description: Electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide (Markovnikov) to an internal alkene; installs a bromine atom on the more substituted carbon to produce 2‑bromopentane. Reaction performed with HBr gas or aqueous HBr at 0 °C to room temperature, often in dichloromethane or ether; no catalyst required under standard conditions.

Phosgenation (acylation) of methylamine hydrochloride; phosgene reacts with the amine salt to give N‑methylcarbamoyl chloride and hydrogen chloride. Conducted at 0 – 5 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, often with a base (e.g., pyridine) to scavenge the generated HCl. The reaction is moisture‑sensitive and typically performed under an inert atmosphere.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (decarbonylation) of formic acid to carbon monoxide and water; conc. H2SO4 protonates formic acid, facilitating loss of water to generate CO. Usually performed by mixing formic acid with concentrated sulfuric acid and heating gently (80–100 °C); CO evolves as a gas and water remains in the reaction mixture.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Purpose: introduce a methyl group para to the hydroxyl of phenol to give p‑cresol. Key transformation: phenol aromatic ring attacks a methyl cation generated from methyl chloride, forming a new C‑C bond; HCl is released. Typical conditions: anhydrous Lewis acid catalyst such as AlCl₃ (or ZnCl₂), inert atmosphere, temperature 0–50 °C. Common solvent: dry dichloromethane, carbon tetrachloride or nitrobenzene.

Strong reduction of an ester (methyl 3‑(methylthio)propionate) with lithium aluminium hydride to the corresponding primary alcohol (3‑(methylthio)propanol); the methyl thio group remains intact and the methoxy portion is released as methanol; carried out in anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under inert gas, followed by careful aqueous work‑up to quench excess LiAlH₄.

Double displacement/acid‑base precipitation; exchange of cations between magnesium dihydrogen phosphate and ammonium hydroxide. Forms insoluble Mg(OH)₂ precipitate and soluble NH₄H₂PO₄. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Lewis‑acid mediated cleavage of an aryl alkyl ether (dealkylation); boron tribromide attacks the C–O bond of pentoxybenzene, generating phenol and pentyl bromide; conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or chlorobenzene at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under nitrogen, then quenched with methanol or water.

Grignard addition to an amide (formylation). Purpose: convert N,N‑dimethylformamide into the tertiary aldehyde pivaldehyde. Key transformation: tert‑butyl‑MgCl adds to the carbonyl carbon of DMF, giving a tetrahedral intermediate that, after aqueous work‑up, eliminates dimethylamine to afford pivaldehyde; MgCl₂ is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: dry ether or THF, temperature −78 °C to 0 °C, inert atmosphere, 1 equiv Grignard. No additional catalyst required.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of a metal carbide. Purpose: convert hafnium carbide to stable hafnium oxide while generating carbon monoxide. Key transformation: O₂ inserts into Hf—C bonds, producing HfO₂ solid and gaseous CO. Typical conditions: temperatures >1500 °C in a flowing O₂ atmosphere, solid‑state reaction, no solvent.

Intramolecular dehydration / cyclization to a lactone (formation of glycolide). Purpose: prepare glycolide, the cyclic dimer used as a monomer for polyglycolic acid. Key transformation: two glycolic acid molecules lose water; the hydroxyl of one attacks the carbonyl of the other, forming a five‑membered cyclic ester; P₂O₅ acts as a dehydrating agent and absorbs the water. Typical conditions: excess P₂O₅, heating 150–200 °C under nitrogen, often solvent‑free or in toluene to aid removal of water.

Oxidative chlorination and trimerization of urea to cyanuric acid. Purpose: synthesize cyanuric acid (a chlorine‑resistant triazine) and calcium chloride as by‑product. transformation: calcium hypochlorite provides hypochlorous species that oxidize urea, forming intermediate isocyanuric fragments that cyclotrimerize to cyanuric acid; Ca²⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give CaCl₂, and water is generated from hydrolysis. Typical conditions: aqueous slurry of calcium hypochlorite, temperature 60–80 °C, pH neutral to slightly basic, vigorous stirring.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of chloric acid with silver oxide. Purpose: prepare silver chlorate salt. Key transformation: Ag₂O reacts with HClO₃, protons transfer to oxide forming water, and Ag⁺ associates with ClO₃⁻ to give AgClO₃; calcium chloride is not involved. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, mild heating (room temperature to ~50 °C), stoichiometric amounts, no special catalyst.

O‑methylation (alkylation) of quercetin using dimethyl sulfate as methyl donor and pyridine as base; pyridine deprotonates the phenolic hydroxyl and captures the sulfate leaving group, forming methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product and yielding tamarixetin (4′‑O‑methylquercetin). Typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, DMF), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation metathesis. Manganese(II) acetate reacts with ammonium hydroxide to give insoluble manganese(II) hydroxide precipitate and soluble ammonium acetate in solution. Usually performed at ambient temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Catalytic peroxide oxidation – glycolic acid is oxidatively cleaved by hydrogen peroxide in the presence of a catalytic amount of transition‑metal ion (e.g., Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺) to afford oxalic acid and water; performed in aqueous solution at moderate temperature (25–60 °C); purpose is conversion of a 2‑carbon α‑hydroxy acid to a dicarboxylic acid.

Double displacement/precipitation (acid‑base) reaction; iron(II) tetrafluoroborate is neutralized by potassium hydroxide, precipitating insoluble iron(II) hydroxide while forming soluble potassium tetrafluoroborate; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; water is the reaction medium.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis/reduction of γ‑butyrolactone to tetrahydrofuran with concomitant formation of water. High‑pressure H₂ (30–60 bar) over a metal catalyst (Raney Ni, Cu‑Zn alloy, or Pd/C) at 120–150 °C reduces the lactone to the corresponding diol, which cyclizes to THF, releasing water. Solvent often is the product THF itself or a high‑boiling ether.

Complexation/salt metathesis in cyanide leaching. Sodium cyanide dissolves gold(I) cyanide to form the linear dicyanoaurate(I) anion, Na[Au(CN)₂]. Reaction occurs in aqueous alkaline cyanide solution at ambient temperature; no additional reagents are needed.

Oxidative ozonolysis of vanillin’s aldehyde group to give vanillic acid. Ozone is bubbled through a solution of vanillin (often in CH₂Cl₂) at –78 °C to form the ozonide, then work‑up with mild oxidant (H₂O₂) or reductant (Me₂S) converts the intermediate to the carboxylic acid, yielding vanillic acid and water. Typical conditions: low temperature, inert atmosphere, aqueous work‑up.

SN1 nucleophilic substitution; replaces the chloride of tert‑butyl chloride with a nitrate to give tert‑butyl nitrate, useful for preparing organic nitrate esters. Typically performed in dry acetone or ether where AgCl precipitates, using an aqueous or acetone solution of AgNO3 at 0 °C to reflux; no additional catalyst required.

Azo coupling (electrophilic aromatic substitution) of benzenediazonium chloride with aniline to form the para‑azo product 4‑(phenylazo)aniline and HCl. Conducted in cold aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH or Na₂CO₃) at 0–5 °C; water is the solvent and the reaction is kept under stirring to maintain low temperature and prevent side reactions.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a propyl isothiocyanate. Water adds across the N=C=S group, yielding propylamine and carbonyl sulfide (OCS). Typical conditions use dilute mineral acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or dilute base at room temperature to 50 °C; aqueous medium is sufficient, sometimes with a co‑solvent such as ethanol to improve solubility.

Halogen oxidation of niobium tetrachloride by chlorine gas to afford niobium pentachloride. The reaction converts NbCl₄ to NbCl₅, effectively increasing the oxidation state of niobium from +4 to +5. Performed in an inert, non‑reactive solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dry dichloromethane) under a flow of Cl₂ at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to avoid side polymerization.

Acidic hydrolysis of N‑nitrosopiperidine to regenerate piperidine and release nitrous acid. The nitrosamine bond is cleaved by water in the presence of dilute acid (commonly 1–2 M HCl) with gentle heating (40–60 °C). The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution, giving piperidine in the organic phase and HNO₂ in the aqueous phase.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; exchanges the ethyl ester of pyridine‑4‑carboxylate for a methyl ester, yielding methyl pyridine‑4‑carboxylate and ethanol. Conducted by refluxing the substrate in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) or a base (e.g., NaOMe). Removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium; no special solvent beyond methanol is required.

Direct synthesis of lutetium(III) chloride by reacting metallic lutetium with chlorine gas; the metal is heated in a stream of dry Cl₂ at 300‑400 °C under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; the reaction proceeds without solvent or catalyst, yielding LuCl₃ as a solid chloride.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 3‑ethylpent‑2‑ene to 3‑ethylpentane; purpose is saturation of the carbon‑carbon double bond; key transformation is addition of H₂ across the C=C bond; typical conditions use H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in a solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, at 25–80 °C.

Borane reduction of an aldehyde; pyridine‑borane transfers hydride to benzaldehyde converting the carbonyl to a primary alcohol (benzyl alcohol) while regenerating pyridine; typically performed in THF at room temperature under inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis/reduction of a carboxylic acid to a diol; lactic acid (2‑hydroxypropanoic acid) is reduced to 1,2‑propanediol by removal of the carboxyl group, usually with high‑pressure H₂ over a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Cu–Cr, or Pd/C in water or alcoholic solvent at elevated temperature.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenolysis of a C–N bond); purpose: removal of an N‑benzyl protecting group to liberate aniline; key transformation: cleavage of the N‑benzyl bond yielding aniline and toluene; typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with 10 % Pd/C at room temperature to reflux; common solvents: ethanol, methanol or THF.

Fischer esterification between acetic acid and 3‑methylpentan‑2‑ol; an acid‑catalyzed condensation that forms the acetate ester (3‑methylpentan‑2‑yl acetate) and water. Typical conditions: catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, reflux in a non‑polar solvent (toluene, benzene) or neat, with water removal (Dean‑Stark) to drive equilibrium.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (dehalogenation) of a benzylic bromide; benzyl bromide undergoes Pd/C‑catalyzed hydrogen addition, cleaving the C–Br bond to give toluene and hydrogen bromide; reaction performed under H₂ gas (1–5 atm) in ethanol, methanol or acetonitrile at 25–80 °C.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; hydroxide ion from sodium hydroxide displaces the chloride in 3‑chloro‑2,2‑dimethylpropan‑1‑ol, yielding 2,2‑dimethyl‑1,3‑propanediol and sodium chloride; carried out in aqueous NaOH or aqueous ethanol, usually refluxed for several hours.

Enzyme‑cataly  oxidative deamination of metanephrine; molecular oxygen oxidizes the amine to an imine that hydrolyzes to 3‑methoxy‑4‑hydroxyphenylglycolaldehyde, releasing ammonia and hydrogen peroxide; occurs in aqueous physiological buffer (pH 7–8) in the presence of monoamine oxidase (MAO) at 37 °C.

Oxidation (air oxidation) of sulfite to sulfate; molecular oxygen oxidizes Na₂SO₃ to Na₂SO₄. Utilized in industrial waste‑water treatment and flue‑gas desulfurization. Carried out in aqueous alkaline medium (pH ≈ 8–10) at 60–90 °C; often accelerated by transition‑metal catalysts such as Co²⁺, Mn²⁺ or Cu²⁺. Solvent is water; no special reagents besides the catalyst.

Acid‑base protonolysis (salt metathesis) of a silyl anion; HCl protonates sodium trimethylsilanide to generate volatile trimethylsilane (CH₃)₃SiH and NaCl; performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (deacetylation) of the side‑chain acetate ester; water converts the acetoxy group to a hydroxy group, releasing acetic acid; performed in aqueous medium (often aqueous ethanol) with a catalytic amount of mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or HCl) under reflux.

Metal reduction of a trialkyl phosphite to the corresponding trialkyl phosphine; purpose is to remove P–O bonds and generate a low‑oxidation‑state phosphorus ligand. Sodium metal donates electrons to the phosphite, cleaving the P‑OEt bonds and forming sodium ethoxide while the phosphorus centre becomes bound to three ethyl groups (triethylphosphine). Typical conditions are anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere, sodium added in small pieces at reflux or 0 °C to control exotherm; no additional catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne (phenylpropiolic acid) to the saturated carboxylic acid (phenylpropionic acid). The triple bond is reduced stepwise by H₂, first to an alkene and then to an alkane, leaving the carboxyl group intact. Commonly carried out with 1–5 atm H₂ using a heterogeneous catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO₂ in ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate at 25–80 °C. The reaction provides a convenient method for converting propiolic acids to propionic acids.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to produce insoluble silver iodide for removal or analysis. Conducted in water at ambient temperature, AgSCN and KI exchange anions to give yellow AgI precipitate and soluble KSCN; no catalyst needed.

Oxidative conversion of a primary heteroaryl‑methanol to the corresponding carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate in alkaline medium. The alcohol is oxidized through a MnO₄⁻/MnO₂ pathway, delivering the nicotinic acid derivative while MnO₄⁻ is reduced to MnO₂ precipitate and K⁺ forms KOH. Conducted in aqueous KOH or NaOH, typically heated under reflux for several hours; the reaction mixture is basic and aqueous, no additional catalyst is required.

Oxidative esterification (chromate ester formation) of a tertiary alcohol; tert‑butyl alcohol reacts with sodium dichromate in concentrated H₂SO₄ to give tert‑butyl chromate ( chromic ester) plus NaHSO₄ and water. Performed at 0–25 °C in the acidic mixture; the reaction is both an oxidation environment and a means to generate a chromate protecting group.

Reductive amination of an α‑keto acid to the corresponding α‑amino acid using molecular hydrogen and ammonia over palladium on carbon. The keto carbonyl is hydrogenated in the presence of NH₃, delivering an amino group and consuming one equivalent of H₂, with water as the only stoichiometric by‑product. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5 % Pd/C, aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., methanol/water), temperature 25–60 °C; the reaction provides a direct route to amino‑adipic acid from the keto precursor.

Acid‑base neutralization forming the caffeine citrate salt. Citric acid protonates the basic sites of caffeine, producing a ionic caffeine‑citrate complex; the process is used to increase caffeine solubility and modify its pharmacokinetics. Performed by dissolving both components in water, adjusting pH to around 4–5, stirring at ambient temperature, then evaporating or lyophilizing to isolate the solid caffeine citrate. No catalyst is required; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution via metal‑halogen exchange; n‑BuLi deprotonates 2‑bromopyridine to give pyridyl lithium, which attacks chlorodiphenylphosphine to form a P‑C bond, yielding 2‑pyridyldiphenylphosphine. Conducted at –78 °C to 0 °C in dry THF under nitrogen; inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Ligand exchange (acid‑base metathesis) between acetic acid and manganese diformate; the acetate replaces formate ligands on manganese, producing manganese acetate and liberating formic acid. Typically performed by stirring the solid mixture or a suspension in excess acetic acid and heating to reflux (≈120 °C) for several hours; solvent can be glacial acetic acid; no catalyst required.

Chlorination with oxidation (gas‑evolving) – technetium dioxide reacts with chlorine gas, converting the oxide to technetium tetrachloride while releasing oxygen gas. Carried out at high temperature (≈400 °C) in a dry Cl₂ atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Type: SN2 alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of a thiol. Purpose: methylate the sulfhydryl group of cysteine to give S‑methylcysteine. Key transformation: the thiolate form of cysteine attacks the methyl carbon of methyl methanesulfonate, displacing methanesulfonate anion, which is protonated to methanesulfonic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous buffered solution (pH 7‑8) at room temperature or mildly elevated temperature (20‑40 °C); water or a water/acetone mixture serves as solvent; no metal catalyst required.

Vapor‑phase tellurization. WO₂ reacts with tellurium vapor at 600–800 °C in a sealed evacuated quartz tube, yielding tungsten telluride and elemental oxygen. No solvent; the reaction proceeds via solid‑gas interaction.

Aqueous redox reduction of tetrachloro‑1,4‑benzoquinone to tetrachloro‑1,4‑hydroquinone using sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) as the reducing agent; sulfite and bisulfite are generated as oxidation products. Performed in water (or aqueous buffer) at ambient temperature, often pH 7–8 to maintain dithionite stability; no additional catalyst needed.

Phosgenation to form tert‑butyl carbamate; phosgene reacts with tert‑butyl alcohol and ammonia released from ammonium carbonate, producing the carbamate and generating CO₂ and HCl as by‑products. Conducted at 0–25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, with an acid‑scavenging base (e.g., pyridine) to trap HCl; inert atmosphere required.

Direct halogenation of ruthenium metal to afford ruthenium(III) iodide (RuI₃); elemental iodine reacts with finely powdered Ru at elevated temperature, yielding the black metal iodide. Typically carried out in a sealed quartz tube or evacuated flask at 300–400 °C for several hours; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Hydrolysis of ammonia‑borane; type is hydrolytic hydrogen release; purpose is generation of H₂ with benign by‑products; key transformation is NH₃BH₃ reacting with water to give ammonia, boric acid and hydrogen gas; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient to 80 °C; reaction rates are often enhanced by transition‑metal catalysts (e.g., Ru, Ir, Mn complexes) or by added base.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); deprotonates diethyl phosphoric acid with NaOH to give sodium diethyl phosphate and water; simple stoichiometric reaction performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst or solvent beyond water is required.

Acid‑metal displacement (redox). Lithium metal reduces perchloric acid, liberating hydrogen gas and forming lithium perchlorate. Typically performed at low temperature under anhydrous, inert conditions to avoid hazardous oxidation; dilute aqueous or alcoholic perchloric acid is added dropwise to powdered Li with stirring.

Alcoholysis (ring‑ transesterification) of β‑butyrolactone with ethanol to afford ethyl 4‑hydroxybutanoate. Usually carried out in excess ethanol (which serves as solvent) with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) or base (NaOMe) at reflux; removal of water drives the reaction to completion.

Carbonation (acid–base precipitation). Zirconium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide to give zirconium carbonate precipitate and water. Usually carried out by suspending Zr(OH)₄ in water and bubbling CO₂ at ambient to 80 °C, sometimes under elevated CO₂ pressure, to promote complete conversion.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – amine alkylation. Sec‑butylamine nucleophilically displaces bromide from ethyl bromide, yielding N‑ethyl‑sec‑butylamine and hydrogen bromide. Performed in anhydrous solvent (e.g., ethanol or THF) at reflux, often with an added base such as triethylamine or excess amine to scavenge the HBr and prevent over‑alkylation.

Boronate ester formation (condensation). Pinacol cond with phenylboronic acid, eliminating two equivalents of water to afford the cyclic phenylboronic acid‑pinacol ester. Conducted by mixing the reagents in toluene or benzene and removing water azeotropically (Dean‑Stark) at reflux, or by using molecular sieves in anhydrous dichloromethane at room temperature.

Solid‑state metathesis / halogenation. Ammonium iodide reacts with praseodymium(III) oxide upon heating, producing praseodymium triiodide, ammonia gas, and water. Typical procedure involves grinding the powders together and heating in a sealed tube or furnace at 250–350 °C under inert atmosphere to drive off NH₃ and H₂O, leaving PrI₃ as the solid product.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; carbonate ion exchanges with lactate ion, precipitating insoluble magnesium carbonate while forming soluble sodium lactate; typically performed at ambient temperature or mild heating with stirring; water is the solvent.

Chlorination (oxidative halogenolysis) of tetraethylgermane using chlorine gas; Ge–C bonds are cleaved to give ethyl chloride and germanium tetrachloride; the reaction proceeds via radical or electrophilic attack of Cl2, often conducted in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or under gas‑phase conditions at low to moderate temperature; excess chlorine is used to drive complete conversion.

Halide exchange (Finkelstein reaction) converting 2‑bromoacetamide to 2‑iodoacetamide using KI. Performed in dry acetone (or ethanol) where KBr precipitates, often refluxed for several hours. No additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation between methanediol and methanol to give dimethoxymethane (an acetal) and water; conducted in excess methanol as solvent, with a catalytic amount of acid such as p‑toluenesulfonic acid or H₂SO₄, and removal of water (e.g., by reflux) to drive the equilibrium.

Fischer esterification of 5‑aminolevulinic acid with methanol catalyzed by p‑toluenesulfonic acid; the carboxylic acid group is converted to a methyl ester, releasing water; typically reflux methanol with a catalytic amount of p‑TsOH, removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark apparatus) to shift equilibrium toward methyl aminolevulinate; no special solvent beyond methanol is required.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on 2,4,6‑trichloro‑1,3,5‑triazine by 2‑chloroaniline; the aniline nitrogen displaces a chloride on the triazine ring, forming a C–N bond and generating triethylammonium chloride as the acid‑base by‑product; carried out in aprotic polar solvents such as acetonitrile or DMF at 0–80 °C; triethylamine is used in stoichiometric excess to neutralize HCl.

Acid–base metathesis between concentrated sulfuric acid and antimony(III) fluoride; fluoride is protonated to release hydrogen fluoride gas while antimony(III) combines with sulfate to give antimony(III) sulfate; performed by mixing solid SbF₃ with hot conc. H₂SO₄ under a fume hood; the reaction is exothermic and generates HF gas that is collected or neutralized.

Alkaline hydrolysis of a nitrile; the cyano group of 2,2-difluoroacetonitrile is converted to a carboxylate under aqueous NaOH, releasing ammonia. Typical conditions are reflux in water or aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) for several hours; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of ethyl butyrate with water to afford butyric acid and ethanol; typically conducted by heating the ester with aqueous dilute acid (e.g., HCl or H₂SO₄) under reflux; the reaction proceeds via protonation of the carbonyl, nucleophilic attack by water, and de‑esterification; the mixture is then separated to isolate the acid and alcohol.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of a primary chloroamine; water acts as nucleophile displacing chloride to give N,N‑dimethylethanolamine and HCl. Typically performed by refluxing the chloroamine in aqueous solution, sometimes with a slight excess of water; no special catalyst required though mild acid or base can accelerate the reaction.

Double‑displacement acid‑base reaction in aqueous medium: mercurous nitrate reacts with sulfuric acid to produce mercurous sulfate precipitate and nitric acid; usually carried out in cold dilute sulfuric acid solution, water as solvent.

Carbothermal reduction of niobium(V) oxide to metallic niobium; purpose is metal production; key transformation: Nb₂O₅ + 5 C → 2 Nb + 5 CO₂ (often shown as C → CO₂); typical conditions: high temperature (1500‑1800 °C) in an electric arc furnace or carbothermic furnace under inert (Ar) or vacuum atmosphere; solid carbon (graphite) is the reductant; no additional solvent; occasionally a catalyst such as calcium is added to lower temperature.

Acid-catalyzed ring opening of β‑propiolactone by hydrogen bromide; nucleophilic acyl substitution converts the four‑membered lactone into 3‑bromopropionic acid. Usually carried out in aqueous HBr or HBr/AcOH, reflux 0–25 °C then heat; solvent can be AcOH or dichloromethane.

Superacid‑mediated substitution of bromoethane in a fluorosulfonic acid/SbF₅ mixture (“magic acid”). The bromide is protonated to HBr and the ethyl cation reacts with the fluorosulfonate anion to give ethyl fluorosulfonate. Performed at low temperature (−78 °C 0 °C) in the neat superacid or in liquid HF; no additional solvent required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive hydrogenolysis) of 3‑methyl‑2‑pentanone to the corresponding secondary alcohol, 3‑methylpentan‑2‑ol. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (or Pt, Ni) catalyst, solvent such as ethanol, methanol or THF, 25–80 °C.

Type: carbothermic reduction. Lead(II) oxide reacts with solid carbon (or carbon monoxide) to yield metallic lead and carbon monoxide gas. Conducted at high temperature (≈900–1000 °C) in a reducing furnace; carbon source may be charcoal or coke, and the reaction is often performed in a sealed retort to contain CO.

Conversion of fluoroacetic acid to fluoroacetyl chloride using phosphorus pentachloride. Reagent‑based chlorination (acyl‑chloride formation) generates fluoroacetyl chloride with HCl and POCl₃ as by‑products. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often in dry CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄, cooling the addition mixture to 0 °C then refluxing.

Acetylation of tri‑n‑butyl citrate with acetic anhydride to give mono‑acetylated tributyl citrate and acetic acid. Typical conditions: catalytic amount of pyridine or DMAP as base, reflux in pyridine or dichlorethane, 1–2 h reaction time.

Transesterification (carbonate exchange); the hydroxyl of 2‑methoxyethanol attacks dimethyl carbonate, displacing methanol and forming the mono‑carbonate 2‑methoxyethyl methyl carbonate. Conducted at 80–120 °C under nitrogen, usually neat or in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene, with a catalytic amount of base (e.g., K₂CO₃) or acid to accelerate the reaction and continuous removal of methanol to shift equilibrium.

Strong hydride reduction of tert‑butyl 2‑phenylacetate with lithium aluminium hydride. The ester is reduced to primary alcohol 2‑phenylethanol while the tert‑butoxy group is released as tert‑butanol. Performed in dry ether (THF or Et₂O) under nitrogen, addition at 0 °C followed by reflux 2–4 h; quench with aqueous Na₂SO₄.

Dehydrative chlorination of a silanol using thionyl chloride. Trimethylsilanol is converted to trimethylsilyl chloride with loss of SO₂ and HCl gases. Reaction proceeds via activation of the Si–OH by SOCl₂, often in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to reflux. A base (pyridine or triethylamine) is commonly employed to absorb HCl and improve yields.

Neutralization/precipitation; aqueous NaOH is added to a solution of uranyl sulfate, hydroxide ions replace sulfate ligands, precipitating uranyl hydroxide (UO₂(OH)₂) while sodium sulfate remains in solution; reaction proceeds at room temperature with vigorous stirring; the solid is filtered and washed.

Metathesis/complexation reaction; forms the soluble hexafluorotitanate salt (NH4)2TiF6 by adding ammonium fluoride to TiF4. Key transformation: TiF4 + 2 NH4F → (NH4)2TiF6. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating; excess NH4F drives formation. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Reaction type: ester hydrolysis (reverse Fischer esterification) – can be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed. Purpose: to regenerate octanoic acid and methanol from the ester, often for recycling or analysis. Key transformation: the ester bond is cleaved by water, yielding the carboxylic acid and alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1–5 % HCl) or dilute base, heated under reflux for several hours; excess water shifts equilibrium to products. The reaction is usually performed in water or a water/organic solvent mixture; no additional catalyst beyond the acid or base is required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation); ammonia attacks the carbonyl of a chloro‑acyl chloride to give a primary amide and HCl; typically performed in anhydrous THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, often with base such as pyridine or excess gaseous NH3 to trap the released HCl.

Fischer esterification of picolinic acid with ethanol to give ethyl picolinate; reaction performed under reflux in excess ethanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) and removal of water (Dean‑Stark or azeotropic) to drive equilibrium.

Staudinger reduction of azide to amine; purpose: convert the azide into a primary amine under mild conditions; key transformation: 2‑azidopentane + PPh3 + H2O → 2‑aminopentane + Ph3P=O + N2↑; typical conditions: PPh3 (1.2 eq) and the azide in dry THF or CH2Cl2 at 0 °C to rt, then addition of water and gentle warming (20–50 °C) for 1–3 h; the reaction generates triphenylphosphine oxide and nitrogen gas; work‑up includes filtration to remove Ph3P=O and aqueous extraction of the amine.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on a pyridine ring; methoxide displaces the chlorine atom, producing a dimethoxy‑substituted pyridine and NaCl; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) with heating (80‑120 °C) to facilitate the substitution.

Selective reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; NaBH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl of benzaldehyde forming benzyl alcohol while NaBH₄ is oxidized to sodium metaborate; usually performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere if needed.

Conversion of a tertiary alcohol to a tertiary chloride via an SN1‑type mechanism; protonation of triphenylmethanol by HCl generates a stable triphenylmethyl carbocation which captures chloride to give triphenylmethyl chloride, releasing water; conducted in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, often using gaseous or conc. HCl.

Hydrolysis (acid chloride hydrolysis); converts trifluoromethanesulfonyl chloride to trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (TfOH) with release of HCl; purpose is to obtain the strong acid from its chloride; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of water on the sulfonyl chloride, forming sulfonic acid and HCl; typical conditions: dilute aqueous medium, temperature 0 °C to rt, stirring until complete; solvent is water (or water/organic co‑solvent), no catalyst required.

Dehydrative chlorination of a carboxylic acid using thionyl chloride; converts 3‑bromopropanoic acid into 3‑bromopropanoyl chloride by replacing the hydroxyl of the carboxyl group with chlorine; by‑products are SO2 and HCl; typically conducted under anhydrous conditions at 0 °C to reflux in a dry solvent such as dichloromethane, with pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize HCl.

Halogen oxidation: arsenous acid (H₃AsO₃) is oxidized by chlorine gas bubbled into an aqueous solution, yielding arsenic acid (H₃AsO₄) and hydrochloric acid (HCl). Purpose is to oxidize As(III) to As(V); performed in water, often acidified, no catalyst needed.

Amide‑type acylation (acetylation) of a primary amine; acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to the amino function of 6‑aminohexano acid, yielding the N‑acetyl product and acetic acid; typically carried out in pyridine or a mild base as solvent at 0 °C to rt, sometimes under reflux to drive completion.

Thermal decomposition of zinc nitrate hexahydrate; upon strong heating (≈300‑400 °C) the solid decomposes to zinc oxide solid, nitrogen dioxide gas, oxygen gas and water vapour; performed in dry conditions, no solvent or catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester saponification: NaOH hydrolyzes sec‑butyl formate to give sec‑butanol and sodium formate; typically carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux (50‑100 °C) with water/ethanol as solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of diphenyl carbonate: water cleaves the carbonate ester to produce phenol and carbon dioxide; usually performed under heating (80‑120 °C) in aqueous or alcoholic medium; reaction may be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed; CO₂ evolves as gas.

Double‑displacement metathesis (acid‑base neutralization): sodium carbonate reacts with dicalcium citrate in water, exchanging cations to form soluble sodium citrate and insoluble calcium carbonate precipitate; ambient temperature, stirring, water as solvent.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation): propargyl alcohol is deprotonated (e.g., with K₂CO₃ or NaH) and reacts with methyl iodide to give propargyl methyl ether, releasing HI; performed in aprotic polar solvent such as acetone, DMF or THF at 0‑25 °C to rt; base scavenges the HI.

Salt formation (acid‑base reaction): eltoprazine (basic amine) is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid to afford eltoprazine hydrochloride; carried out at 0‑25 °C in water or methanol; solvent is removed or the salt is precipitated to isolate the hydrochloride.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a pyridine ring: 2‑benzylpyridine is hydrogenated (3 H₂) in the presence of a metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) under elevated H₂ pressure (30‑80 bar) in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) at 50‑120 °C to give 2‑benzylpiperidine; heterogeneous hydrogenation converts the aromatic pyridine to a saturated piperidine.

Ester hydrogenolysis; catalytic reduction of propyl acetate with hydrogen over a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, Raney Ni) under elevated H₂ pressure (30‑50 bar) and moderate temperature (50‑100 °C) to cleave the C–O bond, yielding ethanol and n‑propyl alcohol; typical solvent is ethanol or a polar aprotic liquid.

Formation of chloroformate via nucleophilic acyl substitution; ethanol reacts with diphosgene (a phosgene equivalent) to give ethyl chloroformate and HCl. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane, often in the presence of a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the generatedCl.

Sulfur alkylation (methylation) of a thiol; dimethyl sulfate alkylates butyl mercaptan in an SN2 fashion to afford methyl butyl sulfide. The reaction is performed in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF) under basic conditions (e.g., NaH, NaOH) at 0 °C to reflux, with careful control because dimethyl sulfate is highly toxic.

Type: Staudinger reduction. Purpose: convert azide to amine under mild, non‑hydrogen conditions. Key transformation: 1‑azido‑3‑methylbutane + PPh₃ + H₂O → 3‑methylbutan‑1‑amine + Ph₃P=O + N₂. Typical conditions: 1–2 equiv PPh₃ in dry THF or CH₂Cl₂, 0 °C to rt, aqueous work‑up to hydrolyze the iminophosphorane intermediate; reaction time 2–6 h.

E2 β‑elimination (Hofmann) using a bulky base; potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 1‑bromo‑1‑methylcyclohexane, eliminating HBr to give 1‑methylcyclohexene, KBr and tert‑butanol. Conducted in polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMSO at 0–80 °C, under anhydrous conditions.

Metathesis/ligand exchange between a metal acetate and a carboxylic acid; zinc acetate exchanges acetate for picolinate to give zinc picolinate and liberates acetic acid; reaction proceeds via proton transfer and coordination of the picolinate ligand to Zn²⁺; commonly run in refluxing methanol or ethanol (or a MeOH/EtOH‑water mix) at 60–80 °C; no extra catalyst required.

N‑alkylation of piperidine (SN2) to form pempidine (N‑benzylpiperidine); benzyl chloride reacts with piperidine in the presence of sodium hydroxide, which neutralizes the HCl byproduct. The reaction is typically conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous–organic solvent (ethanol/water) at reflux, providing the tertiary amine and NaCl as the only by‑product.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); ethyl 2‑methoxyacetate is treated with aqueous NaOH, leading to cleavage of the ester to give methoxyacetic acid and ethanol. The mixture is heated under reflux for several hours, then the reaction mixture is acidified to isolate the acid. Water is the solvent no organic co‑solvent is required.

Hydrolysis of silicon tetrafluoride; SiF₄ reacts with water to form metasilicic acid (H₂SiO₃) and hydrogen fluoride. The reaction proceeds readily at ambient temperature in aqueous solution; excess water drives the equilibrium toward the acid, and the HF formed remains in solution.

Acid‑base neutralization; sodium hydroxide neutralizesoric acid to give water and sodium metaphosphate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water serves as solvent and the reaction proceeds readily without additional catalysts.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration); a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid generates the nitronium ion, which nitrates sec‑butylbenzene preferentially at the para position to afford 4‑nitro‑sec‑butylbenzene and water. Conducted at 0–50 °C under cooling; the mixed acids act as both reagent and solvent; no external catalyst is required.

Metal‑acid single‑displacement reaction; strontium metal reacts with hydrofluoric acid to produce hydrogen gas and strontium fluoride. Performed in aqueous HF, often under reflux or gentle heating to promote reaction; the HF solution itself serves as solvent; inert atmosphere may be used to avoid oxidation.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation (acetal formation); formaldehyde (methanal) reacts with 2‑methylpropane‑1,3‑diol in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid, eliminating water to form trimethylolethane. Commonly carried out under reflux in an aqueous or alcoholic medium with continuous removal of water to drive the equilibrium; sulfuric acid acts as the catalyst.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation using ethylene oxide; benzene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution with ethylene oxide in the presence of aluminum chloride, which opens the epoxide and installs a –CH2CH2OH side chain, yielding phenethyl alcohol and HCl as a by‑product. Reaction requires anhydrous conditions, low temperature (0–30 °C), and a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon disulfide; AlCl₃ is the Lewis acid catalyst.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous solutions of strontium sulfate and lead iodate exchange anions to form insoluble lead sulfate precipitate and soluble strontium diiodate. Conducted at room temperature in water; the formation of the solid PbSO₄ drives the reaction forward.

Esterification (acyl substitution). An acid chloride reacts with methanol to give the corresponding methyl ester and hydrogen chloride. The key transformation is nucleophilic acyl substitution where the alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing chloride. The reaction is typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, and a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) is added to scavenge the evolving HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

Halide exchange (double displacement) precipitation; employed in qualitative analysis to replace bromide with iodide, yielding less soluble mercuric iodide. HgBr₂ + 2 KI → HgI₂ (precipitate) + 2 KBr. Conducted in water, often at ambient temperature; excess KI ensures complete conversion; no catalyst required.

Free‑radical chlorination of a saturated alkane; UV light (or heat) initiates homolysis of Cl₂, generating Cl· radicals that abstract a primary hydrogen from 2,2‑dimethylbutane and recombine to give the mono‑chloro derivative and HCl. Typically performed in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or neat, at ambient temperature.

Hydrolysis of methyl isocyanide to N‑methylformamide; a nucleophilic addition of water across the C≡N bond converting the isocyanide to a formamide. The reaction proceeds via protonation of the terminal nitrogen, water attack, and tautomerization to the amide. Usually carried out in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) or under reflux with a catalytic amount of acid or base; heating (50–100 °C) accelerates the conversion, and the reaction is performed in water or a water‑miscible organic solvent such as methanol.

Condensation / cyclization (Perkin‑type) to synthesize coumarin. Salicylaldehyde undergoes a Knoevenagel‑type condensation with acetic anhydride, followed by intramolecular lactonization to form the heterocyclic lactone coumarin, with liberation of acetic acid as by‑product. The reaction is performed by heating salicylaldehyde neat or in excess acetic anhydride (often 150–200 °C) under reflux; sodium acetate can be used as a catalyst. No external solvent is required, and the crude product is isolated after cooling and aqueous work‑up.

Metal–water hydrolysis (single‑displacement) reaction; provides a route to terbium(III) hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Terbium metal reacts with liquid water or steam, yielding Tb(OH)₃ and H₂. The reaction proceeds slowly at room temperature but is accelerated by heating the metal under reflux in water (often 80–100 °C) or by using steam. Performed in aqueous medium; no additional catalyst needed.

Combustion oxidation. Methyl tert‑butyl ether reacts with molecular oxygen in a flame or high‑temperature furnace, leading to oxidative cleavage of the C–O bonds and formation of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and water. Conditions involve excess O₂, temperatures above the ignition point (~350 °C), and are typically carried out in open air or a controlled combustion chamber; no solvents or catalysts are used.

Oxidative conversion of an aldose to a dicarboxylic acid. Glyceraldehyde is oxidized by dilute nitric acid, where the aldehyde group and adjacent hydroxyls are converted to a carboxylate, yielding tartronic acid (hydroxymalonic acid). Nitric acid is reduced to nitrogen dioxide, which is liberated as a brown gas, and water is formed. The reaction is conducted in aqueous solution (≈1–5 % HNO₃) at ambient temperature or gentle reflux, with vigorous stirring; no additional catalyst is required.

Double displacement precipitation; aqueous magnesium acetate reacts with ammonium fluoride to form insoluble magnesium fluoride and ammonium acetate in solution; typically carried out at moderate temperature (20‑50 °C) in water, no catalyst needed.

Deprotonation (salt formation) of cyclopentadiene. Sodium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (NaHMDS) acts as a strong, non‑nucleophilic base, abstracting the acidic proton of cyclopentadiene to generate the cyclopentadienyl anion as its sodium salt and bis(trimethylsilyl)amine as the by‑product. The transformation is performed under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in an aprotic ether solvent such as THF, typically at 0 °C to –78 °C to control exotherm, then allowed to warm to room temperature.

Oxidative coupling of a dithiocarbamate. Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes sodium diethyl dithiocarbamate, coupling two dithiocarbamate units to give tetraethylthiuram disulfide while reducing H₂O₂ to water and generating sodium hydroxide. The reaction proceeds in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media (e.g., water/ethanol) at 0 °C to room temperature, often under basic conditions no additional catalyst is required.

Acid-base metal deprotonation; purpose is to generate the sodium phenoxide salt as a nucleophilic partner for further substitution or coupling. The phenolic O–H proton is abstracted by metallic sodium, forming Na‑phenoxide and liberating H₂ gas. Typically performed under inert atmosphere in dry ethereal solvents (ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a slight excess of Na metal.

Catalytic partial oxidation of a linear alkane to the corresponding aldehyde; aim is to convert n‑pentane into pentanal while water is produced from the removed hydrogen atoms. In practice the reaction requires elevated temperature (150–200 °C) and a heterogeneous metal catalyst (e.g., V‑Mo oxide, cobalt‑manganese bromide, or supported silver) with O₂ or air as the oxidant. The process is conducted in the gas phase or a high‑temperature flow reactor; no solvent is used.

Halogenation/reduction reaction; conversion of zirconium dioxide to zirconium tetraiodide using hydrogen iodide; zirconium dioxide is treated with excess dry HI at elevated temperature (200–300 °C) in a sealed vessel, producing zirconium tetraiodide and water; the reaction proceeds under an inert atmosphere; no catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of dimethyl sulfoxide to dimethyl sulfone with sodium periodate; employed when a sulfone is needed as a stable S(VI) functional group. NaIO₄ accepts electrons from the(IV) center, yielding NaIO₃ (sodium iodate) and DMSO₂. Usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile at room temperature; the reaction proceeds rapidly and does not require a catalyst.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (acylation) of 2‑ethylhexanol with salicyloyl chloride to form 2‑ethylhexyl salicylate; common route to UV‑absorbing sunscreen esters. The alcohol attacks the acyl chloride, producing the ester and HCl. A base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) is added to neutralize HCl, and the reaction is performed in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to ambient temperature.

Nitrile reduction with lithium aluminium hydride to afford tris(2‑aminoethyl)amine (TREN); the hydride reduces each –C≡N group to a primary amine. Conducted under strictly anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at low temperature (often –78 °C) followed by gradual warming to reflux. Excess LiAlH₄ is quenched carefully, and the resulting polyamine is isolated after work‑up.

Combustion oxidation of tetramethyllead with oxygen producing lead(II) oxide, carbon dioxide and water. Reaction type: combustion (oxidative decomposition); purpose: destroy organolead or generate PbO; key transformation: cleavage of Pb–C bonds, oxidation of carbon to CO₂ and hydrogen to H₂O; conditions: heating in excess O₂ or air, typically in a furnace, no solvent, exothermic reaction.

Alkylation of a heterocyclic organolithium (2‑lithium‑1,3‑benzothiazol‑2‑ide) with methyl iodide; nucleophilic substitution (SN2) at the carbon‑2 position to give 2‑methyl‑1,3‑benzothiazole. Typically performed under inert atmosphere at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in dry THF or ether, then quenched with water.
Acid‑base neutralization of chromium(VI) oxide with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form sodium chromate and water; performed in water at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) cyanation of a primary alkyl halide; methyl bromide is displaced by cyanide from CuCN to give acetonitrile and CuBr. Usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 80–120 °C, often under reflux; CuCN serves as the cyanide source, no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution using a perfluoroacid anhydride. Sodium n‑butoxide reacts with trifluoroacetic anhydride to afford butyl trifluoroacetate and sodium trifluoroacetate. Conducted at 0 °C to 25 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF to avoid hydrolysis; the reaction is fast and does not require a catalyst.

Reductive cyclization (Leuckart‑type) of 2‑aminobenzaldehyde with excess formic acid; formic acid acts as both carbon source and reducing agent, leading to decarboxylation (3 CO₂) and dehydration (3 H₂O) while forming the heterocycle isoindoline; usually performed by heating the mixture in a sealed tube or high‑pressure reactor at 120–150 °C; neat or aqueous formic acid is the reaction medium.

Reductive deoxygenation of an N‑oxide; N,N‑dimethylaniline N‑oxide is reduced to the parent amine N,N‑dimethylaniline using zinc dust in acetic acid. The acid provides Zn²⁺ (forming zinc acetate) and proton source, while zinc serves as a reductant. Conducted by stirring the mixture at reflux in glacial acetic acid under nitrogen.

Oxidative cyclization of 1,6‑hexanediol to ε‑caprolactone catalyzed by TEMPO (2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine‑1‑oxyl) with sodium hypochlorite as the terminal oxidant. The reaction proceeds in aqueous buffered medium (pH ≈ 8–10), often with a small amount of NaBr as co‑catalyst, at 0–25 °C. Water and NaCl are formed as by‑products.

Nucleophilic addition to an isothiocyanate (thiourea formation); hydrazine attacks phenyl isothiocyanate, giving N‑phenyl‑hydrazinecarbothioamide (a phenyl‑substituted thiourea). Usually performed in ethanol or water at 0 °C to room temperature, sometimes with gentle reflux; no catalyst required. The reaction introduces a hydrazine‑linked thiocarbonyl functionality.

Mild reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol with sodium borohydride; a selective hydride reduction. Purpose is to convert 3,4‑dihydroxyphenylacetaldehyde into 3,4‑dihydroxyphenylethanol. Key transformation: –CHO → –CH₂OH, phenolic OH groups remain unchanged. Typical conditions: NaBH₄ (1.2 eq) in methanol or ethanol, 0 °C to rt, 30 min–1 h; quench with water, isolate product; sodium borate is formed as by‑product.

Acid‑base neutralization/salt formation: selenium trioxide (SeO₃), the anhydride of selenic acid, reacts with aqueous barium hydroxide to give soluble barium selenate (BaSeO₄) and water. The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring.

Carbothermal reduction; purpose is to obtain metallic rhodium from its oxide. Carbon acts as a solid reductant, reducing Rh2O3 to Rh metal while being oxidized to CO. Typically performed at 800–1200 °C in a furnace under inert or reducing atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Transesterification of methyl phenyl carbonate with phenol; a carbonate exchange reaction used to synthesize diphenyl carbonate while releasing methanol. Typically carried out under reflux with a catalytic amount of base (e.g., NaOMe, K₂CO₃) or acid (p‑TSA) in an inert solvent such as toluene or anisole, and methanol is removed by distillation to drive the equilibrium.

Electrophilic bromination of 2,2′‑bithiophene with molecular Br₂ to afford 5,5′‑dibromo‑2,2′‑bithiophene; bromine adds to the 5‑positions on each thiophene ring; performed in a non‑protic halogenated solvent (e.g., CHCl₃ or CCl₄) at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required; light protection is advised.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation of isothiazole; bromine adds to the 5‑position to give 5‑bromoisothiazole. Conducted in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often at 0 °C to room temperature. A Lewis acid catalyst (e.g., FeBr₃ or AlCl₃) may be employed to activate Br₂, but direct bromination can also occur with stoichiometric Br₂.

Acetylation of the primary amine of serotonin; an acylation (N‑acetylation) reaction used to modify or protect the amino group. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane with pyridine or triethylamine as base, often catalyzed by DMAP, at room temperature. By‑product is acetic acid.

Redox fluorination of elemental sulfur with oxygen difluoride; sulfur is oxidized to sulfur tetrafluoride while O–F bonds are reduced to molecular oxygen. The reaction is carried out at low temperature (often –78 °C to –30 °C) in a fluorine‑compatible vessel, generally without solvent or in liquid fluorine; it is highly hazardous and requires specialized equipment.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between copper(II) sulfate and diammonium hydrogen phosphate. Forms insoluble copper(II) hydrogen phosphate precipitate while ammonium sulfate remains dissolved. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Anion exchange (metathesis) reaction; purpose: preparation of tetraethylammonium iodide; key transformation: swapping perchlorate anion for iodide, forming tetraethylammonium iodide and potassium perchlorate; typical conditions: aqueous or acetonitrile solution, stirring at rt; common solvent: water or MeCN.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (para‑selective bromination) of toluene using bromine. Typically performed in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, with a Lewis acid catalyst like FeBr₃ to generate the bromonium electrophile. One equivalent of HBr is liberated.

N‑methylation of uracil via SN2 alkylation with methyl iodide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or acetone) in the presence of a base such as potassium carbonate or NaH to deprotonate the uracil nitrogen. Reaction proceeds at room temperature to moderate heating; hydrogen iodide is generated as by‑product.

Oxidation of 3‑phenylpropanal to 3‑phenylpropionic acid using Jones reagent (chromium(VI) oxide in dilute sulfuric acid). Performed in acetone as solvent, typically at 0 °C to 25 °C, with aqueous CrO₃/H₂SO₄ added dropwise. The primary aldehyde is converted to corresponding carboxylic acid; chromium is reduced from Cr(VI) to Cr(III).

Thermal dissociation (salt decomposition) to regenerate the free base and acid. Ethylammonium acetate can be heated (often under reduced pressure or by azeotropic removal with a volatile solvent) to release ethylamine gas and acetic acid. The process may be assisted by a base (e.g., NaOH) to drive the equilibrium toward the free amine. No specific catalyst is required.

Radical halogen exchange (photochemicaliodination). Ultraviolet light cleaves H–I to generate I· radicals which abstract iodine from iododifluorochloromethane, producing molecular iodine and chlorodifluoromethane. Typically performed in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as CCl₄ or benzene under dry, nitrogen atmosphere; no added catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt dissolution). Concentrated hydrochloric acid protonates the oxo ligands of cupr molybdate, converting the copper(II) species to soluble CuCl₂ and generating molybdic acid (H₂MoO₄) which may precipitate as MoO₃·H₂O. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution; no special catalyst needed.

Esterification via acylation of a phenolic hydroxyl (acetylation). Acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to the 5‑hydroxy position of N,N‑dimethyltryptamine, yielding 5‑acetoxy‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine and acetic acid as by‑product. Usually carried out in an anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature, with a catalytic amount of DMAP or pyridine to scavenge the generated acid.

Oxidative transformation of a heterocyclic base (C‑8 oxidation). Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes adenine, inserting an oxygen atom at the C‑8 position to afford 8‑oxoadenine with water as the only by‑product. Reaction is performed in aqueous medium, often buffered at neutral to slightly basic pH, and may be accelerated by mild catalysts such as peroxidases or transition‑metal complexes; ambient temperature is typical.

N‑alkylation via SN2 (nucleophilic substitution). The indole nitrogen of 2‑phenylindole is deprotonated by potassium carbonate and then attacks methyl iodide, forming N‑methyl‑2‑phenylindole and potassium iodide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, acetone) at reflux or elevated temperature; the carbonate serves as base and the reaction is moisture‑sensitive.

Nucleophilic substitution of silicon halides (organolithium alkylation). Ethyl lithium attacks the three Si–Cl bonds of trichlorosilane, replacing each chloride with an ethyl group to give triethylsilane and lithium chloride. Performed in anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, typically at –78 °C to 0 °C to control reactivity; no additional catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduces two nitro groups of 2,6‑dinitrotoluene to amines using H₂ over Pd/C in aqueous HCl, yielding 2,6‑diaminotoluene which is immediately protonated to its dihydrochloride salt. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, room‑to‑50 °C, water or aqueous ethanol as solvent.

Ester aminolysis (transamidation). Aniline attacks the carbonyl of ethyl trifluoroacetate, displacing ethanol and giving N‑trifluoroacetylaniline. Usually performed under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene or xylene with a base (pyridine, TEA) or a catalytic amount of acid (HCl, TsOH) to accelerate the reaction and scavenge the generated ethanol. Removal of ethanol (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) helps drive the reaction to completion.

Acid‑base reaction to generate nitrous acid in situ; hydrochloric acid protonates the nitrite ion, forming HNO₂ and yielding KCl as a by‑product; employed as a preparative step for diazotization or nitrosation; performed in aqueous solution at low temperature (0–5 °C) to minimize decomposition of HNO₂.

Oxidative epoxidation; potassium peroxymonosulfate (Oxone) transfers an electrophilic oxygen to the C=C bond of cyclohexene, producing cyclohexene oxide. Sodium bicarbonate buffers the reaction, neutralizing generated acid and evolving CO₂. Performed in water or water/acetone at ambient temperature; by‑products are potassium bisulfate and water.

Metathesis (acid‑base exchange); HCl reacts with potassium tetrafluoroborate to give tetrafluoroboric acid (HBF₄) and potassium chloride. Usually carried out in anhydrous organic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane to avoid hydrolysis; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement acid‑base reaction; sulfuric acid protonates zinc nitrite, liberating nitrous acid and forming zinc sulfate. Conducted in aqueous medium, often kept cool (0–10 °C) to limit HNO₂ decomposition; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic addition (urea formation) of hydrazine to isocyanic acid, yielding semicarbazide (NH₂NH‑CO‑NH₂); the reaction proceeds readily at ambient temperature in water or aqueous ethanol; often performed under a nitrogen atmosphere to avoid side reactions; no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic bromination of indole. Purpose: synthesize 3‑bromoindole. Key transformation: Br₂ adds electrophilically at C‑3, generating HBr as by‑product. Typical conditions: Br₂ (1.0–1.2 equiv) in CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄, 0 °C to rt, often with a base such as pyridine or NaHCO₃ to trap HBr; reaction completes in 15–60 min.

High‑temperature solid‑state (flux) reaction producing sodium aluminate; Al₂O₃ (amphoteric oxide) reacts with Na₂CO₃, carbonate acts as base and is removed as CO₂ while Na⁺ combines with AlO₂⁻ to give NaAlO₂; purpose is synthesis of soluble aluminate for glass or alumina processing; conducted by intimately mixing the powders and heating at 800‑1000 °C in a furnace; no solvent, catalyst, or additional reagents required; CO₂ evolution drives the reaction forward.

Hofmann (oxidative) rearrangement of cyclobutanecarboxamide using NaOCl/NaOH to cyclobutylamine; general type: Hofmann degradation (base‑mediated oxidative decarboxylation of amide); purpose: convert amide to amine with loss of carbon as CO₂; key transformation: –C(=O)NH₂ → –CH₂NH₂ + CO₂; typical conditions: aqueous NaOCl (bleach, 1.5 equiv) and NaOH (2–3 equiv) at 0–5 °C, then acid work‑up; by‑products: NaCl, CO₂, H₂O.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of cobalt(II) acetate; upon heating to high temperature (≈500–800 °C) in an inert atmosphere the acetate breaks down to cobalt(II) oxide, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and water; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Hydride reduction of a di‑ester to the corresponding diol; LiAlH₄ reduces both ester groups of dimethyl decanedioate to primary alcohols, producing 1,10‑decanediol and methanol as by‑product; carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether solvents such as THF or diethyl ether, typically at 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar).

Metathesis/precipitation double‑displacement; aqueous silver nitrate reacts with sodium propanoate to exchange the ions, forming insoluble silver propanoate (precipitate) and soluble sodium nitrate; performed at room temperature in water, with stirring.

Acid–base exchange (neutralization) in aqueous solution; nitric acid protonates ammonium tellurate, yielding ammonium nitrate and telluric acid (H₆TeO₆); reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water, no special catalyst required.

Metathesis/acid‑base reaction that generates gaseous ammonia; cesium hydroxide neutralizes ammonium chloride, yielding soluble cesium chloride, water, and liberating NH₃ gas; performed in aqueous solution, usually with gentle heating to drive off ammonia; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; aqueous perchloric acid replaces chloride in mercuric chloride, yielding mercuric perchlorate and hydrochloric acid. Key transformation: HgCl₂ + 2 HClO₄ → Hg(ClO₄)₂ + 2 HCl. Performed in water or dilute acid solution at ambient temperature; stirring until dissolution; no catalyst required. Reaction is useful for preparing soluble mercuric perchlorate from the less soluble chloride.

The reaction is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2). The hydroxide ion (from NaOH) displaces the chloride ion in 1-chloro-2-methylhexane, yielding 2-methyl-1-hexanol and sodium chloride. Conditions typically involve aqueous or alcoholic solution with heating. No catalyst required; polar protic solvents like ethanol/water mixtures are common. Purpose is converting alkyl halides to alcohols.

Nucleophilic substitution (alkyl bromide formation) using phosphorus tribromide; PBr₃ converts benzyl alcohol to benzyl bromide while being reduced to phosphorous acid; carried out anhydrously in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, typically 0 °C to room temperature, often with pyridine as a base.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich coupling); N,N‑diisopropylcarbodiimide activates salicylic acid, and DMAP catalyzes acyl transfer to p‑cresol, producing p‑cresyl salicylate and diisopropylurea as the by‑product; performed in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen.

Transesterification between vinyl acetate and methyl propionate to exchange ester groups, yielding acetic acid and vinyl propionate. This is an equilibrium ester exchange used to prepare vinyl esters. Typically performed with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base (e.g., NaOMe) at reflux in an aprotic solvent such as toluene or xylene; removal of the volatile acetic acid drives the reaction forward.

Oxidation of a sulfite ester to a sulfate ester. Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes dimethyl sulfite to dimethyl sulfate, releasing water. The reaction is usually performed in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) under mild temperatures (0 °C → room temp) and may require a catalyst such as a Lewis acid (e.g., titanium tetrachloride) or a base to control over‑oxidation.

Double‑replacement metathesis/precipitation. Aqueous NaOH reacts with cadmium selenite to form soluble sodium selenite and insoluble cadmium hydroxide, which precipitates. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; stirring and filtration isolate the Cd(OH)₂ solid.

Salt metathesis (double displacement). In aqueous solution sodium arsenite exchanges anions with ammonium carbonate, producing sodium carbonate (soluble) and ammonium arsenite (soluble). Reaction proceeds at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Redox reaction in aqueous hydrochloric acid; MnO₂ oxidizes iodide ions to molecular iodine while MnO₂ itself is reduced to Mn²⁺; products are iodine, potassium chloride, manganese(II) chloride, and water; performed at room temperature or with mild heating in water; no additional catalyst required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of a secondary amine. Methyl iodide alkylates N‑methyl‑2‑propen‑1‑amine to give N,N‑dimethyl‑2‑propen‑1‑amine, with HI generated as a by‑product. Performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, often in the presence of a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., triethylamine or NaH) to trap HI and drive the reaction to completion.

Homolytic cleavage (photolytic or thermal radical generation). Trifluoronitrosomethane decomposes under UV irradiation or mild heating to afford a trifluoromethyl radical and nitric oxide radical. Conducted in an inert gas matrix or non‑coordinating solvent (.g., argon‑saturated benzene) at low temperature to stabilize the radicals.

Catalytic hydrogenation; purpose is to reduce the two nitro groups of 4,4'-dinitrobiphenyl to amines, yielding benzidine (4,4'-diaminobiphenyl) with water as the only by‑product. Key transformation: –NO2 → –NH2 via addition of H2. Typical conditions: H2 gas (1–5 atm) passed over Pt/C catalyst at 25–80 °C, often in ethanol or methanol as solvent; reaction proceeds under stirring until gas uptake ceases.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of barium chromate; yields chromium(VI) oxide (CrO₃) and barium oxide (BaO). Key transformation: BaCrO₄ → BaO + CrO₃ with release of oxygen as part of CrO₃ sublimation. Typical conditions: strong heating, generally 800–1000 °C in a dry furnace; no solvent; the volatile CrO₃ sublimes and is collected separately.

Transesterification (alcohol‑ester exchange); ethanol attacks isopropyl formate, swapping the alkoxy groups to give ethyl formate and isopropanol. Key transformation: R¹OH + R²OCOH ⇌ R²OH + R¹OCOH. Common catalysts: mineral acid (e.g., 1–5 % H₂SO₄), solid acid resin, or base (NaOEt). Conditions: refluxing the neat mixture or in toluene/benzene with removal of the formed isopropanol to drive equilibrium, typically 60–80 °C for several hours.

Reductive dehalogenation; zinc metal reduces the heavily iodinated alkene tetraiodoethylene, eliminating two iodine atoms and forming the alkyne diiodoacet while generating ZnI₂. Key transformation: C₂I₄ + Zn → C₂I₂ (diiodoacetylene) + ZnI₂. Typical conditions: Zn dust (excess) in dry ether or THF under nitrogen, gentle heating (0–50 °C) to avoid side polymerization; reaction proceeds via single‑electron transfer.

Halogen exchange/oxidative chlorination; phosphorus pentachloride chlorinates indium(III) oxide, converting the oxide to indium trichloride while the oxygen is transferred to phosphorus to give phosphorus oxychloride. Overall: 3 PCl₅ + In₂O₃ → 2 InCl₃ + 3 POCl₃. Conditions: anhydrous, inert atmosphere, heating to 100–150 °C; the POCl₃ distills off and can be collected; no solvent is required, though carbon tetrachloride has been used as a liquid medium historically.

Free‑radical autoxidation (peroxidation) of an alkene; produces tert‑butyl hydroperoxide, a useful oxidizing agent; isobutylene reacts with O₂ in the presence of a radical initiator (e.g., AIBN, benzoyl peroxide) to give t‑Bu‑OOH; performed at 50–100 °C under O₂ pressure, often in an inert solvent such as cyclohexane or in the gas phase; metal catalysts (Co, Mn) may be employed industrially.

Acid–base double displacement in aqueous solution; sulfuric acid protonates the sulfite anion of ammonium sulfite, forming sulfurous acid (H₂SO₃) and ammonium sulfate. Key transformation: H₂SO₄ + (NH)₂SO₃ → (NH₄)₂SO₄ + H₂SO₃. Conditions: aqueous medium at room temperature; the mixture is typically stirred; sulfurous acid is unstable and may decompose to SO₂ and H₂O, so the reaction is often performed under an atmosphere that can vent the gas.
Neutral hydrolysis of phenyl 2,2‑dichloroacetate; cleavage of the phenoxy ester bond giving phenol and dichloroacetic acid; typically heated water, may be assisted by mild acid; no special catalyst.

α‑Bromination of butan‑2‑one using N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS). The ketone is converted to 1‑bromo‑2‑butanone with succinimide as the by‑product. This electrophilic α‑halogenation proceeds via enol formation and NBS as the bromine source. Common conditions are a non‑nucleophilic solvent like carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, 0 °C to room temperature, often in the dark to suppress radical pathways; a catalytic amount of acid or base may be added to promote enolization.

Acidic hydrolysis of a nitrile; conversion of 2‑(pyridin‑2‑yl)acetonitrile to 2‑pyridineacetic acid. Purpose is to generate the corresponding carboxylic acid. Conducted by refluxing the nitrile in aqueous HCl (6–12 M) for several hours; water is the solvent. No extra catalysts are needed.

Neutralization of an acetamidine·HCl salt with sodium carbonate, releasing free acetamidine and evolving CO₂. Purpose is to liberate the free amidine base. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; sodium carbonate acts as the base, generating NaCl, water and carbon dioxide. No special catalyst required.

Hydrolysis. Reverses esterification, cleaving ester into alcohol and carboxylic acid. Water nucleophilically attacks ester under acidic conditions (e.g., H2SO4), generating 4-methylpentan-2-ol and acetic acid. Requires heating and aqueous solution.

Bechamp reduction of 4,4‑dinitrobiphenyl to benzidine (4,4′‑diaminobiphenyl) using iron powder in aqueous hydrochloric acid. Purpose is to reduce nitro groups to amines, yielding a diamine. Typically carried out by refluxing the nitro compound with excess Fe and conc. HCl (≈6 M) for several hours; water is the solvent. Iron serves as the reducing agent, forming FeCl₃.

Acylation of piperidine hydrochloride with acetyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine. Purpose is to form N‑acetylpiperidine (protected amine). Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt. Triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl, yielding triethylammonium chloride as by‑product.

Aerobic oxidation of 4‑chlorobenzyl alcohol to 4‑chlorobenzaldehyde using molecular oxygen. Purpose is to convert a primary alcohol to an aldehyde. Usually requires a catalyst such as Cu/TEMPO, a base (e.g., NaNO₂ or pyridine), and a solvent like acetonitrile or dichloromethane; reaction proceeds at 25–80 °C under an O₂ atmosphere. Water is formed as the only stoichiometric by‑product.

Oxidative mineralization of a halogenated ethane; strong oxidant KMnO4 in concentrated H2SO4 oxidizes 1,1,2‑trichloro‑1,2‑difluoroethane to CO2 while liberating HCl and HF; inorganic salts (K2SO4, MnSO4) are formed. Typical conditions: aqueous sulfuric acid, excess KMnO4, heating under reflux.

Type: free‑radical halogenation (substitution). Purpose: synthesis of dibromomethane from bromomethane. Key transformation: a hydrogen atom of CH₃Br is abstracted by a bromine radical, producing CH₂Br₂ and HBr; overall Br₂ adds one Br atom to the carbon and the other forms HBr. Typical conditions: UV irradiation or thermal initiation (≈30 °C) in an inert, non‑reactive solvent such as carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) or chloroform; reaction conducted under an inert atmosphere to avoid side oxidation. No catalyst beyond the radical initiator (light).

Catalytic oxidative hydroxylation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes ellipticine in the presence of sodium tungstate (Na2WO4) to give 9‑hydroxyellipticine. Reaction proceeds in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., water/acetone), pH buffered around neutral to mildly acidic, at ambient to 50 °C. Tungstate acts as a catalyst for selective C‑H oxidation.

Acid‑base precipitation reaction of zinc dihydroxide with carbonic acid yielding zinc carbonate and water; conducted in aqueous media at room temperature or mild heating; no catalyst needed, pH adjusted to slightly acidic to favor carbonate formation.

Hydride reduction of nitro groups; lithium aluminum hydride (LiAlH4) reduces the two nitro substituents of ,4‑dinitrophenol to amines, yielding 2,4‑diaminophenol. Conducted in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, typically 0 °C to reflux, with careful quench of excess LiAlH4.

Selective reduction of a nitrile to an aldehyde (nitrile → aldehyde); carried out with diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H) as the reducing agent; typically performed at –78 °C in anhydrous THF or diethyl ether to avoid over‑reduction; reaction is quenched with dilute acid (e.g., aqueous NaHSO₄) to afford 2‑ethylhexanal from 2‑ethylhexanenitrile.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a chloro‑carboxylic acid; sodium hydrosulfide (NaSH) attacks the α‑chloro carbon 2‑chloropropionic acid, displacing chloride to form sodium chloride and 2‑mercaptopropionic acid. Reaction performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑alcoholic medium, mild heating (30–60 °C), often with pH adjusted to keep HS– nucleophilic.

Amine‑aluminum exchange (salt metathesis); trimethylaluminum reacts with dimethylamine to replace Al‑Me bonds with Al‑NMe2 groups, producing tris(dimethylamido)aluminum(III) and releasing methane gas. Carried out in dry ether (e.g., THF or toluene) under inert atmosphere, at 0 °C to room temperature to avoid uncontrolled exotherm.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of toluene with acetyl chloride to give acetophenone and HCl. An electrophilic aromatic substitution where the acylium ion (CH₃CO⁺) generated by AlCl₃ attacks the aromatic ring para‑ to the methyl group. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1–2 equiv) in a dry, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or CS₂, temperature 0 °C to 25 °C, under nitrogen. The liberated HCl is trapped by the aluminum chloride.

Acid‑base neutralization of a metal oxide; zinc oxide reacts with aqueous chloric acid (HClO₃) to give zinc chlorate (Zn(ClO₃)₂) and water. The reaction is performed in aqueous solution, typically with gentle heating to complete dissolution.

Acid–base neutralization with a weak acid; purpose is to produce ammonium acetate and evolve CO2; reaction: NH4HCO3 + CH3COOH → NH4CH3COO + CO2 + H2O; performed in water or aqueous acetic acid solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (ammonolysis) of benzylic chlorides; 1,3‑bis(chloromethyl)benzene is treated with excess aqueous ammonium hydroxide, leading to SN2 displacement of chloride by ammonia and formation of 1,3‑benzenedimethanamine with ammonium chloride as a side product. Reaction is carried out in aqueous NH₄OH at elevated temperature (50‑80 °C) to drive complete substitution.

Fischer esterification (wax‑ester synthesis); hexadecanoic acid reacts with hexadecan‑1‑ol in the presence of a catalytic amount of a strong mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH). The mixture is heated to reflux, often with a Dean‑Stark trap or in a non‑polar solvent such as toluene to remove water, yielding hexadecyl hexadecanoate and water.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; calcium lactate and sodium phosphate in aqueous solution undergo ion exchange to precipitate calcium phosphate while forming soluble sodium lactate. The reaction is typically performed at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the solid calcium phosphate is isolated by filtration and washing.

Oxidation of a secondary α‑hydroxy ester to an α‑keto ester (methyl lactate to methyl pyruvate); purpose is to introduce a carbonyl functionality; key transformation is conversion of the –CH(OH)– group to a C=O group using Cr(VI); performed as a Jones oxidation with aqueous chromic acid (typically CrO₃/H₂SO₄) in acetone or dichloromethane at 0‑25 °C; reaction is acid‑catalyzed and gives water as the only by‑product.

Base‑promoted decarboxylative elimination of cinnamic acid to styrene; purpose is to produce the vinyl arene from a β‑unsaturated carboxylic acid; key transformation is loss of CO₂ from the carboxyl group, forming the C=C double bond of styrene; carried out by heating cinnamic acid with solid sodium carbonate (or NaOH) at 200‑250 °C in a dry‑distillation apparatus; no solvent; the gaseous CO₂ is released.

Double displacement: Cupric acetate exchanges ions with ammonium phosphate to form copper(II) phosphate precipitate and aqueous ammonium acetate. Aimed at isolating copper phosphate via insoluble product formation. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature.

Oxidation of fluoroacetaldehyde to fluoroacetic acid using potassium permanganate; purpose is to convert an aldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid; key transformation is MnO₄⁻ oxidation of the –CHO group to –COOH, producing MnO₂ precipitate; typically performed in aqueous alkaline medium (NaOH or KOH) at 60‑80 °C; water is formed as a by‑product and MnO₂ is removed by filtration.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); L‑glutamic acid is deprotonated by NaOH to produce disodium 2‑aminopentanedioate and water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature using 2 equiv NaOH, stirring until dissolution; no special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Esterification (acylation of alcohol by acetic anhydride); purpose: protect or derivatize the alcohol as an acetate; key transformation: 2‑fluoroethanol + (CH₃CO)₂O → 2‑fluoroethyl acetate + CH₃COOH; typical conditions: 1.1–1.2 eq acetic anhydride, base such as pyridine or DMAP (0.1 eq), 0 °C to rt, often in dichloromethane; common solvent: CH₂Cl₂; catalyst/base is pyridine/DMAP.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of salicylanilide to give 3,4',5‑tribromosalicylanilide; purpose is to install bromine atoms at activated positions on both aromatic rings; key transformation is substitution of hydrogen by bromine via an Br₂ electrophile; reaction is usually conducted in glacial acetic acid (or dichloromethane) at 0‑25 °C, often catalyzed by a Lewis acid such as FeBr₃; stoichiometric bromine is consumed and HBr is generated.

Synthesis of sodium perborate from hydrogen peroxide, sodium hydroxide and sodium metaborate; purpose is to prepare a solid peroxide adduct used as a bleaching agent; key transformation is the formation of the perborate O–O linkage between H₂O₂ and the metaborate anion; carried out in aqueous solution, maintaining p around 10 with NaOH, and adding H₂O₂ at 0‑30 °C under stirring; water is the only small‑molecule by‑product.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; converts the carboxamide group of piperidine‑1‑carboxamide into a carboxylic acid while releasing ammonia. Key transformation: C(=O)‑NH2 → C(=O)‑OH + NH3. Typically performed in aqueous hydrochloric acid (1–6 M) at reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours; water is the solvent.

Oxidative dissolution of silver in hot concentrated sulfuric acid; purpose: form silver(I) sulfate and reduce sulfuric acid to sulfur dioxide; key transformation: 2 Ag + 2 H₂SO₄ (hot) → Ag₂SO₄ + SO₂ ↑ + 2 H₂O; typical conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄ (~95 %), temperature >150 °C, corrosion‑resistant vessel; no catalyst.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization). Hydroxide ion deprotonates the ammonium cation of ammonium metaborate, liberating NH₃ gas and forming sodium metaborate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution; gentle heating helps drive off ammonia. No special catalyst is required; water is the solvent.
