Formation of a Weinreb amide using an anhydride; acetic anhydride acylates N,O‑dimethylhydroxylamine to afford N‑methoxy‑N‑methylacetamide, releasing acetic acid as by‑product. Reaction typically performed in a dry solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or toluene with a base (pyridine, TEA) at 0 °C to rt to neutralize the formed acid.

Oxidation of a lower oxide to a higher oxide. Rhenium dioxide is exposed to excess oxygen at elevated temperature (≈400‑600 °C), converting it to rhenium heptoxide. The reaction is carried out in an O₂ atmosphere, typically in a furnace; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Dehydrative cyclization using POCl₃ (phosphorus oxychloride) as a condensing reagent. The amino‑sulfonamide reacts with POCl₃, which activates the sulfonyl oxygen and promotes intramolecular attack of the amine, forming the 1,2,4‑benzothiadiazine‑1,1‑dioxide ring. Water is added at the end to hydrolyze excess POCl₃ to phosphoric acid. Reaction is usually performed neat or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at reflux temperature under an inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is needed.

Copper(I)-catalyzed cyanation (halogen‑cyanide exchange); converts an aryl iodide to the corresponding nitrile by transfer of cyanide CuCN. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMS, heating to reflux; CuI precipitates and is removed.

Acylation of amiloride (formation of an amide). Benzoyl chloride reacts with the primary amine of amiloride, generating the benzoyl‑substituted product (benzamil) and releasing HCl. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature in the presence of a tertiary amine base such as triethylamine or pyridine to capture the liberated HCl. Inert atmosphere is advisable.

Redox decomposition of hydroxylamine in acidic medium. Three equivalents of hydroxylamine react with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO₂/HCl) to produce nitrogen gas and water. The process involves oxidation of hydroxylamine to N₂ while nitrous acid is reduced, overall consuming protons. Conducted in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C); excess acid ensures complete conversion. No catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution with an organolithium reagent. Ethyl lithium adds to the carbonyl carbon of acetyl chloride, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to expel LiCl, yielding methyl‑ethyl‑ketone (butan‑2‑one). Reaction is performed under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at –78 °C to 0 °C in dry ether or THF to control reactivity and avoid side reactions. No additional catalyst is needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to exchange the acetate and nitrate anions between copper(II) and potassium salts. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating; the salts dissolve and then recrystallize upon cooling. No catalyst required; common solvents are water or dilute mineral acid to aid solubility.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation reaction; thorium acetate reacts with sodium hydroxide to precipitate insoluble thorium hydroxide while forming soluble sodium acetate. Performed in aqueous medium, often at ambient temperature with stirring. No catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated amide; oleamide (cis‑9‑octadecenamide) is reduced by molecular hydrogen over palladium on carbon to give fully saturated stearamide. Conducted in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol under 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, typically 25–50 °C. Pd/C is the catalyst; reaction is exothermic.

Base‑promoted oxidation (haloform‑type reaction); chloral hydrate is hydrolyzed and oxidized by aqueous NaOH to give sodium trichloroacetate and water. Reaction proceeds at ambient or mildly elevated temperature in aqueous solution; no special catalyst required.

Ligand exchange/metathesis forming a metal β‑diketonate complex; silver acetate reacts with acetylacetone, transferring the acetate to form acetic acid and silver acetylacetonate precipitate. Usually performed in refluxing ethanol or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization; yttrium hydroxide reacts with hydrobromic acid (hydrogen bromide) to produce aqueous yttrium(III) bromide and water. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution of Y(OH)₃. No catalyst; water is the reaction medium.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) between ammonium chloride and sodium chlorate to afford ammonium chlorate and sodium chloride. Usually performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; the products remain in solution and can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Metathesis/precipitation. Potassium carbonate in water reacts with cupric acetate to form insoluble copper(II) carbonate precipitate and soluble potassium acetate. Usually performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to improve crystal growth; no special catalyst needed.

Oxidation of monomethylarsonous acid to monomethylarsonic acid using sodium chlorite; carried out in aqueous solution, mildly acidic (pH ~4‑6), typically at 20‑40 °C; sodium chlorite is reduced to sodium chloride; no catalyst required.

Condensation (imide formation) using DCC; purpose is to convert a dicarboxylic acid and a primary amine into an N‑aryl succinimide; DCC activates the carboxyl groups forming an O‑acylurea which cyclizes with the aniline, releasing dicyclohexylurea; typically performed in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often with catalytic DMAP; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidative N‑demethylation (metabolic-like transformation); purpose is to remove a methyl group from caffeine to give paraxanthine and formaldehyde; commonly achieved with oxidizing agents such as hydrogen peroxide, peroxyacids, or enzymatic P450 systems; carried out in aqueous buffer or methanol at ambient temperature; no special solvent beyond the reaction medium.

Hydrolysis of an acid chloride; 2‑ethoxyacetyl chloride reacts with water to regenerate 2‑ethoxyacetic acid and release HCl; typically performed at 0 °C to rt by slow addition of aqueous solution to the acid chloride in an inert solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) followed by basification to neutralize the HCl.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne nitrile. Purpose: saturate the carbon–carbon triple bond to afford the saturated nitrile. Key transformation: H₂ adds across the C≡C bond of but‑2‑ynenitrile, converting it to butanenitrile. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, Pd/C or Raney Ni (5 % w/w), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, 25–50 °C, 1–3 h.

Acid oxidation (redox) of scandium metal; purpose is to synthesize scandium(III) nitrate and release nitrogen dioxide; Sc(0) is oxidized to Sc³⁺ and nitrate ion is reduced to NO₂; performed in aqueous nitric acid (≈2–6 M) with reflux or moderate heating; water serves as the reaction medium, no additional catalyst is used.

Catalytic aerobic oxidation of a secondary alcohol; purpose is to convert 2‑octanol to 2‑octanone using molecular oxygen as the terminal oxidant; palladium on carbon (5–10 % wt) mediates the oxidation; typically run in an inert solvent (toluene, ethanol or acetonitrile) under an O₂ balloon or slight pressure at 50–100 °C; water is formed as a by‑product.

Halide exchange via silver salt precipitation (SN2); cinnamyl bromide reacts with silver acetate to give cinnamyl acetate while insoluble AgBr precipitates, driving the reaction forward.ed in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Eschweiler‑Clarke methylation of an indole amine; purpose is to convert 5‑methoxytryptamine to the N,N‑dimethyl analogue (5‑MeO‑DMT); formaldehyde provides the methyl groups and formic acid serves as the reductant, generating CO₂ and H₂O; typically performed in methanol or aqueous methanol, refluxing for several hours; the reaction is homogeneous and requires no metal catalyst.

Fischer esterification: conversion of 2‑ethylhexanoic acid to its ethyl ester using excess ethanol and an acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄). Reaction is performed under reflux, often with removal of water (azeotropic distillation) to drive equilibrium toward ester formation; ethanol acts as both reactant and solvent.

Condensation. Non-enzymatic formation of L-citrulline from L-ornithine and potassium cyanate. Likely simulates carbamoylation steps of the urea cycle. Requires potassium cyanate as a carbamoyl donor. Typically occurs under heated or alkaline conditions to activate cyanate. No solvent specified; potentially in aqueous media.

Acid‑base/precipitation reaction; neutralizes vanadic (HVO3) acid with ammonium hydroxide to form ammonium metavanadate (NH4VO3) and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the product crystallizes upon cooling or evaporation. No special catalyst needed; water is the medium.

Oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide using peracetic acid (a peroxyacid). The propyl sulfide is converted to propyl sulfoxide while peracetic acid is reduced to acetic acid. Conducted at 0 °C to 25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation to sulfone, often in a dry organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform. No additional catalyst required; the reaction may be buffered with a mild base to control acidity.

Halogen exchange (halogenation) redox reaction; phosphorus trichloride reacts with bromine, swapping chlorine for bromine to give phosphorus tribromide (PBr3) and liberating chlorine gas. Highly exothermic; performed under cold conditions (0 °C to 5 °C) in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, or neat under a nitrogen atmosphere. No catalyst; the stoichiometry controls product distribution.

Phosgenation / carbonate formation used to prepare di‑tert‑butyl dicarbonate (Boc2O), a common protecting‑group reagent. Phosgene reacts with tert‑butanol to give the dicarbonate while pyridine scavenges the generated HCl, forming pyridinium chloride. Carried out in a dry aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature under anhydrous conditions. Pyridine acts as the base/ catalyst; the reaction is typically run under a nitrogen blanket.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization). HBF₄ protonates the phosphate ion of Na₃PO₄, producing phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) and the tetrafluoroborate salt NaBF₄. Conducted in water, often at ambient temperature; no additional catalyst needed.

Amide formation (acetylation) of a secondary amine; α‑methylbenzylamine reacts with acetic anhydride to afford N‑(1‑phenylpropan‑2‑yl)acetamide and acetic acid; usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane, pyridine acting as base to scavenge the generated acetic acid.

Copper‑catalyzed SN2 cyanation (Rosenmund‑von Braun type copper(I) cyanide transfers a CN⁻ to the α‑bromo ketone, affording 3‑cyanobutan‑2‑one and copper(I) bromide. Usually carried out in DMF or DMSO at 80‑120 °C under inert atmosphere; copper(I) bromide can be removed by filtration.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl bromide with azide ion. Potassium azide displaces bromide on 1‑bromopropane to yield 1‑azidopropane and potassium bromide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, usually at 50–80 °C to promote substitution. No catalyst required; the azide ion is the nucleophile.

Oxidation of ethyl sulfide to ethyl sulfoxide with peroxyacetic acid; peroxyacetic acid (generated in situ from acetic acid and H₂O₂) reacts at 0 °C to 25 °C in an organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst and yields acetic acid as the only stoichiometric by‑product.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination (halogenation) of isophthalonitrile to produce chlorothalonil (tetrachloro‑isophthalonitrile). Chlorine gas, activated by catalytic FeCl3 (Lewis acid), substitutes four hydrogen atoms on the aromatic ring. The reaction is performed in a non‑reactive chlorinated solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) at 0 °C to reflux, with excess Cl2 to achieve tetra‑chlorination. FeCl3 serves as the catalyst; the process yields chlorothalonil and HCl (often trapped by a base).

Catalytic hydrogenation of an unsaturated ester; purpose is to saturate the carbon–carbon double bond of ethyl oleate to give ethyl stearate. Key transformation is addition of H2 across the C=C bond. Typical conditions: H2 gas (1–5 atm) with a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO2, or Raney Ni in an inert organic solvent (e.g., ethanol, ethyl acetate) at 25–80 °C.

SN2 alkylation of a carboxylate (Williamson ester synthesis); purpose is to form an ester from potassium benzoate and ethyl bromide. The benzoate anion attacks the primary carbon bearing bromide, displacing KBr. Common conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or dimethylformamide, reflux temperature, stoichiometric KBr precipitates out; no additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of an alkyl chloroformate; water attacks 2‑ethylhexyl carbonochloridate producing 2‑ethylhexanol, carbon dioxide and hydrogen chloride; performed in aqueous or biphasic system, often with a base (pyridine, NaHCO3) to neutralize HCl; mild temperature conditions.

Acid–base neutralization / precipitation reaction; purpose is to convert iron(III) oxide to an insoluble iron(III) phosphate salt. Phosphoric acid protonates oxide, forming water and Fe³⁺ which combines with PO₄³⁻ to give FePO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, heating gently to improve dissolution, stirring; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl halide with ammonia; purpose is to synthesize 2‑fluoroethylamine. Ammonia attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming the amine; ammonium chloride forms as by‑product. Conditions: excess aqueous NH₃, temperature 50–100 °C, aqueous solvent; reaction often performed under reflux; no catalyst required.

Acid–base reaction followed by isomerization (Wöhler synthesis); used to prepare urea from a cyanate salt; potassium cyanate reacts with ammonium chloride in aqueous solution to give ammonium cyanate which rearranges to urea, with potassium chloride as by‑product; typically performed in water under reflux, no additional catalyst required.

Double‑displacement/metathesis in aqueous solution; purpose is to produce a basic aluminum acetate complex while converting aluminum sulfate and sodium hydroxide/acetate into sodium sulfate and water. Aluminum hydroxide formed reacts with acetate to give basic aluminum acetate (Al(OH)(OAc)₂). Typical conditions: aqueous medium, moderate heating (room temperature to 60 °C), vigorous stirring; no special catalyst.

Copper‑mediated alkylation (Ullmann‑type O‑alkylation); methyl iodide reacts with copper(I) acetate to form methyl acetate, with CuI precipitating. Carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at reflux temperature; inert atmosphere often employed to avoid oxidation.

Acid chloride formation using thionyl chloride; conversion of prop‑2‑ynoic acid to the corresponding acyl chloride. The carboxylic acid is treated with excess SOCl₂, often with a catalytic drop of DMF, and refluxed or warmed to 40–60 °C in anhydrous conditions (no external solvent needed or in dry CH₂Cl₂). By‑products sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride are expelled; the product is isolated after removal of volatiles and drying.

Halogen exchange/redox solid‑gas reaction; chlorine oxidizes iodide to iodine while being reduced to chloride, converting ytterbium(II) iodide to ytterbium(II) chloride. Typically carried out in a sealed tube or furnace at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) under anhydrous, inert atmosphere; no solvent is used.

Chlorination of antimony(III) oxide with phosphorus pentachloride; a halogenation/oxidative chlorination that generates volatile phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and antimony(III) chloride (SbCl₃). Conducted in a dry, closed system at 50–100 °C, often in a non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or neat PCl₅; exclusion of moisture is essential.

High‑temperature solid‑state calcination; calcium carbonate thermally decomposes to CO₂, and the liberated oxide reacts with silica to form calcium silicate (CaSiO₃). Performed in a rotary or shaft furnace at >1200 °C in the presence of excess SiO₂; no solvent, atmosphere typically air or nitrogen.

Grignard addition to a nitrile followed by acidic work‑up; methylmagnesium bromide attacks cyclopropanecarbonitrile to give an imine magnesium complex, which upon hydrolysis furnishes cyclopropylacetone (a ketone). Carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen; quenched with dilute acid or water to release the ketone.
Nucleophilic substitution; synthesis of ethylene glycol; two chlorine atoms replaced by hydroxyl groups; hot aqueous potassium hydroxide (aq KOH) as both reagent and solvent; no catalyst required.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation of guaiacol with ethyl chloride and AlCl3; produces 4‑ethylguaiacol and hydrogen chloride; typically carried out in dry dichloromethane or nitrobenzene with excess AlCl3, temperature ranging from 0 °C to reflux.

Hydrogen‑gas reduction of Cr(VI) oxide to Cr(III) oxide with concurrent formation of water; conducted at 500–800 °C in a stream of H₂ (sometimes diluted with inert gas); solid‑gas reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Nitrous‑acid mediated deamination ( diazotization‑decomposition ); the primary amine of N‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)ethylenediamine is converted to a diazonium intermediate by NaNO₂/HCl, which loses N₂ and is hydrolyzed to give 2‑(2‑hydroxyethylamino)ethanol. Reaction performed in cold aqueous acidic solution (0–5 °C), with NaNO₂ added slowly; the gaseous N₂ evolves, and the aqueous layer is worked up to isolate the product.

Acid‑base (metal‑oxide dissolution) reaction of iridium(III) oxide with aqueous hydrochloric acid to afford iridium(III) chloride and water; carried out in aqueous HCl at ambient to reflux temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Enzymatic methyl transfer; S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine donates a methyl group to 1,3,7‑trimethyluric acid, yielding theacrine and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Catalyzed by a caffeine‑xanthine N‑methyltransferase in buffered aqueous media at pH 7–8, typically at 25–37 °C; requires Mg²⁺ or other divalent cations as cofactors.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction; used to prepare silver perchlorate from commercially available silver nitrate. In aqueous solution the two soluble salts exchange anions, yielding ammonium nitrate and soluble silver perchlorate. Typical conditions: dissolve reagents in water at ambient temperature, stir, then isolate AgClO₄ by evaporation or crystallisation; no special catalyst required.

Double‑replacement precipitation reaction; converts nickel(II) acetate and sodium phosphate into insoluble nickel(II) phosphate while forming soluble sodium acetate. Performed in water: aqueous solutions of the two salts are mixed, the nickel phosphate precipitates and is collected by filtration, washed and dried. Heating or gentle reflux can improve yield; no catalyst is needed.

Electrophilic addition of bromine to an alkene (vicinal dibromination); Br₂ adds across the double bond of 2‑norbornene to give 2,3‑dibromonorbornane (anti addition). Reaction is performed in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, with careful control to avoid over‑bromination.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt exchange) reaction; aqueous hydrochloric acid protonates barium chromate, generating chromic acid (H₂CrO₄) and soluble barium chloride. The mixture is typically stirred in water at room temperature or with gentle heating to ensure complete conversion. No catalyst is required; the chromic acid formed can be used in situ as an oxidising agent.

Oxidation of secondary alcohol; MnO₂ converts cyclohexanol toohexanone with formation of MnO and water. Conducted at room temperature to reflux in an aprotic solvent like dichloromethane, chloroform or acetone; excess solid MnO₂ is used. Purpose is selective oxidation to the ketone.

Catalytic carbonyl reduction (hydrosilylation) of a ketone; triethylsilane delivers a hydride to the carbonyl of acetophenone in the presence of a Lewis‑acid catalyst, boron trifluoride etherate, affording the secondary alcohol 1‑phenylethanol. Standard conditions: dry dichloromethane (or CH₂Cl₂) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to rt, catalytic amount of BF₃·OEt₂, stoichiometric Et₃SiH. After reaction work‑up (aqueous work‑up, extraction) the alcohol is isolated by evaporation and purification.

Silyl‑transfer (esterification) of a carboxylic acid; trimethylsilyl triflate reacts with benzoic acid, transferring the trimethylsilyl group to the acid to form trimethylsilyl benzoate while releasing trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (TfOH). Carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; no additional catalyst is required. The silyl ester can be isolated by standard work‑up, and TfOH remains in the reaction mixture or is removed by aqueous extraction.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (alcohol to alkyl chloride) using thionyl chloride; purpose: convert a primary alcohol into the corresponding chloride for further functionalisation; key transformation: the hydroxyl group is replaced by chloride while SOCl2 generates gaseous HCl and SO2 driving the reaction forward; typical conditions: reflux or gentle heating in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine as solvent/base, often under inert atmosphere; common solvents/catalysts: pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl, dichloromethane as reaction medium.

Copper‑catalyzed halogen exchange (Ullmann‑type halogen swap); converts an aryl iodide to the corresponding aryl bromide. Key transformation is replacement of iodine on 3‑iodopyridine by bromide supplied from NaBr, mediated by CuBr as a Lewis‑acid catalyst. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or NMP, often with a nitrogen atmosphere; excess NaBr drives the equilibrium; reaction temperature 80–120 °C.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose: exchange the anions to form an insoluble barium sulfate precipitate while generating soluble zinc fluoride; key transformation: Zn²⁺ pairs with F⁻ to give ZnF₂ and Ba²⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to give BaSO₄ (white solid); typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; common solvents/catalysts: water as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Direct oxidation (combustion) of tungsten metal; forms tungsten dioxide (WO₂), a semiconductor oxide. The process is a simple metal‑oxygen redox where tungsten is oxidized from 0 to +4 oxidation state. Requires high temperature (≈500–1000 °C) in air or flowing O₂; no solvent or catalyst is used. Often carried out in a furnace with controlled oxygen flow.

Type: reductive amination (reductive methylation) of a secondary amine; purpose: install a methyl group on piperidine to give N‑methylpiperidine; key transformation: formaldehyde reacts with piperidine hydrochloride to form an iminium intermediate which is reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to the N‑methyl product, generating NaCl and boric acid as by‑products; typical conditions: mild acidic pH (≈5–6), room temperature or 0 °C to rt, in a mixture of methanol/water; common solvents/catalysts: methanol or ethanol as solvent, NaBH₃CN as the selective reductant, sometimes a buffer (e.g., acetate) to control pH.

Type: N‑alkylation (SN2) of a secondary amine with methyl iodide; purpose: methylate desipramine to afford imipramine (the N‑methyl analogue); key transformation: the lone pair on the nitrogen attacks the electrophilic methyl carbon of CH₃I, displacing iodide and forming a new N‑C bond, with HI as a by‑product; typical conditions: reflux or rt in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, using a base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaHCO₃, or triethylamine) to neutralise the generated HI; common solvents/catalysts: acetonitrile, DMF, and a mild inorganic base.

Carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) mediated amide coupling; synthesis of the racetam nootropic Aniracetam (N‑(4‑methoxybenzoyl)‑2‑pyrrolidone). 4‑Methoxybenzoic acid is activated by CDI to give the corresponding imidazolide, releasing imidazole as by‑product, which then reacts with 2‑pyrrolidone to form the N‑acylated product. Typical conditions: dissolve acid and CDI in dry dichloromethane or THF under nitrogen, stir at 0 °C to rt, then add 2‑pyrrolidone; reaction proceeds at rt to 40 °C; work‑up involves aqueous wash to remove imidazole.

Formation of an alkyl fluorosulfonate (ethyl fluorosulfonate) by esterification of ethanol with fluorosulfuric acid (FSO₃H). The hydroxyl group is converted into the fluorosulfonate leaving group, with water as the only by‑product. Reaction is carried out at 0 °C to 5 °C to control exotherm, in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or chloroform under nitrogen; stoichiometric amount of FSO₃H is added dropwise. No catalyst is required.

Pinnick oxidation (aldehyde to carboxylic acid). 1‑Piperidinecarboxaldehyde is oxidized by sodium chlorite (NaClO₂) in the presence of sodium dihydrogen phosphate as a buffer to give piperidine‑1‑carboxylic acid, with sodium chloride and water as by‑products. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 3–4) containing NaClO₂ and NaH₂PO₄, often with a scavenger such as 2‑methyl‑2‑butene to quench chlorine dioxide; temperature 0 °C to rt; solvent mixture of water and tert‑butanol or acetonitrile.

Reductive amination of phenoxyacetaldehyde with ammonia using sodium cyanoborohydride. The aldehyde condenses with ammonia to form an imine, which is reduced in situ by NaBH₃CN to give 2‑phenoxyethanamine. Conducted in a polar protic solvent (methanol or ethanol) at pH 5–6 (adjusted with acetic acid or buffer) and temperature 0 °C to rt; NaBH₃CN is added portionwise to avoid over‑reduction; the reaction yields the primary amine as the major product.

Acid‑base double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is to convert insoluble strontium chromate into soluble chromic acid while precipitating strontium sulfate; key transformation: SO4^2‑ replaces CrO4^2‑ forming H2CrO4 and SrSO4; typical conditions: aqueous solution, dilute H2SO4, ambient to mild heating; common solvent: water; product SrSO4 precipitates and is filtered off.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a thioester; cleaves benzyl thioacetate to give benzyl mercaptan and acetic acid; protonated carbonyl facilitates nucleophilic attack by water; typical conditions: dilute HCl (1–3 M), heating under reflux; aqueous medium, sometimes with an organic co‑solvent such as ether.

Skeletal isomerization of a branched alkane; purpose is to increase octane rating or obtain a specific isomer; key transformation: migration of a methyl group from C‑3 to C‑4 converting 2,2,3‑trimethylpentane to 2,2,4‑trimethylpentane; typical conditions: gas‑phase or liquid‑phase catalysis at 200‑400 °C over strong acid or metal‑oxide catalysts (e.g., Pt/Al2O3, zeolite HY); common solvents (if liquid) include high‑boiling hydrocarbons; reaction is catalytic and reversible.

N‑acylation of a primary amine (amide formation, Schotten‑Baumann type); propionyl chloride reacts with n‑butylamine to give N‑butylpropionamide and HCl. The reaction is usually carried out in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to 25 °C, with a stoichiometric base (triethylamine, pyridine, or NaHCO₃) to scavenge the generated HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). 1‑Phenylpropan‑1‑ol is treated with stoichiometric PCC in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, under inert atmosphere. PCC selectively oxidizes the alcohol to 1‑phenylpropan‑1‑one while being reduced to chromium(III) chloride; water is generated as a by‑product. The reaction is typically run for 1–2 h, followed by filtration to remove the chromium residue. No additional catalyst is needed.

Radical alpha‑chlorination of acetyl chloride using sulfuryl chloride; purpose is to introduce a chlorine atom at the carbonyl α‑position to give chloroacetyl chloride; key transformation: CH3COCl → CH2ClCOCl with by‑products HCl and SO2; typical conditions: reflux in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often under UV light or heat; radical initiator (e.g., benzoyl peroxide) may be employed.

Alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of a phenolic hydroxyl; methyl iodide reacts with 4‑hydroxyphenylacetone in the presence of potassium carbonate to give 4‑methoxyphenylacetone. Conditions: K₂CO₃ (1‑2 eq), MeI (1.1‑1.5 eq) in dry acetone or DMF, reflux 4‑6 h under nitrogen; the base deprotonates the phenol, generating the phenoxide which undergoes SN2 attack on MeI.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification to synthesize triethylene glycol dimethacrylate; purpose is to prepare a difunctional methacrylate monomer for polymer networks; key transformation: two molecules of methacrylic acid are coupled to the two hydroxyl groups of triethylene glycol, producing the diester and two equivalents of dicyclohexylurea as by‑product; typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in dry dichloromethane or DMF, with catalytic DMAP under inert atmosphere; by‑product dicyclohexylurea precipitates and is filtered off.

Metal‑acid redox (single‑displacement) reaction of vanadium metal with hydrogen chloride; purpose is to generate vanadium(II) chloride and hydrogen gas; key transformation: V + 2 HCl → VCl2 + H2; typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–2 M) heated to reflux or gently warmed; reaction proceeds readily without additional catalyst.

Imine formation (Schiff‑base condensation) of benzophenone with ammonia generated from ammonium acetate; purpose is to produce benzophenone imine, a protective carbonyl derivative; key transformation: Ph2C=O + NH3 → Ph2C=NH plus water and acetic acid; typical conditions: reflux in toluene or benzene with a Dean–Stark apparatus to remove water, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid to accelerate condensation.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation of benzaldehyde with two equivalents of pyrrole to afford dipyrromethane; purpose is to generate the dipyrromethane core used in porphyrin synthesis; key transformation: electrophilic attack of pyrrole on the aldehyde carbon, followed by addition of a second pyrrole and loss of water; typical conditions: catalytic amounts of a strong Lewis or Brønsted acid (e.g., BF3·OEt2, TFA) in dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; water is removed or trapped to drive the reaction.

Base‑induced elimination (E2) of a secondary alkyl chloride. Potassium ethoxide acts as a strong base, abstracting a β‑hydrogen while the chloride leaves, giving the internal alkene but‑2‑ene, potassium chloride, and ethanol (the conjugate acid of the base). Conducted in ethanol solvent, often under reflux, with stoichiometric KOC₂H₅.

Redox generation of chlorine dioxide from sodium chlorite; purpose is in situ production of ClO2 for bleaching, disinfection, or analytical use; key transformation: chlorite (ClO2⁻) is oxidized by acidic conditions and MnO2 to ClO2 gas while MnO2 is reduced to Mn^2+; typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (1‑2 M HCl), low temperature (0‑25 °C) to control gas evolution; MnO2 acts as heterogeneous catalyst; common solvent: water.

Solid‑state/base‑mediated oxide synthesis; aluminum oxide reacts with aqueous barium hydroxide to form soluble aluminate ions which combine with Ba²⁺ on heating to precipitate barium aluminate (BaAl₂O₄). Usually carried out by adding Al₂O₃ to excess Ba(OH)₂ solution, evaporating, then heating the residue at 800‑1000 °C to obtain the crystalline salt; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Reaction type: Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed condensation of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol). Purpose: synthesis of 3‑methylbut‑2‑enyl acetate from acetic acid. Key transformation: protonated carbonyl of acetic acid is attacked by the alcohol, followed by loss of water to give the ester. Typical conditions: reflux in a non‑aqueous solvent (toluene, benzene or solvent‑free) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄), removal of water by Dean–Stark or excess acid to drive the equilibrium forward.

Acidic oxidation/dissolution; concentrated nitric acid oxidizes gallium telluride, converting gallium to soluble gallium nitrate and tellurium to tellurium dioxide while reducing nitrate to nitrogen dioxide gas; performed by refluxing the solid in hot HNO₃, often in a glass vessel; gases are vented; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization; cyclamic acid (a sulfonic acid) is neutralized by calcium hydroxide to give the calcium salt of cyclamate and water. Performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature or with mild heating to drive off water; pH is adjusted to neutral. No catalyst is needed.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of ethyl cyanate; purpose is to generate sodium cyanate. The O‑ethyl bond is cleaved, transferring the cyanate ion to Na⁺ and releasing ethanol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at 50–80 °C with stirring; solvent = water or water/ethanol mixture; no catalyst required.

Hydrolytic decomposition / prodrug activation; molsidomine undergoes aqueous hydrolysis (physiological pH, 37 °C) to cleave the N‑nitroso group, releasing formaldehyde and the active metabolite linsidomine (SIN‑1). Reaction proceeds in buffered aqueous solution; no external catalyst is required.

Redox/halogen exchange between iodine monochloride and potassium iodide in aqueous solution; ICl oxidizes I⁻ to I₂ while Cl⁻ pairs with K⁺ to give KCl; carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic addition of an amine to an isocyanate (carbamoylation); urea reacts with isocyanic acid (HNCO) to give carbamoyliminourea (N‑carbamoyl‑urea). Typically performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as pyridine or THF at 0‑25 °C, sometimes under inert atmosphere; no catalyst is essential, the reaction is driven by the nucleophilicity of the urea nitrogen.

Acid‑base neutralization of an arsenic acid derivative; dimethylarsinic acid is deprotonated by sodium hydroxide to afford sodium dimethylarsenate and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; straightforward stoichiometric neutralization, no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization of a carboxylic acid with sodium bicarbonate; purpose is to generate the sodium salt of 4‑fluorobenzoic acid for isolation or subsequent reactions. Key transformation: 4‑fluorobenzoic acid + NaHCO₃ → sodium 4‑fluorobenzoate + CO₂ ↑ + H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of sodium bicarbonate (excess) added to a solution of the acid in water or a miscible organic solvent (e.g., ethanol/water) at room temperature; vigorous stirring evolves CO₂. The resulting aqueous salt solution can be lyophilized or the salt precipitated by evaporation.

Acid dissolution (double‑displacement) reaction. Purpose: convert the insoluble barium hydrogen phosphate into soluble barium chloride and regenerate phosphoric acid. Key transformation: BaHPO₄ reacts with excess HCl (typically 2 eq) to give BaCl₂ (aq) and H₃PO₄ (aq). Typical conditions: aqueous HCl added to BaHPO₄ at ambient or mildly elevated temperature with stirring until complete dissolution. No catalyst used.

Acid‑base deprotonation (metal‑acid reaction). Sodium metal removes the phenolic hydrogen of (1,1′‑biphenyl)-2‑ol to give sodium 2‑phenylphenoxide and H₂. Purpose: generate a phenoxide salt for nucleophilic substitution or metal‑mediated coupling. Typical conditions: dry ethereal solvent (diethyl ether or THF), Na added under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to rt, stirring until gas evolution ceases. No additional catalyst.

Complete combustion of a saturated hydrocarbon; oxidizes hexane to carbon dioxide and water; same oxidation mechanism as other alkanes; needs sufficient O₂ and an ignition source (≈350 °C); performed in a flame or furnace; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (deprotonation) of a pyridinium salt; NaOH deprotonates pyridinium trifluoromethanesulfonate, producing free pyridine, sodium trifluoromethanesulfonate, and water; performed in aqueous or mixed solvent at ambient temperature, no additional catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of an aryl iodide with methylboronic acid; purpose is to install a methyl group onto the aromatic ring producing 3‑methylphenol (m‑cresol); key transformation: C–I bond is replaced by C–CH3 bond via transmetalation and reductive elimination; typical conditions: Pd(0) source (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 or PdCl2(dppf)), base such as K2CO3 or Na2CO3, mixed solvent THF/H2O or dioxane/H2O, heated 80‑100 °C under inert atmosphere; catalyst loading 0.5‑5 mol %; reaction gives high selectivity for para‑ or meta‑substituted product.

Transesterification (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed exchange of alkoxy groups): Methyl acetoacetate reacts with excess ethanol to give ethyl acetoacetate and methanol. The reaction swaps the methoxy group for an ethoxy group, allowing preparation of the ethyl β‑keto ester. Common conditions employ reflux in ethanol with a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid (0.5–2 % v/v) or a catalytic base such as NaOEt; removal of volatile methanol by distillation drives the equilibrium to the product side. Reaction times are typically 2–6 h; the product is purified by simple distillation or silica gel chromatography.

Acid–base gas‑evolving double displacement reaction; sodium bicarbonate reacts with calcium acetate, producing sodium acetate, calcium carbonate precipitate, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Executed in water at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring helps release CO₂; no catalyst or special solvent is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitroarene; reduces the nitro group of 8‑nitroquinoline to an amine to give 8‑aminoquinoline, with water as the only by‑product. Typically performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over palladium on carbon in ethyl acetate (or ethanol/methanol) at room temperature to gentle reflux.

Ligand‑exchange (chelation) reaction forming a metal β‑diketonate complex; titanium(IV) isopropoxide reacts with acetylacetone replace the isopropoxide ligands by acetylacetonate, yielding titanium(IV) acetylacetonate and liberating isopropanol. Conducted by refluxing the reagents in a non‑coordinating solvent (toluene, benzene) or neat, with removal of the isopropanol (often by azeotropic distillation).

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide by cyanide; sodium cyanide attacks 4‑bromobutyric acid to give 4‑cyanobutyric acid and sodium bromide. Usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to reflux, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst if using aqueous NaCN.

Oxidative coupling of a secondary thiol with elemental iodine; purpose is disulfide formation. Key transformation: two R‑SH react with I₂, producing R‑S‑S‑R and two equivalents of HI. Often carried out in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂, CCl₄) at room temperature; the generated HI may be neutralized with a base.
Acid–base double‑replacement reaction; aqueous HCl protonates zinc oxalate, producing soluble ZnCl₂ and oxalic acid; performed ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition (retro‑urea) of methoxyurea; on heating (≈150–200 °C) methoxyurea breaks down to methyl isocyanate and water. The reaction proceeds in the bulk or in a high‑boiling inert solvent, without catalyst.

Electrophilic addition of bromine to an alkyne (dihalogen addition); purpose is to form a vicinal tetra‑halogenated alkane; key transformation: Br2 adds across the C≡C bond of dichloroacetylene, yielding 1,2‑dibromo‑,2‑dichloroethane; typical conditions: low temperature (0‑5 °C) to avoid over‑reaction, inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; reaction proceeds rapidly and the product precipitates or can be isolated by evaporation.

Condensation (Schiff‑base formation) between an aldehyde and thiosemicarbazide; acetaldehyde reacts with thiosemicarbazide to give the corresponding acetaldehyde thiosemicarbazone, eliminating water. Typically carried out in ethanol or methanol (often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid) under reflux or at ambient temperature.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using silver(I) oxide as the oxidant; the aldehydic carbonyl of 2‑methoxybenzaldehyde is converted to the corresponding 2‑methoxybenzoic acid while Ag2O is reduced to metallic silver. Typically performed in refluxing ethanol or aqueous ethanol; Ag2O is added in stoichiometric amount, and the reaction proceeds under neutral to mildly basic conditions without additional catalyst.

Dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination); purpose is to generate the vinyl difluoride alkene. The strong base KOH abstracts a proton adjacent to the carbon bearing chlorine, expelling Cl⁻ and forming 1,1-difluoroethene, with KCl and water as by‑products. Typically performed in an alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol) under reflux or elevated temperature.
double displacement reaction; precipitation of lead(ii) hydroxide; pb^2+ reacts with oh- from sodium hydroxide to form pb(oh)2; aqueous solution, ambient temperature; no catalyst required

Electrophilic halogen addition; Cl₂ adds across the C=C bond of propadiene (allene) to give the vicinal dichloride 1,2‑dichloro‑1‑propene; usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent such as CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂; no catalyst needed.

Copper‑catalyzed Chan–Lam coupling (oxidative C–N bond formation) between the primary amine of anthranilic acid and phenylboronic acid to give N‑phenylanthranilic acid; bor acid is generated as a by‑product. The reaction is usually run in pyridine, which acts as both solvent and base, with Cu(OAc)2 (10–20 mol %) as catalyst, at 40–80 °C under air or O2 atmosphere. Common bases such as pyridine or triethylamine can be used, and the ligand‑free conditions are typical.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); aqueous solution; Dysprosium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid to give dysprosium(III) sulfate and water; typically carried out by mixing stoichiometric amounts of solid or aqueous Dy(OH)3 with dilute H2SO4 at room temperature or mild heating, stirring until dissolution; water serves as both solvent and product; no catalyst required.

Redox dissolution of cobalt metal by concentrated nitric acid; cobalt is oxidized from 0 to +2, forming cobalt(II) nitrate, while nitric acid is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas and water. The reaction is carried out in refluxing concentrated HNO3 (≈ 68 %); vigorous evolution of reddish‑brown NO2 is observed. No external catalyst is required; temperature control is important to manage the exotherm.

Double‑displacement precipitation: lead(II) bromide solution mixed with silver nitrate precipitates insoluble silver bromide while forming soluble lead(II) nitrate; performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring, no catalyst.

Metathesis/acid‑base exchange between citric acid and ferric nitrate in aqueous solution, producing ferric citrate ( metal‑organic complex) and liberating nitric acid. The reaction is performed by mixing aqueous solutions of the salts, often with gentle heating (40–60 °C) to drive off the generated HNO3 or to aid complexation. No catalyst is needed; the process proceeds under ambient pressure.

Oxidation of chromium(IV) dioxide (CrO2) by molecular oxygen to give chromium(VI) oxide (CrO3). This high‑temperature oxidation is typically conducted in a flow or batch furnace at 300–400 °C in an oxygen‑rich atmosphere. No additional catalyst is required; the reaction is driven by the high temperature and excess O2.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of 1‑bromo‑4‑methylbenzene with potassium vinyltrifluoroborate to afford 4‑methylstyrene. Standard conditions employ a Pd(0) source such as Pd(PPh3)4 or PdCl2(dppf) (1–5 mol %), a mild inorganic base (K2CO3 or Na2CO3), and a mixed solvent system (THF/H2O or dioxane/H2O) at 80–100 °C under N2 atmosphere. The reaction tolerates the trifluoroborate leaving group and delivers the vinyl‑aryl product in good yield.

Acid–base neutralization (acid carbonate reaction). Hydrogen selenide acts as a weak acid and reacts with calcium carbonate in aqueous solution, releasing carbon dioxide gas and water while forming calcium selenide as the inorganic salt. Typically performed by bubbling H2Se gas into a suspension of CaCO3 in water at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required; common solvent is water.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) / amination. Ammonia generated from ammonium hydroxide attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing chlorine in 2‑chloroacetaldehyde, displacing chloride to give 2‑aminoacetaldehyde while forming ammonium chloride. Conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑alcoholic medium at 0–25 °C; excess NH4OH drives the reaction; no special catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; used to exchange anions and isolate insoluble copper(II) carbonate. In aqueous solution CuHPO₄ reacts with Na₂CO₃; copper(II) carbonate precipitates while sodium dihydrogen phosphate remains dissolved. Reaction is performed at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst or solvent beyond the water medium.

Single‑displacement (metal‑acid) reaction. Strontium metal reacts with sulfuric acid, oxidizing the metal to the Sr²⁺ state and reducing protons to hydrogen gas; the insoluble strontium sulfate precipitates. Usually carried out in dilute H₂SO₄ at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) under stirring; no catalyst; aqueous medium.

Dehydrative cyclization (carbodiimide‑mediated anhydride formation). Dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates the carboxyl groups of benzene‑1,2,4‑tricarboxylic acid, promoting intramolecular condensation to give trimellitic anhydride and dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Performed in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or chloroform, typically at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; DCC itself acts as coupling reagent.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a metal cyanamide salt. Calcium cyanamide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid, protonating the cyan anion and liberating free cyanamide (NH₂CN) while forming soluble calcium chloride. Conducted by refluxing CaCN₂ in excess 2 M HCl for 1–2 h; water is the solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Redox (halogen displacement) reaction; chlorine oxidizes bromide ion to bromine while being reduced to chloride ion, yielding KCl and Br₂; carried out by bubbling Cl₂ gas through an aqueous solution of KBr, often at room temperature and in the dark to minimize side reactions; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (alkylation) of benzhydryl chloride by 2-(dimethylamino)ethanol to form diphenhydramine; HCl is generated as by‑product. The reaction is used to synthesize the antihistamine diphenhydramine. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, in the presence of a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to capture HCl.

Acid–base metathesis; generates chloric acid from nitric acid and sodium chlorate; key transformation: HNO₃ protonates ClO₃⁻ to give HClO₃ while Na⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ forming NaNO₃; performed in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine; catalytic hydrogenation (H₂, 1–5 atm) over Pd/C or Raney Ni in ethanol (or methanol) at reflux, or chemical reduction with LiAlH₄, affords 3‑methylphenethylamine from the nitrile.

Type: Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage with HCl (SN2‑type). Purpose: Generate chloromethane (CH3Cl) as a building block and methanol as by‑product. Key transformation: One methyl group is protonated and displaced by chloride, yielding CH3Cl + CH3OH (CH3OCH3 + HCl → CH3Cl + CH3OH). Typical conditions: Gaseous or aqueous HCl, temperature 0–50 °C to minimize side reactions, often under anhydrous conditions. Solvent/catalyst: May be performed in inert solvent such as dichloromethane or in the gas phase; no additional catalyst beyond HCl.

Metathesis salt displacement: Silver nitrate reacts with amino alcohol hydroiodide to form highly insoluble silver iodide precipitate, driving the formation of ethanolammonium nitrate. This aqueous ionic reaction exploits AgI's low solubility product to selectively remove iodide ions from solution.

Halogen exchange/redox reaction; chlorine gas oxidizes iodide in BiI₃ to elemental iodine while substituting chloride to form bismuth trichloride. Usually carried out by passing dry Cl₂ over solid BiI₃ at modest temperature (0‑50 °C) in a dry inert atmosphere; products can be collected by sublimation; no solvent or catalyst needed.

DCC‑mediated amidation (coupling) of DL‑aspartic acid with ammonia to give DL‑asparagine, with dicyclohexylurea formed as insoluble by‑product. This peptide‑bond formation is employed in synthesis of amino‑acid derivatives. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or DMF, ambient temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂), and catalytic amount of DMAP may be added to accelerate the reaction. The precipitated dicyclohexylurea is filtered away.

Chlorination of N,N‑diethylformamide with phosphorus pentachloride to afford N,N‑diethylcarbamoyl chloride, phosphoryl chloride (POCl₃) and gaseous HCl. The transformation converts a formamide into the corresponding acid chloride and is useful for preparing acyl‑chloride reagents. Performed anhydrously in a non‑protic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or CHCl₃ at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen; HCl gas is vented or trapped.

Acid–metal reaction; used to convert metallic magnesium into a soluble fluoride complex while generating hydrogen gas; Mg metal + H₂SiF₆ → MgSiF₆ (magnesium hexafluorosilicate) + H₂↑; performed in aqueous solution, typically at ambient temperature or mild heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Metallothermic reduction of phosphorus trichloride by zinc producing zinc chloride and elemental white phosphorus (P₄). The reaction is a high‑temperature redox displacement used for laboratory preparation of P₄. Carried out in a sealed tube or a high‑temperature furnace at 250–350 °C under an inert atmosphere (argon) to avoid oxidation; solid Zn and PCl₃ are mixed thoroughly before heating.

Base‑promoted O‑methylation of dihydroartemisinin with dimethyl sulfate in the presence of sodium carbonate to give artemether (a methyl ether). This is an SN2 alkylation used to introduce the methoxy group required for antimalarial activity. Typical conditions: biphasic system (e.g., acetone/water) or dry organic solvent, temperature 0–25 °C, sodium carbonate as the base to neutralize generated H₂SO₄; the reaction is quenched with ice and extracted.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) followed by acid work‑up; converts methyl 4‑chlorobenzoate to 4‑chlorobenzoic acid. Key transformations: NaOH attacks the ester carbonyl producing the sodium carboxylate and methanol; subsequent addition of HCl protonates the carboxylate to give the free acid and forms NaCl and water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 1–2 h, then cool and acidify with dilute HCl. Common solvent: water/ethanol mixture; no special catalyst needed.

Fluorination of arsenic(V) oxide with hydrogen fluoride; preparation of volatile arsenic pentafluoride. Key transformation: each As2O5 mole reacts with ten HF molecules to replace all O atoms by F, yielding 2 AsF5 and 5 H2O. Conducted under anhydrous HF gas, often at 0–50 °C in a PTFE‑lined reactor; no solvent other than excess HF; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) in water; exchanges ammonium and rubidium ions between ammonium chloride and rubidium chromate; key transformation: 2 NH₄Cl + Rb₂CrO₄ → (NH₄)₂CrO₄ + 2 RbCl; carried out by dissolving the salts in water and stirring at room temperature; no additional catalyst.

General type: acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: preparation of ammonium phosphate tribasic as a fertilizer or buffering salt. Key transformation: three equivalents of NH4OH neutralize the three acidic protons of H3PO4 to give (NH4)3PO4 and water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, gradual addition of NH4OH to phosphoric acid with stirring; exothermic heat is dissipated. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Chlorination of a cyclic anhydride with phosphorus pentachloride to give an acid chloride (pentanedioyl dichloride). Key transformation: PCl5 converts the two carbonyl oxygens of glutaric anhydride into chloride, producing pentanedioyl dichloride and POCl3 as by‑product. Conducted anhydrous, under nitrogen, at 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑protic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or chloroform. No additional catalyst.

Erbium hydroxide undergoes a straightforward acid‑base neutralization with hydrochloric acid to give soluble erbium(III) chloride and water; carried out in aqueous HCl at room temperature, optionally with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a 2‑bromoethyl side chain by ammonia, yielding tryptamine. Key transformation: NH3 attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing bromide, displacing Br⁻ and forming the primary amine side chain on the indole nucleus; HBr combines with excess ammonia to give NH4Br. Typically carried out in excess gaseous or aqueous NH3 (or 25 % NH3 in ethanol) at 60–100 °C in a sealed tube or pressure reactor; solvent often ethanol or methanol; no metal catalyst required.

Catalytic of a nitro aromatic compound to the corresponding amine using sodium borohydride with nickel(II) chloride as in‑situ catalyst (transfer hydrogenation). Key transformation: NaBH4 reduces NiCl2 to Ni⁰, which mediates electron transfer to the nitro group, converting 4‑nitro‑1,1′‑biphenyl to 4‑aminobiphenyl; by‑products are water and NaCl. Typical conditions: ethanol‑water mixture, ambient to reflux temperature, addition of NiCl2 (5–10 mol %) followed by NaBH4 (2–3 eq). No further reagents required.

This is an acid-base reaction where calcium hydride reacts with carbon dioxide to produce calcium carbonate and hydrogen gas. Its purpose is typically for hydrogen generation or CO2 absorption. Key transformations involve the hydride reacting with CO2 to form carbonate and release hydrogen. Typical reaction conditions are at room temperature or with gentle heating. Common solvents are not usually required, as it can occur in solid-gas phase.
Dehydrohalogenation (thermal elimination) of 1,1,1,2‑tetrafluoroethane to give trifluoroethylene and HF; high temperature (300‑400 °C) often over alumina or silica catalyst, gas‑phase, no solvent.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction) of allyl alcohol with peroxyformic acid to afford glycidol and formic acid; typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0‑25 °C under inert atmosphere.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) of silicon tetrabromide with hydrogen fluoride producing silicon tetrafluoride and hydrogen bromide; performed in a dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or liquid HF) at ambient to moderate temperature; gaseous products are evolved.

Acylation (Schotten‑Baumann amide formation) of 5‑methoxytryptamine with acetyl chloride to yield melatonin and HCl; conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine, 0 °C to room temperature.

Acid‑base reaction of lithium carbonate with iodic acid forming lithium iod, carbon dioxide and water; carried out in aqueous solution, often warmed gently to promote CO₂ evolution; stoichiometric amounts used.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage (O‑dealkylation) of the 3‑methoxy group of codeine using concentrated hydroiodic acid; the methyl group is removed as iodomethane and the phenolic hydroxyl is regenerated to give morphine; typically performed by refluxing codeine in 55 % aqueous HI (often generated in situ with red phosphorus) at 100–150 °C, water or ethanol as solvent, no additional catalyst.

Alcoholysis of methyltrichlorosilane with methanol, affording methyltrimethoxysilane and HCl. Provides a methoxy‑functional organosilane used in coating and cross‑linking chemistries. Conducted in dry methanol, temperature control (0‑10 °C initially, then room temperature or reflux at 65 °C), inert atmosphere, and usually in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to neutralize HCl. Methanol acts as solvent and reagent.

Electrophilic methylation (alkylation) of 2‑naphthol methyl triflate; the phenolic O‑H is converted to an O‑CH₃ ether (2‑methoxynaphthalene); usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature, with a weak base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to neutralize the triflic acid by‑product.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; sulfate ions exchange from Zn²⁺ to Mg²⁺ forming soluble magnesium sulfate, while hydroxide ions transfer to Zn²⁺ precipitating zinc hydroxide; carried out in water ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement metathesis/precipitation; ammonium hydroxide reacts with calcium nitrate to give soluble ammonium nitrate and insoluble calcium hydroxide which precipitates; performed in water at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precipitation; lanthanum(III) chloride hexahydrate in water reacts with phosphoric acid, forming insoluble lanthanum phosphate precipitate and liberating hydrochloric acid into solution. Typically carried out at 50‑80 °C with aqueous media; pH may be adjusted to favor precipitation. No catalyst.

Oxidative acid leaching of indium arsenide with concentrated sulfuric acid; the arsenide is oxidized from As³⁻ to arsenic acid (H₃AsO₄) while indium forms soluble indium sulfate (In₂(SO₄)₃); typically conducted by heating the solid InAs in refluxing 90–98 % H₂SO₄ at 150–200 °C, often under an inert atmosphere; the acid itself acts as both solvent and oxidant, no external catalyst required.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; produces cadmium tellurate and hydrochloric acid. In aqueous solution, telluric acid reacts with cadmium chloride; cadmium ions pair with tellurate to precipitate cadmium tellurate, while chloride ions form HCl in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, room temperature to mild heating, stirring; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Oxidative homocoupling of a diazonium salt (diazo). 4‑Nitroaniline is converted in situ to its diazonium chloride with HCl/NaNO2 at 0–5 °C; CuCl acts as a catalytic oxidant, promoting loss of N₂ and formation of a C‑C bond between two aryl radicals, yielding 4,4′‑dinitrobiphenyl. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium, low temperature for diazotization, then gentle warming; catalyst CuCl (often 0.1 equiv). No special solvent beyond water is required.

Carbonation‑hydrolysis reaction; sodium aluminate reacts with CO2 (bubbled) in water, converting to soluble sodium carbonate and precipitating aluminum hydroxide; typical of the Bayer process, performed in aqueous slurry at 50–80 °C under CO2 pressure; no catalyst, water is the solvent.

Hydrogen‑halide cleavage of an ether (hydrohalogenation). Hydrogen bromide protonates diethyl ether, followed by nucleophilic attack of Br⁻ on the more substituted carbon, yielding ethanol and bromoethane. Typically carried out with excess HBr gas or aqueous HBr, refluxing the mixture (≈80 °C). Common solvents include glacial acetic acid or a mixture of HBr and ether; no additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr). Ammonia displaces the bromine on 1‑bromo‑2,4‑dichlorobenzene, which is activated toward substitution by the two ortho/para chloro groups. The reaction produces 2,4‑dichloroaniline and HBr. Common conditions: excess NH₃ (gas or aqueous) refluxed in ethanol or water, often in a sealed tube; no catalyst needed. Reaction is typically carried out at 80–120 °C.

Williamson ether synthesis (alkylation of a secondary alcohol). Dihydroartemisinin’s hydroxyl group is deprotonated by NaOH and then methylated with methyl iodide to give artemether (the 10‑O‑methyl ether). Typical conditions: aprotic polar solvent such as acetone or DMF, NaOH (1–2 equiv), methyl iodide (1.1‑1.5 equiv), reflux 1–3 h under inert atmosphere. Reaction proceeds by SN2 displacement.

Jones oxidation (primary alcohol to carboxylic acid): 2‑methyl‑1‑butanol is oxidized with Jones reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄ in acetone) at 0 °C to rt. The reaction proceeds through the aldehyde and over‑oxidizes to give 2‑methylbutanoic acid; water is released.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification. Ethanol attacks the carbonyl of pentyl formate, displacing the pentyl alkoxy group, which then abstracts a proton to give pentanol; the ethoxy group remains on the carbonyl, forming ethyl formate. Reaction is usually catalyzed by a strong base (NaOEt or NaOH) or an acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄) in a solvent‑free or refluxing alcohol medium at 60–100 °C. Removal of one product (e.g., by distillation) drives the equilibrium to completion.

Carbothermic reduction; purpose is to produce manganese metal from its oxide; manganese(II) oxide reacts with carbon (often coke) to yield manganese and carbon monoxide; performed at very high temperature (≈ 1200 °C) in a furnace or electric arc furnace; solid‑phase, no solvent.

Solid‑state ceramic synthesis of lead zirconate titanate (PZT) via mixed‑metal nitrate route. Glycine is often used as a fuel/complexing agent; aqueous solutions of lead nitrate, zirconium nitrate, and titanium nitrate are mixed, gelled (often with glycine‑fuel combustion), dried, and then calcined at 800–1000 °C in air to yield the perovskite PZT powder. No liquid catalyst is required beyond water for mixing; high‑temperature solid‑state reaction furnishes the ferroelectric ceramic.

Acid leaching/dissolution of chrysotile asbestos (Mg₃Si₂O₅(OH)₄) with concentrated H₂SO₄. The mineral reacts with three equivalents of sulfuric acid, forming soluble magnesium sulfate, silicic acid (Si(OH)₄), and water. Conditions: excess hot, concentrated H₂SO₄ (typically 90 % w/w), temperature 150–200 °C, reflux for several hours. Reaction proceeds in aqueous medium; no additional catalyst is required.

Synthesis (fluorination) – conversion of silica to ammonium hexafluorosilicate. Fluoride ions from ammonium fluoride attack SiO2, forming the SiF6^2‑ complex and releasing ammonia and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution with excess NH4F, heated under reflux; the product precipitates upon cooling and is isolated by filtration.

Direct combination (redox synthesis) – oxidation of elemental mercury by chlorine gas to give mercuric chloride. Mercury is oxidized from 0 to +2 oxidation state while Cl2 is reduced to chloride. The reaction proceeds at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature in a dry, inert atmosphere; no solvent is required, but it is often performed in a sealed vessel to contain the corrosive HgCl2 vapors.

Thermal dehydration (pyrolysis) of acetic acid to give ketene; used industrially to generate ketene gas. Key transformation is loss of water (‑H2O) from the carboxylic acid, forming the C=C=O moiety. Conducted at 650–750 °C, often under reduced pressure and in the presence of solid acid catalysts (e.g., silica, alumina, CuO). No solvent is used.

Thermal decomposition – heating lithium nitrate causes it to break down into lithium oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. The nitrate anion oxidizes its own nitrogen, releasing NO2 gas, while the lithium forms the oxide. Usually performed in a high‑temperature furnace (≈500–600 °C) under an inert or air atmosphere; the gaseous products are vented and Li2O remains as a solid residue.

Acid dissolution of yttrium phosphate; concentrated hydrochloric acid attacks the insoluble phosphate, converting it back to soluble yttrium chloride and regenerating phosphoric acid in solution. Typically performed with 6–12 M HCl under reflux (80–100 °C) until the solid fully dissolves; the resulting solution can be used for further chloride chemistry.

Acid‑base dissolution of a metal oxide; rhodium(III) oxide reacts with aqueous hydrogen bromide to form rhodium(III) bromide and water. Oxide is protonated, releasing H₂O and producing Rh³⁺ which complexes with Br⁻. Usually performed by refluxing Rh₂O₃ in concentrated HBr solution.

Pictet‑Spengler cyclization (condensation of an amine with an aldehyde followed by intramolecular electrophilic aromatic substitution); phenethylamine reacts with acetaldehyde to form an iminium ion that cyclizes onto the aromatic ring, producing 1‑methyl‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroisoquinoline; typically run in an acidic medium (e.g., acetic acid, trifluoroacetic acid) in methanol, ethanol or water, at reflux or ambient temperature.

Acylation (esterification) of the allylic alcohol 3‑methyl‑2‑buten‑1‑ol with acetic anhydride to produce 3‑methyl‑2‑butenyl acetate and one equivalent of acetic acid; typical conditions use a catalytic amount of pyridine or DMAP as base, solvent dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂) or THF, 0 °C to rt; reaction is usually performed under anhydrous conditions.

This is an acid-base reaction where gadolinium phosphide reacts with hydrochloric acid. The reaction produces phosphine gas and gadolinium chloride in an aqueous solution. Hydrochloric acid acts as the proton source, facilitating the liberation of phosphine. The reaction typically occurs under ambient conditions with no specialized catalyst required. Water serves as the solvent.

Weak‑acid peroxide hydrolysis; generates H2O2 and calcium acetate; O2^2‑ is protonated by acetic acid, Ca2+ forms Ca(CH3COO)2; reaction carried out in water/acetone mixture with excess acetic acid, often refluxed gently to aid dissolution; water (or aqueous acetic acid) solvent, no catalyst.

Acid–base (acid hydrolysis) – lanthanum nitride reacts with nitric acid to form lanthanum nitrate and ammonia. The nitride ion is protonated, releasing NH3, while La³⁺ is coordinated by nitrate anions. Performed in aqueous solution, typically with dilute HNO3 at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; the resulting La(NO3)3 remains dissolved and can be crystallized by evaporation.

Hydrolysis reaction of germanium tetrabromide with water, producing germanium dioxide and hydrobromic acid; performed by mixing GeBr₄ with water under reflux conditions, with aqueous solution as the medium; no catalyst is required.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed). Methyl formate reacts with water under reflux in the presence of a catalytic amount of dilute mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOH). The C‑O bond is cleaved to give formic acid and methanol. Typically performed in aqueous solution at 80–100 °C.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges cations between calcium nitrate and potassium ferrocyanide to form sparingly soluble calcium ferrocyanide (precipitate) and soluble potassium nitrate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Oxidation – hydrogen peroxide oxidizes azepane (a cyclic secondary amine) to azepan‑2‑one, a lactam. The peroxide transfers an oxygen atom to the nitrogen‑adjacent carbon, effecting a net insertion of O and forming the amide carbonyl while reducing H2O2 to water. Commonly carried out in aqueous or mixed organic solvent (e.g., MeCN/H2O) with a metal catalyst such as tungstate, molybdate, or a peracid‑generating system, at 0 °C to room temperature; excess H2O2 is removed by aqueous work‑up.

Reaction type: selective oxidation of a thioether to a sulfoxide; purpose: functional‑group oxidation to increase polarity or serve as a synthetic intermediate; key transformation: hydrogen peroxide delivers an oxygen atom to the sulfur of allyl phenyl sulfide, forming allyl phenyl sulfoxide and water; typical conditions: aqueous or dilute H2O2 (30 %) in a polar aprotic solvent (MeCN, acetone) at 0–25 °C, sometimes with a catalytic amount of a transition‑metal (e.g., Na2WO4, Ti‑icalite) to enhance rate.

SNAr substitution; converts an aryl chloride to an aryl ether. Nucleophilic attack of methoxide on the 4‑position of 4‑chloropyridine displaces chloride to give 4‑methoxides and NaCl. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or MeCN) at reflux temperatures (80‑120 °C). No catalyst required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of 2‑piperidone with methyl iodide; introduces a methyl group on the lactam nitrogen to give N‑methyl‑2‑piperone. Typically carried out with a mild base (e.g., K2CO3 or NaH) in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or acetone at 0 °C to reflux; the reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of the deprotonated lactam nitrogen on the methyl iodide.

Palladium‑catalyzed Buchwald‑Hartwig C‑N cross‑coupling of anthranilic acid with iodobenzene using Pd(OAc)2, PPh3 and Cs2CO3 as base. Forms N‑phenylanthranilic acid by coupling the amino group to the aryl halide. Common conditions: reflux in toluene or dioxane, 80–120 °C, inert atmosphere; cesium carbonate neutralizes the HCl generated and promotes deprotonation of the amine.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between barium oxalate and ammonium carbonate in aqueous solution. Barium carbonate, an insoluble solid, precipitates while ammonium oxalate remains dissolved. Typically performed at room temperature in water with vigorous stirring; the solid BaCO3 is filtered off.

Hydrolysis of a methyl cyanoacetate ester to cyanoacetic acid; water attacks the carbonyl of methyl 2‑cyanoacetate, yielding cyanoacetic acid and methanol; performed under acidic or basic aqueous conditions (e.g., 1 M HCl or NaOH) with heating (reflux); water is the solvent, acid/base serves as catalyst.

SN2 alkylation of dimethylamine with ethyl triflate to afford N,N‑dimethylethylamine. The strong electrophilic ethyl triflate transfers an ethyl group to the nitrogen, generating trifluoromethanesulfonic acid as a by‑product. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at low temperature (0–25 °C); the reaction may be assisted by a non‑nucleophilic base to scavenge the TfOH.

Acid-base neutralization. Purpose: Deprotonation and isolation of free amine. Transformation: Sodium hydroxide deprotonates 1-phenylpropan-2-amine hydrochloride, releasing the amine. Conditions: Typically at low temperature. Solvent: Water or aqueous alcohol.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt hydrolysis) of piperidine·HCl with sodium hydroxide. Hydroxide deprotonates the ammonium salt, liberating free piperidine, water, and forming NaCl. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring ensures complete conversion.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction of trisodium citrate with aluminum chloride in water, producing aluminum citrate complex and three equivalents of NaCl. The metal‑citrate complex may precipitate or stay in solution depending on pH and concentration. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, mild heating if necessary, and removal of NaCl by crystallization or filtration.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to produce insoluble lead(II) fluoride for isolation or removal; aqueous solution of lead(II) nitrate mixed with sodium fluoride, lead fluoride precipitates while sodium nitrate stays dissolved; performed at room temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed). Allyltrimethylsilane is activated by BF₃·OEt₂ to generate an electrophilic allyl species that attacks the electron‑rich 1,2,3‑trimethoxybenzene ring, installing an allyl substituent to yield elemicin. Typically performed in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN) alkylation of imidazole. The nitrogen of imidazole attacks ethyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming the quaternary 1‑ethylimidazolium chloride salt. Commonly carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or DMF, often refluxed for several hours; no additional catalyst is required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of nitazoxanide; purpose to generate the active metabolite tizoxanide; key transformation: nitazoxanide + NaOH → tizoxanide + NaOAc (sodium acetate) + H₂O; performed in aqueous NaOH (often 0.5‑1 M) at room temperature or mild reflux, sometimes with a co‑solvent such as ethanol; NaOH provides the catalytic base, no other catalyst required.

Oxidative cleavage (ozonolysis) of an alkene. Ozone adds across the C=C bond of vinyl acetate to form a molozonide that fragments, yielding acetic acid from the acetate‑bearing carbon and formaldehyde from the vinyl carbon. Conducted at ‑78 °C to 0 °C in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane, with a reductive work‑up (e.g., Me₂S) or oxidative work‑up (H₂O₂) to isolate the carbonyl products.

Base‑promoted elimination (E2) of 1,1,2‑tribromoethane with sodium ethoxide; ethoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen, generating 1,1,2‑tribromoethene while the liberated bromide forms NaBr and the ethoxide is protonated to give ethanol. Typically carried out in ethanol solvent at reflux temperatures; NaOEt serves both base and nucleophile.

Oxidative conversion of a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon to a quinone. Potassium permanganate in alkaline aqueous medium oxidizes the benzylic positions of acenaphthene, inserting two carbonyl groups to give acaphthene‑1,2‑quinone. Typical conditions involve KMnO₄ (excess), NaOH, and heating under reflux (often in acetone‑water) for several hours, followed by filtration of MnO₂ precipitate and acidification to isolate the quinone.

Acid‑catalyzed etherification (condensation) of two alcohols; a mixed secondary/tertiary ether is formed by dehydration. Typically carried out with concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH as catalyst at 120–150 °C, using excess of one alcohol as solvent and removing water azeotropically to drive the equilibrium toward isopropyl tert‑butyl ether.

Metathesis/precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction between oxalic acid and thulium(III) acetate. Oxalic acid replaces acetate, yielding insoluble thulium(III) oxalate as a precipitate and liberating acetic acid into solution. Conducted in aqueous medium, often at room temperature or with gentle heating; the solid thulium oxalate is filtered and washed. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of calcium carbonate with permanganic acid. The carbonate is protonated to carbonic acid, which decomposes to CO₂ + H₂O, while the permanganate anion pairs with Ca²⁺ to form calcium permanganate salt. Performed in aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C to control the vigorous oxidation nature of permanganic acid; the CO₂ gas evolves and the calcium permanganate remains dissolved oritates depending on concentration. No catalyst needed, but protective measures for the strong oxidizer are essential.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 3‑chloropropionitrile by ammonia. Ammonia attacks the primary alkyl chloride, displacing chloride to give 3‑aminopropionitrile; the chloride combines with a second equivalent of ammonia to form ammonium chloride. Usually carried out in excess aqueous or alcoholic ammonia at reflux (≈80 °C) to ensure complete conversion; the by‑product ammonium chloride precipitates out and can be filtered. No additional catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction between oxalic acid and uranyl acetate. Oxalic acid exchanges ligands with the uranyl cation, producing sparingly soluble uranyl oxalate and releasing acetic acid into the solution. Conducted in water, often with gentle heating to dissolve the reactants; the uranyl oxalate precipitates and is collected by filtration. No catalyst is employed.

Acid‑base neutralization of butyric acid with calcium oxide. Two equivalents of the carboxylic acid react with the basic oxide to form calcium butanoate (calcium butyrate) and water. Typically performed by heating the mixture at 100–120 °C to melt the acid and allow solid CaO to react completely, yielding a dry calcium salt after removal of water. No solvent or catalyst is required.

Suzuki‑Miyaura acylative cross‑coupling; used to construct a diaryl ketone. Palladium(0) generated from Pd(OAc)₂/PPh₃ oxidatively adds into the C–Cl bond of 4‑fluorobenzoyl chloride, forming an acyl‑Pd(II) species. Transmetalation with 4‑fluorophenylboronic acid (base‑activated by K₂CO₃) transfers the aryl group to palladium, and reductive elimination furnishes 4,4‑difluorobenzophenone. Typical conditions: anhydrous DMF or dioxane/water (≈5 % water), K₂CO₃ (2 equiv), Pd(OAc)₂ (2–5 mol %), PPh₃ (4–10 mol %), 80–120 °C under nitrogen or argon.

Formylation of hydroxylamine with formic anhydride; acylation gives formylhydroxylamine and releases formic acid. Reaction is carried out in an inert organic solvent such as ether or dichloromethane at low temperature (0–25 °C) under anhydrous conditions; a mild base (e.g., pyridine) may be employed to neutralize the generated formic acid. Used to introduce a formyl protecting group on hydroxylamine.

Acidolysis (hydrolysis) of tetrabutyltin with hydrochloric acid. One butyl group is protonated and eliminated as n‑butanol, while the tin center is converted to tributyltin chloride. Usually carried out by stirring tetrabutyltin in concentrated HCl (aq) at reflux (60‑80 °C); organic solvents such as dichloromethane may be used to aid phase separation.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between a barium salt and a lithium sulfide; purpose is to prepare insoluble barium sulfide and soluble lithium chloride. The reaction proceeds in aqueous or polar organic medium; often performed at ambient temperature with stirring. No catalyst required; product BaS can be isolated by filtration and washing.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using phosphorus pentachloride; a standard acid‑chloride formation. PCl₅ reacts with cyclopropanecarboxylic acid, replacing the –OH by –Cl while generating POCl₃ and HCl as by‑products. Typical procedure: dissolve the acid in dry dichloromethane or chloroform, cool to 0 °C, add PCl₅ (1.2 equiv) slowly, then stir at room temperature (0–25 °C) for 1–2 h. No catalyst needed; work‑up involves quenching excess reagent with ice‑water and extraction.

Nucleophilic substitution (allylic SN2′) of an allylic bromide with acetate ion to give an allylic acetate. Sodium acetate provides the acetate nucleophile, which attacks the allylic carbon, displacing bromide as NaBr. Reaction is usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF, or MeCN at reflux or 50–80 °C. No catalyst required; the product can be isolated after aqueous work‑up and purification.

Solid‑state metathesis/oxide exchange reaction; purpose is to obtain tin(IV) oxide and sodium sulfate from tin(IV) sulfate and sodium oxide; key transformation involves oxide anion from Na₂O swapping with sulfate on tin, yielding SnO₂ solid and Na₂SO₄; performed by high‑temperature fusion (≈500‑700 °C) of the reagents; no solvent or catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an allylic alcohol. 3‑Hexen‑1‑ol is reduced in the presence of palladium on carbon (10 wt % Pd/C) under hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) to saturate the C=C bond, yielding 1‑hexanol while leaving the primary alcohol unchanged.
