Typical conditions: solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, room temperature to 50 °C, stirring under a H₂ atmosphere. The catalyst is filtered off after completion.

Reaction type: nitrosation/esterification of an alcohol with nitrous acid to form an alkyl nitrite. Purpose: synthesis of isoamyl nitrite, a volatile nitrite ester used as a reagent or fragrance. Key transformation: conversion of the –OH group of isoamyl alcohol into a –ONO group, releasing water. Typical conditions: nitrous acid generated in situ from sodium nitrite and a strong acid (e.g., HCl) at 0‑5 °C; the reaction is performed in an ice‑bath aqueous medium, often with the alcohol added dropwise. No special catalyst is required; dilute acidic aqueous solution serves as both solvent and catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization; converts insoluble cadmium hydroxide to soluble cadmium sulfate; hydroxide ions are protonated to water while sulfate anion replaces hydroxide; generally carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Reductive amination of glycolaldehyde with ammonia using sodium cyanoborohydride; the aldehyde condenses with ammonia to form an imine/iminium intermediate that is reduced by NaBH₃CN to give 2‑aminoacetaldehyde. Conducted in methanol or ethanol under mildly acidic (pH 5‑6) conditions at 0 °C to room temperature; NaBH₃CN is the selective reducing agent.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) of hydrogen chloride to an allene; HCl adds across the C=C=C system giving the allylic chloride 3‑chloro‑1‑propene. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) using gaseous or aqueous HCl; no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of a tetraalkyltin compound; water attacks the Sn–C bonds of tetraethyl tin, cleaving them to form ethanol and precipitating tin(IV) oxide. Conducted by stirring the organotin in excess water or aqueous medium, often at reflux; acidic or neutral conditions are common; no special catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation) of pyrazine with chlorine; chlorine substitutes a hydrogen on the aromatic ring to give 2‑chloropyrazine while generating hydrogen chloride as a by‑product. Usually carried out in a non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) with a Lewis‑acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ or under UV irradiation to promote radical chlorination.

Thermal decomposition (redox) of barium bromate; upon heating the solid decomposes to barium bromide and releases oxygen gas (3 O₂ per mole of Ba(BrO₃)₂). Performed by heating the bromate in a sealed tube or furnace at 200–300 °C; no catalyst required, and the reaction is driven by the favorable formation of O₂ and BaBr₂.

High‑temperature redox reduction of silica by carbon monoxide; CO reduces SiO₂ to silicon monoxide while being oxidized to CO₂. Conducted in a flow reactor at 1400–1600 °C under a stream of CO (often diluted with inert gas); solid silica is contacted with the gas phase; no catalyst is normally required, though a slight excess of CO ensures complete reduction.

Reduction of an amide to a primary amine using lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH₄ transfers hydride to the carbonyl of N‑methylpropanamide, converting it into N‑methylpropylamine with loss of the carbonyl oxygen as Al‑O species. Performed in dry ether or THF under anhydrous conditions, typically at 0 °C during addition followed by reflux; the reaction is quenched with cautious addition of water or a protic work‑up.

Redox oxidation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes manganese carbonate yielding manganese dioxide, carbon dioxide and water. Occurs in aqueous medium, often at room temperature or mild heating; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of anthracene; purpose is partial reduction of the central double bond to give 9,10‑dihydroanthracene; hydrogen gas adds across the 9,10‑positions in the presence of palladium on carbon; typically carried out in a protic solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at ambient temperature and 1 atm H₂; reaction time varies until desired conversion is achieved.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of formaldehyde; ozone reacts with the aldehyde to give formic acid and molecular oxygen. Typically performed in a low‑temperature inert solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, with ozone bubbled through the solution under darkness; work‑up may involve quenching with a reductant.

This acid-base reaction between potassium sulfite and hydrochloric acid produces potassium chloride and sulfurous acid. Key transformations involve protonation of sulfite ions. Conducted in aqueous solution under standard conditions, with sulfurous acid potentially decomposing into sulfur dioxide and water.
Simple acid–base salt formation; benzamidine is protonated by hydrochloric acid to afford benzamidine hydrochloride. Typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution at ambient temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic hydration of cyclooctene; water adds across the double bond to give cyclooctanol (Markovnikov addition). Conducted in aqueous acid (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄) or via oxymercuration‑demercuration (Hg(OAc)₂/H₂O, followed by NaBH₄) at 0–50 °C.

Swern oxidation; dimethyl sulfoxide activated by oxalyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine oxidizes cyclodecanol to cyclodecanone. Reaction is carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C, with oxalyl chloride added first, then the alcohol, and finally TEA to quench the intermediate. By‑products are dimethyl sulfide, CO and CO₂.

Acid–base salt metathesis; the strong base KOH deprotonates the ethylammonium cation, liberating free ethylamine and forming potassium acetate and water. Typically carried out in aqueous or mixed water‑ethanol solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no special catalyst is required.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate; the aldehyde is converted to the corresponding acid while MnO₄⁻ is reduced to insoluble manganese dioxide, with water formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions involve an aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH or K₂CO₃) at room temperature to reflux, with KMnO₄ added portionwise to control the reaction rate; the precipitated MnO₂ is filtered off after completion.

Radical dehalogenation (tributyltin hydride reduction); tributyltin hydride, initiated by azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN), abstracts the bromine from 4‑bromo‑1‑butene, yielding 1‑butene and Bu₃SnBr. Typically run in refluxing toluene or benzene under nitrogen, with AIBN (≈10 mol %) as radical initiator.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (ester cleavage); water hydrolyzes 3‑ethylpentan‑3‑yl acetate to give 3‑ethylpentan‑3‑ol and acetic acid. Performed in aqueous acid (e.g., dilute HCl) or under mild heating (50–80 °C); solvent may be a mixture of water and an organic co‑solvent such as THF.
Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); aqueous rubidium hydroxide reacts with hydrofluoric acid to give rubidium fluoride and water; carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst needed.

Intramolecular lactamization (cyclodehydration) of 5‑aminovaleric acid to form 2‑piperidone with loss of water; the amino group attacks the carboxyl carbon, creating a six‑membered cyclic amide. Usually performed by heating the amino acid neat or in a high‑boiling polar solvent (e.g., acetic anhydride, azeotropic removal of water) or with dehydrating agents such as POCl₃ or P₂O₅.

Direct amidation of dodecanoic (lauric) acid with ammonia to give dodecanamide; purpose is synthesis of a primary fatty‑chain amide; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ammonia on the carbonyl carbon of the acid followed by elimination of water; because simple acids are poor electrophiles, the reaction is usually performed under high pressure of NH₃ gas at 150‑200 °C, or by first converting the acid to the acid chloride (e.g., with SOCl₂) then treating with gaseous or aqueous NH₃; solvents such as toluene or THF may be used, and catalysts like metal oxides (Al₂O₃, MgO) can facilitate the condensation.

Acid–base neutralization of adipic acid with potassium carbonate to form potassium adipate; purpose is preparation of the potassium salt and removal of excess carbonate; key transformation is proton transfer from the di‑carboxylic acid to the carbonate anion, generating carbonic acid which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no special catalyst required; water is the reaction medium and the evolved CO₂ is vented.

Enzymatic (or chemical) aldol condensation of pyruvic acid with N‑acetyl‑D‑mannosamine to afford N‑acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac); purpose is construction of the sialic‑acid backbone; key transformation is a C‑C bond‑forming addition of the pyruvate enolate to the C‑2 carbon of the hexosamine, followed by dehydration to give the nine‑carbon α‑keto acid; typically performed in buffered aqueous solution (pH 7‑8) at 25‑37 °C using the enzyme N‑acetylneuraminic acid synthase; chemical alternatives use sodium borohydride or base (e.g., NaOH) in methanol/water, but enzymatic conditions give the highest selectivity; no organic solvent is required.

Sandmeyer‑type nucleophilic substitution; benzenediazonium chloride reacts with azide ion to give phenyl azide and NaCl. Reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C in aqueous or mixed aqueous/acetone solvent to maintain diazonium stability; dark conditions often used. No catalyst required.

Schiff‑base formation (imine condensation) between benzaldehyde and aniline to give N‑[(E)‑benzylideneamino]aniline; purpose is preparation of an imine for further functionalization; key transformation is nucleophilic addition of the aniline nitrogen to the aldehyde carbonyl, followed by loss of water; commonly carried out in ethanol or toluene under reflux with a Dean–Stark apparatus to remove water, or in methanol with a catalytic amount of p‑toluenesulfonic acid; mild acid catalysis accelerates the condensation and drives the equilibrium toward the imine.

Intramolecular dehydration to form citraconic anhydride; the dicarboxylic acid loses water and cyclizes to the five‑membered anhydride. Conducted by heating citraconic acid at 150–200 °C, often under reduced pressure or with a dehydrating agent such as P₂O₅ or acetic anhydride. Solventless or in toluene with a Dean‑Stark trap.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of 1‑hexanol with ethyl acetate to give hexyl acetate and ethanol; purpose is synthesis of a higher‑boiling ester and recovery of ethanol; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of hexanol on the carbonyl carbon of ethyl acetate, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to exchange the alkoxy groups; typical conditions use 5‑10 % NaOMe or K₂CO₃ as catalyst in excess hexanol as solvent, heated to reflux (≈78 °C) for several hours; removal of ethanol by distillation drives the reaction to completion; alternative acid catalysis (H₂SO₄) is possible but base catalysis gives faster rates and fewer side reactions.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is ion exchange to isolate cadmium as an insoluble oxalate. Alkali metal oxalate reacts with cadmium chloride in aqueous solution, exchanging anions and cations to form soluble potassium chloride and precipitate cadmium oxalate. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, stirring at room temperature; no special solvent, precipitation driven by low solubility of CdC2O4.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ketone; purpose is selective reduction of the C=C double bond while preserving the carbonyl group. 1‑Phenylbut‑3‑en‑2‑one is exposed to H2 gas in the presence of palladium on carbon (Pd/C) catalyst, converting the alkene to the saturated ketone 1‑phenylbutan‑2‑one. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol, ethyl acetate or THF; temperature from 25 °C to 50 °C; reaction time 1–4 h.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) thioether formation, analogous to the Williamson ether synthesis; purpose is synthesis of a symmetrical dialkyl sulfide. 2‑Methylpropane‑1‑thiol is deprotonated by a base (e.g., NaOH, K2CO3, or pyridine) to give the isobutyl thiolate, which attacks 2‑methylpropyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming diisobutyl sulfide with generation of HCl (neutralized by the base). Typical conditions: aprotic polar solvent such as acetone or DMF, ambient to reflux temperature, stoichiometric or slight excess base, 2–6 h reaction time.

Acyl chloride esterification of a polyol (tri‑ester formation); purpose is preparation of a triglyceride (glyceryl tridecanoate). Each hydroxyl of glycerol attacks a molecule of decanoyl chloride, forming an ester bond and releasing HCl. The reaction is usually carried out in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or chloroform) with a stoichiometric base (triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge the liberated HCl and prevent polymerization. Conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N2), slow addition of acyl chloride, reaction completion within 1–2 h.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); the carboxylic acid of L‑malic acid is deprotonated by NaOH to give the sodium L‑malate salt and water. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is to exchange anions and precipitate the low‑solubility salt strontium sulfate. In aqueous solution, sodium sulfate reacts with strontium chromate, producing soluble sodium chromate and insoluble strontium sulfate, which precipitates out. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, mild heating or stirring to enhance mixing, filtration to isolate SrSO4; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of an internal alkyne (Markovnikov addition) using mercuric ion catalysis; purpose is conversion of 3‑hexyne to the corresponding ketone (3‑hexanone). Mercuric sulfate (HgSO4) in dilute sulfuric acid generates Hg²⁺, which adds to the alkyne to form a vinyl mercury intermediate; water then attacks, and after protodemetallation and tautomerization the enol converts to the ketone. Typical conditions: aqueous H2SO4 (≈ 5–10 % w/w), catalytic HgSO4 (0.1–0.5 % mol), reflux temperature (80–100 °C), reaction time 1–3 h; product extracted with an organic solvent such as ether.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis) of an alkali metal with a metalloid; forms sodium arsenide (commonly Na₃As) by reacting elemental sodium with elemental arsenic; performed by mixing the powders and heating at 500–700 °C in an inert (argon) atmosphere to prevent oxidation; no solvent, no catalyst.

Cyclocondensation to a heterocycle; chlorosulfonic acid sulfonates ortho‑phenylenediamine and promotes intramolecular N‑S‑N ring closure to give 1,2,4‑benzothiadiazine‑1,1‑dioxide (the sulfonyl‑dioxide heterocycle) with loss of HCl. The transformation is carried out neat or in a non‑coordinating solvent, typically by heating the mixture to 80–120 °C.

Negishi cross‑coupling (palladium‑catalyzed C‑C bond formation); forms a C‑ethyl bond on a 2‑iodo‑imidazole using diethylzinc; purpose is to synthesize 2‑ethyl‑1H‑imidazole; typical conditions: PdCl2 (often generated in situ from PdCl2/phosphine ligand such as PPh3) in anhydrous THF under nitrogen, 0–80 °C, stoichiometric ZnEt2, inert atmosphere; ZnI2 is generated as a by‑product.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ester (vinyl propanoate) to the saturated ethyl propanoate; purpose is to reduce the C=C double bond while leaving the ester intact; typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni) in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, ambient to moderate temperature.

Type: catalytic hydrogenation (reductiveolysis) of a ketone. Purpose: reduce acetophenone to 1‑phenylethanol. Key transformation: H2 adds across the C=O bond on the surface of Pd/C, delivering two hydrogen atoms to give the alcohol. Typical conditions: acetophenone dissolved in ethanol (or methanol), 5–10 wt % Pd/C, H2 pressure 1–5 atm, temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time 2–6 h, followed by filtration of the catalyst and solvent removal.

Swern oxidation of a primary allylic alcohol; oxalyl chloride activates DMSO to form the chlorodimethyl‑sulfonium intermediate, which oxidizes trans‑3‑hexen‑1‑ol to the corresponding aldehyde (trans‑3‑hexenal). Conducted at –78 °C in dry dichloromethane, followed by addition of triethylamine to quench the reaction.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); aqueous medium; Dysprosium(III) sulfate solution is treated with sodium hydroxide, precipitating dysprosium(III) hydroxide while sodium sulfate remains soluble; performed by adding excess NaOH to a Dy2(SO4)3 solution at ambient temperature, maintaining pH ≈10; the solid Dy(OH)3 is filtered and washed; no catalyst needed.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 displacement) of octyl methanesulfonate by potassium methoxide to give octyl methyl ether; purpose is to form an ether from a primary alkyl sulfonate; typical conditions: aprotic polar solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetone), excess KOCH₃, mild heating (40–80 °C) under inert atmosphere; potassium methanesulfonate is the leaving‑group salt.

Acid–base/ gas‑evolution reaction; purpose: generate carbonate precipitate and evolve CO2; key transformation: SrCl2 reacts with two equivalents of NaHCO3 to form solid SrCO3, NaCl, water and carbon dioxide gas; typical conditions: aqueous solution, gentle heating to drive off CO2; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution of a tertiary alcohol with hydroiodic acid (HI) to give 2‑iodo‑2‑methylheptane and water; an SN1‑type iodination/dehydration. Typically performed by heating the alcohol in excess 48 % HI (or refluxing HI/ether) at 80–100 °C, allowing carbocation formation followed by capture by iodide, producing the alkyl iodide in good yield.

Catalytic partial oxidation of ethylene to acetaldehyde (ethanal); ethylene reacts with molecular oxygen in the presence of a palladium(II)/copper(II) chloride redox system (Wacker‑type conditions) to give CH₃CHO and water. Conducted in aqueous acetone or water at 40‑60 °C under a stream of O₂ or air, with PdCl₂/CuCl₂ as the catalyst pair.

Halide metathesis (salt exchange) converting iridium(III) chloride to iridium(III) bromide using hydrogen bromide; purpose is preparation of IrBr₃; typical conditions: aqueous solution of IrCl₃ treated with excess HBr, reflux or gentle heating, followed by removal of HCl gas or aqueous work‑up; no special catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aldehyde (2‑ethoxypropanal) to the corresponding carboxylic acid (2‑ethoxypropionic acid) using potassium permanganate; purpose is functional‑group oxidation; typical conditions: alkaline aqueous medium, KMnO₄ (often 1–2 equiv), heating to reflux, then acidic work‑up; MnO₂ precipitates as solid by‑product, water is also formed.

Type: catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation). Purpose: replace the chlorine atom with hydrogen to afford 1,1-difluoroethane. Key transformation: C–Cl bond is reduced by H₂, generating HCl as by‑product. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over a Pd/C or Raney Ni catalyst, in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, at 25–80 °C.

Transesterification; used to synthesize the sunscreen agent homosalate. The hydroxyl of 3,3,5‑trimethylcyclohexanol attacks the carbonyl of ethyl salicylate, displacing ethanol and forming the ester homosalate. Typically performed with an acid catalyst (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a solid acid resin, at 80–120 °C under reflux; removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium. Solvent may be toluene or the reaction can be run neat; inert atmosphere is optional.

Enzymatic O‑methyltransfer; biological conversion of the isoflavone genistein to biochanin A. The methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) is transferred to the phenolic hydroxyl of genistein, producing S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine (SAH) and the 4′‑O‑methylated product biochanin A. Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 25–37 °C with the appropriate plant or recombinant 4′‑O‑methyltransferase, often requiring Mg²⁺ or other divalent cations; no organic solvent is needed.

Intramolecular Friedel‑Crafts acylation (cyclization) of phenylacetyl chloride to give 1H‑inden‑1‑one. Aluminum chloride acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst, forming the acylium ion from phenylacetyl chloride, which then electrophilically attacks the ortho position of the aromatic ring, followed by ring closure and loss of HCl. Usually carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane, chloroform or carbon disulfide at 0 °C to reflux (≈ 40–80 °C). Reaction is moisture‑sensitive; AlCl₃ is used in stoichiometric or slight excess amounts.

Metal‑acid reduction of aromatic nitro groups to amines (Zn/HCl reduction). Zinc dust reduces the two nitro substituents of 4,4′‑dinitrodiphenyl ether to the corresponding amines in the presence of concentrated hydrochloric acid, yielding 4,4′‑diaminodiphenyl ether and zinc chloride by‑products. The mixture is heated under reflux (≈ 80–100 °C) in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol media; after completion the solid product is filtered, washed, and neutralized if desired.

Direct fluorination of strontium silicide (e.g., SrSi₂) to generate silicon tetrafluoride and strontium fluoride. Fluorine gas reacts vigorously with the silicide at elevated temperatures (300–600 °C) in a nickel or quartz reaction vessel, effecting oxidation of silicon to SiF₄ (volatile) and formation of solid SrF₂. No solvent is used; the reaction is conducted under inert gas flow with strict safety controls due to the corrosive and toxic nature of F₂.

Acid‑base salt formation (hydrochloride formation). Proadifen, a basic amine, is treated with hydrochloric acid (aqueous or gaseous) to protonate the nitrogen and produce proadifen hydrochloride as a crystalline solid. Typically performed by dissolving proadifen in a polar aprotic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, adding one equivalent of HCl at 0–25 °C, stirring until precipitation occurs, then isolating the salt by filtration and drying. No additional catalysts are required.

Fischer esterification of L‑phenylalanine; the carboxyl group is converted to a methyl ester while the amino group remains protonated; carried out in methanol with catalytic H₂SO₄ under reflux; purpose is to protect the acid functionality; common solvent is methanol.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation / O‑acylation; acetyl chloride reacts with naphthol in the presence of AlCl₃ to form naphthyl acetate and HCl; typical conditions are anhydrous, inert atmosphere, low temperature (0 °C) to reflux in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon disulfide; AlCl₃ acts as Lewis‑acid catalyst.

Thermal radical decomposition and dimerization; benzoyl peroxide thermally decomposes to phenyl radicals, which lose CO₂ and couple to give biphenyl; usually performed by heating the peroxide neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., benzene) without added catalyst; the only by‑product is carbon dioxide.

Reductive amination; 4‑methyl‑2‑pentanone reacts with methylamine to form an imine intermediate that is hydrogenated over Pd/C to give 1,3‑dimethylamylamine; commonly carried out in methanol or ethanol, under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–50 °C; Pd on carbon serves as the hydrogenation catalyst.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization); converts tetrafluoroboric acid and potassium silicate into the soluble salt potassium tetrafluoroborate and silicic acid; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required, water serves as solvent.

Acid‑base precipitation (acid decomposition of stannate); aqueous HCl protonates sodium stannate, leading to precipitation of tin(IV) oxide (SnO₂) and formation of NaCl and water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no special catalyst required.

Radical thiol‑ene addition; employed to form thioethers by adding a thiol across an alkene. A radical initiator (e.g., AIBN or UV light) abstracts a hydrogen from butyl mercaptan, generating a thiyl radical that adds to ethylene, followed by hydrogen abstraction to give ethyl butyl sulfide. Commonly performed in an inert solvent such as THF, toluene, or dichloromethane at room temperature under nitrogen.

Silylation of a carboxylic acid; trimethylsilyl trifluoromethanesulfonate (TMSOTf) transfers the TMS group to acetic acid, producing trimethylsilyl acetate and trifluoromethanesulfonic acid; typically run anhydrous in dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; TMSOTf acts as the silyl‑transfer reagent.

Base‑catalyzed ester saponification; lithium hydroxide hydrolyzes ethyl succinate to lithium succinate, releasing ethanol as the by‑product; carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑alcoholic medium, often refluxed; LiOH provides the basic conditions, no additional catalyst needed.

Double (metathesis) reaction; used to exchange anions and generate iron(III) chloride solution. Aqueous solutions of barium chloride and iron(III) nitrate are mixed at ambient temperature; the ions swap to give soluble iron(III) chloride and barium nitrate. No special catalyst; simple stirring in water suffices.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis (ceramic route) of lithium titanium oxide from lithium carbonate and titanium dioxide with release of carbon dioxide; powders are intimately mixed and calcined at ~800–1000 °C in air; no solvent or catalyst required (optional flux).

Oxidative hydroxylation of an aromatic hydrocarbon; converts toluene into 3‑methylphenol (cresol) with water as by‑product. Typically carried out with gaseous O₂ (or air) over a metal oxide catalyst such as V₂O₅, Cu‑Zn‑Al, or TiO₂ at 300–400 °C under pressure. Reaction performed in the liquid phase; solvent is often the substrate itself (toluene) or an inert hydrocarbon diluent.

Reduction of a pyridine N‑oxide to the parent pyridine; zinc dust serves as the reductant in acetic acid, which also provides the acidic medium. Reaction is a redox deoxygenation, usually conducted by refluxing the N‑oxide with excess Zn in glacial acetic acid. No additional catalyst; the mixture is filtered to remove zinc salts, yielding 2‑ethylpyridine and zinc acetate.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution forming a hydroxamic acid; acetyl chloride reacts with hydroxylamine hydrobromide to give acetohydroxamic acid while releasing HCl and HBr. Performed at 0–25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often in the presence of a weak base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the liberated acids. Reaction is moisture‑sensitive and proceeds rapidly under cold conditions.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of an acid chloride with a primary amine; butanoyl chloride reacts with ethylamine to give N‑ethylbutanamide and HCl; usually performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with a base (triethylamine, pyridine) to scavenge the generated HCl; no metal catalyst required.

This reaction represents an N-methylation of 1-phenylpropan-2-amine using methyl iodide, producing N-methyl-1-phenylpropan-2-amine and hydrogen iodide. The amine’s nitrogen acts as a nucleophile attacking methyl iodide’s electrophilic carbon. The process is a classic S_N2 alkylation, typically conducted in an inert solvent like ethanol or water, without requiring strong catalytic systems. The reaction’s purpose is the formation of a secondary amine from a primary amine via alkylation.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) to synthesize a chelating diphosphine ligand; 1,2‑dichloroethane reacts with two equivalents of dimethylphosphine, displacing chloride ions and forming 1,2‑bis(dimethylphosphino)ethane with HCl as a by‑product. Conducted in an inert, aprotic solvent such as THF or toluene under reflux, together with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) to neutralize HCl. No metal catalyst is required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; dimethyl succinate is converted to diethyl succinate by exchange of the methyl ester groups with ethanol, using sodium methoxide as the catalyst. Reaction is run under reflux in excess ethanol, typically 60–80 °C, with catalytic amounts of NaOMe; methanol is generated as the leaving alcohol. After completion, the reaction mixture is neutralized and the diethyl succinate is isolated by distillation or extraction.

Acid–base neutralization; hydrogen cyanide reacts with cadmium oxide to form cadmium cyanide and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution, with gentle heating to promote dissolution; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed terpene isomerization; β‑pinene rearranges to camphene via a 1,2‑methyl shift and allylic isomerization. Conducted at 150–200 °C in the presence of strong solid acids (e.g., phosphoric acid on silica, zeolite) or liquid acid (H₂SO₄); reactions are performed in the liquid phase or gas‑phase flow; no special solvents beyond the acid medium.

Radical chlorination/dealkylation; tetramethylsilane reacts with chlorine to give methyl chloride and trimethyl‑chlorosilane. Initiated by heat or UV light in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; no catalyst is required, but radical initiators (e.g., benzoyl peroxide) may be used to improve rate.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between magnesium chlorate and barium chloride; the chloride and chlorate ions exchange partners to afford soluble magnesium chloride and barium chlorate. Performed in water at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds without catalyst and may be driven to completion by removal of one product if it is less soluble.

Acid‑base neutralization (ion exchange); proton transfer from phosphoric acid to the valerate anion yields free valeric acid while the ammonium cation pairs with phosphate to form ammonium phosphate; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Carbothermic reduction (high‑temperature reduction) of molybdenum trioxide to metallic molybdenum; MoO3(s) + 3 C(s) → Mo(s) + 3 CO(g); conducted in a furnace at 1000–1200 °C in an inert or reducing atmosphere; solid‑state reaction, no solvent; carbon acts as both reductant and fuel; no additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation; nickel(II) sulfate reacts with potassium chromate to form insoluble nickel(II) chromate (green precipitate) and soluble potassium sulfate. Conducted in water at room temperature or with mild heating; stirring promotes ion exchange; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: Nucleophilic addition. Purpose: Carbonate ester synthesis. Key transformation: Methoxide attacks carbon dioxide, forming a carbonate intermediate stabilized by sodium cation. Conditions: Typically conducted in anhydrous conditions (e.g., THF) under CO₂ atmosphere. No additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base dissolution (salt‑acid reaction); concentrated sulfuric acid protonates iron(III) phosphate, yielding phosphoric acid and soluble iron(III) sulfate. Carried out in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution; no catalyst needed, excess acid drives the reaction to completion.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl bromide with potassium selenide to afford diethyl selenide; the selenide anion attacks the primary carbon displacing bromide. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at reflux under inert atmosphere; potassium bromide precipitates.

Amidation (ester‑amine exchange). 3‑Aminopyridine attacks the carbonyl of nicotinic acid ethyl ester, displacing ethanol and forming N‑(3‑pyridyl)nicotinamide. Conducted by heating the reactants neat or in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or MeCN) under reflux; removal of ethanol drives the reaction forward.

Acid–base neutralization (oxide with acid). Beryllium oxide reacts with phosphoric acid to produce beryllium hydrogen phosphate (BeHPO4) and water. Typically performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to dissolve the oxide; stoichiometric H3PO4 is added slowly, no catalyst required.

SN2 alkylation of sodium methyl sulfide (CH₃S⁻) with methyl iodide; produces dimethyl sulfide (CH₃SCH₃) and NaI. Carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, THF, or DMSO at 0–25 °C; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile. Adamantane‑1‑carbonitrile is reduced with H₂ in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni, Pd/C) to give 1‑aminoadamantane. Performed in ethanol or methanol under several bar of H₂ at 25‑50 °C.

Reaction type: acetylation (esterification) of an alcohol with acetic anhydride. Cinnamyl alcohol reacts with Ac₂O to give cinnamyl acetate; a base such as pyridine or a catalytic amount of DMAP accelerates the reaction and scavenges the generated acetic acid. Performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) or neat acetic anhydride; the by‑product is acetic acid.

Selective hydride reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol. Benzaldehyde is reduced by the mild donor KBH₄, delivering a hydride to the carbonyl carbon to give benzyl alcohol; the borate by‑product forms potassium borate. Reaction is usually performed in protic solvents such as ethanol or methanol (or a mixed MeOH/THF) at 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; no catalyst needed.

Transfer hydrogenation of quinoline. Formic acid acts as a hydrogen donor; with Pd/C the quinoline ring is reduced to 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroquinoline. Typical conditions: 80‑100 °C, ethanol or acetic acid as solvent, ambient pressure.

Radical chlorination of acetone. Under UV photolysis chlorine radicals replace all six hydrogens of acetone, producing hexachloroacetone and six equivalents of HCl. Conducted in the gas phase or in a non‑reactive solvent (e.g., CCl₄) under UV light.

Aqueous metathesis between copper(II) sulfate and sodium trifluoroacetate; the sulfate and trifluoroacetate anions swap to generate copper(II) trifluoroacetate and sodium sulfate. Typically carried out in water with stirring at room temperature; the salts remain in solution, and the reaction can be isolated by evaporation or precipitation of the desired copper(II) salt.

SN2 alkylation of methoxyamine with methyl iodide; used to prepare N‑methyl‑O‑methylhydroxylamine (dimethylhydroxylamine). The nucleophilic nitrogen attacks the electrophilic carbon of MeI, displacing iodide and forming the N‑methyl bond while the oxygen remains methylated, releasing HI. Typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or DMF) at 0 °C to rt, often with a base such as triethylamine or NaHCO₃ to trap the generated HI.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis of midodrine hydrochloride; converts the prodrug into the active metabolite desglymidodrine and acetic acid. The acetyl ester of midodrine is cleaved by aqueous HCl, yielding acetic acid and the free amino‑alcohol (desglymidodrine). Common conditions: reflux in 6 M HCl or other concentrated aqueous HCl, 80–100 °C for several hours; aqueous medium is both solvent and reagent.

Thermal decomposition of unstable ammonium chlorate; upon heating it breaks down explosively into nitrogen gas, chlorine gas, oxygen gas and water; usually performed by gentle heating under controlled conditions; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of ferrocene with benzoyl chloride catalyzed by FeCl₃; furnishes benzoyl‑substituted ferrocene (benzoylferrocene). The Lewis acid activates benzoyl chloride to generate a benzoyl electrophile, which undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution on the cyclopentadienyl ring, releasing HCl. Typical protocol: anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ (or CS₂) at 0 °C → rt under nitrogen, catalytic FeCl₃ (10–20 mol %), often with a slight excess of benzoyl chloride.

Dehydrative conversion of N‑methylformamide to methyl isocyanide using POCl₃ in the presence of triethylamine; a method for isocyanide synthesis. POCl₃ activates the amide, promoting loss of water and formation of the isocyanide (CH₃‑N≡C), while triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl to give Et₃NHCl. Reaction is carried out under dry conditions in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, with excess Et₃N (≥3 eq) and POCl₃ (≈1 eq). The inorganic by‑product after work‑up is phosphoric acid.

Acidic or neutral hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution) of chloroacetonitrile; purpose is to replace the chlorine atom with a hydroxyl group to give the cyanohydrin 2‑hydroxyacetonitrile; key transformation is substitution of Cl by OH, producing HOCH2CN and HCl; performed in water, often with mild heating (60‑80 °C) and may be accelerated by acid or base catalysis; solvent is water; no metal catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition of a metal nitrate; heating holmium(III) nitrate pentahydrate above ~400 °C in a furnace in air decomposes the nitrate to holmium(III) oxide while releasing nitrogen dioxide, oxygen, and water vapor. No solvent; the reaction is performed in a dry, inert or oxidative atmosphere.

Halogen‑metal exchange followed by carboxylation: n‑BuLi reacts with 2‑chloroselenophene at low temperature (–78 °C) in THF, producing selenophene‑2‑yl lithium and n‑butyl chloride. The organolithium intermediate then adds to CO₂ to give the selenophene‑2‑carboxylate, which on acidic work‑up affords selenophene‑2‑carboxylic acid. Conditions: strictly anhydrous THF, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), –78 °C to 0 °C for the exchange, then CO₂ gas bubbled in, followed by aqueous NH₄Cl quench.

Catalytic hydrogenation of methyl 5‑nitro‑2‑hydroxybenzoate to the corresponding amino phenol using Raney nickel. The nitro group is reduced to an amine under H₂ pressure, producing methyl 5‑amino‑2‑hydroxybenzoate and water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions: Raney Ni (5–10 wt % of substrate) in ethanol or aqueous ethanol, H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, temperature 25–80 °C, stirring for several hours until completion.

Enzymatic aldose‑ketose isomerization; L‑arabinose is converted to L‑threo‑2‑pentulose by L‑arabinose isomerase; reaction performed in aqueous buffer (pH 7.5–8.5) at 50–60 °C, requiring a divalent metal cofactor such as Mn²⁺ or Co²⁺; no additional solvents or reagents are required beyond the enzyme and water.

Thermal decomposition (solid‑state) of aluminium molybdate upon heating; the salt breaks down to give metal oxides, specifically MoO3 and Al2O3. Typical conditions involve heating the solid to 500–800 °C in air or under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralisation with gas evolution: selenic acid reacts with ammonium carbonate in aqueous solution, releasing CO2 and H2O and forming ammonium selenate as the salt. The reaction is carried out at room temperature to gentle heating in water; the only reagent is the aqueous acid, no catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of thiirane (ethylene sulfide) by ethanol to give 2‑ethoxyethanethiol. Ethanol attacks the less hindered carbon of the strained three‑membered ring, breaking the C‑S bond and forming an ethoxy substituent while liberating a thiol group. The reaction is carried out in excess ethanol (or ethanol/THF mixture) at reflux (≈78 °C) or under milder conditions with a catalytic amount of base (e.g., NaH or K₂CO₃) to deprotonate ethanol. No metal catalyst is required. Product is isolated after removal of solvent and aqueous work‑up.

Acid‑catalysed amide hydrolysis: N‑(4‑methoxyphenyl)‑2‑phenylacetamide is treated with aqueous HCl (often dilute) and heated (reflux, ~80–100 °C). The amide bond is cleaved, yielding phenylacetic acid and 4‑methoxyaniline. Water serves as the solvent; the acid itself acts as the catalyst.

Selective acetylation (acylation) of propylene glycol: one hydroxyl of propylene glycol reacts with acetic anhydride, producing propylene glycol mono‑acetate and acetic acid as by‑product. The reaction is usually performed neat or in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0–50 °C, often with a base catalyst such as pyridine or DMAP to scavenge the generated acetic acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) of a secondary alkyl halide with aqueous ammonia; purpose is to convert 2‑chlorobutane into the corresponding secondary amine, 2‑aminobutane. The chlorine is displaced by NH3, forming the C‑N bond and releasing HCl, which is neutralized by excess ammonia or water. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous or alcoholic NH3 (≈70 °C), often under pressure to keep ammonia in solution. No special catalyst; the reaction proceeds via carbocation formation (SN1) or backside attack (SN2) depending on temperature and solvent.

Sodium‑borohydride reduction of an aldehyde: 1H‑imidazole‑5‑acetaldehyde is reduced to 1H‑imidazole‑5‑methanol using NaBH4 in a protic or aprotic solvent (methanol, ethanol, or THF) at 0 °C to rt. The hydride selectively converts the aldehyde carbonyl to a primary alcohol; no additional catalyst is required.

SN2 azide substitution; purpose is conversion of a primary bromide to an azide for further functionalization; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of NaN₃ on the carbon bearing bromine, forming methyl 3‑azidopropanoate and NaBr; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, 0 °C to reflux, stoichiometric NaN₃, inert atmosphere.

Direct solid‑state synthesis of nickel boride: elemental nickel powder is combined with elemental boron and heated to high temperature (≈800–900 °C) under an inert (argon or nitrogen) atmosphere, often with a slight hydrogen flow to prevent oxidation. The powders react to form nickel boride (NiB or Ni2B), which is used as a catalyst; no solvent or external catalyst is employed.

Transesterification; converts cyclodecyl acetate into cyclodecanol while forming methyl acetate; key alkoxy exchange (R‑OAc + MeOH → R‑OH + MeOAc); typically catalyzed by acidic (e.g., p‑TsOH, H₂SO₄) or basic (NaOMe, K₂CO₃) conditions; reflux in methanol, often using toluene or no additional solvent.

Oxidative conversion of 4‑nitroaniline to 4‑nitrobenzoic acid using potassium permanganate; purpose is to oxidize the aromatic amine to a carboxylic acid; KMnO₄ functions as the oxidant in alkaline aqueous medium, producing manganese dioxide precipitate and potassium hydroxide; typical conditions involve excess KMnO₄, warm or refluxing water, and a base (KOH) to maintain pH; no additional catalysts are needed.

Halogen–cyanide exchange (cyanogen synthesis); iodine reacts with silver cyanide to produce cyanogen gas and precipitate silver iodide; overall redox where I₂ oxidizes CN⁻ to (CN)₂ while being reduced to I⁻ performed in dry, inert atmosphere, often in aqueous or non‑aqueous medium at ambient temperature; solid AgI precipitates and is filtered off.

Oxidative conversion of 5‑methylfurfural to 2,5‑furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA); concentrated nitric acid oxidizes the aldehyde and methyl groups to carboxylates, releasing water and nitrogen dioxide; typically carried out under reflux (150‑200 °C) with excess HNO₃, sometimes with a co‑solvent such as glacial acetic acid; gas‑evolution (NO₂) is vented through a scrubber.

Sulfide oxidation to sulfone; m‑chloroperbenzoic acid oxidizes the vinyl thioether (ethenylsulfanylethene) to the corresponding vinyl sulfone (ethenylsulfonyl ethene); reaction proceeds via sulfoxide intermediate to sulfone; usually performed in dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; stoichiometric m‑CPBA (1.5–2 equiv) with occasional pyridine or NaHCO₃ to neutralize formed acid.

Base‑promoted deprotonation and carbonate decomposition; potassium carbonate neutralizes imidazolidinium chloride, liberating free imidazolidine, carbon dioxide, and water while forming potassium chloride; carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution, often with gentle heating (50‑80 °C) to drive off CO₂; no special catalyst required.

Transesterification (ester exchange); benzyl alcohol attacks methyl salicylate, swapping the alkoxy groups to give benzyl salicylate and methanol; typical acid catalysis (e.g., p‑TsOH, H₂SO₄) or base (NaOMe) under reflux; solvent can be excess benzyl alcohol or an inert solvent such as toluene; removal of methanol (by azeotropic distillation) shifts equilibrium toward product.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of 5,5‑diethylbarbituric acid; sodium ethoxide deprotonates the NH, the resulting anion attacks methyl iodide to give 1‑methyl‑5,5‑diethylbarbituric acid with ethanol and NaI as by‑products. Typically run under anhydrous conditions in ethanol or DMF at reflux, using NaOEt as base and often an inert atmosphere.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; aqueous bismuth trichloride reacts with sodium sulfide to form insoluble bismuth sulfide (Bi2S3) precipitate and sodium chloride in solution; typically performed in water at ambient or gently heated temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a benzylic secondary alcohol to a carboxylic acid (potassium permanganate oxidation). KMnO₄ in hot aqueous medium oxidizes 1-(2‑methoxyphenyl)ethanol first to the corresponding aldehyde and then to 2‑methoxybenzoic acid, with reduction of Mn(VII) to MnO₂. Conducted under reflux in water or aqueous alkaline medium; reaction is stopped by acidification to isolate the acid. No additional catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation of chlorobenzene; Cl2, activated by a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃, substitutes a para hydrogen on the ring to afford mainly 1,4‑dichlorobenzene plus HCl. Conducted in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) at 0–50 °C with FeCl₃ (or AlCl₃) as catalyst.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of a rhenium carbonyl; used to regenerate metallic rhenium and release CO gas. The solid metal carbonyl is heated under an inert atmosphere (typically 150‑250 °C, sometimes up to 300 °C) in a sealed tube or furnace. No solvent is required; the reaction proceeds in the solid/gas phase and produces rhenium metal as a powder and carbon monoxide vapor.

LiAlH₄ reduction of an ester; n‑butyl hexanoate is reduced with excess LiAlH₄ in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, initially at 0 °C then warmed to reflux. The ester is converted to the two primary alcohols n‑butanol and n‑hexanol. Reaction is quenched with water then dilute acid; no additional catalyst needed.

Redox/oxidation reaction used to generate hydrogen peroxide in situ; barium peroxide reacts with aqueous nitric acid, producing H₂O₂, H₂O and soluble Ba(NO₃)₂; typically carried out at 0‑25 °C in water, no catalyst required.

Ester aminolysis (amide formation) of isopropyl acetate with ammonia; NH₃ attacks the carbonyl, displaces isopropanol and yields acetamide. Usually carried out under reflux in excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃, often in a sealed pressure tube, with removal of isopropanol to drive the equilibrium; no catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base neutralization forming barium bromate; two molecules of bromic acid react with Ba(OH)₂ to give Ba(BrO₃)₂ and water. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at room temperature; the bromate salt may precipitate upon cooling.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of tricalcium diphosphate; CaO reacts with P₂O₅ to form Ca₃(PO₄)₂ (calcium diphosphate) with release of heat. Conducted by mixing the powders and heating above ~1000 °C in a furnace; no solvent is used.

Oxidative coupling of thiols; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes allyl mercaptan to form diallyl disulfide with water as by‑product; typically performed at room temperature in a miscible solvent such as methanol or water, no catalyst required.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction); peracetic acid adds an oxygen across the C=C bond of 2‑pentene to give 2‑pentyloxirane and acetic acid; carried out at 0‑25 °C in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform.

Base‑mediated saponification of the sulfonate ester: potassium carbonate hydrolyzes methyl methanesulfonate to give potassium methanesulfonate and methanol; performed in aqueous or aqueous‑acetone medium at room temperature to reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid; potassium permanganate oxidizes ‑pyridinemethanol to 3‑pyridinecarboxylic acid while being reduced to manganese dioxide in basic aqueous solution; reflux in water or dilute NaOH is common.

Full oxidation of a thiol to a sulfonic acid; excess peracetic acid converts ethanethiol to ethanesulfonic acid, generating three equivalents of acetic acid; reaction is run at low to ambient temperature in a non‑aqueous solvent such as dichloromethane or glacial acetic acid.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); selective oxidation that stops at the aldehyde stage; carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; PCC (≈1.2 eq) is added to the alcohol solution, reaction is usually stirred 1–2 h; by‑product is chromium(III) oxide hydrate.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde. Pyridate chlorochromate (PCC) oxidizes veratryl alcohol (4,5‑dimethoxybenzyl alcohol) to veratraldehyde (4,5‑dimethoxybenzaldehyde) while the chromium(VI) is reduced to Cr(III). Reaction is performed in anhydrous dichloromethane (or another non‑protic solvent) at 0 °C to room temperature under an inert atmosphere. Stoichiometric PCC is used; no additional catalyst is needed.

Reductive dissolution of a metal oxide by hydroiodic acid; Au2O3 is reduced by HI to AuI (gold(I) iodide) while iodide is oxidized to iodine and water is formed; typically performed bying the oxide in concentrated aqueous HI.

Direct combination (metal‑halogen synthesis) of uranium metal with iodine to afford uranium(III) iodide (UI₃). Key transformation: elemental uranium reacts with I₂, oxidizing to the +3 oxidation state and forming UI₃ solid. Typical conditions: finely powdered uranium and iodine mixed in an inert‑gas glovebox, heated gently (≈150‑250 °C) under vacuum or dry inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; no catalyst required.

Halogen oxidation/displacement of mercury sulfide; elemental bromine reacts with cinnabar (HgS) to give mercuric bromide (HgBr2) and elemental sulfur; usually conducted by heating the mixture, often in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of aniline in concentrated sulfuric acid/nitric acid mixture; the strong acid protonates aniline to the anilinium ion, making it meta‑directing, thus yielding 3‑nitroaniline. Purpose: introduce a nitro group at the meta position. Key transformation: substitution of a hydrogen on the aromatic ring by a nitro group (NO2). Typical conditions: mixture of conc. H2SO4 and HNO3 kept at 0‑5 °C to control reaction rate and minimize over‑nitration; the sulfuric acid acts as solvent and catalyst. No additional catalysts required.

Formation of an alkyl nitrate (butyl nitrate) by esterification of 1‑butanol with in‑situ generated nitric acid from potassium nitrate and concentrated sulfuric acid. Reaction type: nitric ester synthesis (acid‑catalyzed esterification). Key transformation: conversion of the alcohol O‑H into an O‑NO2 group, producing water as‑product and potassium bisulfate as the acid salt. Typical conditions: mixture of 1‑butanol, solid KNO3 and conc. H2SO4 heated gently (30‑60 °C) under anhydrous conditions; sulfuric acid serves as both catalyst and solvent.

Leuckart–Wallach reaction of o‑chloroacetophenone with formamide; provides 1‑(2‑chlorophenyl)propan‑2‑amine together with CO₂ and H₂O. The ketone condenses with formamide to form a formimidate, which upon heating undergoes intramolecular reduction, releasing CO₂ and water and delivering the amine. Typical conditions: excess formamide (often serves as solvent), sealed tube or pressure‑resistant flask, heating to 150–200 °C for 4–24 h. No external catalyst is employed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); sodium methanethiolate displaces chloride from benzyl chloride to give benzyl methyl sulfide and sodium chloride; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or THF at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of adipic acid with sodium carbonate in aqueous medium. Key transformation: two carboxylic acid groups are deprotonated by carbonate, generating carbon dioxide and water while forming disodium hexanedioate (sodium adipate). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; the reaction proceeds spontaneously, often performed to prepare the sodium salt for polymer nylon synthesis.

Metathesis/neutralization between citric acid and magnesium acetate in water, yielding trimagnesium dicitrate and acetic acid. Key transformation: three magnesium ions replace three acetate ions on the citrate ligands, releasing six molecules of acetic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous solution heated gently (50‑80 °C) to drive off acetic acid and shift equilibrium toward the magnesium citrate salt; no additional catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (precipitation) reaction: magnesium sulfate exchanges anions with lithium carbonate, yielding soluble lithium sulfate and sparingly soluble magnesium carbonate that precipitates. Used to isolate magnesium carbonate or to generate lithium sulfate. Performed in water at room temperature or with mild heating; the solid is filtered and dried. No catalyst needed.

Enzyme‑catalyzed oxidation (oxidative dimerization); purpose is to form the disulfide homocystine and generate hydrogen peroxide; key transformation: two thiol groups of L‑homocysteine are oxidized to a disulfide bond, O₂ is reduced to H₂O₂; typical conditions: aerobic aqueous buffer, catalyzed by homocysteine oxidase (often requires Cu²⁺ or flavin cofactors); solvent: water.

Nitrosation / esterification of methanol with nitrous acid; purpose to form alkyl nitrite (methyl nitrite) as a volatile nitrosyl ester; HONO protonates methanol, substituting OH with ONO group, releasing water; generally carried out at 0‑5 °C in aqueous medium generated from NaNO₂ and HCl; no special catalyst beyond the acidic conditions.

Synthesis (direct combination) reaction: magnesium metal reacts with hydrogen gas to form magnesium hydride (Mg + H2 → MgH2). Performed under H2 pressure (≥1 atm) at 300–400 °C, often in a sealed tube or furnace; inert atmosphere (argon) is used to prevent oxidation; no solvent required, sometimes Ni or Pd catalysts are employed to enhance kinetics.

Transfer hydrogenation (decarboxylative reduction) of methyl pyruvate using formic acid as the hydrogen donor, producing methyl lactate and carbon dioxide. Reaction type: catalytic reduction with simultaneous decarboxylation of formic acid. Key transformation: the keto group of methyl pyruvate is reduced to a secondary alcohol, while formic acid decomposes to CO2, providing two equivalents of hydrogen. Typical conditions: presence of a homogeneous metal catalyst (e.g., Ru‑triphos, Ir‑pincer) or heterogeneous catalyst (Pd/C), solvent such as methanol or ethanol, temperature 80‑120 °C, under inert atmosphere.

Thermal decomposition of uranyl nitrate solid upon strong heating. Reaction type: oxidative thermal decomposition. Key transformation: uranyl nitrate breaks down, releasing nitrogen dioxide and molecular oxygen while forming uranium(VI) oxide (UO3). Typical conditions: dry solid heated to 400‑500 °C in a furnace or tube reactor; no solvent or catalyst is required, and the evolved gases are collected or vented under controlled conditions.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Aqueous solutions of gadolinium(III) sulfate and barium chloride are mixed; insoluble barium sulfate precipitates while gadolinium(III) chloride remains in solution. Usually carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base double displacement (metal salt displacement) that liberates hydrogen bromide gas; solid BiBr₃ reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄ to form Bi₂(SO₄)₃ and HBr; performed under reflux or heating in a dry tube, no solvent needed, apparatus kept dry to collect HBr.

Palladium‑catalyzed Heck cross‑coupling of a vinyl bromide (4‑bromocatechol) with ethylene to afford 4‑vinylcatechol; Pd(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %) with tri‑o‑tolylphosphine ligand and triethylamine base in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, NMP, or dioxane) under inert atmosphere at 80–120 °C; HBr generated is scavenged by the base.
Simple acid–base neutralization; sodium oxalate (Na₂C₂O₄) reacts with aqueous HCl to produce oxalic acid (H₂C₂O₄) and NaCl; carried out in water at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base carbonation reaction; purpose is to generate a soluble magnesium bicarbonate solution; key transformation is dissolution of solid MgCO₃ in water under CO₂ pressure, forming Mg(HCO₃)₂; usually carried out in aqueous medium at ambient temperature or slightly elevated pressure of CO₂, no special catalysts required.

Hydrolysis/decomposition of indium nitride in water to produce indium oxide (often as In(OH)₃ which dehydrates to In₂O₃) and ammonia gas; carried out in aqueous medium with heating (reflux or 100–200 °C); acid or base can accelerate but not essential; no catalyst required.

Condensation/cyclocondensation forming a pyrazole heterocycle; hydrazine reacts with acetonedicarboxylic acid to give 3,5‑dicarboxypyrazole and water; usually refluxed in ethanol or methanol (or aqueous ethanol) to drive off water, often performed without added catalyst.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitro group; 2‑nitrobenzaldehyde is reduced to 2‑aminobenzaldehyde by SnCl₂·2H₂O in aqueous HCl (often with reflux); tin(II) chloride serves as the reducing agent, solvent is water or EtOH/H₂O mixture, reaction proceeds at 60‑80 °C.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal (1,3‑dioxolane) formation of 4‑ethylbenzaldehyde with ethylene glycol. p‑Toluenesulfonic acid protonates the carbonyl, allowing nucleophilic attack by ethylene glycol and subsequent cyclization to the five‑membered dioxolane ring, with water as the only by‑product. Usually carried out in refluxing toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to continuously remove water, using a catalytic amount of p‑TsOH.

Double displacement/precipitation (acid‑base neutralization). Aqueous KOH reacts with zirconium(IV) sulfate to exchange cations, precipitating insoluble zirconium hydroxide while forming soluble potassium sulfate. Typically carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1) of a tertiary alcohol. Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol, facilitating loss of water to give the more substituted 2‑methyl‑2‑butene. Conducted by heating the alcohol in excess sulfuric acid (≈140‑170 °C); no additional reagents needed.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a heteropoly acid salt. Phosphomolybdic acid is deprotonated by NaOH, producing water and sodium phosphomolybdate (Na₃[PMo₁₂O₄₀]). Reaction performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; the salt often precipitates out.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) / base‑promoted hydrolysis of an epibromohydrin. Hydroxide ion from NaOH attacks the carbon bearing bromine, displacing Br⁻ and yielding glycidol (a 2‑hydroxy‑epoxide) and NaBr. Usually carried out in aqueous NaOH (or water/ethanol mixture) at 0‑50 °C; no catalyst required.

Acid leaching / decomposition; used to break down PbTiO₃ and recover lead as a soluble chloride while precipitating TiO₂. Key transformation: PbTiO₃ + 2 HCl → PbCl₂ (aq) + TiO₂(s) + H₂O. Conducted by suspending the solid in aqueous HCl (1–6 M) and heating under reflux (60–100 °C) for 1–3 h. No catalyst; the reaction mixture is filtered to separate the TiO₂ solid.

Jones oxidation (chromic‑acid oxidation) of a secondary alcohol. Hexan‑2‑ol is treated with Jones reagent (CrO₃ in dilute H₂SO₄, usually prepared in acetone) to oxidize the alcohol to hexan‑2‑one, with reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III) sulfate and formation of water. Reaction performed at 0 °C then allowed to warm to room temperature; acetone is the common solvent.

Acylation (N‑acetylation) of taurine using acetic anhydride, pyridine as base/solvent. Pyridine scavenges the generated acetic acid, driving formation of N‑acetyltaurine (the amide). Conducted in pyridine at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; excess acetic anhydride may be used, and the by‑product acetic acid is removed during work‑up.

Double displacement/precipitation metathesis; used to prepare insoluble platinum(II) sulfide from soluble PtCl₂ and Na₂S; sulfide ions replace chloride, forming PtS precipitate and NaCl in solution; typically performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating and stirring; no special catalyst required.

Acid–base metathesis (anion exchange); converts copper(II) chloride to copper(II) tetrafluoroborate, a non‑coordinating‑anion salt useful in catalysis; HBF₄ protonates chloride to give HCl while BF₄⁻ pairs with Cu²⁺; usually carried out in water or a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) between sulfuric acid and calcium chlorate; yields insoluble calcium sulfate precipitate and regenerates chloric acid; performed in aqueous medium, often at moderate temperature to aid precipitation of CaSO₄; no catalyst needed.

Copper‑catalyzed nucleophilic trifluoromethylation (cross‑coupling) of a 5‑iodonucleoside; replaces the iodine with a –CF₃ group using trimethyl(trifluoromethyl)silane (TMS‑CF₃) as the CF₃ source, CuCN as the copper(I) catalyst, and K₂CO₃ as base; delivers the anticancer nucleoside trifluridine; typical conditions: dry DMF or DMSO, inert atmosphere (N₂), 80–100 °C for several hours; no additional catalyst beyond Cu(I).

Simple acid‑base proton transfer (salt dissociation); heating dimethylammonium acetate releases volatile dimethylamine and forms acetic acid; essentially a thermolysis of an ionic salt to its neutral components; performed by gentle heating, often under reduced pressure to remove dimethylamine; no catalyst required.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction in acidic medium; bromate ion oxidizes Fe²⁺ (from ferrous sulfate) to Fe³⁺, being reduced to Br⁻; sulfuric acid provides the acidic environment and forms sodium sulfate; overall yields ferric sulfate, sodium bromide, water, and sodium sulfate; carried out in aqueous solution at moderate temperature (often 25–60 °C); no external catalyst.

Double displacement/precipitation metathesis; exchanges carbonate and chloride ions to precipitate insoluble calcium carbonate while forming soluble strontium chloride; used to separate or recover CaCO₃ or Sr²⁺ ions; performed in aqueous solution with stirring, usually at room temperature or with mild heating; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base metathesis (ion exchange). Ammonium perchlorate reacts with tetrafluoroboric acid in aqueous solution, exchanging the anions to give perchloric acid (strong acid) and ammonium tetrafluoroborate as a solid salt. Typically performed at 0–25 °C in water; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; used to remove an N‑acetyl protecting group and liberate the free aniline. The acetamide is refluxed in aqueous hydrochloric acid (typically 6 M HCl) at 80‑100 °C. Water acts as solvent; the reaction converts the amide bond to a carboxylic acid (acetic acid) and releases 2,6‑dimethylaniline.

Oxidation of cobalt(II) oxide in air to form cobalt(II,III) oxide; heating cobalt oxide in an oxygen‑rich atmosphere (400–600 °C) leads to uptake of O₂ and formation of the mixed‑valence oxide; solid‑state oxidation, no additional reagents.

Double‑displacement precipitation. Barium chloride aqueous solution is mixed with calcium chromate solution; insoluble barium chromate precipitates while calcium chloride remains in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; filtration isolates the BaCrO₄ solid.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol with Dess‑Martin periodinane. 1‑Phenyl‑2‑propanol is treated with Dess‑Martin periodinane in anhydrous dichloromethane (0 °C to rt) to afford phenylacetone (a ketone) while the reagent is reduced to 2‑iodobenzoic acid. Mild, neutral conditions; no additional catalyst needed.

Fischer esterification: p‑hydroxybenzoic acid is condensed with isopropyl alcohol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid, producing isopropylparaben and water; conditions typically involve excess isopropanol, 1–5 % H₂SO₄, reflux for 3–6 h, and removal of water to drive the equilibrium forward.

Base‑promoted E2 dehydrohalogenation. Sodium ethoxide in ethanol abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 1‑chloro‑2‑nitroethane, eliminating chloride to form nitroethene and NaCl. Reaction usually run under reflux in ethanol; no catalyst required.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of gallium nitride. Metallic gallium reacts with gaseous ammonia at 800–1000 °C (often in a flow reactor) to produce gallium nitride and hydrogen gas. No solvent or catalyst; requires inert or reducing atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) of a secondary alkyl chloride with aqueous NaOH to give the corresponding secondary alcohol; purpose is conversion of alkyl halide to alcohol; key transformation Cl → OH; typically reflux in aqueous ethanol or water/ethanol mixture, NaOH (1–2 M); common solvent: ethanol/water.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling. Phenylboronic acid couples with 3‑chloropyridine in the presence of Pd(PPh₃)₄ (5–10 mol %) and potassium carbonate as base, typically in a mixed solvent (e.g., dioxane/water or THF) at 80–100 °C under nitrogen. The reaction yields 3‑phenylpyridine, with potassium chloride and boric acid formed as by‑products.

Selective NaBH₄ reduction of 1,2‑cyclohexanedione to 2‑hydroxycyclohexan‑1‑one; type: chemoselective carbonyl reduction; purpose: obtain a hydroxy‑ketone from a diketone; key transformation: NaBH₄ delivers a hydride to one carbonyl, leaving the second carbonyl untouched; typical conditions: NaBH₄ (1–1.2 eq) in methanol (or ethanol), 0 °C to room temperature, reaction time 30 min–1 h.

Reaction type: peracid oxidation of a thioether to a sulfoxide; purpose: mild, stoichiometric oxidation to the sulfoxide without over‑oxidation; key transformation: m‑chloroperbenzoic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the sulfur of allyl phenyl sulfide, affording allyl phenyl sulfoxide and m‑chlorobenzoic acid; typical conditions: dichloromethane solvent, 0 °C to rt, 1‑1.2 equiv mCPBA, with the reaction mixture often buffered (e.g., NaHCO3) to neutralize the acid by‑product.

Halide‑exchange (metathesis) converting ZrF₂ to ZrCl₂ with simultaneous formation of HF. Conducted at high temperature (several hundred °C) in the gas phase or in a sealed tube, often by passing dry HCl gas over solid ZrF₂. No solvent; may be facilitated by a molten‑salt medium.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification: butanol attacks the carbonyl of 2‑methylpentyl acetate, exchanging the alkoxy groups to produce butyl acetate and regenerating 2‑methylpentanol; carried out at reflux in excess butanol or in toluene with a catalytic amount of NaOMe, K2CO3, or H2SO4, and the equilibrium driven by removal of one product.

High‑temperature solid‑state halogen exchange (iodination) for preparation of a volatile metal iodide; converts carbon tetraiod and hafnium(IV) oxide into carbon dioxide and hafnium(IV) iodide, effectively transferring iodine to the metal; usually carried out in a sealed quartz tube at 400–600 °C under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen); no solvent or catalyst is used.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of aziridine by methanol to give a β‑amino ether (2‑methoxyethylamine); classified as an acid‑catalyzed or thermally induced aziridine opening; usually carried out in methanol as both solvent and reactant, refluxed, often with a catalytic amount of Brønsted or Lewis acid to activate the aziridine; no additional reagents required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange between sodium tungstate and lithium chloride producing lithium tungstate and sodium chloride; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; both salts are soluble, so the reaction proceeds without a catalyst; isolation may involve evaporation or crystallisation.

N‑alkylation of 2‑methoxyethylamine with methyl iodide via an SN2 nucleophilic substitution, generating N‑methyl‑2‑methoxyethylamine and hydrogen iodide; performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature; a base such as triethylamine or NaHCO₃ is added to neutralize the formed HI.

Double‑displacement (salt metathesis) reaction; potassium carbonate replaces acetate, forming soluble potassium acetate and insoluble calcium carbonate precipitate. Carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; the solid CaCO₃ is filtered off; no catalyst is used.

Acid‑metal reaction where acetic acid reacts with magnesium metal to form magnesium acetate and liberate hydrogen gas; classified as a single‑displacement redox reaction; usually carried out in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere, with magnesium activated (e.g., by iodine) and gentle heating to promote hydrogen evolution.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of a heteroaromatic ring; the nitronium ion generated from concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ attacks the 4‑position of 3‑methylpyridine, yielding 3‑methyl‑4‑nitropyridine and water; carried out at 0‑5 °C then warmed to about 50 °C, solvent is the cold acid mixture.

Acid‑mediated decomposition of a peroxide; furnishes water, molecular oxygen and lithium chloride while oxidizing lithium peroxide with hydrochloric acid; the reaction proceeds rapidly at 0–25 °C in aqueous solution, releasing O₂ gas; performed in water as solvent, no catalyst required.
Neutralization reaction between lead hydroxide and hydrochloric acid. Insoluble lead(II) hydroxide reacts with HCl to form lead(II) chloride and water in aqueous medium.

Type: hydrogen reduction (redox). Purpose: convert molybdic acid (H2MoO4) to molybdenum dioxide, a useful catalyst or pigment. Key transformation: H2 reduces Mo(VI) to Mo(IV), producing water and MoO2 solid. Typical conditions: high temperature (300‑500 °C) under flowing hydrogen, often in a furnace; solid‑gas contact, no solvent. Catalyst: none required.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose is to exchange the alkoxy group of octan‑3‑yl acetate with methanol, producing methyl acetate and 3‑octanol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonyl carbon, followed by departure of the original alkoxide. Typical conditions: excess methanol, catalytic H₂SO₄ or NaOMe, reflux (≈65 °C) for several hours; methanol serves as both reagent and solvent.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) azide transfer from organotin azide to allyl bromide. Purpose: synthesis of allyl azide, a versatile azide building block. Key transformation: the bromide on allyl bromide is displaced by the azide group, forming allyl azide and tri‑n‑butyl‑tin bromide. Typical conditions: inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, toluene) at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen; reaction often stirred for 1‑2 h. Catalyst: none needed.

Type: condensation polymerization (phenol‑formaldehyde resin formation, modified with diphenylamine). Purpose: production of phenolic resin (thermosetting plastic) with improved properties. Key transformation: electrophilic addition of formaldehyde to phenol and diphenylamine, followed by dehydration to create methylene‑linked aromatic networks. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic medium, acid (e.g., HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) catalyst, temperature 60‑120 °C, with gradual addition of formaldehyde. Solvent: water or methanol; catalyst as above.

Type: redox (single‑displacement) reaction. Purpose: generate elemental mercury and oxidize tin(II) to tin(IV). Key transformation: Hg²⁺ is reduced to Hg⁰, while Sn²⁺ is oxidized to Sn⁴⁺, forming SnCl₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of both chlorides, often in dilute HCl, at ambient temperature; stirring under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of mercury. Solvent: water; no additional catalyst.

Type: acid‑base metathesis (double‑replacement) reaction. Purpose: exchange of cations to form sodium hydroxide and ammonium dihydrogen arsenate. Key transformation: NH₄⁺ exchanges with Na⁺, yielding NH₄H₂AsO₄ and NaOH. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, room temperature, vigorous stirring. Solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Type: metal‑acid redox (hydrogen evolution). Purpose: production of lithium fluoride and hydrogen gas; illustrates reactivity of alkali metal with HF. Key transformation: Li metal reduces HF, forming LiF solid and H₂ gas. Typical conditions: anhydrous hydrogen fluoride, low temperature (often 0‑20 °C) in a PTFE or nickel vessel, under inert atmosphere; reaction is highly exothermic and must be controlled. Solvent: liquid HF; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a bromide by cyanide; cyanide ion attacks the bromomethane carbon, displacing bromide to give bromomethyl cyanide and sodium bromide; performed in polar protic or aprotic medium such as aqueous ethanol, often with mild heating; water/ethanol as solvent; no catalyst needed.

Thermal or base‑induced decomposition of ethyl N‑phenylcarbamate to phenyl isocyanate and ethanol; an elimination reaction that removes the alkoxy group as ethanol. Performed by heating the carbamate under reduced pressure (150–200 °C) or with catalytic NaOEt in a non‑polar solvent (toluene), with ethanol removed as it forms.

Neutralization/ion exchange; ammonium hydroxide neutralizes lithium dihydrogen phosphate, forming ammonium dihydrogen phosphate and lithium hydroxide. Conducted in water at room temperature; the resulting salts are soluble and the reaction is exothermic but mild.
Zinc‑mediated reductive dehalogenation in acetic acid; Zn dust (excess) in glacial AcOH, refluxed for several hours, reduces the C–Br bond to a C–H bond, producing 2,3‑dihydro‑1H‑indene.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction in aqueous solution; potassium iodide and silver thiocyanate exchange ions to form insoluble silver iodide precipitate and soluble potassium thiocyanate; typically performed at room temperature in water, no catalyst.

Complete combustion of 4‑methylheptane; hydrocarbon reacts with excess oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat; carried out under flame or in a combustion chamber at high temperature, no solvent or catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (heterogeneous reduction) of 2‑nitronaphthalene to 2‑aminonaphthalene; hydrogen gas the presence of palladium on carbon reduces the nitro group to an amine, producing water as by‑product; usually performed in ethanol or methanol under 1–5 atm H₂ at 25–80 °C.

Acid‑atalyzed acetal formation; acetone reacts with methanol in the presence of sulfamic acid to give acetone dimethyl acetal, water is removed; reaction is carried out under reflux in methanol or in toluene with a Dean‑Stark trap, acid catalyst required.

Redox oxidation of a dithiocarbamate coupled with reduction of Cu(II) to Cu(I); sodium diethyl dithiocarbamate is oxidized to tetraethylthiuram disulfide while copper(II) chloride is reduced to copper(I) chloride, liberation of HCl; typically carried out in a mixed water/ethanol medium at ambient temperature with stirring; copper(II) chloride acts as the oxidant, no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reduction of bromomethane by sodium hydride; hydride attacks the methyl carbon displacing bromide to form methane and sodium bromide; carried out in dry THF or ether under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to room temperature.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of an epoxide (addition of amine to epoxide). Purpose: prepare a β‑amino alcohol. Key transformation: ethylamine attacks the less‑substituted carbon of ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring to give 2‑(ethylamino)ethanol. Conditions: ethylamine (gas or aqueous solution) mixed with ethylene oxide under mild pressure or reflux, temperature 0–50 °C, often in water or an alcohol solvent; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst, using excess amine to drive completion.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an allylic alcohol; the C=C double bond of 3‑methyl‑3‑buten‑1‑ol is reduced to give 3‑methyl‑1‑butanol while the alcohol functionality remains intact; performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over 5 % Pd/C in a solvent such as ethanol or THF at 25–50 °C; palladium on carbon is the catalyst.

Carbothermal nitridation of a metal oxide; tantalum(V) oxide reacts with carbon and nitrogen gas to form tantalum nitride (TaN) and carbon monoxide; solid‑state reaction conducted at 1500–1800 °C under flowing N₂ with excess carbon as the reductant; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Acetylation (esterification) of a phenolic hydroxyl group; converts p‑hydroxybenzaldehyde to its acetate protecting group, 4‑acetoxybenzaldehyde, with acetic acid as by‑product. Typically carried out by mixing the phenol with excess acetic anhydride, often in the presence of a base catalyst such as pyridine or DMAP, at 0 °C to reflux; common solvent is dichloromethane or neat acetic anhydride.

Base‑catalyzed ester saponification with concurrent salt neutralization. Ethyl 6‑aminohexanoate·HCl is hydrolyzed by aqueous NaOH, giving the free carboxylic acid 6‑aminocaproic acid, ethanol from the ester, and NaCl from the original hydrochloride. Typical conditions: 1–2 equiv NaOH in water, reflux 1–3 h; after completion the mixture is often acidified to isolate the acid.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of 2‑chloroethyl acetate with NaOH; purpose is to deprotect the acetate and regenerate 2‑chloroethanol. Key transformation: hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of the ester, cleaving the C–O bond and giving the free alcohol and acetate ion (sodium acetate). Conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux or warm stirring (50–80 °C) in water or aqueous ethanol; reaction proceeds to completion without additional catalyst.

Type: oxidation (Jones oxidation). Purpose: convert cycloheptanol (secondary alcohol) to cycloheptanone. Key transformation: removal of two hydrogens from the alcohol carbon to form a carbonyl; Cr(VI) reduced to Cr(III). Conditions: CrO₃ (or Na₂Cr₂O₇) dissolved in concentrated H₂SO₄ to give Jones reagent, usually in acetone as solvent, reaction performed at 0 °C to room temperature, short reaction time to avoid over‑oxidation. By‑products: Cr₂(SO₄)₃ and water.

Chlorination (redox) of cadmium phosphide; elemental chlorine reacts with Cd₃P₂ to produce phosphorus trichloride (PCl₃) and cadmium chloride (CdCl₂). Conducted in a sealed tube or reactor at elevated temperature (≈200–300 °C) under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; no solvent is usually employed, and the reaction is driven by the stoichiometric excess of Cl₂.

Conversion of 4‑nitrobenzyl alcohol to 1‑(chloromethyl)-4‑nitrobenzene using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂). This is a nucleophilic substitution (Appel‑type) where the hydroxyl group is replaced by chlorine, generating SO₂ and HCl gases. Reaction carried out by adding excess SOCl₂ to the alcohol in dry dichloromethane or chloroform, usually at 0 °C to reflux for 1–2 h; pyridine or triethylamine may be added to scavenge HCl.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl sulfonate ester; methoxide ion attacks the ethyl group of ethyl 4‑methylbenzenesulfonate, displacing ethanol and forming methyl 4‑methylbenzenesulfonate. Performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO at ambient temperature; sodium methoxide is used as the nucleophile, often with catalytic amounts of crown ether to enhance solubility.
