Electrophilic aromatic nitration; nitronium tetrafluoroborate (generated from BF₄⁻ and a strong acid) delivers the NO₂⁺ electrophile to the para position of acetanilide, affording 4‑nitroacetanilide and tetrafluoroboric acid as by‑product. Reaction performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or nitromethane) at 0–25 °C under anhydrous conditions.

Diazomethane esterification; diazomethane reacts with heptanoic acid, transferring a methyl group to the carboxylate to give methyl heptanoate while liberating N₂ gas. Conducted at 0 °C (often −5 °C) in an inert, aprotic solvent such as diethyl ether or hexane, with cautious addition of diazomethane to avoid excess heat and side reactions.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of solid gallium nitrate; on heating to 500–600 °C the nitrate decomposes to gallium oxide (Ga2O3) releasing nitrogen dioxide gas and oxygen. Conducted in a furnace under air or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Type: synthesis (direct combination). Purpose: preparation of strontium sulfide. Key transformation: elemental Sr reacts with elemental S to form SrS. Typical conditions: mixture heated under inert atmosphere (400–600 °C); no solvent.

Acid–base neutralization and salt formation; boric acid reacts with carbonate to neutralize the acid, releasing CO₂ and water while forming sodium metaborate. Typically performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to evolve CO₂; water is the solvent and no external catalyst is required.

Acetylation (esterification) of dihydroxy alkyne; two equivalents of acetic anhydride acetylate the hydroxyl groups of 1,4‑dihydroxy‑2‑butyne, producing the diacetate and acetic acid as by‑product. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature; catalytic amounts of pyridine or DMAP are often added to scavenge the generated acid.

Oxime formation (condensation of carbonyl with hydroxylamine); hydroxylamine adds to the carbonyl carbon of acetophenone, followed by dehydration to give acetophenone oxime. Usually carried out in ethanol or ethanol/water (1:1) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; mildly acidic conditions (pH ≈ 5–6) or a catalytic amount of acetic acid facilitate the dehydration step.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; used to separate magnesium as insoluble hydroxide and convert formate to a soluble sodium salt. Key transformation: exchange of anions between Mg²⁺ and Na⁺, forming Mg(OH)₂ precipitate and NaHCOO in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, vigorous stirring; no special catalyst required. Water serves as the solvent.

Oxidative dehydrogenation; potassium permanganate in aqueous sulfuric acid oxidizes abietic acid by removing two hydrogen atoms to afford dehydroabietic acid, while the permanganate is reduced to Mn²⁺ forming manganese(II) sulfate and water. Reaction is performed in aqueous H₂SO₄ at reflux or elevated temperature (≈80‑100 °C); no additional catalyst is needed.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of cerium(III) hydroxide to the oxide. Key transformation: 2 Ce(OH)₃ → Ce₂O₃ + 3 H₂O↑. Heated in a furnace at 400–600 °C in air or inert atmosphere; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

E2 elimination of a secondary alkyl mesylate; pentan‑3‑yl methanesulfonate reacts with KOt‑Bu to give pent‑2‑ene, potassium methanesulfonate, and tert‑butanol; carried out in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (THF, DMSO) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; strong, non‑nucleophilic base drives anti‑periplanar elimination; purpose is synthesis of the internal alkene.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; sodium cyanide exchanges anions with cadmium iodide, yielding soluble sodium iodide and insoluble cadmium cyanide, which precipitates out. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; stirring ensures complete ion exchange; the solid cadmium cyanide is filtered off.

Carbothermic reduction; production of metallic dysprosium. The oxide is mixed with carbon (or coke) and heated to >1500 °C in an electric arc or induction furnace under an inert atmosphere (Ar). Carbon reduces Dy2O3 to Dy metal while being oxidized to CO (or CO2). No solvents or catalysts are used.

Full reduction with lithium aluminium hydride; reduces both the keto carbonyl and the ester carbonyl of methyl pyruvate, yielding 1,2‑propane‑diol (propane‑1,2‑diol) and releasing methanol. Key transformations: –CO– → –CHOH– and –COOCH₃ → –CH₂OH. Performed under anhydrous conditions in dry THF or diethyl ether, LiAlH₄ (2–3 equiv) added at 0 °C, then the mixture is refluxed for 1–2 h under nitrogen. Work‑up with aqueous NH₄Cl quench gives the diol; solvent is removed after extraction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary bromide; aqueous sodium hydroxide attacks the carbon bearing bromine in 1‑bromo‑4‑chlorobutane, displacing bromide to form 4‑chloro‑1‑butanol and sodium bromide. Reaction proceeds at room temperature or mild heating in water or a water/ethanol mixture; no special catalyst is required.

Grignard addition to a nitrile followed by hydrolysis; methylmagnesium bromide adds to phenylacetonitrile, forming a magnesium‑imidate that on acidic or aqueous work‑up gives phenylacetone (1‑phenyl‑2‑propanone). Conducted in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen. After the Grignard step, the reaction mixture is quenched with water (often with dilute acid) to liberate the ketone.

Oxidation of fluorene to fluoren‑9‑one using chromic acid (Jones oxidation). CrO₃/H₂SO₄ in acetone oxidizes the benzylic methylene bridge to a carbonyl, producing water as a by‑product. Conditions: 0 °C to reflux in acetone, aqueous work‑up required.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (Fischer esterification). Salicylic acid reacts with ethyl acetate in the presence of catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid to give ethyl salicylate and acetic acid. Typically performed by refluxing the mixture in ethyl acetate (which also as solvent) with a catalytic amount of p‑TsOH; removal of the generated acetic acid (e.g., by distillation) drives the equilibrium to completion.

Acid‑base salt metathesis (dissolution of a basic oxide). Barium aluminate is treated with excess nitric acid, yielding soluble barium nitrate and aluminum nitrate while water is formed. The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution, usually at ambient or mildly elevated temperature, with dilute HNO₃ as the acid medium.

Simple acid‑base neutralization. Glycolic acid (hydroxyacetic acid) reacts with ammonium hydroxide to give the ammonium glycolate salt and water. Conducted in water at room temperature; stoichiometric amounts are mixed, and the resulting solution contains the ammonium salt, which can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution with cyanide; purpose: form nitrile from alkyl halide; key transformation: C–I displaced by C≡N; typical conditions: KCN in polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) or aqueous ethanol, mild heating; common solvent: DMF/DMSO.

Halogen exchange / protodealkylation of a trialkylborane. HF protonates the B‑Me bonds, cleaving them to release CH₄ while fluorine replaces the alkyl groups on boron, yielding BF₃. Typically performed with anhydrous HF gas at low temperature (0 °C to –20 °C) in a sealed tube; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Intramolecular esterification (lactonization) to form a five‑membered lactone. 4‑Hydroxybutanoic acid undergoes dehydration to give β‑butyrolactone and water. The cyclisation is typically promoted by heating the acid neat or in a high‑boiling aprotic solvent (e.g., toluene) with a catalytic amount of acid (such as p‑TsOH) and removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap) to drive the equilibrium.

Redox (oxygen‑transfer) reaction; triphenylphosphine reduces iodosylbenzene (PhIO) to iodobenzene (PhI) while being oxidized to triphenylphosphine oxide; typically run at room temperature in an aprotic organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform under inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst needed.

Acyl‑chloride esterification; reaction of cyclohexylmethanol with acetyl chloride to afford cyclohexylmethyl acetate and HCl. Purpose is rapid ester formation without water removal. Key transformation: alcohol attacks the carbonyl of acetyl chloride, displacing chloride as HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, with a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or a solid acid scavenger) to neutralize the generated HCl.

Halogenation/dechlorination (chloride transfer) producing sulfuryl chloride. Phosphorus pentachloride reacts with sulfur dioxide to give phosphorus trichloride and sulfuryl chloride (SO₂Cl₂). The reaction is performed in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) under anhydrous conditions; PCl₃ evolves as a gas and is separated from the liquid SO₂Cl₂.

Metathesis (double‑replacement) reaction; concentrates sulfuric acid displaces lead(II) iodide to precipitate insoluble lead(II) sulfate while generating hydrogen iodide gas. Typically carried out by adding solid PbI₂ to excess conc. H₂SO₄, heating gently (often 80–120 °C) under a dry‑air or inert atmosphere. No catalyst; sulfuric acid acts both reagent and solvent, the HI gas is collected by distillation.

Acylation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of O,S‑dimethyl phosphoramidothioate with ketene to afford the organophosphate insecticide Acephate. The phosphoramidothioate oxygen attacks the electrophilic carbonyl of ketene, forming an acetyl‑phosphoramidothioate. Conducted at low temperature (0 °C to room temperature) in an aprotic, dry solvent such as dry toluene or dichloromethane under nitrogen; the reaction does not require a catalyst but may be assisted by a base (e.g., pyridine) to scavenge the generated acid.

Transesterification (alcoholysis) of phenyl methacrylate with n‑butanol; purpose: preparation of n‑butyl methacrylate; key transformation: phenoxy group replaced by butoxy, phenol liberated; typical conditions: acid (p‑TsOH) or base (sodium butoxide) catalysis, reflux in toluene or xylene, continuous removal of phenol drives equilibrium; common solvents: toluene, xylene; catalyst: p‑TsOH or NaOBu.

Acid‑base (metal‑acid) reaction forming sodium acetylide from acetylene and elemental sodium. Sodium metal reacts with acetylene in a dry, aprotic solvent such as liquid ammonia (or THF) at low temperature (−33 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere, generating Na⁺ C₂H⁻ (sodium acetylide) and hydrogen gas. No catalyst is needed; the solvent stabilizes the sodium acetylide ion.

Acid‑catalysed hydrolysis / salt metathesis. Potassium phenylacetate is treated with aqueous sulfuric acid, converting the carboxylate salt to phenylacetic acid while forming potassium hydrogen sulfate. Usually performed at mild heating (50‑80 °C) in water or a water‑acetone mixture. Purpose: liberation of the free carboxylic acid from its potassium salt.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) bromination of 4‑aminobenzenesulfonamide in acetic acid. Bromine adds to the ortho positions relative to the amino group, yielding 4‑amino‑3,5‑dibromobenzenesulfonamide while HBr is liberated. Reaction is typically performed in glacial AcOH at 0–25 °C, with slow addition of Br₂ to control over‑bromination. No external catalyst; AcOH serves as solvent and proton source.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of erucic acid (cis‑13‑octadecenyl acid) to the fully saturated behenic acid. Hydrogen gas adds across the C=C double bond in the presence of a heterogeneous catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, usually in an alcohol solvent (ethanol or methanol) at 1–5 atm H₂ and 25–80 °C. The reaction converts the monounsaturated fatty acid to the saturated C₂₂ fatty acid.

Acid–base salt formation; purpose is to convert basic medetomidine into its hydrochloride salt for improved solubility; key transformation is proton transfer from HCl to the amine nitrogen of medetomidine yielding an ionic pair; typically performed in anhydrous ethanol or methanol at 0–25 °C with stirring; no catalyst required, solvent is often ethanol, methanol, or a water/acetone mixture.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; purpose is to saturate the C=C bond of (1Z)-cyclononene to give cyclononane; key transformation is addition of H₂ across the double bond using Pd/C as catalyst; usual conditions are 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, 5–10 % Pd on carbon, temperature 20–50 °C, in a protic solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate; catalyst is palladium on carbon.

Condensation/cyclocondensation to form a pyrazolone heterocycle; purpose is synthesis of 5‑methyl‑2‑phenyl‑4H‑pyrazol‑3‑one; key transformation involves nucleophilic attack of phenylhydrazine on the carbonyl of acetylacetone, followed by dehydration and intramolecular cyclization with loss of water; typically carried out on silica gel (solid support) at 100–130 °C, often solvent‑free or with a small amount of ethanol; silica surface provides acidic sites, no added catalyst is required.

Redox (oxidation of sulfite, reduction of chlorine) in alkaline medium; purpose is generation of sodium dithionate; key transformation is chlorine reacting with hydroxide to form chloride and hypochlorite, which then oxidizes sulfite (SO₃²⁻) to dithionate (S₂O₆²⁻) while water is formed; carried out in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C with excess NaOH to maintain basic pH; no catalyst needed, simply NaOH, Na₂SO₃ and Cl₂ gases in water.

This is a single displacement reaction where sodium metal reduces boron tribromide to produce elemental boron and sodium bromide. The reaction typically requires high temperatures to initiate the reduction process. An inert atmosphere may be necessary to prevent oxidation. No common solvent or catalyst is involved.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of an alkyl iodide; purpose is to produce 2‑methoxyethanol; key transformation is attack of water on the carbon bearing iodine, displacing I⁻ and forming the alcohol with concomitant generation of HI; usually performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating (reflux) and sometimes in the presence of a base (e.g., NaOH) to neutralize HI; no special catalyst, solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture.

Acid–base metathesis (salt exchange); purpose is to generate thallium(I) chloride and liberate formic acid; key transformation is proton transfer from HCl to the formate anion, producing HCOOH and TlCl precipitate; typically done in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required, solvent is water.

Fischer esterification of 2,2‑difluoroacetic acid with n‑butanol to form butyl 2,2‑difluoroacetate and water; purpose is preparation of the ester. Key transformation: proton‑catalyzed nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on the acid carbonyl, followed by loss of water. Typically carried out with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) in excess n‑butanol as solvent, refluxing 2–4 h; removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium to products.

Reaction type: acid‑base complexation/fluoride synthesis. Purpose: preparation of the soluble metal fluoride complex potassium hexafluorozirconate (K2ZrF6) used in molten‑salt electrolytes and zirconium processing. Key transformation: zirconium carbonate is protonated by hydrofluoric acid, liberating CO2 and H2O, while fluoride ions from HF and KF coordinate to Zr(IV) to form the hexafluoro‑zirconate anion; excess K⁺ from KF balances charge to give K2ZrF6. Typical conditions: aqueous HF solution (often 40–50 % HF) with stoichiometric KF, temperature 50–80 °C, vigorous stirring; no catalyst required. Common solvent: water; equipment must be HF‑compatible.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of the N‑glycosidic bond of cytidine; cleaves the ribose–base linkage to give free cytosine and D‑ribose. Typically performed with 1–2 M HCl at 80–100 °C for several hours, or enzymatically with nucleosidases in buffered aqueous solution (pH 5–6) at 37 °C.

Reaction type: oxidative phenolic coupling (dimerization). Purpose: synthesis of digallic acid, a dimeric phenolic acid useful in tannin chemistry and pharmaceutical intermediates. Key transformation: two gallic‑acid molecules undergo a radical or electrophilic coupling at the phenolic ortho positions, forming a C‑C bond that links the aromatic rings while preserving the carboxyl groups. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 7–8) at ambient temperature, with an oxidant such as FeCl₃, Cu²⁺, K₃[Fe(CN)₆] or enzymatic laccase; reaction time 1–12 h. Common solvent: water or water/acetone mixture; optional catalyst: metal salt or laccase enzyme.

Redox oxidation of iodide; MnO2 oxidizes I⁻ to I2 in acidic medium, producing MnSO4, K2SO4 and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution with dilute H2SO4 at room temperature; water is the solvent, KI provides iodide, MnO2 is the oxidant.

Reaction type: acid‑base salt metathesis with halogen exchange. Purpose: conversion of trichloroisocyanuric acid (TCCA) into sodium dichloroisocyanurate (NaDCC), a stable chlorine disinfectant, while neutralizing excess acidity. Key transformation: carbonate anion deprotonates TCCA, releasing CO₂ and H₂O; chloride ions from TCCA pair with Na⁺ to form NaCl, and one chlorine remains bound to the isocyanurate ring, yielding NaDCC. Typical conditions: aqueous suspension of TCCA added to an aqueous solution of Na₂CO₃ (solid or solution) at 20–40 °C, with vigorous stirring; reaction completes within minutes. No catalyst needed. Common solvent: water.

Reaction type: acylation (esterification) of an allylic alcohol with acetic anhydride. Purpose: synthesis of 3‑methyl‑2‑butenyl acetate, an ester used as fragrance or intermediate. Key transformation: the hydroxyl group of 3‑methyl‑2‑buten‑1‑ol attacks the carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming the acetate ester and liberating one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to reflux (≈ 80 °C) in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or chloroform); catalytic amount of pyridine, DMAP, or 4‑dimethylaminopyridine to accelerate acyl transfer and scavenge the generated acid. Reaction time 1–4 h. Common solvents: CHCl₂, THF; base catalyst: pyridine or DMAP.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution of cyanuric chloride with ethylamine to produce simazine; SNAr on a 1,3,5‑triazine ring where two equivalents of ethylamine replace two chlorine atoms, yielding 2‑chloro‑4,6‑bis(ethylamino)‑1,3,5‑triazine (simazine) and two equivalents of HCl; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, THF, or MeCN) at 0–50 °C with excess ethylamine, which also serves as base; no metal catalyst is required.

Nitrosative fragmentation of [amino(ethylsulfanyl)methylidene]azanium bromide with nitrous acid to generate ethyl isothiocyanate, ammonium bromide and water. Nitrous acid is generated in situ from sodium nitrite and a mineral acid (HCl) at 0–5 °C in aqueous medium. The reaction proceeds via nitrosation of the amidine‑type cation followed by loss of ammonia and rearrangement to the isothiocyanate. No external catalyst is required beyond the acid source for nitrous acid formation.

Reaction type: solid‑state redox reduction (metallothermic reduction). Purpose: generation of thulium(II) iodide, a strong reducing agent and source of low‑valent thulium for organometallic synthesis. Key transformation: lithium metal donates electrons to Tm³⁺ in TmI₃, reducing it to Tm²⁺ and forming LiI as the by‑product. Overall stoichiometry: TmI₃ + Li → TmI₂ + LiI. Typical conditions: finely powdered reagents mixed under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen), sealed in a quartz or stainless‑steel tube, heated to 200–400 °C for several hours to promote diffusion and reaction. No additional catalyst; the metal itself is the reductant. Common medium: dry, oxygen‑free environment; sometimes a molten salt (e.g., NaI/KI eutectic) is used as flux.

Thermal decarboxylation of a β‑keto acid; purpose is to generate a simple ketone and CO₂ from acetoacetic acid. Key transformation: CH₃COCH₂CO₂H → CH₃COCH₃ + CO₂. Typical conditions: heating to 150–200 °C in the melt or in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., xylene), sometimes with a catalytic amount of base (NaOAc) to accelerate CO₂ loss; no external catalyst required.

Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne to an alkane. Purpose: reduction of diphenylacetylene to diphenylethane, a saturated hydrocarbon used in organic synthesis and as a model substrate. Key transformation: addition of two equivalents of H₂ across the carbon–carbon triple bond, converting it first to a cis‑alkene (stilbene) and then to the saturated alkane. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, Pd on carbon (5–10 % Pd) as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol, ethyl acetate or methanol; temperature 25–50 °C; reaction time 1–6 h. Catalyst is usually pre‑activated by washing with solvent; reaction is performed under inert atmosphere until H₂ is introduced. No additional reagents required.

General type: Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; a metal oxidation forming a metal oxide. Purpose: Produces strontium oxide, a basic refractory material. Key transformation: Elemental strontium reacts with diatomic oxygen to give SrO. Typical conditions: Requires heating or ignition in dry air; often performed under a stream of O₂ at temperatures above the ignition point of Sr (~400 °C). No solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑base (metathesis) reaction; ZrO2, an amphoteric oxide, reacts with strong base KOH to form soluble potassium zirconate (K2ZrO3) and water. Usually carried out by heating a mixture of solid ZrO2 and solid or aqueous KOH at 400‑800 °C or in hot concentrated KOH solution; no special catalyst required.

General type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) of an alcohol to a chloride, known as a Lucas test. Purpose: Converts 1‑piperidinol into the corresponding alkyl chloride, 1‑chloropiperidine. Key transformation: The hydroxyl group is replaced by chlorine; ZnCl₂ acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst to generate a better leaving group, while HCl provides the nucleophilic chloride. Typical conditions: Concentrated aqueous HCl with catalytic ZnCl₂, reflux or gentle heating (≈80‑100 °C). Reaction is often run in the aqueous phase; no organic solvent is required.

This is an oxidation (autoxidation) reaction. The purpose is converting acetoin (3-hydroxy-2-butanone) to the diketone 2,3-butanedione. Key transformation: oxidation of a secondary alcohol (–OH) to a ketone (–CO–), driven by molecular oxygen (O2) and yielding water. Conditions: aerobic environment, possibly catalyzed by transition metals (e.g., Cu²⁺ or Fe²⁺), with mild heating in aqueous solution.

Hydrolysis/precipitation reaction: iron(II) oxide reacts with water to form iron(II) hydroxide. FeO + H2O → Fe(OH)2. Occurs in aqueous medium, typically at ambient temperature and neutral to slightly basic pH. No special catalyst; the product precipitates as a green solid.

Friedel‑Crafts electrophilic aromatic chlorination of anisole; AlCl₃ acts as Lewis‑acid catalyst to generate the electrophilic Cl⁺ from Cl₂, leading to ortho‑chlorination (ortho‑chloroanisole) with HCl as by‑product; carried out anhydrous, 0 °C, in solvents such as CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂.

General type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: Isolates dysprosium(III) hydroxide as an insoluble solid while transferring nitrate to calcium. Key transformation: Exchange of the nitrate and hydroxide ligands between dysprosium and calcium ions, producing Ca(NO₃)₂ in solution and precipitating Dy(OH)₃. Typical conditions: Aqueous solutions of Dy(NO₃)₃ and Ca(OH)₂ mixed at ambient temperature; the mixture is often heated gently (≤80 °C) to ensure complete dissolution before precipitation. The precipitate is filtered and washed; no catalyst required.

General type: Protonolysis (alkyl‑halide exchange) of a metal‑alkyl bond. Purpose: Converts trimethylgallium to gallium tribromide while generating methane gas. Key transformation: HBr protonates the Ga–CH₃ bonds, releasing CH₄ and forming Ga–Br bonds. Typical conditions: Either gas‑phase flow of HBr over Ga(CH₃)₃ at 0‑50 °C, or solution in a dry, non‑coordinating solvent such as diethyl ether or THF under an inert atmosphere; stoichiometric HBr (excess) is used. No additional catalyst is needed.

General type: Solid‑state halide metathesis (fusion) reaction. Purpose: Produces praseodymium(III) iodide by replacing chloride ions with iodide ions. Key transformation: NaI and PrCl₃ exchange anions, yielding NaCl (which melts and can be removed) and PrI₃. Typical conditions: The reactants are ground together and heated above the melting point of NaI (≈660 °C) in a sealed, dry, inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) to prevent hydrolysis. The reaction proceeds without solvent or catalyst; the molten NaCl can be decanted after cooling.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; exchanges the alkoxy groups of tert‑butanol and butyl butyrate to give the more volatile tert‑butyl butyrate and n‑butanol. Typically performed with a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) under reflux; the reaction mixture may be azeotropically distilled or the lower boiling n‑butanol removed to drive equilibrium. Common are toluene or the reacting alcohol itself.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of an allene (electrophilic addition of water to 1,3‑dimethylallene) to produce 2‑methyl‑2‑buten‑1‑ol (an allylic tertiary alcohol). Performed in aqueous sulfuric acid, usually at 0–50 °C. Water acts as both solvent and nucleophile; the acid protonates the central carbon of the allene, allowing water attack at the terminal carbon (Markovnikov orientation).

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) of HBr to 1‑chloropropene; Markovnikov addition places bromine on the more substituted carbon yielding 2‑bromo‑1‑chloropropane; usually performed neat or in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., CCl₄) at room temperature, no external catalyst needed.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of iodobenzene with phenylboronic acid catalysed by bis(benzonitrile)palladium(II) chloride in the presence of potassium carbonate as base and water (often with a co‑solvent such as ethanol or dioxane). Forms biphenyl by creating a C(sp²)–C(sp²) bond; typical conditions are 80–100 °C under inert atmosphere.

SN2 substitution of an ethyl tosylate by iodide ion from sodium iodide, producing ethyl iodide and sodium p‑toluenesulfonate; a classic halide exchange (Finkelstein‑type) to generate a more reactive alkyl halide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often refluxed; NaI is used in excess and no additional catalyst is needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction forming cerium() oxalate (cerous oxalate) as an insoluble solid while ammonium sulfate remains in solution. Typically carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the precipitate is isolated by filtration and washing. No special catalyst is required.

Copper‑mediated Chan–Lam coupling (oxidative C–N bond formation) between phenylboronic acid and diethylamine to afford N,N‑diethylaniline. Copper(II) acetate serves as the catalyst, 2,2‑bipyridine as a ligand, and sodium carbonate as base. The reaction proceeds under aerobic conditions, often in a mixed solvent of MeCN/H₂O or EtOAc/H₂O at room temperature to reflux. By‑products include boric acid and sodium acetate.

Aqueous reductive conversion of nitroguanidine to hydroxyguanidine using sodium dithionite as a mild reducing agent. Sodium dithionite reduces the nitro group to a hydroxylamino (‑NHOH) functionality under neutral to slightly basic pH, typically at 0–25 °C. Reaction carried out in water; the process is useful for generating hydroxy‑substituted guanidines without over‑reduction to amines.

Sandmeyer bromination – Similar to the chlorination, the diazonium salt reacts with copper(I) bromide, converting the diazonium group to bromine and producing bromobenzene, nitrogen gas, and copper(II) bromide. Employed for introduction of bromine onto aromatic rings. Reaction conditions parallel the chlorination: aqueous acidic medium (often HCl), low temperature (0–5 °C) followed by warming; copper(I) bromide serves as the halogen source and catalyst.

The reaction is a nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus, phosphorylating aniline. It produces N-(diethoxyphosphoryl)aniline via nucleophilic attack of the aniline nitrogen on the phosphorus center of diethyl chlorophosphate, with hydrogen chloride as a byproduct. The reaction typically occurs in a polar solvent like ethanol or chloroform, often requiring a base such as triethylamine to neutralize HCl.

This is a redox reaction where sodium hypochlorite oxidizes calcium sulfite to calcium sulfate while being reduced to sodium chloride. The purpose is oxidation of sulfite to sulfate. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solutions under ambient conditions.

Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2) where methanesulfonate anion displaces chloride atoms of 1,4‑dichlorobutane to form busulfan (1,4‑butanediol dimethanesulfonate) and NaCl; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often heated (50‑80 °C) to promote substitution.

The reaction is a copper(II)-catalyzed oxidative C–N bond formation between phenylboronic acid and 4-chloro-2-nitroaniline to produce N-phenylaniline. Pyridine acts as a base or ligand, and oxygen serves as the terminal oxidant. Common solvents include polar aprotic media like DMSO or aqueous alcohols under oxygen atmosphere.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination of 1,2,3‑trichlorobenzene to introduce a fourth chlorine atom, giving 1,2,3,4‑tetrachlorobenzene; Cl₂ is activated by a Lewis‑acid catalyst (e.g., FeCl₃ or AlCl₃) or light; reaction performed in an inert solvent like CCl₄ at modest temperature (0‑25 °C).

Oxidation (hypervalent iodine formation); produces iodosylbenzene using hydrogen peroxide as the oxidant in acidic medium; H₂O₂ transfers an oxygen atom to iodobenzene, forming ArIO and water; usually run in aqueous acetic acid (1–2 M AcOH) at 0–25 °C; reaction mixture may be stirred under mild conditions; no catalyst required.

Hydrogen reduction of a metal oxide; conversion of platinum(IV) oxide back to metallic platinum. Key transformation: PtO2 + H2 → Pt + H2O. Performed at 300–400 °C under a flow of hydrogen (or forming gas) in a tube furnace; solid‑gas reaction, no solvent. Used for regeneration of Pt metal from its oxide.

Alkaline hydrolysis of an N‑acetyl aryl amide; NaOH in water (often with EtOH) at reflux cleaves the amide bond to give the free 3‑chloro‑4‑methylaniline, sodium acetate and water; used to deprotect an acetamide protecting group.

Acid–base reaction of a carbonate with hydrofluoric acid; beryllium carbonate reacts with aqueous HF, yielding soluble beryllium fluoride, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Usually performed at room temperature in aqueous HF; the evolution of CO₂ drives the reaction to completion. No catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization forming a borate salt; boric acid reacts with potassium hydroxide in aqueous solution to give potassium metaborate and water. Typically carried out at ambient temperature in water with stoichiometric 1 : 1 molar ratio; no catalyst required.

Partial neutralization (monobasic salt formation) of tartaric acid with potassium hydroxide; yields potassium hydrogen tartrate and water. Conducted in aqueous medium, often at low temperature to promote crystallization of the tartrate. No special catalyst needed.

Redox (acid‑promoted) generation of chlorine dioxide from chlorate and chlorite ions. Dilute sulfuric acid protonates the oxidants, which are reduced to ClO₂ while sulfate is formed. Reaction is performed in cold aqueous solution (0–5 °C) to control gas evolution; no additional catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to a primary amine. 3,5‑Dimethoxyphenylacetonitrile is reduced with molecular hydrogen over platinum on carbon to afford 3,5‑dimethoxyphenethylamine. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm₂, Pt/C (5–10 % loading), ethanol or methanol as solvent, 25–80 °C. Purpose: synthesis of a phenethylamine building block.

Acid–base metathesis (neutralization) of ammonium metavanadate with sodium hydroxide; produces sodium metavanadate, ammonia gas, and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature, using stoichiometric amounts of NaOH; no catalyst needed.

Gem‑dihalogenation of formaldehyde by hydrobromic acid. Two equivalents of HBr add across the carbonyl, substituting the oxygen and forming dibromomethane with release of water. Usually performed in excess concentrated HBr at 0–25 °C, often in aqueous or alcoholic medium; no additional catalyst is required.

Oxidation (peroxide oxidation) of a tertiary amine to its N‑oxide; RuCl₃ acts as a catalyst to transfer an oxygen atom from H₂O₂ to N,N-dimethyldodecylamine, reducing peroxide to water. Typically performed in a mixed aqueous/organic solvent (e.g., water‑acetonitrile or methanol) at 0–25 °C with 1–5 mol % RuCl₃; no additional reagents required.

Redox (single‑displacement) reaction where metallic zinc reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ while being oxidized to Zn²⁺, yielding ZnCl₂ and FeCl₂. Conducted in aqueous solution, often in dilute HCl to maintain solubility of the iron(II) product; ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Coordination‑complex formation (ligand substitution) of Cr³⁺ from chromium(III) nitrate with thiocyanate and ammonia to give ammonium tetrathiocyanato‑diamminechromate(III) and ammonium nitrate as by‑product. Carried out in aqueous solution with excess NH₃ and NH₄SCN, typically at room temperature to gentle reflux; pH kept neutral to slightly basic; no external catalyst.

General type: N‑alkylation of urea using a strong methylating agent (dimethyl sulfate). Purpose: methylate urea to obtain N‑methylurea. Key transformation: one methyl group of dimethyl sulfate is transferred to the nitrogen of urea, producing N‑methylurea and methyl hydrogen sulfate (MeOSO₃H). Typical conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic medium (often NaOH or Na₂CO₃ solution) at 0–25 °C, with careful control of stoichiometry to avoid over‑methylation. Dimethyl sulfate is used as the methyl donor; no additional catalyst is needed, but a base is essential to capture the acidic by‑product.

Acid‑base double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between hydrochloric acid and ammonium iodate, exchanging the cations to afford iodic acid (HIO₃) and ammonium chloride. Performed in dilute aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base protonation of cyanide; generates hydrogen cyanide gas for use as a reagent; NaCN is protonated by acetic acid to give HCN and sodium acetate; performed in aqueous or ethanolic solution at low temperature (0–25 °C) in a sealed apparatus; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 2‑(2‑bromoethyl)pyridine by ammonia, replacing bromide with an amino group to form 2‑pyridineethanamine; the liberated HBr is captured by excess ammonia as ammonium bromide. Usually carried out in refluxing aqueous ammonia or ethanol solvent, with excess NH₃ to drive the reaction; no catalyst needed.

Hydration (solid‑state incorporation of water) of anhydrous calcium hydrogen phosphate to its dihydrate form. Achieved by exposure to moist air or by dissolving the anhydrous salt in water and recrystallizing; ambient temperature and ambient pressure; no catalyst or solvent beyond water is required.

Acid‑base condensation; SO₃ gas reacts with solid potassium sulfite to give potassium metabisulfite (K₂S₂O₅). Typically carried out by passing SO₃ over heated K₂SO₃ (≈100–150 °C) in a dry‐air or inert atmosphere; no solvent needed.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed): ethyl 2‑mercaptoacetate reacts with water (typically in aqueous NaOH, reflux) to cleave the ethyl ester, producing 2‑mercaptoacetic acid and ethanol; after saponification the mixture is acidified to isolate the thiol acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2/SN1) of a secondary alkyl bromide with sodium hydroxide; the bromide is displaced by hydroxide to give 2‑butanol and NaBr. Performed in aqueous NaOH, often at reflux (≈100 °C) or under milder conditions with polar protic solvent; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2/Hydrolysis); 2‑chlorobutane is converted to 2‑butanol by displacement of chloride with hydroxide ion from potassium hydroxide. Usually performed in aqueous KOH or KOH/ethanol solution, refluxing 60–100 °C; product isolated after acid/base work‑up.

Selective carbonyl reduction; the 1,2‑diketone cyclohexa‑3,5‑diene‑1,2‑dione is reduced by sodium borohydride to catechol (1,2‑dihydroxybenzene) with formation of sodium borate as by‑product. Conducted in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt; NaBH₄ added portionwise, reaction quenched with water.

Acid‑base neutralization / double displacement; sodium bisulfate reacts with calcium hydroxide in aqueous solution to give sodium hydroxide, calcium sulfate precipitate, and water. Performed at ambient temperature in water; solid CaSO₄ is filtered off, leaving NaOH solution.

Hydrolysis of phosphorus oxybromide; POBr₃ reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to afford sodium phosphate (Na₃PO₄) and hydrogen bromide gas. Carried out in cold to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) under stirring; HBr is released and can be captured; the phosphate remains in solution.

Direct combination (halogenation) reaction; chlorine oxidizes elemental vanadium to the +3 oxidation state forming vanadium(III) chloride (VCl₃). Typically carried out by passing dry Cl₂ gas over finely divided vanadium metal heated to 300‑400 °C under anhydrous, inert atmosphere; no solvent required.

Cycloaddition of SO₂ to an epoxide (formation of cyclic sulfite); sulfur dioxide adds to ethylene oxide forming ethylene sulfite, a five‑membered cyclic sulfite ester. Conducted under SO₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often with a base catalyst (e.g., pyridine) at 0–50 °C; product isolated by evaporation and purification.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; sodium cyanide exchanges anion with silver iodide soluble sodium iodide and insoluble silver cyanide precipitate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed Diels‑Alder cycloaddition; cyclopentadiene acts as diene and maleic anhydride as dienophile to give the bridged bicyclic 5‑norbornene‑2,3‑dicarboxylic anhydride. AlCl₃ coordinates to the carbonyls of maleic anhydride increasing its electrophilicity. Commonly run in dry dichloromethane or toluene under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux, with catalytic AlCl₃ (5–10 mol %).

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis/decomposition of hexamethylenetetramine (urotropine) by concentrated H₂SO₄, yielding formaldehyde gas and ammonium sulfate as the stable salt. Reaction is carried out by adding solid or aqueous urotropine to hot concentrated sulfuric acid (≈95 %); temperature 80–120 °C; no additional solvent or catalyst needed.

S‑methylation (alkylation) of 2‑mercaptobenzimidazole with dimethyl sulfate, forming a methyl‑thio‑substituted benzimidazole (thiabendazole analogue) and methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, dichloromethane or pyridine) at 0 °C to room temperature, often in the presence of a mild base (e.g., triethylamine) to neutralize the generated acid.

Oxidative leaching (redox) of nickel sulfide with concentrated nitric acid. Nitric acid oxidizes sulfide to sulfur dioxide, reduces to nitrogen dioxide and simultaneously converts nickel to soluble nickel nitrate. Reaction is performed under reflux with 70–95 % HNO₃, typically in a sealed or fume‑hooded vessel; no catalyst required.

Catalytic oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde using TEMPO (2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine‑1‑oxyl) and sodium hypochlorite (bleach). The TEMPO radical mediates selective oxidation of the primary alcohol under mildly basic aqueous conditions (pH 8–9), often with a co‑catalyst such as NaBr. Solvent is water or a water/organic biphasic mixture (e.g., CH₂Cl₂); reaction proceeds at 0 °C to room temperature, producing water and NaCl as innocuous by‑products.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a thione – 2‑Propanethione (CH3C(=S)CH3) reacts with water to regenerate the carbonyl compound acetone (2‑propanone) and release hydrogen sulfide. The hydrolysis is carried out in aqueous acid (e.g., HCl, pH 1–2) or dilute base, heated to reflux for 1–2 h; no special solvent is required beyond water.

Type: Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation of an amine). Purpose: Synthesize 4‑methoxybenzamide from aniline. Key transformation: The lone pair on the aniline nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon of 4‑methoxybenzoyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming the amide; HCl is generated as a by‑product. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, use of a base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to trap HCl, solvent such as dichloromethane, THF or CHCl₃; reaction often performed under inert atmosphere.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of azide). Purpose: Convert 3‑azidopentane to 3‑pentanamine. Key transformation: The azide functional group (‑N₃) is reduced by H₂/Pd‑C to a primary amine (‑NH₂) with liberation of N₂ gas. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm), 10 % Pd on carbon catalyst, solvent like ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate, temperature from 0 °C reflux as needed; reaction carried out under inert atmosphere.

Carbothermic reduction of germanium monoxide; solid GeO is mixed with carbon and heated to high temperature (≈1000 °C) to yield elemental germanium and carbon monoxide gas. The reaction is a solid‑solid reduction; it is performed in a furnace under an inert or reducing atmosphere, without added catalyst.

Type: Hydrolysis/acid‑base precipitation. Purpose: Generate terbium(III) hydroxide from its acetate and produce acetic acid. Key transformation: Water protonates the acetate ligands, releasing acetic acid and precipitating Tb(OH)₃ as the metal hydroxide. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution, often heated gently to promote precipitation; pH adjusted if needed; no special catalyst required.

Reaction type: strong oxidative cleavage of an alkene (KMnO₄ oxidation). Purpose: convert the alkene into the corresponding carboxylic acids. Key transformation: oxidation of the C=C bond in but‑1‑enylbenzene yields benzoic acid (derived from the benzylic fragment) and propanoic acid (derived from the terminal fragment). Typical conditions: treat the substrate with aqueous KMnO₄ (2–3 equiv) in a mixture of water/acetone or t‑butanol, heat under reflux for several hours, then acidify the mixture (e.g., with HCl) to precipitate the acids. The reaction is performed under basic aqueous conditions; no additional catalyst is needed.

Type: Nucleophilic acyl substitution (urea formation). Purpose: Prepare tetramethylurea from dimethylamine and N,N‑dimethylcarbamoyl chloride. Key transformation: Dimethylamine attacks the carbonyl carbon of the carbamoyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming the urea carbonyl; HCl is produced. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, presence of a base (triethylamine, pyridine) to capture HCl, solvent such dichloromethane or THF; reaction performed under inert atmosphere.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction where nickel(II) nitrate and hydroiodic acid exchange anions to give nickel(II) iodide and nitric acid; performed in water at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst is needed.

Type: SN2 alkylation of a carboxylate (Williamson‑type ester synthesis). Purpose: Form allyl benzoate ester. Key transformation: The benzoate anion performs a backside attack on the primary carbon of allyl bromide, displacing bromide and forming the ester linkage. Typical conditions: Polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, DMSO), mild heating (reflux of solvent), often under nitrogen; no catalyst required; sodium bromide remains in solution.

Type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Purpose: Produce insoluble cadmium chromate and soluble ammonium nitrate. Key transformation: Exchange of counter‑ions between ammonium chromate and cadmium nitrate yields cadmium chromate (CdCrO₄) which precipitates and ammonium nitrate remains in solution. Typical conditions: Aqueous solutions mixed at ambient temperature; stirring until precipitation completes; filtration isolates the solid; no catalyst needed.

Redox (metal displacement) reaction; zinc metal reduces TiCl₄ to TiCl₃, forming ZnCl₂; key transformation: Ti⁴⁺ → Ti³⁺, Zn⁰ → Zn²⁺; carried out in a dry, inert environment at high temperature (≈300–400 °C) in a sealed vessel; no solvent or catalyst required.

Oxidative cleavage of an alkene with potassium permanganate. Converts the propenyl group of 5‑propenyl‑benzo‑1,3‑dioxole to a carboxylic acid, yielding 3,4‑methylenedioxy‑benzoic acid. The substrate is treated with aqueous KMnO4 (often 1.5–2 equiv) under basic conditions (e.g., NaOH) and heated (reflux) or performed at 0 °C for milder oxidation. After the reaction, the mixture is acidified to precipitate the benzoic acid, which is filtered, washed, and purified.

Partial reduction (Béchamp reduction) of nitrobenzene to N‑phenylhydroxylamine using zinc dust in glacial acetic acid; the reaction proceeds under reflux in acidic medium, producing zinc acetate as by‑product and water; purpose is to obtain the hydroxylamine intermediate for further functionalization.

Phenolic O‑acetylation (esterification); acetylates 2‑ethyl phenol with acetic anhydride to give 2‑ethyl phenyl acetate and acetic acid. The reaction is typically base‑catalyzed (pyridine or DMAP) to accelerate acyl transfer and absorb the acid formed. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in dichloromethane or pyridine as solvent.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction between lead(II) acetate and sodium sulfite in aqueous solution; lead(II) sulfite, which is poorly soluble, precipitates while sodium acetate remains in solution; typically carried out at ambient temperature with water as solvent.

Acid‑base dissolution of strontium orthophosphate with concentrated hydrochloric acid; the phosphate is protonated to give phosphoric acid and strontium chloride dissolves in the aqueous medium; usually performed with excess HCl and heating to ensure complete conversion.

Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary allylic alcohol using LiAlH4; strong hydride donor that converts the C=O of cinnamaldehyde to a C–OH while preserving the C=C double bond; typically performed in anhydrous ether (Et2O or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; purpose: synthesis of cinnamyl alcohol.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); purpose is to convert cyanic acid to its sodium salt for use as a cyanate source; key transformation is deprotonation of HNCO to give the OCN⁻ anion which pairs with Na⁺ to form NaNCO, with water as the by‑product; typical conditions are aqueous solution at ambient temperature (0–25 °C); common solvent is water; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 2‑chlorobenzonitrile to 2‑chlorobenzoic acid; refluxing the nitrile in aqueous hydrochloric acid (often with a water/acid mixture) converts the –CN group to a carboxyl group, releasing ammonium chloride; purpose is synthesis of the corresponding aryl acid.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; converts the nitrile group of 3‑pyridine carbonitrile to a carboxylic acid, yielding nicotinic acid while the nitrogen is released as ammonium chloride. Typically performed by refluxing the nitrile in aqueous hydrochloric acid (excess water) at 80‑120 °C; water is the solvent and the HCl serves as the catalyst.

Oxidation of bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfide (a thioether) to bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfoxide using hydrogen peroxide in the presence of sodium molybdate as a molybdenum‑based catalyst; the reaction is typically performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent at mild temperature, with water generated as the only stoichiometric by‑product.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; used to exchange anions and isolate insoluble mercuric sulfate. Sodium sulfate and mercuric nitrate are mixed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring, leading formation of solid HgSO4 which precipitates and sodium nitrate remains dissolved. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Transesterification; converts a methyl ester to the corresponding ethyl ester, exchanging the alkoxy group. The methyl 2,2-dichloroacetate reacts with excess ethanol, producing ethyl 2,2-dichloroacetate and methanol. Typically catalyzed by a Brønsted acid (e.g., H2SO4) or a base (e.g., NaOMe) under reflux. Ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent; removal of methanol drives the equilibrium forward.

Anion metathesis (acid–base exchange); hydrochloric acid protonates the nitrate anion of tetrabutylammonium nitrate, producing nitric acid and tetrabutylammonium chloride. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); removes the chloro substituent from 2‑chloro‑N‑phenylacetamide to give N‑phenylacetamide, generating HCl. Typically performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with Pd/C (5–10 % wt) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature to reflux; the reaction is used to deprotect halogenated amides.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of pentan‑3‑yl 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetate back to pentan‑3‑ol and trifluoroacetic acid; purpose is de‑protection of the ester. Key transformation: R‑CH(OCOCF₃)‑R′ + H₂O → R‑CH(OH)‑R′ + CF₃CO₂H. Typical conditions: aqueous dilute acid (e.g., 0.1 M HCl) or aqueous TFA, reflux in a mixture of water/THF or MeOH, 1–4 h; neutralize and extract product.

Double displacement precipitation of mercuric cyanide. Mercuric chloride reacts with ammonium cyanide in aqueous solution, usually kept cold (0–5 °C) to limit decomposition of cyanide. The insoluble Hg(CN)₂ precipitates, while ammonium chloride stays in solution. No catalyst is needed; water is the solvent.

Fischer esterification of a carboxylic acid with ethanol; cinnamic acid is converted to ethyl cinnamate with loss of water. Conducted by refluxing cinnamic acid with excess ethanol and catalytic H₂SO₄ (≈5 % v/v) at 60–80 °C; the reaction is often run in a simple ethanol solvent.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous lead(II) acetate mixed with ammonium carbonate causes insoluble lead(II) carbonate to precipitate and soluble ammonium acetate to remain in solution; performed at room temperature in water.

Catalytic hydrogenation – reduction of an alkene to an alkane. Hydrogen gas adds across the C=C bond of 1‑hexene, converting it to hexane. Typically performed with copper chromite (CuCr₂O₄) as a heterogeneous catalyst under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 50–150 °C. Reactions are often run in an inert solvent such as ethanol, cyclohexane or occasionally neat liquid substrate.

Buchwald‑Hartwig amination (palladium‑catalyzed C–N cross‑coupling) converting 1‑bromo‑4‑fluorobenzene to 4‑fluoroaniline with ammonia as the nucleophile; hydrogen bromide is released. Typical conditions: Pd source (e.g., Pd₂(dba)₃ or Pd(OAc)₂), bidentate phosphine ligand (BINAP, Xantphos), base (NaOtBu or KOtBu), solvent such as toluene or dioxane, temperature 80–120 °C, inert atmosphere. The reaction forms the aryl amine and HBr by‑product.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of codeine to dihydrocodeine using platinum(IV) oxide (Adams catalyst). Hydrogen gas (1–3 atm) is passed through a suspension of codeine and PtO₂ in an alcoholic solvent (methanol or ethanol) at 20–50 °C. The reaction reduces the 7,8‑double bond, yielding dihydrocodeine; the can be filtered off after completion.

Williamson thioether synthesis (nucleophilic substitution, S_N2). Sulfide ion from sodium sulfide attacks ethyl bromide to form diethyl sulfide and sodium bromide. Typically performed in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO, often at reflux temperature; aqueous Na2S or Na2S dissolved in ethanol can also be used.
Hydrolysis of an acetal. Cleavage of the acetal group with water to regenerate the aldehyde and ethanol. Typically catalyzed by acidic conditions (e.g., dilute HCl), moderate heat.

Acylation (acetylation) of an alcohol. The hydroxyl group of methylazoxymethanol reacts with acetic anhydride to give the acetate ester (methylazoxymethanol acetate) and acetic acid as by‑product. Usually carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base catalyst such as pyridine to scavenge the generated acid.

Fischer esterification of creatine. Concentrated sulfuric acid catalyzes the reaction of the carboxylic acid functionality of creatine with methanol, producing the methyl ester of creatine and water. Conducted by refluxing methanol with excess H₂SO₄ (or using a catalytic amount) and removing water (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage (hydrolysis). Concentrated sulfuric acid protonates cyclopentyl methyl ether, leading to cleavage of the C–O bond and formation of cyclopentanol and methanol. Performed by heating the ether with 95–100 % H₂SO₄ (often under reflux); the reaction mixture itself serves as solvent.

Oxidation of methyl phenyl sulfide to the sulfoxide using potassium peroxymonosulfate (Oxone). This is a convenient solid oxidant for selective sulfoxidation. Key transformation: peroxymonosulfate delivers an electrophilic oxygen to sulfur, the S=O bond; by‑products are potassium bisulfate (KHSO₄) and water. Typical conditions: 1.11.5 eq Oxone in a mixture of acetonitrile/water or acetone/water (1:1 to 3:1), at room temperature, pH adjusted ~7–8 (often using NaHCO₃); reaction proceeds within 30 min to 2 h without additional catalyst.

Electrophilic halogen addition; 1‑hexene undergoes addition of Br₂ across the C=C double bond to give 1,2‑dibromohexane; carried out in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, no catalyst required.

Redox oxidation of Cu(I) by hydrogen peroxide. H₂O₂ oxidizes copper(I) chloride to copper(II) chloride while being reduced to water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds readily in mildly acidic media (pH ≈ 5–7) and may be used in catalytic cycles such as Fenton‑type oxidations.

Halide exchange (metathesis) between aluminum bromide and hydroiodic acid. AlBr₃ reacts with HI to replace bromide with iodide, yielding aluminum iodide and hydrogen bromide gas. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often at 0 °C to 25 °C, in an inert atmosphere (dry solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or toluene) to prevent hydrolysis of AlI₃.

Strong oxidizing redox reaction where nitric acid oxidizes arsenous acid (As(III)) to arsenic acid (As(V)) while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas and water is formed. Conducted by heating the mixture of acids (often under reflux) in a glass vessel; acidic aqueous medium.

Nucleophilic substitution between o-cresol and epichlorohydrin under basic conditions. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates the phenolic hydroxyl, forming a phenoxide that attacks the terminal epoxide carbon of epichlorohydrin. The reaction produces o-cresyl glycidyl ether with sodium chloride and water as byproducts. It is typically carried out in aqueous or polar aprotic solvents (e.g., ethanol/water mixtures) at moderate temperatures.

Solid‑state chalcogenide metathesis; high‑temperature synthesis of manganese telluride by exchanging sulfur for tellurium. Typically performed by grinding MnS and elemental Te, sealing in a quartz tube under vacuum, and heating to 800‑1000 °C for several hours; no solvent or catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of iodoethene with phenylboronic acid; purpose is to construct a C(sp²)–C(sp²) bond to afford styrene. Key transformation: CH2=CH‑I + C6H5‑B(OH)2 → C6H5‑CH=CH2 + B(OH)3. Typical conditions: Pd(PPh₃)₄ or PdCl₂(dppf) (2‑5 mol %), base (K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃), mixed solvent (THF/H₂O or dioxane/H₂O), reflux 8‑12 h under N₂.

Base‑promoted O‑alkylation followed by intramolecular cyclization to form 4‑methylangelicin. Sodium hydride deprotonates the phenolic OH of 7‑hydroxy‑4‑methylcoumarin, which then attacks 2‑methylallyl bromide in an SN2 step. The resulting allyl ether undergoes a thermal or acid‑catalyzed Claisen‑type rearrangement to give the angelicin skeleton. Conducted in dry DMF (or THF) under nitrogen, 0 °C to room temperature, with NaH added portionwise.

Metal‑acid reduction of nitrobenzene to aniline using zinc and hydrochloric acid; purpose: synthesis of aniline; nitro group is fully reduced to primary amine with formation of water and ZnCl2; performed by adding Zn powder to aqueous HCl and heating (reflux) or at 60–80 °C; solvent is water.

Phosphorylation condensation to produce the anticancer agent thiotepa. Three equivalents of aziridine act as nucleophiles toward thiophosphoryl trichloride (PSCl₃), forming three P–N bonds and releasing three equivalents of HCl. The reaction is usually run in anhydrous ether or THF at 0 °C to 25 °C, with an external base (e.g., triethylamine) or a solid HCl scavenger to neutralize the acid; no further catalyst is needed.

Hydrogenolysis (catalytic dehalogenation). Purpose: remove the chlorine from 2‑chloroquinoline to regenerate the parent heteroaromatic. Key transformation: C–Cl bond reduced to C–H, producing quinoline and HCl. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–3 atm) over 10 % Pd/C in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol or EtOAc) at room temperature to 50 °C, often under reflux. No additional catalyst needed; HCl is released into the reaction mixture.

Reaction type: conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅). Purpose: generate the acyl chloride for further synthetic steps. Key transformation: –COOH is replaced by –COCl, producing POCl₃ and HCl as stoichiometric by‑products. Typical conditions: addition of solid PCl₅ to the acid in anhydrous solvent at 0 °C, then stirring at room temperature or gentle reflux. Common solvents/catalysts: carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, or dichloromethane; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst, but an inert atmosphere is recommended.

Transesterification; similar alkoxy exchange where ethanol replaces the butyl group of n‑butyl hexanoate to give ethyl hexanoate and n‑butanol. Conducted under acidic (e.g., H₂SO₄) or basic (e.g., NaOEt) catalysis, usually refluxing in a dry solvent like toluene, xylene, or under solvent‑free conditions; removal of n‑butanol or excess ethanol shifts equilibrium toward products.

Acid hydrolysis of metal phosphide; hydrochloric acid protonates zinc phosphide, releasing phosphine gas and forming zinc chloride in solution; typically done in aqueous HCl at low temperature to control gas evolution; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Oxidative redox of iodide by concentrated sulfuric acid; production of iodine and sulfur dioxide. Concentrated H₂SO₄ oxidizes iodide (from HI) to I₂ while being reduced to SO₂, with water formed. Reaction is performed under heating, often in a sealed apparatus; no catalyst required.

Baeyer‑Villiger oxidation of 2‑methoxyacetophenone with m‑chloroperbenzoic acid. The peracid inserts an oxygen adjacent to the carbonyl, converting the ketone into methyl 2‑methoxybenzoate, while the peracid is reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Typically carried out in dry CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to rt, using 1.1–1.2 equivalents of mCPBA; the reaction is quenched with aqueous sodium sulfite.

LiAlH₄ reduction of phenylacetaldehyde to 2‑phenylethanol. The strong hydride donor adds to the aldehyde carbonyl, forming the alkoxide which upon aqueous work‑up gives the primary alcohol. Conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen; the reaction is quenched carefully with water then dilute acid.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Aqueous potassium chromate and mercury(II) nitrate exchange ions; insoluble mercury(II) chromate precipitates while potassium nitrate stays dissolved. Performed at ambient temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base (sulfation) reaction of calcium carbonate with sulfur trioxide. SO₃ acts as an acidic oxide, reacting with CaCO₃ to release CO₂ and form solid calcium sulfate (gypsum). Conducted at elevated temperature (typically 300–500 °C) in a dry gas‑solid or furnace setup; no solvent or catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of α‑pinene. Molecular H₂ adds across the C=C bond of α‑pinene to give the saturated hydrocarbon pinane. Carried out in an inert solvent (e.g., ethanol, ether, cyclohexane) with a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni, at 1–5 atm H₂ and 25–80 °C.

Oxidation (combustion) of terbium phosphide in oxygen; forms terbium phosphate. Key transformation: TbP + 2 O₂ → TbPO₄. Performed by heating the solid phosphide in air or pure O₂ at 300–600 °C; solid‑state, no solvent or catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution forming a hydroxamic acid. Acetyl chloride reacts with N‑methylhydroxylamine (generated from its HCl salt) to afford N‑methylacetohydroxamic acid, with two equivalents of HCl liberated. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (THF or CH₂Cl₂) in the presence of a base such as triethylamine or pyridine, typically at 0 °C to room temperature to neutralize the released HCl.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose is to exchange the methyl ester for an ethyl ester. Sodium ethoxide generated in ethanol deprotonates ethanol, which then attacks the carbonyl of methyl 4‑chlorobenzoate, displacing methoxide and forming ethyl 4‑chlorobenzoate with methanol as by‑product. The reaction is typically refluxed in excess ethanol (or ethanol/solvent) with catalytic NaOEt (10–20 mol %) at 70–80 °C until equilibrium is driven toward product, often aided by removal of methanol.

Oxidative conversion of toluene to benzoate by permanganate. In alkaline aqueous medium (KOH), potassium permanganate oxidizes the methyl group of toluene to a carboxylate, yielding potassium benzoate; MnO₂ precipitates and additional KOH is formed. Reaction is run at reflux (≈80 °C) with excess KMnO₄; after completion the mixture is filtered to remove MnO₂ and the benzoate is isolated by acidification.

Oxidation; converts a hydroquinone-type diol to a quinone using potassium ferricyanide as the oxidant; the two phenolic hydroxyl groups are dehydrogenated to carbonyls forming 1,4‑naphthoquinone; typically performed in aqueous (often slightly alkaline) solution at room temperature; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Single‑displacement redox (metal displacement); copper metal placed in aqueous silver(I) nitrate solution reduces Ag⁺ to metallic silver while being oxidized to Cu²⁺, forming copper(II) nitrate; reaction proceeds at room temperature with stirring, no additional catalyst required.

Aminolysis of an ester (ester‑amide exchange); morpholine attacks methyl nonanoate to give N‑nonanoylmorpholine (an amide) and methanol as the leaving alcohol; generally carried out by heating the ester and amine together, often under reflux in a non‑protic solvent such as toluene or xylene, with removal of methanol to drive the reaction; no catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange; potassium nitrate and lead(II) chromate exchange anions to form potassium chromate and lead(II) nitrate; usually conducted in aqueous solution with both salts dissolved; ambient temperature; water is the reaction medium, no special catalyst.

Hydration (salt hydration); anhydrous magnesium perchlorate absorbs water to form the hexahydrate crystal Mg(ClO₄)₂·6H₂O; achieved by dissolving the salt in water and allowing crystallization upon cooling or slow evaporation at ambient temperature.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) of a. tantalum pentachloride is converted to tantalum pentafluoride while releasing chlorine gas; the reaction involves direct elemental fluorine replacing chloride ligands on Ta; performed in a sealed reaction vessel at elevated temperature (often 200–400 °C) under an inert atmosphere; fluorine gas is the reagent, no catalyst is required.

Precipitation/neutralization double‑displacement; aqueous ammonium hydroxide provides hydroxide ions that react with magnesium iodide to precipitate insoluble magnesium hydroxide and form soluble ammonium iodide; carried out in water at room temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Metathesis precipitation; iron(III) nitrate and potassium ferrocyanide exchange ions to produce insoluble iron(III) ferrocyanide (precursor to Prussian blue) and soluble potassium nitrate; typically performed in aqueous solution with both salts dissolved, often at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (Fischer–Speier ether synthesis); two molecules of 2‑propanol condense under the action of methanesulfonic acid to form diisopropyl ether with loss of water. Conducted by heating the mixture (≈80 °C) in excess methanesulfonic acid, which acts both as catalyst and solvent; water is removed continuously (e.g., Dean‑Stark) to drive the equilibrium.

oxidation (combustion) of gallium sulfide to gallium oxide; purpose is to convert Ga2S3 into the more stable oxide and liberate SO2; key transformation: S2‑ → SO2 and Ga3+ remains in oxide; typical conditions: heating solid Ga2S3 in air or O2 flow at 500‑800 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Kumada coupling (cross‑coupling) of a Grignard reagent with an aryl bromide using CuI as catalyst; purpose is to form a biaryl (biphenyl). Key transformation: phenyl‑MgBr transfers phenyl to bromobenzene, producing biphenyl and MgBr2. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF, inert atmosphere (N2), CuI (5–10 mol %), 0 °C to reflux, 1–4 h.

Disulfur reacts with chlorine gas in a halogenation/disproportionation reaction to give sulfur dichloride and elemental sulfur; typically performed dry, at room temperature or slightly below, under an inert atmosphere without solvent.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt formation); copper(II) oxide reacts with trifluoromethanesulfonic acid to give copper(II) trifluoromethanesulfonate (Cu(OTf)₂) and water. Usually carried out at 0–25 °C in a dry organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN) under inert atmosphere.

Metathesis (salt exchange) reaction; exchanges potassium and sodium cations between hydroxide and dihydrogen arsenate to give sodium hydroxide and potassium dihydrogen arsenate; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration; mixed fuming nitric acid and sulfuric acid generate the nitronium ion which attacks ortho‑nitroanisole to introduce a second nitro group at the para position forming 2,4‑dinitroanisole; carried out at 0–5 °C to control rate, then warmed to room temperature; the reaction medium is the acid mixture itself, no additional solvent or catalyst needed.

Fischer esterification of decanoic acid with tert‑butanol to form the tert‑butyl ester; strong acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) under reflux, often using excess tert‑butanol as solvent and removing water to promote ester formation.

Alcoholysis of a metal halide (vanadium(V) oxytrichloride) in the presence of a base; three equivalents of isopropanol replace the chloride ligands to give vanadium(V) triisopropoxide oxide, while triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl as triethylammonium chloride; conducted under anhydrous conditions (dry inert atmosphere) in a non‑protic solvent such as THF or toluene, often with reflux; no external catalyst.

Enzymatic (PLP‑dependent) decarboxylation of 5‑hydroxy‑L‑tryptophan; converts the α‑carboxyl group of the amino acid to CO₂, producing 5‑hydroxytryptamine (serotonin); key transformation is loss of CO₂ and formation of a primary amine; carried out in aqueous buffer at physiological pH (≈7.0) with pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate as cofactor; no organic solvent required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; water attacks ethyl 4‑chlorobutanoate, cleaving the ester bond to produce 4‑chlorobutanoic acid and ethanol; typically carried out in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., dilute HCl) with heating under reflux; solvent is water or a water‑alcohol mixture; no additional catalyst beyond the acid.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 3‑methylbutyl benzoate; water attacks the ester carbonyl under acidic conditions, regenerating benzoic acid and 3‑methyl‑1‑butanol; performed by refluxing the ester in aqueous HCl (or dilute H₂SO₄) for 1–3 h, then separating the acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alcohol with thionyl bromide to the corresponding alkyl bromide; used to convert 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol into 1‑bromo‑2,2‑dimethylpropane. The alcohol reacts with SOBr₂, typically in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, in the presence of a base such as pyridine to trap HBr. By‑products are sulfur dioxide gas and hydrogen bromide.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation of a transition‑metal chromate; sodium chromate in aqueous solution reacts with nickel(II) nitrate to give insoluble nickel(II) chromate (green precipitate) and soluble sodium nitrate. Conducted in water at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; the precipitate is isolated by filtration and washed.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between a metal bromide and chlorine gas; uranium tetrabromide reacts with chlorine gas to produce uranium tetrachloride and elemental bromine. The reaction requires elevated temperature (often 200–400 °C) in a sealed tube or reactor under an inert atmosphere to prevent side reactions; it is a gas‑solid exchange without solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed epoxide ring‑opening of 2‑butyloxirane with methanol; methanol acts as a nucleophile, attacking the more substituted carbon of the epoxide to give 2‑methoxy‑1‑butanol (a β‑alkoxy alcohol). Typical conditions use a protic acid catalyst such as p‑toluenesulfonic acid or dilute H₂SO₄ in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., methanol itself serves as solvent) at ambient temperature or mild heating.

Oxidation – Oxone (potassium peroxymonosulfate) oxidizes bis(2‑oroethyl) sulfide (a sulfide) to the corresponding sulfoxide. The sulfur atom is converted from a sulfide (S⁰) to a sulfoxide (S⁺⁺=O) while chloride remains attached to the ethyl groups. The reaction is carried out in aqueous media, often at room temperature, using water or a water‑acetone mixture as solvent; no additional catalyst is required. It is employed for detoxification of mustard‑type agents, yielding a less toxic sulfoxide and producing water and potassium bisulfate as by‑products.

Oxidation (halogen oxidation) – Chlorine gas oxidizes rhenium(V) chloride to rhenium(VI) chloride. Two equivalents of ReCl₅ are converted to two equivalents of ReCl₆, with Cl₂ reduced to two equivalents of chloride ion that become part of the ReCl₆ product. The reaction is conducted under anhydrous conditions, typically in a non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dry chloroform, at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) in a sealed tube or under an inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution – Acetyl chloride reacts with ammonium cyanide, where the cyanide anion displaces chloride on the carbonyl carbon to give acetyl cyanide. Ammonium chloride is formed as the inorganic by‑product. The transformation is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dry ether or THF, using a stoichiometric amount of₄CN dissolved in minimal water or ethanol; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Double displacement acid‑base metathesis; purpose is to produce bismuth phosphate precipitate and generate sulfuric acid; key transformation is Bi₂(SO₄)₃(aq) + 2 H₃PO₄(aq) → 2 BiPO₄(s) + 3 H₂SO₄(aq); performed in water, often with gentle heating to dissolve the bismuth sulfate; ambient pressure; water solvent; no catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of phenyl 2‑bromoacetate with sodium cyanide to afford phenyl 2‑cyanoacetate and sodium bromide; cyanide displaces bromide in a single‑step backside attack; reaction is conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) at 50–80 °C under anhydrous conditions; the by‑product NaBr remains in solution.

Syn‑dihydroxylation (cis‑diol formation) – Catalytic osmium tetroxide adds across the double bond of 2,3‑dimethyl‑2‑butene to give the vicinal diol known as pinacol (2,3‑dimethyl‑2,3‑butanediol N‑Methylmorpholine N‑oxide (NMO) serves as a stoichiometric co‑ant that regenerates OsO₄ from the reduced Os(VI) species. Typical conditions are 5 mol % OsO₄, 1–2 equiv NMO, in a mixture of tert‑butanol/water or acetone/water, at 0–25 °C, often under ambient pressure.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) – Potassium hydroxide hydrolyzes 2‑pentyl acetate to give 2‑pentanol and potassium acetate. The ester carbonyl is attacked by hydroxide, leading to cleavage of the C–O bond and formation of the alcohol. The reaction is performed in aqueous KOH, frequently with ethanol or methanol as co‑solvent, and heated under reflux (60–80 °C) until completion. No additional catalyst is required.

Acid–base double displacement (metathesis) to exchange anions; purpose is to produce praseodymium(III) perchlorate and free acetic acid; key transformation is proton transfer from perchloric acid to acetate, forming acetate‑derived acetic acid and perchlorate salt; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the common solvent, no catalyst required.

Nitrosation of a thiol. L‑Cysteine is reacted with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO₂ and HCl) to convert the sulfhydryl group into an S‑nitroso derivative, S‑nitroso‑L‑cysteine, with release of water. Reaction is carried out in aqueous acidic medium (pH ≈ 2–3) at 0–5 °C to minimize side reactions; excess nitrous acid is avoided. No catalyst is required.

Simple acid–base neutralization (metathesis); purpose is to convert lithium acetate to lithium nitrate and liberate acetic acid; key transformation is proton transfer from nitric acid to acetate ion; usually performed in water at room temperature; water serves as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis of an acid chloride (neutralization); purpose is to generate the carboxylate salt (sodium octanoate) while eliminating CO₂ and H₂O; key steps are nucleophilic attack of bicarbonate on the acyl chloride, release of CO₂ and formation of chloride ion; commonly done in an ice‑bath or cold aqueous medium, often with a biphasic organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) to extract the product; sodium bicarbonate acts as the base, no additional catalyst.

Type: Photochemical elimination (photo‑induced fragmentation). Purpose: Generate an o‑quinone methide intermediate for cycloaddition, nucleophilic trapping, or polymerization studies. Key transformation: UV irradiation cle C–O bond of 2‑hydroxybenzyl acetate, expelling acetic acid and forming the conjugated o‑quinone methide. Typical conditions: Irradiation at 300–350 nm in an aprotic solvent (e.g., benzene, acetonitrile, or dichloromethane) under nitrogen; reaction time 10 min to several hours depending on light intensity. No added catalyst.

Borane‑mediated reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol; purpose is to obtain 1‑phenylethanol from acetophenone; key transformation is hydride transfer from pyridine‑borane to the carbonyl carbon, generating the alcohol and free pyridine; typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; pyridine‑borane itself serves as the reducing reagent, no external catalyst.

Transesterification (alkoxy exchange) between methanol and an ethyl ester; purpose is to replace the ethyl group with a methyl group, yielding methyl 3‑(dimethylamino)propanoate and ethanol; key step is nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonyl carbon of the ester, followed by departure of ethanol; commonly performed under reflux with an acid catalyst (e.g., p‑tosic acid) or a base catalyst (e.g., NaOEt) in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or directly under solvent‑free conditions using azeotropic removal of ethanol; catalyst is required to accelerate the exchange.

Acid–base neutralization; strong base (tribasic potassium phosphate) reacts with strong acid (hydrochloric acid) to exchange cations, yielding soluble potassium chloride and phosphoric acid; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with gentle heating to ensure complete conversion; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 2‑chloropentane with sulfide ion; purpose is synthesis of a thioether (di‑n‑pentyl sulfide). The sulfide anion (from Na2S) attacks the primary alkyl chloride, displacing chloride to form the C‑S‑C bond while NaCl precipitates. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at reflux temperature; solid Na2S is used in stoichiometric amount.

Hydrazinolysis (nucleophilic substitution) of N‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)phthalimide with hydrazine; used to deprotect the phthalimide group and liberate ethanolamine while forming phthalhydrazide. Hydrazine attacks the imide carbonyl, opening the ring and releasing the primary amine. Typically performed in refluxing ethanol or methanol, sometimes with a slight excess of aqueous hydrazine, under inert atmosphere.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; employed to precipitate manganese(II) oxalate for purification or analysis; MnSO4·H2O(aq) + K2C2O4(aq) → MnC2O4(s) + K2SO4(aq); done in water at room temperature with stirring; water as solvent; no catalyst.

Acid‑base solid‑gas reaction; preparation of magnesium sulfate; sulfur trioxide gas reacts with solid magnesium oxide to give magnesium sulfate; typically carried out at 200‑300 °C in a dry furnace; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑promoted decomposition of magnesium peroxide; redox/acid‑base reaction. Hydrochloric acid protonates the peroxide, generating hydrogen peroxide which subsequently decomposes to water and oxygen; simultaneously Mg2+ forms MgCl2. Usually carried out in aqueous HCl (≈2 M) at ambient to mild heating, with vigorous stirring; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑base proton transfer (neutralization) between hydrogen bromide and lithium acetate; HBr (strong acid) protonates the acetate ion to give acetic acid, and Li+ pairs with Br− to form LiBr. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; the reaction is rapid and quantitative.

Finkelstein halide exchange (SN2) converting ethyl bromide to ethyl iodide using sodium iodide; purpose is preparation of the more reactive alkyl iodide. Iodide ion displaces bromide on the primary carbon; NaBr precipitates out, driving the reaction forward. Typically run in dry acetone as solvent at reflux; excess NaI and removal of precipitated NaBr enhance yield.

Acid‑base precipitation (double‑replacement) of lead(II) oxide with arsenious acid. Type: precipitation/neutralization reaction. Purpose: form lead arsenite, an insoluble heavy‑metal compound. Key transformation: PbO + H₃AsO₃ → PbHAsO₃ (lead arsenite) + H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring until precipitate forms, filtration and washing. Water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.
