Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation); purpose to synthesize hexan‑3‑yl acetate from hexan‑3‑ol; acetic acid is protonated by catalytic H₂SO₄, the alcohol attacks the carbonyl, and water is eliminated; common conditions: reflux (≈80 °C) with a Dean‑Stark trap or excess acid to remove water; solvent often toluene or the reactants are used neat; sulfuric acid serves both as catalyst and dehydrating agent.

Acid‑base neutralization; the hydroxide ion abstracts a proton from hydrochloric acid producing water and the tetrabutylammonium cation pairs with chloride to give tetrabutylammonium chloride, often used as a phase‑transfer catalyst; typically performed in aqueous solution at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Peracid oxidation of a tertiary amine to its N‑oxide; purpose to generate N,N‑dimethylbenzylamine N‑oxide; m‑chloroperbenzoic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the nitrogen, producing the N‑oxide and m‑chlorobenzoic acid as by‑product; typically carried out in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; stoichiometric mCPBA (≈1.1 eq) is used; reaction mixture may be washed with sodium bicarbonate to remove acid.

Thiourea formation from cyanamide and hydrogen sulfide; a condensation (thio‑addition) where H₂S adds across the C≡N bond to give the thio‑amide (thiourea); performed in aqueous medium at 50–100 °C under an H₂S atmosphere, sometimes with a slight acidic buffer to keep H₂S dissolved; used for laboratory synthesis of thiourea.

LiAlH₄ reduction of an amide to a secondary amine; purpose to convert phenyl(piperidin‑1‑yl)methanone (an amide) into 1‑benzylpiperidine; LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, then the intermediate collapses, yielding the amine and Al‑containing by‑products; carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, initially at 0 °C then refluxed for several hours; reaction is quenched carefully with water then dilute acid.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an unsaturated methyl ester; purpose to saturate the C=C bond of methyl (Z)-octadec‑9‑enoate, giving methyl octadecanoate (methyl stearate); H₂ adds across the double bond in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni; typical conditions: 1–3 atm H₂, solvent ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–60 °C; reaction proceeds to completion without affecting the ester function.

Type: aqueous hydrolysis of a metal fluorosilicate (salt decomposition). Purpose: liberates hydrofluoric acid and converts the silicate to silicic acid while precipitating barium fluoride. Key transformation: H2O attacks the Si–F bonds of BaSiF6, producing 4 HF, H4SiO4 (silicic acid) and BaF2 solid. Conditions: aqueous medium, often heated to promote complete hydrolysis. Solvent/catalyst: water acts as both reactant and solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Type: double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction, acid‑base neutralization. Purpose: preparation of insoluble yttrium phosphate and removal of yttrium from solution. Key transformation: phosphate anions from phosphoric acid combine with Y³⁺ ions to give YPO4 precipitate, while Na⁺ pairs with SO4²⁻ to form soluble Na2SO4; water is formed from acid‑base neutralization. Conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; often the mixture is heated to improve dissolution and precipitation. Solvent/catalyst: water; no catalyst needed.

Type: acid‑base proton transfer (salt metathesis). Purpose: generation of sulfamic acid from its ammonium salt. Key transformation: HCl protonates the sulfamate anion, yielding H2NSO3H (sulfamic acid) and ammonium chloride as by‑product. Conditions: aqueous solution, typically at room temperature; the reaction is rapid and exothermic. Solvent/catalyst: water; no catalyst required.

Oxidative chlorination (halogenation) to regenerate a higher‑valent chloride; ReCl3 is exposed to chlorine gas at 200–300 °C, often in a sealed vessel, resulting in formation of ReCl5. No additional catalyst; the reaction may be conducted in the gas phase or with a slight excess of Cl2 as reagent.

Type: selective reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H). Purpose: obtain 2‑fluoroacetaldehyde while preserving the aldehyde functional group. Key transformation: DIBAL‑H delivers a hydride to the carbonyl carbon of ethyl 2‑fluoroacetate, reducing the ester to the corresponding aldehyde; the ethoxy fragment is released as ethanol. Conditions: low temperature (‑78 °C to ‑20 °C), dry, inert atmosphere; reaction typically run in an aprotic solvent such as THF. Solvent/catalyst: anhydrous THF; DIBAL‑H is the reagent, no additional catalyst.

Redox reduction of iodylbenzene to iodobenzene using sodium sulfite; the IO2 group is reduced from iodine(V) to iodine(I) while sulfite is oxidized to sulfate; serves to quench the oxidant and generate iodobenzene as a benign by‑product; typically performed in a mixed aqueous–organic medium (e.g., water/acetone or water/MeCN) at ambient temperature under neutral to slightly acidic conditions; no catalyst required.

Type: Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed condensation). Purpose: synthesis of propyl acetate from acetic acid and n‑propyl alcohol. Key transformation: the carbonyl oxygen of acetic acid is protonated, facilitating nucleophilic attack by the alcohol; after proton transfers and loss of water, propyl acetate is formed. Conditions: reflux in the presence of excess acetic acid or removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation); reaction time ranges from 1 h to several hours. Solvent/catalyst: concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as the acid catalyst; the reaction can be performed neat or in a non‑reactive solvent such as toluene.

Type: high‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of a metal phosphide. Purpose: convert cadmium phosphide to its oxide and phosphorus pentoxide, often as a step in material processing or waste treatment. Key transformation: elemental oxygen oxidizes Cd₃P₂, breaking P–Cd bonds to give CdO and P₂O₅. Conditions: elevated temperature (typically >400 °C) in a flow of pure O₂ or air; solid‑state reaction. Solvent/catalyst: none; the reaction proceeds thermally without added solvent or catalyst.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of indole at the C‑3 position; purpose is to install a propionyl carbonyl onto the heteroaromatic ring. The electrophile is generated from propionyl chloride and AlCl₃, which also acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst. Typical conditions are anhydrous, inert atmosphere, 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon disulfide. By‑product is HCl, which is scavenged by the excess AlCl₃.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of tert‑butanol to isobutylene using methanesulfonic acid; purpose identical to reaction 3; key transformation is the same E1 elimination; typical conditions are 40‑80 °C with dry methanesulfonic acid (10‑20 mol %) in anhydrous solvent (toluene, CH₂Cl₂) or neat, under inert atmosphere; water formed is removed by azeotropic distillation or by using a Dean‑Stark trap.

Free‑radical bromination (photochemical substitution). Purpose: install a bromine atom on the cyclopropane framework. Key transformation: homolytic cleavage of Br₂ under UV light generates Br· radicals that abstract a hydrogen from methylcyclopropane, forming a cyclopropyl radical which then recombines with Br· to give 1‑bromo‑2‑methylcyclopropane. Typical conditions: UV irradiation (≈254 nm), dilute solution of substrate in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, ambient temperature, inert atmosphere.

Ester reduction with LiAlH4; converts 3‑methyl phenyl acetate to 3‑methyl phenol and ethanol by cleaving the ester C–O bond and reducing the carbonyl to a primary alcohol; typically performed with 1–2 equiv LiAlH4 in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous acidic work‑up.

Acid‑catalyzed ether synthesis; triethyl oxonium tetrafluoroborate activates ethanol to give an ethyl oxonium intermediate that undergoes SN2 with a second ethanol molecule to form symmetrical diethyl ether; by‑product is tetrafluoroboric acid. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile under atmosphere.

Base‑catalyzed saponification – hydrolysis of octyl acetate with sodium hydroxide to give octanol and sodium acetate. Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming the alkoxide (octanol) and acetate anion which pairs with Na⁺. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (0.5–2 M) under heating (60–100 °C) for 1–4 h, usually with reflux. Water or a water/ethanol mixture is used as solvent.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of diethyl maleate to maleic acid and ethanol. Purpose: convert ester to carboxylic acid. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–O bond of the diethyl ester, forming the dicarboxylic acid and releasing ethanol. Typical conditions: aqueous acid (e.g., HCl) or base (NaOH) reflux, followed by acidification if base used. Common solvent: water mixed with ethanol or methanol; catalyst: mineral acid or alkali.

Double displacement (acid–base) in aqueous solution; converts the sulfate salt to palladium(II) hydroxide precipitate while forming soluble Na2SO4; aqueous NaOH is added to an aqueous PdSO4 solution, often with slight heating to aid precipitation; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed oxidative hydrolysis of a nitrile to the corresponding carboxylic acid with release of ammonia. Water provides the oxygen and hydrogen atoms, while molecular O₂ serves as the terminal oxidant. Typical conditions: 5–10 mol % Pd(OAc)₂, aqueous medium (often buffered), O₂ pressure (1–5 atm), temperature 80–120 °C, sometimes with a phosphine or bipyridine ligand to stabilize Pd(II). The overall transformation converts butyronitrile → butyric acid + NH₃.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) between two equivalents of lactic acid and one equivalent of magnesium carbonate. The carbonate is deprotonated by the acids, generating magnesium lactate, carbon dioxide and water. Reaction is carried out in water, gently heated (40–60 °C) to evolve CO₂ and drive the equilibrium to completion. No additional catalyst is required.

S‑alkylation (SN2) of butyl mercaptan with methyl iodide to give methyl butyl sulfide and HI. In practice the thiol is first deprotonated with a base (e.g., NaOH or NaH) to form the butyl thiolate, which then attacks methyl iodide in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF, DMF or acetone at 0 °C to room temperature. The reaction is fast and generally gives high yields of the thioether; the by‑product is hydrogen iodide, which is neutralised by the base.

Strong hydride reduction of an ester – LiAlH4 reduces methyl benzoate to the corresponding primary alcohol (benzyl alcohol) and the released methoxy group is reduced to methanol. Performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere. LiAlH4 used stoichiometrically; reaction quenched with water or dilute acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction. Purpose: Quaternization of secondary amines to form ammonium salts. Transformation: Methylation of dimethylamine via nucleophilic attack on methyl iodide. Conditions: Typically conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solvents at ambient temperature. Solvent: Water or ethanol.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of methyl lactate with n‑butanol to produce n‑butyl lactate and methanol. Typical conditions involve 1–5 % catalytic amount of sulfuric acid, p‑toluenesulfonic acid, or a solid base (e.g., CaO, NaOMe) in excess n‑butanol, reflux (≈ 120 °C) under nitrogen, and removal of methanol (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) to shift equilibrium toward product. No stoometric reagents other than the two esters are required.

N‑acylation (acetylation) of an aryl amine; purpose is to protect the aniline or introduce an acetyl group; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the aniline nitrogen on acetic anhydride, forming N‑(4‑bromophenyl)acetamide and releasing acetic acid; usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert solvent such as pyridine, dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, with pyridine or a catalytic amount of DMAP acting as base; reaction time 30 min to 2 h.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation); condensation of adipic anhydride with excess ammonia to give the diamide (hexanediamide) and water; typically performed by bubbling gaseous or aqueous NH3 through the anhydride at 50‑100 °C, often neat or in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF) under pressure; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (formation of a trifluoromethylsilane, Ruppert‑Prakash reagent); KOtBu deprotonates trifluoromethane generating CF3− which attacks chlorotrimethylsilane to afford Me3SiCF3, with KCl and tert‑butanol as by‑products; usually carried out in dry THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric KOtBu acts as base, no additional catalyst.

Halogenation via phosphorus tribromide; the three hydroxyl groups of 2,4,6‑trihydroxy‑1,3,5‑triazine are replaced by bromine atoms producing 2,4,6‑tribromo‑1,3,5‑triazine and phosphorous acid; conducted by adding PBr3 dropwise to a suspension of the triazine in anhydrous CCl4 or toluene, refluxing for 1–2 h; moisture‑free conditions required, no external catalyst.

Sandmeyer‑type diazonium substitution (azide introduction); the p‑nitro‑diazonium chloride is treated with sodium azide, resulting in nucleophilic attack of N3− on the diazonium carbon and formation of p‑azido‑4‑nitrobenzene with NaCl as the only inorganic by‑product; performed in aqueous medium at 0–5 °C, protected from light, typically with NaNO2 generated in‑situ for the diazonium step; no catalyst needed.

Ozonolysis of an alkene; the C=C bond is cleaved oxidatively to give carbonyl fragments, here formaldehyde from the terminal carbon and hydroxyacetone from the internal carbon; reaction is performed at –78 °C to 0 °C in a non‑protic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂, with O₃ bubbled through, followed by a reductive work‑up (e.g., dimethyl sulfide) to isolate the aldehyde and ketone.

Acid–base neutralization and salt formation; oxalic acid reacts with sodium carbonate in aqueous solution, the carbonate neutralizes the di‑acid to give sodium oxalate while liberating CO2 gas and water; usually carried out at room temperature with stirring; the reaction is exothermic and proceeds to completion; no catalyst required.

High‑temperature oxidation of GaAs in air or pure O₂ at 600‑900 °C, converting the semiconductor into gallium oxide (Ga₂O₃) and arsenic oxide (predominantly As₂O₃ or As₂O₅ depending on oxygen potential); used for waste treatment or to grow surface oxide layers; solid‑state reaction in a furnace, no solvent or catalyst needed.

SN2 substitution of benzyl chloride by methylamine to give the secondary amine N‑methylbenzylamine; hydrogen chloride is formed as a by‑product. The reaction is usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, using an excess of gaseous or aqueous methylamine and a base (e.g., triethylamine or NaHCO₃) to neutralize the HCl.

Direct chlorination (oxidation‑reduction) of lanthanum sesquioxide; chlorine gas converts the oxide to lanthanum chloride (LaCl₃) with evolution of O₂; carried out at high temperature (≈500–800 °C) in an inert atmosphere with Cl₂ flow; no solvent or catalyst required.

Double N‑alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of ethylenediamine with benzyl bromide to form benzathine (N,N′‑dibenzyl‑ethylenediamine); potassium carbonate acts as a mild base, abstracting HBr and generating KBr, CO2 and H2O; reaction is performed in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or acetonitrile at reflux (80‑100 °C) under nitrogen; no transition‑metal catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution on phosphorus (P‑Cl → P‑N3); used to prepare diphenyl azidophosphate as an azide transfer reagent. The azide ion from hydrazoic acid attacks the electrophilic phosphorus of O,O‑diphenyl phosphorochloridate, displacing chloride as HCl. Usually performed at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen in dry dichloromethane or THF, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap the generated HCl.

Cyclocondensation (dehydrative condensation) of a 1,2‑diamine with a 1,2‑dialdehyde; furnishes the fused heterocycle imidazo[1,2‑a]pyrazine and water as by‑product. The two amino groups attack the carbonyl carbons of glyoxal, forming imine intermediates that cyclize and lose water. Conducted in refluxing ethanol, acetic acid, or toluene (often with a catalytic amount of acid) for several hours; removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap) drives the reaction to completion.

Grignard addition to an aldehyde; provides the secondary benzylic alcohol 1‑(4‑fluorophenyl)ethanol. Methylmagnesium bromide acts as a nucleophile, adding to the carbonyl carbon of 4‑fluorobenzaldehyde to give an alkoxide, which is protonated on aqueous work‑up. Performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; the reaction mixture is quenched with dilute ammonium chloride or water.

Peracid oxidation of indole to isatin; converts the indole nucleus into the oxindole (isatin) and generates acetic acid as the reduced by‑product. The peracetic acid delivers an electrophilic oxygen that inserts into the C2‑C3 bond of indole, followed by rearrangement to the lactam. Typically carried out in glacial acetic acid or a mixture of acetic acid and dichloromethane at 0–25 °C; the reaction is often monitored by TLC and quenched with sodium sulfite to remove excess oxidant.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification (Fischer esterification) of formic acid (generated in situ from sodium formate and H₂SO₄) with methanol to give methyl formate and sodium hydrogen sulfate. The strong acid protonates the formic acid, facilitating nucleophilic attack by methanol; water formed is removed by azeotropic distillation. Conducted by refluxing methanol containing catalytic (≈5 %) sulfuric acid and solid sodium formate; the mixture is distilled to collect methyl formate, and the remaining salts are filtered off.

Acid‑base reaction of lithium borohydride with a carboxylic acid; produces hydrogen gas, borane (BH₃) and lithium acetate. The protic acid protonates the hydride, liberating H₂ and converting LiBH₄ into BH₃, while the acetate anion coordinates lithium. Performed in dry THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C under nitrogen to control gas evolution; the generated BH₃ can be trapped or used in situ for further reductions.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a metal sulfate; sulfuric acid protonates zinc oxide, yielding water and soluble zinc sulfate. Typically performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of an epoxide by a primary amine (aminolysis); butylamine attacks ethylene oxide to give the β‑amino alcohol 2‑(butylamino)ethanol. Usually carried out at room temperature in polar aprotic solvents such as THF, MeCN or methanol; no additional catalyst needed.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (DCC coupling) of a fatty acid with an alcohol. Oleic acid is activated by N,N′‑dicyclohexylcarbodiimide, then reacts with n‑butanol to afford butyl oleate, with N,N′‑dicyclohexylurea precipitating as by‑product. Conducted anhydrously in dichloromethane or DMF, 0 °C to rt, often with catalytic DMAP; inert atmosphere recommended.

Substitution (halogenation) of a primary alcohol with phosphorus pentachloride; PCl5 converts one hydroxyl of glycerol to a chloride, producing 2‑chloro‑1,3‑propanediol while generating HCl and phosphorus oxychloride as side products. Reaction is carried out under reflux in dry chlorinated solvents (e.g., chloroform, carbon tetrachloride) or in the absence of solvent, with temperature control to avoid over‑chlorination.

Acid dissolution of a metal sulfide; hydrochloric acid protonates copper(II) sulfide, producing soluble copper(II) chloride and releasing hydrogen sulfide gas. Performed in aqueous HCl, often with gentle heating to evolve H₂S.

Redox reaction of dioxygen difluoride with chlorine; O₂F₂ (a powerful oxidizer) oxidizes Cl₂, yielding molecular oxygen and two equivalents of chlorine monofluoride (ClF). The reaction is highly exothermic, requires cryogenic temperatures (below –130 °C) and an inert matrix, and is studied under controlled low‑temperature conditions.

Oxidation of a phosphorothioate to the corresponding phosphate; hydrogen peroxide transfers oxygen to the sulfur atom of O,O‑diethyl O‑(4‑nitrophenyl) phosphorothioate, producing O,O‑diethyl O‑(4‑nitrophenyl) phosphate and water. Typically performed in aqueous or mixed organic solvent at 0 °C to rt; may be catalyzed by a base or a transition‑metal complex to enhance rate.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Aqueous silver nitrate and potassium arsenate exchange anions to form soluble potassium nitrate and insoluble silver arsenate, which precipitates. Used to isolate or remove silver ions. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); purpose is to convert perillyl alcohol back to perillaldehyde. Key transformation: selective oxidation of the C‑OH bond to a C=O bond without over‑oxidation to the acid. Typical conditions: PCC (1.1–1.5 equiv) in dry dichloromethane, temperature 0 °C to ambient, under nitrogen; reaction typically completed in 1–2 h.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (condensation coupling). Phenol reacts with acetic acid in the presence of diisopropylcarbodiimide (DIC) to yield phenyl acetate while DIC is converted to N,N‑diisopropylurea. Typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF with catalytic DMAP or pyridine, at 0 °C to room temperature.

High‑temperature gas‑phase oxidation (combustion) of methane by dinitrogen tetroxide. N2O4 acts as oxidizer, converting CH4 to CO2, N2 and H2O Carried out at several hundred degrees Celsius in the gas phase; no solvent or catalyst needed, as in rocket‑propulsion contexts.

Hydrolysis of disulfur decafluoride. Water attacks S2F10, breaking S‑F bonds to produce sulfur dioxide and hydrogen fluoride. Reaction is vigorous and exothermic, performed in aqueous media, often at low to moderate temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.
Alkaline hydrolysis (SN2) of 5‑chloromethylfurfural; NaOH in water or aqueous ethanol at reflux converts the benzylic chloride to a hydroxymethyl group, yielding 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural and NaCl.

Base dissolution of alumina to generate potassium aluminate; Al₂O₃ reacts with KOH in water, forming soluble aluminate species (KAl(OH)₄ or KAlO₂) and water; purpose is preparation of aluminate solutions for glass, zeolite, or water‑treatment chemistry; performed by adding Al₂O₃ to a hot (80‑150 °C) aqueous KOH solution under reflux; excess KOH often employed; reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; the carbon‑carbon double bond of trans‑anethole is reduced to give p‑methoxyethylbenzene; common catalysts are palladium on carbon, platinum oxide, or Raney nickel; reaction run in ethanol or methanol under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at room temperature to reflux; solvent is protic; no other reagents needed.

Type: cyclodehydration/carbonylation to form a heterocycle. Purpose: synthesis of 1,2,3‑oxadiazol‑5(2H)‑one. Key transformation: phosgene inserts a carbonyl between the N‑hydroxy and carbonyl groups of N‑hydroxyurea, followed by intramolecular cyclization with loss of HCl. Typical conditions: phosgene (or triphosgene) added dropwise at 0 – 5 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl; the mixture is then allowed to warm to room temperature and stirred until completion. Common solvents/catalysts: dry CH2Cl2, pyridine (HCl scavenger).

Acid‑catalyzed ring‑opening of tetrahydrofuran with hydrogen bromide. HBr adds across the THF ether ring to give 4‑bromo‑1‑butanol. Usually carried out by bubbling HBr gas through THF or reacting THF with aqueous HBr under reflux (0 °C to reflux); THF serves as solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidative conversion of an arylboronic acid to phenol; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes 4‑nitrophenylboronic acid to 4‑nitrophenol while boric acid is formed. Conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., MeOH/H₂O) at 0–25 °C, sometimes with a base (NaOH) to improve solubility; H₂O₂ (1–2 equiv) is the oxidant and no metal catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction. Purpose: Regeneration of sodium octanoate from magnesium salt. Transformation: Ion exchange forming insoluble magnesium carbonate. Conditions: Aqueous solution at room temperature. Solvent: Water.

Acidic decomposition of zinc telluride. Concentrated HCl reacts with ZnTe to form soluble zinc chloride and gaseous hydrogen telluride (H2Te). Performed in aqueous HCl, often with gentle heating to promote gas evolution; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; exchange of the cations between ammonium nitrate and potassium hydrosulfide to give potassium nitrate and ammonium bisulfide; typically carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: acid‑base metathesis (salt‑acid exchange). Purpose: generation of ammonium nitrate (a fertilizer) and recovery of acetic acid. Key transformation: proton transfer from nitric acid to the acetate anion, yielding acetic acid and the ammonium nitrate salt. Typical conditions: mixing aqueous solutions of ammonium acetate and concentrated nitric acid at low to ambient temperature (0‑25 °C) to avoid violent decomposition; the mixture is usually kept dilute and stirred. Water serves as the solvent; no additional catalyst is needed.

Formation of a chloroformate via reaction of an alcohol with phosgene; the hydroxyl of 2‑methoxyethanol attacks phosgene, yielding 2‑methoxyethyl chloroformate and HCl. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, with a base scavenger such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize the generated HCl and prevent side reactions.

Same acid‑base metathesis as reaction 2, but with potassium hydroxide. Produces potassium bicarbonate, ammonia gas, and water. Conducted in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed. Gentle heating may be applied to evolve NH₃.

Acid‑base double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; converts soluble lead(II) acetate and HCl to insoluble lead(II) chloride precipitate and acetic acid; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water as solvent; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) methylation of cytosine using dimethyl sulfate; the nitrogen of cytosine attacks a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, forming 1‑methylcytosine and generating methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product; performed in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF) or aqueous alkaline medium to de‑protonate cytosine; reaction kept cool to control toxicity of dimethyl sulfate; no catalyst other than base.

Acid‑base neutralization of formic acid with potassium bicarbonate; proton transfer converts bicarbonate to carbon dioxide and water while forming potassium formate; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; gas evolution drives reaction to completion; no catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization of pyridine·HCl with aqueous ammonium hydroxide; ammonia deprotonates pyridinium to give pyridine and ammonium chloride; carried out in aqueous medium at 0–25 °C; useful for extracting pyridine into an organic layer.

Hydrobromic acid dehydration of 1‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol to 1‑bromo‑1‑phenylpropane; general type: acid‑catalyzed substitution (SN1-like for secondary benzylic); purpose: generate alkyl bromide from alcohol; key transformation: R‑CH(OH)‑R′ + HBr → R‑CH(Br)‑R′ + H₂O; typical conditions: reflux in conc. HBr (48 % aqueous) or generated HBr gas, often in glacial acetic acid or ether, at 70–80 °C; water removed as by‑product.

N‑acylation of 2‑methylindole with acetyl chloride in the presence of pyridine, which acts as base and solvent; forms N‑acetyl‑2‑methylindole and neutralizes generated HCl; typically run at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction in water; oxalic acid protonates perchlorate salt, exchanging anions to give insoluble barium oxalate precipitate and soluble perchloric acid; typically performed at room temperature; stirring and filtration isolate the barium oxalate; no catalyst.

Protonolysis/ligand‑exchange of a cerium(III) β‑diketonate with hydrogen chloride; HCl protonates the diketonate ligands, releasing three equivalents of pentane‑2,4‑dione and forming cerium(III) chloride; carried out in anhydrous organic solvent such as THF or acetonitrile, often under reflux; stoichiometric HCl gas or solution is used; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation; aqueous cadmium acetate reacts with phosphoric acid, exchanging acetate for phosphate to give insoluble cadmium phosphate precipitate and acetic acid; usually carried out in water with gentle heating to ensure complete reaction.

Strong oxidation of a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon using potassium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid (chromic acid oxidation). Adjacent benzylic carbons of acenaphthene are oxidized to carbonyl groups, yielding acenaphthene‑1,2‑dione. Reaction is carried out under reflux in concentrated H₂SO₄ (often with water); Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) as chromium(III) sulfate.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; used to exchange the methyl ester of methyl methacrylate for an ethyl ester, ethyl methacrylateanol. Ethanol attacks the carbonyl of the ester under acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOMe) catalysis, followed by removal of methanol to drive equilibrium. Reaction is run under reflux in excess ethanol or a suitable solvent such as toluene, often with a Dean‑Stark trap. No special catalyst beyond the acid/base.

Acid‑base dissolution and complexation citric acid protonates the carbonate of ferric carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O while chelating Fe³⁺ to form ferric citrate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution, heated gently to promote CO₂ evolution. No catalyst needed; excess citric acid ensures complete conversion.

Acid displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; nitric acid protonates the chromate anion to give chromic acid (H₂CrO₄) and forms soluble strontium nitrate. Reaction is performed by adding aqueous HNO₃ to a suspension of SrCrO₄, often with gentle heating to increase solubility. No catalyst required.

Acid leaching of a metal arsenide; concentrated HCl attacks cobalt arsenide, producing arsine (AsH₃) gas and cobalt(II) chloride. Reaction proceeds at elevated temperature (e.g., 60‑80°C) in aqueous HCl, with the evolution of toxic arsine gas requiring proper venting. No catalyst, but careful control of temperature and acid concentration is essential.

Acyl‑chloride esterification; the acid chloride reacts with 2‑ethylhexanol to give the corresponding ester (2‑ethylhexyl benzoate) and HCl. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0‑25 °C, in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge the liberated HCl. No additional catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of propane‑1,3‑diol; hydrogen gas under pressure (1–5 atm) with Pd/C (5–10 % wt) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or at 50–100 °C cleaves one C‑O bond to give 1propanol and water; used for selective conversion of a diol to a monohydroxy alcohol.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; n‑butanol reacts with propylparaben in the presence of a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid or sodium methoxide, usually under reflux in toluene or methanol, exchanging the ester group to afford butylparaben and propanol; employed to synthesize a different parabens ester.

Acid‑catalyzed cyclotrimerisation (condensation) of formaldehyde; in the presence of a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H2SO4, HCl, or BF3) and mild heating, three formaldehyde molecules condense with loss of water to give the cyclic trimer 1,3,5‑trioxane. The reaction proceeds in aqueous or alcoholic media and is employed to generate a stable, solid storage form of formaldehyde for later depolymerisation back to monomer.

Acetylation of a metal oxide (acid‑base reaction); mercury(II) oxide reacts with acetic anhydride at room temperature, often neat or in a non‑reactive solvent such as dichloromethane, yielding mercury(II) acetate and acetic acid; a convenient method for preparing a metal acetate salt.

E2 elimination of an alkyl tosylate; pentan‑3‑yl 4‑methylbenzenesulfonate reacts with potassium tert‑butoxide in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature; the strong base abstracts a β‑hydrogen, eliminating the tosylate to form pent‑2‑ene, while the base is protonated to tert‑butanol and potassium 4‑methylbenzenesulfonate is generated; applied for dehydro‑substitution to produce internal alkenes.

Acid‑base metathesis/precipitation forming ferr phosphate; aqueous ammonium dihydrogen phosphate mixed with iron(III) oxide and heated (80–100 °C) undergoes proton transfer, releasing ammonia gas and water and precipitating ferric phosphate (FePO₄ employed for preparation of ferric phosphate and liberation of ammonia.

General type: reduction of a metal fluoride with hydrogen; purpose: convert uranium tetrafluoride to lower‑valent uranium trifluoride and generate hydrogen fluoride; key transformation: hydrogen reduces UF₄, fluorine transfers to H₂ forming HF while UF₄ is reduced to UF₃; typical conditions: gas‑phase reaction at 400‑600 °C under excess H₂, sealed reactor, no solvent, no catalyst required.

General type: solid‑state intermetallic synthesis; purpose: prepare hafnium silicide (HfSi₂) for refractory or semiconductor applications; key transformation: elemental hafnium reacts directly with silicon to form the silicide phase; typical conditions: intimate mixing of powdered Hf and Si, heating to 1000‑1500 °C under inert atmosphere (argon or vacuum), often in a sealed tube; no solvent or catalyst.

General type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitro aromatic; purpose: obtain 2‑naphthylamine from 2‑nitronaphthalene; key transformation: nitro group is reduced to an amine while the aromatic ring remains intact; typical conditions: H₂ gas (1‑5 atm) with Pd/C, Pt, or Raney Ni catalyst in ethanol or methanol solvent, temperature 50‑ °C, reaction performed in a pressure vessel or flask.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction; oxalic acid protonates fluoride ion, yielding sodium oxalate and hydrofluoric acid; performed in aqueous solution, often at low to moderate temperature to control HF evolution; no catalyst needed.

General type: aerobic oxidation of a carbohydrate to a furan dicarboxylic acid; purpose: synthesize renewable 2,5‑furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) as a monomer for bioplastics; key transformation: fructose is oxidized and reorganized to a furan ring bearing two carboxyl groups, with water as the only other product; typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH), temperature 120‑180 °C, O₂ pressure 5‑10 bar, heterogeneous Co‑Mn‑Br catalyst supported on silica or similar, water as solvent.

General type: base‑mediated ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose: cleave isopropyl trifluoroacetate to recover isopropanol and sodium trifluoroacetate; key transformation: hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl, yielding isopropanol and the trifluoroacetate anion which pairs with Na⁺; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1 equiv) at room temperature to reflux, water or water/methanol mixture as solvent, no additional catalyst.

Gas‑phase redox between NO₂ and SO₂. Nitrogen dioxide oxidizes sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide, being reduced to nitrogen monoxide. Takes place at elevated temperatures (~500 °C) and can be catalyzed by metal oxides (e.g., V₂O₅). No solvent; gas‑phase process.

Oxidation reaction; strong oxidizing conversion of ethanol to acetic acid using acidic potassium permanganate; key transformation is oxidation of the primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid while MnO4‑ is reduced to Mn²⁺; performed in concentrated sulfuric acid aqueous solution, heated (typically reflux) to maintain the redox potential; common solvents are water/H₂SO₄ mixture, no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed epoxide ring‑opening (hydrolysis); converts 1,2‑epoxycyclohexane to the vicinal diol 1,2‑cyclohexanediol; the epoxide oxygen is protonated by H₂SO₄, then water attacks to give the trans‑diol; carried out in dilute aqueous sulfuric acid at ambient or slightly elevated temperature (0‑50 °C); solvent is water or aqueous acid.

Thermite (metallothermic reduction) reaction; reduces scandium oxide to elemental scandium while aluminum is oxidized to aluminum oxide; a highly exothermic redox process where Sc³⁺ is reduced and Al⁰ is oxidized; initiated by ignition (e.g., Mg strip) and proceeds at >2000 °C; no solvent, performed as a solid‑state reaction under inert atmosphere or vacuum.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); boric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to yield sodium metaborate (NaBO₂) and water; the B‑O‑H bonds are deprotonated by OH⁻ forming the metaborate anion; conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature or with mild heating; water is the reaction medium, no special catalyst required.

Redox reaction in acidic medium; phosphorous acid oxidizes to phosphoric acid while sodium bromate (BrO3−) is reduced to bromide ion, yielding NaBr and water; executed in dilute acid (e.g., H2SO4) at 20‑70 °C; typically no catalyst is added.

Elimination (E2) reaction: sodium ethoxide (strong base) in anhydrous ethanol (often reflux) dehydrohalogenates 2‑bromobutane, abstracting a β‑hydrogen and expelling bromide to give 2‑butene, sodium bromide and ethanol; used to convert alkyl bromides to alkenes.

Intramolecular Williamson ether synthesis (base‑promoted epoxide formation); sodium hydroxide deprotonates 1‑chloro‑2‑propanol, the resulting alkoxide attacks the adjacent carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and closing a three‑membered epoxide ring to give propylene oxide; by‑product is NaCl and water; performed in aqueous NaOH or dilute NaOH/ethanol mixture, typically at 50‑80 °C; no additional catalyst needed.

Thermal decarboxylation (pyrolytic degradation) of caffeic acid; the carboxyl group is eliminated as CO₂, and the remaining phenylpropanoid fragment rearranges to form 4‑vinylcatechol; generally achieved by heating the acid (200‑300 °C) under inert atmosphere or in the presence of mild oxidants; no solvent is required for the gas‑phase pyrolysis; serves as a method for generating vinyl‑substituted catechols from hydroxycinnamic acids.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a monosaccharide; converts the aldose L‑fucose to the corresponding alditol L‑fucitol by reduction of the aldehyde group to a primary alcohol. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure of 1–5 atm, transition‑metal catalyst (Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂), in aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., MeOH/H₂O) at 25–80 °C. No protecting groups are required.

Oxidative cleavage (Wacker-type aerobic oxidation) of the allyl side chain of 4‑allylphenol to a carbonyl group, yielding 4‑hydroxyacetophenone; catalyzed by palladium(II) chloride with copper(II) chloride as co‑catalyst, using molecular oxygen (or air) and water as the oxidant; typically performed in aqueous acidic media (e.g., dilute HCl or AcOH) at 30–80 °C under O₂ atmosphere.

Reductive nitro‑to‑amine conversion (iron/acetic acid reduction); purpose is to obtain 4‑methylaniline (para‑toluidine) from the nitro compound. Key transformation: Fe⁰ reduces the nitro group (‑NO₂) to an amino group (‑NH₂), generating Fe³⁺ (as iron(III) oxide/hydroxide) and water. Typical conditions: excess iron powder in glacial acetic acid, reflux (80‑100 °C) for several hours the mixture is then filtered to remove iron residues and the product is extracted with an organic solvent.

Urea formation via nucleophilic addition of cyclohexylamine to cyclohexyl isocyanate; a straightforward condensation (no catalyst) that proceeds at ambient temperature in inert organic solvents such as THF, dichloromethane, or even neat; the reaction converts the isocyanate functional group into a dicyclohexylurea linkage.

Oxidation of 2‑methoxyacetaldehyde to methoxyacetic acid using hydrogen peroxide; a mild aldehyde‑to‑acid oxidation that generally employs aqueous H₂O₂ (30 %) with a small amount of a metal catalyst (e.g., Na₂WO₄, Na₂MoO₄) or acidic conditions (dilute H₂SO₄) at room temperature to 50 °C, producing water as the only by‑product.

Metathesis (double‑replacement) reaction between potassium cyanide and mercuric acetate in aqueous solution, forming insoluble mercury(II) cyanide precipitate and soluble potassium acetate; carried out at ambient temperature with stirring; Hg(CN)₂ precipitates out and can be filtered.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 2,2‑dichloroethanol to 1,1‑dichloroethylene; a classic E1 elimination using concentrated H₂SO₄ as both solvent and catalyst, heated to 80–120 °C; water is eliminated to give the gem‑dichloro alkene.

Acyl transfer from 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetic anhydride to dimethylamine, yielding the same amide and one equivalent of 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetic acid. Reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of the amine on one carbonyl of the anhydride. Typical conditions: 0–25 °C in dichloromethane or pyridine as solvent; an excess of amine or a base (e.g., pyridine) may be used to neutralize the generated acid.

Oxidation of a primary alkyl halide; benzyl bromide is first hydrolyzed to benzyl alcohol then oxidized by KMnO₄ to benzoic acid. Conducted in aqueous alkaline solution (often NaOH) with excess KMnO₄, heated to reflux until the purple permanganate color disappears; manganese dioxide precipitate is removed.

Base‑induced E2 elimination of a tertiary alkyl bromide; NaOH abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 2‑methyl‑2‑bromobutane to give the corresponding alkene (2‑methyl‑2‑butene), sodium bromide and water. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic NaOH, reflux or heating, solvent often ethanol/water.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑iodopropane with sodium cyanide; purpose is synthesis of propionitrile; key transformation: CH3CH2CH2I + NaCN → CH3CH2CN + NaI; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetonitrile at 0–50 °C; no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of a tertiary isocyanate; water attacks the carbon of the N=C=O group in 2‑isocyanato‑2‑methylpropane, releasing CO₂ and forming tert‑butylamine; the reaction proceeds at ambient to moderate temperature (20–60 °C) in aqueous media, often in the presence of a mild base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to neutralize any acidic by‑products.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 2‑ethylhexyl acetate; purpose is to generate 2‑ethylhexanol and acetic acid; key transformation is water attack on the ester carbonyl followed by proton transfers; typically carried out by refluxing the ester in aqueous HCl or H₂SO₄ (1–6 M) at 80–110 °C; solvent can be a mixture of water with a water‑miscible organic solvent (e.g., toluene, THF).

Conjugate (Michael) addition of a secondary amine to an α,β‑unsaturated ester; diethylamine adds to the β‑carbon of ethyl acrylate forming ethyl 3‑(diethylamino)propionate. Usually performed at room temperature in polar aprotic solvents such as THF or MeCN, no catalyst required.

Silylation of a tertiary alcohol; 2‑methylpropan‑2‑ol reacts with chlorotrimethylsilane to form Trimethyl‑[(2‑methylpropan‑2‑yl)oxy]silane and HCl; carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) to trap HCl, 0‑25 °C under inert atmosphere.

Metal‑halogen exchange followed by electrophilic carboxylation; n‑butyllithium converts 3‑bromofuran to the 3‑lithiated furan, which is then trapped with carbon dioxide to generate furan‑3‑carboxylic acid after aqueous work‑up. Conditions: -78 °C to 0 °C, inert atmosphere, THF as solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange; potassium carbonate reacts with barium selenate in aqueous solution to form insoluble barium carbonate precipitate and soluble potassium selenate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring.

Redox reduction of ozone by hydrogen; gaseous ozone is reduced by H₂ to give water and dioxygen. Purpose is ozone destruction and water formation. Key transformation: O₃ + H₂ → H₂O + O₂. Typical conditions: elevated temperature (150–300 °C) or catalytic surface (e.g., Pt, Pd, metal oxides). No solvent; gas‑phase reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑iodooctane with hydroxide ion to give 1‑octanol and sodium iodide. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol) and heated under reflux. Polar protic solvent helps solubilize NaOH.

Fischer esterification of a carboxylic acid with methanol; purpose is to convert the acid to its methyl ester. Key transformation: anthranilic acid → methyl anthranilate + H₂O. Typical conditions: reflux methanol containing catalytic H₂SO₄ (or other strong acid) for several hours; water is removed by azeotropic distillation or by using excess methanol. Solvent is the methanol itself.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amine acylation) to form an amide; cyclopropylamine reacts with benzoyl chloride to give N‑cyclopropylbenzamide and HCl; purpose is to install a benzoyl amide protecting group; key transformation is attack of the amine nitrogen on the carbonyl carbon of the acid chloride, followed by loss of chloride as HCl; commonly carried out in a dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane with a stoichiometric base (pyridine or triethylamine) to absorb the generated HCl; reaction is performed at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

Carbothermic reduction (high‑temperature redox) of iron(II) oxide by carbon; solid FeO is reduced to metallic iron while carbon is oxidized to carbon monoxide. Performed in a furnace at ~1000 °C under an inert or reducing atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an acid chloride to an aldehyde; 2,2‑dimethylpropanoyl chloride is reduced by H₂ in the presence of palladium on barium sulfate (Pearlman’s catalyst) to give 2,2‑dimethylpropanal and HCl. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 0–25 °C, solvent such as diethyl ether or dichloromethane.

Acid‑base neutralization; potassium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (KHMDS) deprotonates benzoic acid, forming potassium benzoate and bis(trimethylsilyl)amine as the by‑product. Typically carried out in anhydrous THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (alcohol to alkyl bromide); PBr3 activates the hydroxyl group converting allyl alcohol to allyl bromide while generating phosphorous acid. Typically performed in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Aqueous hydrolysis; converts toxic cyanogen chloride to hydrogen cyanide and hypochlorous acid. ClCN + H2O → HCN + HOCl. Performed in water at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature; no special catalyst required, though alkaline conditions can accelerate the reaction.

Acid‑catalyzed decomposition (hydrolysis) of ferrocyanide. Potassium ferrocyanide K₄[Fe(CN)₆] reacts with hydrochloric acid; the Fe(II) center forms FeCl₂, the cyanide ligands are protonated and released as hydrogen cyanide (HCN) gas, and K⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give KCl. Conducted in aqueous HCl (often 1–6 M) at room temperature to gentle heating; the evolution of HCN requires proper ventilation. No additional catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) via in‑situ generation of an acid chloride; thionyl chloride converts 3,5‑dibromo‑2‑hydroxybenzoic acid to its acid chloride, which then reacts with 4‑bromoaniline to give the amide 3,4′,5‑tribromosalicylanilide, releasing HCl and SO₂. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or toluene, often with pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl, under reflux or at 0 °C‑rt, inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic addition of a primary amine to an isothiocyanate forming a symmetrical N,N′‑dibutylthiourea; usually performed at room temperature in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF; no catalyst required.

Dehydrative conversion of an amide to a nitrile; phosphorus pentoxide acts as a strong dehydrating agent, removing water from butanamide to afford butyronitrile. Reaction is performed by heating the amide with excess P₂O₅, usually neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., toluene) at 150–200 °C under dry conditions.

Direct combination (synthesis) oxidation; elemental antimony is oxidized by bromine to form antimony tribromide, key oxidation of Sb⁰ to Sb³⁺ and reduction of Br₂ to Br⁻; conducted by adding solid Sb to liquid or gaseous Br₂ at room temperature or slight heating; often performed in a dry, inert medium such as carbon tetrachloride, no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction; converts trisodium phosphate and ammonium chloride into ammonium phosphate (tribasic) and sodium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution by mixing stoichiometric amounts of the two salts at ambient temperature. No special catalyst required; the reaction proceeds to equilibrium and the products remain in solution (both are soluble). Often the mixture is evaporated or crystallized to isolate the ammonium phosphate.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (Friedel‑Crafts chlorination); chlorine in the presence of the Lewis acid aluminum chloride chlorinates methyl benzoate preferentially at the meta position, yielding methyl 3‑chlorobenzoate and HCl. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, AlCl₃ (1–2 equiv), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere.

N‑Acylation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of a lactam; acetyl chloride reacts with the nitrogen of 4‑piperidone, and triethylamine neutralizes the generated HCl, affording N‑acetyl‑4‑piperidone. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; triethylamine is used as base, no additional catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration; nitrates pyrene to 1‑nitropyrene using the nitronium ion generated from NO2 and concentrated H2SO4; purpose is introduction of a nitro group onto an aromatic system; typically performed at 0–50 °C in glacial sulfuric acid as solvent, often with stirring under an inert atmosphere.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine; piperidine reacts with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO2 and HCl) to form N‑nitrosopiperidine and water; used to prepare nitrosamines; carried out in aqueous acidic medium at 0–5 °C to control decomposition, with HCl as acid and water as solvent.

Acid–base neutralization; Cr(OH)3 reacts with aqueous H2SO4 to produce soluble Cr2(SO4)3 (written as chromium(III) sulfate) and water. Conducted in aqueous medium, usually with gentle heating to ensure complete reaction; no catalyst.

Free‑radical α‑chlorination of a carboxylic acid; chlorine abstracts a hydrogen from acetic acid under photolytic (UV) or thermal radical conditions to give monochloroacetic acid and HCl; employed for synthesis of halo‑acetic acids; typically performed in an inert solvent such as CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂, with a radical initiator or UV light, at ambient or slightly elevated temperature.

Nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) of an alkyl halide by sulfide; 3‑chloropropionitrile reacts with Na₂S to replace Cl⁻ with –SH, yielding 3‑mercaptopropionitrile and NaCl; conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., ethanol/water) under reflux; excess Na₂S and mild heating promote the substitution.

Strong reduction of diesters to diols; dimethyl azelatedimethyl nonanedioate) is reduced by LiAlH₄ to 1,9‑nonanediol, converting both ester carbonyls to primary alcohols; purpose is to obtain a long‑chain diol for or material synthesis; performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert (N₂ or Ar) at reflux, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Acid‑base neutralization with a carbonate buffer; employed to generate diethylamine while removing the sulfate counter‑ion and eliminating carbon dioxide. Diethylammonium hydrogen sulfate reacts with solid Na2CO3 in water; the carbonate deprotonates the ammonium ion, producing diethylamine, sodium sulfate, water and CO2 gas. Reactions are usually carried out at ambient temperature or with mild heating (30‑50 °C) to drive off CO2; aqueous medium is sufficient and no catalyst is needed.

Single‑displacement (metal‑acid) reaction: Nickel metal reacts with hydrochloric acid, yielding nickel(II) chloride and hydrogen gas. Key transformation: Ni + 2 HCl → NiCl2 + H2. Performed in aqueous HCl (usually 6 M concentrated) with heating or reflux to increase rate, as nickel is relatively inert. No external catalyst; vigorous stirring and mild heating are typical to promote gas evolution.

Metathesis/precipitation double‑displacement reaction between potassium iodide and silver chloride. Purpose is to exchange halides, producing insoluble silver iodide for removal or isolation. Key transformation: I⁻ replaces Cl⁻ on Ag⁺, forming AgI(s) while K⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give KCl(aq). Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; no special catalyst needed.

Chlorination/oxidative cleavage of tetramethyllead. Purpose is to convert organolead compound into methyl chloride and lead(II) chloride. Key transformation: each CH₃–Pb bond is cleaved by Cl₂, yielding CH₃Cl and reducing Pb(IV) to PbCl₂. Typically performed in the gas phase or sealed tube at moderate temperature (0–100 °C) under a chlorine atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑iodopropane with sodium acetate (Williamson‑type alkylation); purpose is formation of propyl acetate ester; key transformation: CH3CH2CH2I + NaOAc → CH3COOCH2CH2CH3 + NaI; commonly performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at reflux; no additional catalyst.

Simple acid‑base salt formation; 2‑aminoacetonitrile dissolved in water or ethanol is treated with concentrated HCl, protonating the amine to afford 2‑aminoacetonitrile·HCl (hydrochloride salt); ambient temperature, aqueous HCl.
Acid–base neutralization; ammonia reacts with sulfuric acid to give ammonium hydrogen sulfate (ammonium bisulfate); carried out in water, often with cooling to control the exotherm.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of dimethyl adipate with ethanol to give diethyl adipate. Purpose is to exchange the alkoxy groups on the ester. Key transformation: ethanol attacks the carbonyl of the methyl ester, displacing methanol and forming an ethyl ester; the process repeats for the second methyl group. Typical conditions: excess ethanol, catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOMe), reflux (≈78 °C) in a suitable solvent or neat ethanol; methanol is removed to drive the equilibrium.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis (carbothermic or direct combination) of hafnium(IV) carbide (HfC); a stoichiometric reaction between elemental hafnium metal and carbon (graphite or carbon black). Key transformation is formation of strong Hf‑C covalent bonds. Conducted under inert atmosphere (argon) or vacuum at temperatures of 1800–2100 °C, often in a graphite crucible or via spark plasma sintering. No solvent or catalyst is employed; the resulting carbide is a refractory ceramic.

Nucleophilic phosphorylation (P‑O bond formation) where the phenoxide of p‑chlorophenol attacks O,O‑diethyl phosphorochloridothioate, displacing chloride to give the organophosphate insecticide Carbophenothion and HCl; typically performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or toluene) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine at 0 °C to reflux to neutralize the generated acid.

Acid‑base hydrolysis of sodium hexafluorosilicate in water, cleaving the SiF6^2− anion to produce sodium fluoride, hydrofluoric acid, and silicic acid; carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to accelerate the reaction, no catalyst required.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); the 4‑bromobenzoic acid undergoes chlorination of the carbonyl, releasing SO₂ and CO gases and furnishing 4‑bromobenzoyl chloride; performed under reflux in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, sometimes with pyridine as HCl scavenger.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange between ferric chloride and sodium sulfate in aqueous solution, yielding soluble iron(III) sulfate and precipitated or soluble sodium chloride; the reaction proceeds at ambient temperature with stirring, no special catalyst needed.

SN2 N‑alkylation of glycine by sodium chloroacetate to form iminodiacetic acid and NaCl; the nucleophilic amino group attacks the electrophilic chloromethylene carbon, displacing chloride; typically conducted in aqueous or alcoholic medium with a base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) to keep glycine deprotonated, at reflux temperature.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); purpose is to replace the bromine atom with hydrogen to give a saturated alkane. Key transformation: C–Br bond → C–H, producing hydrogen bromide as by‑product. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with Pd/C (5–10 wt % Pd) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25‑80 °C.

Ullmann ether synthesis (copper‑catalyzed aryl ether formation). Phenol is deprotonated by pyridine, the phenoxide attacks iodobenzene in the presence of CuI, forming diphenyl ether and regenerating CuI. Typically performed at 120‑180 °C in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO under inert atmosphere.

SN alkylation of sodium carbamodithioate with methyl bromide. The nucleophilic sulfide attacks the primary carbon of bromomethane, displacing bromide and giving methyl carbamodithioate; Na is the by‑product. Conducted at 0‑25 °C to ambient temperature in polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO) or aqueous media.

Reductive carbonylation of tungsten(VI) chloride by copper under CO. Copper metal reduces WCl₆ while CO ligates the reduced tungsten, yielding tungsten hexacarbonyl (W(CO)₆) and copper(II) chloride as the oxidized product. Carried out under a CO pressure (5‑20 atm) at 150‑200 °C in a non‑coordinating solvent such as THF or toluene.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) between aluminum perchlorate and sodium formate; purpose is to exchange anions and form aluminum formate and sodium perchlorate. Key transformation: Al(ClO₄)₃ + 3 NaHCOO → Al(HCOO)₃ + 3 NaClO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring; mild heating may be used to enhance solubility.

High‑temperature redox reaction between zinc metal and manganese dioxide. Zinc is oxidized to ZnO while MnO₂ is reduced to metallic Mn. Reaction proceeds upon heating (≈300‑400 °C) in the solid state or in a molten mixture; no solvent needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of an acid chloride with ammonia to give an amide. (E)-But‑2‑enoyl chloride is bubbled into a solution of dry NH₃ (gas) or added to anhydrous NH₃ in an aprotic solvent (e.g., THF, MeCN) at 0 °C to 5 °C to control exotherm. The amide forms while HCl is generated and trapped by excess NH₃ or a base (e.g., pyridine). The product, (E)-but‑2‑enamide, is isolated after work‑up (extraction, drying). No additional catalyst is needed.

Simple precipitation metathesis of halide salts. Potassium iodide exchanges anions with silver bromide, forming insoluble silver iodide precipitate and soluble potassium bromide. Conducted in water at room temperature; the AgI is filtered off.

Imide formation via nucleophilic acyl substitution; ethylamine attacks maleic anhydride to give N‑ethylmaleamic acid which cyclizes with acetic anhydride to the imide N‑ethylmaleimide, releasing two equivalents of acetic acid. Typically performed in anhydrous inert solvent (e.g., THF or toluene) under reflux; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of guanine at C‑8; hydrogen peroxide acts as the oxidant converting guanine to 8‑oxoguanine with loss of water. Usually carried out in aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8) at room temperature; excess H₂O₂ may be used, no metal catalyst needed.

Fischer esterification of pent‑4‑ynoic acid with ethanol to give ethyl pent‑4‑ynoate; purpose is to convert the carboxylic acid into an ethyl ester; key steps are protonation of the acid carbonyl, nucleophilic attack by ethanol, and loss of water; reflux in ethanol (or a solvent like toluene) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (conc. H₂SO₄, p‑toluenesulfonic acid) at 70‑80 °C, often employing a Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic removal of water to drive the equilibrium; no other catalyst is required.

Amidation (condensation) of 2‑furancarboxylic acid with ammonia to give 2‑furamide; water is eliminated. Typically performed by heating the acid with excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃ (150–200 °C) in a sealed tube or by first converting the acid to the acid chloride (SOCl₂) then treating with NH₃. No special catalyst required; common solvents are toluene or DMF.

Reductive cleavage of a cyclic acetal (acetal reduction). Purpose: deprotect 1,3‑dioxolane to obtain ethylene glycol and methanol. Key transformation: LiAlH4 delivers hydride to both acetal carbons, breaking the C–O bonds and forming two primary alcohols. Conditions: LiAlH4 (1–2 equiv) in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, reflux 1–3 h, followed by careful aqueous work‑up (water then dilute acid). No additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydride reduction) of an alkyl halide; CsH acts as a hydride source, attacking ethyl bromide in an SN2 fashion to give ethane and cesium bromide; performed in dry aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere, often warmed to reflux; no external catalyst required.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitro aromatic to an amine; SnCl₂ in hydrochloric acid reduces 3‑nitrobiphenyl to 3‑aminobiphenyl, with evolution of water and formation of SnCl₄. Reaction is performed by refluxing the substrate in aqueous HCl with excess SnCl₂ under nitrogen.

Reductive elimination/molysis of a diallyl nickel complex; heating diallylnickel under inert atmosphere induces Ni–C bond cleavage, yielding elemental nickel (often as Ni(0) precipitate) and 1,5‑hexadiene via β‑hydride elimination. Performed in a sealed tube or Schlenk flask at 120‑150 °C; no additional reagents.

Oxime formation by condensation; hydroxylamine adds to the carbonyl of formaldehyde, followed by loss of water to give formaldehyde oxime. Usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution at 0‑25 °C, pH adjusted to 5‑6 with acetate buffer; no catalyst required.

Fischer esterification of 4‑chlorobenzoic acid with 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol to give chloroprocaine (an ester) and water; typically performed under reflux with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) in an inert solvent such as toluene or benzene, using a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water and drive the equilibrium.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkyl halide amination) where 1‑chloropropane reacts with excess ammonia to afford propylamine and ammonium chloride; usually carried out in anhydrous ethanol or aqueous ammonia solution at 50‑80 °C, with excess ammonia serving as both nucleophile and base to neutralize HCl.

Alkylation (SN2) of N‑methylhydrazine with methyl iodide to produce,1‑dimethylhydrazine (unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine) and hydrogen iodide; conducted in a dry aprotic solvent such as ether, THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often in the presence of an inorganic base (e.g., NaHCO₃ or K₂CO₃) to scavenge HI.

Acid‑base double displacement precipitation: oxalic acid reacts with iron(III) bromide in aqueous solution to form insoluble iron(III) oxalate and liberate hydrobromic acid; reaction proceeds at ambient temperature with stirring, the solid iron(III) oxalate is filtered off and the filtrate contains HBr.

SN2 substitution of bromocycloheptane with aqueous ammonia yielding cycloheptylamine and ammonium bromide; performed by heating the bromide in aqueous ammonia (or NH₃/ethanol mixture) under reflux (≈80‑100 °C) for several hours, after which the amine can be extracted with an organic solvent and the salt remains in the aqueous phase.

Reaction type: Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation). Purpose: form methyl 2‑methoxyacetate from the corresponding acid. Key transformation: the carboxylic acid function of 2‑methoxyacetic acid condenses with methanol, releasing water. Typical conditions: reflux the acid with excess methanolysis‑grade methanol, often with a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., p‑tosic acid or H₂SO₄) to accelerate the equilibrium; removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark trap) drives the reaction to completion. Solvent can be methanol itself.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of N,N‑diethyl‑m‑toluamide (DEET) in aqueous HCl to give 3‑methylbenzoic acid and diethylammonium chloride; carried out by refluxing the amide with concentrated HCl (6‑12 M) for several hours, then cooling to isolate the carboxylic acid (by precipitation or extraction) while the diethylammonium chloride in.

Halide exchange (metathesis) reaction; converts scandium chloride to scandium fluoride; Cl⁻ is replaced by F⁻ yielding ScF₃ and HCl; generally conducted in aqueous HF or gaseous HF at elevated temperature (≈150‑200 °C); HF solution or gas is the reaction medium, no catalyst required.

Catalytic reduction (hydrogenolysis) of propyl acetate using sodium borohydride in the presence of a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., NiCl₂·6H₂O or CuCl); the ester C–O bond is cleaved to give ethanol from the acetyl fragment and propanol from the alkoxy fragment; typically carried out in THF or methanol, 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere, no external hydrogen source needed.

Thermal decomposition/disproportionation of dinitrogen trioxide (N₂O₃) into nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂); a reversible gas‑phase or low‑temperature solution reaction that proceeds without solvent, catalyst, or added reagents; N₂O₃ is stable only at low temperature (≈ ‑78 °C) and decomposes on warming.

Aqueous hydrolysis of magnesium borate to give two equivalents of boric acid and one equivalent of magnesium hydroxide; water attacks the borate anion, producing H₃BO₃ and Mg(OH)₂; performed by suspending the solid in water and heating to reflux; no catalyst required; solvent is water (sometimes with gentle stirring).

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol with PCC. 2‑Methylcyclopentan‑1‑ol is converted to the corresponding ketone (2‑methylcyclopentan‑1‑one); chromium(III) chloride and water are formed as by‑products. Reaction is performed in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, often under nitrogen. No additional catalyst.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; silver nitrate reacts with sodium thiocyanate to form silver thiocyanate precipitate and soluble sodium nitrate; performed in aqueous solution under ambient conditions; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of the imine N‑[(E)‑benzylideneamino]aniline with water, regenerating benzaldehyde and aniline; typical conditions use dilute mineral acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) in aqueous ethanol, reflux for 1–2 h; solvent is a water/ethanol mixture; heating accelerates the reaction.

Reaction type: esterification (condensation) of a carbamic acid with ethanol to afford an ethyl carbamate. Purpose: synthesize ethyl N,N‑dimethylcarbamate, a protected amine or agrochemical intermediate. Key transformation: ethanol attacks the carbonyl of the carbamic acid, eliminating water to give the ethyl carbamate. Typical conditions: reflux ethanol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base (pyridine); water removal by azeotropic distillation or using a Dean‑Stark apparatus. Reaction time 2–6 h. Common solvents/catalysts: ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent; optional acid or base catalyst.

Redox reaction of elemental iodine with lithium cyanide to form cyanogen (C₂N₂) and lithium iodide; iodine oxidizes CN⁻ to the dimeric cyanogen while being reduced to I⁻; conducted in dry aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑induced Nef reaction of nitrocyclohexane. Type: oxidative cleavage of nitroalkane to carbonyl compound. Purpose: generate cyclohexanone from nitro compound. Key transformation: nitroalkane deprotonated → nitronate → fragmentation giving cyclohexanone + NaNO₂ + H₂O. Typical conditions: 1–2 equiv NaOH in aqueous medium, 0 °C to rt, then acid work‑up; no special catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange; solid copper(II) oxide reacts with aqueous ammonium hydrogen sulfate, yielding copper(II) sulfate, ammonium sulfate, and water. Usually performed by heating the aqueous mixture to promote dissolution and reaction; no external catalyst is required.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of ethyl acetate with benzyl alcohol to afford benzyl and ethanol; typical conditions employ catalytic sodium methoxide, p‑toluenesulfonic acid, or sulfuric acid, reflux in anhydrous toluene or xylene, with continuous removal of ethanol to drive equilibrium; solvent may be the ester itself or an inert high‑boiling solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization (protonation) of disodium methylarsonate with hydrochloric acid; purpose is to generate methylarsonic acid from its salt. Key transformation: replacement of Na⁺ by H⁺, forming methylarsonic acid and NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, dropwise addition of conc. HCl at 0‑25 °C with stirring; final pH kept acidic.

Ester reduction with lithium aluminum hydride; purpose is to convert the ester into the corresponding primary alcohols; key transformation is hydride attack on the carbonyl followed by cleavage of the C–O bond, giving cyclopropanol from the alkoxy side and ethanol from the acyl side; usually carried out in anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen or argon; work‑up involves careful quenching with water or dilute acid.

Ether formation (Williamson‑type, proceeding via SN1/E1) between tert‑butyl chloride and sodium methoxide to give methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE). Key transformation: alkyl chloride converted to ether, NaCl formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous methanol or THF with NaOMe, reflux (≈60‑80 °C); reaction often proceeds through a tert‑butyl carbocation, sometimes acid‑catalyzed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 4,4′‑bis(dimethylamino)benzophenone to the corresponding benzhydrol; purpose is reduction of the carbonyl to a secondary alcohol. Key transformation: C=O → CH‑OH with addition of hydrogen. Typical conditions: H₂ (1‑3 atm) with Pd/C (≈5 wt %) in ethanol or methanol, 25‑50 °C until hydrogen uptake is complete.

Alpha‑halogenation of a ketone: N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) chlorinates the enol form of acetophenone to give 2‑chloroacetophenone. Typically performed in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature; trifluoroacetic acid acts as a Brønsted acid catalyst to promote enol formation. No metal catalyst is required.

Oxidation of a primary benzylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde: hydrogen peroxide oxidizes benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde with loss of two equivalents of water. Because H₂O₂ alone is a weak oxidant for this transformation, the reaction is usually carried out in the presence of a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Ti‑sylicate, Mo‑ or W‑based catalysts) or a homogeneous organocatalyst such as TEMPO. Typical conditions are aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (t‑butanol, acetonitrile) at 0 °C to 40 °C.

Deprotonation of a phenolic ester (acid‑base reaction): sodium hydride abstracts the phenolic hydrogen of methylparaben, generating the sodium methylparaben salt and liberating hydrogen gas. Conducted under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in a dry, aprotic solvent such as THF, DMF, or DME at 0 °C to reflux; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Carbamoylation of phenol with isocyanic acid to give phenyl carbamate (phenyl N‑carbamate). Phenol is mixed with HNCO (often generated in situ from a phosgene or carbamoyl chloride) in an inert solvent such as toluene or THF at 0–25 °C, sometimes in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine) to scavenge HCl. The nucleophilic phenoxide attacks the electrophilic carbon of isocyanic acid, forming the carbamate linkage; the product serves as a protected phenol or a building block for further transformations.

Reaction type: acyl chloride esterification (acylation of an alcohol). Purpose: synthesis of bornyl acetate, a fragrance ester. Key transformation: the hydroxyl of borneol attacks the carbonyl of acetyl chloride, displacing chloride to form the ester and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, often in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or tetrahydrofuran, with a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine, or anhydrous Na₂CO₃) to trap the generated HCl. The reaction is usually performed under inert atmosphere to avoid.

Reaction type: aqueous hydrolysis (saponification) of an alkyl hydrogen sulfate ester. Purpose: regeneration of the free alcohol and recovery of sulfuric acid. Key transformation: water attacks the sulfate ester, cleaving the S–O bond to yield decyl alcohol and H₂SO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, heating to reflux (50‑100 °C); can be acid‑catalyzed (addition of a small amount of H₂SO₄) or base‑catalyzed (NaOH) followed by neutralization. No special solvent is required beyond water.

Reaction type: acid‑base neutralization. Purpose: produce potassium nitrite from nitrous acid. Key transformation: analogous to the Na⁺ case, forming KNO₂ and water. Typical conditions: cold aqueous medium, careful temperature control to avoid HNO₂ decomposition. No catalyst required.

Reaction type: nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) leading to aryl amination. Purpose: synthesis of 1‑(2‑pyridyl)piperazine, a pharmacologically relevant heterocycle. Key transformation: one nitrogen of piperazine attacks the 2‑position of 2‑chloropyridine, displacing chloride. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or NMP; presence of a mild base (K₂CO₃, NaHCO₃, or Cs₂CO₃) to deprotonate the piperazine; heating to 80‑130 °C for several hours. Copper catalysis (CuI) can be employed for Ullmann‑type coupling, but simple SNAr often proceeds without metal under the stated conditions.

Reaction type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: preparation of beryllium azide and recovery of ammonium sulfate; useful for generating soluble beryllium azide for further use. Key transformation: the azide anion exchanges with the sulfate anion, forming Be(N₃)₂ and NH₄₂SO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of both salts mixed at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring; the insoluble beryllium azide precipitates and is filtered. The reaction is performed under inert atmosphere if moisture‑sensitive handling of Be compounds is required.

Reaction type: aminolysis of an ester to form an amide (amide synthesis). Purpose: conversion of ethyl 2‑chloroacetate to chloroacetamide while liberating ethanol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of ammonia on the carbonyl carbon of the ester, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses, expelling ethanol and giving the amide. Typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃, reflux in a solvent such as ethanol or THF; temperature around 60‑80 °C; the reaction may be driven to completion by removing ethanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) or by using an excess of ammonia. No metal catalysts are needed.

Thermal decarboxylative ring‑opening of glycerol carbonate to give glycidol and carbon dioxide. Usually performed by heating the carbonate (≈150–200 °C) in the melt or in a high‑boiling solvent, sometimes under reduced pressure or with a basic catalyst to facilitate CO₂ loss; the process is solvent‑free or uses a high‑boiling inert solvent.

Ester hydrolysis of butyl propionate with water to give n‑butanol and propionic acid; usually performed in aqueous medium under reflux, often acid‑catalyzed (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄) or base‑catalyzed (NaOH), solvent water or water/organic mixture.
Oxidation of 2‑nitrobenzaldehyde to 2‑nitrobenzoic acid using NaOCl (bleach); reaction proceeds in aqueous alkaline conditions (often NaOH) at 0–25 °C, producing water and NaCl as side products.
Thermal decomposition; produces barium oxide as a solid product; barium carbonate decomposes into barium oxide and carbon dioxide; requires high temperature.
Thermal decomposition of hydroxymethanesulfonic acid yielding formaldehyde and sulfurous acid; occurs upon heating an aqueous solution, no catalyst required.

Sulfonylation of benzyl alcohol with methanesulfonyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine to form benzyl methanesulfonate and triethylammonium chloride; typically done in anhydrous dichloromethane, 0 °C to room temperature.

Hydrolysis of an acyl chloride: 4‑bromobenzoyl chloride reacts with water to produce 4‑bromobenzoic acid and hydrogen chloride; usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a biphasic system (e.g., CH₂Cl₂/H₂O) or directly in aqueous media, without any additional catalyst.

Acid‑base gas‑solid reaction with decarbonation; production of sodium sulfate; sulfur trioxide gas reacts with solid sodium carbonate to give sodium sulfate and carbon dioxide; heated to 150‑250 °C under dry conditions; no solvent or catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of diethyl terephthalate with water to afford terephthalic acid and ethanol; performed with aqueous NaOH or KOH at reflux, followed by acid work‑up to precipitate the acid; solvent water/ethanol or mixed aqueous system.

Esterification (condensation) of acrylic acid with pentaerythritol to give pentaerythritol triacrylate; used to prepare UV‑curable crosslinking monomers. Key transformation is formation of three ester bonds with release of three water molecules. Typically carried out under reflux (80‑120 °C) with a strong Brønsted acid catalyst (e.g., sulfuric acid, p‑TsOH, or catalytic DMAP) and removal of water by azeotropic distillation (toluene or xylene as solvent).

Ion‑exchange (metathesis) conversion of a quaternary ammonium halide to its hydroxide. Methyltributylammonium iodide reacts with aqueous NaOH to afford methyltributylammonium hydroxide and NaI. Performed at ambient temperature in a biphasic water/organic system; the hydroxide salt is often used as a phase‑transfer catalyst. No special solvent beyond water is required.

Oxidative dissolution of gold in aqua regia (concentrated HCl/HNO₃, ~3 : 1). Gold is oxidized by nitrate to Au³⁺, which is immediately complexed by chloride to form chloroauric acid (HAuCl₄). Nitrogen oxides generated are reduced to nitrosyl chloride (NOCl) and chlorine (Cl₂), with water as by‑product. Reaction proceeds at ambient to ~50 °C in the liquid acid mixture; no added solvent or catalyst is required.

Fischer esterification between benzyl alcohol and phthalic acid to afford monobenzyl phthalate (a mono‑ester plasticizer) with loss of water. The reaction forms a single ester linkage while the second carboxyl group remains free. Conducted under reflux (120‑150 °C) with an acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid or p‑TsOH, often in toluene or xylene with Dean–Stark apparatus to remove water and drive the equilibrium.

E2 dehydrohalogenation of 3‑chloro‑1‑phenylpropane with potassium tert‑butoxide, producing allylbenzene and potassium chloride.
