N‑ethylation of morpholine with ethyl bromide (SN2 alkylation); purpose is to form N‑ethyl‑morpholine; key transformation is nucleophilic substitution of bromide by the morpholine nitrogen, yielding the product and HBr; usually conducted in dry acetonitrile, DMF or dichloromethane at reflux, employing a base (K₂CO₃, NaH, or triethylamine) to neutralize the acid; morpholine may be used as solvent or in excess.

Base‑promoted Williamson ether synthesis forming an epoxy (glycidyl) ether from o‑cresol and epichlorohydrin. Potassium carbonate acts as base and captures the generated HCl, releasing CO2 and water. Carried out in refluxing acetone or DMF under nitrogen, 60–80 °C, no additional catalyst.

β‑Elimination (E2) of a tosylate ester by strong, non‑nucleophilic base potassium tert‑but, yielding 3‑methyl‑1‑butene and potassium p‑toluenesulfonate. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent (THF or DMSO) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; base itself serves as the promoter.

Acid–base/heterolytic substitution reaction producing monochloramine (NH2Cl) from ammonium hydroxide and hypochlorous acid. Conducted in aqueous solution with pH buffered around 8–9 to favor NH2Cl formation; no catalyst needed.

Radical‑mediated trifluoromethylation (SRN1/SET) of 5‑bromo‑2′‑deoxyuridine to give trifluridine. Potassium persulfate initiates radicals that replace the bromine with a CF3 group supplied by sodium trifluoromethanesulfinate. Typical conditions: aqueous/organic medium (e.g., DMSO/water), 60 °C, under nitrogen; persulfate acts as oxidant/initiator, no additional metal catalyst.

Double‑displacement/halide exchange; used to convert iridium(III) bromide into the water‑soluble hexachloroiridate(III) complex. In aqueous HCl the bromide ligands are displaced by chloride, forming [IrCl6]³⁻ which pairs with Na⁺ from NaCl to give Na₃[IrCl₆]; NaBr remains in solution. Typical conditions: dissolve NaCl, IrBr₃ and excess HCl in water, stir at ambient temperature or mild heating (≤50 °C). No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Co‑precipitation followed by solid‑state oxidation; preparation of barium ferrite (BaFe₁₂O₁₉) nanopowder. NaOH is added to an aqueous mixture of Ba(NO₃)₂ and Fe(NO₃)₃, precipitating Ba(OH)₂ and Fe(OH)₃. The precipitate is washed, dried, and calcined at 800–1000 °C in air, where it transforms into BaFe₁₂₁₉ while releasing water and forming NaNO₃ that stays in the melt or is washed away. Reaction is carried out in water; pH is kept high (≈10–12). No catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitrile to a primary amine; purpose: convert 4‑methoxyphenylacetonitrile into O‑methyltyramine; key transformations: –C≡N reduced to –CH₂NH₂; typical conditions: H₂ (1–5 atm) with Pd/C or Raney Ni in ethanol or methanol at 40–80 °C; common solvent: ethanol or methanol; catalyst: palladium on carbon or Raney nickel.

Aqueous acid‑base hydrolysis of ammonium perchlorate; formation of perchloric acid and ammonia. Dissolving NH₄ClO₄ in water results in proton transfer from NH₄⁺ to H₂O, generating NH₃ (which may escape as gas) and HClO₄. The reaction proceeds at room temperature in water; no catalyst is required. It is often used to obtain dilute perchloric acid solutions.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile; hexadecanenitrile is reduced under H₂ (1–5 atm) over Pd/C to give the primary amine hexadecylamine; performed in ethanol or methanol at 25–80 °C; catalyst loading typically 5–10 % Pd.

Acid–base neutralization; metal oxide reacts with a strong acid to give a soluble metal halide and water; Y2O3 + 6 HCl → 2 YCl3 + 3 H2O; typically performed in aqueous HCl under reflux or gentle heating; water is the reaction medium, no catalyst required.

Condensation (ocondensation) of formaldehyde with thiourea to give 2‑imidazolidinethione. Formaldehyde reacts with two equivalents of thiourea, forming a five‑ed heterocycle and releasing one molecule of water. The reaction is typically performed in ethanol or aqueous ethanol under reflux (60–80 °C) and may be catalyzed by a weak acid (e.g., acetic acid) or by heating alone. It provides a convenient route to thio‑urea‑derived heterocycles.

Double‑replacement metathesis between sodium phosphate (Na₃PO₄) and praseodymium fluoride (PrF₃). In aqueous solution the phosphate anion exchanges with fluoride, precipitating insoluble praseodymium phosphate (PrPO₄) while forming soluble NaF. The mixture is stirred at ambient temperature or gently heated (≤60 °C) to complete the exchange; water is the solvent and no catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of terephthalic acid; purpose to saturate the aromatic ring and produce 1,4‑cyclohexanedicarboxylic acid, a monomer for polymer synthesis. Key transformation: reduction of the benzene ring to a cyclohexane ring while preserving the two carboxylic acid groups. Typical conditions: hydrogen pressure 50–100 atm, temperature 150–200 °C, solid metal catalyst such as Raney nickel, palladium on carbon, or platinum. Common solvents: ethanol, water, or glacial acetic acid.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrosation of N‑ethylurea using sodium nitrite; purpose to generate the carcinogenic/chemotherapeutic intermediate N‑ethyl‑N‑nitrosourea. Key transformation: conversion of the secondary amide nitrogen to an N‑nitroso group (N–N=O) with loss of water; formation of sodium hydrogen sulfate as by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, dilute H₂SO₄ to generate nitrous acid in situ, temperature kept 0–5 °C to avoid decomposition, slow addition of nitrite solution. No additional catalyst; acid serves to produce nitrous acid. Solvent: water, sometimes with a miscible organic co‑solvent (e.g., methanol).

Aqueous double‑displacement metathesis/precipitation; used to prepare insoluble terbium(III) phosphate from terbium(III) sulfate by exchanging sulfate for phosphate anions, yielding solid TbPO₄ and H₂SO₄ in solution; performed in water at ambient or gently heated temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation reaction between lead(II) acetate hydroiodic acid; purpose to obtainuble lead(II) iodide and liberate acetic acid. Key transformation: exchange of acetate anions for iodide anions, yielding solid PbI₂ precipitate and acetic acid in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; reaction proceeds spontaneously. Solvent: water.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of acetyl chloride with sodium hydroxide; purpose to convert an acid chloride to its carboxylate salt and neutralize chloride. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl carbon, producing acetate ion and chloride ion; one molecule of water is generated. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution, initial cooling (ice bath) followed by warming to ambient temperature, vigorous stirring. Solvent: water, optionally mixed with an organic solvent if a biphasic system is used.

Aqueous precipitation/acid‑base reaction; purpose is to isolate copper(II) sulfide and generate nitric acid in solution. Key transformation: Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂S(g) → CuS(s) + 2 HNO₃(aq). Performed by bubbling H₂S through an aqueous Cu(NO₃)₂ solution at ambient temperature, often under slightly acidic conditions (pH ≈ 1–2); water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic addition of sulfenyl chloride to an alkene (mustard‑gas synthesis). Sulfur dichloride adds across the C=C bond of ethylene, forming bis(2‑chloroethyl)sulfide. Usually carried out at 0‑5 °C in anhydrous carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, often with a Lewis‑acid catalyst such as AlCl3 or under UV irradiation to promote the addition.

Acid‑base neutralization between acetic acid and sodium hypophosphite; purpose to prepare hypophosphorous acid and sodium acetate. Key transformation: proton transfer from acetic acid to the hypophosphite anion, forming H₃PO₂ and CH₃COO⁻ Na⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, moderate concentrations, no special catalyst required. Solvent: water.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride; aqueous NaOH provides OH⁻ which attacks the carbon bearing Cl, displacing Cl⁻ to give 2‑fluoroethanol and NaCl. Reaction proceeds at room temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation reaction of ammonium hydroxide with stannous sulfate; purpose to precipitate stannous hydroxide while generating soluble ammonium sulfate. Key transformation: Sn²⁺ reacts with OH⁻ to form insoluble Sn(OH)₂ solid; SO₄²⁻ pairs with NH₄⁺ to give (NH₄)₂SO₄ in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, slight excess of NH₄OH, ambient temperature, continuous stirring. Solvent: water.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of a chloro‑pyrimidine by ammonia; replaces the chlorine with an amino group to give 2,6‑dimethyl‑4‑aminopyrimidine while generating HCl; typically carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at elevated temperature (80‑120 °C); often a base (e.g., triethylamine) is added to neutralize the formed HCl.

Simple double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange between ethylammonium chloride and sodium nitrate; produces sodium chloride and ethylammonium nitrate in aqueous solution; performed at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water serves as the reaction medium.

Epoxide ring‑opening with a Grignard reagent; isopropylmagnesium chloride attacks ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring and, after protonation, yields 2‑methyl‑1‑butanol; typically conducted in dry THF at 0 °C to rt, then the reaction mixture is acid‑quenched (e.g., with NH₄Cl or dilute HCl).

Iodoform (haloform) reaction combined with oxidation of a secondary alcohol; iodine in basic aqueous NaOH oxidizes sec‑butyl alcohol to the corresponding methyl ketone, which then undergoes haloform cleavage to give iodoform (CHI₃) and sodium propionate; carried out in water at room temperature to gentle reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization; converts Gd(OH)3 into soluble gadolinium sulfate by treatment with aqueous H2SO4, producing Gd2(SO4)3 (or Gd(SO4)3) and water; conducted in water at ambient temperature, often with gentle heating to aid dissolution; the reaction proceeds without a catalyst; the product remains in aqueous solution.

High‑temperature ammonolysis (salt metathesis) of silicon tetrachloride with ammonia to form silicon nitride (Si₃N₄) and gaseous HCl; typically performed in the gas phase at 600‑800 °C under flowing NH₃; no solvent; the HCl by‑product is removed as a gas.

Oxidation; primary alcohol to carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate. The reaction oxidizes the terminal CH2OH of 2‑methylheptan‑1‑ol to the corresponding acid, producing MnO2 precipitate and water. Typical conditions are aqueous alkaline KMnO4 (often in dilute NaOH) at room temperature to gentle heating; the reaction is carried out in water or a water‑acetone mixture and the mixture is acidified after completion to isolate the acid.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of an alkyl iodide by azide ion; purpose is to introduce an azide functional group for later reduction to amine or click chemistry; key transformation is replacement of iodine with N3; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 50–80 °C with excess K N3; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 mechanism) of 2,4,4‑trimethylpentan‑2‑ol using concentrated sulfuric acid; eliminates water to give 2,4,4‑trimethylpent‑2‑ene; carried out at 60‑80 °C, often with the alcohol acting as solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Strong hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; purpose: obtain(4‑methylphenyl)ethanol; key transformations: –CO₂H → –CH₂OH; typical conditions: LiAlH₄ (1–2 equiv) in dry THF or diethyl ether, 0 °C then reflux; common solvent: dry THF or ether; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidative cleavage of a non‑2‑ene double bond using hot aqueous potassium permanganate; a strong oxidizing reaction that breaks the C=C bond to give the two terminal fragments as carboxylic acids (acetic acid from the two‑carbon side and heptanoic acid from the seven‑carbon side). Conducted under reflux in dilute KMnO₄ solution, typically in water or aqueous NaOH; no special catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction between aqueous ammonium hydroxide and dysprosium(III) chloride. The base exchanges anions with the metal salt, forming insoluble dysprosium(III) hydroxide precipitate and soluble ammonium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Perkow reaction: dimethyl phosphite reacts with 2,2‑dichloroacetaldehyde (an α‑halo carbonyl) to give the organophosphate dichlorvos (dimethyl 2,2‑dichlorovinyl phosphate) and water. Requires anhydrous, aprotic solvent (e.g., benzene, toluene) and reflux under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Redox/precipitation reaction of potassium cyanide with mercury(I) chloride. Cyanide reduces mercurous ions, yielding mercury(II) cyanide precipitate, elemental mercury, and potassium chloride in solution. Carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature; no catalyst.

Carbamoylation (urea formation) of dimethylamine with potassium cyanate. Nucleophilic attack of the amine on the cyanate ion gives N,N‑dimethylurea after transfer. Usually performed in water or alcoholic, heated gently (50‑80 °C), often under neutral to slightly basic conditions; no catalyst required.

Intramolecular cyclodehydration (heterocycle formation) using thionyl chloride as a dehydrating and oxidizing agent; converts the two adjacent amine groups of o‑phenylenediamine into the fused 1,2,5‑benzothiadiazole ring while releasing HCl and SO₂. Typical conditions: reflux neat SOCl₂ or SOCl₂ in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) under nitrogen; often a base such as pyridine is added to scavenge HCl.

Oxidation of ferrocyanide to ferricyanide in acidic medium; H₂O₂ serves as the oxidant in the presence of nitric acid, converting [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ to [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ with formation of water. Performed in aqueous solution, typically 0–25 °C, under stirring; the acid provides the necessary protons, and no additional catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization forming an acid salt; ammonium hydroxide (aqueous) reacts with sulfuric acid to give ammonium hydrogen sulfate and water. Typically performed in water at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution/opening of epibromohydrin by ethanol to form glycidyl ethyl ether and liberate hydrogen bromide. Ethanol attacks the carbon bearing bromine, displacing Br⁻ and generating the ether. Conducted in anhydrous ethanol or a polar aprotic solvent, often with a base (e.g., NaH, K₂CO₃) to scavenge HBr; reflux conditions are typical.

Acid‑base neutralization: magnesium carbonate reacts with malic acid to form magnesium malate, releasing CO2 gas and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating; CO2 evolution drives the reaction to completion.

Type: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on a pyrimidine ring. Purpose: Replace two chlorine atoms of 2,4‑dichloropyrimidine with amine groups to afford 2,4‑diaminopyrimidine. Key transformation: NH3 (from NH4OH) attacks the electron‑deficient C‑Cl positions, displacing Cl− and generating HCl. Typical conditions: Reflux in aqueous or alcoholic NH4OH (often ethanol/water), excess ammonium hydroxide, temperature 80‑100 °C. No special catalyst; by‑product HCl is scavenged by the excess base.

Type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: Exchange anions and cations to precipitate iron(III) hydroxide. Key transformation: FeCl3 + Sr(OH)2 → Fe(OH)3 (insoluble) + SrCl2 (soluble). Typical conditions: Aqueous solutions mixed at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring; the iron(III) hydroxide precipitates and is filtered. No catalyst required.

Type: Conversion of an alcohol to a chloroate using oxalyl chloride/DMF (Vilsmeier‑type activation). Purpose: Generate benzyl chloroformate, a useful protecting group for amines. Key transformation: Benzyl‑OH reacts with in‑situ‑generated Cl‑C(O)‑Cl (from oxalyl chloride) to give benzyl‑O‑C(O)‑Cl, releasing CO, CO2 and HCl. Typical conditions: Dry dichloromethane or THF, catalytic dimethylformamide (0.1‑1 equiv), oxalyl chloride added at 0 °C under nitrogen, then benzyl alcohol added; reaction warmed to rt and stirred 1‑2 h. By‑products (CO, CO2, HCl) are vented or trapped.

Catalytic hydrogenation; purpose is to saturate the C=C bond of norbornene to give norbornane. Hydrogen adds across the double bond in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni. Reaction is run at 1–5 atm H₂, ambient to 50 °C, in solvents like ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate.

Type: Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: Prepare indium(III) acetate from the hydroxide precursor. Key transformation: In(OH)3 + 3 CH3COOH → In(CH3COO)3 + 3 H2O. Typical conditions: Aqueous or ethanolic solution, gentle heating (50‑80 °C) to aid dissolution, stoichiometric amounts of acetic acid; reaction proceeds to completion with evolution of water. No catalyst required.

Electrophilic addition (halogenation) of the C=C bond in maleic anhydride; chlorine adds across the double bond to give dichloromaleic anhydride. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane under a dry nitrogen atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Intramolecular Wurtz‑type reductive cyclization (dehalogenation) of a 1,9‑dihalide to a cyclononane; purpose: form a nine‑membered carbocycle; key transformations: two C–Cl bonds reduced, radicals couple to give a new C–C bond forming the ring, ZnCl₂ formed; typical conditions: excess zinc dust in dry ether or THF, reflux under inert atmosphere; common solvent: dry ether or THF; metal (zinc) serves as the reductant, no separate catalyst.

Redox (metal fluoride formation). Antimony metal reacts with hydrogen fluoride, oxidizing Sb to Sb(III) and reducing HF to H₂. Typically performed in a sealed tube or pressure reactor at elevated temperature≈150‑200 °C) with anhydrous HF; no additional solvent; hydrogen gas evolves as a by‑product.

Acid‑catalyzed Friedel‑Crafts alkylation. Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates isobutylene to generate a tert‑butyl carbocation which electrophilically attacks the ortho positions of 4‑methylphenol, giving 2,6‑di‑tert‑butyl‑4‑methylphenol (a hindered phenol antioxidant). Usually carried out at 0‑30 °C initially, then warmed to 60‑80 °C, using excess isobutylene gas; the reaction medium is the sulfuric acid itself, and water is removed during work‑up.

Oxidative conversion of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid (Jones oxidation). Salicyl alcohol (2‑hydroxybenzyl alcohol) is oxidized by CrO₃ in the presence of aqueous H₂SO₄, converting the –CH₂OH group to –CO₂H and affording salicylic acid. Typical conditions: CrO₃ (1.5–2 equiv) in acetone or aqueous acetone, dilute H₂SO₄ (≈1 M), temperature 0 °C to room temperature, with vigorous stirring; reaction is quenched with methanol or water.

Base‑catalyzed aldol (Claisen‑Schmidt) condensation. 4‑Hydroxybenzaldehyde condenses with acetone under NaOH to form the α,β‑unsaturated ketone 4‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)but‑3‑en‑2‑one (a chalcone analogue). Conducted in aqueous NaOH (10–30 % w/w) or NaOH/ethanol solution, temperature kept below 25 °C during addition, then refluxed for 1‑2 h to promote dehydration; the product precipitates upon cooling and is filtered.

Free‑radical bromination (substitution, favoring tertiary); gives a tertiary bromoalkane; key transformation replaces the tertiary hydrogen of isopentane with bromine to produce 2‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane and HBr; reaction conditions similar to (3): UV light or heat in an inert solvent (CCl4), often requiring longer reaction times due to bromine’s lower reactivity.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of nitro group). 1‑Nitronaphthalene is reduced with molecular hydrogen over Pd/C to give 1‑naphthylamine; water is formed from the reduction of the nitro oxygens. Performed in a hydrogenation vessel at 1–5 atm H₂, 25‑50 °C, using ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate as solvent; catalyst loading typically 5–10 % Pd on carbon, reaction monitored by TLC or GC.

Fischer esterification. Gallic acid (3,4,5‑trihydroxybenzoic acid) reacts with n‑butanol in the presence of catalytic H₂SO₄ to afford n‑butyl gallate and water. Conducted under reflux (≈110 °C) with excess n‑butanol serving as both reactant and solvent; a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄ (≈0.5 % v/v) catalyze the reaction, and water is removed azeotropically (Dean‑Stark or by nitrogen sweep) to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Ester hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution); purpose is to cleave the sulfonate ester to recover the sulfonic acid and an alcohol. Key transformation: water attacks the sulfonate carbon, displacing the pentyl group as pentanol and generating 4‑methylbenzenesulfonic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, often heated ( reflux ) and may be acid‑catalyzed (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄). Common solvent: water or water‑anol mixture.

Metal sulfide formation (solid‑state redox); purpose is to prepare copper(I) sulfide; key transformation is transfer of sulfur fromyl sulfide to Cu(I) forming Cu2S while carbon is oxidized to CO2; typical conditions involve passing OCS gas over Cu2O at 300–500 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent and the copper oxide itself acts as the reagent/catalyst.

S‑alkylation of thiourea (nucleophilic substitution, SN2) with methyl bromide; purpose is to methylate the sulfur atom, yielding S‑methylthiourea and HBr. Thiourea acts as a nucleophile on the electrophilic carbon of CH₃Br, displacing bromide. Reaction is typically conducted in an aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol) at reflux temperature; a base such as NaOH or Na₂CO₃ is often added to neutralize the generated HBr and drive the reaction to completion. No metal catalyst is needed.

Electrophilic sulfonation; purpose is to introduce a sulfonic acid substituent onto benzene. Key transformation: benzene undergoes SEAr with the electrophile SO₃ (from oleum) to give benzenesulfonic acid. Typical conditions: oleum (20–65 % SO₃ in H₂SO₄) at 0–80 °C; reaction is usually performed in the liquid oleum itself, no external solvent needed.

Oxidative cleavage/oxidation of a dialdehyde; potassium permanganate oxidizes decanedial to the dicarboxylic acid decanedioic acid. Performed in aqueous basic medium (NaOH or KOH, 0.5–1 M) at 60–80 °C; excess KMnO₄ is used (2–3 equiv per aldehyde function) and the reaction mixture is then acidified to precipitate the diacid.

SN2 N‑alkylation of a secondary amine; purpose is to methylate the nitrogen of 1‑(3,4‑dimethoxyphenyl)propan‑2‑amine. Key transformation: methyl iodide transfers a methyl group to the amine nitrogen, forming the N‑methyl product and potassium iodide as by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, acetonitrile) at 0 °C to rt, with potassium carbonate as base to deprotonate the amine.

Alkaline hydrolysis (amide saponification) of acetanilide with aqueous NaOH, heated to reflux. The amide bond is cleaved to give sodium acetate and free aniline; reaction often performed in a mixed water/ethanol solvent, followed by acidification to liberate aniline.

Metathesis/precipitation (silica removal and aluminate formation). Aluminum hydroxide reacts with sodium silicate (water glass) to give soluble sodium aluminate, solid silicon dioxide, and water. Typically performed in aqueous medium under heating (50–80 °C) with vigorous stirring to keep the silica dispersed and to drive the reaction to completion. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Swern oxidation (DMSO‑oxalyl chloride mediated oxidation); purpose is to convert the benzylic alcohol of 2‑(hydroxymethyl)aniline to the corresponding aldehyde (2‑aminobenzaldehyde). Key transformation: DMSO activated by oxalyl chloride forms a chlorosulfonium intermediate that reacts with the alcohol; triethylamine then abstracts a proton, giving the aldehyde and dimethyl sulfide as by‑product. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane, –78 °C to 0 °C for addition of oxalyl chloride/DMSO, then warm to rt after TEA addition. Common solvents: CH₂Cl₂; reagents: DMSO, oxalyl chloride, triethylamine.

Transesterification of methyl 3‑(dimethylamino)propanoate with ethanol forming ethyl 3‑(dimethylamino)propanoate and methanol; purpose is to exchange the alkoxy group of the ester; key transformation is substitution of the methoxy group by an ethoxy group; typically catalyzed by a small amount of acid (H2SO4) or base (NaOEt) under reflux in ethanol, with removal of methanol to shift the reaction forward.

Acyl chloride formation from a carboxylate salt; thionyl chloride converts sodium dichloroacetate into dichloroacetyl chloride while releasing gaseous HCl and SO₂; typical conditions are reflux in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or chloroform) often with a base such as pyridine to trap HCl; by‑product NaCl precipitates, reaction is driven to completion by removal of HCl/SO₂ gases.

Acid dissolution of a mixed manganese oxide; Mn3O4 reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form manganese(II) sulfate and water (Mn3O4 + H2SO4 → MnSO4 + H2O); carried out in aqueous medium with gentle heating; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base protonation of a xanthate salt; aqueous HCl protonates potassium ethyl xanthate to give ethyl xanthic acid and potassium chloride; performed at ambient temperature in water or dilute acid solution; no special catalyst required; the reaction is simply a neutralization‑type conversion from the salt to the free acid.

Neutralization of a carboxylic acid; diclofenac acid reacts with aqueous NaOH to afford the water‑soluble sodium salt of diclofenac and water; carried out in water or a water‑alcohol mixture at room temperature; often used to improve solubility or for salt‑form preparation in pharmaceutical synthesis; no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an unsaturated fatty acid; cetoleic acid (22‑carbon monounsaturated acid) is hydrogenated in the presence of H₂ gas and a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO₂) to give the fully saturated docosanoic (behenic) acid; typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 50–150 °C, solvent such as ethanol, isopropanol or hexane; the reaction removes the C=C double bond without affecting the carboxyl group.

Acid–base double displacement (neutralization) of ammonium nitrate with sodium hydroxide: NaOH converts₄NO₃ to sodium nitrate, liberates ammonia gas, and forms water. Purpose is to generate NH₃ and a sodium nitrate solution. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature by slowly adding NaOH solution to solid or solution of ammonium nitrate; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic chlorination of cyanuric acid to give trichloroisocyanuric acid; chlorine gas is bubbled through an aqueous suspension of cyanuric acid, effecting stepwise substitution of the ring nitrogens with chlorine atoms and generating HCl; the process is conducted at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to control exotherm; the product, trichloroisocyanuric acid, precipitates and is isolated; no additional catalyst is required.

Fischer esterification; converts a secondary alcohol (pentan‑3‑ol) to its acetate ester (pentan‑3‑yl acetate) by reacting with acetic acid. Acid catalyst (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄) and reflux are typical; water formed is removed (Dean‑Stark or azeotropic distillation). Common solvents: toluene, benzene, or xylene.

Oxidation of fluorene to fluorenone; sodium dichromate (Na₂Cr₂O₇) in acidic medium (usually H₂SO₄) oxidizes the benzylic methylene of fluorene to the carbonyl group, yielding fluoren‑9‑one and water. Reaction is carried out under heating, often in aqueous sulfuric acid; no organic solvent is required.

Knoevenagel‑type condensation producing methyl cyanoacrylate (superglue monomer). Formaldehyde condenses with methyl cyanoacetate in the presence of ammonium acetate as a mild base catalyst, eliminating water to form the α,β‑unsaturated nitrile. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or methanol, 60–80 °C, with removal of water to drive the equilibrium.

Acid–base neutralization/precipitation; calcium oxide reacts with phosphoric acid in aqueous solution, forming calcium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate (CaHPO₄·2H₂O) and water. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature; stirring in water followed by cooling yields the crystalline dihydrate, which can be filtered and dried.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of tert‑butyl benzoate; purpose is to cleave the tert‑butyl ester to give the free carboxylic acid. Water attacks the carbonyl, and the tert‑butyl group leaves as tert‑butanol, affording benzoic acid and tert‑butanol. Conducted with aqueous strong acid (e.g., HCl or H₂SO₄) at reflux (≈80–100 °C) in a biphasic mixture of water and a water‑miscible organic solvent such as dioxane or dichloromethane.

Transfer hydrogenation (catalytic reduction) of 1‑nitronaphthalene to 1‑naphthylamine using formic acid as the hydrogen donor over Pd/C. Formic acid decomposes to CO₂ and H₂ while delivering hydrogen to the nitro group, effecting its reduction to the amine. Conducted in polar protic solvent (e.g., methanol or ethanol) at 25–60 °C under atmospheric pressure.

Oxidative conversion of a benzylic methyl group to a carboxylic acid using aqueous alkaline potassium permanganate; typical conditions: reflux in water or aqueous NaOH, excess KMnO₄, temperature 80‑120 °C; MnO₂ precipitates; purpose: synthesis of 2‑chloro‑6‑fluorobenzoic acid.

Mo(VI)‑catalyzed oxidation of phenylacetic acid to mandelic acid. Hydrogen peroxide serves as the oxidant; molybdenum(VI) oxide (MoO₃) activates H₂O₂ to generate peroxy species that hydroxylate the α‑carbon of phenylacetic acid, yielding mandelic acid and water. Reaction is performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic medium (often acetone or methanol) at 0–25 °C, with catalytic amounts of MoO₃ (≈1–5 mol %).

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchange of cations between sodium octanoate and magnesium sulfate produces magnesium octanoate (often less soluble) and sodium sulfate. Performed in aqueous solution, sometimes warmed to improve precipitation; the solid magnesium octanoate is filtered off.

Double displacement reaction. Purpose is precipitation of lead(II) oxalate. Key transformation involves cation exchange between lead(II) nitrate and calcium oxalate in aqueous solution. Reaction occurs in water as solvent without catalyst.

Thermal decomposition reaction. Purpose is decomposition of chromium(III) nitrate under heat. Key transformation is breaking down of chromium nitrate into oxygen, chromium(III) oxide, and nitrogen dioxide. Requires high temperature conditions without catalyst.

Oxidation reaction. Purpose is selective oxidation of cycloheptane to cycloheptanone. Key transformation involves introduction of a ketone functional group via oxygen insertion. Typically requires catalytic transition metals (e.g., Co or Mn) under high-temperature and pressure conditions.

General type: carbamoylation (nucleophilic addition of an amine to cyanate). Purpose: to protect the amino group of β‑alanine as an N‑carbamoyl derivative. Key transformation: the primary amine of β‑alanine attacks the electrophilic carbon of potassium cyanate, forming N‑carbamoyl‑β‑alanine and generating KOH as a by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic solution, mild heating (40–80 °C), neutral to slightly basic pH. Common solvent/catalyst: water or ethanol; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose is to exchange the alkoxy group of decyl acetate for a methyl group, producing methyl acetate and regenerating decanol; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methoxide on the carbonyl, followed by methanolysis; usually carried out in excess methanol with NaOMe (or K₂CO₃) at reflux (≈65 °C) in a sealed tube or with a Dean‑Stark apparatus.

Catalytic aerobic oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde; 4‑bromobenzyl alcohol is oxidized to 4‑bromobenzaldehyde using CuCl₂ as the copper(II) catalyst and molecular O₂ as the oxidant; typical conditions: solvent such as acetonitrile or DMSO, a base (e.g., pyridine or NaOH), temperature 80‑120 °C under an O₂ balloon or air flow; reaction proceeds without stoichiometric oxidant.

Nucleophilic addition of an aromatic amine to isocyanic acid, forming a urea linkage; aniline attacks the electrophilic carbon of HNCO, yielding phenylurea after proton transfer; a straightforward method to synthesize aryl‑ureas; usually performed at room temperature in an inert solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, toluene) or neat, sometimes with a mild base (pyridine) to accelerate proton abstraction; no external catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis (amide deamidation) of L‑glutamine to L‑glutamate and ammonia; purpose is removal of the side‑chain amide in nitrogen metabolism; key transformation is conversion of the amide group to a carboxylate releasing NH3; typically catalyzed by glutaminase in aqueous buffer at neutral to slightly alkaline pH, or chemically with dilute acid or base at elevated temperature; solvent is water.

General type: acid–base neutralization. Purpose: conversion of dithionic acid to its sodium salt (sodium dithionate). Key transformation: H2S2O6 + 2 NaOH → Na2S2O6 + 2 H2O. Typical conditions: dissolve dithionic acid in water, add stoichiometric NaOH solution at room temperature, stir until complete. Common solvent/catalyst: water; reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Type: acid‑base (salt metathesis). Purpose: generate pertechnetic acid (HTcO4) from ammonium pertechnetate. Key transformation: protonation of the pertechnetate anion with HCl to form HTcO4 and NH4Cl. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of NH4TcO4 treated with dilute HCl, often kept cool (0‑5 °C) to avoid decomposition. Common solvent: water.

Metal‑acid redox (single‑displacement) reaction; indium metal is oxidized by hydrogen bromide, producing indium tribromide and hydrogen gas; typically carried out in concentrated aqueous HBr under reflux to ensure complete reaction; no external catalyst, aqueous HBr is both reagent and solvent.

Acid–base (double displacement) metathesis; swaps nitrate for fumarate, producing iron(II) fumarate precipitate and nitric acid in aqueous medium; carried out at ambient or slightly elevated temperature with stirring, no catalyst.

General type: halogenation of cyanide (formation of cyanogen halide) with simultaneous oxidation‑reduction. Purpose: synthesis of cyanogen bromide, a useful electrophilic reagent. Key transformation: NaCN + Br2 → BrCN (cyanogen bromide) + NaBr. Typical conditions: cold (0–5 °C), dark, aqueous or methanol solution of NaCN; bromine added dropwise to control exotherm. Common solvent/catalyst: water or methanol; often a phase‑transfer catalyst (e.g., tetrabutylammonium bromide) is used to improve yields, but not mandatory.

Enzymatic decarboxylation; L‑cysteine sulfinic acid is converted to hypotaurine with loss of CO₂. This reaction is catalyzed by L‑cysteine‑sulfinic‑acid decarboxylase (a PL‑dependent enzyme) in aqueous buffer at physiological pH (≈7.4) and temperature (≈37 °C). It is a key biosynthetic step in the formation of taurine.

General type: amide hydrolysis (cleavage to carboxylic acid and amine). Purpose: to liberate butanoic acid and 2‑phenylethylamine from the protected amide. Key transformation: N‑(2‑phenylethyl)butanamide + H2O → butanoic acid + 2‑phenylethylamine. Typical conditions: aqueous acid (e.g., 6 M HCl) or base (e.g.,  M NaOH), reflux (80–120 °C) for several hours; alternatively, enzymatic hydrolysis at mild pH. Common solvent/catalyst: water; acid catalyst (HCl) or base catalyst (NaOH) is required.

Oxidative cleavage of 2‑methyl‑1,4‑butanediol with concentrated nitric acid; purpose is conversion to methylsuccinic acid; key transformation: strong oxidation of primary alcohol groups to carboxylic acids, releasing nitrogen dioxide and water; typical conditions: fuming nitric acid (≈95‑100 %) heated under reflux at 50‑80 °C in glassware resistant to acid; no catalyst.

Oxidative coupling reaction. Purpose is autooxidation of pyrogallol to form purpurogallin. Key transformation involves dimerization of pyrogallol via phenolic oxidation. Reaction typically proceeds in aqueous solution with a base or enzymatic catalyst (e.g., peroxidase).

Acid‑base double displacement; hydrofluoric acid protonates strontium orthophosphate and precipitates insoluble strontium fluoride while liberating phosphoric acid; performed in aqueous solution at ambient to modest temperature, typically water as solvent, no catalyst required.

Synthesis (acid‑base reaction of a metal oxide with an acid anhydride); used to prepare iron(III) sulfate as a pigment, water‑treatment agent or laboratory reagent; the oxide O²⁻ in Fe₂O₃ is converted to sulfate SO₄²⁻, forming Fe₂(SO₄)₃ while the oxidation state of iron remains +3; typically carried out by passing gaseous SO₃ over finely powdered Fe₂O₃ at 200‑400 °C, often in the presence of excess fuming H₂SO₄; no solvent is required (solid‑state or gas‑phase conditions).

Allotropic conversion; white phosphorus (P4) is thermally rearranged to the polymeric red phosphorus allotrope; carried out by heating white P to ~250 °C in an inert atmosphere (nitrogen or vacuum) in a sealed tube, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Halogen displacement (single‑replacement) reaction; chlorine, being a stronger oxidizing halogen, oxidizes bromide to bromine gas while reducing itself to chloride, converting solid thallium bromide to thallium chloride. Typically carried out by passing dry Cl₂ gas over heated TlBr (200‑300 °C) in a dry tubular furnace; no solvent or catalyst required.

Metal‑acid single replacement; elemental potassium reduces picric acid, producing hydrogen gas and the potassium picrate salt; conducted in dry, aprotic solvents such as anhydrous diethyl ether or THF under inert atmosphere, often at 0 °C to ambient temperature, no catalyst.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling; DCC activates nonanoic acid to form an O‑acylurea intermediate which then reacts with morpholine to give 4‑nonanoylmorpholine and precipitated dicyclohexylurea; typically run at 0 °C to rt in dichloromethane or DMF under nitrogen, DCC acts as coupling reagent.

Acid–base double displacement (metal phosphate dissolution); purpose: solubilize copper(II) phosphate as copper(II) chloride and generate phosphoric acid; Cu(HPO₄)₂ reacts with aqueous HCl to give CuCl₂ (aq) and H₃PO₄; conducted at room temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Thiourea formation from amine, carbon disulfide and ammonia. 2‑Chloroaniline reacts with CS₂ in the presence of aqueous ammonia (or NH₃ in ethanol) at 0–25 °C to give N‑(2‑chlorophenyl)thiourea and hydrogen sulfide (released as gas). The reaction proceeds via formation of the ammonium dithiocarbamate intermediate; a base such as NaOH is usually added to deprotonate the amine.

Acid‑carbonate neutralization; aqueous hydrochloric acid reacts with bismuth carbonate liberating CO₂ and₂O while forming soluble bismuth(III) chloride; performed in water at room temperature or with gentle heating, no catalyst required.

Metathesis/complexation; iron(III) nitrate exchanges its nitrate anions with sodium N,N‑diethyldithiocarbamate to afford the iron(III) diethyldithiocarbamate complex and sodium nitrate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with slight stirring; no additional catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis); primary alkyl bromide is converted to the corresponding primary alcohol; water acts as nucleophile, displacing bromide and generating HBr; typical conditions are reflux in aqueous ethanol or water, sometimes heated; no special catalyst required.

Type: halogen exchange/alkyl halide synthesis. Purpose: generate methyl bromide and boron tribromide (a Lewis acid). Key transformation: each bromine molecule attacks trimethylborane, transferring a methyl group to bromine to form CH3Br while boron ends up as BBr3. Conditions: anhydrous, inert atmosphere (N2), 0‑25 °C, typically in dry diethyl ether or dichloromethane; no additional catalyst required.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis of vicinal dihalide). Purpose: convert 1,2‑dichlorobutane the corresponding diol. Key transformation: hydroxide ions replace the two chlorine atoms, yielding 1,2‑butanediol and NaCl. Conditions: aqueous NaOH solution, reflux (≈80‑100 °C), polar protic medium (water, optionally with ethanol); no catalyst needed.

Type: strong reduction of an ester. Purpose: cleave isobutyl formate into two primary alcohols. Key transformation: LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl, producing isobutanol from the alkoxy fragment and methanol from the formyl fragment. Conditions: dry THF or diethyl ether, 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, work‑up with aqueous acid; LiAlH4 is the sole reagent/catalyst.

Type: haloform reaction (base‑promoted oxidative cleavage). Purpose: convert acetaldehyde into bromoform and a carboxylate. Key transformation: bromination of the α‑carbon three times followed by C‑C bond cleavage, giving CHBr3 (bromoform) and sodium formate. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (10‑20 % w/v), Br2 added at 0‑5 °C, then mixture warmed to 25‑30 °C with stirring; no additional catalyst.

Hydrolysis of a metal halide; indium(III) bromide reacts with water to give insoluble indium(III) hydroxide and hydrobromic acid; key transformation: InBr₃ + 3 H₂O → In(OH)₃ (s) + 3 HBr; usually performed in water, often with gentle heating to complete precipitation; no catalyst.

Type: O‑methylation (alkylation) using dimethyl sulfate. Purpose: methylate naringenin to afford hesperetin. Key transformation: phenolic oxygen attacks a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, displacing methyl hydrogen sulfate. Conditions: polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, or acetonitrile), base such as K2CO3 or NaH to deprotonate the phenol, 0‑25 °C to reflux (40‑80 °C) under inert atmosphere; methyl hydrogen sulfate removed during aqueous work‑up.

Acid-base metathesis reaction. Purpose is synthesis of boron trifluoride from boron monoxide. Key transformation involves oxygen to fluoride substitution using hydrogen fluoride. Likely requires high-temperature conditions; uses no solvent or catalyst.

Type:CC‑mediated amide coupling (carboxylic acid activation). Purpose: synthesis of lidocaine as its hydrochloride salt. Key transformation: activation of 2‑(diethylamino)acetic acid by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide, nucleophilic attack by 2,6‑dimethylaniline to form the amide bond, followed by protonation with HCl to give lidocaine·HCl; dicyclohexylurea is generated as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous organic solvent (CH2Cl2 or DMF), 0 °C to ambient temperature, inert; catalytic DMAP often added to accelerate acyl transfer.

Type: N‑alkylation via SN2 nucleophilic substitution. Purpose: preparation of the bronchodilator enprofylline (3‑propyl‑1‑methylxanthine). Key transformation: deprotonated nitrogen of 1‑methylxanthine attacks the primary carbon of 1‑bromopropane, displacing bromide and forming a propyl substituent; HBr is released. Typical conditions polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, reflux or 80‑100 °C, with a mild base (K2CO3, NaH) to scavenge HBr; reaction often performed under nitrogen.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution of an alcohol (SN2) with chloride ion. Purpose: conversion of a primary alcohol to the corresponding alkyl chloride. Key transformation: protonation of the hydroxyl group of 5‑bromopentanol by HCl, followed by chloride attack on the primary carbon to give 5‑bromo‑1‑chloropentane and water. Typical conditions: excess concentrated HCl (often aqueous) with reflux; optionally a Lewis acid catalyst such as ZnCl2 (Lucas reagent) to increase rate; solvent may be ethanol or just the aqueous acid.

Hydride reduction (dehalogenation) of an alkyl chloride with LiAlH₄; 3‑chloro‑3‑methylhexane is reduced to the corresponding alkane 3‑methylhexane, generating LiCl and AlCl₃ (or Al(OH)₃ after work‑up) as by‑products. Reaction carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under reflux, under anhydrous inert atmosphere.

Type: Thermal/photolytic decomposition. Purpose: generation of carbon monosulfide (CS) and elemental chlorine from thiophosgene. Key transformation: homolytic or heterolytic cleavage of the CSCl2 molecule yields CS (carbon monosulfide) and Cl2. Typical conditions: heating to 150‑200 °C or exposure to UV light; performed in an inert gas flow; no solvent required.

Oxidative cleavage of a vicinal diol using sodium periodate (periodate oxidation). Purpose: convert 1,2‑cyclopentanediol into the corresponding dialdehyde (glutaraldehyde). Key transformation: cleavage of the C‑C bond between the two hydroxyl‑bearing carbons, yielding two aldehyde functions. Typical conditions: aqueous NaIO4 (0.5–1 equiv), 0 °C to room temperature, often in a water/THF mixture; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Type: Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation of an amine). Purpose: mono‑acetylation of p‑phenylenediamine to afford N‑acetyl‑p‑phenylenediamine. Key transformation: the lone pair on one amino group attacks acetyl chloride, forming the amide bond and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: use of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl, solvent CH2Cl2 or pyridine, temperature 0 °C to room temperature; reaction often run under nitrogen to avoid moisture.

Type: Decarboxylation (thermal). Purpose: removal of the carboxyl group from quinoline‑4‑carboxylic acid to regenerate the parent heterocycle. Key transformation: heating induces loss of CO2, yielding quinoline. Typical conditions: high temperature (≥200 °C) often with a solid support or catalyst (e.g., copper oxide, zinc dust, or soda‑lime) in a sealed tube or on a heated oil bath; can be performed neat or in a high‑boiling solvent such as quinoline itself.

Salt metathesis / complex formation; preparation of the fluorometallate KNbF7; NbF5 reacts with KF to give the heptafluoroniobate anion; usually carried out in anhydrous HF or molten fluoride mixture at 150‑250 °C under inert atmosphere; no catalyst, solid‑state or liquid HF solvent.

Acid–base double displacement (precipitation); conversion of BaCrO4 to soluble chromic acid while removing Ba2+ as insoluble BaSO4; H2SO4 protonates chromate and precipitates BaSO4, leaving H2CrO4 in solution; performed in medium temperature, often with diluteSO4; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a catechol to a quinone; 4‑methylcatechol is oxidized by H2O2 to 4‑methyl‑1,2‑benzoquinone with loss of two equivalents of water; typically run in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., MeOH/H2O) at 0‑25 °C; may be catalyzed by a small amount of transition‑metal ion (Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺) or enzyme (peroxidase) but can proceed uncatalyzed with excess H2O2.

Nitrosation (formation of a nitrosamine); guanidine hydrochloride is nitrosated by nitrous acid generated in situ from NaNO2 in acetic acid, yielding N‑rosoguanidine and sodium acetate; reaction is performed at 0‑5 °C to control nitrosation, then allowed to warm to room temperature; aqueous/acetic acid medium, no external catalyst needed.

Hofmann rearrangement (base‑induced amide to amine conversion); isobutyramide is converted to isobutylamine with loss of CO₂ in the presence of Br₂ and NaOH; the bromination of the amide followed by base‑mediated migration gives the primary amine; carried out in aqueous NaOH, Br₂ added slowly at 0‑5 °C then the mixture is warmed to 20‑30 °C; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of phosphite to phosphate; sodium hydrogen phosphite (Na₂HPO₃) is oxidized by H₂O₂ to sodium phosphate, producing water as the only by‑product; reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often under mildly alkaline conditions to keep phosphite soluble; water is the solvent, no catalyst is necessary, though slight acid or base adjustment may be used to control pH.

Oxidative cleavage (periodate cleavage) of a vicinal diol; periodic acid (HIO4 or NaIO4) cleaves the CC bond between the two hydroxyl‑bearing carbons to give two carbonyl fragments (formaldehyde and heptanal). Typically performed in aqueous media with a co‑solvent such as acetonitrile at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation (meta‑chlorination) of nitrobenzene. Chlorine gas in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst (e.g., FeCl₃ or AlCl₃) installs a chlorine atom at the meta position relative to the nitro group, yielding 1‑chlCl as by‑product. Conventional conditions: dry carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane as solvent, catalyst 10 % mol, temperature 0 °C → reflux for 1–3 h; work‑up removes inorganic salts.

Acid‑base double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; concentrated H2SO4 protonates bromide ions from CsBr to generate hydrobromic acid while the cesium cations pair with sulfate to form cesium sulfate. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; no special solvent or catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; soluble cadmium chloride reacts with sodium fluoride to precipitate insoluble cadmium fluoride and produce sodium chloride in solution. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; excess NaF improves yield, filtration isolates CdF2.
Oxidative decomposition; tin telluride is oxidized in air to give SnO₂ and TeO₂; heated in static air or flowing O₂ at 400–600 °C; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Grignard addition to formaldehyde (nucleophilic addition); allylmagnesium chloride reacts with formaldehyde to give the alkoxide of but‑3‑en‑1‑ol, and acidic work‑up furnishes the primary allylic alcohol; typical conditions are dry ether (THF) at 0  by aqueous NH₄Cl or dilute HCl quench.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) reaction; purpose is to isolate insoluble samarium(III) hydroxide; key transformation is exchange of acetate for hydroxide, forming a precipitate of Sm(OH)₃ and soluble sodium acetate; carried out in aqueous NaOH solution at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of anthraquinone; concentrated HNO3 (often in combination with H2SO4 as a catalyst) introduces a nitro group onto the aromatic ring, yielding nitroanthraquinone. Reaction is carried out at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control substitution, then warmed to 50–80 °C; the mixed acid serves both as solvent and nitrating medium.

Mitsunobu alkylation; triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate (DEAD) convert 3‑methylbenzyl alcohol into its N‑alkylated product with piperazine, proceeding via formation of an oxyphosphonium intermediate and inversion of configuration. Triphenylphosphine is oxidized to PPh3O and DEAD reduced to diethyl hydrazine dicarboxylate. Conducted in anhydrous THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere, typically 0 °C to room temperature.

Acetylation (mixed anhydride formation) of a phosphate monoester: Acetic anhydride with the P–OH of dimethyl hydrogen phosphate, forming dimethyl acetyl phosphate and acetic acid. Typically run in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to rt with a base such as pyridineAP to neutralize the generated acetic acid.

This is an acid‑base (oxide‑acid) synthesis reaction in which antimony(V) oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form antimony pentachloride, a strong Lewis acid, and water. The key transformation is exchange of oxide for chloride ligands. Typical conditions involve refluxing solid Sb₂O₅ with excess dry HCl gas or concentrated aqueous HCl, often in a sealed tube to avoid moisture; the reaction is usually carried out at 0–50 °C for gas‑phase HCl or at room temperature for aqueous acid. No additional solvent or catalyst is required beyond the acid medium.

Acid‑base proton transfer between a protic acid and a metal hydride; lithium hydride reacts with acetic acid to produce hydrogen gas and lithium acetate. Usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dry ether under inert atmosphere; gentle warming may be applied to drive off H2. No catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation of styrene using fuming sulfuric acid (oleum, containing dissolved SO3); the sulfonic‑acid electrophile adds para to the vinyl group, yielding 4‑vinylbenzenesulfonic acid and water as the by‑product. Reaction is carried out neat in the acid at 0–5 °C, then allowed to warm cautiously to avoid polymerization; no additional catalyst is needed.

Oxidative side‑chain oxidation of a pyridine methyl group using potassium permanganate in water; purpose is conversion of 4‑methylpyridine to 4‑pyridinecarboxylic acid. Key transformation: KMnO₄ oxidizes the benzylic‑like methyl to a carboxyl group, producing MnO₂ precipitate and KOH in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous KMnO₄ (often 2–3 equiv), pH adjusted to neutral‑basic, reflux or heating under vigorous stirring, followed by filtration to remove MnO₂.

The reaction between resorcinol and p-nitrobenzenediazonium chloride is a diazo coupling reaction used to synthesize the azo dye Disperse Red 60. It occurs under mildly acidic or neutral conditions at low temperatures (typically 0–5°C) to prevent decomposition of the diazonium chloride. The hydroxyl groups on resorcinol activate the aromatic ring for nucleophilic attack, forming an azo bond with the diazonium intermediate. Aqueous or ethanol solvents are commonly used.

Double displacement precipitation reaction; preparation of indium(III) sulfide using ammonium sulfide; sulfide ions from (NH4)2S precipitate In2S3 while ammonium nitrate remains in solution; conducted in aqueous solution, often at room temperature, with exclusion of air; no catalyst required.

Ethene undergoes epoxidation with peroxyformic acid, a peroxycarboxylic acid, to yield ethylene oxide and formic acid. This is an oxygen-transfer reaction where the electrophilic oxygen of the peracid attacks the double bond, forming an epoxide via a concerted cyclic transition state. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions, often in a solvent like dichloromethane or aqueous media.

Base‑promoted intramolecular SN2 (epoxide synthesis). Vicinal diiodopropane reacts with strong hydroxide (KOH) in aqueous or alcoholic solution (often ethanol) at elevated temperature. Hydroxide displaces iodide to form an alkoxide, which then intramolecularly attacks the neighboring carbon, producing propylene oxide and two equivalents of KI; water is formed from the hydroxide proton. No catalyst required.

The reaction of potassium cyanide, copper(I) cyanide, and 1-bromo-4-iodobenzene is a nucleophilic aromatic substitution (Rosenmund-von Braun reaction) that forms 4-bromobenzonitrile. The iodide is displaced by cyanide in the presence of copper(I) as a catalyst, leaving the bromide substituent inert. The reaction requires high temperatures and a polar aprotic solvent like dimethylformamide (DMF) or quinoline.

Chlorine gas oxidizes potassium manganate (K₂MnO₄) to potassium permanganate (KMnO₄), receiving electrons to form potassium chloride. This redox reaction involves manganese in a +6 oxidation state being oxidized to +7, while chlorine (0) is reduced to -1. It typically occurs in solution, often under basic pH conditions to stabilize the permanganate anion.

Oxidation reaction. Purpose to convert secondary alcohol to ketone. Chromic acid (H2CrO4) oxidizes 1-phenylethanol's hydroxyl group to a carbonyl, forming acetophenone. Typically conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid (H2SO4) as solvent and catalyst. Reaction occurs under acidic conditions with heating.

Oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction. Dissolves zinc antimonide (ZnSb₂) using concentrated nitric acid (HNO₃), oxidizing antimony to antimony pentoxide (Sb₂O₅) and zinc to zinc nitrate (Zn(NO₃)₂). Nitric acid is reduced to nitrogen dioxide (NO₂). Conducted under boiling aqueous HNO₃ conditions, yielding NO₂ gas and nitrate salts.

Thermal decarboxylation of 2‑furancarboxylic acid producing furan and CO₂. Typically requires heating to 200–300 °C, often in a sealed tube or under reduced pressure; metal oxides (e.g., CuO) or basic promoters can be used to lower the temperature. No solvent is strictly necessary, but high‑boiling hydrocarbons (e.g., diphenyl ether) may be employed.

Nucleophilic ring-opening of an epoxide. Hydroiodic acid (HI) protonates ethylene oxide, enabling trimethylamine's attack to form choline iodide. Epoxide ring opens via nucleophilic addition, generating a β-hydroxyethylammonium salt. Typically performed in aqueous solution at moderate temperatures.

Oxidation of a primary benzylic alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); mild, non‑aqueous oxidation that stops at the aldehyde stage; performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; by‑products are pyridinium chloride and water.

Salt formation/halogen complexation where tetrabutylammonium iodide reacts with elemental iodine to generate tetrabutylammonium triiodide ([TBA][I₃]); the process provides a soluble source of I⁺; typically performed at room temperature in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane with a 1:1 molar ratio; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid. Sodium chlorite (NaClO₂) oxidizes 2-pyridinecarboxaldehyde in a buffered phosphate solution (NaH₂PO₄) to picolinic acid. Buffer maintains pH, preventing chlorite self-decomposition. Common for aldehyde oxidation, yielding sodium chloride (NaCl) as byproduct. Conducted near room temperature.

Hydroboration-oxidation sequence. Diborane (B₂H₆) adds to 1-butene (anti-Markovnikov), followed by oxidation with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to yield 1-butanol. Reaction occurs in two steps: THF solvent for hydroboration, aqueous NaOH for oxidation. Produces primary alcohol.

Strong base–ammonium bifluoride neutralization. Sodium hydroxide solution is added to ammonium bifluoride (NH4HF2) in water. The OH⁻ deprotonates the ammonium ion and converts the bifluoride to fluoride, yielding sodium fluoride (NaF), ammonium fluoride (NH4F) and water. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aromatic aldehyde to a carboxylic acid;anganate serves as a strong oxidizing agent that converts the aldehyde group of o‑vanillin into the corresponding acid (o‑vanillic acid). Typically performed in aqueous alkaline solution (KMnO₄ in water or dilute NaOH), heated under reflux, followed by acidification of the reaction mixture and extraction. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; forms a C‑C bond between an aryl bromide and phenylboronic acid to give 5‑phenyl‑2‑furaldehyde; key transformation is palladium‑catalyzed transmetallation and reductive elimination; typically run under inert atmosphere with Pd(OAc)2 (5 mol %), tri‑ortho‑tolylphosphine (10–20 mol %), K2CO3 as base in a mixed aqueous/organic solvent such as dioxane‑water or toluene‑ethanol; heated to 80–100 °C for 2–12 h; water is formed as by‑product.

Salt metathesis/precipitation reaction; oxalic acid reacts with magnesium nitrate to form insoluble magnesium oxalate and releases nitric acid into solution. Conducted in water at room temperature with stirring; the magnesium oxalate precipitate is filtered and washed No catalyst needed; water is the reaction medium.

Palladium‑catalyzed Buchwald‑Hartwig C–S cross‑coupling. 4‑Bromopyridine couples with thiophenol using Pd(OAc)₂, triphenylphosphine and Cs₂CO₃ to give 4‑(phenylthio)pyridine, CsBr, CO₂ and H₂O (CO₂/H₂O from carbonate decomposition). Typical conditions: toluene or dioxane, 80‑120 °C, inert atmosphere, with stoichiometric base.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; sulfuric acid protonates the nitrile of methacrylonitrile, water adds across the C≡N bond to give methacrylic acid and liberates ammonia. Conducted in aqueous H₂SO₄ (1–6 M) at 80–120 °C, often in a sealed tube; water is the solvent.

Reaction type: amide hydrolysis (acidic). Purpose: conversion of 2,2,2‑trifluoro‑N‑propylacetamide to 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetic acid and propylamine. Key transformation: protonated amide carbonyl is attacked by water, leading to cleavage of the C‑N bond and formation of the carboxylic acid and the free amine. Typical conditions: strong aqueous acid (e.g., 6 M HCl or conc. H₂SO₄) heated to 100 °C for several hours; the reaction is often performed in a water/organic solvent mixture to improve solubility.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; erbium(III) nitrate reacts with aqueous ammonium hydroxide to form insoluble erbium(III) hydroxide precipitate and soluble ammonium nitrate; performed at room temperature in water with stirring.

Hydrolytic or metabolic cleavage of the phosphorodithioate group in Cartap to produce the active toxin nereistoxin. transformation involves nucleophilic attack on the phosphorus centre, breaking the P–S bond and releasing the thiol‑amine (nereistoxin). Can be achieved chemically under aqueous alkaline conditions (e.g., NaOH, heat) or enzymatically in biological systems. No external catalyst; water serves as solvent.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of phosgene with alkoxide; two equivalents of sodiumoxide attack phosgene, displacing chloride ions and forming diethyl carbonate while generating sodium chloride as by‑product. Performed in anhydrous ethanol or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; sodium ethoxide is prepared in situ from sodium metal and ethanol. No additional catalyst required.

Direct combination synthesis of dysprosium(III) iodide; solid‑state halogenation reaction between Dy metal and I2. Performed by heating the elemental mixture in a sealed quartz tube or inert atmosphere at 500–700 °C to promote vapor‑phase reaction, yielding DyI3 as a solid. No solvent or catalyst is used.

O‑methylation (nucleophilic substitution) of the phenolic hydroxyl of dopamine using dimethyl sulfate; purpose is to protect or modify the catechol to give 3‑methoxytyramine; key transformation is transfer of a methyl group to oxygen, generating methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or dichloromethane with a base (e.g., Na₂CO₃, K₂CO₃) at 0 °C to room temperature; no metal catalyst required.

General type: Transesterification (methanolysis) of an acetate ester. Purpose: Exchange the acetate group for a methyl ester, simultaneously liberating the alcohol. Key transformation: Methanol nucleophilically attacks the carbonyl of 1‑phenylethyl acetate, producing phenylethanol and methyl acetate. Typical conditions: Refluxing methanol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑TsOH, H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOCH3, K2CO3); reaction time 2–6 h. Excess methanol drives the equilibrium toward products. No metal catalyst is required unless a specific homogeneous catalyst (e.g., Ti(OBu)4) is desired for higher rates.

Oxidation; primary benzylic alcohol is oxidized to a carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate. The CH2OH group is converted to CO2H, giving 4‑phenylbenzoic acid. Typical conditions involve an aqueous alkaline KMnO4 solution (often in water/acetone), reflux for several hours, followed by acid work‑up to precipitate the acid. No catalyst is required beyond the oxidant.

Metal‑acid salt formation with hydrogen evolution. Picric acid (2,4,6‑trinitrophenol) is treated with sodium amalgam (Na/Hg) in an aqueous or alcoholic medium at ambient temperature. Sodium ions deprotonate the phenolic OH, producing the sodium salt (sodium picrate) while the liberated hydrogen atoms combine to form H₂ gas. The reaction proceeds without additional catalysts; mercury serves as a medium to moderate the reactivity of metallic sodium.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange anions to isolate lead(II) cyanide, which often precipitates from aqueous solution. Key transformation: Pb(NO₃)₂ + Ba(CN)₂ → Pb(CN)₂ (solid) + Ba(NO₃)₂. Typically performed in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; purpose is to cleave the acetamide protecting group to afford 2‑aminophenol and acetic acid. Key transformation: N‑(2‑hydroxyphenyl)acetamide + HCl + H₂O → 2‑aminophenol + CH₃COOH. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous hydrochloric acid (conc. 1–6 M) for 1–3 h; water or aqueous ethanol as solvent; no additional catalyst.

Reductive amination of a ketone using sodium cyanoborohydride; purpose is to install a methylamino group, yielding 3‑methoxymethamphetamine. Key: 3‑methoxyphenylacetone + CH₃NH₂ → imine intermediate → reduced by NaCNBH₃ → 3‑methoxymethamphetamine + H₂O. Conducted in a protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol (often with a small amount of acid to protonate the imine) at 0 °C to room temperature; NaCNBH₃ acts as the reducing agent; no external catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis (neutralization) of a metal acetate; purpose is to convert neodymium(III) acetate to the insoluble hydroxide while regenerating acetic acid. Key transformation: Nd(CH₃COO)₃ + 3 H₂O → Nd(OH)₃ (solid) + 3 CH₃COOH. Typically performed in water, often with gentle heating to aid precipitation; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and precipitate the insoluble barium fluoride; key transformation is BaCl2 + 2 NH4F → BaF2(s) + 2 NH4Cl; typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Sulfonylation (mesylation) of an alcohol; converts 2‑ethoxyethanol into its methanesulfonate ester, providing a good leaving group for subsequent substitution reactions. The alcohol reacts with methanesulfonyl chloride in the presence of pyridine, which acts as both base and solvent, scavenging the generated HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, often in dichloromethane or neat pyridine, under inert atmosphere.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol using Jones reagent; purpose is to convert 1‑pentadecanol to the corresponding carboxylic acid (pentadecanoic acid); key transformation is 1‑pentadecanol + CrO3/H2SO4 → pentadecanoic acid + Cr^3+ + H2O; carried out in a mixture of acetone and water at 0 °C to 25 °C, usually under an ice bath; Jones reagent (chromic acid generated from CrO3 and concentrated H2SO4) is the oxidant.

Acid–salt metathesis (double displacement) reaction; purpose is to generate selenic acid from the barium salt; key transformation is BaSeO4 + 2 HNO3 → H2SeO4 + Ba(NO3)2; performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution; water is the solvent, no special catalyst required.

High‑temperature redox/halogen exchange reaction; purpose is to reduce plutonium(VI) fluoride to plutonium(IV) fluoride while producing silicon tetrafluoride gas; key transformation is 2 PuF6 + Si → 2 PuF4 + SiF4; carried out in a sealed, dry reaction vessel (e.g., quartz tube) at 300–400 °C under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst, the silicon acts as the reductant.

Strecker-type synthesis of an α‑amino acid derivative; purpose is to form N‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)glycine from 4‑hydroxybenzaldehyde; key transformations are condensation of the aldehyde with NH3 and KCN to give an aminonitrile, followed by aqueous acidic hydrolysis to the amino acid; typically performed in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution at ambient temperature for the condensation step, then heated under acidic conditions (e.g., 1 M HCl) for hydrolysis; KCN supplies cyanide, ammonia provides the amine source; no metal catalyst required.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; purpose is to precipitate nickel(II) hydroxide and generate ammonium sulfate in solution; key transformation is NiSO4 + 2 NH4OH → Ni(OH)2(s) + (NH4)2SO4; carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to a primary amine; ethyl 2‑cyanopropanoate is reduced to ethyl 2‑aminopropanoate; purpose is conversion of a nitrile ester into an α‑amino ester; key transformation is addition of H2 across the C≡N triple bond; typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–50 °C; no special additives needed.

Reaction type: Acyl chloride aminolysis (amide formation). Purpose: Introduce an acetyl protecting group on the amino group of glycine. Key transformation: Nucleophilic attack of the amine nitrogen on acetyl chloride, forming N‑acetylglycine and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (e.g., triethylamine, pyridine) to capture the generated HCl.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt hydrolysis); converts insoluble magnesium stearate into free stearic acid and soluble magnesium chloride; key step is protonation of the stearate anion by HCl, releasing stearic acid and forming MgCl₂; typically performed in aqueous HCl solution, often heated to 60‑80 °C with stirring; water or aqueous ethanol serves as solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed etherification (phenol alkylation) with epichlorohydrin produce resorcinol diglycidyl ether, an epoxy resin precursor; NaOH deprotonates resorcinol to phenoxide, which attacks epichlorohydrin forming a chlorohyd intermediate that undergoes intramolecular ring closure to give the epoxide; carried out in aqueous or mixed organic solvent (e.g., dipropylene glycol monomethyl ether, DMSO, or water/ethanol) at 50‑80 °C; NaOH acts as catalyst; reaction often finished with alkaline work‑up to promote epoxide formation.

Nucleophilic substitution (alcohol chlorination). Primary 1‑octanol is converted to 1‑chlorooctane with thionyl chloride. Key transformation: –OH replaced by –Cl, producing SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous solvent (pyridine, dichloromethane) with pyridine or triethylamine as HCl scavenger; reaction performed under nitrogen; temperature0 °C to reflux.

Formation of N‑phenylbutanamide from butyryl chloride and aniline; this is an amide synthesis via acyl‑chloride amidation (acyl substitution). The reaction liberates HCl, which is neutralized by a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or NaHCO₃). Standard conditions: cool (0 °C) addition of aniline to a solution of butyryl chloride in dichloromethane or THF, then stir at rt; base present in 1‑1.2 equiv relative to amine.

Acetylation of carnitine with acetic anhydride to give O‑acetylcarnitine and acetic acid; esterification of the secondary hydroxyl group; usually performed neat or in pyridine (or a small amount of DMAP) at 0 °C to room temperature.

Nucleophilic addition of ethoxide to carbon disulfide forming aanthate salt (sodium ethyl xanthate); ethoxide attacks CS₂, generating the O‑ethyl dithiocarbonate anion which pairs with Na⁺; performed in anhydrous ethanol at 0‑25 °C under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst needed.

Quaternary ammonium salt formation (nucleophilic substitution followed by acid‑base neutralization); trimethylamine attacks chloroacetic acid, displacing chloride to give the betaine salt 1‑propanaminium, 3‑carboxy‑N,N,N‑trimethyl‑2‑oxo‑inner salt; performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution, typically at ambient temperature or mild heating; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base proton transfer (salt metathesis) between acetic acid and potassium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (KHMDS); the amide anion abstracts a proton from acetic acid, yielding bis(trimethylsilyl)amine (HN(SiMe₃)₂) acetate; usually carried out in THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature under inert gas; no catalyst required.

Condensation of sulfur dioxide with potassium sulfite to give potassium metabisulfite (K₂S₂O₅); SO₂ dissolves in aqueous K₂SO₃ solution forming bisulfite, which then condenses (loss of water) to the metabisulfite ion; performed by bubbling SO₂ gas through a K₂SO₃ solution at 20‑30 °C, followed by evaporation or gentle heating (80‑100 °C) to remove water and crystallize the product; no catalyst needed.

Transesterification of ethylene glycol monostearate with ethanol to produce ethyl stearate and ethylene glycol; ethanol attacks the ester carbonyl, displaces the glycol moiety; typically conducted with excess ethanol as solvent, using a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., 1‑5 % H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOEt), reflux (150‑180°C); removal of ethyl stearate or water drives the equilibrium toward products.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) between calcium gluconate and sodium hydroxide yielding sodium gluconate and calcium hydroxide; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; Ca(OH)₂ precipitates due to low solubility, facilitating separation; no special catalyst needed.

Reductive amination (NaBH4 reduction). The carbonyl of 1‑phenyl‑2‑propanone reacts with methylamine to form an imine intermediate, which is reduced by sodium borohydride to give phenpromethamine, a secondary amine. Typical conditions: methylamine (gas or solution) in methanol or ethanol, NaBH4 added at 0 °C to rt, stir 1–2 h; work‑up with aqueous acid.

Acetylation (O‑acylation) of a primary alcohol using acetic anhydride, catalyzed by DMAP; converts the hydroxy group into an acetate ester while generating acetic acid as by‑product; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF.

Swern oxidation of a) primary alcohol to aldehyde via oxalyl chloride/DMSO/triethylamine; a low‑temperature oxidative transformation. Conducted in CH2Cl2 at –78 °C: oxalyl chloride (1.1 eq) and DMSO (2 eq) generate the activated sulfoxide, the alcohol is added, then triethylamine (2 eq) is introduced to quench, warming to rt affords 2‑(furan‑2‑yl)acetaldehyde.

Oxidation (redox) of hydrogen selenide by ozone; elemental selenium oxidized from the –2 to the +4 oxidation state, yielding selenium dioxide and water; carried out at low temperature (often –78 °C to 0 °C) with ozone gas bubbled through an inert solvent (e.g., dry dichloromethane) under an oxygen‑free atmosphere.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of a methyl ester with a primary aliphatic alcohol; sodium methoxide deprotonates the alcohol, allowing exchange of the methoxy group for a heptyloxy group and releasing methanol; reflux in anhydrous heptanol or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF) under inert atmosphere drives the equilibrium toward the heptyl ester.

Dehydrative chlorination of a phenolic ester using thionyl chloride; the phenolic OH is replaced by chlorine to give an aryl chloride, with simultaneous formation of gaseous HCl and SO₂; usually conducted under reflux in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, which also scavenges the HCl.

Bromination to produce phosphorus oxybromide. Phosphorus pentoxide reacts with anhydrous hydrogen bromide gas (or concentrated HBr) at elevated temperature (≈120–150 °C) in a moisture‑free apparatus, giving PO Br₃ and water. The product POBr₃ is collected by distillation; water is removed by drying agents or trap.

Deoxy‑fluorination of carboxylic acids to acyl fluorides with diethylaminosulfur trifluoride (DAST); each acid is converted to the corresponding acyl fluoride while DAST fragments to give sulfur dioxide, diethylamine, and hydrogen fluoride; reaction is performed at 0 °C to rt in a dry, aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂, often under nitrogen.

Hydrolysis of an acid chloride. Purpose: obtain the free carboxylic acid and release HCl. Key transformation: 3‑nitropropanoyl chloride + H2O → 3‑nitropropionic acid + HCl. Typical conditions: addition of the acid chloride to ice‑cold water or aqueous NaHCO3 at 0 °C to rt; optionally performed in a biphasic system (CH2Cl2/water) with vigorous stirring, then acidify the aqueous layer.

Phosgenation of a diol to form a carbonate ester; phosgene reacts with two equivalents of 2‑ethoxyethanol, producing bis(2‑ethoxyethyl) carbonate and two equivalents of HCl; typical conditions involve cooling (0 °C), anhydrous solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂), and a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to neutralize the liberated HCl.

Perkin condensation; forms an α,β‑unsaturated carboxylic acid (3,4‑dimethoxycinnamic acid) from an aromatic aldehyde and acetic anhydride. Sodium acetate acts as base catalyst. Typical conditions: reflux of the aldehyde with excess acetic anhydride and catalytic NaOAc (0–1 equiv) at 120–150 °C, often neat (acetic anhydride serves as solvent) under an inert atmosphere.

Acetylation (esterification) of a primary alcohol;1‑methoxyethanol reacts with acetic anhydride to give 2‑methoxyethyl acetate and one equivalent of acetic acid. Usually carried out neat or in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature; a base such as pyridine or DMAP may be added to scavenge the generated acetic acid and accelerate the reaction.

Metalation (acid‑base deprotonation) of an aromatic diene. Purpose: generate sodium cyclopentadienide for use as a nucleophile or ligand. Key transformation: sodium metal abstracts the acidic proton of cyclopentadiene, forming NaC5H5 and H2 gas. Conditions: sodium metal added to dry cyclopentadiene in dry THF or ether under inert atmosphere, 0–25 °C, often using excess Na. No catalyst needed.

Hydrolytic decomposition of methylenediurea; water attacks the methylene bridge linking two urea moieties, cleaving it to regenerate formaldehyde and free urea. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution, usually heated to 80‑120 °C and may be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed (e.g., dilute HCl or NaOH) to accelerate cleavage.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of ethoxymethylformamide (EMF); purpose is to decompose EMF into useful small molecules. Key transformation: EMF + HCl/H₂O → HCOOH + CH₃CH₂OH + CH₂O. Conducted in dilute aqueous HCl at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; water is the solvent; no additional catalyst.

Acid–sulfide reaction; terbium sulfide reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce terbium(III) chloride and hydrogen sulfide gas; protonation of sulfide releases H₂S while Tb³⁺ forms TbCl₃; performed in aqueous HCl, often with gentle heating and proper ventilation to vent H₂S; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Reduction (partial) of a Weinreb amide; DIBAL‑H selectively reduces N‑methoxybenzamide to the corresponding aldehyde (benzaldehyde). The aluminum‑hydride donates a hydride to the carbonyl, forming an alkoxy‑aluminum intermediate that, after aqueous work‑up, releases benzaldehyde and the by‑product N‑methoxy‑N‑methylamine. Typical conditions: 0 °C to –78 °C in anhydrous ethers (toluene, THF, or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere; quench with dilute acid or water.

Azo coupling of benzenediazonium tetrafluoroborate with aniline; purpose is to synthesize azobenzene (an azo dye); key transformation is formation of an N=N double bond linking two phenyl rings with loss of N₂ gas; typical conditions: cold aqueous or mixed organic/aqueous medium (0–5 °C) at slightly alkaline pH (≈7) to promote coupling; BF₄⁻ acts as a non‑nucleophilic counter‑ion; no additional catalyst required.

Double‑replacement (acid–base) metathesis; aqueous calcium bromate reacts with nitric acid, exchanging the cations to give bromic acid (HBrO₃), a strong oxidizing acid, and calcium nitrate. Usually performed in dilute aqueous solution at 0–25 °C to avoid decomposition of HBrO₃; no special catalysts required.
