Acid–base neutralization; acetic acid reacts with ammonium hydroxide to form ammonium acetate and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction is exothermic and may be performed with cooling if large quantities are mixed. No special catalyst is required.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann ether synthesis (aryl‑ coupling). Phenanthroline ligates Cu(I) bromide, enabling methoxide (from NaOMe) to displace bromide on bromobenzene, forming anisole and NaBr. Typically performed under inert atmosphere at 100‑130 °C in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO, using NaOMe as base and CuBr/phenanthroline as catalyst system.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange. Barium hydroxide reacts with lithium succinate, swapping cations to give soluble lithium hydroxide and insoluble barium succinate, which precipitates. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Hydroformylation followed by hydrogenation (oxo process). Propylene undergoes syngas (CO/H₂) addition in the presence of a Rh or Co carbonyl catalyst to give branched isobutyraldehyde, which is immediately hydrogenated to isobutanol. Typically carried out at 80‑150 °C, 20‑100 bar CO/H₂ pressure, in a solvent such as toluene or methylcyclohexane.

Acid‑base neutralization/ carbonate decomposition. Potassium carbonate neutralizes propionamide·HCl, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and forming propionamide together with KCl. The reaction proceeds in aqueous or alcoholic medium at room temperature; no catalyst is needed.

Strong reduction of a carboxylic acid; purpose is to obtain tiglic alcohol (trans‑2‑methyl‑2‑butenol) from tiglic acid. Key transformation: carboxyl group is reduced to a primary alcohol using LiAlH4. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, LiAlH4 (2–3 equiv) added at 0 °C, then refluxed gently for 1‑2 h. Reaction is quenched with careful addition of water or dilute acid, and the product is isolated after work‑up.

Peroxide oxidation of a thioether to a sulfone. Bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfide (mustard gas) is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to the corresponding sulfone, bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfone, with water as by‑product. Usually performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., MeCN/H₂O) at 0‑25 °C, optionally with a phase‑transfer or metal catalyst (e.g., Na₂MoO₄) to accelerate oxidation.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification (alkoxy exchange). Sodium methoxide attacks ethyl propionate, displacing the ethoxy group to give methyl propionate and sodium ethoxide. Conducted in methanol or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF) at 40‑80 °C under inert atmosphere; NaOMe serves both as nucleophile and catalyst.

Transesterification of ethyl pyrrole‑2‑carboxylate with sodium methoxide in methanol; base‑catalyzed ester exchange converts the ethyl ester to the methyl ester and releases ethanol. Typically run in methanol solvent at reflux with catalytic NaOMe.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitrosamine. Zinc dust in glacial acetic acid donates electrons to the N‑nitroso group of 1‑nitrosopiperazine, reducing it to the secondary amine piperazine while zinc is oxidized to Zn²⁺ forming zinc acetate. Used to de‑protect nitroso groups or generate piperazine. Typical conditions: reflux in AcOH, excess zinc, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Oxidative coordination complex formation; excess NH₃ and HCl provide a strongly basic, chloride‑rich medium in which Co(II) from cobalt(II) chloride is oxidized by chlorine gas to Co(III). The resulting Co(III) coordinates five ammonia ligands and one chloride to give the octahedral complex chloropentaamminecobalt(III) chloride, [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; Cl₂ is bubbled through the stirred mixture, and the product precipitates on cooling.

Gas‑phase redox fluorination. Hydrogen gas reduces molybdenum hexafluoride (MoF₆, Mo(VI)) to molybdenum pentafluoride (MoF₅, Mo(V)), while H₂ is oxidized to hydrogen fluoride (HF). Reaction proceeds at elevated temperature (≈250–500 °C) in a fluorine‑resistant reactor; no solvent or catalyst required.

Carbon monoxide reduction of tin(II) oxide to tin metal. CO reduces SnO to Sn while being oxidized to CO₂, a common gas‑phase metallurgical reduction. Carried out at 800–1000 °C in a CO‑rich atmosphere; no solvent, catalyst generally unnecessary.

Acid‑base complexation to form aminophylline. Two molecules of theophylline associate with one ethylenediamine through hydrogen‑bonding and ionic interactions, producing the soluble 2:1 theophylline‑ethylenediamine adduct known as aminophylline. Employed to increase theophylline’s water solubility for pharmaceutical use. Typical procedure: dissolve theophylline in ethanol or water, add ethylenediamine, reflux 1–2 h, cool and isolate the crystalline complex; no catalyst needed.

Reductive ozonolysis of a terminal alkene. Ozone adds across C=C bond of tridec‑1‑ene forming a primary ozonide that fragments on work‑up with dimethyl sulfide, a reductive quench, yielding formaldehyde from the terminal carbon and dodecanal from the remaining chain. Purpose: cleavage of alkenes to aldehydes. Conditions: O₃ bubbled at –78 °C to 0 °C in dichloromethane (or CH₂Cl₂), followed by addition of excess dimethyl sulfide, then warming to room temperature; dimethyl sulfide acts as reductant, no metal catalyst.

Acid–base neutralisation of a carbonate. Nitric acid protonates the carbonate ion of rubidium carbonate, releasing CO₂ gas and H₂O while the rubidium cation pairs with nitrate anion to give rubidium nitrate. Simple preparation of the nitrate salt. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring until gas evolution ceases; no catalyst or special solvent required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation; preparation of erbium phosphate from soluble salts. Er(NO₃)₃ exchanges anions with NH₄H₂PO₄, producing solid ErPO₄ and soluble NH₄NO₃ in solution. Conducted in water at ambient to slightly elevated temperature (20–60 °C) with stirring; no catalyst, water is the medium.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration (electrophilic addition) of 2‑methyl‑1‑butene; water adds Markovnikov to the double bond to give the tertiary alcohol 2‑m‑2‑butanol. Typical conditions: dilute H₂SO₄ as catalyst, aqueous medium, 0–50 °C; solvent is water or dilute sulfuric acid solution.

Acid–base neutralization; butanoic acid reacts with lithium hydroxide to form lithium butanoate and water; generally carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Alcoholysis (protonolysis) of sodium triethylborohydride; methanol acts as a proton source, converting the B‑H bond into triethylborane while generating sodium methoxide and hydrogen gas. Performed at ambient temperature, often using excess methanol as both reagent and solvent; inert atmosphere is advisable to avoid moisture‑sensitive side reactions.

Acidic hydration of 2‑methyl‑2‑pentene; water attacks the more substituted carbon of the alkene under acidic conditions to afford 2‑methylpentan‑2‑ol. Usually performed with dilute mineral acid or H₂SO in water, temperature 0–50 °C; aqueous acidic medium serves as both solvent and catalyst.

Condensation of formamide with hydroxylamine to form formamidoxime (amidoxime formation). The nucleophilic –NH₂OH attacks the carbonyl carbon of formamide, followed by loss of water. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solution, often with a mild base (e.g., NaOH) to generate free hydroxylamine, at ambient temperature or slight heating; no metal catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between ammonium sulfate and calcium sulfite in water. Calcium sulfate (CaSO₄) precipitates because of its low solubility, while ammonium sulfite remains dissolved. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of indoxyl acetate (ester cleavage) to give indoxyl and acetic acid. Water attacks the carbonyl carbon the acetate ester, releasing acetate as acetic acid. Usually carried out in aqueous buffer or mild acid/base at elevated temperature (40–80 °C); catalyst can be acid or base to accelerate the reaction, but plain water with heat suffices.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed ethanolysis (transesterification); ethanol replaces the original alkoxy group, giving ethyl hexanoate and hexanol; typical procedure uses excess ethanol with a catalytic base (NaOEt, NaOH, 5‑10 mol %) at 50‑80 °C, or a small amount of acid catalyst (H₂SO₄) under reflux; ethanol serves both as reactant and solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution of cyanogen chloride (ClCN) by sulfide ion from sodium sulfide. The sulfide attacks the electrophilic carbon of ClCN, displacing chloride and forming sodium thiocyanate (NaSCN) and NaCl. Conducted in aqueous solution, often at ambient or mildly heated temperatures; no additional catalyst is required.

Formation of the Grignard reagent octylmagnesium bromide from 1‑bromooctane and magnesium turnings; magnesium inserts into the C–Br bond under anhydrous conditions; carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) with gentle reflux.

Solid-state double replacement (metathesis) reaction; converts yttrium(III) sulfate to yttrium(III) oxide while forming sodium sulfate; key transformation: Y2(SO4)3 + 3 Na2O → Y2O3 + 3 Na2SO4; carried out by grinding the powders together and calcining at 600–800 °C; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Type: halogenation of alcohol (PBr3 mediated substitution). Purpose: convert the primary alcohol of 2‑ethoxyethanol into the corresponding bromide (1‑bromo‑2‑ethoxyethane). Key transformation: replacement of the hydroxyl group by bromide via formation of a phosphite intermediate. Typical conditions: add phosphorus tribromide (1 equiv) to a solution of 2‑ethoxyethanol in anhydrous ether or CH2Cl2 at 0 °C, then allow the mixture to warm to rt and stir for 1–2 h. By‑products are phosphorous acid (H3PO3) and excess PBr3 is hydrolyzed on work‑up.

Halogenation/oxidation; formation of iodine trichloride by electrophilic chlorination of iodine. I2 is treated with Cl2 in the presence of the Lewis acid AlCl3 to generate ICl3. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, typically at 0–25 °C in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; excess chlorine is avoided to prevent over‑oxidation.

Alkylation (O‑methylation); conversion of the primary alcohol of 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural to a methoxymethyl ether using dimethyl sulfate as the methyl donor and sodium carbonate as a base to neutralize the generated bisulfate. The reaction is usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF or DMSO) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, with stirring under nitrogen to avoid moisture.

Reductive dealkylation; reduction of the nitro group of 2‑nitroanisole to an amino group while simultaneously cleaving the methoxy substituent to give methyl iodide. The transformation employs hydroiodic acid and red phosphorus, which generate HI in situ as a reducing agent. Typical conditions involve refluxing the substrate in excess HI (often neat or in aqueous solution) with a few grams of red phosphorus at 100–150 °C until gas evolution ceases.

Oxidative aromatic coupling; two equivalents of 3,5‑dimethylaniline are coupled to afford 3,3′,5,5′‑tetramethylbenzidine. Ferric chloride (FeCl3) serves as a one‑electron oxidant, producing FeCl2 and HCl as by‑products. The reaction is carried out in a dry, non‑coordinating solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen, with the FeCl3 added portion‑wise to control polymeric side reactions.

Acid oxidation and salt formation; terbium oxalate is dissolved in nitric acid, where the oxalate anion is oxidized to carbon dioxide while the terbium cation is converted to terbium nitrate. The mixture is heated to reflux in aqueous solution (often 1–3 M HNO3) until gas evolution, then cooled and the aqueous nitrate solution is filtered to remove any insoluble residues.

Oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid (permanganate oxidation). 3‑Cyclopentylpropanal is oxidized by KMnO₄ in acidic aqueous medium (H₂SO₄) to 3‑cyclopentylpropanoic acid. Reaction is carried out under heating (50–80 °C) with excess KMnO₄; manganese dioxide precipitates and is filtered off.

Amide (acyl‑ chloride) coupling; glycine is acylated with oxalyl chloride to give N‑oxalylglycine while triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl, forming triethylammonium chloride. The reaction is performed in anhydrous dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen. After addition of oxalyl chloride dropwise, the mixture is stirred until gas evolution ceases; the by‑product salt is removed by filtration or aqueous work‑up.

Catalytic hydroamination of ethylene with ammonia to afford ethylamine; a nucleophilic addition of NH₃ across a C double bond. Purpose: synthesis of a primary aliphatic amine. Key transformation: conversion of the C=C bond into a C–N bond forming EtNH₂. Typical conditions: high pressure of ammonia (30–100 atm) and ethylene, temperature 150–250 °C, solid acid or metal catalyst such as Ni, Pd, or zeolite. Often performed in the gas phase without solvent.

Direct redox reaction between cyclooctasulfur and metallic lead producing lead sulfide. Synthesizes PbS semiconductor or mineral galena. Involves heating solid reactants in absence of solvent, proceeding through elemental sulfide transfer.

N‑Methylglycine (sarcosine) acylationuroyl chloride to give lauroyl sarcosine; a nucleophilic acyl substitution forming an amide. Purpose: preparation of an N‑acyl sarcosine surfactant intermediate. Key transformation: the secondary amine attacks the acid chloride, displacing chloride and generating HCl. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or THF as solvent, 0 °C to room temperature, base (pyridine or triethylamine) to capture HCl. Reaction is moisture‑sensitive and carried out under inert atmosphere.

Mannich reaction of indole, formaldehyde and N‑methylpyrrolidine yielding 3‑(N‑methylpyrrolidin‑2‑ylmethyl)‑1H‑indole; a three‑component electrophilic alkylation. Purpose: C‑3 functionalization of indole for heterocyclic synthesis. Key transformation: in‑situ formation of a iminium ion from formaldehyde and the secondary amine, which then undergoes electrophilic attack by the C‑3 of indole, followed by loss of water. Typical conditions: methanol or ethanol as solvent, ambient temperature, optionally a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., acetic acid) to promote iminium formation. Reaction proceeds in 1–6 h.

Esterification of 3‑hexen‑1‑ol with benzoyl chloride to give 3‑hexenyl benzoate; a nucleophilic acyl substitution (acyl chloride esterification). Purpose: preparation of an unsaturated benzoate ester. Key transformation: alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl of benzoyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming the ester, with HCl as by‑product. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or chloroform as solvent, 0 °C to rt, base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize HCl. Reaction is rapid (minutes to 1 h) and the product is isolated by aqueous work‑up.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation of oxalic acid with silver oxide to afford silver oxalate and water. Purpose: preparation of aingly soluble silver salt for analytical or photochemical use. Key transformation: proton transfer from oxalic acid to the oxide, forming water and the silver salt (Ag₂C₂O₄). Typical conditions: aqueous suspension, slight heating (40–60 °C) to promote dissolution of oxalic acid, followed by cooling to precipitate Ag₂C₂O₄. No special solvent beyond water; stirring and filtration isolate the product.

Double‑displacement reaction of Yb(NO3)3·xH2O with hydrofluoric acid to form YbF3 precipitate and HNO3; performed in dilute HF solution at 0–25 °C under stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst, but corrosion‑resistant equipment is essential.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydration of an α,β‑unsaturated ketone; water adds across the C=C double bond of methyl vinyl ketone in a Markovnikov fashion to afford 4‑hydroxy‑2‑butanone. Under dilute mineral acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) at 0–25 °C, or under mild alkaline conditions (NaOH, Na₂CO₃) at room temperature, the reaction proceeds smoothly; no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed Hock rearrangement (oxidative cleavage of an aryl alkyl hydroperoxide). The benzylic O–O bond of ethylbenzene hydroperoxide is protonated, leading to migration of the phenyl group and fragmentation to give phenol and acetaldehyde. Typically performed with strong mineral acid (e.g., 70 % H₂SO₄) at 60–100 °C in a polar solvent such as glacial acetic acid or dichloromethane; water is generated and removed with the acid work‑up.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt formation). Aluminum chloride reacts with three equivalents of acetic acid, abstracting the chloride ions to form aluminum triacetate (Al(OAc)₃) and liberating three equivalents of hydrogen chloride gas. The reaction is usually conducted in an aprotic, dry solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or toluene) under an inert atmosphere at 0–25 °C to avoid hydrolysis of AlCl₃; the HCl is removed by gas‑flow or trapped in a base.

Chemical reduction of a quinone to a hydroquinone. Sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) serves as a two‑electron donor, reducing duroquinone to 2,5‑di‑tert‑butyl‑hydroquinone. The reaction is carried out in aqueous buffer (pH 7–9) or water/ethanol mixture at ambient to 50 °C; excess dithionite is often used to ensure complete reduction. No metal catalyst is required; the by‑product is sulfite/sulfate.

Conversion of an anhydride to the corresponding di‑acid chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂). Glutaric anhydride reacts with SOCl₂, replacing carbonyl oxygens with chloride to afford pentanedioyl dichloride (glutaroyl chloride), with evolution of HCl gas and SO₂. Typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform under nitrogen, with removal of gaseous by‑products by a vented drying tube; reaction time 1–3 h.

Redox oxidation of a diol by a metal nitrate; heating ethylene glycol with aluminum nitrate leads to oxidation of the glycol to oxalic acid, which chelates Al³⁺ to precipitate aluminum oxalate, while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas. The overall process generates water as a by‑product. Typically performed in a sealed tube or reflux apparatus at 150–200 °C; the evolution of NO₂ signals the oxidation, and the solid aluminum oxalate is isolated by filtration and drying.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of hydrazine; isopropyl bromide reacts with hydrazine in the presence of HCl, forming 1‑isopropylhydrazine which is immediately protonated to its hydrochloride salt. The displaced bromide combines with a proton to give HBr. The reaction is usually carried out in ethanol or a water/ethanol mixture at reflux (≈78 °C); the product crystallizes as 1‑isopropylhydrazinium chloride upon cooling.

Oxidative cyclization (heterocycle formation). An O2‑mediated copper(II)-catalyzed C–S coupling converts 2‑aminothiophenol into benzothiazole while reducing Cu(II) to Cu(I). Typical conditions: CuCl2 (10–20 mol %), O2 atmosphere, polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, 80–120 °C for several hours; water is generated as by‑product and CuCl is formed.

Full catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne ester. Ethyl pent‑4‑ynoate is reduced with H2 over Pd/C to give the saturated ester ethyl pentanoate. Common conditions: 1–3 atm H2, 5–10 wt % Pd/C, solvent (EtOH or MeOH), room temperature to 50 °C, reaction time 1–4 h.

Direct synthesis of potassium hydride: elemental potassium reacts with hydrogen gas to form KH (K + ½ H₂ → KH). This metal‑hydrogen formation reaction is performed at elevated temperature (150–250 °C) under hydrogen pressure (1–5 atm) often in liquid ammonia or anhydrous hydrocarbon solvent, with an inert atmosphere; no added catalyst.

Oxidative dimerization of thiamine. Peracetic acid oxidizes two thiamine molecules, forming the disulfide dimer pyritinol with release of acetic acid and water. Typically carried out in a mixed aqueous‑acetone medium at 0–25 °C; peracetic acid is added slowly to control exotherm; the reaction proceeds under ambient pressure.

Complete catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑aturated ketone. Cyclohexenone is reduced with excess H2 (2 equiv) in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO2) to give cyclohexanol. Standard conditions: 3–5 atm H2, 5 wt % Pd/C, solvent such as ethanol or THF, 25–60 °C, 2–6 h.

Acid‑base reaction of a refractory oxide; Al₂O₃ reacts with concentrated hydrochloric acid, often under heating (150‑200 °C), to give aluminum chloride and water; the oxide is converted to the corresponding chloride; heating is essential because Al₂O₃ is relatively insoluble; no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid–metal reaction producing hydrogen gas and a metal fluoride. Cadmium metal reacts with aqueous or concentrated HF (2 equiv) to generate hydrogen gas and cadmium fluoride (CdF2) solid. Reaction is usually performed at 0–25 °C under a fume hood due to HF toxicity; excess HF is used to keep CdF2 suspended.

Metathesis/precipitation double displacement. Aqueous solutions of zinc nitrate (3 equiv) and tribasic potassium phosphate (2 equiv) are mixed, yielding soluble potassium nitrate (6 equiv) and insoluble zinc phosphate (Zn3(PO4)2) which precipitates. Conditions: room‑temperature stirring in water, followed by filtration and washing of the Zn‑phosphate solid.

Thioamide formation (carboxamide sulfurization). The carboxy acid reacts with propylamine in the presence of phosphorus pentasulfide to convert the amide carbonyl into a thiocarbonyl, yielding prothionamide. Used to synthesize thioamide drugs. Typical conditions: reflux in dry pyridine or toluene, inert atmosphere, P2S5 added portion‑wise. No additional catalyst required.

Radical substitution/organomercury coupling. Photolysis of carbon tetrachloride generates trichloromethyl radicals that attack phenylmercuric iodide, producing phenyl‑trichloromethyl‑mercury and elemental iodine as by‑product. Employed to prepare organomercuryents. Conducted under UV irradiation in an inert organic solvent (e.g., benzene or CCl4 itself) at ambient temperature; no added catalyst.

Reaction type: alkoxide hydrolysis (acid‑base proton transfer); purpose: regenerate the primary alcohol and generate sodium hydroxide; key transformation: Na⁺–O⁻ bond is protonated to give hexan‑1‑ol and Na⁺ pairs with OH⁻ to form NaOH; typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient temperature, no catalyst required; common solvent: water (or dilute alcohol/water mixture).

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of a thiazole ring. N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) delivers bromine electrophilically to the 5‑position of 1,2‑thiazole, affording 5‑bromo‑1,2‑thiazole and succinimide as by‑product. Reaction proceeds in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, typically at 0 °C to ambient temperature, in the dark or under mild stirring; no metal catalyst is required.

Acid‑base exchange (proton transfer) between ethylammonium acetate and HCl; purpose is to obtain the ethylammonium chloride salt and free acetic acid; key transformation is protonation of the acetate anion by HCl to give acetic acid and transfer of the chloride to the ethylammonium cation; generally performed in aqueous medium at 0–25 °C; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of beryllium carbonate; the carbonate breaks down upon heating to give beryllium oxide and carbon dioxide gas; performed by heating the solid in a furnace at high temperature (generally >800 °C); no solvent or catalyst, solid‐state reaction in air or inert gas.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) azide transfer. Tri‑n‑butyl‑tin azide displaces bromide from ethyl bromide, affording ethyl azide and tri‑n‑butyl‑tin bromide. Useful for preparing alkyl azides for click chemistry. Performed in an apro such as toluene or THF, refluxed under nitrogen; no external catalyst.

Halide metathesis (precipitation-driven exchange). Benzyl chloride reacts with soluble silver nitrate; Ag⁺ precipitates as insoluble AgCl, shifting equilibrium to form benzyl nitrate. Performed at ambient temperature in a mixed aqueous/organic medium (e.g., water with dichloromethane extraction). No additional catalyst; stirring under dark conditions to prevent photodecomposition.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of octyl octanoate; purpose is to convert the ester into the sodium salt of the fatty acid and liberate the alcohol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the carbonyl carbon, forming sodium octanoate and 1‑octanol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux (60–80 °C) for 2–4 h; after completion, the reaction mixture is acidified (if free acid desired) or the sodium salt is isolated; solvent often water or water/ethanol mixture.

Free‑radical halogenation of methane. Chlorine radicals abstract hydrogen from methane, forming chloromethane which undergoes further chlorination to give dichloromethane and hydrogen chloride. Industrial route to HCl and DCM. Carried out in the gas phase under strong UV light or at 400–500 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acylation (esterification) of a tertiary alcohol. 2‑Methylpentan‑2‑ol reacts with acetic anhydride, transferring an acetyl group to the alcohol to give 2‑methylpentan‑2‑yl acetate and acetic acid. Standard method for preparing acetate esters. Usually refluxed in pyridine or dichloromethane with catalytic DMAP; no additional catalyst is essential.

Conversion of an alcohol to an alkyl chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); purpose is to replace the hydroxyl group with chlorine; key transformation: formation of 1‑chloro‑1‑methylcyclopropane with evolution of SO₂ and HCl gases; typically run at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous pyridine or dichloromethane; pyridine acts as base and HCl scavenger.
Hydration/acid formation; tellurium dioxide dissolves in water to give tellurous acid (H2TeO3). Reaction proceeds upon stirring aqueous suspension, often with gentle heating to promote dissolution.

Acid‑base (protonolysis) reaction: Aluminum ethoxide is added to aqueous nitric acid, the nitro‑acid protonates the ethoxide ligands to release ethanol and generates aluminum nitrate (often as the hydrated salt) in the aqueous phase. Conducted at low temperature (0–25 °C) in water; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic epoxide ring opening. Ammonia attacks the less hindered carbon of 2‑pentyloxirane, opening the ring to afford 1‑amino‑2‑pentanol (a β‑amino alcohol). Employed to synthesize amino‑alcohol building blocks. Conducted in anhydrous ethanol or water/alcohol mixture at 0–50 °C, using excess NH3; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – lithio‑2‑pyridyl anion attacks bromoethane to give 2‑ethylpyridine; lithium bromide is formed as by‑product. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions in THF or Et₂O at –78 °C to 0 °C; no additional catalyst required.

Direct halogenation (synthesis of a metal halide) – red phosphorus reacts with chlorine gas to afford phosphorus trichloride (PCl₃). Conducted in a dry, inert vessel; chlorine is passed over heated phosphorus (often 200–300 °C). No solvent; the reaction is gas‑phase.

Oxidation with hydrogen peroxide; arsenous acid reacts with H₂O₂ in aqueous solution, yielding arsenic acid and water. Typically performed at room temperature or mild heating (20‑40 °C) in acidic to neutral pH; no additional catalyst required, though catalytic amounts of transition‑metal ions (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺) can accelerate the reaction.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative methoxycarbonylation of a nitrile – benzonitrile, carbon monoxide and methanol undergo Pd(OAc)₂/PPh₃‑mediated carbonylation to give methyl benzoate, with PPh₃ acting as ligand. Typical conditions: 5–30 bar CO, 80–120 °C, methanol as solvent, 1–5 mol % Pd, 2–4 mol % PPh₃, reaction time 4–12 h.

Hydrolysis/condensation of chlorosilane – two equivalents of trimethylchlorosilane (₃SiCl) react with water to produce hexamethyldisiloxane (Me₃Si‑O‑SiMe₃) and two equivalents of HCl. Usually carried out at 0 °C to rt in an inert organic solvent (toluene, dichloromethane); a base such as pyridine or triethylamine may be added to neutralize HCl.

Acetylation (acylation) of indoxyl – indoxyl reacts with acetic anhydride to give indoxyl acetate andetic acid. Performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., pyridine, dichloromethane) at 0 °C to reflux; pyridine can serve both as solvent and acid scavenger. Reaction time 1–3 h.

Reductive amination (hydrogenation) of a dialdehyde – pentane‑1,5‑dial is condensed with ammonia, then the resulting imine intermediates are hydrogenated to afford 1,5‑diamino‑pentane (cadaverine) with water as the only by‑product. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–50 atm) using a heterogeneous catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or Pt‑O₂, in ethanol or methanol at 50–100 °C for several hours.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; couples an aryl bromide with a pyridin‑4‑ylboronic acid to give the biaryl 4‑phenylpyridine; by‑product is boric acid. Typical conditions: Pd(0) catalyst (Pd(PPh₃)₄ or PdCl₂(dppf)), base such as K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃, mixed aqueous/organic solvent (dioxane‑water or THF‑water), heated 80‑100 °C under inert atmosphere.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; aqueous ammonium hydroxide reacts with silver nitrate to form insoluble silver oxide and soluble ammonium nitrate, releasing water. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; no special solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of acetic anhydride by lithium amide; the amide anion attacks the carbonyl, yielding acetamide and lithium acetate. Typically performed in dry THF or ether at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; stoichiometric LiNH₂ is used, no catalyst.

Metal‑hydride reduction of a lactone; sodium bis(2‑methoxyethoxy)aluminum hydride (Red‑Al) reduces δ‑valerolactone to the corresponding 1,5‑pentanediol. Reaction carried out in anhydrous THF or toluene, reflux (≈70‑80 °C) under nitrogen; the hydride reagent is used in excess, no additional catalyst.

Palladium‑catalyzed aryl cyanation (cross‑coupling) of 4‑bromo‑1,2‑dimethoxybenzene with potassium cyanide to afford 4‑cyano‑,2‑dimethoxybenzene. Common conditions: Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd₂(dba)₃ with a phosphine ligand, base (e.g., K₃PO₄), polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or NMP, heating at 80‑120 °C under inert atmosphere.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of catechol using N‑bromosuccinimide; regioselective formation of 4‑bromocatechol with succinimide as the by‑product. Usually in anhydrous dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to rt, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid or light; no metal catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) reaction converting silicon tetrachloride to silicon tetrabromide while generating hydrogen chloride; purpose is to replace Si–Cl bonds with Si–Br. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often as a gas‑phase reaction or in a dry inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride; no catalyst is required.

Ester transesterification (alcoholysis) of ethyl propionate with methanol exchanging the ethoxy group for a methoxy group to give methyl propionate and ethanol; used to synthesize a different ester or re‑esterify. Typically performed with excess methanol under reflux, using an acid catalyst (e.g., sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a base catalyst (e.g., NaOMe); methanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

NaBH₄ reduction of a ketone; 2‑methylcyclopentanone is reduced to the secondary alcohol 2‑methylcyclopentan‑1‑ol. Usually performed in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or a MeOH/THF mixture at 0 °C to rt; stoichiometric NaBH₄ (1.1 equiv) gives quantitative conversion.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of hydrogen telluride with sodium hydroxide, producing sodium telluride and water; a straightforward way to generate the telluride salt. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed, water is the solvent.

Acid‑base reaction (carbonate neutralization) of scandium carbonate with acetic acid, yielding scandium acetate, carbon dioxide, and water; employed to prepare soluble Sc(III) acetate. Conducted in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to drive off CO₂; no catalyst required.

Acidic hydrolysis of a metal nitride (acid‑base reaction). Calcium nitride reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid, protonating the nitride ion to release ammonia gas while forming soluble calcium chloride. Performed at ambient temperature by adding HCl solution to calcium nitride powder; the reaction generates NH₃ gas that can be collected, and no catalyst is required.

Fluorination oxidation of potassium sulfide with elemental fluorine, forming sulfur tetrafluoride and potassium fluoride; used to synthesize SF₄, a valuable fluorinating agent. Performed in dry liquid HF or a nickel/steel reactor at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under an inert atmosphere; fluorine is the reagent and no catalyst is used.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) of tert‑butyl chloride with silver nitrite, producing tert‑butyl nitrite and precipitating silver chloride; a method for preparing alkyl nitrites. Typically carried out in dry acetone or ether at room temperature or mild reflux, with AgNO₂ acting as the nitrite source and as a scavenger for chloride; the AgCl precipitate is filtered off.

Salt metathesis/acid displacement; lead azide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to precipitate lead sulfate and liberate hydrazoic acid; performed in cold dilute H₂SO₄ solution, careful temperature control and ventilation required to handle HN₃ safely; water is the reaction medium, no catalyst.

Esterification (acylation) of a primary alcohol using acetic anhydride; the hydroxyl group of cyclodecanol attacks the carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming cyclodecyl acetate and releasing acetic acid. Typically carried out at room temperature to mild heating, often neat or in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) and may be catalyzed by a base such as pyridine or DMAP to speed up acyl transfer.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive nitro‑to‑amine conversion). Molecular hydrogen reduces the nitro group of 2‑nitrobiphenyl to an amine in the presence of a palladium on carbon (Pd/C) heterogeneous catalyst, generating 2‑aminobiphenyl and water as the only by‑product. Common conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 25–80 °C, solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate; catalyst loading 5–10 wt % Pd relative to substrate.

Appel halogenation of 2‑(hydroxymethyl)pyridine using I2 and triphenylphosphine; primary alcohol is converted to the corresponding iodomethyl derivative with formation of triphenylphosphine oxide and HI as by‑products. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF under inert atmosphere. No external catalyst other than the phosphine‑iodine system.

Enzymatic O‑methylation (SAM‑dependent methyl transfer). The methyl group of S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) is transferred to the 2‑hydroxy group of estradiol, producing 2‑methoxyestradiol and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. The reaction is mediated by a catechol O‑methyltransferase (COMT) or related methyltransferase under aqueous, physiological pH (≈7.4) at 25–37 °C, often in a buffered saline solution with Mg²⁺ as cofactor.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on a heteroaromatic chloride. Hydroxide ion attacks the electron‑deficient 3‑position of 3‑chloropyridine, displacing chloride to give 3‑hydroxypyridine and sodium chloride. Typically performed in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol NaOH (1–2 M), refluxed for 1–3 h, then cooled and the product isolated by extraction or crystallization.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Oxalic acid protonates the chloride ligands of manganese(II) chloride, releasing HCl and forming insoluble manganese(II) oxalate (MnC₂O₄·2H₂O). Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the mixture is stirred until precipitation is complete, then the solid is filtered, washed, and dried. No special catalysts required.

Redox dissolution of iron in dilute nitric acid. Iron metal is oxidized to Fe³⁺ while nitrate is reduced to nitric oxide (NO); the overall stoichiometry yields iron(III) nitrate, water, and gaseous NO. Performed in aqueous dilute HNO₃ (≈1–3 M) at room temperature or with gentle heating; gas evolution is vented, and the aqueous iron nitrate solution can be concentrated or crystallized. No external catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalzed Fischer esterification of phthalic anhydride with 1‑butanol and 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol to give the mixed diester butyl isobutyl phthalate; p‑toluenesulfonic acid acts as a Brønsted acid catalyst, water is formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: reflux in an inert organic solvent (toluene or xylene) with azeotropic removal of water or Dean‑Stark trap; reaction generally carried out 3–6 h under nitrogen.

Michaelis–Arbuzov reaction (phosphonate synthesis); trimethyl phosphite undergoes an SN2 attack on ethyl iodide, forming ethyl dimethyl phosphonate (1‑dimethoxyphosphorylethane) and methyl iodide as the side product. Conducted under reflux in anhydrous solvent such as toluene or acetonitrile, 80–120 °C, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Conversion of a secondary alcohol to a bromide via phosphorus tribromide; purpose is to prepare the alkyl bromide for substitution reactions. Cyclooctanol reacts with PBr3, the –OH is replaced by Br, forming bromocyclooctane and phosphorous acid (H3PO3). Typical conditions: anhydrous ether or CH2Cl2, 0 °C to rt, stoichiometric PBr3 added under nitrogen; reaction is exothermic.

Oxidative decomposition (redox) of cadmium antimonide with concentrated nitric acid, yielding soluble cadmium nitrate, antimony oxide precipitate, water and nitrogen dioxide gas. The reaction is carried out by adding solid CdSb to hot (≈70 °C) conc. HNO₃ under a fume hood; mixture is refluxed until gas evolution ceases, then cooled and filtered to isolate the antimony oxide. No special catalyst is required.

Williamson ether synthesis: nucleophilic SN2 substitution of 1,8‑dibromo‑octane with sodium methoxide producing 1,8‑dimethoxyoctane and sodium bromide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as dry DMF or DMSO under inert atmosphere; temperature typically 60–80 °C to drive both displacements to completion. Excess methoxide ensures complete conversion.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation: oxalic acid reacts with cobalt(II) sulfate to form insoluble cobalt(II) oxalate precipitate and sulfuric acid remains in solution. Performed in water at ambient temperature; the mixture is stirred, the cobalt oxalate is filtered, washed and dried. No catalyst is needed.

Redox/acid‑base reaction between ammonium sulfite and sodium hypochlorite in aqueous solution: hypochlorite oxidizes sulfite to sulfate while being reduced to chloride; simultaneously ammonium ions are liberated as ammonia gas. Conducted at room temperature in dilute aqueous media, often with gentle stirring; the reaction proceeds rapidly, liberating NH₃, forming Na₂SO₄, NaCl and water. No additional catalyst is required.

Condensation of a silyl chloride with a silyl alkoxide to give a siloxane; a nucleophilic substitution where the chloride is displaced by the trimethylsilanolate, forming hexamethyldisiloxane and KCl as by‑product. Typically carried out under anhydrous, aprotic conditions (e.g., THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no external catalyst is required.

Wittig olefination: n‑Butyllithium deprotonates methyltriphenylphosphonium bromide to generate the ylide, which then reacts with 4‑chlorobutanal to afford 4‑chlorobut‑1‑ene and triphenylphosphine oxide. Used to convert an aldehyde into a terminal alkene while preserving the chloro substituent. Performed in dry THF (or ether) at –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere; n‑BuLi serves as the strong base.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; cadmium acetate reacts with ammonium carbonate in aqueous solution, forming insoluble cadmium carbonate and soluble ammonium acetate; generally conducted in water at low to moderate temperature to avoid decomposition of ammonium carbonate.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of naphthalene. Sulfuric acid protonates ammonium nitrate to generate the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺), which attacks the 1‑position of naphthalene to afford 1‑nitronaphthalene. The reaction introduces a nitro group for further functionalisation. Conducted in concentrated H₂SO₄ (often with added HNO₃ generated in situ) at 0–50 °C; the acid mixture acts as both solvent and catalyst.

Hydrolytic dechlorination of a gem‑dichloro carboxylic acid; water replaces one chlorine atom, yielding 2‑chloropropionic acid and releasing HCl. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating (e.g., 50–80 °C) to accelerate the substitution; no special catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction used to prepare lead(II) formate; aqueous solution of lead(II) chloride reacts with sodium formate, exchanging anions to give insoluble lead(II) formate (precipitate) and soluble sodium chloride; performed at room temperature with stirring in water, no catalyst required.

Sequential SN2 nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of two bromides by hydroxide; aqueous sodium hydroxide displaces both bromides of 1,5-dibromopentane to give 1,5-pentanediol and sodium bromide; performed by heating the substrate in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol or water as solvent) under reflux; no catalyst required.

Metal‑acid reaction (redox/displacement); used to dissolve terbium metal and generate its chloride salt. Terbium metal reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, producing terbium(III) chloride and hydrogen gas. Typical conditions are a dilute HCl solution (≈1 M) at ambient temperature or with gentle heating (∼50 °C) to increase rate. Reaction is carried out in water; no catalyst is required.

Simultaneous reduction of the nitro group and N‑oxide of 4‑nitropyridine N‑oxide with lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to obtain 4‑aminopyridine; key transformations are reduction of the nitro group to an amine and removal of the N‑oxide oxygen, producing lithium hydroxide and aluminum oxide as inorganic residues; typical conditions: excess LiAlH₄ in dry THF or Et₂O, reflux under nitrogen, followed by aqueous work‑up; solvent is anhydrous ether.

Synthesis of an ammonium dithiocarbamate. Carbon disulfide reacts with pyrrolidine to form the pyrrolidinedithiocarbamate anion, which is protonated/neutralised by ammonium carbonate, giving ammonium pyrrolidinedithiocarbamate while liberating CO₂ and H₂O. This is a thiocarbonylation (dithiocarbamate formation) reaction. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in a polar protic solvent (water or methanol); ammonium carbonate serves as the base and source of CO₂.

Acid–base neutralisation of a citrate salt. Three equivalents of hydrochloric acid protonate the trisodium citrate, converting it to citric acid and generating three equivalents of sodium chloride. Used to obtain the free organic acid from its sodium salt. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring ensures complete dissolution and reaction.

Acid–base neutralization to form a phosphate salt: Sodium bicarbonate deprotonates the P–OH of dimethyl hydrogen phosphate, producing sodium dimethyl phosphate, carbon dioxide, and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst needed.

. Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of acetylide. Purpose: carbon‑carbon bond formation to synthesize a terminal alkyne. Transformation: sodium acetylide (C≡C⁻ Na) attacks the primary carbon of 1‑bromobutane, displacing bromide and giving 1‑hex‑1‑yne; NaBr is formed as by‑product. Conditions: anhydrous ethereal solvent (dry THF or diethyl ether), inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux, generated from sodium metal or NaNH₂ and acetylene. No catalyst required.

Type: Acylation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of an amine with acetic anhydride. Purpose: protect or derivatize the primary amine of taurine, yielding N‑acetyl‑taurine. Transformation: the amino group attacks one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming N‑(2‑acetamido)‑2‑aminoethanesulfonic acid and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Conditions: typically performed in pyridine or a non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; pyridine acts as base and solvent; no metal catalyst.

Type: β‑Elimination (E2) of a benzylic halide. Purpose: dehydrohalogenation to generate the vinyl arene styrene. Transformation: hydroxide abstracts the benzylic hydrogen while bromide leaves from 2‑phenylethyl bromide, forming the C=C double bond (styrene) and water; NaBr is formed. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (often 5–10 M), heated under reflux (≈80–100 °C), sometimes in ethanol or water/ethanol mixture; no catalyst needed.

Type: Nucleophilic alkylation (SN2) of a pyridyl organolithium. Purpose: introduce a methyl group at the 2‑position of pyridine to afford 2‑methylpyridine (picoline). Transformation: lithium 2‑pyridylide (2‑lithiopyridine) attacks the electrophilic carbon of iodomethane, displacing iodide and forming the C–C bond; LiI precipitates. Conditions: anhydrous THF, low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under nitrogen; inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of an alkyl chloride. Purpose: convert 2‑chloro‑1,1,1‑trifluoroethane to the corresponding alcohol, 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol. Transformation: water attacks the electrophilic carbon, displacing chloride as HCl and yielding trifluoroethanol; overall HCl is produced. Conditions: typically performed in aqueous base (e.g., NaOH) at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, followed by acid work‑up to isolate the alcohol; polar protic solvent such as water/ethanol; no metal catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed Cannizzaro disproportionation of a non‑enolizable aldehyde; 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzaldehyde undergoes simultaneous reduction to the benzyl alcohol and oxidation to the benzoic acid, giving both 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzyl alcohol and 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzoic acid; conducted with aqueous NaOH (often 1–2 M) at 0–25 °C; mixture is worked up by acidification and extraction; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑mediated neutralization (alkaline work‑up); regeneration of free propan‑1‑amine from its hydrochloride salt. Hydroxide deprotonates the ammonium ion, producing propan‑1‑amine, NaCl and water Conducted in aqueous NaOH solution at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring suffices.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of 2‑chloroquinoline with hydroxide; OH⁻ displaces the ortho‑chloroquinoline and NaCl; typically refluxed in aqueous NaOH or NaOH/ethylene glycol mixture (100‑130 °C) followed by acid work‑up; no additional catalyst.

Oxidation (sulfoxide to sulfone) using a peracid; purpose is to convert the thioether side chain into a more polar sulfone for increased oxidation state or biological stability. Key transformation: bis(2‑hydroxyethyl) sulfide is oxidized by m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (mCPBA) to the corresponding sulfone, with m‑chlorobenzoic acid formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: 1–1.5 equiv mCPBA in anhydrous dichloromethane, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; reaction quenched with aqueous sodium sulfite or sodium thiosulfate and worked up with extraction. No metal catalyst required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) in aqueous solution; purpose is to synthesize GdF₃ from GdCl₃. Fluoride from ammonium fluoride exchanges with chloride, forming insoluble GdF₃ and soluble NH₄Cl. Usually performed by mixing aqueous solutions of GdCl₃ and excess NH₄F, heating to reflux or 60‑80 °C to promote complete precipitation, then filtering and washing the GdF₃ solid.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of 1,2,2‑trichloropropane; purpose is to remove halogen atoms and obtain the saturated hydrocarbon. Key transformation: three equivalents of H₂ reduce the three C–Cl bonds, producing propane and three equivalents of HCl. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, 5–10 % Pd/C (10 wt % on carbon) as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–60 °C; reaction monitored until gas evolution ceases, then filtered to remove catalyst.

Redox metathesis between calcium chlorate and sodium bisulfite in aqueous solution; chlorate is reduced to chloride while bisulfite is oxidized to sulfate, giving calcium sulfate precipitate, sodium chloride in solution, and water. Typically carried out at ambient temperature in water; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration) of chlorobenzene; purpose is to introduce two nitro substituents for synthesis of dinitro‑aryl intermediates. Key transformation: chlorobenzene undergoes ortho‑ and para‑nitration (relative to the chloro group) to give 1‑chloro‑2,4‑dinitrobenzene; water is generated as a by‑product. Typical conditions: mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and conc. H₂SO₄ (mixed acid), temperature maintained at 0–5 °C during addition then gently warmed to 30–50 °C; reaction performed in the acid medium itself; work‑up involves quenching into ice, neutralization, and isolation by filtration or extraction.

Acid–base salt formation (hydrochloride generation) of 2,3,5,6‑tetramethylpyrazine; purpose is to obtain a water‑soluble, stable salt for handling or pharmaceutical formulation. Key transformation: the basic pyrazine nitrogen accepts a proton from HCl, forming the corresponding hydrochloride salt; no covalent bond changes. Typical conditions: dissolve tetramethylpyrazine in a minimal amount of anhyd organic solvent (e.g., EtOAc or MeCN) and add equimolar aqueous HCl or gaseous HCl at 0–25 °C; the salt often precipitates and is collected by filtration, then dried under vacuum.

Redox/combination gas‑solid reaction where metallic silver reduces hydrogen selenide, yielding silver selenide and hydrogen gas. Conducted by passing dry H2Se gas over heated silver (≈200 °C) in an inert atmosphere; no solvent, catalyst, or added reagents needed.
Double displacement reaction; synthesizes silver tellurite by anion exchange. Occurs in aqueous solution with sodium acetate as a soluble byproduct. No catalyst needed.

Oxidative disulfide coupling using iodine; purpose is to synthesize the disulfide cystamine from the thiol cysteamine. Key transformation: two molecules of cysteamine (as the hydrochloride) are oxidized by I₂ to form the disulfide bond, yielding cystamine; iodine is reduced to two equivalents of hydrogen iodide, and the original HCl from the cysteamine salt is liberated. Typical conditions: 0.5 equiv I₂ per mole of disulfide desired, reaction in a polar aprotic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or a water‑methanol mixture, ambient temperature, stirring until the brown color of I₂ disappears; the mixture is then basified to precipitate cystamine, and the HI/ HCl can be removed by aqueous work‑up.

Type: SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkylation of a secondary amine). Purpose: Form an N‑alkylated pyrrolidine derivative. Key transformation: The lone pair on pyrrolidine attacks the primary carbon bearing bromide in 2‑phenylethyl bromide, displacing Br⁻ and yielding N‑(2‑phenylethyl)pyrrolidine; HBr is neutralized by a base present. Typical conditions: Reaction in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile, DMF, or DMSO at reflux or 80–100 °C, with an added inorganic base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaHCO₃, or excess pyrrolidine) to trap HBr. Reaction time: 4–12 h.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis). Sodium cyanide deprotonates chloroacetic acid, transferring a proton to cyanide to give hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and sodium chloroacetate. Typically performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Mannich/Pictet‑Spengler alkylation followed by N‑methylation. 3,4‑Dimethoxyphenethylamine condenses with formaldehyde to form an iminium intermediate, which cyclizes to a tetrahydroisoquinoline core; methyl iodide then N‑methylates the nitrogen, yielding laudanosine. Conducted in a polar protic solvent (e.g., methanol or ethanol) with an acid catalyst (often HCl) under reflux.

Halide metathesis/halide abstraction. Chlorotrimethylsilane reacts with silver triflate; Ag⁺ precipitates as AgCl, while the trimethylsilyl group is to the triflate anion forming trimethylsilyl triflate (TMS‑OTf), a strong silylating agent. Carried out under anhydrous conditions in a non‑coordinating solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, typically at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Hydrobromic acid protonates terbium(III) hydroxide, producing water and the terbium tribromide salt (TbBr₃). Usually performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to dissolve the hydroxide; no catalyst required.

Methylation of 4‑mercaptobenzoic acid with diazomethane to produce methyl 4‑mercaptobenzoate and nitrogen gas; a mild, non‑acidic esterification where the carboxylate attacks diazomethane, releasing N₂; performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as diethyl ether or dichloromethane using a stoichiometric solution of diazomethane.

Metallothermic reduction of a metal fluoride. Tungsten hexafluoride is reduced by silicon metal, yielding elemental tungsten and silicon tetrafluoride gas (SiF₄). This high‑temperature redox process is performed at 800–1200 °C in a sealed tube or flow reactor under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Ester transesterification (nucleophilic acyl substitution) used to prepare the local anesthetic procaine (Risocaine). The hydroxyl group of 2-(diethylamino)ethanol attacks the methyl ester of p‑aminobenzoic acid, displacing methanol and forming the 2‑(diethylamino)ethyl p‑aminobenzoate ester. Typically performed under reflux in an aprotic solvent (e.g., toluene or xylene) with a catalytic amount of acid such p‑toluenesulfonic acid or HCl. The reaction is driven to completion by removal of methanol.

Double‑displacement (halide metathesis) precipitation. Mixing aqueous solutions of AgCl and tetraphenylphosphonium bromide exchanges the halides, producing insoluble AgBr which precipitates, and soluble tetraphenylphosphonium chloride remains in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; the solid AgBr is filtered and washed.

Acid‑base/precipitation synthesis of zinc telluride. Hydrogen telluride gas reacts with solid ZnCl2, exchanging the halide for telluride to give ZnTe solid and HCl gas. Usually carried out in a sealed tube or reactor under an inert atmosphere, heated (≈200 °C) to promote gas–solid interaction. No catalyst is required; the HCl is removed by gas flow.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (sulfonation); introduces a sulfonic acid group onto the aromatic ring to give ethylbenzenesulfonic acid; key transformation: SO3 adds to the para position of ethylbenzene forming the sulfonic acid; typically carried out by treating ethylbenzene with fuming sulfuric acid (or SO3 in H2SO4) at 0‑30 °C; no additional catalyst required, reaction mixture often run neat or in concentrated sulfuric acid.

Oxidation of anthracene to anthracene‑9,10‑dione (anthraquinone). Potassium dichromate acts as the oxidant in acidic medium (conc. H2SO4) to insert two carbonyl groups at the 9,10‑positions of anthracene. The reaction is performed at 80–120 °C, often in a mixture of acetic acid and water or glacial acetic acid alone. The Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) and the product precipitates on cooling.

Reductive carbonylation to form iron pentacarbonyl. Zinc metal reduces Fe(II) bromide under a pressure of CO (≈5–10 atm) to generate Fe(CO)5, while the zinc is oxidized to ZnBr2. The reaction is carried out in anhydrous, oxygen‑free solvent such as THF or diethyl ether at room temperature or mild heating, under an inert atmosphere. The volatile Fe(CO)5 is distilled off; ZnBr2 remains in solution.

Coordination complex formation of dichloro(1,5‑cyclooctadiene)palladium(II). PdCl2 is dissolved in a non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or chloroform) and treated with 1,5‑cyclooctadiene; the COD ligand displaces coordinated chloride/water to give the neutral PdCl2(COD) complex. The reaction proceeds at reflux or room temperature under nitrogen, often with gentle stirring. No additional catalyst is required; the product precipitates or can be isolated by solvent evaporation.

Oxidative dissolution (acid digestion). Concentrated nitric acid oxidizes iron(II) selenide, reducing nitrate to nitrogen dioxide while releasing elemental selenium and forming ferrous nitrate. Typically performed by heating the solid in refluxing HNO₃, no added catalyst, water is the reaction medium.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution / carbamate synthesis. Aniline attacks diethyl carbonate, displacing ethanol and forming ethyl phenylcarbamate. Conducted under reflux in an anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., toluene or xylene) often with a base such as pyridine to absorb the generated acid; no metal catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (deoxygenation). Antimony pentoxide is heated to high temperature (≈600 °C) causing loss of molecular oxygen and conversion to antimony trioxide. Performed in a furnace or tube oven under inert or air atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Double displacement / complexation (metathesis). Zinc chloride reacts with sodium dimethyldithiocarbamate in aqueous solution, precipitating zinc dimethyldithiocarbamate complex and sodium chloride. Typically carried out at ambient temperature with stirring; water serves as solvent, no additional catalyst.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkyl halide hydrolysis). Aqueous sodium hydroxide attacks 3‑bromohexane, displacing bromide to give 3‑hexanol and NaBr. Reaction proceeds under reflux or gentle heating in water (sometimes with ethanol as co‑solvent); no catalyst required.

PLP‑dependent condensation (transsulfuration) of L‑serine with homocysteine to form cystathionine; key step in the methionine cycle. Key transformation: the β‑carbon of serine attacks the electrophilic carbon of the homocysteine thio‑group, forming a new C‑S bond and releasing water. Catalyzed by cystathionine β‑synthase (CBS) with pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate (PLP) as cofactor, requiring Mg²⁺ and often S‑adenosyl‑methionine as an allosteric activator. Conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 7.5–8.5) at 37 °C, enzyme concentration 0.1–1 µM. No organic solvent; enzyme and PLP act as catalysts.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Aqueous NaOH hydrolyzes ethyl pent‑4‑ynoate, yielding ethanol the pent‑4‑ynoate carboxylate, which upon acid work‑up furnishes pent‑4‑ynoic acid. Conducted by refluxing the ester in water/NaOH, followed by neutralization with dilute acid; no special catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduction of a nitro group to an amine; 3‑nitrobenzenesulfonic acid to 3‑aminobenzenesulfonic acid with H₂, producing water; typically performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at room temperature 50 °C using a palladium on carbon (Pd/C), Pt/C, or Raney Ni catalyst in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol.

Metal‑oxide oxidation; oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; propanal is oxidized by silver(I) oxide (Ag₂O) to propanoic acid while metallic silver precipitates; generally carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic media at reflux, often with a slight excess of Ag₂O and mild stirring.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis of a gem‑dichloride to an aldehyde; aqueous NaOH (often 1–2 M) at reflux in water converts 1,1‑dichloroethane to acetaldehyde, with NaCl and water as by‑products, proceeding via SN1‑type nucleophilic substitution and dehalogenation.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) with a strong amide base; replaces a primary alkyl bromide with an amino group; ethyl bromide reacts with sodium amide (NaNH₂) to give ethylamine and sodium bromide; carried out in dry liquid ammonia as solvent at –33 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere.

Double displacement reaction; produces strontium chloride and ammonia through salt metathesis and thermal decomposition; typically used for ammonia gas preparation; conducted in aqueous solution with heating to drive off volatile ammonia; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (heterogeneous); reduces the aromatic pyridine ring of N‑ethylpyridine to a saturated piperidine while retaining the N‑ethyl group; purpose is to obtain the fully saturated heterocycle; key transformation is addition of 3 H₂ across the ring (C=C → C‑C single bonds); typical conditions: H₂ gas at 1–5 atm, 5–10 % Pd/C, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–80 °C.

Metal‑mediated reduction to form a radical anion (solvated electron complex); lithium metal donates an electron to naphthalene in dry diethyl ether, generating lithium naphthide (C₁₀H₈⁻ Li⁺); performed under anhydrous, oxygen‑free conditions at 0 °C to –78 °C with excess lithium, often used as a strong reducing agent in subsequent reactions.

This is a free radical halogenation reaction, used to produce isotopically labeled compounds like deuterium bromide. The key transformation is the combination of deuterium gas with bromine liquid to form deuterium bromide. Typical conditions involve exposure to light or heat to initiate the reaction, often in the absence of solvents or in an inert gas phase.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction of aluminum nitrate with phosphoric acid, yielding aluminum phosphate precipitate and nitric acid in solution. An acid–base exchange where Al³⁺ combines with PO₄³⁻. Conducted in aqueous medium, typically at ambient temperature with stirring; heating may be used to improve precipitation.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of a carbamate; phenyl carbamate breaks down on heating to give phenol and isocyanic acid; usually requires elevated temperatures (150–250 °C) in the absence of solvent or in a‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., xylene), occasionally catalyzed by acids or bases to facilitate bond cleavage.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification); acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) is hydrolyzed by water to yield salicylic acid and acetic acid; commonly performed under acidic conditions (e.g., dilute HCl, reflux) or basic conditions (e.g., NaOH, reflux followed by acid work‑up); aqueous ethanol or methanol is often used as the solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation (ination); used to introduce an iodine substituent for labeling or SAR studies; replaces the para hydrogen on the aromatic ring of clonidine with iodine via attack of the I⁺ from ICl; typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Esterification (acylation) of 2‑ethylbutanol with acetic anhydride to give 2‑ethylbutyl acetate; purpose is to convert a primary alcohol into its acetate ester. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on the carbonyl of acetic anhydride, loss of acetate anion and formation of ester, generating acetic acid as by‑product. Typically carried out at 0 °C to reflux, often in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, with a base catalyst (pyridine, DMAP, or triethylamine) to neutralize the formed acid and drive the reaction to completion.

Combustion/reductive oxidation; purpose: reduce perchlorate to chloride using carbon as fuel; key transformation: carbon combusts to CO2 while ClO4− is reduced to Cl− producing O2; typical conditions: fine powder mixture of KClO4 and carbon, ignition at 200‑400 °C, conducted in a closed vessel or pyrotechnic composition, no solvent.

Acid–base proton transfer; deprotonation of phenol by ethoxide anion to generate sodium phenoxide and ethanol; essentially a acid‑base neutralization; carried out in ethanol (or a mixture of ethanol and water) at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition of a metal nitrate; employed to produce copper(II) oxide and gaseous nitrogen oxides. Heating solid copper(II) nitrate trihydrate leads to breakdown of the nitrate groups. Key transformation: Cu(NO₃)₂·3H₂O → CuO (solid) + 2 NO₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) + 3 H₂O(g). Typical conditions: dry solid heated to 200‑250 °C in a furnace or heating mantle, often under open air. No solvent or catalyst; the reaction is driven by heat.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (reverse Fischer); n‑butyl hexanoate is heated with excess water and a dilute mineral acid (HCl or H₂SO₄) under reflux, cleaving the ester to regenerate n‑butanol and hexanoic acid. Typical conditions 80–120 °C in aqueous acid; no special solvent beyond water.

Intramolecular SN2 cyclization (dehydrohalogenation) to form an epoxide; glycerol dichlorohydrin undergoes base‑promoted intramolecular nucleophilic attack of an alkoxide on the adjacent carbon, expelling HCl and yielding epichlorohydrin; usually conducted with aqueous NaOH or KOH (10–20 % w/w) at 50–80 °C, often in a water/ethanol mixture; no metal catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; purpose: exchange anions to produce soluble zinc sulfate and free oxalic acid; key transformation: ZnC2O4 + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2C2O4; typical conditions: aqueous solution, often warmed to aid dissolution; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

β‑Elimination (E2) using a bulky strong base, potassium tert‑butoxide; abstraction of a β‑hydrogen and expulsion of chloride give the more substituted alkene 3‑ethyl‑2‑pentene together with KCl and tert‑butanol; conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere.

High‑temperature solid‑state carbothermic reduction;adium nitride reacts with elemental carbon to convert the nitride lattice into vanadium carbide while liberating nitrogen gas; performed in a graphite or carbon crucible at 1500–2000 °C under inert (argon) atmosphere; no solvents or catalysts are used.

Gas‑phase reduction of titanium dioxide by carbon monoxide; purpose is to obtain lower‑valent titanium(II) oxide; CO reduces TiO₂, being oxidized to CO₂ while Ti⁴⁺ is reduced to Ti²⁺; conducted at high temperature (≈900‑1100 °C) in a flow of CO (often diluted with inert gas); no liquid solvent; reaction may be facilitated by a reducing atmosphere but no catalyst is essential.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis/precipitation (metathesis); TiCl₄ is hydrolyzed by aqueous sodium hydroxide, forming insoluble titanium hydroxide precipitate and soluble NaCl; reaction carried out in cold to room‑temperature aqueous solution with vigorous stirring; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base salt formation; hydrogen selenide (a weak acid) reacts with solid strontium oxide to produce strontium selenide and water vapor; typically performed by passing H₂Se gas over heated SrO (≈300 °C) in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Type: salt metathesis (halide exchange). Purpose: preparation of a cyclopentadienyl zirconium complex used as a precursor for organozirconium catalysts. Key transformation: replacement of one chloride ligand on ZrCl4 by a cyclopentadienyl anion, generating NaCl as by‑product and CpZrCl3. Typical conditions: anhydrous, inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), aprotic solvent such as THF or toluene, low to ambient temperature; reaction is stirred until gas evolution ceases and the solid NaCl precipitates, then filtered.

Salt‑base neutralization to liberate a free amine (alkaline extraction). Purpose: convert the amine hydrochloride salt to the free base for further use. Key transformation: 1‑(4‑fluorophenyl)propan‑2‑amine·HCl + NaOH → 1‑(4‑fluorophenyl)propan‑2‑amine + NaCl + H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at 0–25 °C, stirring until gas evolution ceases; the free amine is then extracted into an organic solvent such as dichloromethane or ethyl acetate.

Type: acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis. Purpose: conversion of an acetate ester to the corresponding thiol‑containing alcohol and recovery of acetic acid. Key transformation: cleavage of the C(O)– bond of 2‑mercaptoethyl acetate, yielding 2‑mercaptoethanol and acetic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1 M HCl or H₂SO₄), reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h; solvent is usually water or a water–organic mixture (e.g., water/ethanol). After completion the mixture is neutralized and the products are extracted.

Acidic hydrolysis of a nitrile to a carboxylic acid; converts the –CN group of 2-(4‑methylphenyl)acetonitrile into a –CO2H group yielding 4‑methylphenylacetic acid while releasing ammonia that is protonated to ammonium chloride. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (conc. or 6 M), heat to reflux (80‑100 °C) for several hours; water is the solvent.

Type: nucleophilic substitutionSN2/SN1 mixture, secondary alkyl halide). Purpose: synthesis of a secondary alcohol from the corresponding alkyl chloride. Key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks the carbon bearing the chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ to give 2‑hexanol and NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (5–10 % w/v) or alcoholic KOH, heated under reflux (100–120 °C) for 2–6 h; solvent can be water, ethanol, or a water/tert‑butanol mixture. Reaction may be assisted by phase‑transfer catalysts for improved rate.

Type: alkaline ester hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: cleavage of an aromatic benzo ester to afford the corresponding benzyl alcohol and the benzoate salt. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl carbon of (4‑methoxyphenyl)methyl benzoate, forming 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux (80–100 °C) for 2–4 h; solvent is water or water/ethanol. After reaction the mixture is acidified (e.g., with dilute HCl) to isolate the alcohol, while the benzoate remains as the sodium salt.

Halide metathesis of indium(III) chloride with hydrogen iodide; the iodide replaces chloride on the indium center, generating indium(III) iodide and HCl gas. Conducted in a dry, inert solvent (e.g., THF or dry acetonitrile) under reflux; excess HI drives the reaction to completion, and the evolved HCl can be removed by gas‑flow or trapped with a base.

High‑temperature oxidative degradation (combustion) of an organochlorine pesticide; complete oxidation of hexachlorocyclododecane to CO₂, H₂O and HCl. Conducted in an incinerator or furnace with excess O₂ at ≥800 °C (often 1000 °C) under a flowing air/oxygen stream; no catalyst is usually required. Employed for safe disposal of persistent chlorinated compounds.

Type: alkaline ester hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: generation of the benzoate salt and ethanol from an ethyl ester; a common step in the preparation of carboxylate salts. Key transformation: OH⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethyl benzoate, yielding potassium benzoate and ethanol as the leaving group. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH (1–2 M), reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h; solvent can be water alone or a water‑ethanol mixture. After completion the mixture is cooled and the benzoate salt is isolated by filtration or evaporation.

Acetylation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of an aromatic amine to form an amide; used to protect the amine or modify polarity. The amine attacks acetic anhydride, releasing acetic acid. Typically carried out in an inert solvent such as pyridine, dichloromethane or acetonitrile, often at 0 °C to room temperature, with pyridine or triethylamine serving as a base to scavenge the liberated acid.

Redox reaction of a reactive metal with a carboxylic acid, producing hydrogen gas and the corresponding metal acetate. Neodymium metal dissolves in glacial acetic acid, reducing protons to H₂ while forming neodymium(III) acetate. Conducted by refluxing neodymium filings or turnings in excess concentrated acetic acid under an inert atmosphere; the acid itself acts as solvent and reactant, no additional catalyst required.

Strong hydride reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine. Lithium aluminium hydride delivers hydride to the nitrile carbon, forming an imine intermediate that is further reduced to the amine after work‑up. Performed in dry ether or THF under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful aqueous acid quench to destroy excess LiAlH₄ and isolate butylamine.

Catalytic acetylation (esterification) of a primary alcohol using acetic anhydride activated by a catalytic amount of DMF (Vilsmeier-type activation). The alcohol attacks the activated anhydride to give the acetate ester and a molecule of acetic acid. Reaction is run in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen; DMF is used in catalytic (≈5 mol %) amount, no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidative dissolution of pyrite with concentrated sulfuric acid; a redox process where FeS₂ is oxidized to Fe²⁺ (forming FeSO₄) and sulfur is oxidized to SO₂ while the acid is reduced to water. Typically performed by heating solid pyrite in excess hot (≈90–100 °C) conc. H₂SO₄ in a glass apparatus; no solvent beyond the acid, and the reaction generates SO₂ gas which must be vented or captured.

Electrophilic chlorination (halogen transfer) using trichloroisocyanuric acid as a chlorine source to convert succinimide into N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS), while the cyanuric core is regenerated as cyanuric acid. Conducted in anhydrous organic solvents such as acetone, dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often under nitrogen; the TCICA reagent serves both as chlorine donor and solid support, no external catalyst required.

Acid–base (salt metathesis) reaction where solid copper(II) oxide reacts with ammonium chloride on heating to generate ammonia gas, water and copper(II) chloride; performed by gently heating the dry solid mixture (≈150–200 °C) in a test tube, no solvent required.

Oxidation (redox) of Au(I) to Au(III) by hydrogen peroxide; H₂O₂ oxidizes gold(I) bromide to gold(III) bromide while being reduced to water; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; no additional catalyst required; used to generate Au(III) halide for further synthesis.

Oxidative conversion of glyoxal to glyoxylic acid by concentrated nitric acid; nitric acid acts as both oxidant and acid, yielding nitrogen dioxide gas and water; performed in a sealed glass apparatus at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) to control NO₂ evolution.

Grignard addition to ester yielding aryl methyl ketone; methyl 4‑methylbenzoate reacts with one equivalent of methylmagnesium bromide in dry THF at low temperature (‑78 to 0 °C); the Grignard adds to the carbonyl, displaces the methoxy group and after acidic work‑up (HCl) gives 4‑methylacetophenone; purpose is formation of a benzylic ketone; conditions avoid excess Grignard to prevent over‑addition.

Base‑mediated oxidation of arsenic(III) oxide to arsenic(V) species; arsenic trioxide is dissolved in aqueous sodium hydroxide and exposed to oxygen (air) to form monosodium arsenate, with water as by‑product; the reaction proceeds at ambient temperature or with gentle heating, in aqueous alkaline medium.

Transesterification with methanol; purpose is to exchange the acyl group, forming methyl acetate and pentan-3-ol; methanol acts as nucleophile attacking the ester carbonyl, displacing the original alcohol; commonly catalyzed by an acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid, 1–5 mol %) or a base (e.g., NaOMe, 1 mol %) under reflux in excess methanol (typically 5–10 equiv) for 2–6 h.

Oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde using cerium(IV) sulfate as the oxidant; the reaction is carried out in aqueous acidic medium (often dilute sulfuric acid) at 0–25 °C, producing cerium(III) sulfate and water as the reduced species.

Hofmann‑type rearrangement of N‑methylpropanamide with bromine and potassium hydroxide, converting the amide to N‑methylethylamine with loss of carbon dioxide; performed in aqueous KOH at 0 °C to 20 °C, with Br₂ added dropwise, generating KBr as by‑product.

General type: Acid-base reaction. Purpose: Neutralization to produce hydrazoic acid. Key transformation: Sulfuric acid donates protons to convert azide into hydrazoic acid (HN3). Conditions: Dilute aqueous solution, room temperature. Solvent: Water. Catalyst: None.
Hydrolysis; chromyl fluoride rapidly reacts with water to form chromic acid and hydrogen fluoride, performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; HF evolves, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metath) of ammonium 2‑hydroxypropanoate with potassium hydroxide, producing ammonia, water and potassium 2‑hydroxypropanoate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Oxidation of 1,2‑dihydroxynaphthalene to 1,2‑naphthoquinone using ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN); a single‑electron oxidative dehydrogenation typically performed in a MeCN/H₂O mixture at room temperature, CAN acting as stoichiometric oxidant.

Acid‑base neutralization and salt formation; tartaric acid reacts with calcium carbonate in aqueous medium, usually with gentle heating, to give calcium tartrate, CO₂ (gas) and H₂O; proceeds via proton transfer, no catalyst needed.

Halogen exchange (oxidative fluorination). Fluorine gas oxidizes the bromide ligands of indium tribromide, substituting them with fluoride to give indium(III) fluoride and elemental bromine. Conducted in a fluorine‑compatible reactor, often at low to moderate temperature (0–100 °C) with careful control; usually gas‑phase, no solvent.

Anion exchange / acid‑base neutralization; purpose: generation of tetraethylammonium hydroxide; key transformation: replacement of perchlorate with hydroxide, yielding tetraethylammonium hydroxide and sodium perchlorate; typical conditions: aqueous solution, added NaOH solution at 0 °C to rt; common solvent: water.

Reductive hydrogenation; hydrogen gas reduces gold(III) oxide to elemental gold with formation of water; key step is hydrogen oxidation to H₂O while Au³⁺ is reduced to Au⁰; performed in a tube furnace or flow reactor under H₂ (or H₂/Ar) at 300‑500 °C; the reaction may be facilitated by a catalyst such as palladium or nickel if lower temperatures are desired, though pure Au₂O₃ can be reduced directly by H₂ at elevated temperature.
Base‑catalyzed alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of arecoline with aqueous NaOH, yielding methanol and arecaidine; reflux in water/ethanol for 1–2 h followed by acidification, no catalyst needed.
Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ether cleavage) of methyl propargyl ether with aqueous HCl, giving methanol and propargyl alcohol; heated under reflux in water, acid serves as the catalyst.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of 1‑bromo‑1‑propene with phenylboronic acid to form 1‑phenyl‑1‑propene; requires a Pd(0) catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄), a base such as K₂CO₃, and a THF/H₂O solvent system at 80–100 °C.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) of zinc pyrophosphate from ZnCl₂ and sodium pyrophosphate, producing NaCl as by‑product; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene oxide by the imidazole nitrogen (SN2‑type addition). Purpose: install a 2‑hydroxyethyl side chain on imidazole. Key transformation: N–C bond formation and generation of a primary alcohol. Typical conditions: imidazole (often deprotonated with a mild base such as NaH or K2CO3) in an aprotic polar solvent (DMF, MeCN, THF) at 0 °C to reflux; no metal catalyst required.

Redox (metal‑acid reduction) producing a metal hydride. In aqueous hydrochloric acid, zinc metal reduces antimony trichloride to stibine (SbH₃) while zinc is oxidized to zinc chloride.
