Friedel‑Crafts acylation of benzene with chloroacetyl chloride catalyzed by AlCl3; provides the aryl ketone chloroacetophenone by electrophilic aromatic substitution; key transformation is insertion of the –CO‑CH2Cl acyl group onto the benzene ring with loss of HCl; carried out in a dry, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, CS2 or nitrobenzene at 0–50 °C under anhydrous conditions; AlCl3 acts as the Lewis‑acid catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide with azide ion; yields ethyl azide, a useful precursor for click chemistry, and NaBr as by‑product; reaction proceeds in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO, or acetone) at 0 °C to reflux to favor backside attack; no catalyst is required.

Formation of a polyiodide salt; CsI reacts with elemental iodine to give caesium triiide (CsI₃). This is a halide‑complexation equilibrium where I⁻ adds to I₂ to form I₃⁻. Typically performed in polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or ethanol at ambient temperature; no catalyst required. Useful for preparing polyiodide reagents and studying halogen bonding.

Oxidative dehydrogenation (aromatization) of a flavanone using DDQ as a quinone oxidant; converts 4′‑methoxy‑5,7‑dihydroxyflavanone to the flavone acacetin while DDQ is reduced to hydroquinone; typically run in anhydrous aromatic solvent such as benzene or toluene under reflux or at elevated temperature; DDQ serves both as oxidant and stoichiometric reagent, no metal catalyst is needed.

Catalytic transfer hydrogenation (reduction) of the nitro group in o‑nitroacetanilide to an amine using formic acid as the hydrogen donor and Pd on carbon as the heterogeneous catalyst; produces o‑aminoacetanilide and water; reaction is carried out in a mixed aqueous/organic solvent (e.g., ethanol‑water) at 25–80 °C under an inert atmosphere; Pd/C is the catalyst, and formic acid supplies the required reducing equivalents.

Oxidative coordination (redox‑complexation) of cobalt(II) nitrate in aqueous ammonia, where hydrogen peroxide and chlorine gas oxidize Co(II) to Co(III) and allow ammonia ligands to bind, forming chloropentaamminecobalt(III) chloride; ammonium nitrate is generated as a by‑product; performed in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature, with controlled addition of H2O2 and Cl2 to manage oxidation; no additional catalyst beyond the cobalt salt itself.
Acid‑base neutralization; aqueous HF is neutralized by NaOH to afford soluble NaF and water. Reaction proceeds readily at 20–25 °C in water; stoichiometric amounts are mixed, no catalyst needed.

Metal‑acid reduction; zinc dust reduces dimethylarsinic acid in aqueous HCl to dimethylarsine while being oxidized to ZnCl₂; aqueous medium, excess HCl, reflux or gentle heating; purpose is preparation of the organoarsine gas.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of an ester; LiAlH₄ cleaves the acetate ester (acetyl benzoate) to give the corresponding primary alcohols, benzyl alcohol from the aromatic side and ethanol from the acetyl side; performed in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to reflux, then work‑up with aqueous acid.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); potassium hydroxide deprotonates clavulanic acid yielding water and the potassium salt, potassium clavulanate; performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; used to obtain a more soluble or stable salt form of the β‑lactamase inhibitor.

Oxidation of 1,10‑phenanthroline to 1,10‑phenanthroline‑5,6‑dione using in‑situ generated peracetic acid (acetic acid + H₂O₂); reaction proceeds at 0‑25 °C then warms to room temperature; solvent is glacial acetic acid (often with a small amount of water); no external catalyst required; purpose is introduction of carbonyl groups at the 5,6‑positions.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (aqueous hydrolysis) of hexyl butyrate to give butyric acid and 1‑hexanol; typically carried out in water with a mineral acid (e.g., HCl or H₂SO₄) under reflux; purpose is cleavage of the ester into its component acid and alcohol.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; sodium carbonate exchanges cations with silver selenite, forming soluble sodium selenite and insoluble silver carbonate which precipitates; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; used to isolate or remove silver ions.

Halogen‑exchange redox reaction; fluorine gas oxidatively fluorinated nitrosyl chloride, producing nitrosyl fluoride and chlorine monofluoride; conducted in the gas phase, often at low temperature in a fluorination apparatus under inert atmosphere; purpose is conversion of NOCl to the more reactive fluorinated species.

Metallothermic reduction (aluminothermic). Aluminum reduces ruthenium(III) chloride to elemental ruthenium while being oxidized to aluminum chloride. Typically carried out at high temperature (700–1000 °C) in the solid state under an inert atmosphere; no solvent is used.

Salt metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation; AgPF₆ exchanges its anion with cyanide from NaCN, forming insoluble AgCN (precipitate) and soluble NaPF₆. Conducted in aqueous solution or polar aprotic solvent (e.g., water or MeCN) at ambient temperature, with stirring and subsequent filtration to isolate AgCN.

Free‑radical benzylic chlorination. Chlorine abstracts a hydrogen atom from the benzylic position of ethylbenzene, forming a benzylic radical that recombines with chlorine to give 1‑chloro‑1‑phenylethane. Conducted under UV light or heat, often in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or in the gas phase; no catalyst required.

Dehydrative halogenation of a tertiary alcohol with phosphorus pentachloride. PCl₅ converts 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol into the corresponding tertiary chloride (2‑chloro‑2‑methylbutane) while generating phosphorus oxychloride as a by‑product. Usually performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature, then warmed to reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑base metathesis (double displacement). Sulfuric acid protonates the phosphate anion of copper(II) phosphate (tricopper diphosphate), releasing phosphoric acid and forming copper(II) sulfate in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution; no special catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (phenolic O‑methylation). Methyl iodide alkylates the two phenolic hydroxyl groups of 6,7‑dihydroxy‑2H‑1‑benzopyran‑2‑one in the presence of potassium carbonate, producing 6,7‑dimethoxy‑2H‑1‑benzopyran‑2‑one and potassium iodide. Typically run in dry acetone or DMF under reflux; the carbonate acts as the base, no additional catalyst is needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement/decomposition reaction; sulfurous acid (H2SO3) reacts with silver carbonate (Ag2CO3) in water, yielding silver sulfite (Ag2SO3) as a precipitate and carbonic acid (H2CO3), which promptly decomposes to CO2 and H2O; typical conditions are ambient temperature in aqueous solution.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene to an alkane; prop‑1‑en‑2‑ylbenzene (α‑methylstyrene) is hydrogenated to isopropylbenzene (cumene) using H₂ gas and a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni. Reaction is performed in a solvent like ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate at 1–5 atm H₂ and 20–60 °C; the catalyst enables selective reduction of the C=C bond.

Metathesis / acid‑base exchange (strong‑acid displacement). Potassium methanesulfonate is treated with sulfuric acid (often concentrated) to give methanesulfonic acid and potassium hydrogen sulfate (KHSO₄). Reaction is done in aqueous or mixed solvent at low to moderate temperature; excess H₂SO₄ drives the equilibrium. No catalyst required.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution/halogenation of a polyol (HCl‑induced chlorination). Purpose: Introduce chloro substituents on glycerol to give a mono‑inated diol. Key transformation: Two of the three hydroxyl groups of glycerol are replaced by chloride, forming 1,3‑dichloro‑2‑propanol and water. Typical conditions: excess conc. HCl (≈12 M) heated under reflux for 1–3 h; sometimes ZnCl₂ or a Lewis acid is added to accelerate substitution. Common solvent: aqueous HCl (no additional solvent needed).

Oxidative conversion of a primary bromomethyl group to a carboxylic acid; a strong oxidation (KMnO₄) of 1-(bromomethyl)naphthalene to 1‑naphthoic acid. Conditions: aqueous KMnO₄ (0.5–1 M) under alkaline pH (NaOH) and reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours; water is the solvent, solid MnO₂ precipitates as by‑product.

Acid‑chloride formation using oxalyl chloride. Bromoacetic acid is converted to bromoacetyl chloride, with evolution of CO, CO₂ and HCl as gaseous by‑products. The reaction is carried out in an inert, dry organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to ambient temperature under nitrogen, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to accelerate the conversion.

Oxidative phenol coupling (radical dimerisation). Sodium persulfate acts as a one‑electron oxidant, generating phenoxy radicals that couple at the para positions to give 4,4′‑biphenol. The reaction proceeds in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media (often Na₂S₂O₈ in alkaline solution or with NaOH) at 60–80 °C; sodium sulfate is formed as the inorganic by‑product.

Acidic redox oxidation of chloride by permanganate. In concentrated HCl, KMnO₄ oxidises chloride ions to chlorine gas while being reduced from Mn(VII) to Mn(II). The stoichiometric reaction produces water, potassium chloride, manganese(II) chloride and chlorine. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at elevated temperature with vigorous stirring; the mixture is acidic and generates gaseous Cl₂.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation; forms magnesium carbonate from the chloride and sodium carbonate. Key transformation: MgCl₂·6H₂O + Na₂CO₃ → MgCO₃↓ + 2 NaCl + 6 H₂O. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with vigorous mixing; solid MgCO₃ is filtered. No catalyst required.

General type: deprotonation of a terminal alkyne (acid‑base reaction) using a strong organolithium base. Purpose: generation of lithium phenylacetylide for subsequent C‑C bond‑forming steps; tert‑butane is formed as a volatile byproduct. Key transformation: t‑BuLi abstracts the acidic proton of phenylacetylene, yielding lithium phenylacetylide and tert‑butane (t‑BuLi + Ph‑C≡CH → LiC≡C‑Ph + t‑BuH). Typical conditions: dry THF or diethyl ether, low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C), inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst; reaction relies on the basicity of t‑BuLi.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde with Dess‑Martin periodinane. Tridecan‑1‑ol is converted to tridecanal; the hypervalent iodine reagent is reduced to iodobenzene and acetic acid as side products. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane under inert atmosphere, usually in the dark to avoid decomposition.

Redox neutral acid‑base reaction between sulfite and bromate in strong acid. In the presence of sulfuric acid, sodium sulfite reduces bromate to bromide while being oxidised to sulfate; both sodium and potassium ions end up as their respective sulfates (Na₂SO₄, K₂SO₄) and KBr is formed. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; the mixture is acidic and the reaction proceeds without gas evolution.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction in aqueous solution; potassium iodide exchanges anions with antimony(III) nitrate to form soluble potassium and insoluble antimony triiodide precipitate; carried out at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Double displacement precipitation in water; potassium hydroxide neutralizes neodymium(III) chloride producing soluble potassium chloride and insoluble neodymium(III) hydroxide precipitate; performed at ambient temperature; no catalyst.

Basic hydrolysis/precipitation in aqueous alkaline medium; sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes ammonium hexafluorotitanate yielding titanium dioxide solid, sodium fluoride, ammonium fluoride and water; mild heating often applied to drive hydrolysis; no catalyst.

Reaction type: metal‑acid reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an aniline (iron/HCl reduction). Purpose: convert 1‑methoxy‑4‑nitrobenzene to 4‑methoxyaniline. Key transformation: Fe metal donates electrons to the nitro group in the presence of HCl, reducing –NO2 to –NH2; the methoxy group remains unchanged. Typical conditions: excess iron filings (≈5 equiv) in aqueous HCl (3‑6 M) heated to reflux for several hours; after cooling, the mixture is filtered, basified, and the product extracted. Common solvent: water (aqueous); catalyst/reagent: iron metal, concentrated HCl.

Reaction type: Acyl chloride esterification (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Purpose: Form octyl acetate efficiently using a more reactive acyl donor. Key transformation: Octanol attacks acetyl chloride, displacing chloride to give the ester and HCl. Typical conditions: Performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize HCl; reaction completes within minutes to an hour.

Thermal decomposition of solid holmium(III) nitrate upon strong heating (≈400‑600 °C); decomposes to holmium(III) oxide solid, nitrogen dioxide gas and oxygen gas; performed in a dry furnace; no solvent or catalyst.

Hydride reduction of an alkyl halide; iodomethane is reduced by lithium aluminum hydride in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, giving methane, lithium iodide and, after work‑up, aluminum hydroxide; reaction run from 0 °C to reflux; LiAlH4 is the reagent, no additional catalyst.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2) in aprotic solvent; phenol is deprotonated (e.g., with NaOH or K2CO3) to phenoxide which attacks 1‑iodo‑2‑methoxyethane, forming 2‑methoxyethyl phenyl ether and hydrogen iodide (or its salt); typically performed in acetone or DMF under reflux; no metal catalyst needed.

Esterification with diazomethane; converts the carboxylic acid into its methyl ester (methyl 3‑hydroxybenzoate) while releasing nitrogen gas; key step is nucleophilic attack of diazomethane on the carbonyl followed by loss of N₂; carried out at 0 °C to rt in dry diethyl ether or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

High‑temperature solid‑state double decomposition where barium carbonate reacts with tungsten trioxide to give barium tungstate (BaWO4) and carbon dioxide. Conducted by thoroughly mixing the powders and heating in a furnace at 800–1000 °C for several hours; atmosphere can be air or inert gas; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization; lithium hydroxide neutralizes arsenic acid to afford lithium arsenate. Key transformation: replacement of acidic protons by lithium ions forming the salt and water. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation of neodymium(III) chloride with sodium hydroxide; purpose is isolation of neodymium(III) hydroxide; key transformation is NdCl₃ + 3 NaOH → Nd(OH)₃(s) + 3 NaCl; usually carried out by mixing aqueous solutions of NdCl₃ and NaOH at room temperature with vigorous stirring, adjusting pH to about 10; water is the reaction medium and the solid hydroxide is filtered and washed.

High‑temperature chlorination/reduction of titanium dioxide; H₂ and Cl₂ react with TiO₂ to generate titanium tetrachloride and water. Type: redox/halogenation. Key transformation: conversion of the oxide lattice to a volatile chloride while oxygen is reduced to water. Conducted in a sealed reactor at 400–600 °C (often higher, up to 900 °C) under a flow of chlorine/H₂ gases; inert carrier gas may be used; no catalyst needed; gas‑phase conditions.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of methylamine with acetic anhydride; the amine attacks the anhydride carbonyl, displacing acetate to afford N‑methylacetamide and acetic acid as by‑product. Usually performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to rt, often with a base such as triethylamine to neutralize the generated acetic acid. Purpose: preparation of a simple amide.

Nucleophilic substitution of sulfuryl chloride by a methyl organolithium reagent; methyllium attacks the sulfur centre, displacing chloride to give methylsulfonyl chloride and lithium chloride. Type: organolithium addition to a sulfonyl chloride. Performed at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in dry ether or THF under nitrogen or argon; the reaction mixture is quenched with aqueous work‑up. No additional catalyst.

Acid dissolution/metathesis of thorium silicate with nitric acid; the silicate is broken down, yielding thorium nitrate and silicic acid while water is released. Type: acid‑salt metathesis. Conducted by refluxing ThSiO₄ in concentrated HNO₃ (typically 4 eq.) in water; temperature 80–120 °C for several hours. No catalyst; aqueous medium.

Type: SN2 O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis). Purpose: Convert phenolic OH groups of resorcinol to methoxy groups, forming 1,3‑dimethoxybenzene. Key transformation: Two phenolic hydrogens are displaced by methyl groups from methyl iodide, generating potassium iodide as by‑product. Typical conditions: Anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, or DMSO), potassium carbonate as base, reflux under inert atmosphere; reaction proceeds at 50–80 °C for several hours.

Type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: Exchange anions to isolate insoluble silver sulfate and generate soluble thallium nitrate. Key transformation: Silver(I) cations pair with sulfate anions forming precipitated Ag₂SO₄, while thallium(I) cations pair with nitrate to give TlNO₃ in solution. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring; the mixture is filtered to remove the Ag₂SO₄ solid.

Salt metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction; exchange of K⁺ and Ca²⁺ ions between potassium acrylate and calcium chloride to produce calcium acrylate and potassium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; no special catalyst required.

Direct acid‑catalyzed substitution of a primary alcohol with hydrogen bromide; produces bromomethane and water. Concentrated aqueous or gaseous HBr protonates methanol, followed by SN2 attack of bromide. Reaction is run at reflux or 30–80 °C in aqueous HBr (the alcohol can act as solvent) and requires no catalyst.

Formation of a sulfonate ester (mesylation); the primary alcohol of ethylene glycol monoethyl ether reacts with methanesulfonyl chloride to afford 2‑ethoxyethyl methanesulfonate and HCl. Performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, in the presence of a base (triethylamine, pyridine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Type: Electrophilic aromatic nitration (mixed‑acid nitration). Purpose: Introduce a nitro substituent onto the aromatic ring of 2‑methylnaphthalene to afford 1‑nitro‑2‑methylnaphthalene. Key transformation: Generation of the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) from HNO₃/H₂SO₄, which attacks the aromatic ring preferentially at the position ortho to the methyl group. Typical conditions: Concentrated H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ (≈95 % and 70 %), temperature controlled at 0–5 °C initially, then allowed to rise to 30–40 °C; reaction performed in glassware resistant to acid, often with the substrate dissolved in glacial acetic acid or carbon disulfide.

Type: Pinnick oxidation (oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid using NaClO₂). Purpose: Oxidize 3‑chlorobenzaldehyde to 3‑chlorobenzoic acid while scavenging chlorine dioxide. Key transformation: Sodium chlorite oxidizes the aldehyde carbonyl to a carboxylic acid; 2‑methyl‑2‑butene acts as a chlorine‑dioxide trap, preventing side reactions. Typical conditions: Aqueous phosphate buffer (NaH₂PO₄/Na₂HPO₄) at pH ≈ 3.5–5, NaClO₂ added portionwise at 0–25 °C, often with a co‑solvent such as tert‑butanol or dioxane; reaction completed within 1–2 h, then acidified to isolate the acid.

Type: Acid‑catalyzed skeletal isomerization (hydroisomerization) of a straight‑chain alkane. Purpose: Rearrange n‑heptane to the more branched, higher‑octane‑number isomer 2,2,3‑trimethylbutane. Key transformation: Intramolecular hydride shifts and carbocation rearrangements under acidic sites, converting a linear C₇ chain into a highly branched C₇ skeleton. Typical conditions: High‑pressure hydrogen (≈30–60 bar), solid acid catalyst (e.g., Pt‑Zeolite, H‑ZSM‑5) at 150–250 °C; liquid‑phase or vapor‑phase flow reactors are employed.

Hydrolysis of diglycolic anhydride; purpose: convert anhydride to diglycolic acid; key transformation: ring opening of anhydride by water to give di‑carboxylic acid; typical conditions: aqueous medium, mild heating (room °C to 80 °C), optionally acid or base catalyst; solvent water.

Acid‑carbonate reaction (neutralization/precipitation); sulfuric acid protonates strontium carbonate, liberating carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O) and forming insoluble strontium sulfate precipitate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Knoevenagel condensation/decarboxylation; benzaldehyde condenses with malonic acid in the presence of a base (e.g., piperidine or pyridine) to give an α,β‑unsaturated intermediate that decarboxylates, yielding cinnamic acid plus CO₂ and H₂O. Typically performed in ethanol or methanol under reflux; catalytic base and sometimes a mild acid additive are used.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous Fe³⁺ ions exchange anions with Ag⁺ ions, producing insoluble silver chloride precipitate and soluble iron(III) nitrate. Carried out in water at room temperature; no special catalyst needed.

Oxidation (aldehyde to carboxylic acid); potassium permanganate oxidizes 2‑methoxybenzaldehyde to 2‑methoxybenzoic acid; performed in aqueous alkaline KMnO₄ solution (often warm) followed by acidification to isolate the acid.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) hydrolysis; hydroxide attacks the electron‑deficient 1,3,5‑trichlorobenzene, displacing three chloride ions to afford phloroglucinol and three NaCl salts. Requires concentrated NaOH, elevated temperature (150–200 °C) in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol medium; pressure vessel may be used, no additional catalyst.

Fischer esterification; 3,4‑dihydroxybenzoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid, forming ethyl 3,4‑dihydroxybenzoate and water. Conducted under reflux in excess ethanol; acid catalyst drives equilibrium, and water removal (e.g., Dean–Stark) improves yield.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation; anisole undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution with 2‑hydroxybenzoyl chloride in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst (commonly AlCl₃), forming 2‑hydroxy‑4‑methoxybenzophenone and releasing HCl. Reaction is performed in anhydrous non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon disulfide at 0 °C to room temperature; AlCl₃ (or similar) is essential catalyst.

Metathesis precipitation; thulium triiodide reacts with aqueous ammonium hydroxide, yielding a precipitate of thulium hydroxide while ammonium iodide remains in solution; performed in water, usually at modest temperature; no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of hafnium tetrachloride; precipitation of hafnium dioxide with concomitant formation of hydrochloric acid; aqueous solution of HfCl₄ added to excess water, often refluxed with vigorous stirring; temperature 80‑120 °C; no catalyst, water is the solvent and acid is generated in situ.

Halide metathesis (solid‑state double displacement); used to prepare gallium(III) fluoride from readily available gallium trichloride and sodium fluoride. Key transformation: exchange of Cl⁻ for F⁻ yielding NaCl precipitate and GaF₃. Typically performed by grinding anhydrous NaF and GaCl₃ together and heating at 200–300 °C under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); can be done neat or in a high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF) if a melt is desired.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis) of silver metal with elemental selenium to form silver selenide (Ag2Se). Typically carried out by heating the solid reactants together at 200‑400 °C in an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) in a sealed tube; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Esterification (acetylation) of a primary alcohol with acetic anhydride; purpose is synthesis of isobutyl acetate (a flavor/fragrance ester). Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on the carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming the acetate ester and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Common conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base catalyst such as pyridine or a catalytic amount of DMAP to scavenge the generated acid. Reaction can be run neat (excess acetic anhydride) or in dichloromethane/methyl‑tert‑butyl ether as solvent.

Redox (hydrazine reduces Cu(II) to Cu⁰ in basic medium); hydrazine is oxidized to nitrogen, copper(II) sulfate is reduced to metallic copper, sodium hydroxide maintains alkalinity and precipitates Cu as a solid, and sodium sulfate is formed from the anion exchange. Purpose: preparation of finely divided copper metal; classic demonstration of hydrazine as a reducing agent. Key transformation: N₂H₄ → N₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻; Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu⁰. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, NaOH (1–2 M) added to keep pH >10, mixture stirred at room temperature or slightly warmed (25‑40 °C); CuSO₄ added dropwise to avoid vigorous gas evolution. No organic solvent needed.

SN1 aqueous hydrolysis of a tertiary alkyl chloride; purpose is to convert the halide into the corresponding alcohol while generating HCl; key transformation is cleavage of the C–Cl bond and addition of OH from water to give 1‑methylcyclohexanol; typically performed with excess water under reflux or gentle heating, sometimes with a mild acid catalyst, solvent is water or water/acetone mixture.

Acid‑base reaction generating nitrous acid in situ; employed as a source of HNO₂ for subsequent nitrosation or diazotization steps. Key transformation: proton transfer from HCl to the nitrite ion, producing HNO₂ and RbCl. Performed in aqueous solution at 0–5 °C to minimize decomposition of HNO₂; dilute acid (≈0.1 M) and rubidium nitrite are mixed, often under stirring and inert gas to avoid oxidation.

Cyclocondensation (dehydrative cyclization) of thiosemicarbazide with formic acid to afford 1,3,4‑thiadiazol‑2‑amine. The reaction involves nucleophilic attack of the thiosemicarbazide terminal –NH₂ on the carbonyl of formic acid, followed by intramolecular cyclization and loss of two molecules of water. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or methanol (or a water/ethanol mixture) for 2–6 h, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acetic acid to promote condensation. Reaction is conducted under nitrogen to avoid oxidation.

Reductive amination of piperazine with 4‑chlorobenzaldehyde using sodium cyanoborohydride; provides 1‑(4‑chlorophenyl)piperazine, a key intermediate for pharmaceuticals. Key steps: formation of an iminium ion between the secondary amine of piperazine and the aldehyde, followed by selective reduction with NaBH₃CN. Conducted in methanol or ethanol with a mild acid (e.g., acetic acid, pH ≈ 5) at 0 °C to room temperature, stirring for several hours; NaBH₃CN is added portionwise to control gas evolution (HCN).

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of N,N‑dimethylurea to dimethylamine and isocyanic acid. This is a single‑molecule cleavage where the C–N bond adjacent to the carbonyl breaks, generating volatile dimethylamine and isocyanic acid gases. Performed by heating the solid or melt of N,N‑dimethylurea at 150–250 °C under reduced pressure or in a flow of inert gas (N₂). No solvent or catalyst is required; the reaction is driven by temperature.

Type: Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 O‑alkylation). Purpose: convert the phenolic OH of 3‑methoxyphenol into a second methoxy group to afford 1,3‑dimethoxybenzene. Key transformation: K₂CO₃ deprotonates the phenol to give a phenoxide, which attacks methyl iodide in an SN2 step, forming an OCH₃ bond and releasing I⁻. Typical conditions: reflux in a polartic solvent such as acetone or DMF, solid K₂CO₃ as base, reaction time 2–12 h.

Partial reduction of an ester using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H); purpose is to stop at the aldehyde stage. One equivalent of DIBAL‑H adds a hydride to the carbonyl of methyl 4‑chlorobenzoate at low temperature (‑78 °C to ‑20 °C) in a dry solvent such as toluene or THF, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide that, upon work‑up with methanol or aqueous acid, gives 4‑chlorobenzaldehyde and methanol. The reaction is performed under inert atmosphere.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; purpose is to prepare the nitrate salt of tetrabutylammonium. Silver nitrate precipitates bromide as AgBr, leaving tetrabutylammonium nitrate in solution: TBA⁺Br⁻ + Ag⁺NO₃⁻ → TBA⁺NO₃⁻ + AgBr(s). Conducted in aqueous (or water/acetone) solution, kept in the dark to avoid photodecomposition, at room temperature; the AgBr solid is filtered off. No catalyst required.

Type: Halogen exchange (nucleophilic substitution of Cl by F). Purpose: replace the chlorine atom in 1,1‑difluoro‑2‑chloroethane with fluorine to generate 1,1,2‑trifluoroethane. Key transformation: fluoride from HF attacks the carbon bearing Cl, displacing Cl⁻ and forming a new C‑F bond while HCl is liberated. Typical conditions: liquid HF or HF‑pyridine (Olah’s reagent) often with a Lewisacid catalyst such as SbF₅ or AlF₃, temperature 50–150 °C.

Type: Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Purpose: oxidize furfuryl alcohol to 2‑furoic acid. Key transformation: oxygen (O₂) or a stoichiometric oxidant converts the –CH₂OH group first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid, producing water as a by‑product. Typical conditions: catalytic aerobic oxidation using a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, Cu‑TEMPO) in aqueous or alcoholic solvent at 80–120 °C; alternatively, stoichiometric oxidants such as KMnO₄ in alkaline medium.

Type: Jones oxidation (Cr(VI) oxidation of aldehyde to acid). Purpose: oxidize 2‑(2‑hydroxyethoxy)acetaldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid. Key transformation: CrO₃/H₂SO₄ in acetone converts the aldehyde carbonyl to a carboxyl group while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III). Typical conditions: freshly prepared Jones reagent added dropwise to a solution of the substrate in dry acetone at 0 °C, then stirred at room temperature for 1–2 h; work‑up with water and dilute acid.

Metal displacement (single‑replacement) with hydrogen evolution; analogous to reaction 2, producing potassium selenide. Potassium metal reacts with H2Se, liberating H2 and forming K2Se. Conducted in dry, aprotic solvents (liquid ammonia, THF, or ether) under inert gas, often at 0 °C to −20 °C; no catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition; barium peroxide is heated, breaking the O–O peroxide bond to yield barium oxide solid and release molecular oxygen gas. Typical conditions: direct heating to 400‑500 °C in a furnace; no solvent or catalyst required.

Type: Acid‑metal reaction (metal dissolution in acetic acid). Purpose: produce scandium(III) acetate and hydrogen gas from elemental scandium. Key transformation: Sc metal is oxidized to Sc³⁺, while protons from acetic acid are reduced to H₂. Typical conditions: excess glacial acetic acid, reflux (≈80–100 °C) under inert atmosphere; stirring is required as the reaction proceeds slowly.

Type: Reduction of aldehyde to primary alcohol (LiAlH₄ reduction). Purpose: convert the bicyclic aldehyde myrtenal into the corresponding alcohol myrtenol. Key transformation: hydride transfer from LiAlH₄ to the carbonyl carbon forms an alkoxide, which is subsequently protonated to give the –CH₂OH group. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether), addition of LiAlH₄ at 0 °C under nitrogen, then stirring at room temperature or gentle reflux for 1–3 h, followed by careful quench with water or dilute acid.

Double displacement (metathesis/precipitation) reaction; performed in water, typically at room temperature or with gentle warming. Iron(II) bromide reacts with sodium carbonate, yielding insoluble iron(II) carbonate and soluble sodium bromide: FeBr2 + Na2CO3 → FeCO3(s) + 2 NaBr. No catalyst; stirring promotes complete ion exchange.

Reaction type: nitrosylation/alkyl nitrite formation. Purpose: convert a tertiary alcohol into the corresponding alkyl nitrite. Key transformation: tert‑butanol O‑H is replaced by a nitroso group from nitrosyl chloride, yielding tert‑butyl nitrite and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous solvent (e.g., dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; a base such as pyridine or triethylamine is often added to trap the generated HCl.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange cations and precipitate the insoluble calcium sulfate while forming soluble sodium acetate; key transformation is Ca²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → CaSO₄(s) and Na⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ → NaCH₃COO(aq); typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Acid–base displacement reaction; concentrated sulfuric acid protonates nitrate ion of potassium nitrate, liberating nitric acid, which is distilled off, leaving potassium bisulfate in the reaction mixture. Typically carried out by adding solid KNO₃ to 95–98 % H₂SO₄ and gently heating under reflux; apparatus for distillation required; no solvent other than the acid.

Acid‑base hydrolysis (neutralization) of boron trichloride with sodium hydroxide; yields boric acid and sodium chloride. The reaction consumes three equivalents of NaOH per BCl3, converting BCl3 to H3BO3 while neutralizing the released HCl. Conducted in aqueous solution, usually at 0‑25 °C to control the exotherm; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Reaction type: acid‑base precipitation (salt metathesis). Purpose: generate tungstic acid from ammonium tungstate and isolate it as a solid. Key transformation: the tungstate anion is protonated by sulfuric acid to give H2WO4 (tungstic acid) while ammonium ions combine with sulfate to form NH4)2SO4. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, addition of concentrated H2SO4 to a cooled solution of ammonium tungstate, stirring at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; the tungstic acid precipitates and is filtered.

Williamson ether synthesis; sodium ethoxide (NaOEt) in dry ethanol or THF reacts with 1‑bromopentane via SN2 to afford ethyl pentyl ether and NaBr; the mixture is heated under anhydrous conditions, often under nitrogen.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis: ethyl but‑2‑ynoate is hydrolyzed by aqueous HCl to produce but‑2‑ynoic acid and ethanol; the mixture is refluxed in aqueous acid (sometimes in a water/ethanol co‑solvent) until complete conversion, then the product is isolated after neutralization.

Reaction type: copper‑catalyzed oxidative bromination of arylboronic acids (Chan‑Lam‑type coupling). Purpose: replace the boronic acid group with a bromine atom to afford an aryl bromide. Key transformation: 4‑methoxyphenyl‑B(OH)2 is converted to 4‑bromo‑1‑methoxybenzene, with boric acid as the stoichiometric by‑product. Typical conditions: CuBr2 (10–20 mol %) as catalyst, pyridine (acts as ligand and solvent), O2 atmosphere as oxidant, often in MeCN or DMF, temperature 40–80 °C under stirring.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (water cleavage of an ester). Purpose: convert an ethyl ester into the corresponding carboxylic acid and ethanol. Key transformation: the carbonyl carbon of ethyl valerate is attacked by water, leading to cleavage of the C–OEt bond and formation of valeric acid and ethanol. Typical conditions: aqueous acid (e.g., 1–2 M H2SO4) or reflux in water; heat (80–100 °C) for several hours; sometimes a small amount of catalyst (HCl, H2SO4) is used to accelerate the reaction.

Hydrolysis of a secondary amide to the corresponding α‑amino acid. 2‑(Methylamino)acetamide is treated with water (often heated and acid or base catalyzed) leading to cleavage of the terminal amide bond. The product is N‑methylglycine (sarcosine) and liberated ammonia. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl or NaOH, reflux for several hours, followed by neutralisation to isolate the amino acid.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) with acetate anion. Purpose: synthesize the acetate ester of a benzylic chloride. Key transformation: acetate ion displaces chloride on 4‑methoxybenzyl chloride, yielding 4‑methoxybenzyl acetate and NaCl. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, sodium acetate (1–2 equiv), reflux temperature (≈50–80 °C) for several hours; the reaction is often performed in a sealed tube to avoid moisture.

Acid‑base neutralization of antimony(V) oxide; antimony pentoxide reacts with sodium hydroxide to produce sodium antimonate and water. Type: oxide‑base salt formation. Conducted in aqueous NaOH solution, often heated gently (50–80 °C) to dissolve the antimony oxide fully. No catalyst; water serves as solvent.

Oxidation reaction. Converts a sulfoxide to a sulfone using sulfur trioxide as a strong oxidizing agent. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions, often in inert solvents like dichloromethane at moderate temperatures.

Transferase (methylation) reaction. Involved in natural product biosynthesis, transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to isoliquiritigenin to form cardamonin. Requires enzymatic catalysis (e.g., O-methyltransferase) under physiological conditions (aqueous buffer, ~pH 7-8, 37°C).

Redox reaction. Dissolves cerium metal in methanesulfonic acid, producing hydrogen gas and cerium(III) methanesulfonate. Driven by cerium's high reactivity; conducted at elevated temperatures (reflux) with excess acid.

Acid–base double displacement (neutralization) of aluminum phosphate with aqueous NaOH, forming soluble sodium aluminate and sodium phosphate; performed in water, usually heated (e.g., 80–100 °C) to drive reaction to completion.

Acid-base/condensation reaction. Forms zirconium phosphate from phosphoric acid and zirconium tetrachloride, releasing hydrogen chloride. Typically requires high-temperature hydrothermal or solvothermal conditions to drive HCl evolution.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an amide; purpose is to cleave N‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)acetamide to give 2‑aminoethanol (ethanolamine) and sodium acetate; NaOH deprotonates water, generating OH⁻ which attacks the amide carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses, releasing acetate anion and the free amine; usually performed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) with heating (80–100 °C) for 1–2 h; solvent is water.

Halogen-exchange reaction. Produces chlorodifluorophosphorus oxide by reacting POCl3 with HF. Requires anhydrous conditions, often performed neat or in non-nucleophilic solvents (e.g., CCl4) at elevated temperatures.
Redox/displacement reaction. Bromine oxidizes iodide in ammonium iodide to form iodine and ammonium bromide. Proceeds spontaneously in aqueous solution at room temperature without catalysts.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis – converts bromochloroacetonitrile to bromochloroacetic acid while protonating the liberated ammonia to ammonium chloride; typically performed by refluxing the nitrile in aqueous hydrochloric acid (excess HCl, 1 M) for several hours; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Metal‑acid displacement (salt formation) – sodium metal reacts with monochloroacetic acid to generate sodium chloroacetate and hydrogen gas; carried out under inert atmosphere in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to control rapid H2 evolution; the reaction is a straightforward acid‑base neutralization with a reactive metal.

LiAlH4 reduction of a carboxylic acid – lithium aluminium hydride reduces palmitic (hexadecanoic) acid to hexadecanol (palmityl alcohol); usually performed in anhydrous diethyl ether or THF at 0 °C then refluxed, followed by careful quench with water or dilute acid; purpose is to obtain the fatty primary alcohol from the corresponding acid.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acyl chloride using thionyl chloride; purpose is activation of the acid for further acylation reactions. Key transformation is formation of a chlorosulfite intermediate that collapses to release SO₂ and HCl gases, yielding 2‑nitroacetyl chloride. Typical conditions: add SOCl₂ dropwise to a solution of 2‑nitroacetic acid in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or CHCl₃, reflux gently (40–60 °C) for 1–2 h; gaseous by‑products are vented.

Acid‑base neutralization to a metal lactate – magnesium oxide neutralizes lactic acid to form magnesium lactate and water; commonly executed by heating a mixture of the solid acid and MgO in a sealed vessel or by dissolving lactic acid in water and adding MgO with gentle warming; no special catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrocracking) of a straight‑chain alkane – octane undergoes C–C bond cleavage in the presence of hydrogen over a metal catalyst (e.g., Pt, Ni, or bifunctional zeolite‑metal system) at elevated temperature (300–450 °C) and pressure (30–80 atm) to yield n‑heptane and methane; the reaction is used for selective shortening of hydrocarbon chains.

Halide exchange/metathesis to prepare a metal chalcogenide – hydrogen telluride reacts with gallium chloride at elevated temperature (typically 150–300 °C) in an inert atmosphere (often in sealed quartz tube) to produce gallium telluride and hydrogen chloride gas; the process is a solid‑state or gas‑phase synthesis of the binary gallium‑tellurium semiconductor material.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (glich esterification) of p‑aminobenzoic acid with 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol to give Risocaine; DCC activates the carboxyl group, DMAP catalyzes acyl transfer, and dicyclohexylurea precipitates; usually performed in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature.

Cross‑Aldol condensation between benzaldehyde and hexanal followed by dehydration to afford α‑hexylcinnamaldehyde (an α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde) with loss of water; carried out with a base such as NaOH or KOH in ethanol or aqueous ethanol at 0–25 °C, then warmed to promote dehydration.
Halide metathesis reaction. Purpose: Synthesis of cyanuric fluoride. Reaction conditions: Typically conducted under elevated temperature, sometimes solventless. No catalyst required.

Lucas substitution (SN1) of cyclohexanol to cyclohexyl chloride using concentrated HCl and ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent); reaction proceeds at room temperature or with gentle heating, typically in aqueous HCl or a HCl/acetone mixture; water is generated.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); purpose is to obtain the stable hydrochloride salt of guanidine. Guanidine reacts with hydrogen chloride (gas or aqueous HCl) to give guanidine·HCl. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the salt precipitates upon cooling or evaporation of solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification of perindoprilat with ethanol to produce perindopril (ethyl ester) and water; catalytic mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) in refluxing ethanol, with water removed (Dean‑Stark or azeotropic distillation) to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; used to exchange ions and isolate insoluble silver cyanide; aqueous solution, typically at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion of a phenol to a benzoic acid (oxid reaction); purpose is to oxidize the phenolic group to a carboxylic acid while the permanganate is reduced to manganese dioxide; performed in aqueous medium, often under alkaline or neutral conditions with heating (reflux); common solvents are water or dilute NaOH solution; potassium permanganate serves as the oxidant, MnO₂ precipitates as a by‑product.

Fischer esterification of 2‑methylpentanoic acid with methanol to afford methyl 2‑methylpentanoate. The carboxylic acid is protonated, methanol attacks, and water is eliminated. Conducted by refluxing the acid in excess methanol with catalytic sulfuric acid (or p‑TSA); the reaction is equilibrium‑controlled and removal of water drives it forward.

Ammonolysis of an ester (nucleophilic acyl substitution) to form an amide; purpose is to convert a methyl ester into the corresponding amide (glycinamide) while liberating methanol; typically carried out in anhydrous or aqueous ammonia, heated under reflux; solvent may be ethanol, methanol or water; excess ammonia drives the reaction, no external catalyst needed.

Oxidative electrophilic aromatic iodination of clonidine; purpose is to introduce an iodine atom at the 4‑position of the aromatic ring; potassium peroxymonosulfate oxidizes I₂ to an electrophilic I⁺ species; reaction is usually performed in a mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile/water or acetone/water) at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; no metal catalyst is required, KHSO₅ acts as the oxidant.

Acidic cleavage of a methyl ether with hydroiodic acid; purpose is to break the ether bond, yielding methanol and the corresponding alkyl iodide (1‑pentyl iodide); conducted by refluxing the ether in excess concentrated HI (often aqueous) at 120–150 °C; water/HI mixture serves as both solvent and reagent; no additional catalyst is needed.

Redox decomposition reaction. Purpose: Oxidative degradation of silver diethyldithiocarbamate. Key transformations: Dithiocarbamate oxidation to CO2 and diethylamine, sulfur reduction to Ag2S. Conditions: Aqueous solution at ambient or mild heating.

General type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation from acid chloride). Purpose: synthesize a secondary amide (4‑nonanoylmorpholine). Key transformation: morpholine nitrogen attacks nonanoyl chloride, displacing chloride; triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl, forming triethylammonium chloride. Typical conditions: dry dichomethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere. Base (triethylamine) is essential; no metal catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis (or transesterification) of dimethyl terephthalate to terephthalic acid and methanol; generally performed by aqueous alkaline saponification followed by acidification, converting the ester back to the diacid; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at 180–200 °C in a pressurized reactor, then acid work‑up (HCl) to precipitate terephthalic acid; water acts as solvent and methanol is liberated.

Thermal decomposition: solid barium iodate is heated strongly (≈350‑400 °C), breaking down to barium iodide and releasing oxygen gas. No solvent; performed in a dry furnace or sealed tube under inert atmosphere to collect O₂.

General type: nitrosation (formation of nitrosamine). Purpose: generate N‑nitrosodimethylamine (a nitrosamine) from dimethylamine. Key transformation: the nitroso group is transferred from butyl nitrite to the secondary amine, producing N‑nitrosodimethylamine and releasing n‑butanol as the leaving group. Typical conditions: mild (often 0–25 °C), usually in an aqueous or mixed organic‑aqueous medium; may be performed under neutral or slightly acidic conditions. No metal catalyst; reaction proceeds via a nitrosyl intermediate.

N‑alkylation of tryptamine with ethyl bromide; SN2 substitution where the amine nitrogen attacks the ethyl carbon of EtBr, displacing bromide to give N‑ethyltryptamine. Carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, MeCN, DMSO) with a base such as K₂CO₃, Na₂CO₃, or triethylamine to capture the liberated HBr. Temperatures range from 0 °C to reflux, often 50‑80 °C for complete conversion.

General type: transesterification (urea exchange). Purpose: exchange the ethoxy group of ethyl carbamate with a propoxy group to obtain n‑propyl carbamate. Key transformation: propanol attacks the carbonyl of ethyl carbamate, displacing ethanol and forming the new carbamate ester. Typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous solvent (e.g., toluene or xylene) with acidic (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or basic (e.g., NaOMe) catalyst; removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium to the product side. No metal catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; silver nitrate solution is added to thiocyanic acid solution, resulting in the precipitation of silver thiocyanate (AgSCN) and formation of nitric acid (HNO₃) in the filtrate. Performed in cold water, protected from light because AgSCN is photosensitive; no catalyst required.

Type: Hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed) of carbonyl sulfide. Purpose: decompose OCS to simple gaseous products. Key transformation: OCS + H₂O → H₂S + CO₂. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, mild heating (50–100 °C); reaction can be accelerated by dilute acid (HCl) or base (NaOH). No special solvent beyond water required.

General type: direct halogenation (synthesis of metal halide). Purpose: prepare antimony trichloride from elemental antimony. Key transformation: elemental chlorine reacts with antimony metal, oxidizing antimony and forming SbCl₃. Typical conditions: chlorine gas passed over heated antimony (200–300 °C) in a sealed tube flow reactor; reaction may be conducted under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture. No solvent; the reaction is a gas‑solid combination.

Thermal decarboxylation; used to convert nitrilotriacetic acid (NTA) into the chelating ligand iminodiacetic acid (IDA) by loss of one carboxyl group as CO₂; key transformation is removal of a CO₂ molecule from the three‑carboxyl NTA skeleton; typically performed by heating solid NTA at 200–300 °C under reduced pressure or in an inert atmosphere; no solvent required, sometimes carried out in a quartz tube or sealed tube.

Thermal cracking of hexane to butane and ethene; similar high‑temperature (≈500‑750 °C) pyrolysis causing C‑C bond scission that produces a C₄ alkane and a C₂ alkene; performed under inert atmosphere, no solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); purpose is to remove the bromine atom from 1-(5-bromothiophen-2-yl)ethanone giving 2-acetylthiophene while preserving the carbonyl group; key transformation is C–Br → C–H; typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over Pd/C or Raney Ni at room temperature to reflux; common solvent: ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate.

Ullmann ether synthesis (aryl–carboxylate coupling): copper(I) bromide catalyzes the formation of a C–O bond between bromobenzene and potassium 2,2-difluoroacetate, yielding phenyl 2,2-difluoroacetate and KBr; typical conditions include CuBr (10–20 mol %), pyridine as ligand/base, anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO), heated 100– °C under inert atmosphere.

Type: halogen–metal exchange (metal‑halogen exchange). Purpose: generate phenyl‑lithium reagent while releasing the alkyl halide. Key transformation: electrophilic bromine on bromobenzene is transferred to n‑BuLi, giving phenyl‑Li and n‑butyl‑Br. Typical conditions: –78 °C to –20 °C, dry ether solvent (THF, Et₂O), nitrogen or argon atmosphere. No catalyst needed.

Chromic acid oxidation (secondary alcohol to ketone); conversion of indan‑1‑ol to 1‑indanone using CrO₃/H₂SO₄ (Jones reagent); reaction carried out in acetone/water (≈1:1) at 0 °C to room temperature, with vigorous stirring; work‑up with aqueous sodium bisulfite to quench excess oxidant.

Claisen‑type condensation / Dieckmann cyclization. Purpose: construct the five‑membered lactone ring of tetronic acid from diethyl oxalate and 2‑butanone. Key transformation: base‑catalyzed condensation of the enolate of 2‑butanone with diethyl oxalate, followed by intramolecular Dieckmann cyclization and subsequent hydrolysis/acid work‑up to afford tetronic acid. Typical conditions: strong base such as sodium ethoxide or potassium tert‑butoxide in ethanol, reflux for several hours, then acidification (e.g., dilute HCl) to cyclize and precipitate the product. No special catalyst beyond the base.

Base‑catalyzed methanolysis (transesterification) of ethylene carbonate; purpose is to generate dimethyl carbonate (a green methylating agent/solvent) and recover ethylene glycol; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methanol on the cyclic carbonate, opening the ring and forming dimethyl carbonate and ethylene glycol; usually carried out with excess methanol as both reactant and solvent at 60–120 °C in the presence of a basic catalyst such as K₂CO₃, NaOH, or ZnCl₂; inert atmosphere not mandatory.

Halogen–lithium exchange on aane (metallation); purpose is to replace the bromine on a bromosilane with an n‑butyl group, forming n‑butylsilane; key transformation is formation of a Si–C bond and precipitation of LiBr; reaction is performed at low temperature (‑78 °C to ‑40 °C) in anhydrous ether or THF under nitrogen or argon; stoichiometric n‑butyl lithium is used, no additional catalyst.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction between calcium sulfate and sodium hydroxide producing calcium hydroxide and sodium sulfate. Usually carried out in aqueous solution with heating to improve solubility; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of 2‑methoxy‑4‑methylphenol with concentrated nitric acid; purpose is to introduce a nitro group ortho to the phenolic OH; key transformation is attack of the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) on the activated aromatic ring forming 2‑methoxy‑4‑methyl‑6‑nitrophenol and water; typical conditions: temperature 0‑5 °C to control regioselectivity, mixed acid medium (conc. HNO₃ often with conc. H₂SO₄ as a catalyst), reaction in the acid mixture; water is generated as by‑product.

General type: Base‑induced elimination (E2). Purpose: Dehydrohalogenate alkyl halide to produce the corresponding alkene. Key transformations: Alcoholic KOH a β‑hydrogen while chloride leaves, forming propene, KCl, and water. Typical conditions: Reflux in dry ethanol (or isopropanol) with excessOH, temperature 78‑85 °C, reaction time 1‑2 h. Common solvents/catalysts: Ethanol as solvent, potassium hydroxide as strong base.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction: permanganate oxidizes Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ while Mn(VII) is reduced to Mn²⁺. Occurs in aqueous solution, often neutral to slightly acidic; no special catalyst required. Products are CaSO₄ (precipitate), Fe₂(SO₄)₃, and MnSO₄ in solution.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aryl nitro group to an amine; purpose is to convert 4-bromo-2-nitrophenol into 4-bromo-2-aminophenol while retaining the bromine substituent. Key transformation: – H₂ reduces –NO₂ to –NH₂. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, 5–10 % Pd/C (by weight), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–50 °C.

Acylation of a primary alcohol with acetyl chloride in the presence of pyridine; yields furan‑2‑ylmethyl acetate and hydrogen chloride (neutralized by pyridine); typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, pyridine as both solvent and base, often performed in dichloromethane; the reaction proceeds rapidly (minutes to an hour).

Copper‑catalyzed Kumada cross‑coupling (aryl‑alkyl coupling); purpose is to install methyl groups at the 3‑ and 4‑positions of 3,4‑dibromothiophene, yielding 3,4‑dimethylthiophene; key transformations are two successive transmetalations of MeMgBr to copper(I) and reductive elimination to form C–C bonds; typical conditions: 1–5 mol % CuI (or CuBr) as catalyst, anhydrous THF as solvent, 0 °C to reflux temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); Grignard reagent added dropwise.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; purpose is to exchange ions to produce soluble ammonium nitrate and less‑soluble lithium oxalate, which can precipitate; key transformation is swapping of Li⁺ with NH₄⁺ between oxalate and nitrate anions; carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required; the solid lithium oxalate can be isolated by filtration.

Selective ester reduction to aldehyde using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H); purpose is to convert methyl salicylate into salicylaldehyde while preserving the phenolic OH; key transformations are hydride delivery to the carbonyl carbon, formation of an alkoxide intermediate, and controlled work‑ that releases methanol and aldehyde; performed at ‑78 °C to 0 °C in anhydrous THF or toluene under nitrogen; typically 1 equiv DIBAL‑H is used, and the reaction is quenched with a mild protic work‑up (e.g., aqueous Rochelle’s).

Acyl substitution (acid chloride amidation); purpose: install a benzoyl group on glycinamide nitrogen to give N‑benzoylglycinamide; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the amine on benzoyl chloride with loss of chloride, generating HCl; typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, with a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge the HCl.

General type: hydrolysis of a metal sulfide. Purpose: conversion of aluminum sulfide to the amphoteric hydroxide and liberation of H2S gas. Key transformation: Al2S3 + 6 H2O → 2 Al(OH)3 + 3 H2S. Typical conditions: solid Al2S3 is added to warm water (ambient to 80 °C); the reaction proceeds spontaneously, often under acidic to pH to control H2S release. No catalyst needed; water acts as both solvent and reactant.

Acid‑salt reaction of a lanthanide sulfide; lanthanum(III) sulfide is protonated by nitric acid releasing hydrogen sulfide gas and forming soluble lanthanum nitrate; typically done in dilute HNO₃ aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature to avoid oxidation of sulfide, no catalyst.

General type: acid‑base (neutralization) reaction of a metal oxide. Purpose: conversion of cobalt(II) oxide to the soluble bromide salt. Key transformation: CoO + 2 HBr → CoBr₂ + H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous HBr (conc. 48 %) added to CoO at room temperature or with gentle heating (50‑80 °C) to ensure complete dissolution. Common solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Thionation with Lawesson’s reagent; purpose: replace the carbonyl oxygen at position 4 of uracil with sulfur to give 4‑thiouracil; key transformation: C=O → C=S conversion; typical conditions: 1–2 equiv Lawesson’s reagent, dry toluene or THF as solvent, reflux at 80–110 °C under nitrogen, reaction time 2–6 h, no additional catalyst required.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed hydrosilylation (reductive deoxygenation) of an aldehyde; purpose: convert 3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde to 3‑pyridinemethanol; key transformation: triethylsilane delivers a hydride to the carbonyl carbon in the presence of BF₃·OEt₂, forming the primary alcohol after aqueous work‑up; typical conditions: dichloromethane or toluene, 0 °C to rt, catalytic amount of BF₃·OEt₂, inert atmosphere.

Acid–base transfer (hydrolysis of alkoxide); purpose: generate ethanol and lithium hydroxide from lithium ethoxide; key transformation: water protonates the ethoxide anion, yielding ethanol and Li⁺·OH⁻; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no additional solvent required.

4-Fluorotoluene + Sodium dichromate + Sulfuric acid -> 4-Fluorobenzoic acid  
**Type:** Oxidation. **Purpose:** Converts a benzyl methyl group to a carboxylic acid. **Key transformations:** Sodium dichromate in acidic medium oxidizes the methyl group using Cr(VI). **Conditions:** Reflux in concentrated sulfuric acid. **Solvents/catalysts:** H2SO4 provides acidic medium; Na2Cr2O7 as the oxidizing agent.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling (peptide‑type synthesis); purpose: form the amide bond of capsaicin from 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzylamine and 8‑methyl‑6‑nonenoic acid; key transformation: DCC activates the carboxylic acid to an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is then attacked by the amine to give the amide and dicyclohexylurea by‑product; typical conditions: dichloromethane or DMF, 0 °C to rt, often with catalytic DMAP to improve rate, under nitrogen.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (cleavage); purpose is to regenerate phenethyl alcohol and acetic acid. Water attacks the protonated carbonyl of 2‑phenylethyl acetate, leading to cleavage to the alcohol and acid. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous 1–6 M HCl (or H₂SO₄) for 2–12 h; sometimes a co‑solvent such as THF, MeCN or toluene is used to improve miscibility. The reaction is driven to completion by excess water.

Salt formation (acid‑base neutralization) of the basic amine Mexiletine with hydrogen chloride to afford Mexiletine hydrochloride; used to improve solubility and stability of the drug. Typically the free base is dissolved in a polar solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol and treated with gaseous or aqueous HCl at 0‑25 °C, the salt precipitates and is filtered.

Double‑replacement metathesis/precipitation reaction between zinc bromide and potassium stearate yielding zinc stearate and potassium bromide. Purpose: preparation of zinc stearate as a lubricant or soap. Conducted in water or aqueous ethanol at ambient temperature; zinc stearate precipitates, is filtered and washed. No catalyst required.

Photochemical free‑radical halogenation (substitution) of fluoroethane with chlorine under ultraviolet light, producing hydrogen chloride and 1‑chloro‑1‑fluoroethane. Typical conditions: dilute chlorine gas bubbled through fluoroethane in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, irradiated with a mercury lamp at room temperature.

Solid‑state synthesis (high‑temperature metathesis) of lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO₄) from phosphoric acid, lithium carbonate and iron(II) phosphate. The stoichiometric powders are thoroughly ground, then calcined under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at 600‑700 °C for several hours, yielding LiFePO₄ together with CO₂ and H₂O. No solvent or catalyst is used; reaction proceeds via solid‑state diffusion.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (amide cleavage) of acetaminophen in aqueous hydrochloric acid, giving 4‑aminophenol as its hydrochloride salt and acetic acid. Conducted by refluxing acetaminophen in 1‑6 M HCl (often in aqueous ethanol) at 80‑100 °C for 2‑6 h, then cooling to crystallize 4‑aminophenol·HCl.

Reductive dehalogenation of 1,2,2‑tribromopropane with sodium amalgam, removing two bromine atoms to afford 2‑bromopropane and sodium bromide. Performed in anhydrous THF or ethanol at 0‑25 °C under inert atmosphere; sodium amalgam serves as the electron donor, no additional catalyst required.

Type: Strong reducing reaction (LiAlH4 reduction of an acid anhydride). Purpose: Convert a sterically hindered acid anhydride into the corresponding primary alcohol. Key transformation: Both acyl groups of 2,2‑dimethylpropanoic anhydride are reduced to 2,2‑dimethylpropanol, with evolution of Al–O and Li–O salts. Typical conditions: Anhydrous ether or THF, inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), addition of LiAlH4 at 0 °C followed by reflux for 1–3 h. Common solvents/catalysts: Dry diethyl ether, tetrahydrofuran; work‑up with aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) to decompose excess LiAlH4.

Acidic (or neutral) hydrolysis of an acetate ester; purpose is to cleave the ester to release the corresponding alcohol and acid; key transformation: cyclopropyl acetate + H2O → cyclopropanol + acetic acid; typical conditions: aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or simply refluxing water, 80‑100 °C for several hours; solvent may be a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (e.g., dioxane) to improve solubility.

Type: LiAlH4 reduction of a chlorinated carboxylic acid. Purpose: Produce a chlorinated primary alcohol from 2,2‑dichloroacetic acid. Key transformation: The C=O of the acid is reduced to CH2‑OH, giving 2,2‑dichloroethanol; lithium and aluminum are converted to lithium hydroxide and aluminum hydroxide as inorganic by‑products. Typical conditions: Anhydrous THF or ether, addition of LiAlH4 at 0 °C, then stirring at reflux (≈66 °C) for 2–4 h. Work‑up: aqueous acidic quench (e.g., dilute HCl) to destroy excess hydride and precipitate Al(OH)3.

Thermal cracking (pyrolysis) of a long‑chain alkane; purpose is to break the C24 hydrocarbon into shorter hydrocarbon fragments for fuel or feedstock. The C–C bonds are cleaved to give a C12 alkane (dodecane) and a C12 terminal alkene (1‑dodecene). Typical conditions are temperatures of 500–800 °C in the gas phase, often over a solid acid catalyst such as a zeolite or silica‑alumina. No solvent is used; the reaction is carried out under inert or nitrogen atmosphere.

Type: Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation) using an ionic liquid as catalyst. Purpose: synthesis of heptyl p‑hydroxybenzoate (a parabens ester). Key transformation: the carboxyl group of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid reacts with n‑heptanol, eliminating water and forming the corresponding ester. Typical conditions: heating at 100–120 °C, often under solvent‑free or minimal‑solvent conditions, with 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate (BMIM‑BF₄) as a recyclable acidic ionic liquid catalyst. Common solvent/catalyst: BMIM‑BF₄ (ionic liquid) can act as solvent and catalyst; sometimes a co‑solvent such as toluene is used to aid removal of water.

Sulfide oxidation to sulfoxide with DMDO; purpose: selective oxidation of diphenyl sulfide to diphenyl sulfoxide; key transformation: diphenyl sulfide + DMDO → diphenyl sulfoxide + acetone; typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, aprotic solvent; common solvent: dichloromethane or chloroform; DMDO generated in situ.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride with ammonia. Purpose: Introduce an amino group to form 3‑(aminomethyl)pentane. Key transformation: The chloride is displaced by NH3, generating the primary amine and HCl as the by‑product. Typical conditions: Excess gaseous or aqueous ammonia (often 2–5 equiv), sealed tube or pressure reactor at 50–100 °C for several hours. Solvent: Anhydrous ethanol, methanol, or neat liquid ammonia. The generated HCl is often removed by passing the reaction mixture through a base trap or by using an excess of ammonia to neutralize it.

Type: Aminolysis (ring‑opening) of a lactone by ammonia. Purpose: preparation of γ‑aminobutyric acid (GABA). Key transformation: ammonia attacks the carbonyl carbon of β‑butyrolactone, opening the four‑membered lactone ring to give a primary amine and a carboxy acid that together constitute GABA. Typical conditions: aqueous or gaseous NH₃ in excess, heated to 80 °C under pressure or in a sealed tube; reaction can be performed in water or a water‑miscible solvent such as ethanol. No additional catalyst is required.

Metathesis/base preparation; tetrabutylammonium bromide is treated with aqueous ammonium hydroxide, exchanging bromide for hydroxide to produce tetrabutylammonium hydroxide (a strong organic‑soluble base) and ammonium bromide; performed in water at ambient temperature, often followed by extraction into an organic solvent such as dichloromethane; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous AgNO₃ reacts with NaBr to precipitate insoluble AgBr and form NaNO₃ in solution; carried out at room temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction; purpose is to oxidize Fe(II) to Fe(III) and reduce NO₂ to NO. Iron(II) oxide donates electrons to nitrogen dioxide, producing iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃) and nitric oxide gas. Conducted as a solid‑gas reaction at elevated temperatures (≈300–500 °C) in a flow of NO₂; no solvent or catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; cyanide ion displaces the methanesulfonate to produce butyronitrile (1‑cyanopropane); reaction is usually run in DMF or DMSO at 0–25 °C to minimize elimination, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst for aqueous KCN.

Type: Halide exchange (metathesis) between a mercuric salt and hydrochloric acid. Purpose: Replace the nitrate ligand in phenylmercuric nitrate with chloride to give phenylmercuric chloride, simultaneously producing nitric acid. Key transformation: An anion exchange where Cl‑ displaces NO3‑ coordinated to HgPh, forming HgPhCl and HNO3. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution of phenylmercuric nitrate cooled to 0–5 °C, addition of concentrated HCl dropwise with stirring. The mixture is then allowed to warm to ambient temperature; the phenylmercuric chloride precipitates and is filtered. No external catalyst is required; the reaction relies on the higher affinity of Hg for chloride under these conditions.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of a nonyl benzoate ester; an alkoxide reduction (hydride reduction) that cleaves the C=O–O bond to give the corresponding primary alcohols, benzyl alcohol from the acyl fragment and nonanol from the alkoxy fragment. Typically carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, refluxing LiAlH4 under nitrogen, followed by careful aqueous work‑up.

Fluorination/acid‑base conversion of antimony trioxide to antimony(III) fluoride; Sb2O3 reacts with excess hydrogen fluoride gas to give SbF3 and water. Performed in a sealed PTFE or quartz vessel with gaseous HF (often excess) at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C); no solvent is required, and the reaction is conducted under rigorously dry, corrosion‑resistant conditions.

Metal‑acid redox synthesis of potassium azide; hydrazoic acid (HN3) reacts with elemental potassium metal, reducing the azide proton to hydrogen gas and forming potassium azide (KN3). Conducted in anhydrous liquid ammonia or dry ether at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere to control the highly exothermic and potentially explosive nature of the reagents.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of phenol with acetyl chloride in the presence of aluminum chloride; electrophilic aromatic substitution delivers primarily the para‑acylated product, 4‑hydroxyacetophenone. Reaction is carried out anhydrously, typically in carbon disulfide, dichloromethane or nitrobenzene, with AlCl3 (1–1.5 equiv) at 0 °C to room temperature; the mixture is quenched with ice‑water after completion.

Aqueous metathesis/precipitation reaction between ethylenediamine dihydroiodide and mercury(II) chloride; the iodide ions exchange with chloride to form insoluble mercury(II) iodide (HgI2) precipitate and the soluble ethylenediammonium chloride remains in solution. Performed in water (or dilute aqueous acid) at temperature with stirring; the solid HgI2 is filtered off and washed.

Acid dissolution / halogenation of a metal dioxide; osmium dioxide reacts with concentrated hydrochloric acid to furnish osmium tetrachloride (OsCl₄) and water; employed to convert OsO₂ into a soluble chloride for further synthesis; typically refluxed in 6–12 M HCl at 70–100 °C; aqueous HCl serves as both solvent and reagent; no additional catalyst.

Oxidation of dimethyl sulfide to dimethyl sulfone using m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA); the sulfoxide intermediate is oxidized, while each equivalent of m‑CPBA is reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Conducted in an aprotic, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, with 2 equiv of m‑CPBA; the reaction mixture is worked up by aqueous wash to remove the benzoic acid by‑product.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; forms a biaryl C‑C bond between 4‑bromophenol and 4‑tert‑butylphenylboronic; K2CO3 acts as base; Pd(PPh3)4 is the catalyst; typically run in THF (often with a small amount of water) at 80‑100 °C under nitrogen; used to construct aryl‑aryl linkedol.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of calcium carbonate; yields calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. CaCO3 is heated to ≥825 °C in a furnace, causing irreversible breakdown to CaO solid and CO2 gas. No solvent; carried out in air or inert atmosphere, no catalyst required.

Acid‑chloride amide formation; N‑methylglycine (sarcosine) is acylated by dodecanoyl chloride to give N‑lauroylsarcosine; triethylamine scavenges the released HCl forming TEA·HCl; performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; synthesizes a surfactant‑type amide.

Hydrogen reduction (gas‑solid reduction): germanium nitride is reduced by hydrogen gas to give germanium metal and ammonia. Conducted at 400–600 °C under a continuous flow of H₂, often in a quartz tube. Occasionally a metal catalyst such as nickel or palladium is employed to enhance hydrogen activation. No solvent; reaction gases are the reagents.

Ester hydrolysis (neutral or base‑catalyzed); hexan‑3‑yl acetate reacts with water to yield hexan‑3‑ol and acetic acid; commonly carried out with aqueous base (NaOH or KOH) at reflux, followed by acidification to isolate the acid; purpose is cleavage of ester to alcohol and acid.

Acid‑catalyzedioester hydrolysis; propyl thioacetate is protonated by HCl, water attacks to give propyl mercaptan and acetic acid; performed in aqueous HCl, often with heating (reflux); converts a thioester to a thiol.

Single displacement/redox acid‑metal reaction; zinc metal is oxidized to Zn²⁺ forming zinc nitrate while nitrate ion is reduced to nitrogen monoxide gas; carried out in dilute aqueous HNO₃ at room temperature, no catalyst required.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation); purpose is to convert acetic acid to the chloroethyl acetate ester. Acetic acid reacts with 2‑chloroethanol, eliminating water to form 2‑chloroethyl acetate. Typical conditions: reflux in a non‑aqueous solvent such as toluene or benzene with catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark trap) drives the equilibrium to products.

Benzoin condensation (cyanide‑catalyzed umpolung); two benzaldehyde molecules form benzoin via cyanide activation; KCN serves as catalyst, generating a cyanohydrin intermediate; usually conducted in ethanol or aqueous ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; provides an α‑hydroxyketone from aldehyde.

LiAlH4 reduction of amide; azepan‑2‑one is reduced to azepanea secondary amine) using LiAlH4; reaction run in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; converts a lactam to a saturated cyclic amine.

Acid-base metalation; preparation of lithium tetramethylpiperidide (LiTMP) by deprotonating 2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine with tert‑butyllithium. Conducted under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) at low temperature (−78 °C) in anhydrous THF or Et₂O. By‑product is gaseous tert‑butane; no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation; chlorine adds to the ortho position of 1‑methoxy‑4‑methylbenzene under the directing influence of the methoxy group. Typical conditions: Cl₂ gas (1 equiv) a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ (10–20 mol %) in an inert, non‑protic solvent (CS₂, CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to room temperature. The reaction yields 2‑chloro‑1‑methoxy‑4‑methylbenzene.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; purpose is qualitative detection of copper(II) as insoluble sulfide; key transformation is Cu2+ + S2‑ → CuS solid and generation of HCl; performed by bubbling H2S gas through an aqueous CuCl2 solution at room temperature; water is the solvent.

Double displacement precipitation (acid‑base type); converts a soluble carbonate and a strong base into insoluble calcium carbonate and soluble potassium hydroxide; CO₃²⁻ from K₂CO₃ combines with Ca²⁺ from Ca(OH)₂ to precipitate CaCO₃ while K⁺ pairs with OH⁻ to give KOH; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary tosylate by ammonia to give 2‑fluoroethylamine. Usually performed in a polar protic (ethanol or water/ethanol mixture) with excess NH₃ (gas or aqueous solution) at 50–80 °C, sometimes under reflux. The tosylate group leaves as p‑toluenesulfonic acid (or its salt), which can be neutralized by the excess ammonia.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of ethyl 4‑hydroxybenzoate to 4‑hydroxybenzoic acid. Conducted with aqueous NaOH or KOH (1–2 equiv) in a water/ethanol mixture, heated under reflux (≈80 °C). After completion, the reaction mixture is acidified (e.g., with dilute HCl) to precipitate 4‑hydroxybenzoic acid; ethanol is liberated as the by‑product.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction forming silver iodide and iodine azide (I(N₃)). Performed in anhydrous, aprotic solvent such as dry CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN at 0 °C to −20 °C under inert atmosphere and protected from light. Silver azide reacts with I₂, precipitating AgI (white solid) while generating the highly sensitive iodine azide in solution; no catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement (ion‑exchange) reaction between sodium oxalate and lithium bromide in aqueous solution. The mixture is stirred at ambient temperature; Na⁺ exchanges with Li⁺ to give lithium oxalate and sodium bromide. No special reagents or catalysts are needed; solubility differences may drive the equilibrium.

Selective sulfide oxidation to sulfoxide. CAN transfers an oxygen atom to thioanisole, converting the thioether to methyl phenyl sulfoxide while avoiding over‑oxidation to the sulfone. The reaction is usually run in acetonitrile/water (often 4 : 1) at 0 °C to room temperature, with 1–2 equiv of CAN as the stoichiometric oxidant.

Acid‑base precipitation (double replacement) reaction; used to recover phosphate as a soluble sodium phosphate while precipitating chromium(III) hydroxide; phosphate anion is transferred to sodium, and chromium(III) forms an insoluble hydroxide precipitate; conducted in aqueous solution by adding aqueous sodium hydroxide solution to a suspension of chromium(III) phosphate, often at room temperature or with slight warming; excess NaOH ensures complete precipitation; no catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 substitution); purpose is to prepare ethylene glycol dibutyl ether as a non‑polar solvent; the alkoxide of 2‑butoxyethanol attacks n‑butyl bromide displacing Br– and forming the second ether linkage, with NaOH neutralizing the generated HBr to water; typically performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO under reflux, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst, no additional metal catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization; purpose is to obtain lutetium(III) iodide, a soluble lanthanide salt; hydroiodic acid protonates the hydroxide ligands of Lu(OH)₃, yielding water and LuI₃; carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to dissolve the solid, no special catalyst, water is the solvent.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert octanoic acid into octan‑1‑ol for further functionalization; LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl, forming an aldehyde intermediate that is further reduced to the alcohol, with LiOH and Al(OH)₃ as by‑products; performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, quench with water then dilute acid; LiAlH₄ itself is the reagent, no catalyst needed.

Sulfoxidation (oxidation of thioether): performic acid oxidizes the sulfur of DL‑methionine to the corresponding sulfoxide, producing DL‑methionine sulfoxide and formic acid. Reaction is carried out in water or aqueous methanol at 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation; stoichiometric amount of performic acid, no metal catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a ketone; purpose is to reduce menthone to menthol, a valuable flavor and fragrance compound; hydrogen adds across the carbonyl C=O bond on the Pd/C surface, converting the ketone to the secondary alcohol; reaction is run at 1–5 atm H₂, Pd on carbon (10 % Pd) as catalyst, in ethanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature to 50 °C, typically under nitrogen purge to remove oxygen.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a polyunsaturated fatty alcohol; purpose is to saturate linoleyl alcohol (C18:2) to give stearyl alcohol (C18:0), improving melting point and stability; H₂ across each C=C double bond on a metal catalyst surface; common conditions include 3–5 atm H₂, Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂ as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol, temperature 50–100 °C, reaction time several hours.
