Base‑catalyzed ester alcoholysis (transesterification) of methyl pivalate with sodium methoxide; purpose is to generate sodium pivalate and release methanol, often used to prepare the pivalate salt; methoxide attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing methoxide as methanol and forming the carboxylate anion; usually carried out in methanol as solvent at room temperature or mild reflux, with NaOMe as both base and nucleophile, no additional catalyst required.

Reduction of an azido aldehyde to the corresponding azido alcohol; nucleophilic hydride reduction (NaBH4) of the carbonyl group while leaving the azide intact. Typically carried out in methanol, ethanol or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required. Key transformation: –CHO → –CH2OH.

Acid‑catalyzed thioacetal formation (protecting group installation). Acetaldehyde reacts with 1,2‑ethanedithiol in the presence of catalytic HCl, forming the cyclic thioacetal 4‑methyl‑1,3‑dithiolane and water as by‑product. Typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or toluene under reflux, using a few drops of concentrated HCl as catalyst and a Dean–Stark trap to remove water.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein) reaction converting a dibromoalkane to a diiodoalkane. SN2 substitution of bromide with iodide using sodium iodide in an aprotic polar solvent (commonly acetone) where NaBr precipitates, driving the reaction forward. Usually refluxed for several hours; no additional catalyst.

Peroxidation (formation of a cyclic organic peroxide, diacetone peroxide); acetone reacts with hydrogen peroxide under acid catalysis to give a 1,2‑dioxane dimer; typical conditions are 0–5 °C in the presence of a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄, using acetone as both substrate and solvent; the peroxide precipitates and is filtered under cold conditions.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of a secondary alcohol to an internal alkene; E1 elimination of water from 2‑heptanol to give hept‑2‑ene. Performed with strong acids such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH at 130–180 °C, often in the absence of solvent or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., toluene). Key transformation: –OH and adjacent H removed to form C=C.

Peracid oxidation of a secondary arylamine (acetylaminofluorene) to the N‑hydroxy derivative; N‑oxidation using peracetic acid. Conducted in an inert, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0–5 °C under nitrogen; the peracid transfers an oxygen to the nitrogen, yielding N‑hydroxy‑2‑acetylaminofluorene and acetic acid as by‑product.

Kolbe‑Schmitt carboxylation of p‑cresol to 2‑hydroxy‑p‑toluic acid. Phenolate (generated by NaOH) reacts with CO₂ under pressure (≈1–3 atm) at 100–150 °C, followed by acid work‑up to afford the ortho‑carboxylated phenol. Aqueous NaOH solution is the typical medium; no additional catalyst required.

Alcoholysis of a chlorosilane to form a trialkoxysilane; nucleophilic substitution of Si–Cl bonds by methanol. Performed by refluxing 3‑chloropropyltrichlorosilane in excess methanol, often in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine) to neutralize the generated HCl. Results in 3‑chloropropyltrimethoxysilane and HCl.

Hydrolysis/acid‑base exchange of deuterium fluoride; DF reacts with water to give hydrofluoric acid (HF) and deuterium oxide (D2O). The key transformation is proton exchange between fluorine‑bearing hydrogen isotopes. Conducted by bubbling DF gas into liquid water or by mixing aqueous DF solution with water at ambient temperature; aqueous medium serves as both solvent and reactant; no additional catalyst is needed.

Ester hydrolysis (acid or base catalyzed) of hexadecyl acetate with water to give hexadecanol and acetic acid; typically performed in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) or base (NaOH) at reflux, using a water/ethanol mixture as solvent and heating to drive the equilibrium toward products.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction between sodium fluoride and calcium hydroxide; fluoride exchanges with hydroxide to give insoluble calcium fluoride (CaF2) which precipitates, while sodium hydroxide remains in solution; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent.

Fischer esterification of hexan-3-ol with acetic acid to form hexan-3-yl acetate; performed with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) under reflux in toluene or benzene, with continuous removal of water (Dean–Stark apparatus) to shift the equilibrium toward the ester.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification betweenyl p‑aminobenzoate and 2‑diethylaminoethanol producing procaine and ethanol; uses p‑toluenesulfonic acid (≈10  %) in anhydrous toluene, refluxed while azeotropically removing ethanol (Dean–Stark) to drive the reaction to completion.

Oxidation of tri(2‑ethylhexyl) phosphite (P III) to tris(2‑ethylhexyl) phosphate (P V) by hydrogen peroxide; carried out in an organic solvent such as dichloromethane or heptane at 25–60 °C, sometimes with a catalytic amount of base (NaOH) or a metal catalyst to accelerate the oxidation, producing water as the only by‑product.

Double displacement/precipitation; copper(II) ions replace sodium in sodium ferrocyanide to give insoluble copper ferrocyanide (Cu2[Fe(CN)6]) and sodium sulfate remains in solution. Performed by mixing aqueous solutions of Na4[Fe(CN)6] and CuSO4 at ambient temperature. Water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Acyl chloride amidation with aqueous ammonia: 2‑furancarbonyl chloride is treated with aqueous NH₃ to form furan‑2‑carboxamide and release HCl. The reaction proceeds at 0 °C to room temperature, often in a biphasic mixture (e.g., THF/water) with excess ammonia; the generated HCl is neutralized by the excess NH₃, and the amide is isolated after extraction and drying.

Redox/displacement reaction; chlorine gas oxidizes iodide to elemental iodine while being reduced to chloride; LiI provides I⁻ which is oxidized to I₂, and Cl₂ is reduced to Cl⁻ forming LiCl; usually carried out by bubbling Cl₂ through an aqueous LiI solution at 0‑25 °C; the liberated iodine may be extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane), while LiCl stays in the aqueous phase.

Double‑replacement precipitation of mercury(I) oxide from mercurous nitrate and sodium hydroxide; aqueous NaOH is added to a solution of mercurous nitrate at room temperature, causing yellow Hg₂O precipitate to form while sodium nitrate remains in solution; the solid is filtered and washed.

Appel-type halogenation; converts a primary alcohol to the corresponding alkyl bromide. The hydroxyl group is replaced by bromine via activation with triphenylphosphine and N‑bromosuccinimide, producing succinimide and phosphine oxide as by‑products. Typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, using stoichiometric PPh₃ and NBS.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification); the carboxylic acid 6‑oxohexanoic acid is coupled with ethanol in the presence of dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to afford ethyl 6‑oxohexanoate, with dicyclohexylurea precipitating as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP to accelerate acyl transfer; reaction run under inert atmosphere for 2–12 h.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of a metal sil reduces chromium(III) oxide with silicon to form silicon dioxide and a chromium silicide (e.g., CrSi₂). Conducted by intimately mixing fine powders of Cr₂O₃ and Si and heating in an inert atmosphere (argon) or vacuum at 1500–1800 °C for several hours. No solvent; the reaction relies on thermal energy.

Selective ester‑to‑aldehyde reduction; DIBAL‑H adds one hydride equivalent to methyl 4‑methoxybenzoate, stopping at the aldehyde stage to give 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde and methanol. Conditions: 1 equiv DIBAL‑H in dry toluene or CH₂Cl₂, −78 °C to 0 °C, inert atmosphere, quench with methanol or dilute acid.

Oxidative regeneration of a leuco dye; ammonium persulfate oxidizes leucomalachite green (the reduced, colorless form) to malachite green (the colored cation). The persulfate serves as a strong oxidant, generating sulfate radicals that abstract electrons. Carried out in aqueous solution, often at ambient temperature and neutral to slightly basic pH; no catalyst is required.

Reaction type: metal‑hydride reduction of an ester (LiAlH₄ reduction). Purpose: fully reduce the ester to the corresponding primary alcohols. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl of propyl hexanoate, yielding 1‑hexanol (from the acyl side) and 1‑propanol (from the alkoxy side) after work‑up. Typical conditions: dry ether solvent (diethyl ether or THF), addition of LiAlH₄ (1–2 equiv) at 0 °C followed by stirring at reflux temperature (≈ 65 °C for THF) for 1–3 h. Reaction is quenched with careful addition of water then dilute acid.

Acid‑base neutralization of a metal oxide; purpose is to form mercury(II) perchlorate and water. HgO(s) reacts with H⁺ from aqueous perchloric acid to give Hg²⁺ (as Hg(ClO₄)₂) and H₂O. Conducted in dilute HClO₄ at room temperature, often with gentle heating to dissolve the oxide; water is the medium, no catalyst needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation; ammonium hydroxide reacts with yttrium sulfate to precipitate yttrium hydroxide while forming soluble ammonium sulfate. The reaction proceeds at room temperature with vigorous stirring in water; the insoluble Y(OH)₃ is isolated by filtration and washing.

Aqueous metathesis/precipitation reaction: zinc acetate reacts with aqueous ammonia to precipitate zinc hydroxide, while ammonium acetate remains in solution; performed at room temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Base‑promoted dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination); sodium hydroxide abstracts a proton adjacent to the chlorine on 2‑chlorocyclohexan‑1‑one, eliminating HCl to give the α,β‑unsaturated ketone 2‑cyclohexen‑1‑one. Usually performed in aqueous NaOH or NaOH/ethanol mixture, heated under reflux (≈80 °C) for 1–2 h; the reaction is driven to completion by removal of NaCl.

Oxidative conversion of acetaldehyde to acetic acid using peroxymonosulfuric acid; similar aqueous acidic conditions as above, low to ambient temperature, water solvent, with H2SO4 and water formed as by‑products.

Copper‑catalyzed aryl‑aryl coupling (Ullmann‑type) using a diazonium salt; benzenediazonium tetrafluoroborate transfers a phenyl group to biphenyl in the presence of CuBr, forming p‑terphenyl. The reaction is carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or acetonitrile, 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of Cu(I) and sometimes a base (e.g., K₂CO₃) to neutralize generated acid.

Amidation via mixed anhydride formation; purpose is to link arachidonic acid to 4‑hydroxyphenyl group forming a bioactive amide; key transformation is conversion of the carboxylic acid into an isobutyl mixed anhydride (by isobutyl chloroformate) which then reacts with the amine of 4‑aminophenol; typical conditions involve cooling the reaction mixture to 0 °C then stirring at room temperature under inert atmosphere; common solvent is dry dichloromethane or THF and N‑methylmorpholine acts as base to scavenge HCl.

Acid‑base neutralization forming an aluminum nicotinate salt; purpose is to prepare a metal‑nicotinate complex; key transformation is deprotonation of nicotinic acid by basic sites on Al₂O₃ water and the aluminum‑nicotinate solid; usually performed by grinding the solid reagents and heating to 200–300 °C in a dry furnace; no solvent; the reaction proceeds ambient or slightly elevated temperature depending on desired conversion.

Fischer esterification of chloroacetic acid with methanol yielding methyl 2‑chloroacetate and water; acid‑catalyzed condensation to form a methyl ester. Common conditions: excess methanol, catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, reflux (≈60–80 °C), removal of water to drive equilibrium.

Haloform (iodoform) reaction analogous to 1 but using KOH; acetone is converted to iodoform and potassium acetate under aqueous KOH and I₂, typically at room temperature; water (or water/ethanol) serves as solvent.

Copper‑catalyzed cyanation (Rosenmund‑von Braun type) using copper(I) cyanide; replaces bromide with a nitrile group. Bromoacetone is reacted with CuCN (1–2 equivalents) in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as dimethylformamide (DMF) or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) at 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere. The copper(I) cyanide transfers the cyanide to the alkyl carbon, forming cyanoacetone and precipitating copper(I) bromide. The reaction may be aided by a catalytic amount of copper(I) iodide to improve solubility.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of tris(2,4‑pentanedionato)cobalt(III); purpose is to generate cobalt oxide and small organic volatiles; key transformation is breakdown of the acetylacetonate ligands to give acetone and carbon dioxide while the cobalt center is reduced/oxidized to mixed‑valent Co(II,III) oxide; typical condition is heating the solid to 300–400 °C under nitrogen or argon; no additional reagents or solvents are required.

N‑alkylation of adenine (SN2) with benzyl bromide to afford N⁹‑benzyladenine (benzylaminopurine); purpose is synthesis of a plant cytokinin; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the adenine nitrogen on the benzylic carbon displacing bromide; reaction is usually carried out in dry DMF or DMSO with a mild base such as K₂CO₃ or NaH, at 60–80 °C for several hours; hydrogen bromide is generated as a by‑product and is trapped by the base.

Conversion of phenylphosphonic acid to phenylphosphonic dichloride using oxalyl chloride, releasing CO, CO₂ and HCl; typically carried out in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature under nitrogen, with the volatile gases allowed to escape to drive the reaction forward.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to a primary amine; uses H2 gas with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni or Pt in a protic solvent (ethanol or methanol) under 1–5 atm pressure at room or elevated temperature, converting the C≡N group of 2‑cyanopyridine into a CH2NH2 side chain to give pyridine‑2‑ylmethanamine.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of nitrobenzene to give 3‑bromonitrobenzene; purpose is regioselective meta bromination; key transformation is generation of the Br⁺ electrophile from Br₂ activated by FeBr₃, which attacks the meta position of the electron‑deficient nitrobenzene ring; typical conditions are addition of Br₂ (1.1 equiv) to nitrobenzene in carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature with catalytic FeBr₃ (5–10 mol %); hydrogen bromide is released during the process.

Acid‑base salt formation with a corrosive acid; used to produce terbium(III) fluoride. Terbium(III) oxide reacts with aqueous hydrofluoric acid, forming terbium(III) fluoride and water. Performed in water (often in PTFE vessels) at low to moderate temperature (0‑50 °C) to control HF vapor; no additional catalyst. Careful handling of HF is required.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation of anthraquinone with methyl iodide to afford 2‑methylanthraquinone; purpose is introduction of a methyl substituent; key transformation is generation of a methyl cation equivalent from CH₃I by AlCl₃ Lewis acid, which attacks the 2‑position of anthraquinone; reaction is performed anhydrously in dichloromethane or CS₂ at 0 °C to reflux, using excess AlCl₃ (1.5–2 equiv); hydrogen iodide is produced as a by‑product.

Carbonation of strontium hydroxide; acid‑base neutralization forming a carbonate precipitate; Sr(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) → SrCO3(s) + H2O(l); done in aqueous solution at room temperature or slightly warmed; water is the solvent, no catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is to exchange cations and precipitate insoluble samarium(III) carbonate. Potassium carbonate and samarium(III) chloride are mixed in aqueous solution, often heated gently; the resulting Sm2(CO3)3 precipitates, while KCl remains soluble. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Acid‑chloride mediated amide formation (acylation of an amino acid); produces 2‑methylhippuric acid (benzoylglycine) and HCl. Glycine is reacted with 2‑methylbenzoyl chloride in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, in the presence of a base (e.g., NaHCO3, Na2CO3, or pyridine) to capture the liberated HCl. No additional catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of a disulfide to a thiosulfinateformation of allicin) using a peracid; the peracid (meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid) is reduced to meta‑chlorobenzoic acid. The reaction is performed in a‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, under inert atmosphere. No catalyst; mCPBA serves as both oxidant and source of the by‑product acid.

Fluoride‑mediated desilylation of an ethyl trimethylsilyl ether; purpose is to deprotect the silyl ether and release the free alcohol; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of fluoride on silicon, breaking the Si–O bond and forming trimethylsilyl fluoride while the ethoxy group is protonated to ethanol; typical conditions employ tetrabutylammonium fluoride (TBAF) in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at room temperature; the reaction proceeds cleanly without additional catalyst.

O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of a phenol with dimethyl sulfate; yields 2,4‑dichloroanisole and methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product. The phenol is deprotonated with a mild base (e.g., K2CO3 or NaOH) in a polar aprotic solvent like acetone or DMF, and the reaction proceeds at 0 °C to reflux. No catalyst required.

Thionyl‑chloride mediated conversion of an ester to an acyl chloride with concurrent formation of an alkyl chloride; methyl salicylate gives salicyloyl chloride and methyl chloride. The reaction is carried out in anhydrous non‑protic solvent (e.g., chloroform or carbon tetrachloride) under reflux, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to accelerate chloride exchange. No external catalyst beyond SOCl₂.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction used to prepare neodymium fluoride; fluoride ions from hydrofluoric acid replace nitrate ions of neodymium nitrate, forming insoluble NdF3 which precipitates while nitric acid and water are generated; typically performed in aqueous HF at low to ambient temperature with vigorous stirring, no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis (saponification). Aqueous NaOH (often refluxing in water or aqueous ethanol) converts the C≡N group of pentanenitrile into a carboxylate a‑ion, releasing ammonia; after acid work‑up the product is sodium pentanoate. No special catalyst is required beyond the hydroxide.

Birch‑type dissolving‑metal reduction of pyridine to a 1,4‑dihydropyridine; sodium metal in liquid ammonia provides electrons, while a small amount of an alcohol (e.g., ethanol) serves as proton source. The reaction is performed at –33 °C under inert atmosphere, typically in a dry ammonia bath; no additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (sulfonyl azide synthesis). Sodium azide attacks methanesulfonic anhydride to give methanesulfonyl azide and sodium methanesulfonate. Typically performed an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere. No catalyst required. Used to prepare sulfonyl azides for azide‑transfer or click chemistry.

Oxidative cleavage of an alkene (permanganate oxidation). Trans‑β‑methylstyrene is oxidized by aqueous alkaline KMnO₄, breaking the C=C bond to afford acetaldehyde and benzaldehyde. Conducted in water or dilute alkaline solution, often heated to reflux. No additional catalyst; KMnO₄ acts as oxidant. Used to fragment alkenes into carbonyl fragments.

Acid dissolution of a silicate; magnesium trisilicate reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid, breaking the silicate framework to give soluble magnesium chloride and silicic acid (Si(OH)₄). Conducted in water with excess HCl, typically heated to reflux to ensure complete conversion. No catalyst needed; the reaction is driven by acid‑base neutralization and silicate hydrolysis.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Ethyl 2‑butoxyacetate reacts with NaOH, yielding ethanol and the sodium 2‑butoxyacetate salt. Typically carried out in aqueous NaOH/ethanol mixture, refluxing 1–2 h. No catalyst beyond NaOH. Produces carboxylate salt and liberates the alcohol.

Chlorination of boron sulfide (halogen exchange). Boron sulfide (B₂S₃) reacts with Cl₂ gas to form boron trichloride (BCl₃) and elemental sulfur. Conducted in the gas phase at elevated temperature (≈300 °C) under inert atmosphere. No solvent; reaction is driven by heat. Provides volatile BCl₃ and sulfur.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a heteroaromatic. 2‑Methylpyridine is hydrogenated with H₂ in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd, Raney Ni, or Pt) to give 2‑methylpiperidine. Reaction performed in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at 50–100 °C under 30–50 atm H₂ pressure. No other reagents. Reduces aromatic ring to saturated piperidine.

Double‑replacement precipitation. Lead(II) acetate in aqueous solution reacts with potassium bromide, precipitating insoluble lead(II) bromide while forming soluble potassium acetate. Performed at room temperature in water; the solid PbBr₂ is filtered off; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (thioether formation). Decanethiol is deprotonated (often with a mild base like triethylamine) to generate a thiolate that attacks ethyl bromide in an SN2 fashion, producing decyl ethyl sulfide and HBr. Conducted in an aprotic solvent (THF, DMF) at room temperature. No metal catalyst required. Used to synthesize alkyl thioethers.

SN2 alkylation of a thiol. Propyl mercaptan is deprotonated (e.g., with NaH, NaOH, or similar base) to generate a propyl thiolate, which attacks ethyl bromide in an SN2 displacement to give ethyl propyl sulfide and HBr. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetone at 0–50 °C; a base is required to form the nucleophilic thiolate.

Acid‑base neutralization / double displacement; used to convert soluble iodic acid into the sparingly soluble barium iodate salt; HIO3 proton transfers to OH forming water and Ba²⁺ combines with IO3⁻ to give Ba(IO3)2; performed in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Metathesis (cation exchange) double displacement; employed to swap sodium and potassium counter‑ions between carbonate and cyanate; Na2CO3 + 2 KOCN → K2CO3 + 2 NaOCN; carried out in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to improve solubility; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening (ammonolysis) of a strained oxabicyclic ether to yield an amino‑alcohol; gives 2‑aminocyclooctanol. Ammonia acts as nucleophile, attacking the electrophilic carbon of the oxabicyclic ether and opening the ring, forming a primary amine and a secondary alcohol on the eight‑membered ring. Typical conditions involve refluxing the substrate in aqueous ammonia or in liquid NH3 (or NH3 in MeOH) at 50‑80 °C; the reaction proceeds without metal catalyst, though the use of a small amount of acid or base can accelerate the opening.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis (SN2) of an alkyl aryl sulfonate; converts the sulfonate ester into 4‑methylbenzenesulfonic acid and releases the corresponding primary alcohol (3‑methyl‑1‑butanol); aqueous NaOH attacks the benzylic carbon, displacing the sulfonate group; typically reflux in water or mixed water/ethanol; NaOH serves as both reagent and catalyst; no additional catalyst required.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; purpose is to prepare lutetium triiodide; lutetium metal is oxidized from 0 to +3 while iodine is reduced to I⁻ forming LuI₃; typically carried out by heating elemental lutetium with excess iodine vapour in a sealed tube under inert atmosphere at 500–600 °C; no solvent required.

Acetylation of o-phenylenediamine via reaction with acetic anhydride, producing o-aminoacetanilide. One amine group acts as a nucleophile, opening the acetic anhydride ring to form an amide (acetanilide) while releasing acetic acid as a byproduct. The reaction often occurs under mild heating in a solvent like acetic acid or water, with acid catalysis (e.g., H2SO4) sometimes employed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (Williamson‑type esterification) of a carboxylate with an alkyl halide; sodium benzoate attacks n‑propyl bromide to give propyl benzoate and NaBr; carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as dry acetone or DMF to keep NaBr precipitated; reaction is heated under reflux; no catalyst is needed, the carboxylate anion is the nucleophile.

SN2 alkylation of a secondary amine; N‑methylpiperazine nucleophilically substitutes the bromide of benzyl bromide giving 1‑benzyl‑4‑methyl‑piperazine with concomitant formation of HBr; usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile, DMF) at 0 °C to room temperature; a mild base (e.g., NaHCO₃ or triethylamine) is often added to trap the released HBr; no metal catalyst required.

Knoevenagel condensation between paraformaldehyde (­dehyde source) and butyl 2‑cyanoacetate to afford butyl 2‑cyanoacrylate with loss of water; the activated methylene of the cyanoacetate is deprotonated by a weak base (piperidine, ammonium acetate) forming a carbanion that adds to the aldehyde, followed by elimination of water; typical conditions use ethanol or toluene as solvent, catalytic amount of base, and gentle heating with azeotropic removal of water; no transition‑metal catalyst needed.

Decarboxylation (dry distillation) of gallic acid to pyrogallol; used to synthesize pyrogallol from the natural phenolic acid. Key transformation: loss of a carboxyl group as CO₂, converting the benzoic acid ring to a trihydroxybenzene. Typical conditions: heating the solid at 200‑300 °C in a furnace or tube furnace often in the presence of a copper or metal oxide catalyst to promote CO₂ release. No solvent; reaction carried out in the gas‑phase or under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑fluorination (acid‑base) reaction of aluminum titanate with hydrofluoric acid; employed to convert the mixed oxide into aluminum fluoride and titanium dioxide. Key transformation: fluoride ions replace oxide ligands on aluminum, forming AlF₃ (often reported asF₆³⁻ in solution) and liberating water while Ti remains as TiO₂ solid. Typical conditions: aqueous HF (≈ 5‑10 M) at 50‑100 °C with vigorous stirring; reaction performed in PTFE‑lined equipment. No additional catalyst required.

Metathesis/complexation in aqueous solution to prepare ferric citrate and potassium nitrate. The nitrate anion exchanges with citrate to give the soluble ferric citrate complex, while K⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻. Conditions: dissolve iron(III) nitrate and potassium citrate in water, adjust pH to neutral‑slightly acidic, stir at ambient temperature or mild heating (30‑60 °C) until complete. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (organolithium alkylation of silicon). Used to form a Si–C bond and generate a trialkylsilane, often for protecting groups or organosilicon synthesis. The carbon‑lithium bond attacks bromotrimethylsilane, displacing bromide to give n‑butyltrimethylsilane and LiBr. Typically carried out in anhydrous THF at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen or argon, with strict exclusion of moisture; no additional catalyst is required.

Fluorination/halogen exchange; antimony tribromide is fluorinated by F₂ to give antimony trifluoride with bromine released, key replacement of bromide by fluoride; performed by exposing SbBr₃ to dilute F₂ gas at 0–25 °C in an inert carrier gas (e.g., N₂ or Ar); no solvent, strict safety controls, no catalyst.

Condensation dehydration of methacrylic acid to its anhydride. This is a typical acid‑anhydride formation used to obtain methacrylic anhydride for polymer chemistry. Key transformation: two carboxyl groups lose one molecule of water, forming the anhydride linkage. Typical conditions: excess methacrylic acid with a strong acid catalyst (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid or sulfuric acid) or a dehydrating agent such as DCC, heated at 80‑120 °C under reflux in toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water. Dry inert atmosphere is common.

Hydrolysis of a silyl ester; purpose is to cleave the Si–O bond and recover the free acid. Trimethylsilyl 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetate reacts with water to give trimethylsilanol and 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetic acid. The reaction is performed at rt in a polar aprotic solvent (THF, MeCN) with a slight excess of water; mild acid or base may be used to accelerate the cleavage.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of methyl gallate with dodecanol to give dodecyl gallate and methanol. Purpose: synthesis of long‑chain alkyl gallate esters for antioxidant or surfactant applications. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of dodecanol on the ester carbonyl, displacement of methanol. Typical conditions: NaOH (5‑10 mol % relative to ester) in a polar aprotic solvent such as tert‑butanol or a mixture of ethanol/water, reflux at 80‑100 °C, removal of methanol by azeotropic distillation or nitrogen sweep. Reaction proceeds until methanol evolution ceases.

Simple acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of hydrobromic acid with ethylamine to afford ethylammonium bromide. Used to generate the hygroscopic salt for various synthetic or analytical purposes. Conditions: mix aqueous HBr (or aqueous solution of HBr) ethylamine gas or aqueous ethylamine solution at 0‑25 °C, stir until gas evolution stops; the resulting solid can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Esterification (Fischer esterification); converts the primary alcohol 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol and acetic acid into the acetate ester 2‑(diethylamino)ethyl acetate with loss of water. Typically performed under reflux with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or using a Dean–Stark trap to remove water. Common solvents: toluene, benzene, or dichloromethane.
Thermal decomposition; heating lutetium carbonate converts it to lutetium oxide and releases CO₂; performed by calcination at 600‑1000 °C in a dry furnace; no solvent, no catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination; bisphenol A undergoes four successive brominations on the two phenolic rings in the presence of bromine and catalytic FeBr₃, yielding tetrabromobisphenol A and releasing HBr. Reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform or dichloromethane; FeBr₃ acts as Lewis‑acid catalyst to generate the electrophilic Br⁺ species.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) of a nucleobase; 5‑iodouracil reacts with silver fluoride, where F⁻ replaces the iodine atom to give 5‑fluorouracil and precipitates insoluble AgI. The reaction proceeds in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) at 80–120 °C under anhydrous conditions to drive the exchange. Silver iodide precipitates and is removed by filtration.

Oxidative cleavage/oxidation of 1‑chloropropylbenzene with hot aqueous potassium permanganate to produce 3‑phenylpropionic acid. The benzylic side chain is fully oxidized to a carboxylic acid while the chloride is displaced as KCl. Typical conditions: excess KMnO₄ (2–3 equiv) in alkaline aqueous solution (often NaOH) heated to reflux (≈80 °C) for several hours. After completion, the mixture is cooled, acidified (often with dilute H₂SO₄) to precipitate the acid, and the manganese dioxide by‑product is filtered off. No additional catalyst required.

Type: Double nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzylic bromides by ammonia (alkylation of ammonia). Purpose: synthesis of 1,3‑bis(aminomethyl)benzene (benzene‑1,3‑dimethanamine). Key transformation: each benlic bromomethyl group of 1,3‑bis(bromomethyl)benzene is displaced by an ammonia molecule, forming a primary amine and releasing hydrogen bromide. Typical conditions: excess liquid ammonia (or gaseous NH₃ under) at reflux temperature (≈−33 °C for liquid NH₃ or 80–100 °C in a sealed vessel), often in an inert solvent such as ethanol or THF. A base (e.g., excess ammonia) scavenges the generated HBr.

Double‑displacement precipitation with acid‑base decomposition; aqueous silver nitrate reacts with ammonium bicarbonate, forming insoluble silver carbonate precipitate and ammonium nitrate in solution; carbon dioxide evolves and water is produced; the reaction is performed at ambient temperature in water, without catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes benzyl salicylate, cleaving the ester bond to produce benzyl alcohol and the sodium salt of salicylic acid (sodium salicylate). Reaction carried out in aqueous NaOH solution, typically at 60–100 °C; after completion the mixture may be acidified to isolate benzyl alcohol, while sodium salicylate remains in the aqueous phase.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt hydrolysis); concentrated nitric acid reacts with aluminum metaphosphate, protonating the phosphate anion to form phosphoric acid and converting aluminum to aluminum nitrate. Performed in aqueous medium under reflux; the reaction proceeds readily at 80–120 °C, yielding soluble Al(NO₃)₃ and H₃PO₄ in the aqueous layer.

Condensation (acylhydrazide formation).boxlic acid reacts with hydrazine to give the corresponding hydrazide and water. Typically performed by refluxing butyric acid with an excess of hydrazine hydrate in anhydrous ethanol or methanol; sometimes a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., HCl) is added to promote activation of the carbonyl. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of hydrazine on the carbonyl, followed by loss of water.

Acid‑base metathesis; used to synthesize terbium fluoride (TbF₃), an important inorganic salt; Tb³⁺ replaces nitrate with fluoride ions from HF, forming solid TbF₃ and releasing HNO₃ into solution; conducted in dilute aqueous HF, often at low temperature (0–25 °C) to control HF volatility; water solvent, no catalyst, but careful HF handling required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement precipitation). Aqueous solutions zinc sulfate and ammonium pyrophosphate exchange anions to produce insoluble zinc pyrophosphate, which precipitates, while ammonium sulfate remains in solution. The mixture is stirred at ambient temperature or mildly heated; the solid product is filtered, washed and dried. No special catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) cyanation of an alkyl halide; converts ethyl bromide to ethyl cyanide by displacement of bromide with CuCN. Typically performed under reflux in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO; copper(I) cyanide acts as both cyanide source and catalyst; by‑product copper(I) bromide precipitates.

Nophilic substitution (SN2) to form a thioether. Pentane‑1‑thiol is deprotonated with a base such as NaH or NaOH to give the pentanethiolate, which attacks methyl iodide in an aprotic polar solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO, acetone) at 0 °C to room temperature. The reaction yields pentyl‑methyl sulfide and iodide ion; work‑up typically involves aqueous quench and extraction.

Electrophilic nitration (nitro‑esterification). Isosorbide mononitrate is converted to the dinitrate by reaction with dinitrogen pentoxide, a strong nitrating agent that generates the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺). The reaction is carried out at low temperature (0–5 °C) in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as nitromethane or dichloromethane under a dry atmosphere. Nitric acid is formed as a by‑product and is removed during work‑up.

Interesterification (acid‑catalyzed ester exchange). Propionic acid and butyl acetate undergo acyl‑group swapping to give butyl propionate and acetic acid. A solid acid catalyst such as Amberlyst‑15, sulfonated zeolite, or Nafion resin is employed, typically at 120–180 °C under solvent‑free conditions or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., toluene). Removal of the volatile acetic acid drives the equilibrium toward product formation.

Hydrolysis of phosphorus pentafluoride. PF₅ reacts rapidly with water to produce phosphoric acid and hydrogen fluoride. The reaction proceeds exothermically in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; excess water ensures complete conversion. No catalyst is required, but the mixture must be handled in corrosion‑ resistant equipment due to HF generation.

Ring‑opening polymerization of ethylene oxide initiated by ethylene glycol; a step‑growth oligomerization to give pentaethylene glycol (a diol). Purpose: synthesis of a defined oligomeric ethylene glycol chain. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the glycol hydroxyl on the epoxide ring, sequential opening of four ethylene oxide units. Typical conditions: anhydrous conditions, 120‑180 °C, often with a catalytic amount of alkali metal hydroxide (e.g., KOH) or an organic base; water‑free solvent such as toluene or performed bulk (solvent‑free). By‑product: none (polymer formed).

Conversion of a dicarboxylic acid (azelaic acid) to its acid chloride using thionyl chloride; an acid‑chloride formation (chlorination) reaction. Purpose: activation of the carboxyl groups for subsequent coupling (esterification, amide formation). Key transformation: replacement of the –OH of each –COOH with –Cl, generating azelaic acid dichloride. By‑products: gaseous HCl and SO₂. Typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, addition of a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl; temperature 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of octan‑3‑yl acetate. Purpose: liberate 3‑octanol and acetic acid. Key transformation: acetate ester cleavage, R‑OCOCH₃ → R‑OH + CH₃COOH. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) at 70‑100 °C. Solvent: water or water/tert‑butanol; acid serves as catalyst.

Carbamoylation of 1‑naphthol with N‑methylcarbamoyl chloride to afford carbaryl (1‑naphthyl N‑methylcarbamate); an esterification that forms a carbamate linkage. Purpose: preparation of the insecticide carbaryl. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the phenolic oxygen on the carbonyl carbon of the carbamoyl chloride, displacement of chloride as HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, presence of a base (pyridine) to capture HCl. Work‑up includes aqueous wash to remove pyridinium chloride.

Reduction of 3‑iodopropanoic acid with lithium aluminium hydride to give 3‑iodopropan‑1‑ol; a selective carboxylic‑acid reduction to primary alcohol. Purpose: preparation of an iodo‑functionalized alcohol for further substitution chemistry. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, converting –CO₂H to –CH₂OH while the iodine substituent remains unchanged. Typical conditions: dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C addition followed by reflux; reaction quenched with aqueous acid (e.g., dilute HCl) to decompose excess LiAlH₄.

Skraup quinoline synthesis; aniline, glycerol, concentrated H2SO4 and nitrobenzene undergo acid‑catalyzed dehydration of glycerol to acrolein, condensation with aniline, and oxidative cyclization to quinoline; purpose is construction of the quinoline heterocycle; conditions: neat mixture, 120–140 °C, nitrobenzene as oxidant, sulfuric acid as catalyst/media; water released as by‑product.

N‑acylation (carbamation) of aniline with ethyl chloroformate; forms ethyl N‑phenylcarbamate and releases HCl; usually carried out in an aprotic solvent (dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to rt in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or NaHCO₃) to capture the generated HCl; the base also promotes nucleophilic attack of the amine on the carbonyl carbon.

Strong reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine (LiAlH₄ reduction); 2‑(4‑methylphenyl)acetonitrile is reduced to 2‑(4‑methylphenyl)ethanamine. Conditions: LiAlH₄ (2–3 eq) added to a dry THF solution of the nitrile at 0 °C, then reflux 2–4 h; after completion, quench cautiously with aqueous NH₄Cl or dilute acid, filter off aluminium hydroxide salts, and extract the amine.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between potassium iodide and mercuric sulfate in aqueous solution, forming insoluble mercury(II) iodide and soluble potassium sulfate. Purpose: synthesis of HgI₂, often for analytical uses. Key transformation: exchange of anions (I⁻ for SO₄²⁻). Typical conditions: aqueous medium, ambient temperature, stirring; product precipitates as bright red HgI₂ crystals which are filtered, washed, and dried. No special catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of epibromohydrin by methanol to give glycidyl methyl ether; purpose is preparation of a monofunctional epoxy ether; key step is attack of methanol on the bromine‑bearing carbon, displacement of bromide as HBr while the epoxide ring remains intact; typically performed by refluxing excess dry methanol, often with a base such‑as pyridine or triethylamine to trap the liberated HBr; methanol serves as both reagent and solvent.

Redox reduction of Cr(VI) in barium chromate by sodium dithionite, concurrently oxidizing dithionite to sulfate and precipitating barium sulfate; purpose is conversion of toxic hexavalent chromium to trivalent chromium and analytical removal of BaSO₄; key transformations: S₂O₄²⁻ → 2 SO₄²⁻, CrO₄²⁻ → Cr³⁺ which forms Cr₂(SO₄)₃; carried out in aqueous solution, usually under mildly acidic conditions (pH 2–4) at room temperature; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Amide formation by direct amidation; 2‑ethoxybenzoic acid reacts with ammonium hydroxide to give 2‑ethoxybenzamide and water; the carboxyl group is activated by heating with excess aqueous ammonia, often under reflux (≈120‑130 °C) and sometimes with a coupling agent (e.g., EDC/HOBt) or a dehydrating agent such as DCC to improve yield; solvent is typically water or a water‑ethanol mixture.

Acidcatalyzed hydrolysis of (4‑methoxyphenyl)methyl benzoate to benzoic acid and 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol; purpose is deprotection of the benzoate ester; key step is cleavage of the ester C–O bond by water, giving the carboxylic acid and the benzyl alcohol; performed by refluxing the ester in aqueous strong acid (e.g., 6 M HCl) or by base‑mediated saponification (NaOH) followed by acid work‑up; solvent mixture of water with a miscible organic co‑solvent (e.g., ethanol) is common; acid or base acts as catalyst.

Zinc‑mediated reduction of nitrocyclohexane to cyclohexylamine in glacial acetic acid; purpose is conversion of a nitro compound to the corresponding primary amine; key steps: nitro group (‑NO₂) is reduced stepwise to ‑NH₂ while Zn is oxidized to Zn²⁺ forming zinc acetate; reaction is run by adding zinc powder to a refluxing solution of nitrocyclohexane in excess acetic acid (6 equiv), typically for 2–4 h; acetic acid acts as solvent and proton source; no external catalyst is needed.

SN2 alkylation of ethanethiol with propyl trifluoromethanesulfonate to afford ethyl‑propyl sulfide; purpose is synthesis of a thioether; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the thiolate (generated in situ from the thiol) on the electrophilic propyl carbon, displacing triflate and generating trifluoromethanesulfonic acid; reaction performed at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere, often in an aprotic polar solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with a mild base (e.g., triethylamine) to neutralize the formed HOTf; no metal catalyst required.

Carbothermal reduction of molybdenum nitride with carbon to produce molybdenum carbide and nitrogen gas; solid‑state high‑temperature synthesis, typically heated to 1100–1500 °C under an inert atmosphere (Ar or N₂) with intimately mixed powders, no solvent, often in a graphite crucible.

Hydride reduction of benzoin to hydrobenzoin using lithium aluminum hydride; LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl of the α‑hydroxyketone, converting it to a 1,2‑diol; performed in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, followed by aqueous acidic work‑up.

Oxidation of a vicinal diol to a diketone using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); pentane‑2,3‑diol is converted to pentane‑2,3‑dione; typically performed in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; PCC serves as the oxidant; no additional catalyst required.

Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis; purpose is to break down isocyanic acid; key transformation: H2O attacks the carbonyl carbon of HNCO leading to cleavage into CO2 and NH3; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating; common solvent: water, no catalyst required.

Solid‑state acid‑base synthesis of lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4); a neutralization/precipitation reaction where phosphoric acid reacts with lithium hydroxide and iron(II) oxide to form water and the battery cathode material LiFePO4. Typically carried out by grinding the solid reactants together and heating at 700–800 °C in an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon); no solvent, catalyst not required.

Double‑replacement metathesis in water giving silver phosphate precipitate and sodium chloride; Na₃PO₄ reacts with AgCl to form insoluble Ag₃PO₄ and soluble NaCl; performed at room temperature with stirring, then the yellow Ag₃PO₄ is filtered and washed.

Jones oxidation of 1‑octen‑3‑ol to 1‑octen‑3‑one using chromium trioxide and sulfuric acid; Cr(VI) oxidizes the secondary allylic alcohol to the corresponding ketone; typically done in acetone (or dichloromethane) with dilute H₂SO₄ at 0‑25 °C, quenched with methanol or isopropanol.

Nef reaction (base‑induced cleavage of a nitroalkane); nitroethane is deprotonated with a strong base such as NaOH to give a nitronate ion, then acidified (e.g., with HCl) to afford acetaldehyde and nitrous acid (HNO2). Conducted in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solvent at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no catalyst.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis (calcination); purpose is the preparation of the spinel magnesium aluminate (MgAl2O4). A intimate mixture of MgCO3 (or MgO) and Al2O3 is heated to 1300–1500 °C for several hours in air or an inert atmosphere. During heating MgCO3 decomposes to MgO and CO2, and MgO reacts with Al2O3 to give MgAl2O4 while releasing CO2 gas. No solvent or catalyst is employed; the reaction proceeds in the solid state.

Acid–base metathesis (ion exchange). Proton transfer from sulfuric acid to acetate converts acetate to acetic acid while tetramethylammonium cation pairs with hydrogen sulfate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water or dilute methanol serves as solvent.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a benzylic bromide with aqueous ammonia; converts the bromomethyl group to an aminomethyl group on the pyridine ring, producing 3-(aminomethyl)pyridine and ammonium bromide. Typically performed by refluxing the bromide in water or a water‑ethanol mixture with excess NH3 (aq); the reaction proceeds at ambient to reflux temperature and requires no additional catalyst.
Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of 2,3‑oxiranedione; heating in the gas phase or sealed tube; the unstable anhydride breaks down to carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide gases.

Acid–base protonation; hydrogen iodide protonates triethylamine to give the ammonium salt triethylammonium iodide. Typically performed in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Gas‑solid single displacement (metal‑acid) reaction; purpose is to produce beryllium sulfide and liberate hydrogen gas. Key transformation: 2 Be(s) + H₂S(g) → BeS(s) + H₂(g). Typical conditions: heating the metal in a flow of H₂S at 300–500 °C, sometimes under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation. No solvent; no catalyst required.

Oxidation–reduction (acid oxidation). Concentrated nitric acid oxidizes arsenite (As^III) to monosodium arsenate (As^V) while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas and water. Carried out in aqueous solution, usually with heating; no additional catalyst; water is the reaction medium.

Oxide–acid reaction (neutralization). Calcium oxide (quicklime) reacts exothermically with glycolic acid, forming calcium 2‑hydroxyacetate and water. Reaction is conducted with careful addition of the acid to powdered CaO in a dry or minimally wet medium, often at 0–25 °C to control heat; the product is typically isolated from the slurry after cooling.

Hydrolysis of anhydrous phosphate. Aluminum metaphosphate reacts with water to yield phosphoric acid and insoluble aluminum phosphate precipitate. Typically performed by stirring the phosphate in water with gentle heating; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.
Double displacement reaction; formation of lead (II) bromide precipitate; ammonium and lead exchange anions; conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; water as solvent.

Reductive amination of benzaldehyde with methylamine using sodium cyanoborohydride; the aldehyde carbonyl is reduced after imine formation, affording N‑methylbenzylamine. Typical conditions: MeOH or EtOH as solvent, pH adjusted to ~5–6 with acetic acid, temperature 0 °C to rt, NaBH₃CN (1.2–1.5 eq) added slowly; no external metal catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; ammonium dihydrogen phosphate reacts with cobalt(II) nitrate in water, exchanging ions to produce soluble ammonium nitrate and insoluble cobalt(II) phosphate, which precipitates. Performed at room temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst required.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (acyl substitution). Methanol attacks pivaloyl chloride, displacing chloride to give methyl pivalate ester and hydrogen chloride. Usually carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to trap HCl. No additional catalyst needed.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation (E2) of 1,2‑dibromoethane with sodium ethoxide; ethoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen, eliminating HBr to give bromoethene (vinyl bromide) while the liberated HBr is neutralized by NaOEt to form ethanol and NaBr; typically performed in anhydrous ethanol under reflux.

Iron(III)‑catalyzed oxidative hydroxylation of quinoline using hydrogen peroxide; FeCl₃ generates •OH radicals that functionalize the C‑2 position of quinoline to afford 2‑hydroxyquinoline with water as by‑product; carried out in aqueous solution (often acidic) at ambient to mild‑heat temperatures.

Reductive chlorination (hydrogen reduction) of tantalum(V) chloride; used to access lower‑valent tantalum halides. H₂ gas reduces TaCl₅ to TaCl₃ while generating HCl. Conducted in a sealed tube or flow reactor at 400–600 °C under a stream of H₂ (often diluted with an inert gas such as Ar). No solvent; solid‑state reaction. No catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1,2‑dichloropropane with sodium hydrosulfide; two equivalents of HS⁻ replace the chloride atoms, yielding 1,2‑propanedithiol and NaCl; the reaction is usually run in aqueous ethanol or water/ethanol mixture with gentle heating.

Oxidation of strontium sulfide to strontium sulfate by hydrogen peroxide; H₂O₂ supplies oxygen atoms, converting S²⁻ to SO₄²⁻ while producing water; performed in aqueous media, often at elevated temperature (50‑80 °C) with excess peroxide.

Redox oxidation of thulium metal by nitric acid; thulium is oxidized to thulium(III) nitrate while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide and water; carried out in aqueous HNO₃ (2–6 M) with gentle heating, no catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (acidol of cyclohexyl acetate; catalytic H₂SO₄ protonates the carbonyl, water attacks, and the ester splits to give cyclohexanol and acetic acid; reflux in aqueous sulfuric acid solution is typical.

Metathesis (acid‑base exchange) between trifluoroacetic acid and lead(II) acetate; the acids swap anions to form lead(II) trifluoroacetate and acetic acid; generally carried out at room temperature in a polar solvent such as water or acetonitrile.

Double displacement/acid‑base neutralization and precipitation; used to remove aluminum ions from solution. Carbonate ion neutralizes acidic aluminum sulfate, generating carbon dioxide gas, water, soluble sodium sulfate and insoluble aluminum hydroxide precipitate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Single‑displacement/redox reaction: metallic lanthanum is oxidized by water to form lanthanum(III) hydroxide while water is reduced to hydrogen gas. Purpose is to prepare the hydroxide or liberate H2. Key transformation: La → La³⁺ + 3 e⁻, H₂O + e⁻ → ½ H₂ + OH⁻. Typically carried out with powdered lanthanum in water; reaction is slow at room temperature but accelerates with heating or steam (reflux). No catalyst required; solvent is water (aqueous medium).

Acid‑base double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to prepare selenic acid while precipitating calcium sulfate; anion exchange between SeO4²⁻ and SO4²⁻; carried out in aqueous solution with excess concentrated H₂SO₄, often warmed to encourage CaSO₄ precipitation; water solvent, no catalyst required.

Combustion/oxidation reaction; oxidation of tetraphosphorus trisulfide (P4S3) by molecular oxygen. The phosphorus‑sulfur bonds are broken, forming tetraphosphorus hexoxide (P4O6) and sulfur dioxide; elemental sulfur may also be produced. Conducted at elevated temperature (200‑400 °C) in the gas phase or a sealed tube; no catalyst, inert carrier gas (e.g., N2) be used.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of carbamoyl chloride with aniline to form phenylurea; aniline attacks the carbonyl, chloride is expelled as HCl; reaction is usually conducted in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to 25 °C with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl.

Catalytic oxidative dehydrogenation (oxidation) of carboxylic acids; converts butyric acid to the α‑unsaturated but‑2‑enoic (crotonic) acid while reducing O2 to water. Requires a metal‑oxide catalyst (e.g., CuO, V2O5) and high temperature (300‑500 °C) in the gas phase or in a high‑pressure reactor; inert solvent such as toluene can be employed if run in liquid phase.

Nitro‑bromo condensation synthesis of bronopol (2‑bromo‑2‑nitro‑1,3‑propane‑diol); glycerol reacts with bromine in the presence of sodium nitrite (source of nitrous acid) under acidic aqueous conditions. The process introduces a bromine and a nitro group onto the glycerol backbone, yielding bronopol and sodium bromide, with water formed from neutralization. Typically run at 0‑5 °C to control exotherm, in water or aqueous acetic acid; no additional catalyst required.

Redox disproportionation of nitrogen oxides in basic medium; dinitrogen tetroxide reacts with potassium hydroxide to give potassium nitrate (oxidized nitrogen), potassium nitrite (reduced nitrogen) and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; excess KOH ensures complete conversion; no catalyst is needed.

Acid-base reaction; carbonate reacts with strong acid to give a soluble metal chloride, carbon dioxide gas and water; typically performed in aqueous solution with excess hydrochloric acid at ambient or gently refluxed temperature; no special catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid (Pinnick oxidation). Sodium chlorite oxidizes cyclopropanecarboxaldehyde, while catalytic hydrogen peroxide re‑oxidizes hypochlorous species. By‑products are water and sodium chloride. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 3–4, NaH₂PO₄), NaClO₂ (1–2 equiv), 0.5 equiv H₂O₂, room temperature to 40 °C, mixed organic/aqueous solvent such as THF/H₂O.

Conversion of a primary alcohol to an alkyl chloride using phosphorus trichloride. Three molecules of 1‑decanol react with PCl₃, undergoing an SN2 substitution to give three equivalents of decyl chloride and phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃) as the stoichiometric by‑product. Reaction is usually performed under anhydrous conditions in a dry ether or dichloromethane solvent, often with pyridine or a tertiary amine to scavenge HCl, at 0 °C to reflux.

Acid–base metathesis (double displacement) between zinc ricinoleate and sodium hydroxide. The zinc carboxylate exchanges its cation with Na⁺, producing insoluble zinc hydroxide precipitate and two equivalents of sodium ricinoleate in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; the mixture is typically stirred until Zn(OH)₂ precipitates, then filtered.

Thermal decarboxylation of a β‑keto acid. Purpose: generate the conjugated ketone 3‑buten‑2‑one from 2‑oxo‑4‑pentenoic acid. Key transformation: loss of CO₂ from the β‑keto acid furnishes the vinyl ketone. Typical conditions: the β‑keto acid is heated neat or in a high‑boiling solvent such as xylene at 150–200 °C, often without additional catalyst; sometimes a solid acid (e.g., CuO) is employed to promote decarboxylation.

Oxidation (hydroboration‑oxidation) of vinylborane: the organoborane undergoes oxidative cleavage with hydrogen peroxide in a basic medium to afford ethanol and boric acid. Typical conditions involve adding H₂O₂ (30 % aq.) to a solution of vinylborane in THF or ether, with NaOH or KOH as base, at 0‑25 °C.

Nucleophilic addition of a Grignard reagent to an acid chloride to afford a ketone. Methylmagnesium bromide adds to trifluoroacetyl chloride, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses on work‑up to give 1,1,1‑trifluoroacetone. Performed under anhydrous conditions in dry diethyl ether or THF, usually at 0 °C to –20 °C during addition, then allowed to warm to room temperature before aqueous quench.

Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzyl chloride with ethylamine to form N‑benzylethanamine and HCl. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; a base (e.g., triethylamine, pyridine) is added to trap the generated HCl. Purpose: synthesize a secondary amine via alkylation of a primary amine.

Alkylation of a carboxylate (SN2 ester formation); purpose to synthesize a methyl ester; key transformation: sodium propanoate nucleophilically substitutes methyl iodide, giving methyl propanoate and NaI; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO), reflux, dry, often with excess alkyl halide.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; purpose is to exchange cyanide for chloride producing insoluble copper(I) cyanide; key transformation: Cu⁺ exchanges its chloride for cyanide ion, forming CuCN(s) and NaCl in solution; typical condition: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; common solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of methyl bromide with ammonia to give methylamine. Key transformation: CH₃Br + NH₃ → CH₃NH₂ + HBr. Performed in excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃ (or NH₃ in ethanol) at 0–50 °C; the HBr formed is often neutralized by an added base (e.g., NaOH) or the product isolated as the hydrochloride salt.

Palladium‑catalyzed hydrocyanation of 1,3‑butadiene; purpose is to synthesize allyl cyanide (3‑butenenitrile). Key transformation is the addition of HCN across the diene to give a terminal nitrile. Typically generated in situ from PdCl2 and PPh3 (forming a Pd(0)–phosphine complex), carried out under anhydrous conditions in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or toluene, often at 0 °C to 25 °C and under a slight pressure of HCN gas.

Halogen exchange (F‑for‑Cl) at the α‑carbon of chloroacetic acid; nucleophilic substitution of chloride by fluoride to afford fluoroacetic acid. Usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or DMF) with potassium fluoride as the fluoride source, heated gently (40–80 °C) to drive the reaction to completion, and yields potassium chloride as the inorganic by‑product.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; exchange of anions between sodium chloride and ammonium bromide to form ammonium chloride and sodium bromide; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required; used for salt preparation or purification.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) where chloroacetyl chloride reacts with pyrrolidin‑1‑amine to give N‑(chloroacetyl)pyrrolidine and HCl; usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or TEA) is added neutralize the generated HCl; purpose is synthesis of a chloro‑acetyl‑substituted heterocyclic amide.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); converts 1‑bromo‑3‑fluoropropane to the azide for downstream click‑type transformations; the bromide is displaced by N₃⁻ giving 1‑azido‑3‑fluoropropane and NaBr; typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 50‑80 °C with excess NaN₃, under anhydrous conditions.

Nucleophilic substitution (Williamson‑type thioether synthesis) where two equivalents of 2‑bromobutane react with sodium sulfide to afford sec‑butyl sulfide and two equivalents of sodium bromide; conducted in polar aprotic solvents like DMF or DMSO, often under reflux; inorganic base (Na2S) provides sulfide nucleophile; useful for constructing thioethers.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification); fluoroacetic acid is activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) and coupled with 2‑ethylhexanol to form 2‑ethylhexyl fluoroacetate, with dicyclohexylurea as by‑product; reaction performed in dry dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, typically with a catalytic amount of DMAP to accelerate acyl transfer; employed for preparing fluorinated esters under conditions.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride to 1,1‑dichloropropene (rohalogenation); adds HCl across the C=C bond to give 1,1,2‑trichloropropane. Typical conditions involve bubbling HCl gas into the alkene in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often at reflux temperature (≈ 60 °C) to ensure complete addition.

Redox disproportionation/oxidation where hydrogen peroxide oxidizes potassium chlorite to potassium chlorate, producing water as the only other product; performed in aqueous solution, often mildly acidic, and may be heated to accelerate the reaction; no special catalyst is needed; used in analytical chemistry for generating chlorate or in waste‑treatment processes.

Nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus (S_N2) where azide from silver azide displaces chloride of O,O‑diphenyl phosphorochloridate, precipitating AgCl and yielding diphenyl azidophosphate. Performed in anhydrous polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; silver chloride is removed by filtration.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); converts hexyl 2‑methylprop‑2‑enoate into methacrylic acid and hexanol; typically performed by refluxing the ester with aqueous strong acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄ or HCl) in water or a water‑organic mixture; no special catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Esterification (condensation) of sulfurous acid with ethanol to give diethyl sulfite and water. Conducted by bubbling SO₂ gas into excess ethanol (often with a catalytic amount of mineral acid) and refluxing; water formed is removed by azeotropic distillation or using a Dean‑Stark trap. Typical solvent is the ethanol itself; temperature 60–80 °C.

Aqueous double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction between silver nitrate and hydrazine sulfate exchanging anions, producing only slightly soluble silver sulfate (Ag₂SO₄) which precipitates and hydrazinium nitrate remaining in solution. Carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid Ag₂SO₄ is filtered off.

Hydrolysis of a phosphorochloridate; water attacks the phosphorus center, replacing the Cl with OH to give diethyl hydrogen phosphate and HCl. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature or mild heating; no catalyst required, but buffering may be used to control acidity.

Jones oxidation: primary alcohol of but‑2‑yn‑1‑ol is oxidized by chromium(VI) reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄ in acetone) to the corresponding carboxylic acid, but‑2‑ynoic acid, while the alkyne moiety is retained. Reaction is run at 0 °C to room temperature, typically with 1.5–2 equiv of Jones reagent, then quenched with isopropanol or methanol.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of one aryl chloride in 1,2‑dichlorobenzene, replacing Cl with H to give chlorobenzene and HCl. Conducted under H₂ pressure (5–50 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or Pt‑O₂ at 100–200 °C in a solvent like ethanol, THF or acetic acid. The generated HCl is usually removed in the gas stream.

Nucleophilic halogen‑cyanide displacement forming cyanogen iodide. I₂ reacts with KCN in aqueous or alcoholic solution (often in the dark, 0–25 °C) to give KI and ICN. The reaction is fast; ICN can be extracted into organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) for use as a cyanogenating agent.

Thiocyanate‑to‑isothiocyanate rearrangement: methyl thiocyanate is isomerized to methyl isothiocyanate; type – S‑N isomerization (thermal or Lewis‑acid catalyzed); purpose – preparation of the isothiocyanate functional group; key transformation – CH3–S–C≡N → CH3–N=C=S; typical conditions – heating to 150–200 °C or using a Lewis acid such as AlCl3, ZnCl2, or CuCl in anhydrous solvent (toluene, dichloromethane) under reflux.

Acid leaching with sulfuric acid; purpose is to produce soluble nickel sulfate and H₂S gas from the sulfide. NiS reacts with aqueous H₂SO₄, yielding NiSO₄ in solution and H₂S. Conducted at 60–100 °C in dilute to concentrated sulfuric acid; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis: 3‑methyl‑3‑butenyl acetate reacts with water to give 3‑methyl‑3‑buten‑1‑ol and acetic acid; type – hydrolysis (saponification) of an acetate ester; purpose – cleavage of the ester bond to regenerate the alcohol and acid; key transformation – ester + H2O → corresponding alcohol + acetic acid; typical conditions – aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M H2SO4) or base (NaOH) at reflux; often performed in a water‑organic biphasic system (toluene, THF) to improve phase contact.

LiAlH4 reduction of an ester: hexyl acetate is reduced to ethanol (from the acyl fragment) and 1‑hexanol (from the alkoxy fragment); type – strong reduction of an ester to two primary alcohols; purpose – conversion of both ester moieties into alcohols; key transformation – RCOOR' + LiAlH4 → RCH2OH + R'CH2OH; typical conditions – anhydrous ether or THF, reflux under inert atmosphere, followed by cautious quench with water and dilute acid.

Fischer esterification: benzoic acid reacts with 2‑ethylhexanol to form 2‑ethylhexyl benzoate and water; type – condensation (esterification) of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol; purpose – synthesis of the ester; key transformation – RCOOH + R'OH → RCOOR' + H2O; typical conditions – excess 2‑ethylhexanol, catalytic amount of strong acid (H2SO4 or p‑TsOH), reflux (≈120–130 °C); removal of water by Dean‑Stark or azeotropic distillation, solvent may be the alcohol itself or toluene.

Acid‑base salt metathesis: zinc selenite reacts with hydrochloric acid to give selenous acid and zinc chloride; type – protonation of a metal selenite (acid‑base reaction); purpose – generation of aqueous H2SeO3; key transformation – ZnSeO3 + 2 HCl → H2SeO3 + ZnCl2; typical conditions – aqueous solution at ambient temperature or gentle heating; water is the solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Solid-state acid‑base/decomposition reaction; lithium carbonate reacts with tungsten trioxide at high temperature (≈800‑900 °C) in a dry solid mixture to yield lithium tungstate (Li₂WO₄) and release CO₂; no solvent, often performed in a furnace with thorough grinding of the powders.

Anion exchange (metathesis) between 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium bromide and potassium acetate. In a polar protic solvent such as water or methanol, acetate replaces bromide to give 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium acetate and potassium bromide. The reaction is usually stirred at 50‑80 °C; the solid KBr can be filtered off and the ionic liquid isolated. No catalyst is needed.

High‑temperature solid‑state ceramic synthesis; mixed oxides of lead carbonate, TiO₂ and ZrO₂ are intimately ground and calcined/sintered at 1200‑1300 °C to form the perovskite ferroelectric material lead zirconate titanate (PZT); the process involves diffusion of cations in the solid state, no solvents, occasionally a brief pre‑calcination step.

Free‑radical hydrogen‑atom transfer (radical substitution) using tributyltin hydride as a hydrogen donor and AIBN as radical initiator; the bromide substrate is reduced to the alkene 2‑methylprop‑1‑ene while forming tributyltin bromide; typically carried out under reflux in an inert organic solvent such as toluene or benzene at 80‑110 °C under nitrogen.

Acid‑base displacement (gas‑generating) reaction; sulfuric acid protonates sodium hydrogen difluoride, converting it to hydrofluoric acid (HF) and sodium hydrogen sulfate; performed in aqueous medium or with concentrated acids at low to moderate temperature, with careful temperature control to contain the evolved HF gas; no catalyst required.

Neutralization (acid‑base) reaction; aqueous sodium hydroxide is added slowly to aqua regia (a mixture of HCl and HNO₃), quenching the mixture and producing water, sodium chloride and sodium nitrate; the addition is done in an ice bath or with cooling due to the exothermic nature; carried out in water, no catalyst needed.

Alkali‑mediated hydrolysis/salt formation; maleic anhydride reacts with sodium carbonate aqueous solution (often warmed to 80‑100 °C) to give disodium 2‑butenedioate (sodium maleate) together with CO₂ and H₂O; this is an acid‑base reaction that opens the anhydride ring; no additional catalyst required.

Thermal decarboxylation of an aromatic carboxylic acid; salicylic acid loses CO₂ to afford phenol; usually requires heating to 200–250 °C, often in the presence of a metal‑oxide catalyst such as CuO or ZnO (or under basic conditions); the reaction can be run neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., diphenyl ether); no solvent or catalyst is strictly required if performed in the melt.

Esterification (Fischer esterification); converts one hydroxyl of ethylene glycol into an acetate ester to give 2‑acetoxyethanol and water; typically catalyzed by a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄), refluxed in anhydrous acetic acid or toluene with Dean‑Stark water removal.

Nucleophilic substitution/cyclization (thiolysis); potassium sulfide attacks the two bromomethylene carbons of 1,2‑dibromoethane, displacing bromide and forming the three‑membered episulfide ring (ethylene sulfide) with 2 KBr as by‑product; carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at elevated temperature.

Salt metathesis (double‑displacement precipitation); calcium chloride exchanges cations with lithium succinate, producing sparingly soluble calcium succinate (precipitates) and soluble lithium chloride; performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating and stirring to aid precipitation.

Direct metal oxidation; elemental niobium reacts with molecular oxygen to form niobium monoxide (NbO); requires high temperature (typically >800 °C) in a flow of dry O₂ or air, sometimes under inert‑gas protection before ignition.

Aminolysis (ammonolysis) of an ester; reaction of ethyl cyclopentanecarboxylate with ammonia gives cyclopentanecarboxamide and ethanol. Usually carried out by refluxing the ester in excess aqueous or alcoholic ammonia (often 2–5 M NH3) for several hours. The reaction may be performed in ethanol or MeOH as solvent; excess ammonia drives the equilibrium toward amide formation.

Ester hydrolysis (acidic or neutral aqueous hydrolysis); the acetate ester of methylazoxymethanol is cleaved by water to yield free methylazoxymethanol and acetic acid; usually carried out in aqueous buffer or mild acid at room temperature or slight heating.

Double‑displacement precipitation/acid‑base reaction; ammonium bifluoride supplies fluoride which reacts with lanthanum nitrate to precipitate insoluble lanthanum trifluoride, while NH₄⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to give ammonium nitrate and HF is liberated; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with stirring and filtration to collect LaF₃.

Acid‑base precipitation reaction; HF is neutralized by Ca(OH)₂, yielding insoluble CaF₂ precipitate and water. Typically carried out in water at room temperature; the solid CaF₂ is filtered off, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization (dissolution) reaction; converts solid iron(II) hydroxide into soluble iron(II) chloride while generating water; Fe(OH)₂ reacts with HCl, protonating OH⁻ to form H₂O and pairing Fe²⁺ with Cl⁻; typically conducted in aqueous solution at 0 °C to 25 °C; dilute HCl is added slowly to the suspension with stirring; water is the medium, no catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis; used to produce the ether 2‑ethoxy‑2‑methylbutane; nucleophilic substitution of chloroethane by sodium 2‑methyl‑2‑butoxide giving the ether and NaCl; typically carried out in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (THF, DME) under inert atmosphere with mild heating (40‑80 °C); no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to cleave the ester bond to give the corresponding carboxylate salt and alcohol; key transformation: cyclobutylmethyl acetate + OH⁻ → cyclobutylmethanol + acetate ion; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 1–3 h; solvent mixture often water/ethanol or water alone; work‑up involves acidification to isolate the alcohol.

Enzymatic transamination (aminotransferase reaction); 4‑hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid transfers its keto group to L‑glutamate, forming 4‑hydroxyphenylglycine and α‑ketoglutarate; requires pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate (PLP) as cofactor; carried out in aqueous phosphate buffer (pH 7.5–8.0) at 30–37 °C, often with recombinant aromatic amino‑acid aminotransferase.

Acid‑base/complexation (salt formation); preparation of bismuth subsalicylate, the active ingredient in some antacids; salicylic acid deprotonates and coordinates to Bi(III) from bismuth subnitrate, releasing nitric acid and water; performed in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol medium, heated to reflux with slight acid pH; no special catalyst.

Acid‑base conversion of potassium tellurite with sulfuric acid to give tellurous acid and potassium sulfate; conducted in water, often with gentle heating to complete the reaction; no catalyst employed.

Acid‑base neutralization; conversion of ammonium hydrogen phosphate to phosphoric acid and ammonium iodide; proton transfer from hydroiodic acid to the phosphate and ammonium ion exchange; simply dissolve the solids in water and stir at ambient temperature; aqueous solution, no catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (cyanation of anhydride); cyanide attacks one carbonyl of acetic anhydride producing acetyl cyanide and acetate ion which pairs with Na⁺; carried out in dry aprotic solvent such as DMF or THF at 0‑25 °C to avoid side reactions; NaCN is the nucleophile, no additional catalyst.

Redox oxidation of silicon by oxygen difluoride; silicon is oxidized to silicon tetrafluoride while OF₂ is reduced, liberating O₂; gas‑phase reaction at elevated temperature (≈300‑600 °C) in a flow or sealed reactor; no solvent, excess OF₂ often used; no catalyst.

Esterification with diazomethane (Schiemann methylation); pyridine‑4‑carboxylic acid reacts with diazomethane to give methyl pyridine‑4‑carboxylate and N₂ gas; performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or hexane) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; diazomethane is the reagent, no catalyst.

Double displacement precipitation; purpose is to prepare lead azide, a primary explosive; key transformation is exchange of bromide and azide ions forming insoluble lead azide and soluble sodium bromide; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring, followed by filtration; no catalyst required; water is the common solvent.

Acid–base displacement (salt metathesis) reaction; concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium bromide to liberate hydrogen bromide gas and form sodium hydrogen sulfate (or sodium sulfate with excess acid); used generate anhydrous HBr gas for synthesis; carried out by adding NaBr to cold (0–5 °C) conc. H₂SO₄ in a dry apparatus, avoiding high temperature that could oxidize Br⁻ to Br₂; no solvent or catalyst, but temperature control is critical.

Acid‑base neutralization; forms ammonium formate salt; key step is proton transfer from formic acid to ammonia producing the ionic ammonium cation and formate anion; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst needed; water acts as the solvent.

Double displacement metathesis precipitation; aqueous solution; fluoride ion replaces chloride to give sparingly soluble TbF3 and soluble KCl; often conducted with excess KF to drive reaction to completion; ambient temperature, water as solvent, no catalyst.

Metal‑mediated reductive dehalogenation of 3‑chloro‑1H‑indole using zinc dust in acetic acid; the zinc reduces the C–Cl bond, generating indole and zinc acetate while liberating HCl. Usually performed by refluxing the substrate with excess Zn powder in glacial acetic acid (or a mixture of acetic acid and water) for several hours under nitrogen to avoid oxidation of the metal.

Acid‑base reaction with strong mineral acid; conc. sulfuric acid protonates the carboxylate to liberate hexanoic acid while forming ammonium sulfate; usually done in aqueous or mixed solvent, temperature 0‑50 °C to avoid side reactions; no catalyst.

Grignard addition to an aldehyde; synthesizes a secondary allylic alcohol (but‑3‑en‑2‑ol); vinylmagnesium bromide adds to the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde forming an alkoxide which is protonated on work‑up; performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen or argon; no catalyst other than the Grignard reagent itself.

Sol‑gel hydrolysis‑condensation of a metal alkoxide; converts titanium tetrapropoxide to titanium dioxide while releasing propanol; water hydrolyzes Ti–OPr bonds to Ti–OH, which then condense to TiO2 polymeric network; usually carried out by adding stoichiometric water to a solution of the alkoxide in an alcohol solvent (often isopropanol) with stirring at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base protonolysis with a carboxylic acid; dimethylzinc reacts with acetic acid to afford zinc acetate and methane. Used to prepare metal acetates and safely dispose of organozinc. Key transformation: each Zn–CH3 bond is protonated by the acidic proton of acetic acid, yielding CH4; Zn becomes Zn(OAc)2. Conditions: excess glacial acetic acid, 0‑25 °C, inert atmosphere, slow addition to control gas evolution. Solvent is the acetic acid itself; no catalyst required.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis; combines sodium metal with red phosphorus to form sodium phosphide (Na3P); reaction is conducted under inert atmosphere (argon) in a sealed tube or glovebox, heating to melt sodium (~98 °C) and allow diffusion into phosphorus; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Esterification (Fischer esterification) of docosanoic acid with methanol to form methyl docosanoate; purpose is to produce a fatty‑acid methyl ester; key transformation: carboxylic acid + alcohol → ester + water; typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol with catalytic H₂SO₄ or HCl, removal of water (Dean‑Stark) drives equilibrium; methanol acts as both reactant and solvent.

Free‑radical halogenation (chlorination) of an alkane. Chlorine abstracts a hydrogen atom from 2,4‑dimethylpentane, primarily at the tertiary carbon (C‑2), forming a carbon‑centered radical that recombines with Cl· to give 2‑chloro‑2,4‑dimethylpentane and HCl.
