Initiated by UV light or heat, typically conducted in an inert, non‑polar solvent like carbon tetrachloride. No additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of the allylic alcohol linalool to give α‑ocimene; purpose is to generate a conjugated diene from an alcohol; key transformation: elimination of water from an allylic/tertiary alcohol to form C=C bonds; typical conditions: dilute strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or solid acid catalyst (zeolite) at 80‑120 °C; solvent may be toluene or the substrate itself; water is removed to shift equilibrium.

Negishi cross‑coupling of 4‑bromoanisole with phenylzinc bromide to afford 4‑methoxy‑biphenyl; purpose is to construct a biaryl C–C bond; key transformation: Pd‑catalyzed transmetalation and reductive elimination between an aryl halide and an arylzinc reagent; typical conditions: 0‑5 % Pd(0) catalyst such as Pd(PPh₃)₄ in THF, inert atmosphere, 25‑80 °C; THF or diethyl ether is common solvent; no external base required.

Acid‑metal sulfide reaction; converts cobalt(II) sulfide to cobalt(II) sulfate with release of H2S gas. CoS reacts with aqueous sulfuric acid to give CoSO4 in solution and H2S gas. Typically carried out with dilute or concentrated H2SO4, often with gentle heating to promote gas evolution; water is the medium; no catalyst required.

Direct fluorination of silicon nitride (Si₃N₄) with elemental fluorine to yield nitrogen trifluoride and silicon tetrafluoride; purpose is to convert refractory Si‑N material into volatile fluorides; key transformation: oxidation/halogenation of Si and N atoms; typical conditions: excess F₂ gas at 200‑400 °C in a corrosion‑resistant reactor (e.g., nickel or Monel); no solvent; highly exothermic reaction requiring careful temperature control.

Oxidation of sodium selenide (Na₂Se) by hydrogen peroxide to produce sodium selenite; purpose is to raise selenium from the –II to the +IV oxidation state; key transformation: Se²⁻ + H₂O₂ → SeO₃²⁻ + H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, neutral to mildly acidic pH, dropwise addition of H₂O₂; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization. Purpose: generate the sodium salt of sorbic acid (sodium sorbate) for improved solubility or as a food preservative. Key transformation: sorbic acid + NaOH → sodium sorbate + H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric NaOH (1 equiv.) at ambient temperature; stirring until dissolution. No special solvent beyond water; reaction is exothermic but mild.

Mixed‑acid nitration of adamantane using concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ to give 1‑nitroadamantane; purpose is to introduce a nitro group onto a tertiary carbon of a saturated hydrocarbon; key transformation: electrophilic substitution (or radical) of a C–H bond by NO₂⁺ generated in the acid mixture; typical conditions: cooled (0‑5 °C) mixture of conc. H₂SO₄ and HNO₃, slow addition of adamantane, reaction maintained at low temperature then quenched; the acid mixture serves as solvent; water is formed as by‑product.

Alkaline oxidative conversion of 4‑nitroaniline to 4‑nitrobenzoic acid using potassium permanganate; the aromatic amine is oxidized, the side chain is eliminated as water, and MnO4⁻ is reduced to MnO₂. Conducted in aqueous NaOH solution, heated (80–100 °C) until the purple permanganate color fades, then the mixture is acidified to precipitate MnO₂ and isolate the nitrobenzoic acid. Typical work‑up includes filtration of MnO₂ and neutralization of the filtrate.

General type: carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich‑type coupling). Purpose: convert the carboxylic acid into the corresponding ethyl ester under mild conditions. Key transformation: activation of 2‑methylbutanoic acid by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, nucleophilic attack by ethanol, and release of dicyclohexylurea (DCU). Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂) or THF as solvent; often a catalytic amount of 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP) is added to accelerate acyl transfer. Reaction time 1–12 h depending on scale.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (oxime cleavage); reverses the oxime formation, yielding benzaldehyde and hydroxylamine; useful for recovering the aldehyde or for analytical purposes; usually carried out in aqueous acidic medium (e.g 1 M HCl) or aqueous NaOH at reflux temperatures.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; exchanges counter‑ions between a copper(II) salt and a sodium benzoate salt; yields copper(II) benzoate and sodium perchlorate; carried out in aqueous solution or polar aprotic solvent (e.g., MeCN) at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Esterification (acylation of a polyol); three acryloyl chloride groups acylate the three hydroxyls of trimethylolpropane to give trimethylolpropane triacrylate, releasing three equivalents of HCl; performed under inert atmosphere with a base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to trap HCl, in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, at 0 °C to rt.

The reaction involves nucleophilic ring-opening of oxirane-2-sulfonic acid by ammonia, producing 2-aminoethanesulfonic acid (taurine) and water, typically occurring in aqueous ammonia at elevated temperatures.

Copper‑catalyzed oxidative C‑N coupling (Chan–Lam coupling); aniline couples with a phenylboronic acid pinacol ester in the presence of Cu(OAc)₂ and pyridine to afford diphenylamine; acetic acid and pinacol are generated as by‑products; reaction conducted under air or O₂, in methanol or dichloromethane at rt to 40 °C; pyridine acts as base/ligand.

Catalytic hydrogenation/deoxygenation of 5-(hydroxymethyl)furfural to 2,5-dimethylfuran; purpose is to convert a biomass‑derived platform chemical into a high‑energy biofuel. Key transformation is reduction of the aldehyde group to a methyl group and concurrent removal of the furan oxygen (hydrogenolysis). Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 3–5 MPa, temperature 150–200 °C, using a metal catalyst such as Cu‑Cr, Pd/C, Raney Ni or a bifunctional metal/acid system. Reactions are usually run in an aprotic solvent (toluene, THF, cyclohexane) or under solvent‑free conditions.

Acid–hydride protonolysis (acid‑base reaction); strong sulfuric acid protonates LiAlH₄, leading to rapid evolution of H₂ gas and formation of aluminum sulfate and lithium sulfate salts; typically performed by adding dilute H₂SO₄ dropwise to a suspension of LiAlH₄ in dry ether at 0 °C under inert atmosphere to control gas evolution; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of an alkyl carbonate (carbonate ester cleavage). The reaction hydrolyzes 1‑chloroethyl phenyl carbonate with water, yielding phenol, 1‑chloroethanol and carbon dioxide. It proceeds via nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon, followed by decarboxylation. Typical conditions are aqueous medium, heating (80‑100 °C) if the carbonate is not highly reactive. Common solvent is water or a water‑compatible organic solvent such as THF; no catalyst is required, although mild base (e.g., NaHCO₃) can accelerate the reaction.

Acid‑base double displacement (neutralization) producing gaseous base. Magnesium hydroxide reacts with ammonium chlorate, exchanging cations and anions to give magnesium chlorate, water and ammonia gas. The key transformation is proton transfer from NH₄⁺ to OH⁻, releasing NH₃. The reaction is performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; gentle heating may be applied to drive off the volatile ammonia. No special catalyst is needed; the reaction is straightforward stoichiometric neutralization.

Wurtz‑type coupling (reductive homocoupling) of alkyl halides. Two equivalents of 1‑bromo‑4‑chlorobutane are reduced by metallic sodium, generating alkyl radicals that couple to form the C8halide 1,8‑dichlorooctane while sodium bromide precipitates. The reaction is carried out in dry aprotic ether (e.g., dry diethyl ether or THF) under an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at reflux temperature (≈ 35‑40 °C for ether). Sodium metal is the reducing agent; no additional catalyst is required, but the reaction must be kept moisture‑free.

Double displacement/precipitation with bicarbonate decomposition. Potassium hydrogen carbonate reacts with strontium chloride in aqueous solution; the carbonate anion combines with Sr²⁺ toitate insoluble strontium carbonate, while CO₂ and H₂O are released from the bicarbonate anion, and KCl remains in solution. The reaction is typically performed at room temperature or with gentle heating to evolve CO₂. No catalyst is needed; water is the solvent and the driving force is the low solubility of SrCO₃.

Halide metathesis (salt exchange) to prepare a metal iodide. Sodium iodide exchanges iodide for chloride with scandium(III) chloride, yielding scandium(III) iodide and sodium chloride. The reaction is usually conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile, where NaCl precipitates out, allowing isolation of ScI₃. Mild heating (50‑80 °C) may be employed to improve solubility and precipitation. No catalyst is required; the driving force is the formation of the poorly soluble NaCl.

Hydrolysis (quench) of an organolithium reagent. Lithium 1‑H‑naphthalen‑1‑ide reacts with water, undergoing proton transfer to give neutral naphthalene and lithium hydroxide. This is a typical work‑up step for organolithium chemistry, converting the strong base into a benign product. The reaction is performed at low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) in an ethereal solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, with careful addition of water to control exotherm. No catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds rapidly upon protonation.

Thermal decomposition of a metal nitrate; purpose: obtain zirconium dioxide and gaseous by‑products; key transformation: Zr(NO3)4 → ZrO2 + 4 NO2 + O2 (overall); heated in a furnace to 400‑600 °C in air; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid–base salt formation with gas evolution; ammonium carbonate reacts with hexafluorosilicic acid in aqueous solution, the carbonate is protonated and decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O while the ammonium cation pairs with the hexafluorosilicate anion to give ammonium hexafluorosilicate. Conducted at room temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic organolithium addition to elemental selenium; two equivalents of ethyl‑Li attack selenium, coupling the ethyl groups to form the C–SeC bond of diethyl selenide and generating lithium selenide as the inorganic by‑product. Typically performed in dry THF under nitrogen at –78 °C to 0 °C, then warmed to room temperature; inert atmosphere required, no added catalyst.

N‑acylation of L‑proline with succinic anhydride (nucleophilic acyl substitution) to give N‑succinyl‑L‑proline and a molecule of succinic acid; serves as a protecting or functionalization step; amine attacks one carbonyl of the anhydride forming an amide and opening the ring; carried out in anhydrous pyridine or DMF, often with catalytic DMAP, under reflux or gentle heating.

Metathesis/precipitation; dysprosium(III) bromide hydrate reacts with sodium hydroxide to precipitate dysprosium(III) hydroxide and form sodium bromide in solution; carried out in water at ambient temperature, pH adjusted with NaOH.

Reductive conversion of a nitro aromatic to an aniline derivative using tin(II) chloride in hydrochloric acid (SnCl₂/HCl reduction). The nitro group of 2,6‑dichloronitrobenzene is reduced to an amine, producing 2,6‑dichloroaniline while Sn(II) is oxidized to Sn(IV) chloride. Reaction is carried out in aqueous HCl, refluxing (≈80–100 °C) for several hours; water is the solvent, no external catalyst beyond SnCl₂.

Enzymatic methyl‑transfer from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine to β‑alanyl‑L‑histidine; a histidine N‑methyltransferase transfers the methyl group of SAM to the imidazole nitrogen of the dipeptide, yielding anserine and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Occurs in physiological buffer (pH ≈ 7.5) at 37 °C in the presence of the specific methyltransferase; no synthetic reagents or solvents required.

Oxidative cleavage (ozonolysis) of the terminal alkene in 1‑ethenyl‑4‑methylbenzene. Ozone adds across the C=C bond to give a molozonide that fragments, yielding formaldehyde from the terminal carbon and 4‑methylbenzaldehyde from the internal carbon. Typically performed at –78 °C in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane, followed by a reductive work‑up (Zn/AcOH) or oxidative work‑up (H₂O₂) to isolate the aldehydes.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of europium selenide; elemental europium and selenium are mixed in a 1:1 molar ratio and heated under an inert atmosphere (argon) in a sealed quartz ampoule, typically at 600–800 °C, to produce EuSe. No solvent or catalyst; the reaction proceeds by direct combination of the metals.

Reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol; sodium borohydride donates hydride to the carbonyl carbon of 4‑heptanone, yielding 4‑heptanol. Typically carried out in protic solvents such as methanol, ethanol or isopropanol at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is quenched with water after completion.

Bimolecular elimination (E2) using a bulky strong base; potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 1‑iodohexadecane, while iodide leaves, forming the terminal alkene hexadec‑1‑ene and KI. Typical solvent is polar aprotic (THF, DMSO) at 60–100 °C; the bulky base favors elimination over substitution.

Formation of a sulfonyl anhydride by condensation of trifluoromethanesulfonic acid with its acid chloride; the process releases hydrogen chloride and produces trifluoromethanesulfonic anhydride (Tf₂O). Conducted at low temperature (0–5 °C) in an aprotic solvent like dichloromethane or toluene under inert atmosphere; a tertiary amine base (e.g., pyridine) is often added to trap the generated HCl.

Reductive dehalogenation of 2,4,6‑tribromoanisole to anisole; zinc dust reduces the carbon‑bromine bonds in the presence of acetic acid, forming anisole and zinc bromide as by‑product. Reaction is performed by refluxing the mixture in glacial acetic acid, often with excess zinc, and proceeds under acidic conditions.

Strong reduction of an amide to a primary amine; lithium aluminum hydride supplies hydride to the carbonyl carbon of N‑phenylbutanamide, converting it to N‑phenylbutylamine. Conducted in dry, aprotic ether solvents (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful aqueous work‑up to quench excess LiAlH₄.

Oxidation of 2‑methylnaphthalene to 2‑methyl‑1,4‑naphthoquinone using a chromium(VI) oxidant; potassium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes the benzylic methyl group and the aromatic ring, producing the quinone and reducing chromium(VI) to chromium(III) sulfate. Typically carried out by heating the substrate in aqueous H₂SO₄ with K₂Cr₂O₇ at reflux; water is the solvent and the reaction is performed under acidic, strongly oxidizing conditions.

Oxidative acid leaching; zinc sulfide is dissolved by concentrated nitric acid, oxidizing sulfide to sulfur dioxide and nitrate to nitrogen dioxide; yields zinc nitrate, NO2, SO2 and water; usually performed by refluxing ZnS with 6–12 M HNO₃ under atmospheric pressure, generating brown NO₂ gas; no additional solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑base proton transfer (salt metathesis). Sodium cyanide reacts with methanol, the methanol donates a proton to the cyanide ion forming volatile hydrogen cyanide gas, while the sodium cation pairs with the methoxide anion. Typically carried out in anhydrous methanol or aqueous/alcoholic solution at temperatures below 0 °C to suppress HCN loss; sealed or reflux apparatus may be used. No catalyst required.

Single‑displacement redox (metal‑acid reaction). Potassium metal reduces protons from hydroiodic acid to molecular hydrogen and is oxidized to potassium ions, which combine with iodide to give potassium iodide. Conducted in aqueous HI at ambient temperature; the reaction is highly exothermic and proceeds spontaneously. No solvent beyond the aqueous acid and no catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation (salt metathesis). Zinc chlorate reacts with ammonium hydroxide; insoluble zinc hydroxide precipitates, while the ammonium cation pairs with chlorate to give soluble ammonium chlorate. Performed in aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C to avoid thermal decomposition of the chlorate. No catalyst; water acts as the solvent.

Oxidative deamination; converts an aromatic amine to the corresponding carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium; the amine group is removed, forming 1‑naphthoic acid while MnO2 precipitates and KOH remains in solution; typical conditions: aqueous KMnO4, reflux or heating, neutral to mildly alkaline pH, water as solvent.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium nitrate; purpose is to generate nitrous oxide gas; key transformation: heating ammonium nitrate yields nitrous oxide and water vapor; typically heated to 170–240 °C; may be catalyzed by metal oxides (e.g., CuO, Fe₂O₃) to favor N₂O; performed in a sealed vessel or furnace; no solvent.

KMnO4 oxidation of an aldehyde; purpose is oxidative conversion of decanal to the carboxylic acid decanoic acid; key transformation is addition of oxygen to the aldehyde carbonyl, reducing Mn(VII) to Mn(IV) as MnO2 and generating water; usually conducted in aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH or KOH) at 0–25 °C, followed by acid work‑up to isolate the acid; manganese dioxide precipitates and is filtered off.

Alkyl halide alkylation. Nucleophilic substitution of tert-butylamine with n-butyl bromide yields N-butyl-tert-butylamine, with hydrogen bromide generated as a byproduct. Typically conducted in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF) with a base to neutralize HBr.

Alkaline hydrolysis / halogen exchange of N‑halo‑hydantoin. In aqueous sodium hydroxide, 1‑bromo‑3‑chloro‑5,5‑dimethylhydantoin undergoes nucleophilic attack by hydroxide, releasing bromide and chloride as sodium salts and generating hypohalite ions (OCl⁻ and OBr⁻) together with the parent hydantoin. Reaction is performed in water at 0–25 °C; the mixture is kept basic to prevent re‑halogenation. No additional catalyst.

Metal‑halogen exchange to form an organolithium reagent. Phenyl bromide reacts with finely activated lithium metal (often activated by ultrasound) to give phenyl lithium and lithium bromide. Conducted under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in dry ether solvents such as THF or diethyl, typically at −78 °C to 0 °C to control reactivity. No added catalyst; ultrasonic activation aids lithium surface cleaning.

Type: Acid chloride hydrolysis (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Purpose: Convert sulfonyl chloride to the corresponding sulfonic acid. Key transformation: H2O attacks the sulfonyl chloride, releasing HCl and forming 2‑naphthalenesulfonic acid. Conditions: Aqueous medium, often at 0 °C to room temperature; can be performed in water or a water‑organic mixture. No catalyst required; excess water drives reaction to completion.

Type: Catalytic semihydrogenation (selective hydrogenation). Purpose: Reduce one of the two double bonds in norbornadiene to give the mono‑alkene norbornene. Key transformation: H2 adds across one C=C bond under the influence of Lindlar catalyst, affording the cis‑2‑norbornene product while leaving the second double bond untouched. Conditions: H2 gas (1–3 atm), Lindlar catalyst (Pd/CaCO₃ poisoned with lead acetate and quinoline), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, ambient temperature; reaction stops when gas uptake ceases.

Type: Metathesis/acid–base double displacement. Purpose: Exchange anions between sulfuric acid and praseodymium(III) acetate to form praseodymium(III) sulfate and free acetic acid. Key transformation: 3 H₂SO₄ + 2 Pr(OAc)₃ → Pr₂(SO₄)₃ + 6 HOAc. Conditions: Aqueous solution, heating gently (≈50–80 °C) to promote complete salt formation; no special catalyst required.

Single‑displacement/redox acid–metal reaction; magnesium metal reacts with hydroiodic acid, producing magnesium iodide and hydrogen gas (with possible side oxidation of I⁻ to I₂). Carried out in aqueous HI, often refluxed to ensure complete reaction; water/HI solution is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of a secondary alcohol to an alkene using concentrated sulfuric acid; purpose is to form hex‑3‑ene from hexan‑3‑ol; key transformation is elimination of water to give a double bond (E1 mechanism); typical conditions are heating the alcohol with excess conc. H2SO4 at 140–150 °C; solvent is the concentrated acid itself, no additional catalyst.

Type: Dithiocarbamate synthesis followed by alkylation (nucleophilic substitution). Purpose: Prepare methyl N,N‑dimethylcarbamodithioate, a thio‑carbamate ester. Key steps: (i) CS₂ reacts with dimethylamine in basic medium to give the dimethyl dithiocarbamate anion; (ii) methyl iodide alkylates the sulfur atom, yielding the methyl dithiocarbamate; NaI and water are by‑products. Conditions: NaOH (1–2 eq) in water or aqueous ethanol, 0–25 °C for dithiocarbamate formation, then addition of MeI at 0 °C to room temperature; stirring until completion.

Synthesis of fluorosulfonic acid (a super‑acid); type is acid halide formation via reaction of SO₃ with HF. Key transformation: SO₃ (a sulfur trioxide electrophile) reacts with gaseous HF to give HSO₃F (fluorosulfonic acid). Performed anhydrously at low temperature (≤0 °C) in a PTFE or nickel vessel; HF is bubbled through liquid or gaseous SO₃. No solvent is required; the product is collected as a liquid acid.

Type: Halide exchange (metathesis) producing an acid fluoride. Purpose: Convert oxalyl dichloride to oxalyl difluoride, a useful fluorinating reagent. Key transformation: Cl⁻ ions are exchanged for F⁻ via precipitation of insoluble AgCl. Conditions: Anhydrous, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), solvent such as dry CH₂Cl₂ or CHCl₃, low temperature (0–25 °C) to prevent decomposition; stoichiometric AgF (2 eq) is filtered off as AgCl precipitate.

Grignard carboxylation; purpose is to form a benzoic acid derivative; the aryl‑MgBr adds to CO2 giving a magnesium carboxylate which is acid‑work‑up to 4‑fluorobenzoic acid and MgBr2; typically performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to rt under CO2 gas, followed by aqueous HCl quench; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic halogenation of an organolithium; converts neopentyl lithium to neopentyl chloride while generating LiCl; Neopentyl‑Li + Cl₂ → Neopentyl‑Cl + LiCl; carried out under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in dry ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether) at low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) to control reactivity; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base (proton transfer) / salt metathesis; purpose is to generate tetrafluoroboric acid from its sodium salt; HCl protonates BF4⁻ yielding HBF4 and NaCl; usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special solvent or catalyst needed.

Double‑replacement acid‑base reaction; purpose is to exchange acetate for sulfate, forming scandium(III) sulfate and liberating acetic acid; Sc(OAc)₃ reacts with H2SO4 to give Sc₂(SO₄)₃ and 6 HOAc; conducted in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to drive off acetic acid; no catalyst required.

Precipitation / double‑replacement reaction; purpose is to obtain insoluble rhodium(III) sulfide; Rh(NO₃)₃ reacts with Na₂S to form Rh₂S₃ solid and NaNO₃ in solution; performed in water, usually at reflux to ensure complete precipitation; filtration isolates the black Rh₂S₃; no catalyst needed.

Methyl carbamimidothioate reacts with ammonia in a nucleophilic substitution (thiol-amine reaction). The purpose is to form guanidine and methanethiol. Key transformation involves ammonia displacing the thioate group. Reaction conditions typically require heating in a polar protic solvent like water or ethanol without a catalyst.

Alcohol‑to‑alkyl chloride conversion using thionyl chloride (Appel‑type substitution); purpose is to replace the hydroxy group of 2‑hydroxyethyl acrylate with chlorine, yielding 2‑chloroethyl acrylate; SOCl₂ reacts with the alcohol producing HCl and SO₂ as gases; carried out in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of ammonium thiosulfate; purpose is to liberate ammonia gas and form sodium thiosulfate; NaOH deprotonates NH₄⁺ to NH₃ and H₂O while exchanging Na⁺ for NH₄⁺; performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off NH₃; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization forming an ammonium salt; benzoic acid is deprotonated by ammonium bicarbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O while generating ammonium benzoate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating to drive off CO₂; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Complexation/fluorination reaction in hydrofluoric acid medium; titanium dioxide reacts with HF and ammonium fluoride to produce the coordination complex ammonium hexafluorotitanate and water.ed in aqueous HF (often concentrated) at room temperature or slight heating in a Teflon‑lined vessel; the solvent is HF/H₂O mixture, no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution of alcohols on phosphorus trichloride; three ethanol molecules replace the three chlorine atoms of PCl₃, yielding triethyl phosphite and three equivalents of H. Usually carried out neat (ethanol acts as solvent) or in excess ethanol under reflux with a simple gas‑scrubbing system for HCl; inert atmosphere optional, no catalyst.

Acid dissolution of a metal sulfide (acid‑metal reaction). Iron(II) sulfide is treated with hydrochloric acid, liberating hydrogen sulfide gas and forming soluble iron(II) chloride. Usually performed in aqueous HCl at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (de‑protection) of a 1,3‑dithiane protecting group to reveal the corresponding aldehyde; purpose is to convert 2,2‑dimethyl‑1,3‑dithiane into 2,2‑dimethylpropanal. Key transformation: protonation of the dithiane sulfur atoms followed by water attack and cleavage of the C‑S bonds, yielding the aldehyde and mercapto‑by‑products (e.g., methanethiol). Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–3 M) or p‑TsOH in a miscible organic solvent such as THF or MeCN, heated to reflux (≈80 °C) for 1–4 h; acid acts as catalyst.

Nucleophilic addition / condensation of phenylhydrazine to phenyl isocyanate to give diphenylcarbazide. The terminal –NH₂ of phenylhydrazine attacks the electrophilic carbon of the isocyanate, forming a urea‑type intermediate that cyclizes/condenses to the carbazide product. Usually performed in anhydrous ethanol or THF under reflux (≈80 °C) for several hours; no catalyst is required, but an inert atmosphere can be used to avoid side oxidation.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (alkaline cleavage) of the benzoyl amide bond in benzoylecgonine, converting it to benzoic acid and the free ecgonine moiety. Performed in aqueous NaOH (often 1–2 M) with heating (reflux) for 1–2 h, then acidification to liberate benzoic acid; water or aqueous ethanol is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Acid–saltathesis (double displacement) where barium acetate reacts with hydrobromic acid to give acetic acid and barium bromide. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, and the reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Fischer esterification of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid with ethanol to afford ethyl p‑hydroxybenzoate (ethylparaben) and water; acid‑catalyzed condensation used to make a preservative; carried out by refluxing the acid in excess ethanol with catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, often using ethanol as both reagent and solvent.
Reduction of arsenic(III) oxide by hydrogen gas; a high‑temperature gas‑phase reduction (≈500‑600 °C) used to obtain elemental arsenic; no solvent performed under a flow of H₂ in a tubular furnace.

Oxime formation from a ketone; hydroxylamine adds to the carbonyl of 4‑piperidone and eliminates water to give the corresponding oxime; typically carried out in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to reflux, often with a mild base (e.g., pyridine) to neutralize the formed acid.

Acid–base reaction of a carbonate salt; hydroiodic acid protonates lead(II) carbonate, releasing carbon dioxide gas and water and forming insoluble lead(II) iodide; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating to drive off CO₂.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an ester; potassium hydroxide attacks methyl propionate, cleaving the ester to produce methanol and potassium propionate; conducted in aqueous KOH (or KOH in ethanol/water) with heating under reflux.

Acetylation (esterification) of an alcohol; 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol reacts with acetic anhydride in the presence of N‑methylmorpholine, which scavenges the generated acetic acid, yielding 4‑methoxybenzyl acetate; usually performed at 0 °C to rt in dichloromethane or THF.

Precipitation/hydrolysis reaction; purpose is to convert soluble bismuth(III) bromide into the insoluble mixed oxide‑halide bismuth oxybromide; key transformation: BiBr3 + 2 NaOH → BiOBr(s) + 2 NaBr + H2O; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with an excess of NaOH; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base deprotonation of a terminal alkyne with n‑butyllithium to generate the lithium acetylide, followed by silylation with trimethylsilyl chloride to give trimethylsilyl‑acetylene; LiCl is formed as a by‑product. Performed in dry THF at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane to 2,3-dimethyl-2-butanol. Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN1). Purpose: Alkyl halide conversion to tertiary alcohol. Key transformation: Chloride departure generates a tertiary carbocation, attacked by water. Conditions: Aqueous solution, mild heating.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation. Purpose: isolate neodymium hydroxide from its chloride. Key transformation: NdCl3 + 3 NaOH → Nd(OH)3↓ + 3 NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, addition of NaOH solution to NdCl3 solution with vigorous stirring; precipitate filtered; water as solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of anisole using nitronium tetrafluoroborate. The nitronium ion attacks the aromatic ring (predominantly para to the methoxy group) to afford nitroanisole; boron trifluoride and hydrogen fluoride are produced as side‑products. Conducted at 0–25 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane; no external catalyst besides the reagent.

SN2 alkylation/esterification: sodium fluoroacetate anion displaces bromide on 2‑ethylhexyl bromide to give 2‑ethylhexyl fluoroacetate; typically run in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at 0–80 °C with slight excess carboxylate; NaBr precipitates and is filtered off.

Base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (saponification): N‑acetylanthranilic acid is hydrolyzed by aqueous NaOH, cleaving the N‑acetyl group to afford anthranilic acid, water and sodium acetate; usually refluxed 1–3 h in water or aqueous ethanol, followed by acidification to isolate the free acid.

Acid–base displacement: Lithium formate reacts with sulfuric acid (often dilute) to give formic acid and lithium hydrogen sulfate (LiHSO₄) in solution. The reaction proceeds at modest temperature (0–25 °C) and is employed when a bisulfate salt is desired.

Simple double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution: Ag⁺ from silver benzoate exchanges with K⁺ from potassium hydroxide to give insoluble silver hydroxide (precipitates as Ag₂O/AgOH) and soluble potassium benzoate. Typically carried out in water at room temperature; precipitation drives the reaction forward.

Alcohol‑to‑chloride conversion with thionyl chloride: 3‑hydroxypropanamide reacts with SOCl₂, yielding 3‑chloropropanamide together with HCl and SO₂ gases; performed under anhydrous conditions in dry DCM or pyridine at 0 °C to reflux, with pyridine or a tertiary amine scavenging HCl.

Acid‑base salt metathesis: hydrochloric acid protonates lithium orotate, liberating orotic acid and forming soluble lithium chloride; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, then the free acid is isolated by pH adjustment and extraction.

Double‑displacement precipitation (neutralization): aqueous ammonia reacts with aluminum sulfate; Al³⁺ precipitates as aluminum hydroxide while sulfate pairs with ammonium to give ammonium sulfate in solution; performed at room temperature with excess NH₄OH, followed by filtration of Al(OH)₃.

Metal‑catalyzed oxidation (Fenton‑type): 1‑pentanol is oxidized by H₂O₂ in the presence of FeCl₃ (catalytic) to form pentanal; conducted in a water‑organic solvent mixture (e.g., water/acetonitrile) at 0–40 °C under mildly acidic conditions (pH≈3) to avoid over‑oxidation to the acid.

Base‑induced elimination (E2) of an alkyl sulfonate ester; potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts the β‑hydrogen from 2‑methylpropyl 4‑methylbenzenesulfonate, expelling the sulfonate leaving group to give the alkene 2‑methylpropene and potassium 4‑methylbenzenesulfonate. Typical conditions: dry aprotic solvent (THF, DMSO), 0 °C to reflux, inert atmosphere.

Condensation of formamide with ammonia to give formamidine (formimidamide); an amidine‑forming reaction that eliminates water. Conducted by mixing excess gaseous or aqueous ammonia with formamide and heating (≈150–200 °C) to drive off water; sometimes a Dean‑Stark trap is used. No catalyst is essential, though a weak acid can accelerate the process.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification; ethanol from ethyl gallate is exchanged with propanol to afford propyl gallate and ethanol as by‑product. Usually performed with excess 1‑propanol, catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid or sodium methoxide, refluxing in toluene or xylene, with removal of ethanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) to drive equilibrium.

Alcoholysis (transesterification) of 3‑ethyl phenyl acetate with ethanol; converts the aromatic acetate into 3‑ethyl phenol and ethyl acetate. Typically carried out by refluxing ethanol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOH). No additional solvent is required beyond the ethanol used as both reactant and medium.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: prepare cobalt(II) sulfite by swapping the sulfate for sulfite. Key transformation: CoSO4 (aq) + Na2SO3 (aq) → CoSO3 (s) + Na2SO4 (aq). Typical conditions: aqueous medium, room temperature or slight warming to improve dissolution, stirring. Common solvent: water. No catalyst needed.

O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of a phenol; purpose is to convert the phenolic OH into a methoxy group forming 2‑amino‑4‑bromoanisole; key transformation is phenol O‑H → O‑CH3 using methyl iodide; base K2CO3 deprotonates the phenol, generating KI as by‑product; typical conditions: reflux in polar aprotic solvent (DMF or acetone) under inert atmosphere; K2CO3 (2–3 equiv) as base; methyl iodide (1.1–1.5 equiv).

Simple acid–base neutralization forming the hydrochloride salt of benoxathian. The amine nitrogen is protonated by HCl, yielding benoxathian·HCl. Conducted at room temperature in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol, methanol or water; no catalyst required.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to the acid chloride using oxalyl chloride (Schmidt chlorination). Chloroac acid reacts with oxalyl chloride, producing chloroacetyl chloride while liberating CO, CO₂ and HCl gases. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to temperature; catalytic DMF (a few drops) often added to accelerate formation of the acyl chloride.

High‑temperature fluorination/reduction of sulfur hexafluoride with elemental silicon. Si reduces SF₆, yielding silicon tetrafluoride gas and elemental sulfur. The reaction requires temperatures above ~800 °C in a furnace or plasma reactor, under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Acetylation of a primary amine with acetyl chloride in the presence of pyridine; an acid‑chloride acylation that forms the same N‑(2‑hydroxyphenyl)acetamide. Pyridine acts as both solvent and base, trapping HCl as pyridinium chloride. Reaction is typically performed at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen. By‑product is pyridinium chloride.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of a metal carbonate; purpose is to obtain manganese(II) oxide; key transformation: MnCO3(s) → MnO(s) + CO2(g); carried out by heating the solid to 400–600 °C in a furnace, usually in air; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Metathesis/precipitation of lanthanum nitrate with hydrofluoric acid to produce lanthanum trifluoride and nitric acid. Used for preparing LaF₃ as a low‑solubility fluoride. Conducted in aqueous solution, adding excess cold HF to a nitrate solution at 0‑25 °C, stirring until the white LaF₃ precipitates forms; the solid is filtered, washed and dried. No catalyst required.

Oxidation of a vicinal diol to a 1,2‑diketone using chromic acid (Jones oxidation). Cyclohexane‑1,2‑diol is oxidized by CrO₃/H₂SO₄ in aqueous acetone, converting both secondary alcohols to carbonyl groups to give 1,2‑cyclohexanedione. Typically carried out at 0–25 °C; the reaction is quenched with isopropanol or ethylene glycol after completion.

Reductive amination; purpose is to convert cyclohexanone into a tertiary amine (N,N-dimethyl‑cyclohexylamine). Key steps are formation of an iminium intermediate from dimethylamine and cyclohexanone, followed by reduction with sodium triacetoxyborohydride. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid to promote iminium formation; NaBH(OAc)₃ serves as the reductant.

Double‑displacement/precipitation (neutralization) reaction; purpose is to exchange cations and anions, precipitating insoluble aluminum hydroxide while forming soluble potassium sulfate. The hydroxide ions from KOH replace the sulfate ligands on Al³⁺, yielding Al(OH)₃ (solid) and K₂SO₄ (aqueous). Conducted in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; no special catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement (salt metathesis) reaction; magnesium sulfide dissolved in water reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to give magnesium hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium sulfide; carried out at room temperature in water, no catalyst.

Radical‑radical termination: hydroxymethyl radical combines with a hydroperoxy radical producing formaldehyde and hydrogen peroxide; gas‑phase process typical of the troposphere; occurs without added solvent or catalyst.

Metal‑alcohol (acid‑base) reaction; magnesium reacts with methanol to give magnesium methoxide and hydrogen gas; Mg⁰ abstracts a proton from MeOH forming Mg(OCH₃)₂ and H₂; carried out in dry methanol, usually under reflux with a clean magnesium surface; no external catalyst, inert atmosphere often employed.

Oxidative dehydrogenation (redox) of a 1,4‑dihydropyridine using chloranil as the oxidant; purpose is to aromatize the heterocycle to pyridine while reducing chloranil to tetrachlorohydroquinone. Key transformation: loss of two hydrogen atoms from the dihydropyridine to give pyridine, concurrent two‑electron reduction of tetrachloro‑1,4‑benzoquinone. Usually performed in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, reflux or gentle heating, under nitrogen; no additional catalyst needed.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis). Elemental nickel and selenium are intimately mixed and heated (≈400–600 °C) in an inert atmosphere or sealed tube, forming nickel selenide (NiSe). No solvent; reaction proceeds by diffusion.

Acid-base neutralization reaction. Al(OH)₃ acts as a base neutralizing sulfuric acid, yielding aluminum sulfate and water. Occurs in aqueous solution under normal temperature and pressure. Water serves as the solvent, and no catalyst is necessary.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt displacement); purpose is to liberate oxalic acid from its magnesium salt and generate magnesium sulfate. Sulfuric acid protonates the oxalate anion, producing free oxalic acid, while Mg²⁺ pairs with sulfate to give MgSO₄. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to ensure dissolution; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration – water adds across the C=C bond of cyclohexene in a Markovnikov fashion to give cyclohexanol. The reaction is usually performed with a dilute mineral acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) or a catalytic amount of HgSO₄ in aqueous ethanol, heated to reflux.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl bromide with nitrite ion; purpose is to synthesize ethyl nitrite (an alkyl nitrite) and sodium bromide. The nitrite anion attacks the primary carbon of ethyl bromide, displacing bromide. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or dry ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature to favor SN2 over elimination; no catalyst needed.

Double displacement reaction; forms silver formate and ammonium nitrate through ion exchange. Silver nitrate donates silver ions (Ag⁺) to coordinate with formate (HCOO⁻), while nitrate (NO₃⁻) pairs with ammonium (NH₄⁺). Reaction typically occurs in aqueous solution, solubility of products determining extent.

Double‑displacement/precipitation metathesis; purpose is to exchange anions between lead(II) acetate and ammonium chloride, precipitating insoluble lead(II) chloride while forming soluble ammonium acetate. Reaction proceeds in aqueous medium at room temperature with stirring; the low solubility of PbCl₂ drives the reaction; no catalyst required.

Diketene + Isopropanol → Isopropyl acetoacetate  
General type: alcoholysis of a β‑keto lactone (esterification via ring opening). Purpose: prepare a β‑keto ester for further condensations. Key transformation: isopropanol attacks the carbonyl of diketene, opening the ring and forming the isopropyl ester of acetoacetic acid. Typical conditions: reflux or 25 °C with excess isopropanol; may add a mild base (pyridine) to scavenge the liberated acid. Common solvents/catalysts: neat isopropanol (acts as solvent), or isopropanol/THF with catalytic pyridine.

A metathesis/complexation reaction that converts zinc(II) nitrate, manganese(II) nitrate and sodium ethylenebis(dithiocarbamate) into the mixed‑metal dithiocarbamate fungicide Mancozeb, while sodium nitrate precipitates. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with pH adjusted to about 5–6; no special catalyst is required.

Halogen‑exchange (hydrofluorination) of trichlorofluoromethane with HF to give dichodifluoromethane and HCl; performed in the gas phase at 300‑400 °C using a fluoride‑acid catalyst such as AlF₃ or SbF₅; no solvent required.

Acid–base neutralization. Purpose: convert neodymium hydroxide to its soluble chloride. Key transformation: Nd(OH)3 + 3 HCl → NdCl3 + 3 H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, stoichiometric or excess HCl, room temperature, water as solvent.
Acid‑base neutralization of gluconic acid with sodium bicarbonate, generating sodium gluconate, carbon dioxide and water; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with gentle stirring.

Alkaline hydrolysis (ring opening) of BIT; purpose is to regenerate 2‑aminothiophenol and obtain formate. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack hydroxide on the carbonyl carbon of BIT, cleavage of the C‑N bond and formation of sodium formate and the free aminothiophenol. Typical conditions: refluxing BIT (1 eq) in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M 1–2 h at 60–80 °C. Solvent: water; after reaction, acidification (e.g., with HCl) affords the free amine‑thiol.

Hydride reduction of an imine. Sodium borohydride supplies hydride to the C=N bond of N,1-diphenylmethanimine, affording N‑phenylbenzylamine. Reaction is usually carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a brief work‑up to quench excess borohydride. Provides a mild, selective method for imine → amine conversion.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann ether synthesis: phenol couples with bromobenzene to form diphenyl ether; CuI with 1,10‑phenanthroline as ligand, K₂CO₃ base, in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) at 120‑150 °C under inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenation of N-propylidenehydroxylamine (oxime) to 1-propanamine; purpose: reduction of an oxime to a primary amine; key transformation: C=N–OH reduced to C–NH₂ with water as by‑product; typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm), Pd/C or Raney Ni catalyst, ethanol or methanol solvent, 25‑80 °C.
Thermal decomposition of cesium azide producing nitrogen gas and metallic cesium; solid CsN₃ is heated to high temperature (≈300 °C) under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous mixing of ammonium phosphate and praseodymium(III) nitrate leads to formation of insoluble praseodymium(III) phosphate precipitate and soluble ammonium nitrate; typically performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis/metathesis; aqueous zinc iodide reacts with excess sodium hydroxide (and water) to generate sodium iodide and soluble sodium zincate complex (Na2[Zn(OH)4]); carried out in water, often with heating to ensure complete dissolution; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfone using a hyperval iodine reagent; thioanisole is oxidized by iodosylbenzene, yielding iodobenzene as the reduced iodine by‑product and phenyl sulfone (methyl phenyl sulfone) as the oxidized product; typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at room temperature; no external catalyst beyond the iodosylbenz.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of guanine; methyl p‑toluenesulfonate transfers a methyl group to O6 position of guanine, producing O6‑methylguanine and p‑toluenesulfonic acid; usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) with a mild base to neutralize the acid; reaction proceeds at room temperature to gentle heating.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of a secondary alkyl chloride using H₂; purpose is removal of halogen to afford the alkane; key transformation C–Cl → C–H; conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni or PtO₂, temperature 50–100 °C; solvent often ethanol or ethyl acetate.

Hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid; benzoic acid is reduced by sodium bis(2‑methoxyethoxy)aluminum hydride to give benzyl alcohol; performed in anhydrous ether solvents such as THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Free‑radical addition of hydrogen chloride to 3‑methyl‑1‑butene in the presence of a peroxide initiator (e.g., benzoyl peroxide) giving anti‑Markovnikov 1‑chloro‑3‑methylbutane. Reaction proceeds at 0–25 °C in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; peroxide initiates the radical chain.

Hydrolysis of a Weinreb amide; N‑methoxyacetamide is cleaved by water (often under acidic or buffered conditions) to give acetic acid and methoxyamine. Typically heated in aqueous HCl or dilute NaOH, then neutralized.

Reaction type: Ozonolysis oxidation. Purpose: Converts geminal methyl groups in a biphenyl compound to carboxylic acid groups. Key transformation: Cleavage of methyl groups adjacent to aromatic rings by ozone, followed by oxidative work-up to form carboxylic acids. Conditions: Ozone gas bubbled into an inert solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at low temperature (-78°C), followed by aqueous hydrogen peroxide or reductive work-up.

Reaction type: Condensation/cyclization. Purpose: Synthesizes a phenoxazinone derivative via an oxidative coupling. Key transformation: Nitrosobenzene condenses with o-aminophenol, followed by cyclization and elimination of water. Conditions: Acidic conditions (e.g., HCl) or oxidative environment (e.g., air or H2O2), ethanol or aqueous solvent.

High‑temperature chlorination of nickel(II) boride with chlorine gas to form nickel(II) chloride and boron trichloride; a halogenolysis/oxidative chlorination typically carried out in a sealed tube or flow reactor at 200–400 °C under an inert atmosphere; no solvent is used.

Halogenation of a carboxylic acid to an acyl halide using phosphorus triiodide; converts acetic acid to acetyl iodide while generating phosphorous acid; the carbonyl oxygen attacks PI₃ and iodine replaces the hydroxyl group; usually carried out in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux, with careful exclusion of moisture.

Reaction type: Rosenmund reduction. Purpose: Converts acyl chlorides to aldehydes under controlled hydrogenation. Key transformation: Selective hydrogenation of the acyl chloride’s carbonyl group to an aldehyde using poisoned catalyst. Conditions: Hydrogen gas, palladium-on-barium sulfate catalyst poisoned with sulfur, solvent like quinoline or toluene.

Redox oxidation‑reduction; ozone acts as an oxidant converting sulfite (SO3²⁻) to sulfate (SO4²⁻) while being reduced to molecular oxygen. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient to moderate temperature, often under mildly acidic conditions; no external catalyst required.

Reaction type: synthesis/halogenation (direct combination). Purpose: preparation of aluminum iodide, a Lewis acid used in specialized organic reactions. Key transformation: Al oxidized to Al³⁺, I₂ reduced to I⁻, giving AlI₃. Typical conditions: I₂ vapor passed over heated Al (≈300‑350 °C) in a sealed, dry environment; the product sublimes as pale yellow crystals. No solvent; inert gas atmosphere is required.

Type: catalytic hydrogenation (azide hydrogenolysis). Purpose: reduce azide to primary amine. Key transformation: 3‑azidopentane → 3‑aminopentane with loss of N₂. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over 10 % Pd/C, 25–100 °C, inert solvent such as EtOH, MeOH or EtOAc; reaction time 1–12 h.

Oxidation of a thiol to a sulfonic acid; methanesulfonic acid is a strong, non‑corrosive acid used in organic synthesis and electrochemistry; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes methanethiol through sulfenic and sulfinic intermediates to the sulfonic acid, with water as by‑product; typically performed in aqueous solution, often acidic (pH ≈ 2–3) and at 0–25 °C initially, then warmed to reflux; catalytic amounts of transition‑metal ions (e.g., Fe²⁺) may be added to accelerate the reaction.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolysis of methyl 3‑methylbutanoate); purpose is to obtain the free acid. Water attacks the ester carbonyl, yielding 3‑methylbutanoic acid and methanol. Conditions: reflux in aqueous strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or use of aqueous base followed by acid work‑up. Common solvent: mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (e.g., THF) if needed.

Reaction type: Oxidative coupling. Purpose: Synthesizes azobenzene via oxidation of phenylhydrazine. Key transformation: Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes two phenylhydrazine molecules to form an azo bond. Conditions: Acidic environment (e.g., HCl), aqueous or ethanolic solvent, room temperature or mild heating.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; used to exchange anions and isolate insoluble lead(II) carbonate; lead(II) nitrate reacts with sodium carbonate in aqueous solution forming a white precipitate of PbCO3 and soluble NaNO3; typically carried out at room temperature with stirring, no special catalyst, water as solvent.

Complexation (acid–base deprotonation and metathesis) to form a thulium(III) acetylacetonate. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates acetylacetone to give sodium acetylacetonate; the anion then displaces chloride from thulium trichloride, yielding Tm(acac)3, NaCl and water. Typically performed in refluxing ethanol or methanol under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑metal single‑displacement (hydrogen‑evolution) reaction. Strontium metal reacts with acetic acid, liberating H2 gas and forming strontium acetate. Conducted in excess glacial acetic acid, often at mild heating (40–60 °C); the reaction proceeds without catalyst, though stirring and inert atmosphere prevent oxidation of the metal.

Oxidative epoxidation of an alkene; ethyl hydroperoxide transfers an oxygen atom to ethylene forming ethylene oxide, and the remaining fragment is reduced to ethanol. Conducted in organic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) with a metal catalyst such as Ti‑silicalite or a Lewis‑acid (e.g., Fe, Mn) at 50‑120 °C; peroxide is used stoichiometrically.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis of an alkyl tosylate). Water attacks the octyl p‑toluenesulfonate (SN1/SN2 depending on conditions), converting the leaving group to p‑toluenesulfonic acid and releasing 1‑octanol. Usually carried out in refluxing aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution, sometimes with mild heating; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑metal sulfide reaction; purpose is to dissolve copper(I) sulfide and generate hydrogen sulfide gas. Key transformation: protonation of sulfide to H₂S and formation of copper(I) chloride as the soluble metal salt. Typical conditions: aqueous hydrochloric acid at ambient temperature, stirring; gas evolved is collected. No special catalyst required.

Oxidation of a phosphite to phosphate (autoxidation). Trimethyl phosphite reacts with molecular oxygen to give trimethyl phosphate. The reaction proceeds via radical chain oxidation often catalyzed by a small amount of transition‑metal (e.g., CuCl, Co‑salts) or a radical initiator (AIBN) at 50–100 °C under an O2 atmosphere; solvent can be acetonitrile or neat.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange. Sodium fluoride exchanges with copper(II) sulfate in aqueous solution, producing sodium sulfate and copper(II) fluoride. Performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the reaction may be driven to completion by removal of CuF2 (e.g., by precipitation or evaporation). No additional catalyst is required.

Thermochemical reduction; hydrogen gas reduces samarium(III) oxide to metallic samarium while forming water. Typically carried out at 1000–1500 °C in a flowing H₂ atmosphere in a sealed furnace; no solvent, inert gas purge may be used.

Metallothermic reduction; reduces tantalum(V) bromide to elemental tantalum using potassium metal; key transformation is TaBr5 + 5 K → Ta⁰ + 5 KBr; typically carried out in a sealed tube under inert atmosphere (argon) at temperatures (400–600 °C); solid‑state reaction, no solvent, precaution to exclude moisture and air.

General type: O‑alkylation (SN2) of an oxime. Purpose: protect the oxime oxygen as a methoxy group or generate a methoxyimino derivative. Key transformation: the oxime oxygen attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide to give benzaldehyde O‑methyl oxime. Typical conditions: syn‑benzaldehyde oxime is treated with NaH or K2CO3 as base in dry DMF or DMSO, methyl iodide is added dropwise at 0 °C to 25 °C, reaction proceeds 1–2 h, then quenched and extracted.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation; Li2O reacts with phosphoric acid to form lithium phosphate (Li3PO4) and water; purpose is synthesis of an insoluble lithium phosphate material; key transformation is basic oxide + polyprotic acid → phosphate salt + H2O; conducted in water with heating to aid dissolution and precipitation; no catalyst.

Fluorination/halogen exchange (oxidative fluorination); fluorine gas oxidizes terbium(III) chloride to terbium(IV) fluoride, releasing chlorine; overall 4 F₂ + 2 TbCl₃ → 2 TbF₄ + 3 Cl₂; performed in a fluorine‑compatible reactor (e.g., nickel or Monel) at 200–400 °C under dry, inert conditions; no solvent, gas‑phase reaction; safety measures for handling F₂ and Cl₂ gases.

Base‑promoted nitrosamine hydrolysis; aqueous NaOH cleaves N‑nitrosoguanidine, yielding guanidine, sodium nitrite and water. The nitroso group is reduced to nitrite while the guanidine core is released. Reactions are usually carried out at ambient temperature to 60 °C in aqueous solution, with stoichiometric NaOH; the mixture is then acidified to isolate guanidine if desired.

Base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (alkaline hydrolysis); aqueous NaOH cleaves the amide bond of phenyl(piperidin‑1‑yl)methanone to give benzoic acid and piperidine; key steps: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on carbonyl, formation of carboxylate and release of piperidine; typically refluxed in water or aqueous ethanol for 2–4 h; after completion the mixture is acidified to precipitate benzoic acid and extract piperidine; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization to form a metal carboxylate; two equivalents of butanoic acid react with zinc oxide to give zinc butyrate and water: 2 C₃H₇CO₂H + ZnO → Zn(C₃H₇COO)₂ + H₂O; carried out by heating a suspension of ZnO in excess butanoic acid (or in a non‑protic solvent such as toluene) to 120–150 °C to drive off water; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

This is an acid-base reaction where octan-1-amine reacts with hydrochloric acid to form a water-soluble ammonium salt. The primary amine acts as a base, protonating to form octylammonium chloride. The reaction occurs in aqueous or alcoholic solution under ambient conditions. Hydrochloric acid serves as the proton donor and no catalysts are required. This reaction is commonly used to isolate amines as stable solid salts.

Protonation of cyanide (acidic liberation of HCN); aqueous hydrochloric acid protonates barium cyanide, releasing hydrogen cyanide gas and forming barium chloride: Ba(CN)₂ + 2 HCl → 2 HCN↑ + BaCl₂; performed at low temperature (0–5 °C) in a well‑ventilated fume hood or closed system to contain toxic HCN; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed aldose‑ketose isomerization (Lobry de Bruyn–Alberda van Ekenstein transformation) – D‑Mannose in aqueous sodium hydroxide undergoes enediol‐mediated tautomerization, interconverting to D‑glucose (another aldose) and D‑fructose (a ketose). The reaction is carried out at ambient to moderate temperatures (20–50 °C) in aqueous solution; the hydroxide ion acts as both catalyst and solvent.

Reductive conversion of a carboxylic acid to an aldehyde (acid → acyl chloride → aldehyde); pyridine‑3‑carboxylic acid is first activated by thionyl chloride to the acyl chloride, which is then reduced in situ by diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H) to 3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde; by‑products are HCl, SO₂ and diisobutylaluminum chloride; typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF under nitrogen at –78 °C to 0 °C, then warmed to room temperature; DIBAL‑H is the reducing agent, thionyl chloride serves as activating reagent.

Allylic oxidation using selenium dioxide; converts the allylic C–H of α‑ionone into a carbonyl group to give α‑irone; employed to introduce an aldehyde/ketone functionality; typically carried out with catalytic or stoichiometric SeO₂ in refluxing 1,4‑dioxane or tert‑butanol, often with a co‑oxidant such as tert‑butyl hydroperoxide; reaction proceeds under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of melamine; water attacks the triazine ring leading to cleavage of two exocyclic amino groups as NH₃ and formation of ammelide (2‑amino‑4,6‑dihydroxy‑1,3,5‑triazine); used for degradation of melamine; performed by heating melamine in excess water at 150–200 °C, optionally with dilute HCl or NaOH to accelerate the reaction.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide; purpose: convert the alkene into an alkyl bromide; key transformation: proton adds to the less substituted carbon to give the more stable secondary carbocation, which is trapped by Br⁻ to produce 2‑bromopentane (Markovnikov addition); typical conditions: aqueous HBr (48 %) or anhydrous HBr gas in a non‑polar solvent such as CCl4, temperature 0–25 °C, no peroxides present.

Hydrolytic decomposition of ethoxymethylformamide; nucleophilic attack of water on the N‑C and C‑O bonds yields formic acid, ethanol, and formaldehyde; serves as a route to cleave protected formyl groups; conducted in aqueous medium at 80–120 °C, often under mild acidic conditions (pH ≈ 3–) to promote cleavage.

General type: redox (oxidation–reduction) reaction. Purpose: generates elemental iodine and water from iodide; used analytically to produce I2 or in oxidative disposal of HI. Key transformation: iodide ions are oxidized to I2 while molecular oxygen is reduced to H2O (2 HI + ½ O2 → I2 + H2O). Typical conditions: aqueous solution, often heated gently; can be catalyzed by metals such as platinum or palladium. Common solvent: water or dilute acid; no special catalyst required for the basic stoichiometric reaction.

Acetylation (acylation) of 2‑naphthylamine with acetic anhydride; the amine nitrogen attacks the anhydride, forming N‑acetyl‑2‑naphthylamine and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid; a common method to protect aromatic amines; typically refluxed in pyridine or dichloromethane with catalytic pyridine at 60–80 °C for 1–2 .

Dissolving‑metal reduction (Birch‑type) of cyclopentene to cyclopentane; sodium metal in liquid ammonia donates electrons to the alkene, generating a radical anion that is protonated by ammonia, yielding the saturated alkane; used for catalytic‑free hydrogenation of simple alkenes; performed at –33 °C under dry liquid NH₃, using Na metal (1–2 equiv.) and often a small amount of a proton source such as tert‑butanol.

Acidic ester hydrolysis (acid‑catalyzed saponification). Methyl 3‑methylbut‑3‑enoate is cleaved by aqueous HCl to afford the corresponding carboxylic acid, 3‑methylbut‑3‑enoic acid, and methanol. Conditions: excess aqueous HCl (1–6 M), reflux 4–8 h, water (often with a co‑solvent such as THF or acetone) as medium; work‑up involves removal of methanol and isolation of the acid.

Oxidation of thioanisole to methyl phenyl sulfoxide with hypochlorous acid; HOCl transfers an oxygen atom to the sulfide, forming the sulfoxide and producing HCl; a selective method to obtain sulfoxides without over‑oxidation to sulfones; carried out in aqueous NaOCl (generated in‑situ) at 0–25 °C, pH 5–6, optionally with a buffer (acetate) to control acidity.

Double‑displacement (acid‑base metathesis) used to exchange acetate for formate; formic acidates acetate to give acetic acid while Pb²⁺ pairs with formate to form lead(II) formate; typically carried out in aqueous solution with gentle heating or reflux; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Amidation of an acyl iodide with an aromatic amine (aniline) to afford N‑phenylbenzamide and HI. Conducted in an inert, aprotic solvent (CH2Cl2, THF) at 0 °C to rt, with an amine base such as triethylamine or pyridine present in excess to scavenge the hydrogen iodide and improve yield.

Hydrolysis of an acyl fluoride; water attacks the carbonyl carbon of trifluoroacetyl fluoride, displacing fluoride and yielding trifluoroacetic acid and hydrogen fluoride; performed in aqueous media at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; water is both reactant and solvent; no additional catalyst needed.

Acylation (acetylation) of a primary amine; 5‑aminotetrazole nucleophilically attacks one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming the N‑acetyl amide (5‑acetylaminotetrazole) and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid; usually run in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile with a base or pyridine to scavenge the acid; catalytic DMAP or pyridine often employed; temperature from 0 °C to reflux.

Enzymatic oxidation (monooxygenase) of N‑methylnicotinamide; purpose is metabolic conversion to N‑methyl‑4‑pyridone‑5‑carboxamide; key transformation is incorporation of one atom of O2 into the N‑methyl group to form a lactam and reduction of the other O atom to H2O2; typical conditions are aqueous buffer at physiological pH (≈7.4), 37 °C, with the flavin‑dependent N‑methylnicotinamide oxidase and molecular oxygen; solvent is water.

Acylation of morpholine with chloroacetyl chloride; nucleophilic acyl substitution in a polar aprotic solvent (CH2Cl2 or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, usually in the presence of a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to capture HCl, producing N‑chloroacetyl‑morpholine (an amide) and hydrogen chloride; used to protect the nitrogen or introduce a chloroacetyl group.

Reduction of aldehydes to primary alcohols using sodium borohydride; nucleophilic hydride reduction; converts a carbonyl group to a primary alcohol via hydride transfer to the carbonyl carbon followed by protonation; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in protic solvents such as methanol, ethanol, isopropanol or THF/water mixtures; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile; purpose is to reduce the nitrile directly to a primary amine. Molecular hydrogen adsorbs on palladium metal, facilitating addition of two equivalents of hydrogen to the C≡N to give 2‑methoxybenzylamine. Typical setup: 1–5 atm H₂, 5–10 % Pd/C, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–80 °C, under nitrogen until H₂ is introduced.

Esterification of an allylic alcohol with an anhydride; linalool attacks isobutyric anhydride to give the corresponding ester (linalyl isobutyrate) andobutyric acid as the by‑product; typical conditions use a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) and a catalytic base such as pyridine or DMAP; reaction is run at 0 °C to room temperature, sometimes with gentle heating.

Acid‑base reaction of a metal carbonate with hydrogen fluoride; HF protonates carbonate forming CO₂ and H₂O while the fluoride anion coordinates Al³⁺ to give aluminum fluoride (AlF₃); performed in aqueous HF or neat HF at low to moderate temperature; excess HF drives the reaction to completion; no separate catalyst required.

Carbothermic reduction (metallothermic reduction) of a metal fluoride; solid thorium tetrafluoride is mixed with carbon and heated to very high temperature, reducing ThF₄ to metallic thorium while carbon is oxidized to carbon tetrafluoride gas. Reaction type: high‑temperature reduction. Conditions: temperatures of 1500–1800 °C in an inert atmosphere (Ar) or vacuum; solid‑state mixing, no solvent.

Williamson ether synthesis (O‑alkylation) of phenol with methyl bromoacetate; phenol is deprotonated by a base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaH) to generate phenoxide, which displaces bromide in an SN2 step to afford methyl 2‑phenoxyacetate, releasing HBr that is neutralized by the base; carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as acetone, DMF, or DMSO at reflux; catalytic amounts of phase‑transfer agents may be used, but no metal catalyst is needed.

Acid‑salt double displacement (acid‑base) reaction; converts insoluble cadmium phosphate to soluble cadmium chloride while liberating phosphoric acid; key transformation is protonation of phosphate and formation of CdCl2; typically carried out in aqueous HCl solution, often heated to aid dissolution; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic aza‑Michael addition of allylamine to maleic anhydride forming N‑allyl maleamic acid (an amic acid); purpose is to generate a functional monomer for polymer or medicinal chemistry; the amine attacks one carbonyl of the anhydride, opening the ring to give a mono‑acid mono‑amide; usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of a tertiary amine to its N‑oxide using oxone (potassium peroxymonosulfate); purpose is to prepare the amine N‑oxide surfactant or oxidation intermediate; oxygen is transferred from peroxymonosulfate to the nitrogen, yielding N,N‑dimethyldodecylamine N‑oxide and potassium bisulfate; conducted in aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 8) at 0–25 °C, often with water or water/acetone as solvent; no additional catalyst is required.

Citrate reduction of chloroauric acid to colloidal gold (Turkevich method); purpose is the synthesis of gold nanoparticles; citrate acts as both reducing agent (oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O) and stabilizer, converting Au³⁺ to Au⁰ while producing NaCl; performed in water by boiling a AuCl₃ solution, adding trisodium citrate rapidly, refluxing for several minutes, then cooling; water is the solvent and no external catalyst is used.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a chloro‑nitrile with aqueous NaOH. 3‑Chloropropionitrile undergoes hydroxide attack to replace Cl with OH, yielding 3‑hydroxypropanenitrile and NaCl. Conducted in water or aqueous NaOH solution, typically refluxed for several hours; excess base ensures complete conversion. No special solvent is needed beyond the aqueous medium.

Type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (acid‑chloride to amide). Purpose: convert 2‑ethoxybenzoyl chloride into the corresponding amide. Key transformation: the chloride leaving group is displaced by ammonia, forming 2‑ethoxybenzamide and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: reaction performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap the generated HCl.

Halide metathesis (anion exchange) between hydrofluoric acid and copper(II) chloride; purpose is to generate copper(II) fluoride and regenerate HCl; fluoride ions replace chloride on Cu²⁺, giving CuF₂, while chloride is protonated to HCl; conducted in aqueous HF (or HF gas bubbled into solution) at ambient temperature; water is the medium, and no catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene oxide by cyclobutylamine to afford 2‑(cyclobutylamino)ethanol; purpose is synthesis of a β‑amino alcohol; the amine attacks an electrophilic carbon of the strained epoxide, opening the ring and introducing a hydroxyl group; typically carried out in water or ethanol at 0–50 °C, often with a slight excess of ethylene oxide; no catalyst is necessary.

Azo coupling (condensation) between phenylhydrazine and nitrosobenzene to form azobenzene; phenylhydrazine reduces nitrosobenzene and water is eliminated. Typically performed in ethanol or glacial acetic acid at room temperature; no external catalyst required.

Double displacement/precipitation; used to prepare a magnesium citrate salt from aqueous solutions of sodium citrate and magnesium nitrate. Key transformation: exchange of Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions forming soluble sodium nitrate and sparingly soluble trimagnesium dicitrate that precipitates. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, ambient to mild heating, stirring until complete mixing; pH generally remains near neutral to slightly acidic. No special catalyst required; common solvent is water.

Chromic‑acid oxidation of a primary alcohol; ethanol is oxidized to acetic acid while sodium chromate is reduced from Cr(VI) to Cr(III) forming chromium(III) sulfate, with sulfuric acid providing the acidic medium. Carried out in aqueous solution under reflux (≈100 °C); sodium chromate/H₂SO₄ act as the stoichiometric oxidant, no additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; zinc dichloride solution reacts with sodium sulfide solution, exchanging anions to give insoluble zinc sulfide solid and soluble sodium chloride; performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; ZnS precipitates and is collected by filtration.

Reduction of an alkyl bromide with lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH₄ acts as a strong nucleophilic hydride source that replaces the bromide at the terminal carbon of 6‑bromo‑1‑ with hydrogen, yielding 1‑hexanol. Key transformation: C–Br bond cleavage and formation of C–H bond; lithium bromide is generated as a by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous diethyl ether or THF, 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). No catalyst; LiAlH₄ is the reducing agent.

Carbamoylation of L‑glutamic acid with potassium cyanate in acidic medium; the cyanate ion adds to the α‑amine of glutamic acid forming N‑carbamoyl‑L‑glutamic acid, while HCl supplies chloride to give KCl. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the amine on the electrophilic carbon of the cyanate (OCN⁻) forming a urea‑type linkage. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, pH adjusted with HCl (often 0.5–1 M), temperature 25–60 °C, stirring until completion. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Reduction of niobium dioxide (NbO₂) by hydrogen gas; a high‑temperature gas‑phase reduction yielding niobium monoxide (NbO) and water vapor. Key transformation: transfer of hydrogen to oxide, lowering the oxidation state of niobium from +4 to +2. Typical conditions: flow of pure H₂ over solid NbO₂ at 600–900 °C in a tubular furnace; inert carrier gas may be used. No solvent; catalyst is the metal oxide itself.

Acid‑metal reaction between thiocyanic acid (HSCN) and elemental nickel; nickel is oxidized to Ni²⁺ while HSCN is deprotonated, producing nickel(II) thiocyanate and liberating hydrogen gas. Key transformation: redox where Ni⁰ → Ni²⁺ and 2 H⁺ → H₂. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic solution (often dilute HSCN), moderate heating (50–80 °C) with stirring; reaction may be performed under reflux to collect H₂. No external catalyst; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride aqueous ammonia; amination of 2‑oro‑4‑methylpentane to give 2‑amino‑4‑methylpentane and HCl; typically performed by refluxing the chloride in excess NH₃ (aqueous or ethanolic) at 50‑100 °C.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between sodium sulfate and ammonium chloride in aqueous solution; produces sodium chloride and ammonium sulfate; usually carried out by dissolving the salts in water and heating to crystallize (NH₄)₂SO₄.

Enzymatic oxidative deamination; purpose: catabolism of norepinephrine; key transformation: removal of the amine group and oxidation of the side chain to give 3,4‑dihydroxyphenylglycolaldehyde, with formation of hydrogen peroxide and ammonia; conditions: physiological pH, presence of monoamine oxidase enzyme, molecular oxygen as oxidant, aqueous medium; no external solvent or catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of zinc diethyldithiocarbamate; on heating the solid in an inert atmosphere it breaks down to carbon disulfide, diethylamine, and zinc sulfide; no solvent, temperatures ~200‑300 °C.

Base‑mediated dissolution (alkali titanate synthesis); transforms titanium(IV) hydroxide into sodium titanate, a soluble precursor for ceramics or pigments; hydroxide groups are deprotonated by sodium hydroxide, producing Na₂TiO₃ (or its hydrated form) and water; reaction performed in aqueous NaOH solution at 60‑80 °C; no special catalyst required.

Condensationester) of 4‑nitrophenol with dimethyl dithiophosphoric acid to afford methyl parathion and water; commonly conducted under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (pyridine or toluene) with removal of water, sometimes using a base catalyst.
Catalytic hydrogenolysis (dehalogenation) of 3,4‑dibromothiophene using H₂ and Pd/C to give thiophene; performed in an alcohol solvent (ethanol or methanol) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25‑80 °C.
Oxidation of elemental tellurium by hydrogen peroxide to form tellium dioxide; carried out in aqueous medium, often acidic, at room temperature to 60 °C, yielding water as a by‑product.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of chloromethane: hydrogen gas reduces the C–Cl bond to give methane and hydrogen chloride. Requires a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Pt, or Raney nickel, performed under pressure (1–5 atm H₂) at 50–150 °C in a solvent like ethanol or methanol.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose to generate hydrogen chloride gas while precipitating insoluble barium sulfate; key ion exchange: K⁺ exchanges with Ba²⁺ producing BaSO₄(s) and KCl(aq) with release of HCl(g); typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating to drive off HCl; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

NaBH₄ reduction of a ketone: sodium borohydride delivers hydride to the carbonyl of 4‑methoxyacetophenone, yielding the secondary alcohol 1‑(4‑methoxyphenyl)ethanol. Typically performed in methanol, ethanol, or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction quenched with water. No catalyst required.

Acid–base protonation: hydrochloric acid protonates acetamidine to give the acetamidinium chloride salt. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric HCl neutralizes the amidine.
Acid–base neutralization: hydrobromic acid reacts with nickel(II) hydroxide to produce water and nickel(II) bromide, a soluble salt. Usually carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature.

Oxidation (combustion) of uranium nitride. Uranium nitride (UN) is exposed to O₂ at elevated temperature, forming uranium dioxide (UO₂) and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) gas. The reaction is used to convert nitride fuel to oxide for handling or re‑processing. Typical conditions: flow of O₂ gas, temperatures 800–1200 °C in a furnace or controlled‑atmosphere furnace.

Transesterification: p‑cresol attacks methyl salicylate, exchanging the alkoxy groups to form p‑cresyl salicylate and methanol. Catalyzed by acids (e.g., H₂SO₄) or bases (e.g., NaOMe) under reflux in an inert solvent such as toluene or the phenol itself; removal of methanol drives equilibrium.

Acid‑base neutralization; converts solid calcium carbonate into soluble calcium hydrogen phosphate while liberating carbon dioxide and water; key transformation is protonation of carbonate and precipitation of CaHPO4; usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, with phosphoric acid added slowly to a slurry of CaCO3 and stirring; water is the solvent.

Acid-base (neutralization) reaction; purpose is to convert insoluble terbium(III) oxide into a soluble nitrate salt; key transformation is protonation of the oxide to form water and coordination of nitrate to Tb³⁺; typically carried out by adding solid Tb₂O₃ to hot (80‑100 °C) aqueous nitric acid under reflux; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Oxidative chlorination (halogen metathesis) of a metal silicide; purpose is to generate iron(II) chloride and volatile silicon tetrachloride; key transformations are Cl₂ oxidizing FeSi, yielding FeCl₂ (solid) and SiCl₄ (gas); performed at elevated temperatures (200‑400 °C) in a dry chlorine gas stream, often in a sealed quartz tube; no solvent or catalyst, just gaseous chlorine and solid reactant.

Ligand exchange/coordination complex formation; sodium acetylacetonate reacts with iron(III) chloride to produce iron(III) acetylacetonate and NaCl, with water released from the hydrates; usually carried out in refluxing ethanol‑water mixture, inert atmosphere optional, precipitation of Fe(acac)₃ drives the reaction.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of an epoxide by a secondary amine; purpose is to synthesize a β‑amino alcohol; key transformation is attack of diisopropylamine nitrogen on the less hindered carbon of ethylene oxide, producing 2‑(diisopropylamino)ethanol; usually done in an aprotic solvent such as THF or MeCN at 0 °C to rt; no external catalyst, the amine itself acts as nucleophile and base.

SN2 quaternization (alkylation) of triethylamine with 2‑bromoethanol; purpose is to prepare the quaternary ammonium salt triethyl(2‑hydroxyethyl)ammonium bromide (triethylcholine bromide); key transformation is nucleophilic substitution of bromide by the lone pair on nitrogen, forming a permanent N⁺‑C bond; conducted in polar protic or aprotic solvents (ethanol, acetonitrile) under reflux or at rt with excessethylamine; no catalyst required.

E2 alkaline elimination using alcoholic KOH; purpose is formation of the alkene from the alkyl halide; key transformation involves removal of a β‑hydrogen and loss of Cl to give 1‑methylcyclohexene, KCl and water; typical conditions are KOH dissolved in ethanol, reflux temperature (≈60‑80 °C).

Acylation of sec‑butylamine using acetic anhydride to afford N‑sec‑butylacetamide; the amine attacks the anhydride, generating the amide and acetic acid as by‑product; typically run neat or in a solvent such as pyridine which also scavenges the acid; mild heating (50‑80 °C) is common.
