Conducted in a fluorination furnace at 300–500 °C, using dry HF gas; no solvent, and the reaction vessel is typically made of nickel or monel alloy.

Metathesis (acid dissolution) of a rare‑earth phosphate; aqueous nitric acid protonates dysprosium phosphate, liberating phosphoric acid and forming soluble dysprosium nitrate. Performed in water at 50–80 °C with stirring; excess HNO₃ ensures complete dissolution, and no catalyst is required.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an oxime; water attacks acetone oxime, cleaving the N‑O bond to regenerate acetone and release hydroxylamine. Usually carried out in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1–2 M HCl) or with mild base at 80–100 °C; solvent is water or a water‑alcohol mixture, and the reaction is homogeneous.

Nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus (P‑alkylation). Methanol attacks phosphorus of phosphorothioic tribromide, displacing bromide to give trimethyl phosphorothioate and HBr. Performed under anhydrous conditions, often at reflux, using an inert atmosphere; methanol serves as both reactant and solvent, sometimes with a base (e.g., pyridine) to trap HBr.

Fenton‑type oxidative hydroxylation. Fe(II) catalyzes decomposition of H₂O₂ to hydroxyl radicals, which hydroxylate 3,5‑dichlorophenol to 3,5‑dichlorocatechol, producing water as by‑product. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at ambient to slightly elevated temperature, pH≈3‑4; iron(II) sulfate acts as catalyst, no organic solvent required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of acetyl chloride with 3‑methylbutan‑2‑amine to afford N‑(3‑methylbutan‑2‑yl)acetamide and HCl; carried out in an inert solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or THF with a base (pyridine, Et₃N) at 0 °C to room temperature to trap the released HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (de‑acetylation) of the acetate protecting group on ethyl 4‑(acetyloxy)butanoate, yielding the free hydroxy ester ethyl 4‑hydroxybutanoate and acetic acid. Performed with dilute aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) and heating (reflux) in a water/organic mixture such as THF/H₂O.

Halogenation/oxidation of a metal silicide. Chlorine gas chlorinates manganese disilicide, producing manganese(II) chloride and silicon tetrachloride. Typically performed in a sealed tube or flow reactor at elevated temperature (150‑300 °C) under dry conditions; no solvent is used, and the reaction proceeds via direct gas‑solid interaction.

Allylic nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis). Aqueous NaOH attacks 1,3‑dichloropropene, displacing one chloride to give 3‑chloroprop‑2‑en‑1‑ol and NaCl. Conducted in water (or dilute aqueous NaOH) at room temperature or mild heating; the reaction follows an SN2′ pathway characteristic of allylic halides.

Enzymatic transamination (aminotransferase) reaction; L‑cysteine transfers its amino group to α‑ketoglutarate producing mercaptopyruvic acid and L‑glutamic acid; typically performed in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) with pyridoxal‑phosphate (PLP) as cofactor, often in the presence of the enzyme cysteine aminotransferase; no organic solvents required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination). Bicyclo[2.2.1]heptan‑2‑ol loses water under the action of a strong acid (e.g., conc. H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or solid acid (Al₂O₃, zeolite) at 80–130 °C, forming the corresponding alkene bicyclo[2.2.1]hept‑2‑ene. The reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate; removal of the β‑hydrogen gives the double bond. Purpose: generate the norbornene framework from the alcohol.

Direct halogenation (chlorination); exposure of solid AlSb to chlorine gas at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) in a dry, inert atmosphere yields aluminum chloride and antimony trichloride. This is a redox oxidation where chlorine oxidizes both metals. No solvent; gas‑phase reaction.

Stoichiometric oxidation with chromium(VI) in sulfuric acid. Chromium(VI) oxide (as chromic acid in H₂SO₄) oxidizes 9,10‑dihydroanthracene to anthraquinone, reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III) which forms chromium(III) sulfate. Carried out in concentrated H₂SO₄ under reflux (≈180 ); the medium provides both oxidant and solvent, and the reaction is driven by the strong oxidizing power of Cr(VI).

Redox/decomposition reaction; hydrogen peroxide reduces trichloroisocyanuric acid, oxidizing the chlorine atoms to chloride while releasing oxygen; yields hydrochloric acid, water, and cyanuric acid. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required; pH may be adjusted with buffer.

Palladium‑catalyzed Sonogashira cross‑coupling; aryl bromide (bromobenzene) couples with terminal alkyne (phenylacetylene) to a C≡C‑linked diaryl alkyne (diphenylacetylene). Triethylamine acts as base, CuI as co‑catalyst, Pd(dba)₂ as Pd(0) source. Usually carried out under nitrogen or argon in an aprotic solvent such as THF, DMF or toluene at 50–80 °C. By‑ are triethylammonium bromide and copper(I) bromide.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an aromatic aldehyde; vanillin is reduced by H₂ over palladium on carbon to the corresponding primary alcohol (vanillyl alcohol). Reaction conducted in an alcohol solvent (ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate) at 1–5 atm H₂, typically 25–50 °C. Purpose is to convert the aldehyde functional group to an alcohol.

Fischer esterification; acetic acid reacts with 2‑heptanol to give 2‑heptyl acetate and water. Acid catalyst (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) is used, and the mixture is refluxed in a non‑aqueous solvent such as toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water. Reaction proceeds at 100–120 °C until equilibrium shifts toward ester formation.

Metal‑acid displacement/chelation reaction; aluminum metal reacts with citric acid in aqueous solution, producing hydrogen gas and forming soluble aluminum citrate complexes. Reaction is exothermic and performed at room temperature or mild heating, often with stirring to promote metal dissolution. No catalyst is required; excess acid drives the reaction to completion.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of a primary amine; furfurylamine reacts with methyl iodide to give N‑methyl‑furfurylamine and hydrogen iodide as by‑product. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature. A basee.g., triethylamine) is often added to neutralize the generated HI, though not shown in the stoichiometry.

Acid–base reaction (acid digestion). Magnesium silicate is protonated by sulfuric acid, yielding soluble magnesium sulfate and silicic acid while consuming a molecule of water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, reflux or gentle heating, excess H2SO4. Common solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed transetherification; the methyl ether group in 2‑methoxy‑2‑methylbutane is exchanged with ethanol to give the ethyl ether 2‑ethoxy‑2‑methylbutane and methanol as by‑product. Typical conditions use a strong acid catalyst (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid or H2SO4) or a Lewis acid (e.g., BF3·OEt2) under reflux in anhydrous toluene or benzene, with continuous removal of methanol to shift equilibrium.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration). 1,2,4,5‑Tetrachlorobenzene undergoes nitration with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid to introduce a nitro group at the position ortho to the existing chlorines, forming 1,2,4,5‑Tetrachloro‑3‑nitrobenzene. Conditions: mixture of conc. HNO3/H2SO4, temperature 0–5 °C initially, then 30–40 °C for completion. Solvent: the acid mixture itself; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid (Pinnick oxidation). 2‑Chlorobenzaldehyde is oxidized by sodium chlorite to 2‑chlorobenzoic acid. Reaction is usually performed in aqueous buffer (e.g., NaH2PO4, pH ≈ 6.5) with a chlorine scavenger such as 2‑methyl‑2‑butene to suppress side reactions. Conditions: room temperature to 40 °C, mild stirring. Solvent: water/acetone mixture; catalyst: none (chlorite is the oxidant).

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation. Lithium sulfate and barium cyanide exchange ions in aqueous solution, precipitating insoluble barium sulfate while forming soluble lithium cyanide. Reaction is carried out in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the BaSO4 precipitate is filtered off. No catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of a metal halide. Dipotassium hexachloroosmate reacts with water, undergoing ligand exchange to give osmium dioxide (OsO2), hydrochloric acid, and potassium chloride. Typically performed by adding solid K2OsCl6 to hot aqueous solution, refluxing for several hours. Solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Oxidative chlorination of a sulfinate (halogenation). Chlorine gas reacts with sodium methanesulfinate to produce methanesulfonyl chloride and sodium chloride. The reaction is carried out in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often under inert atmosphere to control exotherm. No additional catalyst is required.

General type: acid‑catalyzed esterification; purpose: prepare the methyl ester of isethionic acid; key transformation: carboxylic acid of isethionic acid reacts with methanol to give methyl isethionate and water; typical conditions: reflux methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H2SO4 or HCl) for several hours; common solvent/catalyst: methanol serves as both reactant and solvent, acid catalyst as above.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamate formation). Primary alcohol attacks carbamoyl chloride to give propyl carbamate; HCl is released and usually scavenged by a base such as pyridine or triethylamine. Performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) under inert atmosphere.

Kumada‑type cross‑coupling (aryl‑alkyl C–C bond formation). Bromobenzene couples with n‑propylmagnesium bromide in the presence of catalytic CuI to afford propylbenzene. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF, inert gas, 0 °C to reflux, stoichiometric Grignard reagent, catalytic CuI (5–10 mol %).

Acid‑base neutralization/metal soap synthesis. Two equivalents of stearic acid react with calcium carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and forming calcium stearate. Conducted by heating a slurry of the solid reagents (150–200 °C) or in melt; no solvent required.

Hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution) of ethyl iodide with water; water acts as nucleophile displacing iodide to give ethanol and hydrogen iodide. Typically performed in aqueous medium, often heated to reflux; no additional catalyst required, polar protic solvent (water) suffices.

Conversion of 1‑hexanol to 1‑chlorhexane using the Lucas reagent (conc. HCl with ZnCl₂); proceeds via SN1 (or SN2 for primary) substitution, ZnCl₂ acting as a Lewis‑acid catalyst; reaction conducted in refluxing aqueous HCl or neat HCl/ZnCl₂ mixture at 60–80 °C, generating water as the by‑product.

Type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (acetylation). Purpose: protect thiourea by introducing acetyl groups on both nitrogens. Key transformation: both NH groups of thiourea react with acetic anhydride to give N,N'-diacetylthiourea, releasing acetic acid. Typical conditions: heating or reflux, often in pyridine or anhydrous dichloromethane; pyridine acts as base and solvent to scavenge acid.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; cobalt(II) bromide exchanges anions with carbonate from potassium carbonate to give insoluble cobalt(II) carbonate precipitate and soluble potassium bromide; carried out in water with stirring, often with mild heating; no catalyst is needed.

Alcoholysis of a metal halide to prepare a metal alkoxide. TiCl₄ reacts with excess isopropanol in the presence of pyridine, which scavenges the released HCl as pyridinium chloride, affording titanium(IV) isopropoxide. Performed under anhydrous, inert conditions (dry CH₂Cl₂ or toluene) at 0 °C to room temperature; pyridine is used in catalytic or stoichiometric amount to neutralize HCl.

Acid–base/esterification (mesylation) of a diol: 1,4‑butanediol is converted to its bis‑methanesulfonate (Busulfan) by reaction with methanesulfonyl chloride in the presence of the nucleophilic catalyst DMAP (often together with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine). The two primary alcohol groups are transformed into O‑SO2CH3 groups, releasing HCl. Typical conditions are anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, under inert atmosphere.

Single‑displacement (metal‑water) reaction; elemental barium reacts with water to produce aqueous barium hydroxide and hydrogen gas; vigorous reaction, typically carried out with the metal in liquid water or steam at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature; water is both reactant and solvent; no catalyst; used to prepare Ba(OH)₂ solution and generate H₂.

Acid–base neutralization forming a metal iodate: Zinc oxide reacts with iodic acid in aqueous solution to give zinc iodate and water. The oxide acts as a base, accepting protons from HIO3 and exchanging the anion. Reactions are usually performed at ambient to mild heating, with water as solvent; no catalyst is required.

Metathesis (double‑replacement) between a metal acetate and nitric acid: Mercury(II) acetate exchanges its acetate ligands for nitrate when treated with nitric acid, producing mercury(II) nitrate and acetic acid. Conducted in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature; no special catalyst needed.

Combustion (oxidation) of 2‑butyne: Two molecules of 2‑butyne are rapidly oxidized by excess O2, yielding carbon dioxide and water with a large exotherm. The reaction proceeds at flame temperature (≈800 °C) in open air; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Halide exchange (metathesis): rhenium trichloride reacts with hydrogen bromide gas, swapping chloride for bromide to give rhenium tribromide and hydrogen chloride gas. Performed in the gas phase or in a dry, non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) at elevated temperature (≈150–250 °C). No catalyst needed.

Wurtz coupling of a secondary alkyl iodide with sodium metal; forms a new C–C bond yielding 3,3,4,4‑tetramethylhexane. Performed under dry, aprotic conditions (dry ether or THF) with excess metallic sodium, reflux, inert atmosphere; side reactions include elimination and coupling of radicals.

Radical oxidation of catechol by a hydroxyl radical to form ortho‑benzoquinone; OH· abstracts a hydrogen atom from catechol, producing water and the o‑quinone; occurs in aqueous solution during advanced oxidation processes; ambient to mild temperature; typically performed in water without added catalyst.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of GaAs: Arsenic trichloride reacts with elemental gallium at elevated temperature (600–800 °C) in a sealed ampoule or under vacuum. Gallium reduces the arsenic halide, forming the binary semiconductor gallium arsenide and liberating chlorine gas. No solvent; the reaction relies on thermal activation and the volatility of Cl2.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a diene; adds H2 across the two C=C bonds of norbornadiene to give saturated norbornane. Typical conditions: H2 pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C, PtO2 or Raney Ni as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, at room temperature to reflux.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to generate insoluble barium carbonate and soluble ammonium nitrate; key transformation is exchange of Ba²⁺ and NH₄⁺ ions producing BaCO₃ solid and NH₄NO₃ in solution; performed in aqueous medium at room temperature with stirring; product BaCO₃ is filtered and washed, NH₄NO₃ remains in the filtrate.

Thionyl chloride mediated chlorination (nucleophilic substitution) of an alcohol; purpose is to replace the hydroxyl group with a chlorine atom; key transformation converts 8‑chloro‑octan‑1‑ol to 1,8‑dichlorooctane while generating HCl and SO₂ gases; typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, at 0 °C to reflux, with pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl; the reaction mixture is vented through a gas trap for SO₂.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of a lactone; purpose is to open the γ‑butyrolactone ring to afford the sodium salt of γ‑hydroxybutyrate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl carbon, yielding sodium γ‑hydroxybutyrate and water; carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at ambient temperature or under gentle reflux; the reaction may be conducted in water or a water/ethanol mixture; the product is isolated by evaporation and acidification if needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to a primary amine; purpose is to convert dodecyl cyanide into dodecylamine; key transformation reduces the –C≡N triple bond to –CH₂NH₂; performed under high‑pressure hydrogen (30–50 bar) at 100–150 °C in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂; common solvents are ethanol, methanol, or water; after reaction the mixture is filtered to remove the catalyst and the amine is isolated.

Solid‑state double‑salt formation (ionic exchange) between aluminum fluoride and potassium fluoride; purpose is to produce a mixed fluoride salt (often written KAlF₄, potassium aluminum fluoride); key transformation combines AlF₃ with KF to give the complex fluoride anion; typically carried out by mixing the powdered reagents and heating to 500–650 °C in a dry oven or by dissolving both in water and evaporating to crystallize the product; no additional catalyst is required; the solid is washed and dried.

Cyclodehydration of N‑hydroxyurea to 1,2,3‑oxadiazol‑5(2H)‑one using triphosgene. Triphosgene activates the carbonyl of N‑hydroxyurea, promoting intramolecular attack and loss of two equivalents of HCl. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl. The reaction yields the heterocycle and HCl (captured by the base).

formation of methyl methanesulfonate from methanesulfonyl chloride, methanol and pyridine; reaction type is nucleophilic substitution (sulfonate esterification); the alcohol oxygen attacks the sulfonyl chloride, pyridine scavenges the generated HCl as pyridinium chloride; typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, anhydrous dichloromethane (or chloroform) as solvent, pyridine as base and often solvent, inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base reaction of a metal carbonate with hydrofluoric acid; purpose is to generate bismuth(III) fluoride while releasing carbon dioxide; key transformation protonates the carbonate, producing CO₂ and H₂O and simultaneously replaces carbonate with fluoride to give BiF₃; carried out in aqueous HF, often in excess HF, at 0–25 °C with vigorous stirring; the reaction evolves CO₂ gas; after completion the solution is evaporated to obtain solid BiF₃, which may be washed with cold HF solution.

Acid–base metathesis (salt exchange) converting indium(III) acetate to indium(III) chloride by treatment with aqueous HCl; generates acetic acid as by‑product. Typically performed in water at ambient or slightly elevated temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular cyclization of citronellal using catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid to give rose oxide (a cyclic ether). The reaction proceeds via protonation of the aldehyde, formation of a hemiacetal, and ring closure. Typically run at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, often under air‑free conditions.

Acid‑catalyzed trimerization of formaldehyde to 1,3,5‑trioxane. Trifluoroacetic acid acts as a strong protic acid catalyst, promoting condensation of three formaldehyde molecules with loss of water. Reaction is carried out in anhydrous TFA or a TFA/H₂O mixture at 0–25 °C; removal of water drives the equilibrium.

Halogen‑exchange (halide metathesis) where HBr converts chloroiodomethane to bromoiodomethane with release of HCl. Typically proceeds via SN2 substitution of chloride by bromide in the presence of excess HBr. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile under reflux; no additional catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of thallium(I) carbonate to thallium(I) oxide and carbon dioxide. Heating the solid carbonate at 300–600 °C in air or inert atmosphere causes release of CO₂ and formation of Tl₂O (or Tl₂O depending on stoichiometry). No catalyst needed.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of ethyl 2,5‑dihydroxycinnamate with methanol to give the methyl ester and ethanol. Usually performed with excess methanol, catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOMe), under reflux (50–80 °C) to drive equilibrium toward the methyl ester; removal of ethanol can shift equilibrium.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous exchange of ions between barium acetate and praseodymium(III) sulfate to precipitate insoluble barium sulfate while forming soluble praseodymium(III) acetate; typically performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Esterification (acylation) of the allylic alcohol linalool with acetic anhydride, yielding linalyl acetate and acetic acid as by‑product; often conducted under reflux in anhydrous solvents such as dichloromethane or toluene, using a catalytic amount of pyridine, DMAP or a Lewis acid to accelerate acyl transfer and neutralize the liberated acid.

Electrophilic halogen addition across the C=C bond of but‑2‑ene, producing 2,3‑dichlorobutane; carried out by bubbling Cl₂ gas through the alkene dissolved in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) at 0 °C to 25 °C to control the reaction rate; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration); introduces a nitro group para to the chlorine on chlorobenzene; key transformation is substitution of an aromatic hydrogen by NO₂⁺ generated from concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄; performed with mixed concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids at 45‑55 °C (often with an ice bath), the acid mixture acts as solvent and catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration) of fluoranthene using nitronium tetrafluoroborate as the nitrating agent; the nitronium cation attacks the aromatic system to install a nitro group, while BF₄⁻ decomposes to BF₃ and HF; performed at low temperature (−10 °C to 0 °C) in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or nitromethane; BF₃ acts as a Lewis acid catalyst inherent to the reagent.

Acid‑base neutralization; Li2O (basic oxide) reacts with aqueous H2SO4 to give lithium sulfate salt and water; purpose is salt formation; key transformation is oxide + strong acid → salt + H2O; typically performed in water at ambient to moderate temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of ferrous hydroxide (Fe(OH)₂) by molecular oxygen to form ferric hydroxide (Fe(OH)₃); a redox and precipitation process that occurs readily when Fe(II) solutions are exposed to air or O₂ gas under neutral to mildly alkaline aqueous conditions; no additional catalyst required.

High‑temperature carbothermic chlorination of titanium dioxide with carbon in the presence of chlorine gas to produce titanium tetrachloride and carbon dioxide; an industrial chlorination/reduction step (as in the Kroll process) carried out in a furnace at ~1000 °C under a flow of Cl₂, with solid TiO₂ mixed with carbon; no solvent; reaction is driven by heat.

Electrophilic aromatic halogen of a nucleoside; N‑bromosuccinimide delivers a bromine electrophile that substitutes at the C‑5 position of the pyrimidine ring of 2'-deoxyuridine to give 5‑bromo‑2'-deoxyuridine. Purpose is to introduce a reactive handle for further functionalization or labeling. performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or aqueous acetate buffer at 0 °C to room temperature; no metal catalyst required. By‑product succinimide is formed.

Perester‑mediated epoxidation of cyclooctene using tert‑butyl peroxybenzoate. Homolytic O–O cleavage generates tert‑butoxy and benzoyloxy radicals that transfer an oxygen atom to the alkene, affording cyclooctene oxide while producing benzoic acid tert‑butanol as by‑products. Conducted in an inert, non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

Thermal decomposition of perchlorate; upon strong heating, magnesium perchlorate decomposes to release oxygen gas and form magnesium chloride (often via intermediate MgCl₂ formation in the presence of chloride ions); requires high temperature (typically >300 °C) in a dry environment, sometimes under inert atmosphere.

Oxidation (Jones oxidation); primary alcohol to carboxylic acid with chromium(VI) reagents. 2‑Methylheptan‑1‑ol is treated with Jones reagent (CrO3 in conc. H2SO4) in acetone, usually at 0 °C then allowed to warm to rt. The alcohol is oxidized through the aldehyde stage to the acid, and chromium is reduced to Cr(III) sulfate. The work‑up involves quenching with isopropanol or water and extracting the acid.

Combined catalytic hydrogenation and O‑methylation of morphine; under H₂ pressure and Pd/C, the 7,8‑double bond of morphine is reduced, while methyl iodide in the presence of potassium carbonate alkylates the phenolic hydroxyl to give dihydrocodeine. Purpose is to convert the analgesic morphine into the more lipophilic dihydrocodeine. Typical conditions: 1–3 atm H₂, Pd/C (10 wt %), MeI (1–2 equiv), K₂CO₃ (excess), in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or acetone at 25–50 °C.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑chloro‑2‑methylpropan‑2‑ol with aqueous sodium hydroxide to afford 2‑methyl‑1,2‑propanediol and sodium chloride. Reaction is run in water or aqueous ethanol, typically heated to reflux (60–80 °C) for several hours, and the diol is isolated after acidification and extraction.

Condensation/oxidative rearrangement of alloxan with ammonium hydroxide to produce murexide (ammonium purpurate); ammonia adds to the carbonyl groups of alloxan, followed by dehydration and oxidation to generate the colored heterocyclic dye murexide, with water as the only small‑molecule by‑product. Performed in aqueous NH₄OH, often with gentle heating (50–80 °C) to drive the reaction to completion.

Acid‑base neutralsaponification) of a fatty acid with sodium methoxide; NaOCH₃ deprotonates palmitic acid, forming sodium palmitate and methanol. This straightforward salt‑formation step is used to prepare the sodium salt of the fatty acid. Typically carried out in methanol (or a methanol/water mixture) at room temperature or with mild heating; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization of a carboxylic acid with a metal carbonate; purpose is to generate the corresponding metal acetate while releasing carbon dioxide and water; key transformation: two equivalents of acetic acid protonate strontium carbonate to give strontium acetate, CO₂ and H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous–organic medium, gentle heating to drive off CO₂; common solvent: water or water/ethanol; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralisation (salt metathesis). Benzamidine hydrochloride is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide, liberating the free base benzamidine, while forming NaCl and water. The reaction is carried out in water at ambient temperature; stoichiometric NaOH (1 equiv) is sufficient, and the product can be extracted into an organic solvent or isolated by adjusting pH to precipitate the free base.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 3‑hydroxypropionaldehyde to 1,3‑propanediol; the aldehyde is reduced under hydrogen gas in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni, Pd/C, or Cu–Cr alloy). Typical conditions: 30–50 bar H₂, 80–150 °C, in water or an alcohol solvent; the reaction converts the carbonyl group to an additional hydroxyl, giving the diol.

Oxidation of benzyl bromide (or the benzyl group) with potassium permanganate to benzoic acid; strong oxidizing conditions in aqueous alkaline medium (KMnO₄ with NaOH or K₂CO₃) heated under reflux; manganese dioxide precipitates and potassium bromide is formed as a side product.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange between calcium nitrate and sodium valproate; purpose is to prepare calcium valproate, a less soluble pharmaceutical salt; key transformation: Ca²⁺ exchanges nitrate for valproate anion, yielding Ca(valproate)₂ and 2 NaNO₃; typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at ambient temperature, optionally gentle heating to promote precipitation; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid; purpose is to convert 2‑chloropropionic acid to 2‑chloropropanol while retaining the chloro substituent; key transformation: the C(O)OH group is reduced to CH₂OH, producing LiCl and Al(OH)₃ after aqueous work‑up; typical conditions: dry ether (diethyl ether or THF), low temperature (0 °C) during addition, then reflux under nitrogen; reagent LiAlH₄ is used stoichiometrically; external catalyst.

Ozonolysis of an alkene with dimethyl sulfide work‑up; purpose is oxidative cleavage of the C=C bond to give aldehydes; key transformation: prop‑1‑ene is cleaved to acetaldehyde (from the internal carbon) and formaldehyde (from the terminal carbon); typical conditions: ozone bubbled through a solution of the alkene in dichloromethane at –78 °C, followed by addition of dimethylide at the same temperature and gradual warming to room temperature; solvent: CH₂Cl₂; dimethyl sulfide acts as a reductive quench, no other catalyst.

Transesterification between phenol and methyl acetate; purpose is to synthesize phenyl acetate and release methanol; key transformation: phenoxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of methyl acetate, displacing methanol; typical conditions: catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOMe), reflux in anhydrous solvent such as toluene or xylene, with removal of methanol by azeotropic distillation; solvent: inert organic solvent; catalyst: acid or base as indicated.

Metathesis (acid‑base neutralization) forming an aluminum salt; purpose is preparation of aluminum nicotinate, a vitamin‑B3 supplement. Nicotinic acid (pyridine‑3‑ylic acid) reacts with aqueous aluminum sulfate, exchanging cations to give aluminum nicotinate precipitate and liberate sulfuric acid. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, heating to 60‑80 °C to promote salt precipitation; pH adjusted to near neutral. Common solvent: water; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (base‑promoted hydrolysis) of bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfide (mustard gas) with aqueous ammonium hydroxide; purpose is detoxification to the much less toxic diol, 2,2‑thiodiethanol. Hydroxide (from NH4OH) attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming two primary alcohol groups. Conditions: aqueous NH4OH (≈10‑20%); temperature 0‑50 °C; reaction monitored until gas evolution ceases. Solvent: water; no metal catalyst needed.

Acidic hydrolysis of a cyclic anhydride; converts glutaric anhydride to the dicarboxylic acid glutaric acid. Water attacks the carbonyl, opening the ring and yielding two –COOH groups. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, mild heating (50‑80 °C); can be catalyzed by a trace of acid or base to accelerate the opening. Solvent: water or a water‑acetone mixture; no catalyst required.

Incomplete combustion of propane. Type: combustion (incomplete). Purpose: generate carbon monoxide and water. Key transformation: propane (C₃H₈) partially oxidized to carbon monoxide and water. Conditions: limited oxygen supply, ignition or high temperature (typically 600–800°C), no explicit catalyst or solvent.

Acid‑activated oxidation of sodium chlorite by acetic acid to chlorine dioxide gas and water, with formation of sodium acetate as the salt. Conducted in aqueous solution, the reaction is temperature‑controlled (0–25 °C) to avoid rapid gas evolution; often used in analytical chemistry and water treatment for in‑situ ClO₂ generation.

Thermal decomposition/disproportionation of a high‑valent metal chloride; solid ReCl5 is heated under an inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) at 300–400 °C, releasing Cl2 gas and converting to lower‑valent ReCl3. No solvent or catalyst; the reaction is performed in a sealed tube or furnace.

Acidic decomposition of silver acetylide where hydrochloric acid protonates the acetylide, releasing acetylene gas and forming insoluble silver chloride precipitate. Performed in cold dilute HCl solution, often under a fume hood to capture the evolved C₂H₂; no catalyst.

Reduction of an organic azide to a primary amine using lithium aluminium hydride; employed to convert the azido group into an amino group while retaining the secondary alcohol; the azide (–N₃) is reduced to –NH₂; typically performed with LiAlH₄ (1–2 equiv) in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere, quenched with water or dilute acid after completion.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (Friedel‑Crafts alkylation) of phenol with tert‑butyl chloride in the presence of AlCl₃. The Lewis acid generates a tert‑butyl carbocation which attacks the activated ortho positions of phenol, yielding 2,4‑di‑tert‑butylphenol. Purpose: synthesis of a hindered phenolic antioxidant. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1‑1.5 eq), dry solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon disulfide, temperature 0 °C reflux under nitrogen; reaction quenched with ice water. Catalyst: aluminum chloride; solvent: dry CH₂Cl₂ (or CS₂).

SN2 alkylation of acetate by 1‑bromopropane using tetraethylammonium acetate as nucleophile source. The acetate anion displaces bromide to form propyl acetate, while the tetraethylammonium cation pairs with the liberated Br⁻ to give tetraethylammonium bromide. Purpose: preparation of an ester via a convenient phase‑transfer system. Conditions: polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF or acetonitrile), temperature 25‑60 °C, inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation. No additional catalyst; the tetraethylammonium salt serves both as nucleophile carrier and phase‑transfer agent.

Acid–base metal reaction; phenol is deprotonated by metallic sodium to generate sodium phenoxide and hydrogen gas. Used to prepare phenoxide salts for further nucleophilic substitution. Typically performed in dry ether or THF under an inert atmosphere at 0 °C to room temperature, with addition of sodium pieces to avoid vigorous H₂ evolution.

Acid–base neutralization/protonation; transforms dipotassium molybdate into molybdic acid while forming potassium sulfate. K2MoO4 reacts with H2SO4 to give H2MoO4 and K2SO4 in solution. Performed in aqueous medium, often with dilute H2SO4 at moderate temperature; no catalyst needed.

Reduction of a nitrile to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride; low‑temperature (‑78 °C) addition of DIBAL‑H to acetonitrile in an aprotic solvent such as THF; results in partial reduction giving ethanal; reaction is quenched with methanol or saturated NH₄Cl solution.

Acid–carbonate reaction; manganese carbonate reacts with hydrofluoric acid to evolve carbon dioxide, form water, and produce manganese difluoride (MnF₂). Serves to generate soluble MnF₂ or to neutralize HF waste. Performed in aqueous HF solution, generally at 0 °C to room temperature with appropriate PTFE or glass‑lined equipment due to HF corrosion; stoichiometric HF is added slowly to the carbonate suspension.

Acid–base/neutralization reaction; aqueous sodium molybdate (Na2MoO4) is protonated by hydrochloric acid to give molybdic acid (H2MoO4) and sodium chloride. Typically performed in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; common solvent is water.

Strong oxidative oxidation of 3‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)propionic acid with potassium permanganate; alkaline KMnO₄ in aqueous solution at reflux oxidizes the propionic side chain, yielding 4‑hydroxybenzoic acid, carbon dioxide, manganese dioxide precipitate, and water; reaction is conducted under basic conditions and then acidified to isolate the benzoic acid product.

Nucleophilic substitution at germanium using an organolithium reagent; dimethylgermane dichloride (Me₂GeCl₂) undergoes two methyl‑transfer steps with MeLi to give tetramethylgermanium (Me₄Ge) and lithium chloride as by‑product. Useful for preparing tetra‑alkylgermanes. Reaction is carried out in dry THF or Et₂O under nitrogen, at –78 °C to 0 °C, with careful control of stoichiometry (2 equiv MeLi) and quenched with aqueous ammonium chloride.

Acidification of disodium fumarate with hydrochloric acid; purpose is to regenerate fumaric acid from its sodium salt; the chloride anion replaces the sodium cations, precipitating fumaric acid and forming NaCl in solution; usually carried out in water, often at 0 °C to 25 °C to control exotherm; aqueous HCl is the reagent and solvent.

Oxidative dehydrogenation with selenium dioxide; 2‑methyl‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroquinoline is oxidized to the corresponding aromatic 2‑methylquinoline, with water and selenous acid (H₂SeO₃) formed as by‑products. Employed to aromatize partially saturated heterocycles. Typically run in refluxing 1,4‑dioxane or refluxing acetic acid/water mixtures at 100–130 °C, using catalytic or stoichiometric SeO₂, and the reaction mixture is later filtered to remove selenium residues.

Condensation (lactonization) of glycolic acid using dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) as a dehydrating coupling agent; forms the di‑ester glycolide and dicyclohexylurea byproduct. Typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; DCC activates the carboxyl groups, promoting intramolecular esterification. Used to synthesize monomers for biodegradable polyesters.

Metal‑mediated detonation to form phenoxide; 2‑chlorophenol reacts with sodium metal in dry ether (e.g., THF) inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, giving sodium 2‑chlorophenoxide and evolving hydrogen gas.

Anion exchange (metathesis) to convert 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium chloride into its acetate salt using sodium acetate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; after mixing, sodium chloride precipitates (or remains soluble) and the ionic liquid acetate is isolated by evaporation or extraction. Provides a basic, nucleophilic ionic liquid useful as a solvent or catalyst in organic synthesis.

Nitration (formation of a nitrate ester) of 1,3‑propanediol with a mixed acid system of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid. The sulfuric acid acts as a protonating and dehydrating agent, generating the nitronium ion that reacts with a primary hydroxyl to give 3‑nitrooxy‑propanol and water. Reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C initially, then gently warmed, with the acid mixture serving as the solvent; careful temperature control is required due to exotherm and potential explosivity.

Reductive amination of phenylpropionaldehyde with ammonia in the presence of molecular hydrogen. Catalyzed by a hydrogenation metal (e.g., Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂) in a polar protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol, under H₂ pressure (1–10 atm) at50–100 °C. The aldehyde condenses with ammonia to form an imine, which is subsequently reduced to the primary amine, 3‑phenylpropylamine, with water as the only by‑product.

Acid–base exchange (double displacement) between acetic acid and potassium oxalate; mixing aqueous acetic acid with solid potassium oxalate at room temperature; yields oxalic acid and potassium acetate in stoichiometric amounts.

Carbamoyl‑chloride formation using a phosgene equivalent; purpose is to convert a secondary amine into a dimethylcarbamoyl chloride (a useful acyl‑chloride intermediate). Dimethylamine reacts with triphosgene to give dimethylcarbamoyl chloride and HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in dry CH2Cl2 or CHCl3, with an acid‑scavenging base such as triethylamine or pyridine (1–2 equiv) to neutralize the generated HCl. Reaction is usually carried out under nitrogen.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular dehydration (cyclodehydration) of 1,4‑butanediol to form tetrahydrofuran (THF). Industrially carried out with strong mineral acids (e.g., 5–10 % H₂SO₄) or solid acid catalysts (e.g., zeolites, AlCl₃) at 150–200 °C under reduced pressure to remove water. The reaction proceeds via protonation of a hydroxyl group, loss of water, and ring closure, yielding THF, a valuable solvent and monomer.

Oxidation; selective oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide using hydrogen peroxide as oxidant and molybdenum(VI) oxide as a heterogeneous catalyst; water is the only by‑product; typically carried out at 0–25 °C in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile dichloromethane under stirring.

Condensation polymerization (phenol‑formaldehyde resin synthesis); boric acid acts as a mild Lewis‑acid catalyst to promote electrophilic aromatic substitution of phenol by formaldehyde, forming methylene and hydroxymethyl bridges that generate a thermosetting phenolic resin; usually performed at 60–120 °C in aqueous or alcoholic medium, sometimes with additional acid or base to control pH.

Neutralization (acid–base) to give a salt; aqueous barium hydroxide is added to selenous acid, producing barium selenite and water. The reaction proceeds readily at room temperature in water; stoichiometric amounts (1 equiv Ba(OH)2 per 1 equiv H2SeO3) are mixed, and the resulting solution may be concentrated to crystallize BaSeO3 if desired.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol); pentanal is reduced to 1‑pentanol using molecular hydrogen in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C or Pt‑O₂; reactions are conducted at 1–5 atm H₂, 50–100 °C in solvents like ethanol, isopropanol or water.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of chloroacetic acid by hydrosulfide; NaHS attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming thioglycolic acid while NaCl precipitates; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient to reflux temperature, pH kept near neutral to avoid side reactions.

Haloform (iodoform) reaction; iodine in basic aqueous Na oxid the methyl ketone pinacolone, leading to triiodination at the α‑carbon, cleavage to iodoform (CHI₃) and formation of the carboxylate 2,2‑dimethylpropanoate (pivalate); performed at 0–25 °C then warmed, water is the solvent, excess NaOH required.

Oxidation of L‑lactaldehyde to lactic acid by hydrogen peroxide; converts the aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid with formation of water; often used for synthesis of lactic acid; carried out in aqueous hydrogen peroxide, usually at pH ~ 7–8 and ambient temperature, sometimes with a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Fe²⁺, Ti‑silicalite) to accelerate oxidation; no organic solvent required.

preparation of n‑butyl methanesulfonate from methanesulfonyl chloride, n‑butanol and triethylamine; nucleophilic substitution to give a sulfonate ester; triethylamine captures the liberated HCl forming triethylammonium chloride; typically conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange; used to replace the chloride anion of the imidazolium salt with nitrate and precipitate AgCl. The reaction is performed in aqueous solutionoften water or dilute aqueous ethanol) at ambient temperature with stirring; the insoluble AgCl is filtered off, leaving the 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium nitrate in solution. No catalyst is required.

Grignard nucleophilic addition to an acyl cyanide; methylmagnesium bromide attacks the carbonyl of acetyl cyanide, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide that after aqueous work‑up yields 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanenitrile. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, followed by protonation with dilute acid. No additional catalyst.

Free‑radical nitration of an aliphatic hydrocarbon; purpose: introduce a nitro substituent onto cyclohexane; key transformation: hydrogen atom abstraction followed by addition of a NO2 radical to give nitrocyclohexane and water; typical conditions: mixture of concentrated HNO3 and H2SO4 (often 1:1), temperature 50–80 °C with careful cooling to avoid over‑oxidation; solvent: the acid mixture itself acts as solvent; no external catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization forming an ammonium salt; cinnamic acid reacts with ammonium bicarbonate to give ammonium cinnamate while the bicarbonate decomposes to carbonic acid, which instantly releases CO₂ and H₂O. The reaction is carried out in water at mild temperature (often with gentle heating to drive off CO₂). No catalyst required.

Salt formation via nucleophilic fluorination; fluoride ion from sodium fluoride attacks phosphorus pentafluoride to generate the hexafluorophosphate anion, producing sodium hexafluorophosphate. Performed in anhydrous, non‑protic media such as liquid HF, anhydrous HF/amine mixtures, or dry acetonitrile under atmosphere; the reaction may be cooled to 0 °C–−20 °C to control exotherm. No catalyst.

Hydrolysis of a metal halide; antimony pentachloride reacts with water to give hydrogen chloride gas and antimony oxychloride (SbOCl). Typically conducted by adding SbCl₅ dropwise to cold water or aqueous acid at room temperature; HCl evolves and SbOCl precipitates. No catalyst needed.

Carbamoylation (acyl substitution) of an amino acid; carbamyl chloride acylates the α‑amino group of L‑glutamic acid to afford carglumic acid (N‑carbamoyl‑L‑glutamic acid) with liberation of hydrochloric acid. The reaction is usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as pyridine or DMF, which also serves as a base to scavenge HCl, at 0 °C to room temperature. No additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of an aryl iodide to the corresponding amine by removal of the iodine atom. The 4‑iodoamphetamine is treated with Pd/C (5–10 % Pd) under an H₂ atmosphere (1–3 atm) in ethanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature (or slightly elevated temperature), yielding amphetamine after filtration of the catalyst and work‑up.

Oxidation; primary benzylic alcohol is oxidized to a carboxylic acid. KMnO4 acts as a strong oxidant in aqueous alkaline medium, typically heated under reflux. The alcohol carbon is converted to a carbonyl and then to aboxyl group, producing benzoic acid, water, and insoluble MnO2 precipitate. No additional solvent beyond water is required.

Redox/halogenation; antimony trioxide is oxidized by elemental fluorine to antimony pentafluoride whileine is reduced to oxygen. The reaction is carried out in the gas phase or in a fluorine‑resistant container at elevated temperature (often 200‑300 °C) under an inert atmosphere. No solvent or catalyst is used.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2 or SN1); 2‑octyl chloride undergoes hydrolysis to give 2‑octanol. Typical conditions use aqueous NaOH or KOH, heating under reflux (often 80‑100 °C). After completion the reaction mixture is acidified to liberate the alcohol. Water is the solvent; no catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization with gas evolution; hydrobromic acid reacts with lithium carbonate to release carbon dioxide, form water, and produce lithium bromide. The reaction is performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating. No special catalyst; water acts as solvent.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution of 1,4‑dibromobenzene with sodium amide in liquid ammonia; purpose is to convert one bromine to an amino group forming p‑bromoaniline; key transformation Ar‑Br → Ar‑NH₂; conditions: NaNH₂ in dry liquid NH₃, temperature around –33 °C, inert atmosphere; solvent is liquid ammonia.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2); ethyl bromide alkylates sodium phenolate to afford ethyl phenyl ether and sodium bromide. The reaction is performed in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dry THF or DMF) at reflux temperature, under inert atmosphere to prevent moisture. No additional catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous mixing of barium chloride and potassium iodate exchanges anions to form insoluble barium iodate precipitate and soluble potassium chloride; usually performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring, no catalyst required.

LiAlH4 reduction of an ester; performed in dry ether (THF or Et2O) under inert atmosphere, LiAlH4 donates hydride to the carbonyl of methyl 2‑ethylhexanoate, ultimately yielding 2‑ethylhexanol (primary alcohol) while the methoxy group is reduced to methanol.

Acid‑carbonate neutralization; gaseous or aqueous hydrogen bromide reacts with solid calcium carbonate to produce calcium bromide, water and carbon dioxide gas; proceeds at ambient temperature in aqueous solution with effervescence of CO₂ indicating completion.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous silver perchlorate reacts with rubidium iodide to exchange anions, producing insoluble silver iodide precipitate and soluble rubidium perchlor; performed in water at room temperature, simple filtration isolates AgI; no catalyst required.

Ozonolysis of an α,β‑unsaturated carboxylic acid. But‑2‑enoic acid is exposed to O₃ at low temperature (–78 °C) in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or methanol. Oxidative cleavage of the C=C bond yields glyoxylic acid and acetaldehyde after a reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH) or oxidative work‑up (H₂O₂). No metal catalyst is required.

Direct metal‑halogen combination (synthesis) reaction; purpose: produce the stable fluoride of erbium; key transformation: oxidation of elemental erbium to Er³⁺ and reduction of fluorine to F⁻ forming ErF₃; typical conditions: exposure of finely divided erbium metal to fluorine gas at 300–500 °C in a nickel or Monel reactor, often with a purge of inert gas; no solvent or catalyst.

Acid–base metathesis; concentrated nitric acid protonates praseodymium fluoride, liberating hydrogen fluoride and converting the metal to soluble praseodymium nitrate; typically conducted in aqueous medium with gentle heating to drive off HF; no special catalyst.

Fischer esterification (methyl ester formation): phenylacetic acid is reacted with methanol in the presence of a catalytic acid (H₂SO₄, HCl, or p‑TsOH) under reflux. The acid is converted to methyl phenylacetate with water as the by‑product. Methanol serves as solvent and reactant; water removal or excess methanol pushes the reaction to completion.

Reductive amination of phenylpropanal; the aldehyde reacts with ammonium acetate to form an imine/iminium intermediate which is reduced by sodium triacetoxyborohydride to give 3‑phenylpropylamine, with acetic acid generated as by‑product; usually performed in dichloromethane or THF at rt under inert atmosphere; NaBH(OAc)₃ serves as the mild hydride source.

Free‑radical chlorination; 1,3‑dichloropropane is exposed to chlorine gas under UV light or thermal initiation, abstracting a hydrogen and substituting a third chlorine to afford 1,2,3‑trichloropropane; conducted in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or neat liquid, chlorine in excess; radical chain propagates without added catalyst.

Hydrolysis of oxalyl chloride; a nucleophilic acyl substitution where water attacks the acid chloride yielding oxalic acid and two equivalents of HCl; typically performed in aqueous medium at room temperature or with gentle heating; no special catalyst required, often carried out in water or dilute acid.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 2‑methylbutane‑2,3‑diol; removal of two hydroxyl groups as water forms the alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑butene; carried out with concentrated H₂SO₄ at 100–150 °C; the acid serves as both catalyst and solvent; water is eliminated.

Oxidation; sodium hypophosphite is oxidized by molecular oxygen to sodium dihydrogen phosphate (NaH2PO4); usually carried out in aqueous solution under air or O2 pressure, sometimes with trace transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Fe²⁺) and mild heating (50–80 °C).

Acid‑base proton transfer to generate peroxydisulfuric (persulfuric) acid; ammonium peroxydisulfate is protonated by excess sulfuric acid, forming H2S2O8 and ammonium bisulfate; conducted in concentrated H2SO4, usually at 0–25 °C to avoid decomposition; no additional catalyst.

Oxidative conversion of a nitrile to a carboxylic acid; KMnO₄ in aqueous alkaline medium oxidizes 3,5‑dimethylbenzonitrile to 3,5‑dimethylbenzoic acid, with MnO₂ and potassium carbonate as by‑products. Typical conditions: dilute KMnO₄ (0.5–1 M) in water with NaOH or KOH, reflux 3–6 h; reaction mixture then acidified to isolate the acid.

Double‑displacement/precipitation (metathesis); purpose is to form uranyl oxalate precipitate while liberating acetic acid; uranyl acetate reacts with oxalic acid, exchanging ligands; performed in aqueous solution, sometimes with mild heating to improve dissolution; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Salt metathesis/neutralization of anilinium bromide with ammonium hydroxide; the base deprotonates the anilinium ion, liberating free aniline, water, and forming ammonium bromide; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; product aniline is often extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., ether).

Carbothermic reduction; high‑temperature solid‑state conversion of samarium oxide to metallic samarium while carbon is oxidized to carbon monoxide. Purpose: production of elemental samarium. Key transformation: Sm2O3 + 3 C → 2 Sm + 3 CO. Typical conditions: temperatures of 1500–1800 °C in an inert or slightly reducing atmosphere (Ar or N2) in a furnace or electric arc furnace. No solvent; carbon acts as reductant; reaction may be assisted by excess carbon or using a graphite crucible.

The reaction involves leucine and 3-deoxyglucosone undergoing a Strecker-like degradation, leading to decarboxylation and aldehyde formation (2-amino-3-methylbutanal). Likely occurs under thermal conditions, possibly in aqueous solution, relevant to Maillard reaction pathways.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a dinitroarene. Purpose: reduce both nitro groups to amines, yielding 3‑phenylenediamine Key transformation: each –NO2 group is reduced to –NH2 with release of water. Typical conditions: molecular hydrogen (1‑5 atm) in the presence of a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO₂, in an alcohol solvent (ethanol, methanol) or aqueous/alcohol mixture, temperature 25‑80 °C.

Reductive conversion of a nitrile to a primary amine using a morpholine‑borane complex; morpholine‑borane donates hydride to acetonitrile, reducing it to ethylamine while morpholine is regenerated and boric acid is formed as the oxidized boron species; generally performed in anhydrous THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere, refluxing for several hours; the borane complex serves as both reducing agent and ligand.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of 2‑butyne (Kucherov reaction) to give 2‑butanone; Hg²⁺ (e.g., HgSO₄) in aqueous H₂SO₄ activates the alkyne, water adds regioselectively to give the enol which tautomerizes to the methyl ketone; reaction carried out at 50–80 °C in aqueous sulfuric acid with catalytic mercury(II) sulfate; solvent is water/H₂SO₄ mixture.

Raschig (or Olin Raschig) process for hydrazine synthesis; ammonia reacts with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of ferrous sulfate as a catalyst, effecting oxidative coupling to hydrazine while water is formed; performed in aqueous solution at pH≈10, temperature 50–70 °C, under controlled addition of H₂O₂ to avoid over‑oxidation; iron(II) sulfate acts as the key catalyst.

Cross-coupling reaction (Suzuki-Miyaura); forms biaryl compounds by reacting aryl halides with boronic acids; key steps include oxidative addition of aryl halide to palladium, transmetallation of boronic acid, and reductive elimination; conditions typically involve aqueous or biphasic solvents (e.g., water/ethanol), a base (potassium carbonate), and a palladium catalyst (palladium(II) acetate with triphenylphosphine ligand).

Halogen‑lithium exchange (metal‑halogen exchange); replaces the aryl chlorine with lithium to afford 4‑lithiopyridine and n‑butyl chloride; performed at –78 °C in anhydrous ether (THF or Et₂O) under inert atmosphere; n‑BuLi is added dropwise to a solution of the substrate, no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation reaction; converts fluorene to fluorenone via oxidation of a hydrocarbon to a ketone; uses o-iodoxybenzoic acid (IBX) as an oxidant; typically performed in solvents like DMSO or acetonitrile under mild conditions; no additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis and acid-base neutralization; benzoyl chloride undergoes hydrolysis to form benzoic acid and HCl, which reacts with potassium carbonate to produce CO2, H2O, KCl, and potassium benzoate; occurs in aqueous or polar solvents (e.g., water or ethanol) at or near room temperature; no added catalyst required.

Reductive dehalogenation; removes bromide from 1-bromo-2,3-dihydro-1H-indene using zinc as a radical reductant; acetic acid acts as proton donor and solvent; conducted under reflux conditions; zinc dust functions as the reducing agent.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of a ketone; reduces benzophenone to diphenylmethanol; hydride addition to the carbonyl forms an alkoxide which after acidic work‑up yields the secondary alcohol; lithium aluminate is formed as a by‑product; conditions: dry ether (THF or diethyl ether), 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction; nitric acid protonates fluoride ion to give sodium nitrate and hydrofluoric acid; conducted in aqueous medium, usually at room temperature with careful HF handling; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (salt metathesis); produces silver sulfide by exchanging sulfide and carbonate ions; typically occurs in aqueous media; driven by the low solubility of silver sulfide; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (salt metathesis); forms barium fluoride and sodium carbonate via anion exchange; commonly requires solid-state heating conditions to drive reaction via thermal energy; no solvent or catalyst specified.

Acid–base (salt‑forming) reaction; cerium(III) oxide dissolves in hydrochloric acid, producing aqueous cerium(III) chloride and water. General equation: Ce₂O₃ + 6 HCl → 2 CeCl₃ + 3 H₂O. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle reflux; water is the solvent.

Acid‑base metathesis (double displacement). Purpose: liberate free stearic acid and form cobalt(II) sulfate. Key transformation: proton transfer from H₂SO₄ to cobaltous stearate releases stearic acid and generates CoSO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, often heated to reflux; solvent water or aqueous; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an imide. Purpose: open the heterocyclic 1‑phenylpyrrole‑2,5‑dione to give N‑phenylsuccinamic acid. Key transformation: water adds across the C=O and C‑N bonds under HCl, yielding a linear amide (‑phenylsuccinamic acid). Typical conditions: aqueous HCl, reflux (≈80–100 °C); solvent water or water/ethanol mixture; no additional catalyst.

Hydrolysis of arsenic trichloride. Purpose: convert AsCl₃ to arsenic(III) oxide while generating HCl gas. Key transformation: water attacks As–Cl bonds, producing As₂O₃ and HCl. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, often at room temperature or mild heating; no catalyst; reaction may be performed in a sealed vessel to contain HCl.

Acid–base salt metathesis; protonation of potassium salicylate by conc. H₂SO₄ liberates salicylic acid and forms potassium hydrogen sulfate. Conducted by adding the solid or aqueous salt to cold concentrated sulfuric acid, then heating gently (50‑80 °C) to ensure complete conversion; no additional solvent required.

High‑temperature solid‑state metathesis to synthesize zirconium nitride. Purpose: prepare ZrN and NaCl, releasing nitrogen gas. Key transformation: NaN₃ provides nitride; exchange with ZrCl₄ yields ZrN and NaCl, with N₂ evolving from azide decomposition. Typical conditions: finely powdered ZrCl₄ and NaN₃ mixed, heated in a sealed inert tube (≈600–900 °C) under Ar or N₂; no additional catalyst.

Silyl ester formation (acid‑base/alkylation) where trimethylsilyl chloride reacts with acetic acid to give trimethylsilyl acetate and HCl. The Si–Cl bond is replaced by Si–OAc. Usually carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF. A base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) is added to trap the evolved HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

Acid–base exchange between nitrous acid and cyanide; HNO₂ reacts with NaCN in cold aqueous solution to give sodium nitrite (NaNO₂) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN); serves to generate HCN or to neutralize nitrous acid; reaction is performed at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to limit HCN loss, using water as solvent.

Redox (single‑displacement) reaction in aqueous solution; iodide reduces cobalt(III) to cobalt(II) while being oxidized to iodine; key transformation I⁻ → I₂ and Co³⁺ → Co²⁺; typically carried out by dissolving the salts in water and stirring at room temperature or with mild heating; no special catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Formation of a Grignard reagent. Purpose: generate 3‑pyridylmagnesium chloride for organometallic synthesis. Key transformation: magnesium inserts into the C–Cl bond of 3‑chloropyridine, forming the Mg–Cl bond and the organomagnesium species. Typical conditions: anhydrous diethyl ether or THF, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), gentle reflux; magnesium may be activated with a trace of iodine; strictly dry environment.

Acid‑base salt formation. Purpose: produce lidocaine hydrochloride, a water‑soluble pharmaceutical salt. Key transformation: protonation of the tertiary amine of lidocaine by HCl yields the HCl salt. Typical conditions: dissolve lidocaine base in ethanol or isopropanol, add aqueous HCl at 0–25 °C, stir; isolate by evaporation or crystallization; no catalyst needed.

Solid‑state high‑temperature ceramic synthesis; formation of calcium zirconate perovskite. CaO + ZrO2 → CaZrO3. Mixed oxide powders are calcined at 1300–1500 °C (often in air or inert atmosphere) to achieve complete reaction; no solvent or catalyst, sometimes mechanical milling is used to improve mixing.

Amide hydrolysis: water‑mediated cleavage of 1‑naphthaleneacetamide to give 1‑naphthaleneacetic acid and ammonia. Purpose is to convert an amide into the corresponding carboxylic acid. Key transformation is C–N bond breakage forming a carboxyl group and releasing NH₃. Typically performed by heating the substrate in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base at reflux; aqueous medium, no special solvent beyond water.

Acid‑base neutralization: deprotonation of methanearsonic acid by sodium hydroxide to form monosodium methanearsonate and water. Purpose is to generate a water‑soluble arsenic salt. Key transformation is proton transfer. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of a metal fluoride; vanadium(III) fluoride reacts with water to generate vanadium(III) hydroxide and hydrofluoric acid (VF3 + 3 H2O → V(OH)3 + 3 HF); performed in aqueous solution, often at room temperature or mild heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Redox/acid‑metal reaction of tetrafluoroboric acid with zinc. Zinc metal reacts with aqueous HBF₄ to form zinc tetrafluoroborate and hydrogen gas. Conducted similarly to the magnesium case: aqueous acid, ambient to 60 °C, and stirring. The reaction proceeds readily with powdered or granulated zinc; no extra catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine); purpose: obtain 3‑phenylpropylamine from 3‑phenylpropanenitrile; key transformation: H₂ adds across the C≡N bond, first forming an imine then fully reducing to the amine while retaining the nitrogen; typical conditions: 50‑100 bar H₂, 80‑150 °C, catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂, solvent like ethanol, methanol or water, several hours reaction time.

Dehydration: phosphorus pentoxide acts as a powerful dehydrating agent, removing water from ethanol to produce ethylene gas. Purpose is industrial synthesis of eth from alcohol. Key step is elimination of H₂O from ethanol to give a C=C bond. Conducted by heating ethanol with excess P₂O₅ at 140–180 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent needed.

Precipitation (acid–base neutralization) reaction; aqueous sodium hydroxide neutralizes lead(II) trifluoroacetate, forming insoluble lead(II) hydroxide precipitate and sodium trifluoroacetate in solution. Conducted by slowly adding aqueous NaOH to a solution of lead(II) trifluoroacetate at 0 °C to rt, followed by filtration of the white Pb(OH)₂ solid.

Acylation/esterification: glycerol reacts with lauric anhydride, one hydroxyl group is acylated to give glyceryl monolaurate while the other acyl portion is released as lauric acid. Purpose is to prepare a mono‑ester surfactant. Key transformation is nucleophilic attack of a glycerol OH on the anhydride carbonyl. Typically carried out at 80–120 °C in an aprotic solvent such as pyridine or DMF, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP; no additional catalyst required.

Michael (thiol‑addition) reaction: methyl mercaptan adds conjugatively to the β‑carbon of ethyl acrylate, forming ethyl 3‑mercaptopropionate. Purpose is to synthesize a thio‑functionalized ester. Key transformation is thiolate attack on the activated double bond. Usually carried out in an inert solvent (e.g., THF or DMSO) at room temperature with a base catalyst such as triethylamine or a Lewis acid (e.g., ZnCl₂) to generate the thiolate.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkyl halide to ester). Acetate anion from lithium acetate attacks ethyl bromide, displacing bromide to form ethyl acetate and LiBr. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF) at reflux; lithium salts can enhance nucleophilicity.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis. Water attacks the carbonyl of salicylanilide, breaking the C–N bond to give salicylic acid and aniline. Usually carried out under reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 6 M HCl) or strong base followed by acid work‑up.

Type: direct synthesis (redox combination). Purpose: preparation of copper(I) iodide, a white precipitate used in organic synthesis and photography. Key transformation: 2 Cu(s) + I2(s) → 2 CuI(s). Typical conditions: react copper metal with iodine vapor or in a non‑aqueous solvent (e.g., dry acetonitrile, ether, or acetone) under gentle heating (50–80 °C) in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation to Cu(II). No catalyst; solid CuI precipitates out.

Oxime formation (condensation of an aldehyde with hydroxylamine); used to protect the carbonyl or to prepare precursors for further transformations. Phenylacetaldehyde undergoes nucleophilic addition of hydroxylamine, followed by dehydration to give phenylacetaldoxime and water. The reaction is usually carried out in ethanol or methanol, often buffered (pH ≈ 4‑6) with a weak acid or pyridine, at 0 °C to rt; no catalyst beyond the solvent system is typically needed.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). 2‑Chloroethanol is treated with PCC in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; PCC selectively oxidizes the –CH₂OH group to chloroacetaldehyde while suppressing over‑oxidation to the acid. Water and pyridinium chloride are formed as by‑products.

Hydrolysis of a metal alkoxide (sol‑gel type). Water protonates the isopropoxide ligands on Ta(V), producing isopropanol and converting the metal center to tantalum(V) oxide (Ta₂O₅ polymeric species). Conducted at ambient or gently heated temperature in aqueous medium; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (ether formation). Sulfonic acid protonates tert‑butanol, generating a tert‑butyl carbocation that combines with another tert‑butanol molecule to afford di‑tert‑butyl ether and water. Performed at 0–30 °C with concentrated H₂SO₄ to suppress elimination to isobutene; excess alcohol often used as solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of a cyclic ether. Hydrogen in the presence of a nickel metal catalyst cleaves the C–O bond of tetrahydrofuran, hydrogenating the opened chain to give 1‑butanol. Typically run under H₂ pressure (30–80 bar) at 120–180 °C in a sealed reactor; THF serves as both substrate and solvent.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: generate the alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the carbonyl carbon of heptyl acetate, forming heptanol and sodium acetate. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), heating at 60–100 °C (reflux) until complete. Common solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture.

Radical benzylic bromination using N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS). A homolytic abstraction at the benzylic position of 3‑ethylpyridine generates a radical that captures bromine from NBS, converting the ethyl group to a bromomethyl group and producing succinimide as the by‑product. Conducted under reflux or photochemical initiation in a non‑protic solvent such as CCl₄, CH₂Cl₂, or DMF.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction; phosphoric acid donates protons to chloride ions of MgCl₂, liberating gaseous HCl while the magnesium cation pairs with the hydrogen phosphate anion to form magnesium hydrogen phosphate. Usually performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to evolve HCl gas; no special catalyst is required.

Acid–base gas‑evolution reaction; ammonium chloride reacts with sodium bicarbonate to yield sodium chloride, ammonia gas, carbon dioxide gas and water; typically performed by mixing the solid reagents or their aqueous solutions at room temperature or with gentle heating; water serves as the medium and no catalyst is required.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of butyl 2‑methylpropanoate with potassium hydroxide, yielding potassium 2‑methylpropanoate and n‑butanol. Performed in aqueous KOH under reflux; similar conditions to the NaOH version, with water (or water/ethanol) as solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Salt formation (acid‑base reaction) where tocainide, a secondary amine, is protonated by hydrochloric acid to give tocainide hydrochloride; performed by dissolving tocainide in an appropriate solvent (e.g., ethanol, isopropanol or methanol) and adding aqueous or gaseous HCl at 0–25 °C, followed by removal of solvent and isolation of the crystalline hydrochloride salt.

Enzyme‑catalyzed acyl transfer (acetylation); acetyl‑CoA transfers its acetyl group to the amino nitrogen of L‑alanine, producing N‑acetyl‑L‑alanine and CoA; occurs in aqueous buffer at physiological pH under the action of an N‑acetyltransferase enzyme.

Base‑promoted nucleophilic substitution / hydrolysis; converts the α‑bromo ketone to the corresponding α‑hydroxy ketone (hydroxyacetone). Key transformation: CH₃COCH₂Br + K₂CO₃ → CH₃COCH₂OH + 2 KBr + CO₂ (carbonate supplies OH⁻ and is converted to CO₂). Performed in aqueous or alcoholic medium at room temperature to gentle reflux; stirring is sufficient, no extra catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of an acyl chloride to the corresponding carboxylic acid; trichloroacetyl chloride reacts with water to give trichloroacetic acid and releases HCl; the reaction is typically conducted in a water‑ice bath or at 0–25 °C to control vigor, often in a biphasic system (e.g., water/diethyl ether) to extract the acid, with the liberated HCl remaining in the aqueous layer.

Pyridine N‑oxide formation using peracetic acid; another electrophilic oxidation of the pyridine nitrogen to the N‑oxide; key transformation is similar O‑atom transfer from peracetic acid to the nitrogen, yielding 2‑ethylpyridine N‑oxide and acetic acid; usually performed in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to ambient temperature, with stoichiometric or slight excess of peracetic acid and often a buffer to control acidity.

Hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed) of phenyl N,N‑dimethylcarbamate to regenerate phenol, release dimethylamine, and evolve carbon dioxide. Typically carried out in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base at reflux; water is the reaction medium.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; silver nitrate exchanges its nitrate anion with the bromide of copper(I) bromide, yielding insoluble silver bromide precipitate and soluble copper(I) nitrate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the formation of the white AgBr solid drives the reaction to completion; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base carbonate decomposition: lithium carbonate is treated with aqueous hydrogen chloride, yielding lithium chloride, carbon dioxide gas and water; usually performed at ambient temperature with dilute HCl, gentle heating may be applied to drive off CO2, no catalyst required.

Neutralization/acid‑base reaction of benzenesulfonyl chloride with sodium carbonate; the carbonate deprotonates the sulfonyl chloride, generating sodium benzenesulfonate, carbon dioxide and water, with NaCl as by‑product; typically carried out in a mixed solvent (e.g., aqueous sodium carbonate with a co‑solvent such as acetone) at 0–25 °C, with evolution of CO₂ gas indicating completion.

Acid–base double displacement precipitation; purpose is to convert soluble lead carbonate into insoluble lead phosphate while releasing CO₂ and H₂O; key transformation is protonation of carbonate and exchange of anions yielding Pb₃(PO₄)₂ solid; typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or slightly warmed with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Sandmeyer bromination; replacement of the diazonium group with bromide to give bromobenzene; used to prepare aryl bromides from anilines; key transformation: Ar‑N₂⁺ BF₄⁻ + CuBr → ArBr + N₂↑; conditions similar to the chlorination: acidic aqueous solution (HBF₄), 0–25 °C, copper(I) bromide as bromide source; solvent water or water/acetone; copper(I) bromide serves as catalyst.

Methanolysis (transesterification) of an acetate; excess methanol with catalytic acid or base (e.g., H₂SO₄ or NaOCH₃) at reflux exchanges the alkoxy group of hexan‑2‑yl acetate to give methyl acetate and hexan‑2‑ol; solvent methanol, temperature ~65 °C.

Meerwein‑Ponndorf‑Verley (MPV) catalytic transfer hydrogenation; reduces acetophenone to 1‑phenylethanol using isopropanol as hydride donor and aluminum isopropoxide as Lewis‑acid catalyst; key hydride transfer from isopropanol generates acetone; typically run neat or in excess isopropanol at 80‑120 °C under inert atmosphere.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation reaction between barium dithiocyanate and lead nitrate; purpose is to exchange cations and isolate lead dithiocyanate. Barium cations combine with nitrate anions to give soluble Ba(NO₃)₂, while lead cations pair with dithiocyanate to form Pb(S₂CN)₂, which precipitates. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with vigorous stirring; the solid product is filtered and washed, no catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination; purpose is to install a third chlorine atom onto 1,2‑dichlorobenzene; key transformation is substitution of a hydrogen by chlorine via the Cl2/FeCl3 (or AlCl3) Lewis‑acid catalyst, yielding 1,2,3‑trichlorobenzene; typical conditions involve refluxing the aromatic substrate in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform or dichloromethane with a catalytic amount of FeCl3; the reaction is usually performed under an inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation) of β‑alanine with carbamoyl chloride to give N‑carbamoyl‑β‑alanine; HCl is released; commonly performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

Chromium(VI) oxidation of furfuryl alcohol to furfural; sodium dichromate in aqueous sulfuric acid oxidizes the primary alcohol to the aldehyde while reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III); usually carried out at 0‑50 °C in water/H₂SO₄ medium.

Double‑replacement/precipitation (acid‑base neutralization) using ammonium hydroxide; used to obtain Al(OH)₃ while keeping the ammonium nitrate in solution. Al(NO₃)₃ aqueous solution is treated with NH₄OH, yielding a white Al(OH)₃ precipitate and NH₄NO₃ in the supernatant; performed at room temperature under gentle stirring, typically with a slight excess of NH₄OH.

Carbonylation of an alcohol (hydrocarbonylation); ethanol reacts with CO under pressure in the presence of an acid or metal carbonyl catalyst (e.g., Rh or Co complexes) to afford ethyl formate; typical conditions are 50–150 °C, 10–30 bar CO, and a catalytic amount of acid or phosphine‑ligated metal; solvent may be the alcohol itself.

Acid‑base exchange/fluorination of disodium hydrogen phosphate with hydrofluoric acid to give sodium monofluorophosphate and water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Simple acid‑base neutralization (basification) of the hydrochloride salt of N‑methyl‑1‑phenylpropan‑2‑amine with aqueous NaOH to liber the free amine; generates NaCl and water; typically done at 0‑25 °C in water, followed by extraction of the amine into an organic solvent (e.g., ether or dichloromethane).

Oxymercuration–demercuration (hydration) of 1‑butene to give 2‑butanol. Mercuric acetate adds to the alkene to form a cyclic mercurinium ion, water attacks the more substituted carbon to yield an organomercury intermediate, and NaBH₄ (or NaBD₄) reduces the C–Hg bond to give the Markovnikov alcohol. Typical conditions: Hg(OAc)₂ (0.1 eq) in THF/H₂O at 0 °C to rt, followed by NaBH₄ in methanol at 0 °C to rt.

Fischer esterification of decanoic acid with methanol to give methyl decanoate; acid-catalyzed condensation that replaces the –OH of the carboxylic acid with –OCH₃, releasing water. Typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), often using a Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic removal of water. No special solvent beyond methanol is required.

Cu(II)‑catalyzed oxidative hydroxylation of 3‑methylphenol with hydrogen peroxide to afford 3‑methylcatechol and water; copper(II) sulfate acts as a catalyst in aqueous solution, often at room temperature; excess H₂O₂ (30 % solution) is added dropwise under stirring.

Acid‑base neutralization and salt formation; barium hydroxide neutralizes fluorosic acid, producing water and the inorganic salt barium hexafluorosilicate (BaSiF₆). Conducted aqueous solution, often at room temperature or with mild heating to ensure complete dissolution of reagents; the reaction proceeds without additional catalysts.

Ligand exchange/metathesis in basic medium; zinc dimethyldithiocarbamate reacts with sodium hydroxide, the hydroxide displaces the dithiocarbamate ligands to give soluble sodium dimethyldithiocarbamate and precipitate zinc hydroxide. Typically performed in water at room temperature with stirring; the solid Zn(OH)₂ can be filtered off; no external catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; mixing lead(II) nitrate and hydrochloric acid produces lead(II) chloride precipitate and nitric acid. Lead(II) chloride may partially precipitate depending on solubility. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature. Water is solvent.

Acid–base neutralization; forms sodium bisulfate and releases CO₂; key transformation: H₂SO₄ protonates HCO₃⁻ to produce NaHSO₄, CO₂, and H₂O; generally performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt‑to‑acid conversion); purpose: liberate free 2‑methylpropanoic acid from its sodium salt; key transformation: CH3CH2C(O)ONa + HCl → CH3CH2C(O)OH + NaCl; typical conditions: aqueous medium, often performed at 0 °C to control exotherm; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; MgCl2 exchanges its anion with NaF to give insoluble MgF2 and soluble NaCl; carried out in aqueous solution, usually at ambient temperature or with mild heating to increase ion mobility; no catalyst required.
