Acid–base neutralization/complexation: oxalic acid reacts with europium hydroxide in aqueous solution to neutralize the base and form the insoluble salt dieuropium trioxalate (Eu₂(C₂O₄)₃) while water is released. Typically performed at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of an alkene ether: propyl vinyl ether is treated with ozone at low temperature (−78 °C) in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform. After the ozonide is formed a reductive work‑up (e.g., dimethyl sulfide) yields formaldehyde and propyl formate as the carbonyl fragments.

Hydride reduction of an aldehyde: octanal is reduced by sodium borohydride to 1‑octanol. The reaction is performed in protic solvents such as methanol or ethanol at 0 °C room temperature. Sodium borate is generated as the by‑product.

Hydrolysis of silicon tetrafluoride; a moisture-driven hydrolysis reaction converting the highly fluorinated SiF4 into hydrofluoric acid and orthosilicic acid. Key transformation: Si–F bonds replaced by Si–O bonds with release of HF. Typically performed by bubbling SiF4 into water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required. Aqueous medium is the solvent.

Protonolysis of tetraethyl tin with hydrogen bromide; an acid-mediated cleavage of a Sn–C bond (organotin dealkylation). Produces ethane as the reduced alkane and triethyl tin bromide as the tin bromide product. Usually carried out by stirring tetraethyl tin with excess gaseous or aqueous HBr at (~80 °C) in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or toluene. No additional catalyst needed.

This is a dehydration reaction where praseodymium(III) chloride hexahydrate loses water molecules to form anhydrous praseodymium(III) chloride. The reaction is driven by heating, often under vacuum or at elevated temperatures (e.g., 100–200°C), to remove water vapor. No solvent or catalyst is involved.

Halogenation of n‑butyllithium with bromine; a lithium‑halogen exchange/alkyl halide formation reaction. The butyl organolithium transfers the butyl group to bromine, giving n‑butyl bromide and lithium bromide. Conducted at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in anhydrous ether solvents (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions. No catalyst required.

Preparation of nickel boride (Ni) by reduction of nickel(II) chloride with potassium borohydride; a metal‑boride synthesis that also generates hydrogen gas. Potassium borohydride reduces Ni²⁺ to a nickel‑boride solid while liberating H₂ and forming KCl. Typically performed in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution at room temperature under nitrogen or argon; the reaction mixture is stirred vigorously. No external catalyst; the nickel boride formed is itself used as a heterogeneous hydrogenation catalyst.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (aqueous acid). Purpose: convert an ester into the corresponding carboxylic acid and alcohol. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–O bond of propyl 2‑oxopropanoate to give pyruvic acid (2‑oxopropanoic acid) and propanol. Typical conditions: reflux in a mixture of water with a mineral acid such as H₂SO₄ or HCl (10–20 % v/v), often 2–4 h. Common solvent: water (sometimes a water/organic co‑solvent like dioxane).

Tin(II) chloride reduction in acidic medium; reduces 2‑nitrobenzaldehyde to 2‑aminobenzaldehyde, generating SnCl₄ as by‑product. Conducted in a mixture of SnCl₂ (excess) and concentrated HCl, often in ethanol or water, heated to reflux; after completion the reaction is neutralized and extracted.

Nucleophilic substitution of phosphorus trichloride by dimethylamine to form dimethylphosphoramidous dichloride and HCl; carried out under inert atmosphere in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to rt; HCl gas evolved.

Aerobic catalytic oxidation of phenol to para‑benzoquinone; an oxidation reaction using molecular oxygen as the oxid in the presence of a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., CuCl₂, FeCl₃, or a cobalt complex). Phenol is converted to p‑benzoquinone with concomitant formation of water. Commonly performed in acetonitrile or a mixed water‑organic solvent at 60–100 °C under an O₂ atmosphere (balloon or flow). The metal catalyst facilitates electron transfer; no stoichiometric oxidant other than O₂ is required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkylation of amine); methylamine attacks the primary ethyl p‑toluenesulfonate, displacing the tosylate leaving group to give N‑methylethylamine and p‑toluenesulfonic acid; typically carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF, DMSO or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required, base may be omitted because the tosylate is a good leaving group.

Acid‑base double displacement (metathesis) reaction; ammonium thiocyanate protonates the basic nickel(II) oxide, releasing ammonia and water while nickel(II) assembles with thiocyanate anions to form nickel(II) thiocyanate; performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating (≈80–100 °C) to promote gas evolution; no special catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an unsaturated heterocycle; 3,6‑dihydro‑2H‑pyran is hydrogenated over palladium on carbon to saturate the C=C bond, yielding tetrahydropyran; conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate at 25–50 °C; Pd/C serves as the heterogeneous catalyst.

Oxidative redox (combustion‑type) reaction; purpose is complete oxidation of glycerol to carbon dioxide and water while reducing permanganate to Mn(II); glycerol carbon atoms are converted to CO2, KMnO4 (Mn(VII)) is reduced to MnSO4 (Mn(II)), K+ forms K2SO4; typically carried out in concentrated H2SO4 as both solvent and oxidizing medium, glycerol added dropwise to cold acidic KMnO4 solution, exothermic mixture often cooled initially then allowed to warm to reflux.

Esterification via acyl‑chloride intermediate (carbodiimide‑free coupling); anthranilic acid reacts with ethyl chloroformate in the presence of pyridine, which scavenges the generated HCl and activates the carboxyl group, affording ethyl anthranilate; the reaction is usually run at 0 °C to ambient temperature in pyridine or a pyridine‑containing solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) under an inert atmosphere; pyridine acts both as solvent and base.

Direct combination (halogenation) synthesis; elemental titanium reacts violently with chlorine gas to form titanium tetrachloride, a volatile liquid; carried out in a dry, inert‑gas‑purged reactor at controlled temperature (often 200–300 °C) to avoid uncontrolled exotherm; no solvent or catalyst is required, but chlorine is introduced slowly and the system is cooled to condense TiCl₄.

Acid‑base neutralization of a carbonate: phosphoric acid protonates calcium carbonate, releasing carbon dioxide gas and water while forming calcium dihydrogen phosphate (Ca(H₂PO₄)₂). The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring accelerates CO₂ evolution.

Carbothermic reduction of tin(IV) oxide with carbon; purpose to recover metallic tin from the oxide; SnO2 is reduced by solid carbon to Sn and CO2; performed at very high temperature (≈1200‑1400 °C) in a carbon‑rich environment such as a graphite crucible, often under an inert or reducing atmosphere; solid‑state reaction with no solvent or catalyst.

High‑temperature solid‑state metathesis (thermal exchange). Purpose: to convert germanate to germanium dioxide and generate soluble sodium silicate, useful in material synthesis. Key transformation: Na₂GeO₃ + SiO₂ → Na₂SiO₃ (soluble) + GeO₂ (solid). Typical conditions: thoroughly mixed dry powders heated to 600–800 °C in a furnace, often in air or an inert atmosphere; reaction proceeds without a solvent or catalyst. No catalyst.

Vicinal diol oxidative cleavage (periodic acid oxidation); converts a 1,2‑diol on a cyclohexane ring to the open‑chain dialdehyde (1,6‑hexanedial) while reducing HIO4 to HIO3; typically carried out in aqueous acidic medium at 0–25 °C, often in water or a water‑miscible organic solvent such as t‑butanol; no catalyst required.

Acid‑salt metathesis (double displacement) between sulfuric acid and an iron(II) molybdate; protonates the molybdate anion to give molybdic acid (H₂MoO₄) and forms iron(II) sulfate in solution; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, with stirring; no special reagents beyond the acids and salts.

Cyanohydrin formation (nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde). Formaldehyde undergoes attack by the cyanide ion of HCN, followed by proton transfer to give 2‑hydroxyacetonitrile. Performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., MeOH/H2O) under mildly acidic to neutral pH, 0–25 °C; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization; calcium hydroxide (a strong base) reacts with formic acid to form the calcium salt of formic acid (calcium formate) and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Electrophilic bromination of a furan‑2‑carboxylic acid using N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS); regioselectively introduces bromine at the 5‑position of the furan ring, yielding 5‑bromo‑2‑furancarboxylic acid and succinimide as the by‑product; conducted in an inert, non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄) at room temperature, often under light or a radical initiator; no additional catalyst is required.

Oxidative conversion of cyanide to cyanate with sodium hypochlorite; cyanide ion is oxidized to cyanate (OCN⁻) while hypochlorite is reduced to chloride, giving potassium cyanate and sodium chloride; carried out in aqueous solution under basic or neutral pH, typically at 0–25 °C with controlled addition of NaOCl to avoid over‑oxidation; no extra catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of fluoroacetonitrile to fluoroacetic acid; nitrile is protonated and sequentially hydrated to the amide and then the carboxylic acid, producing ammonium chloride as the acid‑base by‑product; performed in aqueous HCl under reflux (≈80–100°C) until completion; no additional reagents beyond the acid and water.

Preparation of phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) by reaction of phosphoric acid with thionyl chloride; thionyl chloride acts as a dehydrating and chlorinating agent, converting PO(OH)₃ to POCl₃ while generating HCl and SO₂ gases; typically run under reflux in a dry, inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or pyridine) with an efficient gas‑escape system; no catalyst is required.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation; purpose is to introduce a tert‑butyl group onto an aromatic ring. The Lewis acid AlCl3 coordinates to tert‑butyl chloride, generating a tert‑butyl cation electrophile that undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution on benzene to give tert‑butylbenzene and HCl as by‑product. Typical conditions are anhydrous AlCl3 (1–2 equiv), an inert atmosphere, temperature 0–50 °C, and a non‑protic, non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, nitrobenzene or chloroform.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary bromide by cyanide ion; one bromine of 1,4‑dibromopane is displaced by CN⁻ to afford 4‑bromobutyronitrile and NaBr. The reaction is carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile) at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (20–80 °C) under anhydrous conditions to avoid hydrolysis of cyanide.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (acetoxylation); replaces bromine with an acetate group to give pentan‑2‑yl acetate (an alkyl acetate ester). Sodium acetate acts as nucleophile; NaBr precipitates. Commonly carried out in dry acetone or DMF at reflux; acetone also drives the equilibrium by precipitating NaBr.

Comproportionation (redox) between tin(IV) chloride and elemental tin metal to give tin(II) chloride: SnCl₄ + Sn → 2 SnCl₂. The reaction proceeds in a dry, inert solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, usually under reflux and exclusion of moisture and air. The mixture is often stirred for several hours until the color changes from yellow (SnCl₄) to pale green (SnCl₂).

Acid‑base neutralisation / salt formation; the basic amine functional group of oxybuprocaine reacts with aqueous HCl to produce oxybuprocaine hydrochloride, a water‑soluble salt. The process is performed in aqueous HCl (≈1 M), at 0–25 °C, with stirring until dissolution is complete; the product may be isolated by evaporation or precipitation with a non‑solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction: phosphoric acid exchanges its protons with lithium nitrate to give lithium phosphate and nitric acid. The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating (50–80 °C) to drive off the more volatile HNO₃, which can be collected by distillation. Excess phosphoric acid may be used to shift equilibrium toward nitrate formation.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation: Aqueous potassium fluoride and barium chloride exchange ions to form insoluble barium fluoride precipitate and soluble potassium chloride; carried out in water at ambient temperature, solid BaF₂ is filtered off.

Double displacement/acid‑base neutralization. Purpose: to convert sparingly soluble barium selenate into soluble barium chloride and generate selenic acid in solution. Key transformation: exchange of chloride and selenate anions (2 HCl + BaSeO₄ → H₂SeO₄ + BaCl₂). Conditions: aqueous medium, ambient to mild heating, stirring. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Redox oxidation; peroxide oxidizes Chromium(IV) oxide to Chromium(VI) oxide while being reduced to water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution, often acidic, at ambient temperature; no additional solvent beyond water is required.

Acidic chromic oxidation (oxidative dearomatization); potassium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes phenanthrene to phenanthrene‑9,10‑dione, introducing two carbonyl groups at the 9,10‑positions. Reaction proceeds with heating under reflux in aqueous H₂SO₄; potassium sulfate is formed as the chromium(VI) reduction product. Common solvent is the acid medium itself.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation; exchanges bromide for PF6– by reacting tetraethylammonium bromide with silver hexafluorophosphate, precipitating insoluble AgBr; purpose is to obtain tetraethylammonium hexafluorophosphate with a PF6– counter‑ion; carried out in water or acetonitrile, often in the dark; filter off AgBr; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination; bromine, activated by catalytic FeBr₃, undergoes electrophilic substitution on naphthalene to give 1‑bromonaphthalene, with HBr generated as a by‑product. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; FeBr₃ is used in catalytic amounts.

Acetylation (esterification) of a primary alcohol; acetic anhydride reacts with 4‑hydroxyvaleric acid to form the acetate ester (4‑acetoxyvaleric acid) while liberating one equivalent of acetic acid. Usually performed under gentle heating (40–60 °C) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, with pyridine or DMAP as a base/catalyst to scavenge the produced acid.

Ester hydrolysis (acidic or basic saponification); dimethyl phthalate reacts with water to cleave both methyl ester groups, producing phthalic acid and two equivalents of methanol. Typically performed under reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., dilute HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) followed by acid work‑up; common solvent is water or a water‑alcohol mixture.

Fischer esterification of glycol monobutyl ether with acetic acid; purpose is to produce the acetate ester. Key transformation: condensation of –OH with –COOH to give –OCOCH₃ and water. Typical conditions: reflux in an inert solvent (toluene, benzene, or excess acetic acid) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH). Water is removed by azeotropic distillation (Dean‑Stark) or by using excess acid.

Base‑catalysed ester hydrolysis (saponification). An ester group is cleaved by hydroxide to give the corresponding alcohol (methanol) and the carboxylate salt (sodium acetate). Carried out in aqueous NaOH (often 1 M) with reflux; a water/ethanol mixture is common, and no external catalyst is required.

Reaction type: Double displacement. Purpose: Precipitation of bismuth carbonate. Key transformations: Bismuth nitrate reacts with sodium carbonate, forming water-insoluble bismuth carbonate and soluble sodium nitrate. Conditions: Aqueous solution at room temperature. Solvents: Water.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to the corresponding acid chloride using thionyl chloride; 2‑ethoxybenzoic acid reacts with SOCl₂, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases to give 2‑ethoxybenzoyl chloride. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often in dry dichloromethane or neat SOCl₂, with gentle reflux; a catalytic drop of DMF can accelerate the reaction.

Acid–base neutralization of a weak acid; acetic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to afford sodium acetate and water; performed in water at room temperature; often used to prepare acetate buffer; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (dehydration) of calcium hydroxide; heating Ca(OH)2 results in loss of water to give calcium oxide (quicklime); performed by calcining the solid at 400‑600 °C in a furnace; solid‑state, no solvent or catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution forming a phenylurea (synthesis of monolinuron). Dimethylcarbamoyl chloride reacts with the amino group of 4‑chloroaniline to give a urea linkage while releasing HCl. The reaction is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with a stoichiometric base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge the HCl.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Silver carbonate reacts with ammonium chloride, precipitating insoluble silver chloride and generating soluble ammonium carbonate in solution. Typically carried out in water at ambient temperature; gentle stirring promotes complete precipitation of AgCl, which is removed by filtration.

Full reduction of an ester with lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄); the carbonyl carbon is reduced to a primary alcohol, and the alkoxy fragment is also reduced, overall yielding two equivalents of hexanol (commonly reported as hexanol as the major product); performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere (N₂) at 0 °C to reflux, with careful quenching of excess LiAlH₄ by aqueous acid or water.

Halide exchange precipitation (metathesis) reaction. Sodium iodide displaces bromide from silver brom, forming the highly insoluble silver iodide precipitate while sodium bromide remains in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium (or acetone for the classic Finkelstein variant) at room temperature; the solid AgI is isolated by filtration.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a bicyclic alkene (bornylene) to the saturated hydrocarbon bornane. Molecular hydrogen adds across the C=C bond in the presence of a metal catalyst, eliminating the double bond. Standard conditions employ H₂ gas (10–50 atm) with a catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney nickel in a solvent like ethanol, methanol, or THF, at 25–80 °C.

Acid–base neutralisation producing a sulfonate salt. Trifluoromethanesulfonic acid reacts with lithium bicarbonate, yielding lithium trifluoromethanesulfonate (lithium triflate), carbon dioxide, and water. Performed in aqueous solution, often at 0 °C to control CO₂ evolution; the resulting salt is usually isolated by evaporation or crystallisation.

PLP‑dependent hydrolytic cleavage of 3‑hydroxykynurenine by kynureninase to afford 3‑hydroxyanthranilic acid and L‑alanine. The enzyme uses pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate to form a Schiff‑base with the substrate, facilitating C‑α–C‑β bond cleavage and water addition. Occurs in aqueous buffer (pH ≈7.5–8.0) at 30–37 °C, requiring PLP as cofactor and often Mg²⁺.

Nucleophilic silylation (protecting group installation); the Grignard acetylide (ethynylmagnesium chloride) attacks trimethylsilyl chloride, transferring the TMS group to form trimethylsilylacetylene while MgCl₂ precipitates; typically performed in anhydrous THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (hydrazide formation); hydrazine opens the maleic anhydride ring by nucleophilic attack on a carbonyl, yielding maleic hydrazide and water; commonly carried out in aqueous ethanol or ethyl acetate with reflux heating (≈80 °C), often using a slight excess of hydrazine to drive the reaction to completion

Acid‑base halogenation (tin oxide to tin chloride conversion); dibutyltin oxide reacts with aqueous or gaseous HCl, protonating the oxide and replacing the Sn–O bonds by Sn–Cl bonds to give dibutyltin dichloride and water; the transformation is usually conducted in a polar protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol at room temperature or gentle reflux.

Acid‑base neutralization producing sodium metaphosphate; sodium carbonate neutralizes two equivalents of metaphosphoric acid (HPO₃), releasing carbon dioxide and water while forming sodium metaphosphate; the reaction is performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to evolve CO₂, and the resulting salts are isolated after evaporation or crystallization.

Copper‑catalyzed halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type substitution); sodium iodide and catalytic CuI promote the replacement of the two bromine atoms on 5,7‑dibromo‑8‑hydroxyquinoline with iodine, affording 5,7‑diiodo‑8‑hydroxyquinoline; the reaction proceeds in dry dimethylformamide (DMF) or N‑methyl‑pyrrolidone at 80–120 °C under an inert atmosphere, with CuI acting as a Lewis‑acid catalyst to facilitate oxidative addition/reductive elimination cycles.

SN2 alkylation of a metal acetylide (C‑C bond formation); sodium amide deprotonates acetylene to generate sodium acetylide in liquid ammonia, which then attacks 1‑bromobutane in a bimolecular substitution to give hex‑1‑yne and NaBr; typical conditions involve cooling the ammonia solution to –78 °C for deprotonation, then warming to –33 °C (boiling point of NH₃) for the alkylation step, with no additional catalyst required.

RuCl₃/NaIO₄ oxidation (ruthenium‑catalyzed periodate oxidation); oxidizes a benzylic primary alcohol to the aldehyde. Catalytic RuCl₃ (1–5 mol %) activates periodate, which oxidizes the alcohol to 4‑bromobenzaldehyde while generating Ru‑oxo species regenerated by excess NaIO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous acetone or MeCN/H₂O, ambient to 40 °C, periodate in excess; reaction proceeds under air.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and isolate cobalt(II) phosphate as an insoluble solid while forming soluble potassium chloride; key transformation: Co²⁺ ions combine with phosphate to give Co₃(PO₄)₂ precipitate and K⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give KCl in solution; typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at ambient temperature; common solvent: water; no catalyst required; product is filtered and washed.

Williamson ether synthesis (alkylation of morphine phenolic OH). Purpose: preparation of ethylmorphine, a more lipophilic opioid derivative. Key transformation: deprotonated phenoxide of morphine attacks ethyl iodide, displacing I⁻; K₂CO₃ neutralizes the generated HI (Morphine + EtI + K₂CO₃ → Ethylmorphine + KI + K₂CO₃·H₂O). Conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, reflux temperature, inert atmosphere; potassium carbonate acts as base, no additional catalyst.

Base‑induced E2 dehydrohalogenation; purpose is to produce the terminal alkene 1‑phenylpropene from the bromide; key transformation is abstraction of a β‑hydrogen by potassium tert‑butoxide with simultaneous departure of bromide, giving the alkene, KBr and tert‑butanol; typical conditions use excess KOtBu in tert‑butanol or THF, heated to reflux (≈80–100 °C); no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution of 2‑chloroacetaldehyde with ammonia to give 2‑aminoacetaldehyde; ammonia displaces chloride in an SN2 process, generating hydrogen chloride; performed in aqueous or ethanolic ammonia, often at low temperature (0‑25 °C) with a base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to absorb HCl; purpose is preparation of α‑amino aldehyde.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of phenylboronic acid pinacol ester with bromobenzene; reaction type: palladium‑catalyzed C–C cross‑coupling; purpose: formation of a biphenyl C‑C bond; key transformations: oxidative addition of Pd(0) to the aryl bromide, transmetalation with the aryl boronate, reductive elimination to give biphenyl; typical conditions: Pd(PPh₃)₄ (5 mol %), K₂CO₃ (2 eq) in a mixture of water and a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF, dioxane, or ethanol/water), heated to 80‑100 °C under inert atmosphere.

Dehydration of an oxime (N‑[(2‑fluorophenyl)methylidene]hydroxylamine) to the corresponding nitrile, 2‑fluorobenzonitrile; purpose is conversion of an oxime to a nitrile; key transformation: removal of water from the oxime, forming a C≡N triple bond; typical reagents/conditions: dehydrating agents such as POCl₃, P₂O₅, or SOCl₂ in pyridine or DMF, heated 80‑120 °C; solvent often pyridine which also scavenges HCl; catalytic amounts of acid may be employed; water is the only by‑product.

Metathesis/precipitation double‑replacement; aqueous thallium(I) nitrate reacts with sodium hydroxide, producing thallium(I) hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium nitrate; carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst.

Phosphorylation of uridine using phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) to afford uridine‑5′‑monophosphate (UMP); purpose is synthesis of a nucleoside monophosphate; key transformation: POCl₃ activates the 5′‑hydroxyl of uridine, which is then displaced by inorganic phosphate (generated in situ from water) to form a phosphate ester and release HCl; typical conditions: POCl₃ added dropwise to uridine suspended in pyridine at 0 °C, then warmed to room temperature; pyridine acts as solvent and HCl scavenger; work‑up yields UMP after neutralization and purification.

Non‑enzymatic Maillard/Strecker-type decarboxylation; purpose: generate flavor aldehyde methional from L‑methionine and 3‑deoxy‑D‑glucosone; key transformation: L‑Methionine + 3‑deoxy‑D‑glucosone → CH₃SCH₂CH₂CHO + CO₂ + NH₃; typical conditions: aqueous or food matrix, heating at 80‑120 °C, neutral to slightly basic pH, no added catalyst; reaction proceeds via condensation, decarboxylation and deamination.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution (SN1) of 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol with hydrogen chloride to give 2‑chloro‑2‑methylbutane; purpose is preparation of a tertiary alkyl chloride; key transformation: protonation of the hydroxyl group, loss of water to generate a tertiary carbocation, followed by capture by Cl⁻; typical conditions: excess concentrated HCl, often with ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent) at 0‑25 °C; solvent can be aqueous HCl or a non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane; the only by‑product is water.

Reaction type: Acid‑base/carbonation reaction forming a bicarbonate. Purpose: generate soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate from calcium oxide. Key transformation: CaO reacts with water to give Ca(OH)₂, which then absorbs CO₂, forming Ca(HCO₃)₂. Typical conditions: aqueous suspension of CaO, CO₂ gas bubbled at ambient temperature and pressure, vigorous stirring. No special solvent beyond water is required.

Oxidation of 2‑propylpentan‑1‑ol to valproic acid using chromic acid (Jones oxidation); purpose is conversion of a primary alcohol to the corresponding carboxylic acid; key transformation: sequential oxidation of the alcohol to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid; typical conditions: Jones reagent (CrO₃ in aqueous H₂SO₄) in acetone, added at 0 °C and stirred while warming to room temperature; solvent system is acetone/water; chromium(VI) species serves as the oxidant; reaction is quenched with a reductante.g., isopropanol) before work‑up.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage; used to convert a tert‑alkyl ether into the corresponding tert‑alcohol and tert‑alkyl halide. The strong proton source (hydrogen chloride, often as aqueous HCl or gaseous HCl bubbled through) protonates the ether oxygen, forming a good leaving group and generating tert‑butyl cation which is captured by chloride to give tert‑butyl chloride while water attacks the other side to give tert‑butanol. Typical conditions: 0 – 50 °C, aqueous HCl or HCl gas in excess; solvent water or dilute acid solution; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation and rearrangement; converts propargyl bromide into the allene propadiene. Sodium amide dissolved in liquid ammonia acts as a strong non‑nucleophilic base, deprotonating the alkyne to give an acetylide, which undergoes β‑elimination of bromide to afford an allenyl anion that is protonated by the NH₃ solvent to give propadiene. Conditions: liquid NH₃ (−78 °C to −33 °C), excess NaNH₂, inert atmosphere; no catalyst, ammonia serves as both solvent and proton source.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde over Pd/C; selective hydrogen addition to the C=C bond to give hydrocinnamaldehyde (phenylpropionaldehyde) while leaving the aldehyde functional group intact; common conditions: H2 pressure 1–5 atm, solvent such as EtOAc, MeOH or ethanol, room temperature to 50 °C; purpose: saturation of the alkene.

Thermal dehalogenation / cracking; octafluorocyclobutane undergoes high‑temperature pyrolysis to produce tetrafluoroethylene (TFE); carried out at 800–900 °C in inert gas flow, often over a metal catalyst (e.g., nickel or copper) in a quartz reactor to generate the monomer for polymer production.

Acidic carbonylation (hydrocarbonylation) of an alkene; furnishes isovaleric acid from 3‑methyl‑1‑butene by incorporation of CO and water under strong acid. Sulfuric acid provides a highly acidic medium and acts as solvent; CO is introduced at elevated pressure (≈5–30 atm) and the mixture is heated (≈100–150 °C). The acid protonates the alkene, allowing insertion of CO and subsequent hydroxyl attack to give the carboxylic acid. Typical reagents: CO, H₂O, conc. H₂SO₄; conditions: high pressure CO, 100–150 °C, aqueous sulfuric acid medium.

Acid‑ decomposition of ammonium chromate; generates chromium(VI) oxide (CrO₃) and ammonium chloride. Adding concentrated HCl to aqueous ammonium chromate protonates the chromate anion, producing chromic acid which dehydrates to CrO₃ upon heating. Water is formed as a by‑product. Conditions: aqueous solution, cold to ambient temperature, excess concentrated HCl; often performed in a glass apparatus to avoid reduction; no catalyst.

Reduction of a quinone to a hydroquinone (2‑methyl‑1,4‑naphthalenediol). Can be achieved by catalytic hydrogenation (H₂, 1 atm, Pd‑C, ethanol) or by chemical hydride donors such as NaBH₄ in methanol at 0 °C to rt. The reaction reduces both carbonyl groups to hydroxyls, giving the diol in high yield; work‑up typically involves filtration of catalyst and removal of solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 3‑bromopropionitrile with dimethylamine; dimethylamine attacks the primary bromide carbon, displacing Br⁻ and forming 3-(dimethylamino)propanenitrile with HBr as by‑product; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF, DMF or MeCN at 0 °C to reflux; excess dimethylamine (often as a gas or aqueous solution) is used to neutralize HBr.

Protonation acid–base reaction to form an ionic salt; pyridine accepts a proton from hexafluorophosphoric acid, yielding pyridinium hexafluorophosphate. The reaction is typically carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or acetone to dissolve both reagents and avoid hydrolysis of PF₆⁻. Conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, stoichiometric amounts, inert atmosphere optional; no catalyst needed.

Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an oxime to an amine. Purpose: convert the N‑hydroxyimino intermediate into the free primary amine. Key transformation: cleavage of the N–O bond with addition of two hydrogen atoms, yielding 2‑phenylethylamine and water. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol or isopropanol) at room temperature to reflux; reaction time 1–12 h. No additional reagents required.

Acid‑base neutralization. Barium hydroxide reacts with boric acid to give barium metaborate and water; carried out in water at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, stoichiometric amounts, no catalyst needed.

Oxidative redox preparation of sodium permanganate; basic chlorate oxidizes manganese dioxide from Mn(IV) to Mn(VII). In aqueous NaOH, NaClO₃ acts as a strong oxidizer, while MnO₂ is reduced to MnO₄⁻, producing NaMnO₄; chloride is liberated as NaCl, and water is formed. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, NaOH excess, heating to 60–80 °C, often under reflux; stoichiometry as written; no external catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction of cadmium chloride with potassium cyanide to produce cadmium cyanide and potassium chloride. The reaction is performed by mixing aqueous CdCl₂ and KCN solutions at room temperature; Cd(CN)₂ precipitates and is collected, while KCl remains in the aqueous phase. No catalyst is required.

Oxidative preparation of palladium(II) acetate; metal oxidation. Palladium metal is oxidized by oxygen in glacial acetic acid to give Pd(OAc)2 and water. Typical conditions: reflux of acetic acid under an O₂ atmosphere (1 atm) for several hours; no additional solvent needed; reaction is carried out in a sealed flask or under reflux condenser.

Transesterification of 2‑pentyl acetate with methanol; ester exchange. The alkoxy group of the acetate is swapped for a methyl group, yielding methyl acetate and 2‑pentanol. Commonly catalyzed by a Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or a base (e.g., NaOMe). Reaction performed under reflux in excess methanol, often with removal of the formed methyl acetate by distillation to drive equilibrium.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of an aryl chloride by hydroxide. Aqueous NaOH attacks the carbon bearing chlorine ortho to the nitro group, displacing Cl⁻ and forming 2‑nitrophenol; sodium chloride remains in solution. Typical conditions: refluxing aqueous NaOH (10–20 % w/v) possibly with a co‑solvent such as ethanol, 1–2 h reaction time.

Catalytic partial oxidation of decane to decanal; selective alkane oxidation. Decane reacts with molecular oxygen in the presence of a metal oxide catalyst (e.g., Mo‑V‑Te, Co‑Mn, or supported Cu) to give decanal and water as the only by‑product. Gas‑phase reaction at 150–200 °C, 1–5 atm O₂, often in a fixed‑bed reactor; inert carrier gas (N₂) may be used.

Catalytic hydrogenation of phenylcyclohexene to cyclohexylbenzene; alkene reduction. The C=C bond of phenylcyclohexene saturated using H₂ gas and palladium on carbon (10 wt % Pd/C). Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 25–50 °C, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, stirring for 1–3 h until consumption of the alkene.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (demethylation) of furfural methyl ether to furfuryl alcohol; C–O bond cleavage. Pd catalyzes cleavage of the methyl ether under H₂, producing furfuryl alcohol and methane. Conditions: 1–3 atm H₂, 25–80 °C, solvent like methanol or ethanol, catalyst loading 5–10 wt % Pd, reaction time 2–6 h.

Acidolysis/halogen exchange of a trialkylborane. Purpose: to produce the strong Lewis acid BF₃ and methane gas from trimethylborane. Key transformation: HF protonates a B–C bond, leading to cleavage and formation of BF₃ and CH₄ (HF + B(CH₃)₃ → BF₃ + 3 CH₄). Conditions: anhydrous hydrogen fluoride (liquid or gas), low to moderate temperature, inert atmosphere; reaction typically performed neat in HF, no separate solvent or catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an allylic chloride with aqueous sodium hydroxide to afford the corresponding allylic alcohol; purpose is conversion of 3‑chloro‑1‑butene to 3‑hydroxy‑1‑butene. The reaction is typically carried out in water or a water‑ethanol mixture at reflux, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst. Sodium chloride precipitates and is removed during work‑up.

Alkylation (methylation) of the secondary amine hexahydro‑1,4‑diazepine by dimethyl sulfate, forming the N‑methylated product and methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product. The transformation proceeds via an SN2 attack of the nitrogen on a methyl‑sulfonate group in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often at 0 °C to room temperature. A base (e.g., triethylamine) is usually added to neutralize the acidic by‑product.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution with cyanide; cyanide ion displaces the methanesulfonate to afford butyl cyanide and sodium methanesulfonate. Typically run in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO with NaCN (0.5–1 M) at 0‑50 °C; no catalyst; solvent: DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile.

Nucleophilic substitution of phosphorus trichloride with sodium ethoxide to generate triethyl phosphite and sodium chloride (a classic preparation of trialkyl phosphites). The reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions in ethanol or ether, refluxing the mixture under nitrogen; the NaCl precipitate is filtered off after completion.

Catalytic hydrogenation of myrtenol using palladium on carbon to reduce the carbon‑carbon double bond, yielding dihydromyrcenol. Typical conditions involve hydrogen gas at 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), and a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature to reflux. The reaction is monitored until the disappearance of the alkene signal.

Nucleophilic substitution of an alcohol using PBr3; primary allylic alcohol (pent‑4‑en‑1‑ol) is converted to the corresponding bromide (4‑pentenyl bromide) with formation of phosphorous acid; PBr3 replaces the OH group with Br via an SN2‑type pathway; carried out anhydrously at 0 °C to reflux in solvents such as CH2Cl2 or CCl4, under inert atmosphere; PBr3 itself acts as reagent, no additional catalyst.

Halogen‑mediated thiol oxidation; converts a thiol to a disulfide using elemental iodine as the oxidant. Iodine oxidizes two equivalents of butyl mercaptan, forming dibutyl disulfide while producing hydrogen iodide as a by‑product. The reaction is usually run in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride, chloroform) at 0 °C to room temperature, and the mixture is worked up to remove iodine and HI.

Hydrolysis of iodoacetamide in water to give glycolamide (2‑aminoacetamide) and hydrogen iodide. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of water on the carbon bearing iodine; it is usually carried out under mildly acidic or basic conditions, at ambient temperature or gentle heating, and the liberated HI is neutralized or removed during work‑up.

Cyanohydrin formation (nucleophilic addition of CN⁻ to aldehyde); benzaldehyde reacts with NaCN to give mandelonitrile (benzaldehyde cyanohydrin). Key transformation: CN⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide that is protonated to the cyanohydrin; NaOH is generated as a by‑product. Performed in aqueous NaCN at 0‑5 °C (often in ice bath) to limit side reactions; the reaction medium or water is the solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction of cobalt(II) iodate with hydrochloric acid, producing cobalt(II) chloride in solution and iodic acid as the other product. The reaction is performed in aqueous medium at room temperature; the resulting CoCl₂ remains soluble while HIO₃ may precipitate or be isolated by evaporation.

Halogen‑lithium exchange (nucleophilic substitution) on a germanium halide; methyl lithium attacks bromogermane, displaces bromide to give methylgermane and LiBr; performed at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in dry ethereal solvent such as THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralization between phosphoric acid and iron(II) carbonate; carbonate is protonated, releasing CO₂ and H₂O while iron(II) phosphate precipitates; carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off CO₂; no solvent beyond water.

Simmons‑Smith cyclopropanation; zinc (or Zn‑Cu couple) reacts with diiodomethane to generate a iodomethylzinc carbenoid that adds across the C=C of ethylene to afford cyclopropane, with ZnI₂ as by‑product; typically conducted in dry diethyl ether or THF at room temperature or reflux under inert gas.

Combustion (oxidation) reaction: methylhydrazine reacts with oxygen to produce nitrogen gas, carbon dioxide, and water. Occurs under flame conditions or in a combustion chamber with excess O₂ at high temperature; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Fischer esterification of nicotinic acid with methanol catalyzed by p‑toluenesulfonic acid; the acid protonates the carboxyl group, methanol attacks, and water is eliminated to give methyl nicotinate; reflux in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of PTSA, removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) improves yield.

Base‑promoted E2 elimination of ethyl 2‑chloro‑2‑methylpropanoate using triethylamine to generate the α,β‑unsaturated ester ethyl methacrylate; triethylamine abstracts a β‑hydrogen while chloride leaves, forming triethylammonium chloride; typically run in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, THF, or toluene at 0 °C to room temperature.

Direct metal halogenation (redox) of uranium metal with hydrogen bromide gas; uranium is oxidized to uranium(III) bromide while HBr is reduced, liberating H₂; performed at elevated temperature (often >200 °C) in a sealed tube or reactor with a stream of dry HBr; no liquid solvent, inert atmosphere required for safety.

Oxidation/halogenation: Chlorine gas oxidizes PbCl2 (PbII) to PbCl4 (PbIV). The reaction converts lead(II) chloride to tetrachloroplumbane by a redox process, releasing no by‑products. Typically performed by passing dry Cl2 over solid PbCl2 at elevated temperature (≈150 °C) under anhydrous conditions; the product sublimes and is collected in a dry, inert atmosphere. No solvent or catalyst is required.

Oxidative cyclization (heterocycle formation): Ferric chloride acts as an oxidant to cyclize 2‑aminothiophenol into benzothiazole. The amine and thiol groups undergo intramolecular condensation while FeIII is reduced to FeII, generating HCl as a by‑product. Commonly carried in refluxing ethanol or glacial acetic acid, with FeCl3 (≈1–1.5 equiv) as the sole catalyst/oxidant. The reaction mixture is then worked up to isolate benzothiazole; ferrous chloride remains in solution.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (deacetylation): Aqueous hydrochloric acid hydrolyzes 1‑acetylpiperidin‑2‑one, cleaving the acetyl amide to afford acetic acid and 2‑piperidone. The reaction proceeds via protonation of the carbonyl, nucleophilic attack by water, and subsequent de‑acetylation. Typical conditions are reflux (≈80–100 °C) in 6 M HCl for 2–4 h. Water serves as both solvent and reactant; no external catalyst is required.

Thermal condensation (decomposition): Heating solid urea induces a condensation reaction where two urea molecules eliminating ammonia and forming biuret (NH2‑CO‑NH‑CO‑NH2). The process occurs at 150–200 °C under anhydrous, inert atmosphere. No solvent or catalyst is employed; the reaction is driven solely by temperature.

Double displacement (acid–base) reaction; converts ammonium ferric sulfate to soluble iron(III) chloride and ammonium chloride while liberating sulfuric acid; typically performed in aqueous solution with excess concentrated HCl at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of sec‑butyl chloride by acetate ion to form sec‑butyl acetate and NaCl; an esterification via alkyl halide; carried out by refluxing sodium acetate in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often with azeotropic removal of NaCl; no catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; barium acetate reacts with cobalt(II) sulfate to give soluble cobalt(II) acetate and insoluble barium sulfate, which precipitates; performed by mixing aqueous of the two salts at room temperature; no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of 1,2,3‑tribromopropane to propane, with concurrent formation of hydrogen bromide; uses H₂ gas and palladium on carbon (Pd/C) under moderate pressure (1–5 atm) and mild heating (25–80 °C) in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate; Pd/C acts as the catalyst.

Acid–base neutralisation of a carboxylate salt; purpose is to liberate the free hydroxy acid. Sodium 2‑hydroxypropanoate is protonated by aqueous HCl, giving 2‑hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid) and NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, addition of conc. HCl at 0 °C to control exotherm, stirring at rt; water is the solvent.

Acid–salt double displacement; concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with calcium pyrophosphate to produce phosphoric acid and insoluble calcium sulfate; conducted in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to ensure dissolution; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl bromide by aqueous ammonia, yielding ethylamine hydrogen bromide; typically performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution with excess NH₃, sometimes heated to reflux; the HBr formed is neutralized by excess ammonia or a base; no catalyst.

Amide coupling (carbodiimide-mediated condensation). Purpose: connect the carboxyl group of arachidonic acid to the amine of 4‑aminophenol to form a long‑chain amide. Key transformation: activation of the fatty acid by EDC·HCl to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate, which is stabilized by HOBt, followed by nucleophilic attack of the phenolic amine to give the n‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)icosa‑5,8,11,14‑tetraenamide. Typical conditions: reaction performed in anhydrous DMF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often with a tertiary amine base (e., DIPEA) to scavenge HCl. No metal catalysis required.

Base‑catalyzed aldose‑ketose isomerization (Lobry de Bruyn‑Alberda–Van Ekenstein transformation). Purpose: convert the aldose sugar L‑fucose into its corresponding ketose, L‑fuculose. Key transformation: enolization of the aldehyde carbonyl under NaOH, followed by tautomerization to the keto form. Typical conditions: aqueous sodium hydroxide (0.1–1 M) at 20–40 °C for minutes to a few hours; reaction is quenched with acid and the product isolated by chromatography or crystallization. No special solvents beyond water are required.

Catalytic hydrogenation; purpose is to convert an alkene to the corresponding saturated alkane. The C=C double bond is reduced by molecular hydrogen in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO2, or Raney Ni. Typical conditions are H2 pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–80 °C, often in a solvent like ethanol, methanol or dichloromethane; the reaction proceeds smoothly without additional reagents.

Formylation (amide formation) of a primary amine. 2,2‑Dimethylpropylamine reacts with formic acid, undergoing condensation to afford N‑(2,2‑dimethylpropyl)formamide with loss of water. Conducted by heating the mixture (reflux) in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or xylene, often with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water or using a dehydrating agent (e.g., DCC). Purpose: protection of the amine or synthesis of a formamide derivative.

This is a radical dimerization (head-to-head coupling) reaction. Two ethyl radicals combine to form n-butane via a carbon-carbon bond. It proceeds under radical initiation conditions (e.g., UV light, high temperature, or peroxide initiators). The product is a saturated alkane with all single bonds. The reaction is non-selective if other radicals are present.

Jones oxidation (chromium(VI) oxidation of a primary alcohol). Purpose: oxidize citronellol’s primary allylic alcohol to the corresponding carboxylic acid, citronellic acid. Key transformation: chromium(VI) species (CrO₃ in aqueous H₂SO₄, generating the Jones reagent) oxidizes the alcohol first to the aldehyde and then to the acid, with reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III) oxide (Cr₂O₃) and formation of water. Typical conditions: cold acetone solution (0 °C) with addition of Jones reagent dropwise, then stirring at 0–25 °C until completion; reaction is quenched with methanol or isopropanol to destroy excess oxidant. Solvent is usually acetone; acidic aqueous environment is essential.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) and acid‑base precipitation. Purpose: generate insoluble strontium carbonate while converting the nitrate salts to soluble sodium nitrate. Key transformation: Sr²⁺ combines with CO₃²⁻ from the decomposition of NaHCO₃, precipitating SrCO₃; bicarbonate decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O, and Na⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to give NaNO₃ in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, moderate heating (≈50 °C) to drive off CO₂; stirring until cessation of gas evolution. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne ester; purpose is full reduction of the C≡C bond to a saturated C–C bond while retaining the ester functionality, yielding ethyl propanoate. Ethyl propiolate is hydrogenated over Pd/C under H₂ (1 atm) in ethanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature to 50 °C. The Pd/C catalyst facilitates transfer of hydrogen to both carbons of the alkyne, giving the saturated ester.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl halide. Purpose: synthesize ethyl methanesulfonate (ethyl mesylate) from ethyl iodide. Key transformation: the methanesulfonate anion (CH₃SO₃⁻) attacks the electroph carbon of ethyl iodide, displacing I⁻ to give the sulfonate ester and potassium iodide as by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile; temperature 0 °C to reflux (often 40–80 °C) to ensure complete conversion. The reaction proceeds without metal catalysis.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of a metal carbonate. Purpose prepare insoluble copper(II) carbonate and convert soluble bromide to potassium bromide. Key transformation: CO₃²⁻ from K₂CO₃ pairs with Cu²⁺ from CuBr₂ to form CuCO₃ precipitate; K⁺ pairs with Br⁻ to give soluble KBr. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at ambient temperature; the precipitate is filtered and washed. No catalyst needed; water serves as the reaction medium.
Combustion of ethylene: complete oxidation of C₂H₄ with O₂ producing CO₂ and H₂O; occurs as a high‑temperature flame (~1800 °C) in excess oxygen at atmospheric pressure; no catalyst or solvent.

Double‑displacement precipitation; copper(II) sulfate in water reacts with sodium sulfide to form a black precipitate of copper(II) sulfide (CuS) and soluble sodium sulfate. Performed in aqueous solution, often at ambient temperature; no catalyst.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type) reaction; converts a secondary alkyl chloride to the corresponding iodide to improve leaving‑group ability. Performed under anhydrous conditions with aluminium triiodide as a Lewis‑acid halide‑exchange reagent, often in a non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, at reflux or gentle heating under inert atmosphere. The AlI₃ abstracts chloride, forming AlCl₃ and delivers iodide to the substrate.

Nucleophilic addition of an organolithium reagent to selenium dioxide followed by aqueous work‑up; a organoselenium acid (methyl seleninic acid). Methyl lithium adds to the electrophilic SeO₂ to form a lithium selenite intermediate, which on protonation with water gives CH₃SeO₂H. Conducted at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in an aprotic ether solvent such as THF, then quenched with cold water or dilute acid. No external catalyst is needed.

Acid–base proton transfer; generation of hypobromous acid (HOBr) in situ from sodium hypobromite. Acetic acid protonates the hypobromite anion, producing HOBr and sodium acetate. Performed in aqueous solution, often at 0–25 °C to avoid decomposition of HOBr. No catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization; formation of silver nitrite from nitrous acid. Silver hydroxide (AgOH) deprotonates nitrous acid, yielding AgNO₂ and water. Carried out in aqueous medium, usually at ambient temperature. The insoluble silver nitrite can be isolated by filtration. No catalyst needed.

Redox/disproportionation reaction between iodine trichloride and elemental aluminum. Aluminum reduces ICl₃, producing aluminum iodide (AlI₃) and liberating chlorine gas. Typically performed in a sealed, dry vessel at elevated temperature (100–200 °C) under an inert atmosphere to control the vigorous evolution of Cl₂. No additional catalyst; the metal itself serves as the reductant.

Acid–base neutralization; scandium oxide reacts with sulfuric acid to form scandium sulfate. The oxide is added to concentrated aqueous H₂SO₄ and heated (often 80–120 °C) to ensure dissolution, giving Sc₂(SO₄)₃ in solution and water. No catalyst needed; water is the reaction medium.

Solid‑gas redox/O2‑release reaction (oxygen‑candle chemistry); purpose is to generate oxygen; key transformation is BaO2 + CO2 → BaCO3 + O2; performed by heating a mixture of barium peroxide and carbon dioxide at about 300‑400 °C; no solvent, solid‑state reaction.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (deoxygenation) of phenol to benzene. Molecular hydrogen cleaves the C–O bond of phenol in the presence of a metal hydrogenation catalyst (e.g., Pt, Pd, Ni, or Raney nickel), yielding benzene and water. Conducted at high H₂ pressure (10–50 atm) and elevated temperature (150–300 °C) in a solvent such as ethanol or toluene. The metal catalyst enables the reduction and removal of the hydroxyl group.

Hydrolysis/decomposition of trisodium thiophosphate; water attacks the P=S bond, yielding sodium phosphate (e.g., Na₃PO₄ or Na₂HPO₄ depending on pH) and hydrogen sulfide gas. No catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds in aqueous solution, commonly with gentle heating to evolve H₂S. pH controls the phosphate speciation.

Aqueous alkaline hydrolysis of 1‑bromo‑4‑methylcyclohexane to give the corresponding alcohol; NaOH acts as nucleophile, substituting bromide and forming 4‑methylcyclohexanol; reaction proceeds by SN1/E2 pathway depending on conditions. Conducted in water or aqueous ethanol, heated under reflux (80–100 °C). Sodium bromide is formed as by‑product.

Cyclotrimerization (cycloaddition) of thioformaldehyde to give 1,3,5‑trithiane; purpose is to obtain a stable cyclic sulfide that can serve as a protected formaldehyde equivalent. The reaction proceeds by spontaneous condensation of three CH2S units, often accelerated by mild acid or by heating under pressure (e.g., 1–5 atm, 20–80 °C). No solvent is required for the gas‑phase process; when conducted in solution, inert solvents such as THF or diethyl ether are used.

Catalytic hydrogenation of benzonitrile to benzylamine using copper chromite as heterogeneous catalyst; type: reductive hydrogenation of a nitrile. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 50–100 atm, temperature 150–200 °C, in a polar protic solvent (ethanol, methanol or water). Copper chromite (Cu₂Cr₂O₅) provides the active surface for hydrogen activation. Purpose: convert a nitrile functional group to a primary amine.

Salt‑acid displacement (acidification); calcium fumarate reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid, liberating fumaric acid (which may precipitate) and forming soluble calcium chloride; typically carried out at mild heating (40–60 °C) to improve dissolution; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Metathesis precipitation; synthesis of erbium phosphate using sodium phosphate as the phosphate source. Er(NO₃)₃ reacts with Na₃PO₄, forming insoluble ErPO₄ and soluble NaNO₃. Performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating (30–70 °C) to improve crystallization; no catalyst needed, water as solvent.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of 7‑bromoindole with methylboronic acid to afford 7‑methylindole, with boric acid as the by‑product; type: palladium‑catalyzed sp²–sp³ coupling. Typical conditions: 1–5 mol % Pd(PPh₃)₄ or PdCl₂(dppf), base such as K₂CO₃ (2–3 equiv), solvent mixture of toluene/H₂O or dioxane/EtOH, heated to 80–100 °C for 6–12 h under N₂. Purpose: install a methyl substituent on an indole ring.

Selenium dioxide oxidation of 3,4‑dimethoxytoluene to 3,4‑dimethoxybenzaldehyde; type: benzylic (or allylic) oxidation. Conventional conditions: stoichiometric SeO₂ (1.1–1.5 equiv) in 1,4‑dioxane or tert‑butanol, reflux (80–120 °C) for 2–6 h, often with a small amount of water to facilitate the reaction. The methyl group is oxidized to an aldehyde, while selenium is reduced to elemental Se. Purpose: functional‑group interconversion of a benzylic methyl to an aldehyde.

Intramolecular SN2 cyclization of 1,5‑dibromopentane with potassium sulfide to give thiane (six‑membered cyclic thioether) and 2 KBr; type: nucleophilic substitution/ring‑closing reaction. Typical conditions: excess K₂S (or KSH) in polar aprotic solvent such asF or DMSO, heated to 80–120 °C for several hours. The sulfide anion attacks one bromomethylene, displaces bromide, and then closes the six‑membered ring by a second SN2 step. Purpose: synthesis of saturated sulfur heterocycles.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination (EAS) of 3‑trifluoromethyl‑aniline with N‑bromosuccinimide; purpose is to install a bromine para to the amino group for further functionalization. Key transformation is substitution of a hydrogen by bromine at the 4‑position. Typical conditions: NBS (1.0‑1.2 equiv) in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature, sometimes with a mild acid or light; succinimide is formed as the by‑product.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between a zinc carboxylate and sodium carbonate. Zinc butyrate exchanges its butyrate anion for carbonate, yielding zinc carbonate precipitate and soluble sodium butyrate. Conducted in water or aqueous ethanol, often with gentle heating to improve solubility; no catalyst required.

Reduction of methyl phenyl sulfoxide to thioanisole using sodium bis(2‑methoxyethoxy)aluminum hydride (Red‑Al) ; type: selective sulfoxide → sulfide reduction. Conducted at 0 °C to 25 °C in THF or toluene under inert atmosphere (N₂), typically using 1.2–1.5 equiv of Red‑Al. The aluminum hydride delivers hydride to the sulfur, converting the S=O bond to S–H and then to the thioether after work‑up. Purpose: generate the corresponding sulfide (thioanisole) from a sulfoxide precursor.

Oxidation of 2‑methoxyethanol to 2‑methoxyacetaldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); purpose is to obtain the aldehyde without over‑oxidation to the acid; primary alcohol is converted to an aldehyde while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) species; typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric PCC supplies the oxidant and pyridine is released as a by‑product.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification/saponification forming a carboxylate salt; sodium methoxide attacks the ester carbonyl, displacing methanol and generating sodium cinnamate; conducted in methanol with NaOCH₃ at ambient temperature; provides the cinnamate anion for subsequent acid‑base or coupling chemistry.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of ethanol to diethyl ether; purpose is ether synthesis; key transformation is bimolecular electrophilic attack of protonated ethanol by a second ethanol molecule, forming the ether and water; typical conditions: excess ethanol, concentrated sulfuric acid, temperature controlled at 140 °C (lower temperatures favor ether, higher temperatures give ethylene); often carried out in a sealed tube or reflux apparatus.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl chloride by hydroxide; base‑promoted hydrolysis of 2‑chloroethyl acrylate to give 2‑hydroxyethyl acrylate. Typically carried out in aqueous sodium hydroxide (1 equiv) at 0 – 25 °C to avoid unwanted polymerisation of the acrylic double bond. Water or a water‑acetone mixture serves as solvent; the reaction yields sodium chloride as by‑product.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of phenol (bromate oxidation). o‑Cresol is oxidized by sodium bromate aqueous sulfuric acid to the quinone 2‑methyl‑1,4‑benzoquinone, with reduction of bromate to bromide and formation of NaHSO₄ and water. Purpose: synthesis of a methyl‑substituted benzoquinone. Conditions: aqueous H₂SO₄ (≈1 M), NaBrO₃ added at 0–25 °C then warmed to 60–80 °C, vigorous stirring; additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of propionyl chloride with lithium methanolate to give methyl propionate and lithium chloride. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent (THF, CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Carboxylation of a Grignard reagent; purpose is to extend the carbon chain by one carbon to produce heptanoic acid. Heptylmagnesium bromide in dry ether is exposed to a stream of dry CO₂ gas at 0 °C to rt, forming the magnesium carboxylate intermediate. Subsequent aqueous work‑up with dilute HCl protonates the carboxylate, giving heptanoic acid and magnesium bromide. Reaction is performed under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture before CO₂ addition.

Type: thermal decomposition (salt breakdown). Description: Lithium tetrafluoroborate decomposes upon heating to give solid lithium fluoride and volatile boron trifluoride gas. Typical conditions involve heating the solid to 200–300 °C under an inert atmosphere or vacuum to remove BF3. No solvent; performed in a sealed tube or flash‑pyrolysis apparatus.

Acid‑base salt formation (neutralization). The weakly acidic imide NH of phenytoin is deprotonated by sodium carbonate, giving the sodium salt of phenytoin and producing NaHCO₃. Purpose: preparation of a more soluble phenytoin salt. Conditions: aqueous or ethanolic solution, mild heating (30–50 °C) to dissolve reagents; reaction proceeds at ambient pH, no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange. Potassium iodide exchanges anion with cerium(III) nitrate to afford potassium nitrate and cerium(III) iodide. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, equimolar mixing at room temperature, stirring until complete; both salts remain soluble, so isolation may require evaporation or precipitation with a non‑solvent.

Metathesis/precipitation; lead(II) nitrate supplies Pb²⁺ that reacts with sulfide to give black lead sulfide precipitate, leaving barium nitrate in solution; performed in water under ambient conditions, PbS is filtered off.

Base‑promoted dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination). Potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 3‑chloro‑1‑butene, eliminating HCl to form conjugated diene 1,3‑butadiene; the tert‑butoxide is protonated to tert‑butanol and KCl is produced. Purpose: generation of a diene from an allylic halide. Conditions: anhydrous THF or DMF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; stoichiometric KOt‑Bu, no additional catalyst.

SN2 halide exchange with bromide; KBr supplies bromide ion that attacks the primary carbon, giving butyl bromide and potassium methanesulfonate. Performed in polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF) with excess KBr, usually under reflux; no catalyst; solvent: acetone or DMF.

Hydrolysis of an acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Water attacks the carbonyl carbon of 1‑naphthoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give 1‑naphthoic acid and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: aqueous medium (often 1 M NaOH or pyridine to scavenge HCl), 0–25 °C to control exotherm, followed by acidification; solvent may be a mixture of water and a miscible organic (e.g., dioxane).

Acid–base salt formation; used to convert the free base of orphenadrine into a pharmaceutically useful hydrochloride salt that is more water‑soluble; the amine nitrogen is protonated by HCl giving orphenadrine·HCl; typically performed in aqueous or ethanol solution at ambient temperature, often with HCl gas or concentrated aqueous HCl; no catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion of formaldehyde to formic acid with peroxymonosulfuric acid; conducted in dilute aqueous acid at low temperature, water as solvent, producing H2SO4 and water alongside the formic acid.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride (chlorination); employed to activate picolinic acid for subsequent amide or ester formation; the hydroxyl of the carboxyl group is replaced by chlorine, producing picolinoyl chloride with evolution of SO₂ and HCl gases; carried out in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, often at 0 °C to reflux, with a catalytic drop of DMF to accelerate the reaction; no external catalyst beyond the thionyl chloride itself.

High‑temperature carbothermic reduction (solid‑state redox); used to prepare lower‑valent vanadium(II) oxide from vanadium(V) oxide; carbon reduces V₂O₅, removing oxygen to form VO and carbon monoxide; performed in a quartz or alumina tube furnace at 900–1100 °C under an inert (argon or nitrogen) atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst, the solid reagents are mixed and heated.

Oxidation of a primary benzylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde using manganese dioxide; provides 2‑methylbenzaldehyde without over‑oxidation to the acid; MnO₂ abstracts two hydrogens from the –CH₂OH group, forming the carbonyl and reducing to MnO; usually carried out at room temperature in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, chloroform, or dry ether; stoichiometric MnO₂ is used, no additional catalyst.

Reductive fluorination (gas‑phase redox) of arsenic pentafluoride by hydrogen; generates arsenic trifluoride and hydrogen fluoride; H₂ donates electrons to AsF₅, reducing it from +5 to +3 while producing HF as a by‑product; conducted in a sealed reaction vessel at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) under anhydrous conditions; no solvent the reaction is typically driven by excess H₂ and may be catalyzed by a metal surface, but no specific catalyst is required.

Acid‑promoted decarboxylation of a β‑keto carboxylate; converts sodium 3‑oxopentanoate to 2‑butanone while releasing CO₂; typically performed by heating the sodium salt in aqueous conc. H₂SO₄ (reflux), water is the solvent and the acid itself serves as catalyst.

Hydrogen reduction (hydrogenolysis) of a metal sulfide; purpose: recover metallic molybdenum and generate hydrogen sulfide gas. Key transformation: MoS2 + 4 H2 → Mo + 2 H2S. Performed at 500‑900 °C under flowing hydrogen; solid‑gas system, no catalyst or solvent required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of fluorene using nitronium tetrafluoroborate; introduces a nitro group onto the fluorene framework to give nitrofluorene, with concomitant formation of BF₃ and HF from the BF₄⁻ counter‑ion; the NO₂⁺ electrophile attacks the aromatic ring; performed in an aprotic, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; the nitronium salt itself serves as the nitrating agent; no additional catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution; amide synthesis. Lithium amide attacks acetyl chloride, displacing chloride to give acetamide and LiCl. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Oxidation (Jones oxidation); conversion of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Phenoxyethanol is oxidized by sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid, producing phenoxyacetic acid, water, and Cr(III) sulfate. Conducted in aqueous H₂SO₄ (often 1 M) with the dichromate solution added dropwise at 0 °C then warmed to reflux; acetone is a common co‑solvent.

Imine hydrolysis; purpose: deprotect the imine to regenerate benzaldehyde and methylamine; key transformation: acid‑catalyzed addition of water across the C=N bond with cleavage to give the aldehyde and amine; typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) at reflux or room temperature, often in a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent such as THF or dioxane.

Halogen exchange/fluorination; replacement of iodine atoms by fluorine. Carbon tetraiodide reacts with elemental fluorine, yielding elemental iodine and diiododifluoromethane (CF₂I₂). Requires excess F₂ gas, low‑temperature control (often –78 °C to 0 °C) in an inert fluorinated solvent such as liquid HF or perfluorohexane; reaction is highly exothermic and must be performed in specialized fluorine‑compatible equipment.

Oxidation of sulfide to sulfone; catalytic oxidation. Diphenyl sulfide is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide in the presence of sodium tungstate (Na₂WO₄) as a catalyst, affording diphenyl sulfone and water. Typical conditions: aqueous H₂O₂ (30 %), Na₂WO₄ (1–5 mol %), temperature 25–60 °C, solvent mixture of water/methanol or acetonitrile.
Thermal decomposition reaction; selectively produces molybdenum tetrachloride and chlorine gas; occurs upon heating (typically above 180°C); no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid–base salt formation; preparation of an amine hydrochloride. Methoxamine (a primary amine) reacts with hydrochloric acid to give methoxamine hydrochloride. Usually performed by bubbling HCl gas into an aqueous or ethanolic solution of methoxamine at 0 °C to 25 °C, followed by evaporation of solvent to isolate the crystalline salt.

Strong reduction; conversion of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Lithium aluminum hydride (LAH) reduces 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoic acid to 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanol, with Al(OH)₃ formed as a by‑product. Conducted in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen, LAH added at 0 °C then the mixture warmed to reflux; work‑up involves careful quenching with dilute acid.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (reverse Fischer esterification); purpose is to regenerate cyclohexanol from cyclohexyl acetate. Key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl of the ester, breaking the C–O bond and producing cyclohexanol and acetic acid. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous dilute acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) for several hours; acidic medium protonates the carbonyl to facilitate nucleophilic attack. Solvent: mixture of water and a water‑miscible organic solvent (e.g., THF) may be used; no catalyst beyond the acid.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous mixing of tin(II) chloride and potassium sulfide forms insoluble tin(II) sulfide precipitate and soluble potassium chloride; carried out at ambient temperature in water.

Direct combinationsolid‑state synthesis) of elemental zinc and antimony to afford zinc antimonide; performed by heating the elemental mixture under inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) at 500‑600 °C, often in a sealed tube; no solvent required.

Type: Base‑mediated decomposition (neutralization) of a peracid. Purpose: Convert unstable trifluoroperacetic acid into a stable carboxylate and generate hydrogen peroxide. Key transformation: CF3C(O)OOH + OH⁻ → CF3COO⁻ + H2O2. Conditions: Aqueous NaOH solution, typically 0 °C to 25 °C to avoid side reactions. Solvent: Water (no additional catalyst).

Formylation (amide formation) of guanidine with formic acid, yielding N‑formylguanidine and water. The carbonyl carbon of formic acid is attacked by the guanidine nitrogen, followed by loss of water to give the formamide. Usually carried out by heating guanidine in neat formic acid or in a mixture of formic acid and a minimal amount of water at 80–120 °C under reflux; excess formic acid drives the equilibrium to product.

Condensation (heterocycle formation); purpose: synthesis of pyrazole ring. Hydrazine‑carboxaldehyde reacts with the 1,3‑diketone acetylacetone, the two carbonyl groups condense with the –NH‑NH2 segment to give 3,5‑dimethylpyrazole and water. Typically performed by refluxing equimolar amounts in ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid; the reaction proceeds at 70‑80 °C for 2–6 h.

Base‑promoted E2 dehydrohalogenation; potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 1‑chloro‑1‑ethoxyethane, displacing chloride to give ethoxyethene (vinyl ether) and tert‑butanol; typically run in an aprotic solvent such as THF or DMSO at 0 °C to room temperature.

Double displacement precipitation; aqueous solutions of lead nitrate and rubidium molybdate exchange ions, precipitating insoluble lead molybdate while forming soluble rubidium nitrate; performed at room temperature with stirring.
Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution; acetic acid reacts with sodium bicarbon to produce sodium acetate, water and carbon dioxide gas; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature.

Dehydration of an amide to a nitrile using phosphorus oxychloride; POCl₃ activates isobutyramide, and in the presence of a base (often pyridine) the amide loses water to afford isobutyronitrile; reaction carried out under anhydrous conditions, typically in pyridine or dichloromethane, from 0 °C up to reflux.

Acid–base/halide exchange reaction; nitride is protonated by HCl to release NH3 and the uranium is converted to a chloride salt; typically carried out at elevated temperature (300–400 °C) using gaseous or aqueous HCl; no special catalyst; solid UN reacts with HCl gas or conc. HCl solution

Acid–base neutralization; sodium hydroxide deprotonates difluorophosphoric acid to give sodium difluorophosphate and water. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is both solvent and reaction medium, no catalyst required.

N‑alkylation of a primary amine; tryptamine is deprotonated sodium hydride to generate the nucleophilic amide anion, which undergoes two successive SN2 substitutions with allyl bromide to afford N,N‑diallyltryptamine. Typical conditions: dry DMF or THF, 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, NaH (1.2 eq) followed by excess allyl bromide (2 eq); no additional catalyst needed.

Metal‑halogen displacement (redox) reaction; elemental lithium reduces iodine to lithium iodide, forming two equivalents of LiI. Conducted in anhydrous ether (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, often at 0 °C to avoid vigorous exotherm; no catalyst required.

Selective ester‑to‑aldehyde reduction; DIBAL‑H reduces the methyl ester of 2,4‑dihydroxy‑6‑methylbenzoate to the corresponding aldehyde (2,4‑dihydroxy‑6‑methylbenzaldehyde) while leaving the phenolic OH groups intact. Typically carried out in dry THF at –78 °C (dry‑ice/acetone bath) with 1.0–1.2 eq DIBAL‑H, then quenched with methanol and aqueous work‑up; inert atmosphere is employed, no additional catalyst.

Phenol deprotonation (acid‑base neutralization); pentachlorophenol reacts with sodium hydroxide to give the sodium pentachlorophenate salt and water. Performed in aqueous NaOH solution at mild temperature (room temperature to 60 °C); water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic reduction of a nitrile with lithium aluminium hydride; used to obtain the primary amine from a protected aromatic nitrile. Transformation: –C≡N → –CH2CH2NH2. Conditions: LiAlH4 (1‑1.5 eq) added to a solution of the nitrile in dry THF or diethyl ether, reflux under nitrogen atmosphere, then carefully quench with water followed by dilute HCl. Solvent: anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether).

Carbamate formation using a phosgene equivalent; triphosgene reacts with 1‑naphthol and methylamine to generate 1‑naphthyl N‑methylcarbamate, releasing hydrogen chloride. The reaction proceeds via formation of an intermediate chloroformate which couples with the amine. Standard conditions: dry dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen; a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) is often added to scavenge the generated HCl, though the stoichiometry shown includes HCl as a product. No metal catalyst is required.

Elimination (E2) reaction: a strong, non‑nucleophilic base (potassium tert‑butoxide) abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 2‑chloro‑2‑methylhexane, displacing chloride as potassium chloride and forming the alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑hexene; tert‑butanol is generated from proton transfer to the base. Usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF, DMSO) at elevated temperature.

Metal‑acid redox/acid‑base reaction: zinc metal reduces the hydrofluoric component of ammonium bifluoride, producing zinc fluoride and hydrogen gas; the ammonium ion is deprotonated to give ammonia. Typically performed in aqueous or molten conditions, often at reflux, with zinc metal in excess.

Alkoxide exchange (transesterification) similar to #3; titanium(IV) isopropoxide reacts with methanol to produce titanium(IV) methoxide and isopropanol; carried out by refluxing the metal alkoxide in dry methanol, often with azeotropic removal of isopropanol; inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (azide transfer) to form a sulfonyl azide: trimethylsilyl azide attacks p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride, displacing chloride as trimethylsilyl chloride and yielding p‑toluenesulfonyl azide. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile, usually at 0 °C to room temperature, without additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Calcium carbonate reacts with adipic acid; the carbonate is protonated to release carbon dioxide and water while the calcium cation binds the adipate dianion to give calcium adipate. Typically performed by heating a suspension of the solids in water or aqueous ethanol (reflux); no catalyst is required.

Transesterification (ester exchange) reaction; converts esters to other esters via alcoholysis; key transformation involves ester bond cleavage, with methanol’s oxygen incorporating into the new ester; catalyzed by acids (e.g., H2SO4), bases, or lipase enzymes; solvents may include toluene or ethanol for methanolysis.

Aminolysis of an ester (amidation): ammonia attacks the carbonyl carbon of n‑butyl acetate, displacing n‑butanol and forming acetamide. The reaction is driven by excess ammonia and heat (reflux) and may be performed neat with gaseous NH₃ or in a polar solvent (e.g., ethanol) under sealed‑tube conditions.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation): hydrogen gas, in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or Pt‑O₂, cleaves the C–Cl bond of 1‑chloro‑1,1,2‑trifluoroethane, yielding hydrogen chloride and the dehalogenated alkane 1,1,2‑trifluoroethane. Reaction is run under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a protic or aprotic solvent (ethanol THF) at moderate temperature.

General type: condensation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) forming a cyclic hydrazide. Purpose: synthesize phthalhydrazide, a building block for dyes and pharmaceuticals. Key transformation: hydrazine attacks both carbonyl groups of phthalic anhydride, opening the anhydride ring and then cyclizing with loss of one molecule of water to give the five‑membered imide ring of phthalhydrazide. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or aqueous ethanol, excess hydrazine (often as 80 % aqueous solution), removal of water by azeotropic distillation or by using a Dean–Stark trap. Common solvents/catalysts: ethanol, sometimes a catalytic amount of acetic acid to promote ring closure; no metal catalyst required.

Acid‑base (salt metathesis) reaction; protonation of sodium hydrogen phosphite with aqueous HCl produces phosphorous acid and NaCl; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature using dilute HCl.

Acyl transfer (esterification) of cyclopropanol with acetic anhydride: the alcohol attacks one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming cyclopropyl acetate and releasing acetic acid as the by‑product. Usually performed at room temperature or with gentle heating, using a base catalyst (pyridine, DMAP) in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or without solvent.

Cannizzaro-type base‑induced disproportionation of 4‑fluorobenzaldehyde with sodium hydroxide, yielding 4‑fluorobenzyl alcohol and 4‑fluorobenzoic acid. One molecule of aldehyde is reduced to the primary alcohol while another is oxidized to the carboxylic acid. Reaction is performed in aqueous NaOH (often 10–20 % w/v) at 0 °C to reflux, sometimes with ethanol as co‑solvent; no external catalyst is needed.
