Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous sodium hydroxide added to nickel(II) cyanide at room temperature; forms insoluble nickel(II) hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium cyanide; used to separate nickel from cyanide; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration (electrophilic addition) of 1‑methylcyclopentene to give 1‑methylcyclopentanol. Purpose: convert the alkene into a secondary alcohol via Markovnikov addition of water. Key transformation: protonation of the double bond, nucleophilic attack of water on the more substituted carbon, and deprotonation to afford the alcohol. Typical conditions: dilute aqueous H₂SO₄ or HCl, reflux in a mixed organic solvent (e.g., THF, acetone) or oxymercuration‑demercuration (Hg(OAc)₂, NaBH₄) if acid‑sensitive. Solvent: water with a co‑solvent as needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduces the aromatic pyridine ring of 4‑benzylpyridine to the saturated piperidine ring, preserving the benzyl substituent. Typically performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over 10 % Pd/C in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at 25–50 °C. Used to increase basicity and flexibility of heterocycles for medicinal chemistry.

Halogen displacement (redox) reaction; iodine is reduced to iodide while bromide is oxidized to elemental bromine. Usually carried out at ambient temperature in an inert solvent (e.g., acetonile) without a catalyst. Serves to generate Br₂ in situ from inexpensive HBr and I₂.

Halogenation (chlorination) of zirconium nitride; converts Zr–N bonds to Zr–Cl bonds while releasing N2. Used to produce zirconium tetrachloride from the nitride. Typically carried out in the gas phase at 400–600 °C under an inert atmosphere (e.g., Ar) with a continuous flow of dry Cl2; no solvent required.

Salt metathesis (halide exchange); ammonium fluoride exchanges its fluoride ions with chloride ions of TiCl₃ to give titanium(III) fluoride and ammonium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution, often at 0–25 °C to minimize hydrolysis of Ti³⁺. No catalyst required; the reaction proceeds by simple ion exchange.

Direct fluorination redox reaction; elemental manganese is oxidized by fluorine gas to give manganese(III) fluoride (MnF₃); requires anhydrous conditions, excess F₂ gas, and elevated temperatures (≈200–300 °C) in a fluoropolymer or nickel reactor; no solvent or catalyst, but rigorous moisture exclusion is essential.

Dimerization equilibrium; nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) reversibly combines to form dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄). Favored at lower temperatures (e.g., < 25 °C) and shifts toward monomeric NO₂ on heating. No reagents or catalysts are needed; the process is governed by temperature and pressure.

Selective reduction; ketone reduction to secondary alcohol using sodium borohydride. 1‑Hydroxybutan‑2‑one (hydroxyacetone) is reduced at the carbonyl carbon to give 1,2‑butanediol while the pre‑existing hydroxyl group remains unchanged. Typical conditions: NaBH4 (1–2 eq) in methanol or ethanol, 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; reaction quenched with water and extracted.

Acid-base neutralization reaction; hydrofluoric acid reacts with gold sesquioxide to produce gold(III) fluoride and water. Key transformation: Au₂O₃ acting as a base reacting with HF as an acid. Reaction conditions: requires heating; HF acts as both reactant and solvent.

Buchwald‑Hartwig C‑N cross‑coupling of an aryl iodide with piperazine; Pd(OAc)2/dppf and NaOtBu replace the iodine with a nitrogen of piperazine to give 1‑(4‑methoxyphenyl)piperazine, generating HI as a by‑product; run under inert atmosphere in toluene or dioxane at 80‑110 °C.

Catalytic hydrogenation of cyclohex-3-en-1-ol; type: hydrogenation (reduction of C=C bond); purpose: saturate the cyclic alkene to afford the saturated secondary alcohol; key transformation: addition of H2 across the double bond converts cyclohex-3-en-1-ol to cyclohexanol while leaving the hydroxyl intact; typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, 10 % Pd/C (10–20 wt % relative to substrate), solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate, temperature ranging from ambient to reflux; reaction carried out under nitrogen or argon until uptake is complete.

Catalytic hydrogenation reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Purpose is to convert 2‑ethylbutanoic acid into 2‑ethylbutanol. Key transformation: –COOH → –CH2OH. Typical conditions: high‑pressure H2 (50–100 atm) with 5–10 % Pd/C catalyst in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at 50–80 °C. Reaction may require a small amount of acid or base to activate the acid; reaction time 12–24 h.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; zinc nitrate exchanges its nitrate anions with chloride ions from lithium chloride, producing zinc chloride and lithium nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution, typically with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution. No catalyst is required.

Dehydrogenative dehydration (cracking) of n‑butanol to 1,3‑butadiene; removes two molecules of hydrogen and one molecule of water from the alcohol, yielding conjugated diene. Requires high temperature (500–700 °C) over solid metal‑oxide catalysts such as Cu‑Zn‑Al mixed oxides or alumina‑supported catalysts. Used industrially to produce butadiene from renewable alcohol feedstocks.

Oxidation (Pinnick oxidation) of 1‑naphthaldehyde to 1‑naphthoic acid; sodium chlorite supplies the oxo‑transfer while hydrogen peroxide scavenges chlorine dioxide; usually carried out in an aqueous buffer (pH 3–5) with a co‑solvent such as t‑butanol at 0–25 °C; water and NaCl are formed as by‑products.

Metathesis/precipitation double‑replacement of yttrium(III) acetate with oxalic acid; acetate ligands are exchanged for oxalate, giving insoluble yttrium oxalate and liberating acetic acid and water; performed in aqueous solution, often heated or refluxed; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base (salt formation) reaction; holmium oxide reacts with aqueous sulfuric acid to give holmium sulfate solution and water; typically carried out by adding Ho2O3 to dilute (≈1 M) H2SO4 and heating gently (60‑80 °C) with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed nucleophilic substitution of 2‑pentyl acetate with HBr; the acetate group is displaced to afford 2‑bromopentane and acetic acid; typically done by refluxing the ester in concentrated HBr (aqueous or gas) possibly using a solvent such as ether; no metal catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of phosphite to phosphate using hydrogen peroxide; potassium dihydrogen phosphite is converted to potassium dihydrogen phosphate with water as the only by‑product. Performed in aqueous medium, often at room temperature to mild heating; may be acid‑catalyzed (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄) but often proceeds without added catalyst.

Base‑promoted Williamson etherification of triethylene glycol with epichlorohydrin to produce triethylene glycol diglycidyl ether; potassium carbonate abstracts HCl, forming KCl, CO₂ and water; reaction is run under reflux in an aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or THF) at 50–80 °C; the epoxy diglycidyl ether is obtained as the product.

Carbotherstate) reduction of zirconium nitride; expelled as N2 and carbon inserts into the metal lattice to form zirconium carbide. Employed for synthesis of ZrC for high‑temperature ceramics. Conducted at very high temperatures (≈1500–1800 °C) in a sealed tube or furnace under inert gas (Ar or N2); no solvent or catalyst.

Copper(II) chloride‑catalyzed aerobic oxidative condensation of benzaldehyde with pyrrole to give a dipyrrin (bis‑pyrrole ligand); O₂ serves as the terminal oxidant, reducing Cu(II) to Cu(I); commonly carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at ambient to moderate temperature; water and CuCl are generated as by‑products.

Type: Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Purpose: introduce an acetyl group para to the chlorine on chlorobenzene, yielding 1‑(4‑chlorophenyl)ethanone. Key transformation: AlCl₃ complexes with acetyl chloride to generate the acylium ion, which attacks the aromatic ring; HCl is released as a by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1–2 equiv) in dry solvent such as CH₂Cl₂, CS₂ or nitrobenzene, reaction started at 0 °C then warmed to reflux, under nitrogen or argon. AlCl₃ acts as Lewis‑acid catalyst; moisture must be excluded.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of benzanilide; NaOH cleaves the amide bond to yield aniline and sodium benzoate; performed by refluxing the amide in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol or water as co‑solvent) for several hours; no additional catalyst is required.

Acidic cleavage (SN2) of an aryl methyl; HBr protonates the methoxy group of 5‑methoxyresorcinol facilitating nucleophilic attack on the methyl carbon, producing methyl bromide and the demethylated phenol (orcinol); typically performed with concentrated aqueous HBr, heated under reflux, no additional catalyst.

Ullmann‑type hydroxylation (nucleophilic aromatic substitution) of iodobenzene with aqueous sodium hydroxide; OH⁻ displaces I⁻ to give phenol while NaI remains in solution; usually carried out at 180‑200 °C in a sealed pressure tube, often in the presence of a copper(I) or copper(II) salt (e.g., Cu₂O) as catalyst and water or ethanol as solvent.

LiAlH₄ reduction of an ester to primary alcohols. LiAlH₄ donates hydride to the carbonyl of methyl 2‑chloroacetate, producing 2‑chloroethanol from the acyl fragment and methanol from the alkoxy fragment. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon atmosphere; work‑up with aqueous NaKHCO₃.

Ozonolysis of 1-methylnaphthalene leading to oxidative cleavage of the methyl group, forming 1-naphthoic acid and formaldehyde. Reaction conditions involve ozone gas in an inert solvent (e.g., methanol, dichloromethane) followed by reductive or oxidative workup. Purpose: oxidizes an aromatic methyl group to a carboxylic acid.

Redox displacement (metal‑metal exchange) where elemental gallium reduces mercury(II) chloride to elemental mercury and itself is oxidized to gallium(III) chloride; a solid‑state reaction performed by mixing fine powders of Ga and HgCl₂ and heating (≈200‑300 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction of hydrogen telluride with silver perchlorate; H₂Te acts as a weak acid, exchanging protons for Ag⁺ to form soluble perchloric acid and insoluble silver telluride (Ag₂Te) precipitate; carried out in aqueous solution at low temperature (0‑25 °C) under inert atmosphere to contain the toxic H₂Te gas; no catalyst needed.

Type: thermal dehydration of a hydrate. Purpose: obtain anhydrous lanthanum(III) chloride from its hexahydrate. Key transformation: loss of six water molecules coordinated to LaCl3·6H2O, yielding dry LaCl3 solid. Typical conditions: gentle heating (≈100‑200 °C) under dry inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) to avoid hydrolysis. No solvent or catalyst required.

Direct combination (high‑temperature solid‑state synthesis) of titanium metal with red phosphorus to afford titanium phosphide (TiP); the elements are mixed and heated in a furnace at ≥1500 °C under argon or vacuum to prevent oxidation; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Aqueous precipitation of a lanthanide hydroxide; ammonium hydroxide provides OH⁻ that reacts with Gd³⁺ from gadolinium(III) chloride to form insoluble gadolinium(III) hydroxide while NH₄Cl stays dissolved; typically performed at ambient temperature with stirring in water, adjusting pH to ~9‑10, followed by filtration and washing of the precipitate.

Acid anhydride hydrolysis; converts trimellitic anhydride to the corresponding tri‑carboxylic acid by ring‑opening with water; typically performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating or reflux; acid or base catalyst can be used to accelerate the reaction; water is both reagent and solvent.

Generation of a lithium alkoxy‑borohydride (LiEt₃BH, “Superhydride”) by metal‑hydride formation. Lithium metal reduces triethylborane in the presence of hydrogen gas, producing the lithium triethylborohydride hydride donor. Conducted in dry ethereal solvents (THF or diethyl ether) under an inert atmosphere, often at 0 °C to room temperature, with hydrogen supplied at low pressure. The reagent is used as a strong, non‑nucleophilic reducing agent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; potassium sulfate reacts with calcium chloride in aqueous solution to exchange cations, forming soluble KCl and sparingly soluble calcium sulfate which precipitates; conducted at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the reaction medium, no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a primary isocyanide to a isocyanate using hydrogen peroxide; converts the C≡N−R group into N=C=O−R with loss of water; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) or aqueous medium at 0–25 °C; peroxide acts as the oxidant without additional catalyst.

Reductive cleavage of sulfur dichloride; lithium metal reduces SCl₂, yielding dilithium sulfide (Li₂S) and chlorine gas; performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (e.g., Ar) in a dry ether or hydrocarbon solvent at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) to control vigorous gas evolution; lithium is the reduct, no catalyst.

DCC‑mediated amidation to form a Weinreb amide; acetic acid is activated by dicyclhexylcarbodiimide (DCC) and coupled with N,O‑dimethylhydroxylamine, giving N‑methoxy‑N‑methylacetamide and dicyclohexylurea as by‑product; performed in dry aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature; often a catalytic amount of DMAP is added to accelerate acyl transfer; no metal catalyst.

N‑alkylation (double SN2) of a primary amine. Tryptamine’s side‑chain amine undergoes two successive allylations with allyl bromide in the presence of cesium carbonate, a strong, non‑nucleophilic base. The reaction is usually run in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or acetonitrile at room temperature (or slightly elevated), often with catalytic 18‑crown‑6 to enhance Cs⁺ solubility. The product is N,N‑diallyltryptamine; bromide is converted to cesium bromide.

Reaction type: Williamson ether synthesis (SN2) between an alkoxide and an alkyl halide. Purpose: formation of a mixed ether, hexyl methyl ether. Key transformation: NaO‑(CH₂)₅CH₃ (sodium hexan‑1‑olate) attacks methyl iodide, displacing I⁻ to give CH₃O‑(CH₂)₅CH₃ and NaI. Typical conditions: dry, aprotic solvent (THF, DME) at 0 °C to reflux, inert atmosphere to avoid moisture. No additional catalyst is required; the sodium alkoxide itself serves as the nucleophile.

Carboxylation of an aryl lithium reagent; converts 4‑(trifluoromethyl)phenyllithium to the corresponding benzoic acid after acidic work‑up. The organolithium adds to CO₂, forming a lithium carboxylate which on protonation yields 4‑(trifluoromethyl)benic acid. Typical protocol: generate the aryl lithium in dry THF at –78 °C, bubble CO₂ gas into the solution, stir while warming to 0 °C, then quench with dilute aqueous acid (e.g., NH₄Cl or HCl) and extract.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of an alkyl methanesulfonate; hydroxide attacks the ethyl carbon of ethyl methanesulfonate, cleaving the S–O bond to give methanesulfonate anion (as potassium salt) and ethanol. Conducted in aqueous KOH, usually warmed to reflux (≈80 °C) for several hours; the reaction mixture then cooled and the products are isolated by extraction or evaporation.

High‑temperature solid‑state redox (reduction of a metal nitrate by carbon). Carbon acts as a reducing agent, converting Cu(II) nitrate to metallic copper while oxidizing to CO₂; nitrate anion decomposes to nitrogen dioxide. Performed in a quartz or alumina tube furnace at 300–500 °C under flowing inert gas to avoid oxidation of the copper product; stoichiometric carbon (e.g., charcoal) is mixed intimately with the nitrate powder before heating.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of a sparingly soluble metal azide. Sodium azide exchanges its anion with silver bromide, forming insoluble silver azide as a yellow precipitate and soluble sodium bromide. Carried out in cold aqueous solution (0–5 °C) to minimize decomposition of AgN₃; the suspension is filtered, and the AgN₃ is washed with cold water. Protective measures are required because silver azide is shock‑sensitive.

Acid‑base fluorination (salt metathesis) producing cobalt(II) fluoride and nitric acid. Hydrogen fluoride protonates nitrate, releasing HNO₃, while fluoride anion coordinates cobalt(II) to give insoluble CoF₂. Typically performed in anhydrous HF or aqueous HF solution at 0–25 °C; the CoF₂ precipitates and is filtered, and the supernatant contains nitric acid. The reaction must be handled in HF‑compatible equipment and with proper safety precautions.

Sulfonylation (mesylation) of a diol; purpose is to convert the two hydroxyl groups of ethylene glycol into mesylate leaving groups. The OH groups are replaced by –O‑SO2‑CH3, generating ethylene glycol dimethanesulfonate and HCl (neutralized by pyridine). Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or directly in pyridine, using pyridine as base; no additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of an acid chloride; purpose is to obtain the corresponding carboxylic acid. Hexanoyl chloride reacts with water, the acyl‑Cl bond is cleaved and a proton is transferred to give hexanoic acid and HCl. Usually carried out at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often by adding the acid chloride to an ice‑cold aqueous solution or by shaking the chloride in a dry organic solvent (e.g., ether) followed by aqueous work‑up. No catalyst is needed; a base (NaOH, pyridine) may be added to trap HCl.

Oxidative chlorination of a metal halide; purpose is to raise the oxidation state of rhenium from +4 in ReCl4 to +5 in ReCl5. Chlorine gas oxidizes ReCl4, yielding ReCl5 and no organic by‑products. Conducted in the solid state or in a dry non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) at elevated temperature (≈150–200 °C) under an inert atmosphere. No catalyst is required.

Selective reduction of an aldehyde; purpose is to convert the 5‑formyl group of uracil to a primary alcohol, giving 5‑(hydroxymethyl)uracil. Sodium borohydride delivers a hydride to the carbonyl carbon, forming the alcohol and generating sodium borate. Typically performed in methanol, ethanol, or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is rapid and does not need a catalyst.

Conversion of a dicarboxylic acid to its di‑acid chloride using thionyl chloride; purpose is to prepare sebacoyl chloride for polymer‑building (e.g., nylon synthesis). Sebacic acid reacts with excess SOCl2, each –COOH becomes –COCl, releasing HCl and SO2 gases. Reaction is carried out under reflux (≈80–100 °C) in a dry solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to activate SOCl2. No additional catalyst beyond the reagent is required.

Alkylation (methylation) of N,N‑dimethylurea with dimethyl sulfate; purpose is to synthesize tetramethylurea. Each dimethyl sulfate transfers a methyl group to a nitrogen atom via an SN2 mechanism, producing tetramethylurea and two equivalents of methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product. Conducted in an aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C), typically in the presence of a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to neutralize the acidic by‑product. Dimethyl sulfate acts as both methyl donor and electrophile; no separate catalyst is needed.

Decarboxylation of phenazine-1-carboxylic acid to phenazine; thermal elimination of CO₂ often achieved by heating the acid neat or in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., quinoline) at 150‑200 °C, no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of cyclopentene to cyclentanol; electrophilic addition of water (Markovnikov) carried out in dilute H₂SO₄ aqueous solution at 0–50 °C or under reflux, sulfuric acid serves as catalyst.

Neutralization of hydrogen sulfide by rubidium hydroxide; the strong base deprotonates H₂S, giving rubidium sulfide and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; no special catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precipitation between lithium hydroxide and holmium nitrate forming soluble lithium nitrate and insoluble holmium(III) hydroxide; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, the hydroxide precipitates and is isolated by filtration.

Strong hydride reduction of an aldehyde with lithium aluminium hydride. Benzaldehyde is dissolved in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, and LiAlH₄ is added at 0 °C, then the mixture is refluxed. After reaction, the mixture is carefully quenched with water, then dilute acid, furnishing benzyl alcohol in high yield.

Acid–base (fluorination) reaction of yttrium oxide with hydrofluoric acid; purpose is to form yttrium fluoride, a soluble fluoride salt; key transformation: Y₂O₃ + 6 HF → 2 YF₃ + 3 H₂O; carried out in aqueous HF (or gaseous HF) at 0–50 °C with stirring; reaction proceeds readily without additional catalyst; excess HF may be used to ensure complete conversion.

Meyer–Schuster rearrangement of propargyl alcohol to acrolein with loss of water; heated concentrated H₂SO₄ (140‑180 °C) acts as both acid catalyst and solvent, effecting an acid‑catalyzed 1,2‑shift and dehydration.

Carboxylation of Grignard reagent: the 4‑methylphenylmagnesium bromide reacts with CO₂ (dry ice or CO₂ gas) in anhydrous ether at 0 °C to rt, then acidic work‑up., dilute HCl) furnishes 4‑methylbenzoic acid; the key transformation is addition of CO₂ to form a magnesium carboxylate followed by protonation.

SN2 azidation of phenethyl bromide with sodium azide to give phenethyl azide; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 50‑80 °C, sodium bromide is the by‑product, no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidative coupling of cysteamine·HCl using sodium hypochlorite to afford cystamine·2HCl (disulfide); carried out in aqueous buffer (pH≈7‑8 at room temperature, NaOCl acts as oxidant, water and NaCl are formed as side products.

Oxidative degradation of uric acid with concentrated nitric acid to afford alloxan. Nitric acid acts as a strong oxidant, converting the heterocyclic uric acid skeleton into the dioxo‑pyrimidine alloxan, with release of carbon dioxide and water. The reaction is performed at low temperature (0 °C) initially, then gently warmed, typically in the acid medium itself (no additional solvent). Careful temperature control is essential to prevent over‑oxidation or explosive decomposition.

Selective reduction of the aldehyde group in succinic semialdehyde to a primary alcohol using sodium borohydride; yields γ‑hydroxybutyric acid and sodium borate as by‑product; carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, neutral or mildly basic conditions, no additional catalyst needed.

Type: Metal‑acid reaction (deprotonation) producing a metal‑imidazolate and hydrogen gas. Purpose: Prepare sodium imidazolate in a dry, non‑aqueous form. Key transformation: Sodium metal donates an electron to the N‑H of imidazole, forming Na⁺‑imidazolate and H₂. Typical conditions: Sodium metal is added to imidazole dissolved in dry THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen or argon; the mixture is kept at 0 °C to rt to control H₂ evolution. The reaction is highly exothermic and must be performed in a dry, inert environment.

Fischer esterification of propargyl alcohol with acetic acid catalyzed by sulfuric acid; forms propargyl acetate and water; reflux the mixture in a suitable organic solvent (often toluene or xylene) with a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄, removal of water by azeotropic distillation (Dean‑Stark) to drive equilibrium.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 3‑methyl‑1‑hexene to 3‑methylhexane; addition of H₂ across the C=C bond; performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) using a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Ni‑Raney in an inert solvent (e.g., ethanol, methanol) at room temperature to 50 °C.

Hofmann elimination of trimethyl(prop‑2‑enyl)azanium bromide with aqueous potassium hydroxide; yields trimethylamine, propene, water and KBr; heated aqueous KOH (often 2‑4 M) at 80–120 °C, reaction proceeds via deprotonation of the β‑hydrogen and loss of the quaternary ammonium group; no external catalyst required.

Alkaline oxidation of hexanol to hexanoic acid using potassium permanganate; primary alcohol is oxidized to the corresponding carboxylic acid while KMnO₄ is reduced to MnO₂ and KOH forms; carried out in warm aqueous solution (often 60–80 °C) with excess KMnO₄, stirring until the purple color disappears; the solid MnO₂ is filtered off after completion.

Nucleophilic substitution (allylic SN2′) of cinnamyl chloride by methylamine to replace the chloride with a methylamino group, forming cinnamedrine and releasing HCl. Typically carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or ethanol, often with a base (e., triethylamine) to neutralize the generated HCl; reflux conditions are common.

Fischer esterification: condensation of acetic acid with octanol to give octyl acetate and water; acid catalysis (commonly concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) under reflux, often using excess alcohol or a Dean–Stark trap to remove water; solvent may be none (neat) or a non‑reactive solvent like toluene.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (hydrolysis of an acid chloride); converts 4‑fluorobenzoyl chloride to the corresponding carboxylate. Typically performed by treating the acid chloride with aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction mixture is aqueous or a water/THF blend. The base neutralizes the acid chloride, giving sodium 4‑fluorobenzoate, NaCl and water as by‑products.

Thermal or catalytic cracking of n‑decane to produce a mixture of smaller hydrocarbons, here represented as n‑pentane (alkane) and 1‑pentene (alkene); carried out at high temperatures (≈ 700–900 °C) in the presence of steam or a solid acid zeolite catalyst; no solvent is required.

Acid‑base neutralization (double displacement) between hydrobromic acid and barium hydroxide yielding soluble barium bromide and water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Esterification of methacrylic acid with glycidol to afford glycidyl methacrylate and water; usually catalyzed by a Brønsted acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a coupling agent such as DCC; carried out at 60–80 °C in an aprotic solvent like dichloromethane under inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of N‑methylcarbamoyl chloride by ammonia; the amine attacks the carbonyl, displacing chloride to form N‑methylurea and HCl. Performed in aqueous or alcoholic NH3 at 0–25 °C, often with a base (e.g., NaHCO3) to capture HCl.

Hydrolytic cleavage of a chloroformate with decarboxylation. Benzyl chloroformate reacts with water, hydrolyzing the carbonate linkage to give benzyl alcohol, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen chloride. The reaction proceeds readily at ambient temperature; acid or base can be used to neutralize the generated HCl. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, 0‑25 °C, sometimes with a mild base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to trap HCl. Water is the solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 1,3‑dinitrobenzene to meta‑phenylenediamine; hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) with palladium on carbon (Pd/C) as catalyst in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) at 25–80 °C; each nitro group is reduced to an amine, generating water as the only by‑product.

N-alkylation via SN2 nucleophilic substitution; the secondary amine N‑methyltryptamine attacks 1‑bromobutane to give N‑methyl‑N‑butyltryptamine and HBr. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile) at reflux with a mild base (e.g., K2CO3 or triethylamine) to neutralize the generated HBr.

Hydrolytic decomposition of N,N‑dimethylurea; water at elevated temperature cleaves the urea carbonyl, producing ammonia, carbon dioxide, and dimethylamine. Conducted by heating an aqueous solution (often 150‑200 °C) under sealed‑vessel or reflux conditions; no special catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); caesium oxide reacts with phosphoric acid to give caesium phosphate and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating; water serves as solvent and the reaction proceeds spontaneously without a catalyst.

Oxidative fluorination to a hexafluoride. Selenium tetrafluoride reacts with additional fluorine gas to afford selenium hexafluoride (SeF₆). Performed at modest temperatures (0–50 °C) under pressure of F₂, often in a fluorination apparatus made of nickel or Monel; no external catalyst is typically needed, though inert surfaces help prevent side reactions.

Formation of an alkyl nitrite (esterification of an alcohol with nitrous acid); tert‑butanol reacts with in‑situ generated HNO2 (from NaNO2 and HCl) to give tert‑butyl nitrite and water. The reaction is kept cold (0–5 °C) in a biphasic water/tert‑butanol mixture; acid (HCl) is essential for nitrous acid generation.

Oxidative cleavage of 6‑gingerol to zingerone; the side‑chain double bond is oxidatively shortened, converting the phenolic alkenyl side chain to a β‑keto‑aryl compound (zingerone). Commonly achieved by refluxing gingerol in aqueous base or with oxidants such as MnO2, Pb(OAc)4, or NaOCl/H2O2 at 80–120 °C; the reaction removes three carbon atoms from the side chain.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; sodium sulfide reacts with thallium(I) bromide to exchange anions, precipitating thallium(I) sulfide (Tl2S) and forming soluble sodium bromide. Performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the insoluble Tl2S is filtered off.

Acylation of an aromatic amine (acetylation) – nucleophilic attack of the aniline nitrogen on acetic anhydride forming an N‑acetyl amide and releasing acetic acid; used to protect or modify the amine functionality. Typical conditions: neat or in anhydrous pyridine or dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, often with catalytic DMAP; reaction is exothermic and the acid by‑product is scavenged by the base.

Gas‑phase chlorination (oxidation) of iron silicide; chlorine gas reacts with FeSi at elevated temperature (≈400‑600 °C) to produce iron(II) chloride (FeCl2) and silicon tetrachloride (SiCl4) vapor; conducted in a flow reactor, often with inert carrier gas; no catalyst.

Thermal decomposition of urea hydrochloride; upon heating, the salt eliminates isocyanic acid (HNCO) and generates ammonium chloride (NH4Cl). Conducted by heating the solid (≈200 °C) under an inert atmosphere or reduced pressure to remove volatile HNCO; no additional reagents are required.

Oxidation (TEMPO‑ated). Converts primary alcohol to aldehyde without over‑oxidation. 1‑Propanol is oxidized to propanal using catalytic TEMPO (≈5–10 mol %) with sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) as the terminal oxidant, often in a biphasic mixture of dichloromethane or acetonitrile and aqueous NaOCl, buffered to pH 8–9 (NaHCO₃). Reaction proceeds at 0 °C to rt, producing water as the only stoichiometric by‑product.

Acid-base reaction with carbonation. Nickel(II) hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide to form nickel(II) carbonate and water. Carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, which protonates the hydroxide. Typically conducted in aqueous solution under elevated CO2 pressure or ambient conditions.

Type: silyl ester exchange (formation of a silyl acetate). Purpose: generate trimethylsilyl acetate from acetic acid. Key transformation: transfer of the TMS group from the trifluoroacetate to the acetate anion, producing trimethylsilyl acetate and trifluoroacetic acid. Typical conditions: acetic acid (1 equiv) mixed with TMS‑TFA (1.1 equiv) in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to rt, stirring 30 min–1 h. No catalyst required; the reaction is driven by the volatility and acidity of the released TFA.

Nucleophilic substitution of an aryl diazonium (Sandmeyer‑type reduction). Phenyl diazonium tetrafluoroborate reacts with sulfide ion (Na₂S) to give thiophenol and nitrogen gas, with NaBF₄ regenerated. Performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic solvent at 0 °C to 25 °C under inert atmosphere; Na₂S provides S²⁻ nucleophile, and the diazonium is usually prepared in situ from aniline, NaNO₂ and HBF₄. No additional catalyst required.

Acid‑chloride formation using triphosgene. Propane‑1,3‑dicarboxylic acid (malonic acid) is converted to its di‑acid chloride (propanedioyl dichloride) by reaction with triphosgene in the presence of pyridine, which scavenges the liberated HCl. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to rt. By‑products are carbon dioxide and HCl (captured by pyridine), giving a clean conversion to the reactive acid chloride for subsequent coupling reactions.

Copper‑catalyzed N‑alkylation (Ullmann‑type coupling). Ethylenediamine is bis‑benzylated by benzyl chloride in the presence of CuI (5–10 mol %) and potassium carbonate as base, producing benzathine (N,N′‑dibenzyl‑1,2‑ethanediamine). The reaction is carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 80–120 °C. Potassium carbonate decomposes to KCl, CO₂ and H₂O, which are the inorganic by‑products.

Esterification with diazomethane. Butyryl chloride reacts with diazomethane to give methyl butyrate and nitrogen gas. The highly nucleophilic diazomethane inserts a methyl group onto the acyl chloride, forming the methyl ester. Performed at 0 °C to rt in dry ether, THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen; no catalyst is required, and the only stoichiometric waste is N₂.

Oxidative conversion of barbituric acid to violuric acid. Barbituric acid is oxidized by potassium permanganate in concentrated sulfuric acid, yielding violuric acid, water, and precipitated MnO₂. The reaction is carried out under reflux (≈80–100 °C) in aqueous H₂SO₄, with KMnO₄ added portionwise to control oxidation. MnO₂ precipitates as a brown solid, and violuric acid is isolated as a red‑colored salt, often used as a redox indicator.

Reduction of a phosphonic acid to a primary phosphine; LiAlH4 supplies hydride to convert the P=O group of methylphosphonic acid into a P‑H bond, releasing water. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF, typically at reflux under nitrogen or argon atmosphere; LiAlH4 is the catalyst/reducing agent.

Palladium‑catalyzed aryl amination (Buchwald‑Hartwig type) of 2‑iodoanisole with ammonia to give 2‑methoxyaniline and HI. Uses a Pd0 source (e.g., Pd2(dba)3) with a bulky phosphine ligand (BINAP, Xantphos) and a base, in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or dioxane, heated to 80–120 °C under inert gas. Purpose is formation of a primary aryl amine via C–N bond formation.

Formation of a Grignard reagent (oxidative insertion of Mg into C–I bond); purpose: generate an organomagnesium halide for carbon‑carbon bond‑forming reactions; key transformation: Mg inserts into the C–I bond to give isopropylmagnesium iodide; typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), dry Mg turnings, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), gentle reflux; iodine seed sometimes used to initiate the reaction.

Halide metathesis (halogen exchange) converting phosphorus pentachloride and sodium fluoride to phosphorus pentafluoride and sodium chloride. Typically performed anhydrously, in a sealed tube or gas‑flow apparatus at elevated temperature (100–150 °C) because PF5 is volatile; no catalyst required, solid NaF and PCl5 react directly.

Eschweiler‑Clarke reductive methylation of 6‑methoxytryptamine using excess formaldehyde and formic acid to afford 6‑methoxy‑N,N‑dimethyl‑1H‑indole‑3‑ethanamine (6‑MeO‑DMT). Reaction proceeds via formation of iminium intermediates reduced by formic acid. Conducted in methanol or aqueous methanol, refluxed for several hours; no metal catalyst needed.

Acid‑promoted redox disproportionation of bromide by bromate in concentrated sulfuric acid, generating elemental bromine, water, and potassium sulfate. Carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; the strong acid provides the medium for the redox couple BrO3⁻ + 5 Br⁻ + 6 H⁺ → 3 Br2 + 3 H2O. No additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of α‑chloroacetophenone with aqueous ammonium hydroxide to give phenacylamine, ammonium chloride and water. Reaction performed in water or a water/ethanol mixture, typically at reflux or mild heating, with excess NH4OH to drive substitution. No metal catalyst is needed.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling of 2‑chloroselenophene with phenylboronic acid; purpose is to forge a C(sp²)‑C(sp²) bond delivering 2‑phenylselenophene. Key transformation: oxidative addition of Pd(0) into the C–Cl bond, transmetalation with the phenylboronate, and reductive elimination to afford the coupled product; K₂CO₃ serves as base, generating potassium phenylboronate as the leaving species. Typical conditions: Pd(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %), often with a phosphine ligand (e.g., PPh₃), in a mixed solvent such as toluene/water or dioxane/water, heated to 80–100 °C under nitrogen or argon; K₂CO₃ (2–3 equiv) as base.

Nucleophilic epoxide ring‑opening by cyanide; KCN provides CN⁻ which opens ethylene oxide to form 2‑cyanoethanol. Conducted in polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO) or aqueous/ethanol mixture, often at ambient temperature; sometimes a catalytic amount of crown ether (e.g., 18‑crown‑6) is added.

Acid–base neutralization; metal oxide reacts with a strong acid to form the corresponding metal chloride salt and water; typically performed in aqueous solution using dilute hydrochloric acid, often at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no special catalyst required.

Radical O‑alkyl (radical ether synthesis); phenol is converted to tert‑butyl phenyl ether while the tert‑butyl peroxide fragments to give tert‑butanol. Typically initiated by heat or a metal catalyst (e.g., Cu(I) salts) in an inert solvent such as benzene or toluene; the reaction proceeds via homolytic cleavage of the O–O bond and radical attack on phenolic oxygen.

Hydride reduction of an aldehyde; lithium aluminium hydride supplies a nucleophilic hydride that reduces 4‑methylphenylacetaldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol, 1‑(4‑methylphenyl)ethanol. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst required.

Strong‑base induced dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination); potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from tert‑butyl bromide, forming the alkene 2‑methylpropene and potassium bromide as the salt. Reaction is performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF, often at 0–25 °C, under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Metal‑catalyzed oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone; hydrogen peroxide, activated by tungstic acid (H₂WO₄), oxidizes 5‑methyl‑2‑hexanol to 5‑methyl‑2‑hexanone with water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions involve aqueous acidic medium, reflux temperature, catalytic amount of tungstic acid (5–10 mol %), and may be carried out in water or a water‑miscible organic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile).

Acid‑base salt formation; addition of aqueous hydrochloric acid to isoguvacine protonates the basic nitrogen(s), yielding isoguvacine hydrochloride as a crystalline salt. Performed in aqueous HCl (often 1 M), often at ambient temperature, followed by isolation of the solid salt by filtration or evaporation.

Redox reaction of a metal with a strong acid; cadmium metal reacts with hydrobromic acid to generate hydrogen gas and cadmium bromide (CdBr₂). Conducted in aqueous HBr solution, usually warmed to moderate temperature to accelerate gas evolution; no solvent beyond the aqueous acid is required.

Esterification via mixed anhydride formation; used to synthesize menthyl anthranilate (a fragrance ester). The carboxylic acid of 2‑aminobenzoic acid is activated by ethyl chloroformate to give a mixed anhydride, which is attacked by menthol in the presence of triethylamine that scavenges the generated HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, dichloromethane or THF as solvent, slow addition of ethyl chloroformate, then stirring at room temperature. No additional catalyst is required.

LiAlH₄ reduction of an aromatic ester; ethyl benzoate is reduced to benzyl alcohol (C₆H₅CH₂OH) and ethanol as the by‑product. Conducted in dry ether or THF, 0 °C to reflux, using 2–3 eq LiAlH₄ under nitrogen. Reaction quenched with aqueous work‑up (e.g., NaK tartrate) to afford the two alcohols.

Oxidative cleavage of a ketone; converts 3‑heptanone into the shorter carboxylic acids butyric acid and propionic acid. Potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium oxidatively breaks the C–C bonds α to the carbonyl. Conditions: aqueous KOH or NaOH, excess KMnO₄, reflux (80–100 °C) until the purple permanganate is exhausted; work‑up with acidification. Solvent is water or water/acetone mixture; no catalyst beyond the permanganate.

Acyl chloride esterification of salicylic acid to give acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin). The phenolic OH reacts with acetyl chloride, forming an acetyl ester and releasing HCl. Performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., pyridine or dichloromethane) with pyridine or triethylamine as base to trap HCl, usually at 0 °C to room temperature. Provides a rapid, high‑yield synthesis of aspirin.

Dehydrative condensation to form an acid anhydride; 2 equiv of acetic acid lose water to give acetic anhydride. In practice the reaction is driven a strong dehydrating agent (e.g., P₂O₅, acetic anhydride itself, or catalytic acetyl chloride) or by azeotropic removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap with toluene). Conditions: reflux of acetic acid with P₂O₅ (or other dehydrant) under nitrogen, removal of water as it forms. No solvent is required when using solidant; otherwise inert organic solvent such as toluene is used.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of gallium nitride; 4 GaN react with 3 O₂ to give 2 Ga₂O₃ and N₂ gas. This solid‑state reaction is performed in air or oxygen at temperatures ≥800 °C, often in a furnace or tube reactor. No solvent; the process is driven by heat, and the products are solid gallium oxide and molecular nitrogen.

Acid‑base proton transfer between water and sodium cyanide, producing hydrogen cyanide and sodium hydroxide. Simple aqueous reaction; no special catalyst or solvent required beyond water as the medium.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution of propargyl alcohol with HCl, converting the primary alcohol to 3‑chloroprop‑1‑yne while liberating water. Conducted by treating the alcohol with concentrated aqueous or gaseous HCl, often at reflux in ether or dichloromethane; sometimes ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent) is added to accelerate the reaction.

Nucleophilic acyl addition of a Grignard reagent (3‑butenylmagnesium bromide) to acetyl chloride, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to the ketone hex‑5‑en‑2‑one after work‑up; a common method for preparing unsaturated ketones. Conducted at low temperature (0 °C to –20 °C) in anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere, followed by aqueous quench.

Gas‑phase synthesis of indium arsenide from indium trichloride and arsine (AsH3); hydrogen chloride is liberated as a by‑product. Reaction is a typical precusor‑reaction for MOVPE/CVD growth of InAs thin films. Conducted at 500–700 °C, low pressure (0.1–10 Torr), with H2 or N2 as carrier gas; the HCl by‑product is removed by gas‑phase scrubbing.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a dinitrile (2‑methylpentanedinitrile) using H₂ and 10 % Pd/C to reduce both nitrile groups to primary amines, yielding 2‑methylpentanediamine; a standard route to diamines. Performed in ethanol or methanol under 1–5 atm H₂ pressure at room temperature to reflux, with the palladium catalyst filtered off after reaction.

Reductive amination of 3,4‑methylenedioxyphenyl‑2‑propanone with dimethylamine in the presence of sodium cyanoborohydride, forming an iminium ion that is reduced to N,N‑dimethyl‑3,4‑methylenedioxyamphetamine; used for amphetamine synthesis. Carried out in methanol or dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often with a weak acid (AcOH) to promote imine formation, and NaBH₃CN as the mild reductant.

Aerobic copper‑mediated oxidation of cyclopentanol to cyclopentanone using Cu(OAc)₂ as catalyst under an O₂ atmosphere; converts a secondary alcohol to the corresponding ketone. Typical conditions employ acetonitrile or DMSO as solvent, 1–5 mol % Cu(OAc)₂, O₂ balloon or gentle pressure, and heating to 50–80 °C, sometimes with a co‑oxidant such as TEMPO.

Base‑mediated neutralization (recovery of free amine); sodium hydroxide deprotonates cyclohexylammonium nitrate, regenerating cyclohexylamine, sodium nitrate and water. Performed in aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C; the amine can be extracted with an organic solvent after neutralization.

Finkelstein halogen exchange (SN2) of benzyl chloride with sodium iodide in acetone, producing benzyl iodide and precipitating sodium chloride; a common method to generate more reactive alkyl iodides. Reaction is refluxed in dry acetone (polar aprotic solvent) where NaI is soluble and NaCl precipitates, driving the equilibrium to completion.

Oxidative cleavage; acetone is oxidized by sodium dichromate in hot concentrated sulfuric acid, converting one methyl group to acetic acid and the other to carbon dioxide while dichromate is reduced to Cr³⁺; carried out in aqueous H₂SO₄ under, no additional catalyst.
Acid‑base protonation; sodium glyoxylate reacts with hydrochloric acid to release glyoxylic acid and form sodium chloride; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation; aqueous sodium silicate exchanges ions with barium chloride to give soluble sodium chloride and insoluble barium silicate precipitate; run water at room temperature with stirring, product isolated by filtration.

Acid–base reaction with gas evolution; calcium carbonate reacts with formic acid, neutralizing the acid and releasing carbon dioxide gas while forming calcium formate and water. Conducted in water, often with gentle heating to dissolve the carbonate and to promote CO₂ release; no catalyst needed.

Preparation of hypervalent iodine(III) reagent; iodosylbenzene reacts with acetic anhydride (in the presence of acetic acid) to afford iodobenzene diacetate (PhI(OAc)₂) with formation of water; typically conducted in glacial acetic acid/anhydride mixture, reflux or gentle heating, under inert atmosphere, no external catalyst.

Redox dissolution of lead; hot concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes metallic lead to lead(II) sulfate while reducing sulfate to sulfur dioxide, producing water; performed with lead metal in boiling conc. H₂SO₄ (≈340 °C) in a suitable vessel, no added reagents.

Acid‑base salt formation; oxalic acid reacts with aluminium oxide to give aluminium oxalate and water; carried out in aqueous oxalic acid solution, often with gentle heating to aid dissolution, no catalyst needed.

Catalytic transfer hydrogenation; reduces the aromatic nitro group to an aniline while oxidizing isopropanol to acetone. Key transformation: –NO2 → –NH2 and secondary alcohol → ketone. Typical conditions: Pd/C (5‑10 wt %) in refluxing isopropanol, inert atmosphere, ambient pressure. Solvent acts as hydrogen donor; no additional hydrogen gas needed.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution); installs a benzoyl carbonyl onto benzene to form benzophenone. Key transformation: benzene + benzoyl chloride → benzophenone + HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1‑2 equiv) as Lewis acid catalyst, low temperature (0 °C) then gradual warming, solvent such as carbon disulfide, CH₂Cl₂ or nitrobenzene, under nitrogen.

Thermal decomposition of dazomet; employed to generate fumigant gases for soil sterilization. Upon heating, the heterocyclic dazomet ring fragments, releasing methyl isothiocyanate, dimethylamine, and carbon disulfide. Reaction is carried out by heating the solid (70–100 °C) in a sealed vessel, often under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Ester aminolysis (amide formation); ammonia attacks butyl propionate, displacing n‑butanol and yielding propanamide. Key transformation: R‑COO‑R′ + NH₃ → R‑CONH₂ + R′‑OH. Typical conditions: excess aqueous or gaseous NH₃, reflux (100‑150 °C) in a sealed tube or autoclave; sometimes a catalytic amount of base is used to accelerate the reaction.

Oxidation of leucomalachite green to malachite green; hydrogen peroxide in acidic medium generates per‑sulfuric acid which oxidizes the leuco‑amine to the colored cationic dye. Key transformation: leucomalachite green → malachite green (loss of two electrons, formation of iminium). Typical conditions: aqueous H₂O₂ (30 %) with conc. H₂SO₄, temperature 0‑5 °C initially then allowed to warm to room temperature; water is the reaction medium.

Aromatic nitration (electrophilic substitution); mixture of conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ generates the nitronium ion which substitutes a methyl‑substituted benzene to give 2‑nitro‑1,4‑dimethylbenzene. Key transformation: para‑xylene + NO₂⁺ → nitro‑dimethylbenzene + H₂O. Typical conditions: reaction mixture cooled to 0‑30 °C, then stirred 30‑60 min; sulfuric acid acts as solvent and catalyst; work‑up with ice water.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of methyl bromide with ammonia yielding methylamine; ammonium bromide is generated as the by‑product. Reaction proceeds readily with excess NH3 at ambient to reflux temperatures; solvent may be liquid NH3 or an alcohol; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution forming a carbamate; ammonium hydroxide attacks benzyl chloroformate, displacing chloride and yielding benzyl carbamate (Cbz‑NH₂). Key transformation: PhCH₂OCOCl + NH₄OH → PhCH₂OCONH₂ + NH₄Cl + H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous NH₄OH (1‑2 M) at 0‑25 °C, often in a mixed organic/aqueous solvent such as THF or dioxane; the generated HCl is neutralized as NH₄Cl.

Transesterification; exchange of the ethoxy group of ethyl valerate with the isopropoxy group of isopropanol to give isopropyl valerate and ethanol. Used to modify ester alkoxy groups or produce alternative esters. Key step is nucleophilic acyl substitution at the carbonyl carbon. Typically catalyzed by a strong acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOMe) under reflux in anhydrous solvent such as toluene or methanol; removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium.

Base‑catalyzed epoxy formation (alkoxylation) of glycerol with epichlorohydrin to afford triglycidyl glycerol, a trifunctional epoxy monomer. Sodium carbonate deprotonates glycerol, forming glyceroxide that attacks epichlorohydrin; subsequent intramolecular ring closure gives epoxide rings while NaCl and water are released. Conducted under microwave irradiation at 120–150 °C, often solvent‑free or in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF); the microwave provides rapid heating and higher yields.

Prilezhaev epoxidation of styrene with peracetic acid; furnishes styrene oxide and acetic acid; purpose is preparation of the epoxide for further transformations; key transformation is peracid oxygen transfer to the C=C double bond forming the three‑membered epoxide; typically run at 0–25 °C in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, with stoichiometric peracetic acid (often generated in situ from acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide).

Hydrolysis (hydration) of solid silicon dioxide to monomeric silicic acid (Si(OH)4). Represents dissolution of silica in water under aggressive conditions. Usually performed at elevated temperature (≥200 °C) and pressure, often in the presence of a mineral acid (e.g., HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) to accelerate dissolution; the reaction yields a clear aqueous silicic acid solution.

Oxidation‑reduction (oxidation of a primary alcohol). Ethanol is oxidized by silver permanganate, a strong oxidizer, to give acetaldehyde while the oxidant is reduced to solid manganese dioxide and elemental silver; water is formed as a by‑product. Typically carried out in an alcoholic or aqueous medium at room temperature to 50 °C, without additional catalyst; the reaction is driven by stoichiometric amounts of AgMnO₄.

Anion exchange (metathesis) between tetrabutylammonium nitrate and sodium chloride to give tetrabutylammonium chloride and sodium nitrate; all species are generally soluble, so the reaction proceeds in aqueous solution or a biphasic water‑organic system; often used in phase‑transfer catalysis to deliver chloride to the organic phase; carried out at ambient temperature with stirring.

Simple acid–base neutralization. Purpose: prepare the lithium salt of trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (lithium triflate) for use as a non‑coordinating electrolyte. Key transformation: proton transfer from CF₃SO₃H to LiOH, forming LiCF₃SO₃ and water. Typical conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic medium (e.g., water/THF), ambient temperature, 1 equiv LiOH per acid. Stir until gas evolution ceases; isolate the solid by evaporation or crystallisation. No catalyst required.

Direct nitridation of indium metal with ammonia gas to form indium nitride (InN) and hydrogen. Solid‑gas reaction used to prepare the III‑V semiconductor InN. Conducted at high temperature (500–900 °C) under a flow of NH3 (sometimes diluted with inert gas); no solvent, and the metal surface is often pre‑cleaned to promote reaction.

Esterification (Fischer esterification); converts methacrylic acid and cyclohexanol into cyclohexyl methacrylate and water; acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) is used, often under reflux with a Dean‑Stark trap or in toluene/benzene to remove water; purpose is to synthesize the cyclohexyl methacrylate monomer.

Acid–base neutralization of nalidixic acid with sodium bicarbonate to produce sodium nalidixate, releasing carbon dioxide and water. Used to convert the acidic drug into its water‑soluble sodium salt for formulation or purification. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously upon addition of excess NaHCO3 with gentle stirring.

Oxidative rearrangement/aromatization; chromium(VI) oxide oxidizes α‑humulene, removing hydrogen and cyclizing the sesquiterpene framework to give the azulene‑type hydrocarbon guaiazulene. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or acetone) with a catalytic amount of acid at 0 °C to room temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a trityl (triphenylmethyl) salt; water attacks the electrophilic trityl cation of triphenylmethyl hexafluorophosphate, forming triphenylmethanol and releasing hexafluorophosphoric acid. Usually carried out at ambient temperature in a biphasic system (e.g., CH₂Cl₂/H₂O) with gentle stirring.

Oxidative dimerization/condensation of a chlorophenol to a dioxin; 2,4,5‑trichlorophenol undergoes thermally induced coupling in the presence of an oxidant (often Cu²⁺ or Fe³⁺) to give 2,3,7,8‑tetrachlorodibenzo‑p‑dioxin and water. Conducted at high temperature (250–400 °C) in a sealed vessel; no special solvent, sometimes using inert matrix.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to form calcium carbonate from calcium sulfate dihydrate and potassium carbonate, yielding potassium sulfate in solution; aqueous mixing of CaSO₄·2H₂O with K₂CO₃ results in exchange of ions, precipitation of CaCO₃ and liberation of water; performed at room temperature in water; no catalyst needed; reaction: CaSO₄·2H₂O + K₂CO₃ → CaCO₃↓ + K₂SO₄ + 2 H₂O.

Nucleophilic addition to a cyclic anhydride; phenyl lithium adds to one carbonyl of maleic anhydride; after protonation the product is phenylsuccinic anhydride; conducted in dry THF at –78 °C to rt under nitrogen, often with slight excess of PhLi.

Acyl‑substitution (esterification) of an alcohol with an acyl chloride; ethanol reacts with pivaloyl chloride to furnish ethyl pivalate and HCl. The reaction is typically in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, using a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Precipitation of a metal acetylide; acetylene gas is passed through an aqueous solution of silver nitrate (often containing excess ammonia) to generate silver acetylide (AgC≡CH) as a pale brown precipitate. The process is carried out at low temperature, in the dark, and the solid is filtered and washed with cold ether.

Heterocycle N‑oxidation; 4‑methoxypyridine is oxidized by m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA) to its N‑oxide, while the peracid is reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Conducted in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, typically with one equivalent of m‑CPBA and under anhydrous conditions.

Transesterification; converts a benzoate ester to a methyl ester while releasing benzyl alcohol. Key transformation: exchange of the alkoxy groups between methanol and benzyl benzoate. Typically performed under reflux in excess methanol with an acid catalyst (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) or a catalytic amount of sodium methoxide. Solvent is methanol itself; reaction time 2–12 h depending on temperature.

Alkene epoxidation with m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (mCPBA); the peracid oxidizes 2‑pentene to the corresponding epoxide, 2‑pentyloxirane, with formation of m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Conducted in dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; a buffering agent (e.g., NaHCO₃) may be added to neutralize the acidic by‑product.

Solid‑state metathesis (double displacement) synthesis of zinc phosphide. Reactants ZnCl₂ and Na₃P undergo ion exchange to give NaCl and Zn₃P₂. Usually carried out in a sealed tube or furnace at 400– °C under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) to avoid oxidation. No solvent; the product Zn₃P₂ is recovered after washing away NaCl.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of 3‑hexenyl acetate. NaOH attacks the carbonyl, yielding 3‑hexen‑1‑ol and sodium acetate. Conducted in aqueous NaOH or aqueous ethanol, heated to reflux (≈80 °C) for 1–3 h. Reaction then acidified if the free alcohol is desired. No additional catalyst required.

Acid–base protonation (salt formation) of hydrazine with nitric acid to give hydrazinium nitrate. Hydrazine acts as a base, accepting a proton from HNO₃. Performed in ice‑cold aqueous solution (0–5 °C) to minimize oxidation of hydrazine; the hydrazinium nitrate precipitates or remains in solution and can be crystallized. No catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of a metal fluoride; tellurium hexafluoride reacts vigorously with water to produce tellurium dioxide and fluoride. Purpose is to decompose TeF6 and recover TeO2. Key transformation: TeF6 + 2 H2O → TeO2 + 6 HF. Performed in aqueous medium, often with cooling due to exotherm; water is the solvent, no catalyst.

Esterification of a phosphoric mono‑ester with methanol to give dimethyl phosphate; reversible condensation reaction; generally carried out by refluxing methyl dihydrogen phosphate in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) and continuous removal of water to drive the equilibrium toward product.

Acid‑base neutralization between a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (HCO₃⁻). Produces water and sodium carbonate. Occurs readily in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; often used to generate carbonate buffer or to remove CO₂ from solutions. No catalyst required.

Hydrolysis/decomposition of N‑chlorosuccinimide in water. Purpose: in‑situ generation of hypochlorous acid (HOCl) or quenching of excess NCS. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the N‑Cl bond cleaves it, yielding succinimide and HOCl. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at 0–25 °C; reaction proceeds spontaneously without added catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of isobutyl bromide with silver nitrite to afford isobutyl nitrite. Silver nitrite provides NO₂⁻ as nucleophile; AgBr precipitates, driving the reaction forward. Conducted in dry aprotic solvent such as acetone or ether at 0 °C to room temperature, often under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst; the silver salt itself facilitates the reaction.

Fischer esterification of acetic acid with 3‑heptanol to afford heptan‑3‑yl acetate and water. Catalyzed by a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid), refluxed in a suitable solvent like toluene or the excess alcohol itself, with continuous removal of water (e.g., Dean–St trap) to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Fischer esterification of a dicarboxylic acid; purpose is to prepare the di‑isopropyl ester of 2,3‑dihydroxysuccinic acid. Two equivalents of isopropanol react with the two carboxyl groups, releasing two molecules of water and yielding di‑isopropyl 2,3‑dihydroxysuccinate. Conducted under reflux in an azeotropic solvent (toluene, benzene, or xylene) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., conc. H₂SO₄). Removal of water by azeotropic distillation or by using a Dean‑Stark apparatus improves yield.

Oxidative disulfide formation; iodine serves as a mild oxidant that couples two molecules of cysteamine (2‑mercaptoethylamine) to give the disulfide cystamine, with concomitant generation of two equivalents of hydrogen iodide. Usually carried out in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature. A base (e.g., triethylamine or NaHCO₃) is often added to neutralize the formed HI and prevent acid‑catalyzed side reactions.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; sodium phosphate reacts with zinc sulfate in water to exchange anions, forming insoluble zinc phosphate precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. The reaction is performed at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the precipitated zinc phosphate is isolated by filtration and washing. No additional catalysts are required; the process is driven by the low solubility of zinc phosphate in water.

Condensation of 2‑methylpropanal with hydroxylamine to form the corresponding oxime (NE‑N‑(2‑methylpropylidene)hydroxylamine) with loss of water; a classic oxime formation reaction carried out in ethanol or methanol, often at 0 °C to rt, sometimes with a mild base (pyridine) to promote dehydration.

Acid–base reaction and gas‑evolving decomposition; nitrous acid (generated in situ from a nitrite source and a mineral acid) protonates rubidium carbonate, leading to release of carbon dioxide gas and water while forming rubidium nitrite salt. Typically conducted in aqueous solution at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control the rapid decomposition of nitrous acid. Excess nitrous acid is avoided; the reaction mixture is stirred and the evolved CO₂ is vented safely.

Enzymatic aldose‑ketose isomerization; D‑ribose‑5‑phosphate is converted to D‑ribulose‑5‑phosphate by ribose‑5‑phosphate isomerase (RpiA); the reaction proceeds in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 25–37 °C, often requiring Mg²⁺ as a cofactor; no external reagents or solvents beyond water are needed.

Thermal disproportionation/decomposition of copper(I) oxide; upon heating, Cu₂O decomposes to elemental copper and oxygen gas. The reaction requires elevated temperatures (generally >200 °C) in an inert or open atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is needed. The liberated oxygen can be collected, and the resulting copper metal is obtained as a solid residue.

Combustion reaction; complete oxidation of 2,3,3‑trimethylpentane to CO₂ and H₂O; purpose is energy release and combustion analysis; key transformation is C‑H and C‑C bonds broken, forming gaseous CO₂ and H₂O; typically performed in the gas phase at high temperature (≈800‑1200 °C) in excess O₂ or air; no solvent, often in a flame or bomb calorimeter.

Oxidative N‑demethylation; conversion of 7‑methylxanthine to xanthine with release of formaldehyde; purpose is removal of a methyl group from a nitrogen heterocycle (e.g., metabolic or synthetic de‑methylation); key transformation is cleavage of N‑CH₃ bond with insertion of O to give formaldehyde; commonly achieved with aqueous H₂O₂, peracid, or enzymatic systems (e.g., cytochrome P450) under mild temperatures (0‑40 °C) in water or buffered aqueous medium; no metal catalyst required, though metal–oxo reagents can be used.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol with lithium aluminium hydride; transforms 3,3‑dimethylbutyric acid into 3,3‑dimethyl‑1‑butanol; purpose is to obtain the corresponding alcohol from the acid; key transformation is conversion of the –CO₂H group to –CH₂OH via two hydride transfers; typical conditions: LiAlH₄ (1–2 equiv) in dry diethyl ether or THF, added at 0 °C then stirred at reflux (≈35 °C) under nitrogen; quench with careful addition of water then dilute acid.

Fischer esterification of acetic acid with 1‑hydroxy‑2‑butanone (hydroxyacetone) to give 2‑oxobutyl acetate; purpose is formation of an acetate ester from a carboxylic acid and a secondary alcohol bearing a carbonyl; key transformation is condensation of the –OH of hydroxyacetone with the –COOH of acetic acid, eliminating water; typical conditions: catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), reflux in toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water; alternative: use of azeotropic removal of water or molecular sieves; inert solvent not required beyond the acid itself.

Acid‑base (protonolysis) quench an organolithium; n‑butyllithium reacts with water to afford n‑butanol and lithium hydroxide. Performed at 0 °C to ambient temperature in an aprotic ether solvent such as THF or diethyl; water is added dropwise to control the exotherm. Purpose: neutralization of the reactive organolithium and preparation of the corresponding alcohol.

Oxidative condensation (perborate synthesis); generates sodium perborate, a solid oxidizing agent, from metaborate, hydrogen peroxide and base; in alkaline medium (NaOH) the metaborate reacts with H₂O₂ to form the perborate anion (BO₃⁻) and water; typically performed in aqueous solution at 0–5 °C with slow addition of H₂O₂ to avoid decomposition; water is the solvent, NaOH provides the alkaline environment, no additional catalyst.

Stille cross‑coupling between 1‑chloronaphthalene and tributyl(phenyl)stannane; produces 1‑phenyl‑naphthalene and tributyltin chloride; purpose is formation of a C‑C bond between an aryl halide and an aryl‑stannane; key transformation is palladium‑catalyzed transmetalation and reductive elimination; typical conditions: Pd(PPh₃)₄ (5‑10 mol %), often in DMF, THF, or toluene at 80‑110 °C under nitrogen or argon; stoichiometric amount of the organostannane; by‑product tributyltin chloride is removed during work‑up.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (acidic hydrolysis). Purpose: convert an amide into the corresponding carboxylic acid and amine. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–N amide bond with addition of water, generating propionic acid and dibutylamine. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) for several hours. Common solvent: water or aqueous acid; no special catalyst beyond the acid.

Acetylation – para‑Aminophenol reacts with acetyl chloride to give acetaminophen (N‑acetyl‑p‑aminophenol) with release of HCl; conducted in an aprotic base solvent (pyridine or triethylamine) at 0 °C to room temperature, under inert atmosphere, the base scavenges the HCl.

Esterification (acylation) of a primary alcohol; DMAP catalyzes the transfer of an acetyl group from acetic anhydride to 2-(hydroxymethyl)tetrahydrofuran, yielding tetrahydrofurfuryl acetate and acetic acid as by‑product. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; catalytic amount of DMAP (≈10 mol %) is used.

Acid dissolution/metathesis; conversion of insoluble Ag₂MoO₄ into soluble silver nitrate and molybdic acid. The solid is treated with aqueous HNO₃ (1–3 M) at room temperature or with gentle heating (≤60 °C). Ag⁺ is released as AgNO₃ (soluble) while MoO₃ is protonated to H₂MoO₄, which may precipitate. No catalyst; water is the reaction medium.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; calcium acetate reacts with magnesium sulfate in aqueous solution to exchange anions, forming insoluble calcium sulfate (gypsum) which precipitates and soluble magnesium acetate remains in solution. Carried out at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent.

Lithium‑halogen exchange (metalation); n‑butyllithium reacts with 2‑bromothiophene to generate the organolithium species 2‑lithiothiophene and n‑butyl bromide as the leaving group. Conducted at low temperature (≈ −78 °C) in dry ether or THF under a nitrogen or argon atmosphere; reagents are added dropwise to maintain temperature control.

Halide exchange (oxidative halogenation) reaction; bromine oxidatively replaces chloride ligands in tantalum(V) chloride to give tantalum(V) bromide while liberating chlorine gas. Usually performed in a sealed tube or under an inert gas stream at elevated temperatures (100–200 °C); no solvent is required, though inert‑gas conditions prevent side reactions.

Oxidative coupling of a thiol; iodine acts as a mild oxidant converting methanethiol into dimethyl disulfide while being reduced to hydrogen iodide. Typical conditions are 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; no catalyst is required. The reaction is used to generate symmetrical disulfides for further synthetic manipulation.

Alkaline hydrolysis (amidolysis) of N‑methylformamide; aqueous sodium hydroxide attacks the amide carbonyl, cleaving the C–N bond to furnish methylamine and sodium formate. The reaction is heated under reflux (typically 80–100 °C) in water; excess NaOH drives the reaction to completion and the amine may be removed by distillation or gas‑stripping.

Acid–carbonate reaction; purpose is to dissolve manganese(II) carbonate and generate carbon dioxide; key transformation: MnCO3(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → MnCl2(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l); carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or slightly warmed with stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Salt metathesis (anion exchange) reaction; ammonium perchlorate exchanges its perchlorate anion with scandium chloride, producing soluble scandium perchlorate and ammonium chloride. Carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; both salts remain in solution, and the reaction proceeds without the need for a catalyst.

Reductive amination (Mannich-type) of glycine with formaldehyde; NaBH₃CN reduces the imine intermediate to give N‑methylglycine (sarcosine). Purpose: Introduce a methyl group on the nitrogen of an amino acid. Key transformation: primary amine → secondary amine via imine formation and hydride delivery. Typical conditions: aqueous methanol or ethanol, pH 6–7 (adjusted with acetate buffer), NaBH₃CN added portionwise at 0 °C to rt. No special catalyst needed; NaBH₃CN acts as the reducing agent.

Oxidation of a 1,2,5‑oxadiazole with meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA) to generate the N‑oxide heterocycle known as furoxan. Purpose: Convert the neutral oxadiazole into its high‑energy N‑oxide (furoxan) for use as energetic material or NO donor. Key transformation: peracid adds an oxygen to the ring nitrogen, forming the N‑oxide. Typical conditions: dilute m‑CPBA (70 % in AcOEt) in dichloromethane, 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen; reaction monitored by TLC. Quench with aqueous sodium sulfite to remove excess oxidant.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction between sodium carbonate and diammonium hydrogen phosphate in aqueous solution, yielding sodium hydrogen phosphate and ammonium carbonate. Purpose: Exchange of cations to form different soluble salts, often for buffer preparation or analytical work. Key transformation: carbonate anion swaps with phosphate anion. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water, stir at ambient temperature; may gently heat to ensure complete ion exchange. No catalyst required; reaction proceeds spontaneously in solution.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑norbornene to norbornane. Purpose: Saturate the carbon‑carbon double bond to obtain the fully hydrogenated bicyclic hydrocarbon. Key transformation: alkene → alkane by addition of H₂ across the C=C bond. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm), 5–10 % Pd/C or PtO₂ as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–50 °C. Reaction completed in a few hours with stirring under inert gas background.

Reaction type: Direct combination (synthesis) of a metal with a liquid halogen; purpose: preparation of nickel(II) bromide. Key transformation: nickel metal is oxidized to Ni²⁺ and bromine is reduced to Br⁻, yielding NiBr₂. Typical conditions: bromine is added dropwise to heated nickel powder (150–250 °C) in a glass reactor under a nitrogen blanket to control the exotherm; the reaction is often performed in the melt (no solvent). The resulting NiBr₂ can be isolated as a solid or dissolved in aqueous HBr for purification.

Hydrolysis of cyanogen chloride (ClCN) in water to give hydrochloric acid and isocyanic acid (HNCO). Purpose: Decompose toxic ClCN into less hazardous species; HNCO can be further transformed or. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the carbon of the –C≡N group, displacing chloride and forming HNCO plus HCl. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, often mildly acidic or neutral pH, temperature 20–60 °C; reaction may be accelerated by a small amount of base (e.g., NaOH) to neutralize generated HCl. No catalyst required.

Acid–base protonation of a phosphate salt; disodium pyrophosphate reacts with aqueous HCl to give pyrophosphoric acid (H₄P₂O₇) and sodium chloride; performed in water at room temperature, stoichiometric HCl added until the solution is acidic, then the acid can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Base‑cataly amide hydrolysis (saponification) of N‑acetyltaurine; used to regenerate the free amino‑sulfonic acid taurine and to produce sodium acetate. Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of the N‑acetyl group, leading to cleavage of the amide bond and formation of acetate ion, which pairs with Na⁺. The reaction is typically carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2  at 60–100 °C for several hours, often under reflux. Water is the solvent; no additional catalyst is required.

Mitsunobu amination of a secondary benzylic alcohol; the alcohol is first activated by triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate (DEAD), forming an alkoxyphosphonium intermediate that undergoes SN2 attack by dimethylamine, giving N,N‑dimethyl‑2‑phenylpropan‑1‑amine with inversion of configuration; typical conditions: dry THF or dichloromethane, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; stoichiometric amounts of PPh₃ and DEAD/DIAD are required; by‑products are triphenylphosphine oxide and diethylhydrazinedicarboxylate.

Acid‑base neutralization to form a mixed sodium/ammonium tartrate salt; purpose is preparation of a buffered tartrate or a crystalline salt. Key transformation: deprotonation of both carboxyl groups of tartaric acid by NaOH and NH4OH, yielding water and the Na⁺/NH4⁺ tartrate. Typical conditions: dissolve reagents in water, stir at ambient temperature, then cool to crystallize; no special catalyst needed.

Redox (oxygen‑atom transfer) reaction of a hydroperoxide with triphenylphosphine; purpose is reduction of cyclohexyl hydroperoxide to cyclohexanol while oxidizing PPh₃ to phosphine oxide. Key transformation: transfer of an oxygen atom from the O‑O bond to phosphorus, breaking the O‑O bond and forming the alcohol. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane (or CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to rt, 1 equiv PPh₃, inert atmosphere; reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Pyridine N‑oxide formation (oxidation). 2,4‑Dimethylpyridine is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to the corresponding N‑oxide, 2,4‑dimethyl‑1‑oxidopyridin‑1‑ium, with water as by‑product. Typical procedure: H₂O₂ (30 % aq) added to a solution of the pyridine in acetic acid or methanol at 0–25 °C, stir 0.5–2 h; neutralize and isolate the N‑oxide.

Acid–base (hydrolysis) reaction; sodium hydride reacts with water to generate a strong base (NaOH) and hydrogen gas; used to quench excess NaH or produce H2; typically performed at ambient temperature with careful addition of water to solid NaH; aqueous medium or in a polar aprotic solvent (THF) under inert atmosphere to control H2 evolution.

Carbamoylation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of a primary alcohol with carbamoyl chloride; pyridine serves as base and HCl scavenger. Purpose is synthesis of a benzyl carbamate protecting group. Key transformation: attack of the alcohol oxygen on the carbonyl carbon of the carbamoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give the carbamate; pyridinium chloride is formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: dry pyridine as solvent, 0 °C to rt, stoichiometric pyridine; inert atmosphere, no extra catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization (double displacement) where calcium bicarbonate reacts with aqueous sulfuric acid, producing calcium sulfate precipitate, carbon dioxide gas and water; performed in water at room temperature, typically with dilute acid and stirring.

Metal‑acid displacement; produces calcium phosphate and hydrogen gas. Calcium metal reacts with concentrated phosphoric acid (typically aqueous) according to 3 Ca + 2 H3PO4 → Ca3(PO4)2 + 3 H2. Reaction is performed at 0–50 °C to control vigorous H2 evolution; no catalyst, water acts as solvent.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation) of hexafluoroisopropanol alkoxide with iodomethane; purpose is formation of hexafluoroisopropyl methyl ether. Key transformation: deprotonation of HFIP by NaH to generate the alkoxide, followed by nucleophilic attack on MeI, displacing iodide. Typical conditions: dry THF or DMF, NaH (1.1 equiv) at 0 °C then warmed to rt, inert atmosphere; sodium iodide precipitates as by‑product.

Oxidation of a vicinal diol (1,2‑dihroxynaphthalene) to the corresponding quinone using silver(I) oxide; purpose is conversion to 1,2‑naphthoquinone. Key transformation: two‑electron oxidation of each hydroxyl to carbonyl, forming the quinone ring and reducing Ag₂O to metallic silver. Typical conditions: reflux in a non‑protic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile, stoichiometric Ag₂O (1‑1.5 equiv), dark or limited light to avoid silver reduction side reactions; filtration to remove silver metal.

Acyl transfer (esterification) using ac anhydride; purpose is to convert a primary alcohol to its acetate ester. Key transformation: decanol oxygen attacks the carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming decyl acetate and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: heating to 80–120 °C, often neat (acetic anhydride acts as solvent) or in toluene; sometimes a catalytic amount of pyridine or a weak base is added to neutralize the formed acid.

Double displacement reaction. Calcium hydroxide reacts with sodium sulfate to produce calcium sulfate precipitate and aqueous sodium hydroxide. Driven by the low solubility of calcium sulfate. Reaction occurs in aqueous solution at room temperature.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and precipitate the insoluble barium sulfate. Key transformation: sulfate from potassium sulfate combines with barium cation to give BaSO₄ solid, while thiocyanate pairs with potassium to give soluble KSCN. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions mixed at ambient temperature; stirring until BaSO₄ precip, then filtration. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Double‑replacement (acid–base) reaction in aqueous solution; purpose is to generate ammonium sulfide from sodium sulfide and ammonium chloride. Key transformation: sulfide ion pairs with two ammonium cations to give (NH₄)₂S, while sodium cations pair with chloride to give NaCl.
