Halogen exchange/metathesis between phosphorus pentachloride andolinium oxide; PCl₅ reacts with Gd₂O₃ to give phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and gadolinium(III) chloride; usually performed neat or in a non‑coordinating solvent such as CCl₄, heating to 150–200 °C under anhydrous conditions; no catalyst.

Reduction of an ester to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; typically carried out in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere, converting the carbonyl of ethyl furan‑2‑carboxylate to a hydroxymethyl group (furan‑2‑methanol) while the ethoxy fragment is reduced to ethanol.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; LAH donates hydride to the carbonyl of 2‑pyrimidinecarboxylic acid, converting the –COOH group to –CH₂OH and generating aluminium hydroxide on work‑up; carried out in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, followed by careful quench with methanol or aqueous acid; no catalyst.
Thermal decomposition of magnesium bicarbonate on heating produces magnesium carbonate, carbon dioxide and water; typically performed by heating the solid at 100–150 °C without solvent.

Double‑displacement precipitation in aqueous solution: Cu²⁺ from CuSO₄ reacts with [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ from K₄[Fe(CN)₆]·3H₂O to precipitate copper ferrocyanide (Cu₂[Fe(CN)₆]) while K⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to form soluble K₂SO₄. Conducted at room temperature in water; no special reagents or catalysts needed.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of tert‑butanol to isobutylene (E1 elimination); purpose is to generate the terminal alkene for further reactions or as a feedstock; key transformation is loss of water from the tertiary alcohol to give C₄H₈; typical conditions employ dry trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (≈10‑20 mol %) at 0‑25 °C in an anhydrous, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; the reaction is often run under nitrogen and the volatile isobutylene is removed by gas‑flow or trapped.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation forming bismuth subsalicylate; bismuth acetate exchanges its acetate ion with the salicylate ion of sodium salicylate, producing soluble sodium acetate and insoluble bismuth subsalicylate which precipitates; conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature, often adjusted to pH 5–6 to improve precipitation; no catalyst.

Reaction type: Acid‑chloride formation (carboxylic‑acid activation). Purpose: Convert picolinic acid into the more reactive acid chloride for subsequent amide or ester synthesis. Key transformation: Replacement of the hydroxyl group of the carboxyl by a chlorine atom, generating picolinoyl chloride. Typical conditions: Dissolve picolinic acid in dry dichloromethane (or chloroform) under nitrogen, cool to 0 °C, add a catalytic amount (≈0.1 eq) of DMF, then add oxalyl chloride dropwise (1.2 eq). Stir at 0 °C for 30 min then allow to warm to rt for 1–2 h. By‑products CO, CO₂ and HCl are evolved. The crude acid chloride is used directly or distilled under reduced pressure.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration) of furan; purpose is to install a nitro group at the 2‑position; key transformation is replacement of the C‑2 hydrogen by NO2 with loss of water; typically performed with dilute nitric acid (often in acetic acid or acetyl nitrate) at 0–5 °C to minimize polymerisation; common solvent mixture is furan itself or acetic acid, reaction run under cooling and inert atmosphere.

Redox (halogen–sulfide) reaction: bromine oxidizes sulfide ion to elemental sulfur while being reduced to bromide, forming barium bromide. Typically carried out in aqueous solution or refluxing solvent; no catalyst required, moderate temperature suffices.

Reaction type: base-induced elimination (E2). Purpose: elimination of vicinal dihalide to regenerate alkene. Key transformation: strong base abstracts proton, facilitating loss of chlorine atoms to form double bond. Conditions: elevated temperature (~70-100°C). Catalyst: potassium tert-butoxide acts as base. Solvents: tert-butyl alcohol.

Fischer esterification: carboxylic acid (3‑methylbenzoic acid) reacts with methanol to give the methyl ester and water. Acid catalyst (e.g., catalytic sulfuric or hydrochloric acid) and excess methanol as solvent; reflux conditions to drive equilibrium toward ester formation.

Strong oxidative cleavage (KMnO₄ oxidation): 1,16‑hexadecanediol is oxidized in alkaline aqueous potassium permanganate to the corresponding dicarboxylic acid (hexadecanedioic acid). Reaction proceeds under heating (reflux) in water; MnO₂ precipitates as by‑product; no additional catalyst needed.

Mitsunobu coupling: primary alcohol (benzyl alcohol) is converted into the corresponding N‑alkylated amine (N‑benzyltryptamine) using triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate (DEAD) as reagents. Anhyd aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or dioxane), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazinedicarboxylate are formed as by‑products.

Acyl chloride esterification (acetylation): benzyl alcohol reacts with acetyl chloride in the presence of pyridine, which acts as base and nucleophilic catalyst, yielding benzyl acetate and pyridinium chloride. Conducted at 0 °C to ambient temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or neat pyridine; no metal catalyst required.

Salt metathesis/precipitation reaction: soluble silver nitrate exchanges anions with lutetium(III) bromide, forming insoluble silver bromide precipitate and soluble lutetium(III) nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; stirring until complete precipitation; no catalyst needed.

Amide formation via direct condensation of a carboxylic acid with ammonia; the carboxyl group is activated by heating so that the amine attacks the carbonyl, releasing water and giving 2‑iodopropanamide. Typically performed neat or in a high‑boiling aprotic solvent (e.g., toluene) under reflux with excess NH3; removal of water drives the equilibrium.

Base‑promoted intramolecular lactonization (four‑membered β‑propiolactone formation) from 3‑chloropropionic acid. NaOH deprotonates the acid to the carboxylate, which then displaces chloride in an intramolecular SN2 step, yielding β‑propiolactone and NaCl. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often 1 M) at 50–80 °C; phase‑transfer catalysts can be added to improve yield.

Base‑induced epoxide synthesis (intramolecular cyclization) of 2‑chloroethanol to ethylene oxide. NaOH abstracts the hydroxyl proton, generating an alkoxide that attacks the adjacent carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming the three‑membered ring. Reaction carried out in aqueous NaOH at elevated temperature (80–120 °C) or in polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMSO) with solid NaOH; water is a by‑product.

Oxidative coupling of a xanthate; potassium ethyl xanthate is oxidized by iodine to form diethyl dixanthogen (the disulfide) and potassium iodide; usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as acetone or ethanol at ambient temperature, with equimolar I₂, the reaction proceeds rapidly and the KI by‑product remains in solution.

Acid–base deprotonation of oxalic acid by potassium hydride, producing potassium oxalate and hydrogen gas. Each KH abstracts a proton, forming H₂ and the oxalate anion; the reaction is highly exothermic and moisture‑sensitive. Performed under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in dry THF or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature; stoichiometric amounts of KH are used.

Esterification (condensation) of thiophosphoric acid with methanol to give dimethyl thiophosphate. The P–SH group is protonated, allowing nucleophilic attack by methanol; each substitution releases water. Typically reflux methanol serves both reactant and solvent, often with catalytic H₂SO₄ or an acid‑base buffer to promote ester formation; water is removed by azeotropic distillation or molecular sieves.

Catalytic hydrogenation of the furan ring of furfuryl acetate to tetrahydrofurfuryl acetate. Molecular hydrogen adds across the two C=C bonds of the heterocycle, saturating it to a tetrahydrofuran ring while the acetate substituent remains unchanged. Conducted with 5–10 % Pd/C or Raney Ni under 1–5 atm H₂ in ethanol or ethyl acetate at 25–80 °C; reaction usually completes within a few hours.

Type: organolithium oxidation / acid‑quench preparation. Purpose: synthesize phenyl seleninic acid (C6H5SeO2H). Key transformation: phenyl‑Li attacks selenium dioxide, forming a phenyl‑selenate intermediate that is protonated by water to give the seleninic acid. Typical conditions: add phenyl‑lithium (generated in THF or Et2O) to SeO2 at –78 °C to 0 °C, then warm and quench with aqueous work‑up. Solvent: dry THF or diethyl ether; no metal catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation). The lone pair on the secondary amine N‑methyl‑aniline attacks acetyl chloride, producing N‑methyl‑acetanilide and HCl. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HCl. Reaction time 1‑2 h; work‑up includes aqueous wash to remove salts.

Type: high‑temperature solid‑state redox (metallurgical reduction). Purpose: reduce Nb(V) oxide to Nb(IV) oxide while oxidizing aluminum to Al2O3. Key transformation: Al metal donates electrons to Nb2O5, converting Nb5+ to Nb4+ (forming NbO2) and Al3+ (forming Al2O3). Typical conditions: intimate powder mixture heated to 1300–1600 °C in an inert or reducing atmosphere (e.g., Ar). No solvent; reaction performed in a furnace.

Type: catalytic reductive amination (hydrogenation of imine). Purpose: attach a propan‑2‑yl group to tryptamine nitrogen, yielding N‑[2‑(1H‑indol‑3‑yl)ethyl]propan‑2‑amine. Key transformation: condensation of acetone with tryptamine to form an imine, followed by catalytic hydrogenation of the C bond to a secondary amine; water is released. Typical conditions: Pd/C (5–10 % loading) under 1–5 atm H2, 25–50 °C, in ethanol or methanol solvent. Reaction is run until gas uptake stops; then filtered to remove catalyst.

Type: acid‑mediated salt hydrolysis / gas‑generating reaction. Purpose: generate hydrogen telluride (H2Te) gas from strontium telluride. Key transformation: protonation of Te2‑ by H2SO4 yields H2Te, while Sr2+ combines with sulfate to form insoluble SrSO4 precipitate. Typical conditions: add solid SrTe to concentrated aqueous H2SO4, gently heat (50–80 °C) to evolve H2Te gas, which is collected under inert atmosphere. Solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Type: catalytic hydrogenation of a fluorinated olefin. Purpose: saturate the C=C bond of hexafluoropropene to give 1,1,1,3,3,3‑hexafluoropropane. Key transformation: addition of H2 across the double bond. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO2, or Raney nickel, temperature 50–150 °C, often in a inert fluorinated solvent (e.g., perfluorohexane) or solvent‑free in the gas phase. Reaction proceeds to completion with full conversion of the alkene.

Type: directed metalation followed by formylation (organolithium addition to DMF). Purpose: convert 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzene into its corresponding aldehyde. Key transformation: n‑BuLi deprotonates the aromatic ring ortho/para to the methoxy groups, generating an aryl‑lithium species; this nucleophile attacks DMF, and subsequent acidic work‑up yields 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzaldehyde, with n‑butane released as a by‑product. Typical conditions: THF, –78 °C addition of n‑BuLi, then DMF added at low temperature, followed by warm‑up and aqueous quench. No additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic iodination of a phenol with iodine monochloride (ICl); installs an iodine para to the phenolic OH to give 2,6-bis(isopropyl)-4-iodophenol with generation of HCl. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or chloroform solvent at 0 °C to room temperature.

Esterification (Fischer esterification) of propionic acid with ethanol; purpose is to form the ester ethyl propionate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ethanol oxygen on the carbonyl carbon of propionic acid followed by loss of water; typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous solvent (toluene or benzene) with catalytic amount of strong acid such as sulfuric acid; water is often removed by a Dean‑Stark trap to drive equilibrium toward product.

Nucleophilic substitution (alcohol to alkyl chloride). Thionyl chloride converts 3‑methyl‑1‑heptanol into 1‑chloro‑3‑methylheptane, releasing HCl and SO₂ gases. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature; pyridine or a tertiary amine scavenges the HCl.

Basic ester hydrolysis (saponification). Sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes 2,2,2‑tribromoethyl acetate to give 2,2,2‑tribromoethanol and sodium acetate. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol as co‑solvent) and heated under reflux.

Base‑promoted ether cleavage (alkoxy cleavage). Sodium hydroxide attacks the methyl ether of 2‑methoxy‑2‑methylbutane, breaking the C–O bond to give the tertiary alcohol 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol and methanol. Typically carried out in aqueous NaOH (10–20 % w/v) under reflux (80–100 °C). No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Sulfonamide formation via in‑situ sulfonyl chloride. Thionyl chloride activates 4‑aminobenzenesulfonic acid to its sulfonyl chloride, which then condenses with 2‑amino‑4‑methylpyrimidine to afford sulfamerazine, releasing HCl, SO₂ and water. Reaction is carried out in a dry aprotic solvent (e.g., pyridine, DMF) at 0–25 °C, with pyridine acting as base.

Combustion (oxidation) of tetraethylsilane. In the presence of excess O₂, tetraethylsilane burns to produce carbon dioxide, water vapor and silicon dioxide. Requires ignition and high temperature; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Type: Acid‑catalyzed epoxide ring opening. Purpose: Convert an epoxide into a halohydrin. Key transformation: Protonation of propylene oxide followed by nucleophilic attack of Cl⁻ at the more substituted carbon, giving 2‑chloropropan‑1‑ol. Typical conditions: aqueous or gaseous HCl (1–3 M), solvent such as dichloromethane or acetone, 0 °C to ambient temperature. No additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic alkylation (ester formation). Sodium salicylate (the carboxylate of salicylic acid) attacks benzyl bromide in an SN2 fashion to give benzyl salicylate and NaBr. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often under reflux; addition of a catalytic amount of KI can accelerate the reaction.

Multinitration of nitromethane (formation of trinitromethane). Concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ mixture nitrates nitromethane, replacing the hydrogen with three nitro groups to afford trinitromethane (nitroform), with water as by‑product. Conducted at low temperature (0–5 °C) then warmed, using the mixed acid as both nitrating and dehydrating medium.

Hydrolysis (decomposition) of hydroxyurea; purpose is to break the N‑C(O)‑NHOH bond to generate hydroxylamine and urea; key transformation: H2O attacks the carbonyl of hydroxyurea, cleaving it into NH2‑C(O)‑NH2 (urea) and NH2‑OH (hydroxylamine); typically performed by heating an aqueous solution of hydroxyurea at 80–120 °C, often under acidic or basic catalysis (e.g., dilute HCl or NaOH) to accelerate the reaction; solvent is water, no special catalyst required.

High‑temperature solid‑state redox (metal reduction) of zirconium(IV) bromide by aluminum; purpose is to access lower‑valent Zr(III) bromide; key transformation: Al metal is oxidized from 0 to +3, forming AlBr3, while Zr(IV) is reduced to Zr(III), giving ZrBr3; carried out in a sealed tube or molten‑salt medium at 300–500 °C under an inert atmosphere (argon); often the reactants are mixed as powders and heated; no additional solvent, but the reaction may be performed in molten bromide flux as a medium.

Thermal decomposition of stannous oxalate; purpose is to produce tin(II) oxide and gaseous carbonides; key transformation: SnC2O4·nH2O decomposes on heating to SnO (tin(II) oxide) plus CO2 and CO gases; typically heated in a crucible under an inert gas (N2 or Ar) from 350 °C to 500 °C; no solvent; the reaction proceeds spontaneously once the decomposition temperature is reached, sometimes with a brief dwell to ensure complete gas evolution.

Reaction type: acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: preparation of lead(II) selenate. Key transformation: selenic acid donates protons to lead(II) hydroxide, producing water and the lead(II) selenate salt. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring until complete dissolution. Common solvents/catalysts: water; no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction between oxalic acid and gadolinium(III) acetate; purpose is to precipitate insoluble gadolinium oxalate while generating acetic acid; key transformation: two acetate ions exchange with two oxalate ions, giving Gd2(C2O4)3 (often written as GdOxalate) as a solid precipitate and 6 CH3COOH in solution; carried out in aqueous medium, usually by mixing aqueous solutions of the reagents at room temperature and then heating gently (50–80 °C) to drive off acetic acid; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction of nitric acid with barium chlorate; purpose is to exchange anions, forming barium nitrate and chloric acid; key transformation: HNO3 protonates the chlorate ion, producing HClO3 (chloric acid) while Ba2+ pairs with NO3− to give Ba(NO3)2 in solution; performed in dilute aqueous solution at low temperature (0–25 °C) to avoid decomposition of the unstable chloric acid; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aromatic aldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid using a Cr(VI) oxidant (Jones oxidation). The aldehyde carbonyl is converted to a carboxyl group while potassium dichromate is reduced from Cr(VI) to Cr(III), giving chromium(III) sulfate. Typically performed in aqueous sulfuric acid, often with a water‑acetone or water‑dichloromethane mixture, at 0 °C to room temperature. No additional catalyst; the dichromate/H₂SO₄ system supplies the oxidizing power.

Amidation of 4‑aminosalicylic acid with benzoyl chloride in the presence of pyridine (Schotten‑Baumann conditions). Pyridine acts as a base and HCl scavenger, allowing the amine to be acylated to give 4‑(benzoylamino)‑2‑hydroxybenzoic acid. The reaction is usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, at 0 °C to rt, under an inert atmosphere. No metal catalyst is required.

Selective reduction of an acyl chloride (octanoyl chloride) to the corresponding aldehyde (octanal) using lithium triethylborohydride (Superhydride). One equivalent of LiEt₃BH delivers a hydride to the carbonyl carbon, forming the aldehyde while generating triethylborane and lithium chloride as by‑products. Conducted at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in dry ethers (diethyl ether or THF) under inert gas. No additional catalyst needed.

Transesterification of trimethylsilyl acetate with isobutyl alcohol; yields isobutyl acetate and trimethylsilanol, a route to ester formation while removing a TMS protecting group. The isobutyl alcohol attacks the carbonyl of the TMS acetate, displacing TMS‑OH. Conducted at rt to mild reflux in solvents such as CH₂Cl₂, toluene, or THF, often with a catalytic amount of an acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a nucleophilic catalyst (pyridine, DMAP) to accelerate the acyl transfer.

In‑situ generation of hydrogen sulfide from thioacetamide and precipitation of cadmium sulfide. Heating an aqueous mixture of cadmium acetate and thioacetamide causes thioacetamide to decompose to H₂S, which reacts with Cd²⁺ to form insoluble CdS; concomitantly acetic acid and acetamide are produced. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, 80–100 °C, stirring for 1–2 h. No external catalyst; water serves as the solvent.

Mild oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). The primary hydroxyl of 2‑chloropropan‑1‑ol is converted to the corresponding aldehyde (2‑chloropropanal) while water is released. Reaction is carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at room temperature under an inert atmosphere.

High‑temperature oxidation of molybdenum(III) sesquioxide (Mo₂O₃) to molybdenum(VI) trioxideMoO₃). Solid Mo₂O₃ is heated in a stream of oxygen or air, allowing oxygen to oxidize Mo(III) to Mo(VI), yielding MoO₃ as a crystalline solid. Conditions: 500–650 °C in a furnace or tube reactor, solid‑state, no solvent or catalyst required.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of 1‑bromo‑3‑chlorobenzene with potassium vinyltrifluoroborate to afford 3‑chlorostyrene. The aryl bromide undergoes palladium‑catalyzed transmetalation with the vinyl boron reagent, followed by reductive elimination to install a vinyl group while the chlorine remains untouched. Typical system: Pd(0) catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄), base such as K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃, solvent mixture of THF/H₂O or toluene/H₂O, heated to 80–100 °C under nitrogen. No stoichiometric metal reagents are needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduction of the cyclic disulfide in α‑lipoic acid to the dithiol form (dihydrolipoic acid). H₂ gas is passed over Pd/C in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, typically at ambient temperature to a few atmospheres of pressure. The reaction converts the 1,2‑dithiolane ring into two free thiol groups, yielding the biologically active reduced antioxidant.

Reaction type: electrophilic addition (bromination) of an alkene using N‑bromosuccinimide. Purpose: synthesis of 2‑bromo‑1,1‑diethoxyethane. Key transformation: the C=C bond of 1,1‑diethoxyene attacks the Br⁺ generated from NBS, forming a bromonium intermediate that is opened by bromide to give the vicinal bromo‑acetal. Typical conditions: solution in an inert organic solvent (CCl₄, CH₂Cl₂, or CHCl₃) at 0 °C to room temperature, often protected from light to avoid radical pathways. Common solvents/catalysts: carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; occasionally a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., AcOH) to favor the ionic route.

Metathesis/alkylation of a metal halide; methyl lithium transfers methyl groups to mercury(II) bromide to give dimethylmercury and lithium bromide. Performed under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in a dry ether solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, typically at −78 °C to 0 °C to control the highly reactive organolithium reagent. The reaction provides an organomercury compound for further synthetic use.

Thermal decomposition (disproportionation) of bismuth pentafluoride; heating BiF₅ causes it to release fluorine gas while forming bismuth trifluoride. Requires high temperature (often >300 °C) in a sealed, fluorine‑compatible reactor, usually under inert gas to avoid side reactions. The process is a method for generating elemental fluorine from a high‑oxidation‑state fluoride.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous sodium sulfide reacts with mercury(II) nitrate to exchange anions, precipitating insoluble mercury(II) sulfide while forming soluble sodium nitrate. Carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; the black/red HgS solid is filtered off. This reaction is commonly used for mercury ion removal or for preparing HgS pigment.

Chlorination/dehydration of a phosphine oxide; thionyl chloride converts diphenylphosphine oxide into chlorodiphenylphosphine, releasing HCl and SO₂ gases. Typically run in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to reflux, with careful venting of gaseous by‑products. The transformation replaces the P=O group with a P‑Cl bond, useful for synthesizing phosphorochloridates.

Oxidative coupling (FeCl3‑mediated electrophilic condensation) of indole with indole‑3‑carboxaldehyde to construct a carbazole framework; the iron(III) Lewis acid activates the aldehyde for a Friedel‑Crafts‑type attack by indole, followed by oxidative dehydrogenation to give 6‑formylindolo[3,2‑b]carbazole. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, FeCl3 (0.1–0.5 equiv) at ambient temperature under inert atmosphere; work‑up with aqueous base.

Acylation of a primary alcohol with acetic anhydride; purpose is to synthesize decyl acetate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the anhydride carbonyl, forming the ester and generating acetic acid as by‑product; typical conditions: catalytic DMAP or pyridine (1–5 mol %) in anhydrous dichloromethane or neat, gentle heating (30–50 °C) under nitrogen; reaction proceeds rapidly and is quenched with aqueous NaHCO₃.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of the phenolic/alcoholic OH of pindolol by chloroacetonitrile to afford the O‑cyanomethyl ether (cyanopindolol) with loss of HCl. Usually performed in polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO) with a mild base (pyridine, triethylamine, or NaHCO₃) to scavenge the generated HCl, at 0 °C to room temperature.

Partial reduction of an ester to an aldehyde; DIBAL‑H reduces the methyl ester to 4‑fluorobenzaldehyde while releasing methanol; performed at low temperature (≈ −78 °C) in dry THF or toluene, using 1 equiv DIBAL‑H, followed by careful quench with methanol or aqueous acid.

Hydrogen reduction of molybum dioxide to elemental molybdenum. Solid MoO₂ is exposed to a flow of H₂ gas at high temperature (600–800 °C) in a tubular furnace; the reaction proceeds via stepwise hydrogenolysis to yield Mo metal and H₂O vapour. No solvent; inert carrier gas (Ar or N₂) may be used.

Oxidation by ozone; ozone reacts with elemental sulfur to produce sulfur dioxide and sulfur trioxide; a gas‑phase redox reaction carried out at low to moderate temperatures, often in a flow reactor; no solvent, ozone itself serves as the oxidant.

Reductive amination of a ketone; 2‑tetralone reacts with ammonium acetate to form an imine (or iminium) which is reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to give 2‑aminotetraline; acetic acid is released as a by‑product; typical conditions: mildly acidic pH (≈5–6), room temperature to 40 °C; solvent: methanol, ethanol, or a mixture of methanol/water; NaBH3CN is the selective reducing agent.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of mesityl oxide (4‑methyl‑3‑penten‑2‑one) to diacetone alcohol (4‑hydroxy‑4‑methyl‑2‑pentanone). Conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid (1–5 % H₂SO₄) at 0–25 °C, then warmed to 40–60 °C to drive the addition of water across the α,β‑unsaturated carbonyl. The reaction is reversible; removal of product by extraction improves yield.

Williamson ether synthesis: SN2 displacement of the tosylate group of ethyl p‑toluenesulfone by ethoxide ion, forming diethyl ether and sodium‑toluenesulfonate. Carried out in anhydrous ethanol or THF with sodium ethoxide (1–1.2 equiv) at reflux (≈78 °C for EtOH) under nitrogen; the by‑product salts remain in the polar phase and are removed by aqueous work‑up.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of the hydroxyl group of DL‑carnitine with acetyl bromide to give acetyl‑DL‑carnitine. The reaction is carried out in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dry dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, using a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HBr. It is used to prepare the biologically active acetyl‑carnitine ester.

Acid–base neutralization of trifluoroacetic acid with potassium bicarbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and forming potassium trifluoroacetate. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required. Serves to neutralize TFA or generate the potassium salt.

Nucleophilic addition of methylmagnesium bromide (Grignard reagent) to S‑ethyl propanethioate followed by work‑up, giving butan‑2‑one (a methyl ketone) and ethanethiol as the leaving group. Performed under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF, typically at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen. Used for ketone synthesis from thioesters.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of chloroacetone with ammonia to afford aminoacetone and ammonium chloride. Carried out in aqueous or alcoholic ammonia, often under reflux or mild heating. Provides a route to α‑amino ketones from α‑haloketones.

Oxidation of fluorene to fluorenone using chromium(VI) oxide in sulfuric acid (Jones oxidation). Reaction is done in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or dichloromethane at 0–25 °C, with catalytic amounts of H₂SO₄ to maintain Cr(VI) in solution. Converts the benzylic secondary carbon of fluorene to a carbonyl, yielding fluorenone.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); used to deprotect the acetate and afford the allylic alcohol as its sodium salt. Hydroxide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon of (E)-hex‑2‑enyl acetate, giving (E)-hex‑2‑en‑1‑ol and acetate anion, which forms sodium acetate. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (0.5–2 M), reflux 50–100 °C, often in a water/ethanol or water/methanol mixture. No additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed intermolecular transesterification (interesterification) between propionic acid and n‑butyl acrylate, swapping the acyl groups to give acrylic acid and n‑butyl propionate. Conducted with a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄) at 120–150 °C, often under reduced pressure to remove the more volatile acrylic acid and drive the equilibrium. Used to prepare the desired ester and recover acrylic acid.

Acid‑chloride formation using phosgene; salicylic acid reacts with phosgene (COCl2) to give salicyloyl chloride, generating HCl and CO2 as by‑products; carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in dry aprotic solvents (e.g., CH2Cl2) with a base such as pyridine to scavenge HCl; the reaction is highly toxic and requires fume‑hood protection.

Ester aminolysis (amidation) of a fatty acid methyl ester with monoethanolamine to give a fatty acid monoethanolamide and methanol; used to synthesize surfactant amides. Typically heated to 120‑180 °C in a polar aprotic solvent (toluene, DMF) or under solvent‑free conditions with excess ethanolamine; removal of methanol drives the equilibrium. Acidic catalysts (p‑TsOH) or molecular sieves are sometimes added.

Oxidation of a thioether (tetrahydrothiophene) to the corresponding sulfoxide using hydrogen peroxide; a mild, selective sulfoxidation. Performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a miscible solvent such as methanol, acetone or dichloromethane; often in the presence of a catalytic amount of acid or a metal‑based catalyst (e.g., tungsten or vanadium salts) to accelerate the reaction.

Acid–base neutralization; phosphoric acid protonates acetate ion, yielding acetic acid and sodium dihydrogen phosphate. Key transformation: NaCH₃COO + H₃PO₄ → CH₃COOH + NaH₂PO₄. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water acts as solvent; no catalyst needed.

NaBH4 reduction of 2,5‑hexanedione to 2,5‑hexanediol; a selective carbonyl reduction converting both ketone groups to secondary alcohols. Conducted in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to ambient temperature; NaBH4 is added portion‑wise, and the reaction is quenched with water or dilute acid after completion.

Halogen exchange on a sulfonyl chloride: cesium fluoride reacts with methanesulfonyl chloride to give methanesulfonyl fluoride and cesium chloride. This nucleophilic is carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvent (acetonitrile, DMF, or DMSO) at room temperature under inert atmosphere; excess fluoride drives the exchange to completion.

N‑methylation of 3‑aminopyraz via SN2 alkylation with methyl bromide using sodium hydride as base. The reaction is performed in dry THF or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; NaH deprotonates the pyrazole nitrogen, and methyl bromide adds to give 1‑methyl‑3‑aminopyrazole, with NaBr formed as by‑product.

Calciothermic (metallothermic) reduction of neodymium(III) oxide – reduction with calcium metal to produce Nd and CaO. This is a common laboratory and industrial route to reactive lanthanide metals. Reaction is performed at 800–1 200 °C in a sealed steel or tantalum crucible under argon; calcium is used as a molten metal, no solvent; the oxide layer on Nd may be removed by leaching the CaO with dilute acid if needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of O‑propan‑2‑yl ethanethioate with hydrochloric acid; cleavage of the thioester to regenerate ethanethioic acid and propane‑2‑ol; reflux in aqueous HCl (often water/EtOAc mixture), protonation of carbonyl facilitates nucleophilic attack by water.

Diazotization of N,N‑dimethylaniline with NaNO2/HCl followed by coupling with o‑enylenediamine and subsequent cyclization/oxidation to produce the phenazine dye Neutral Red. Conducted in aqueous HCl at 0‑5 °C to generate the diazonium salt, then added to a cold suspension of o‑phenylenediamine; the mixture is warmed gently and oxidized (often by air or additional acid) to afford Neutral Red, with water and NaCl as side products.

Redox/oxidation reaction in acidic medium: copper(I) cyanide is oxidized by concentrated nitric acid, converting Cu(I) to Cu(II) nitrate, while the cyanide carbon and nitrogen are oxidized to carbon dioxide and nitrogen dioxide, with water formed. Performed in aqueous solution, typically with heating; no catalyst needed.

Hydrogen reduction of molybdenum(V) chloride; converts MoCl5 to the lower oxidation state MoCl3 while generating hydrogen chloride. Key transformation: MoCl5(s) + H2(g) → MoCl3(s) + 2 HCl(g). Conducted at 250–350 °C in a quartz tube or furnace with a flowing H2/Ar mixture; the reaction is gas‑phase, no solvent, and may be assisted by a slight excess of H2 to drive completion.

Ester hydrolysis (alkyl acetate cleavage); water attacks chloromethyl acetate yielding acetic acid and chloromethanol; typically performed under acidic or basic aqueous conditions, reflux, solvent water or water/organic co‑solvent.

Carbodiimide‑mediated Steglich esterification; benzyl alcohol and cinnamic acid coupled to give benzyl cinnamate using DCC and catalytic DMAP; carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

N‑nitrosation of guanidine; nitrosonium tetrafluorobor provides NO⁺ which reacts with guanidine to afford N‑nitrosoguanidine and BF₄⁻; performed in dry aprotic solvent (acetonitrile) at 0–5 °C, under inert atmosphere, dark.

Reaction of ammonia with chlorine to form monochloramine; Cl₂ reacts with NH₃ in aqueous solution, producing HCl and NH₂Cl; carried out at low temperature (0–5 °C) with excess NH₃ to favor NH₂Cl, typical of water‑treatment processes.

Base‑induced deprotonation of 5,5‑diphenylhydantoin; sodium ethoxide abstracts the acidic hydrogen, forming the sodium salt of phenytoin and ethanol; performed in dry ethanol, often at reflux or ambient temperature.

High‑temperature combustion/oxidation of boron carbide; B₄C reacts with O₂ and H₂O to give CO₂ and H₃BO₃ (boric acid); requires furnace temperatures (>1000 °C) in an oxygen‑rich atmosphere, solid‑gas reaction.

Metathesis (double displacement) ion‑exchange reaction in aqueous solution; purpose is to exchange the cations of two soluble to give ammonium cyanide and lithium chloride. Typically performed by mixing aqueous solutions of NH4Cl and LiCN at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required; water or dilute ethanol can serve as the solvent.

Quaternary ammonium formation (N‑alkylation of N,N‑dimethylbenzylamine) – yields benzyltrimethylammonium iodide, often used as a phase‑transfer catalyst. The nitrogen lone pair attacks methyl iodide in an SN2 step. Conditions: reflux in a polar solvent (acetonitrile, ethanol, or neat methyl iodide), sometimes with gentle heating; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation of azulene; chlorine adds to the most electron‑rich position (C‑1) to give 1‑chloroazulene. Usually carried out with Cl2 in a non‑protic, inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform or dichloromethane, in the presence of a Lewis‑acid catalyst (e.g., FeCl3 or AlCl3) at 0 °C to room temperature, protected from light.

Oxidation of an aldehyde a carboxylic acid using hydrogen peroxide in acetic acid (peroxyacid oxidation). Cuminaldehyde (4‑isopropylbenzaldehyde) is converted to 4‑isopropylbenzoic acid with water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions involve stirring the aldehyde in glacial acetic acid with aqueous H2O2 (30 %) at 40–60 °C; catalytic amounts of tungstate or molybdate salts may be added to accelerate the reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide by acetate ion to form an ester (ethyl acetate). Sodium acetate reacts with ethyl bromide in a polar aprotic solvent such as dry acetone or DMF, usually under reflux. The reaction proceeds without added catalyst; the by‑product is sodium bromide, which precipitates out of solution.

Alkylation of a primary amine (N‑methylation) via SN2. Phenethylamine is deprotonated by potassium carbonate and then reacts with methyl iodide to give N‑methylphenethylamine and KI. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, acetonitrile) at 0 °C to rt; excess base and inert atmosphere are often used to suppress over‑alkylation.

Acyl transfer (acetylation) of the amine function of desglymidodrine with acetic anhydride to afford midodrine and acetic acid. Typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to rt, with pyridine or triethylamine acting as a base to scavenger the generated acetic acid. No metal catalyst is required.

Fischer esterification of gallic acid with ethanol using catalytic sulfuric acid; converts the carboxylic acid to ethyl gallate and releases water; used to protect the acid or increase lipophilicity; typically reflux ethanol (serves as solvent) with 0.1–1 equiv conc. H₂SO₄, often with azeotropic removal of water (Dean‑Stark) for several hours.

Chlorination of phenylphosphonic acid using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) to afford phenylphosphonic dichloride, with evolution of SO₂ and HCl gases; performed under reflux in dry dichloromethane or toluene under nitrogen, with the gaseous by‑products vented or scrubbed.

Acid‑base reaction forming a sparingly soluble salt; purpose: prepare strontium oxalate precipitate; key transformation: SrCO3 + H2C2O4 → SrC2O4 + CO2 + H2O; carried out in aqueous oxalic acid, often with gentle heating (40‑60 °C); water as solvent; no catalyst.

Reduction; conversion of a nitro group to an amine lithium aluminum hydride. LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the nitro functionality, ultimately forming the primary amine (4‑aminobiphenyl) after aqueous work‑up that generates water. Performed under anhydrous conditions, typically in dry (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, with careful quenching of excess LiAlH4 with water or dilute acid.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of methyl gallate back to gallic acid; regeneration of the free acid from its methyl ester. Key transformation: MeOOC‑Ar(OH)₃ + H₂O → HOOC‑Ar(OH)₃ + MeOH. Conducted by refluxing methyl gallate in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl or 5 % H₂SO₄) or, alternatively, by base‑mediated saponification followed by acid work‑up; water or a water/organic solvent mixture is used as reaction medium.

E2 elimination using a bulky, non‑nucleophilic base; potassium tert‑butoxide promotes removal of H and Br from 2‑bromo‑3‑methylheptane to give the Hofmann product 3‑methyl‑1‑heptene and KBr. Conducted in anhydrous tert‑butanol or THF at reflux, under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Fluorination to give phosphorus oxyfluoride. Anhydrous hydrogen fluoride gas reacts with phosphorus pentoxide under dry, low‑temperature conditions (often 0–25 °C) to produce volatile PO F₃ and water vapor. The reaction is conducted in a sealed, corrosion‑resistant apparatus (e.g., PTFE) with excess HF to drive the equilibrium.

Acid-base (metathesis) reaction; used to convert ytterbium(III) phosphate to ytterbium(III) fluoride. Hydrofluoric acid provides fluoride ions to replace phosphate, forming ytterbium(III) fluoride precipitate and phosphoric acid. Excess HF required. Typically performed in aqueous solution under acidic conditions.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) reaction. In aqueous solution, Nd(ClO₄)₃ exchanges anions with Na₂C₂O₄, forming insoluble neodymium(III) oxalate precipitate and soluble sodium perchlorate. Purpose: isolation of neodymium oxalate as a solid precursor for further processing (e.g., calcination to Nd₂O₃). Typical conditions: aqueous medium, mild heating (30–60 °C) to enhance precipitation; filtration to collect the solid; no catalyst needed.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation; methyl chloride acts as the alkylating agent and AlCl3 as a Lewis‑acid catalyst to generate a methyl cation that electrophilically attacks 2‑methylnaphthalene, giving 2,6‑dimethylnaphthalene and releasing HCl. Conducted in anrous, non‑protic solvent (e.g., CS₂, CCl₄, or dry dichloromethane) under nitrogen at 0–50 °C; the reaction mixture is quenched with water to remove AlCl₃ complexes.

Nucleophilic addition of phenylmagnesium bromide (a Grignard reagent) to acetone followed by acidic work‑up, giving 2‑phenyl‑2‑propanol, a tertiary alcohol. Purpose: carbon–carbon bond formation at a carbonyl carbon. Key transformation: Ph–MgBr adds to the carbonyl C of acetone, forming a magnesium alkoxide, which on protonation yields the tertiary alcohol. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether or THF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; after addition, the reaction mixture is quenched with dilute NH₄Cl or aqueous NH₄OH.

Acid‑base/condensation to a heteropoly acid; excess hydrochloric acid protonates phosphoric acid and sodium molybdate, leading to precipitation of NaCl and formation of phosphomolybdic acid (H₃[PMo₁₂O₄₀]) in aqueous solution, with water as a by‑product. Carried out in water at ambient temperature; heating may be applied to drive off water and ensure complete conversion. No special organic solvents are required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive amination); molecular hydrogen reduces the nitro group of 3‑nitrobenzamide to an amino group, affording 3‑aminobenzamide. Typical catalysts are Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO₂, in solvents such as ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate, under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–80 °C. After reaction, the mixture is filtered to remove catalyst and purified.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2); sodium methoxide reacts with 1‑iodobutane to produce methyl butyl ether and NaI; used to prepare ethers; typical conditions: anhydrous methanol or dry THF as solvent, NaOMe as nucleophile, reflux temperature; no extra catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization of a fluorinated acetate salt; purpose: generate difluoroacetic acid from its sodium salt; key transformation: proton transfer from HCl to sodium 2,2‑difluoroacetate forming difluoroacetic acid and NaCl; typical conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric HCl, room temperature or slight heating; no special solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑base (fluorination) reaction: indium(III) oxide is dissolved by hydrofluoric acid to form indium(III) fluoride and water. Conducted at room temperature to moderate heating in aqueous HF or anhydrous HF gas in a sealed vessel; excess HF drives the reaction, no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑base precipitation and gas evolution; sulfuric acid protonates barium azide, precipitating insoluble barium sulfate while liberating hydrazoic acid (HN₃) as a volatile, toxic gas. Conducted in dilute aqueous H₂SO₄ at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control HN₃ release; the solid BaSO₄ is filtered off, and the acidic aqueous phase contains dissolved HN₃.

Oxidative conversion of a hydroxylamine to a nitroxyl radical (TEMPO); copper(II) chloride oxidizes N‑hydroxy‑2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine to the stable radical 2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidin‑1‑oxyl, while Cu(II) is reduced to Cu(I) chloride and HCl is generated. Typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or acetonitrile at room temperature under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric CuCl₂ is used, and the reaction mixture is worked up to isolate TEMPO.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr). Cyanide ion from sodium cyanide displaces bromide on the electron‑deficient pentafluorobenzene ring, converting it to a nitrile. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, 80–120 °C, often under inert atmosphere. No catalyst required; NaBr is formed as by‑product.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) of an alkyl bromide by a thiolate. Purpose: synthesize a thioether (hexyl phenyl sulfide). Key transformation: deprotonated phenyl mercaptan (PhS⁻) attacks the primary carbon of 1‑bromohexane, displacing bromide forming the C–S bond; HBr is generated as by‑product. Typical conditions: generate the thiolate in situ using a base (NaH, K₂CO₃, or NaOH) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetone; heat to 50–80 °C for 2–6 h. No metal catalyst required.

Reaction type: methanolysis (transesterification). Purpose: exchange the propyl ester for a methyl ester. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonyl carbon of propyl 2‑oxopropanoate, producing methyl 2‑oxopropanoate and propanol. Typical conditions: excess methanol, acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOMe), reflux ( °C) for 2–6 h. Common solvent/catalyst: methanol serves as both reagent and solvent; catalytic amount of acid or base.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction). Molecular hydrogen reduces the carbonyl group of pinocarvone to the secondary alcohol pinocarveol. Commonly performed with 1–5 atm H₂ and a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni) in ethanol or methanol at 25–80 °C. The reaction consumes H₂ and yields the alcohol.

Catalyzed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Manganese dioxide acts as a solid catalyst to decompose H₂O₂ into water and molecular oxygen. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at room temperature or modest heating; MnO₂ is not consumed and can be recovered.

Acid–base neutralization of a basic oxide with a strong acid; converts magnesium oxide to magnesium sulfate and water. Typically performed by adding solid or aqueous MgO to an aqueous solution of sulfuric acid, often with gentle heating to drive the reaction to completion. No catalyst is needed; the process proceeds in water as solvent.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on a pyrazine. One nitrogen of piperazine, deprotonated by potassium carbonate, attacks the 2‑chloro position of 2,6‑dichloropyrazine, displacing chloride to give 2‑chloro‑6‑(piperazin‑1‑yl)pyrazine. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, NMP) at reflux (80–120 °C). Potassium chloride precipitates or remains soluble.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of 2‑bromobutane over palladium on carbon under hydrogen gas; the C–Br bond is cleaved and a hydrogen atom is added, yielding butane and HBr. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in an inert solvent such as ethanol or THF at ambient temperature or mild reflux.

Copper‑catalyzed oxidative C–O coupling (Ullmann ether synthesis) producing dibenzofuran from 2‑bromophenol and phenol; copper (Cu powder, CuCl, or CuO) facilitates intramolecular aryl‑oxygen bond formation while eliminating HBr; carried out at 180–220 °C in a high‑boiling solvent (NMP, o‑dichlorobenzene, or quinoline) often with a base (K₂CO₃) under inert atmosphere.

One‑pot Knoevenagel condensation/esterification to form an alkyl cyanoacrylate. Cyanoacetic acid condenses with formaldehyde in the presence of zinc acetate (Lewis‑acid catalyst) to give the α‑cyanoacrylic acid intermediate, which is then esterified with isobutyl alcohol (2‑methyl‑‑propanol) to afford isobutyl 2‑cyanoacrylate. Typical conditions: reflux in toluene or xylene with azeotropic removal of water, Zn(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %), sometimes a catalytic amount of p‑toluenesulfonic acid. Water is generated as the only by‑product.

Prilezhaev epoxidation of a vinyl arene; the alkene of styrene is oxidized to the corresponding epoxide (styrene oxide) by transfer of an oxygen atom from trifluoroperacetic acid, generating trifluoroacetic acid as the by‑product. The reaction proceeds at 0 °C to ambient temperature in dry dichloromethane or acetone, usually under an inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduces the C=C double bond of cinnamic acid to give the saturated carboxylic acid 3‑phenylpropanoic acid. Performed with H₂ (1–5 atm) over Pd/C (10 % Pd) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at 25–80 °C. Purpose: saturation of the alkene for later functionalization.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of a primary alkyl iodide with potassium hydroxide; OH⁻ attacks the carbon bearing iodine in 1‑iodohexadecane, producing 1‑hexadecanol and KI. Conducted in aqueous ethanol or a water/tert‑butanol mixture, heated under reflux; excess KOH helps ensure complete conversion.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. In aqueous solution, potassium oxalate reacts with cobalt(II) nitrate; the insoluble cobaltous oxalate precipitates out, while soluble potassium nitrate remains in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid cobalt oxalate can be filtered and washed.

Oxidative cleavage of vicinal diols (periodate oxidation). Sodium periodate cleaves 2,‑butanediol into two molecules of acetaldehyde, water and sodium iodate. Performed in aqueous medium (often water/acetone or MeCN) at 0 °C to room temperature with stoichiometric NaIO₄. Purpose: fragment a 1,2‑diol into aldehydes.

Oxidation of benzotriazole to 1‑hydroxybenzotriazole (BHO) using hydrogen peroxide. Typical conditions: aqueous or methanol‑water solution, pH neutral to slightly basic, 0–25 °C; water is the only by‑product.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt exchange). Sulfuric acid reacts with thulium(III) nitrate in aqueous solution to give thulium(III) sulfate and nitric acid. Typically carried out in water with gentle heating to evolve HNO₃; no special catalyst required. Purpose: of thulium sulfate or liberation of nitric acid.

SN2 N‑alkylation (second methylation) of methylamine with dimethyl sulfate; methylamine attacks a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate to afford dimethylamine and methyl hydrogen sulfate. Same conditions as reaction 4: methylamine (as aqueous or methanolic solution) mixed with dimethyl sulfate at 0–25 °C in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., methanol or acetonitrile), sometimes with a mild base to neutralize the generated acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (alcohol halogenation). Isopropyl alcohol is converted to isopropyl iodide by reaction with hydrogen iodide, producing water. Conducted by refluxing the alcohol with excess HI (often generated in situ with red phosphorus) at 50‑100 °C in anhydrous or aqueous HI. Reaction proceeds via an SN1 pathway for the secondary alcohol. Purpose: synthesis of an alkyl iodide.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Sodium oxalate mixed with an aqueous solution of cerium(III) sulfate exchanges ions to form insoluble cerium(III) oxalate precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate in solution. Performed at ambient temperature with stirring; filtration isolates the cerium oxalate. No catalyst required. Purpose: isolation of cerium(III) oxalate or removal of cerium ions from solution.

Oxidation of dimethylarsine to its oxide; hydrogen peroxide serves as the oxidant, converting CH3)2AsH into dimethylarsine oxide with the formation of water. The reaction proceeds in aqueous or mixed organic solvent (e.g., ethanol/water) at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to avoid over‑oxidation. No catalyst is generally required, though the reaction may be accelerated by slight acidification.

Reaction type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation). Purpose: prepare N‑methylbutanamide as an amide building block. Key transformation: the carbonyl chloride of butanoyl chloride is attacked by methylamine, forming the amide bond and liberating hydrogen chloride. Typical conditions: add a solution of methylamine (often as the aqueous 2 M solution or as its free base in THF) dropwise to a solution of butanoyl chloride in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to 5 °C, in the presence of a tertiary amine base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to trap the generated HCl. The reaction proceeds under inert atmosphere (N₂) and is usually completed within 1–2 h.

Mannich-type dearomative alkylation; purpose is to install a primary amine at the 9‑position of anthracene and partially reduce the central ring. Key transformation is condensation of formaldehyde with ammonia to generate an iminium (CH2NH2+) which adds to the 9‑position of anthracene, followed by proton that give 9‑aminomethyl‑9,10‑dihydroanthracene. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or aqueous ethanol, catalytic acid (often p‑TsOH) to promote iminium formation; reaction time 2–6 h; work‑up includes neutralization and extraction. No special catalyst beyond the acid; solvent is ethanol or a mixture of ethanol/water.

Catalytic hydroisomerization of 2‑methylhexane to n‑heptane; purpose is conversion of a branched alkane to the normal paraffin for fuel applications; key transformation involves migration of the methyl group via C–C bond scission/reformation under hydrogen, preserving saturation; conducted at 300–500 °C, 10–30 bar H₂, using a bifunctional catalyst such as Pt or Ni on an acidic zeolite (e.g., H‑ZSM‑5); gas‑phase operation, no solvent.

DCC‑mediated amide coupling; purpose is to convert indole‑3‑propionic acid into its primary amide, 3‑(1H‑indol‑3‑yl)propanamide. Dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates the carboxyl group to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is then attacked by ammonia to give the amide and dicyclohexylurea precipitate. Typical conditions: dissolve acid and DCC (1.1–1.2 eq) in dry dichloromethane, cool to 0 °C, add aqueous or gaseous ammonia (or NH₄OH), stir to rt 12–24 h. Often a catalytic amount of DMAP is added to accelerate acyl transfer. Solvent: anhydrous CH₂Cl₂; by‑product is filtered off.

Acidic dichromate oxidation (Jones oxidation); purpose is to oxidize the primary alcohol of 2‑pyrimidinemethanol to the corresponding carboxylic acid, 2‑pyrimidinecarboxylic acid. Sodium dichromate in conc. H₂SO₄ generates chromic acid (H₂CrO₄) which abstracts hydrogen from the alcohol, sequentially forming the aldehyde and then the acid. Typical conditions: aqueous H₂SO₄ (≈ 1 M), Na₂Cr₂O₇ (1.2 eq), temperature 60–80 °C, reaction 1–3 h. Water is the solvent; the reduced chromium(III) sulfate is formed as a by‑product.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose is to exchange the alkoxy group of hexyl acetate with methanol, yielding methyl acetate and hexan‑1‑ol. Sulfuric acid protonates the carbonyl of the acetate, increasing its electrophilicity; methanol attacks, followed by departure of hexanol. Typical conditions: excess methanol (5–10 eq), catalytic H₂SO₄ (0.5–2 mol %), reflux 2–6 h. Solvent is often the excess methanol itself; the reaction is driven to completion by removal of the more volatile methyl acetate or by using a large excess of methanol.

Base‑induced elimination (E2) of 3‑bromobutan‑2‑ol with sodium ethoxide yielding but‑2‑ene, sodium bromide and ethanol. NaOEt abstracts a β‑hydrogen while the C–Br bond leaves, forming the internal alkene; the resulting HBr protonates ethoxide to ethanol. Performed in dry ethanol solvent at reflux temperature, using stoichiometric NaOEt as strong base.
Chlorination/oxidation of Ti(II) chloride to Ti(III) chloride; gaseous chlorine is bubbled through a solution of TiCl₂ (often in THF) at low to ambient temperature, converting TiCl₂ to TiCl₃.

Jones oxidation of an aldehyde; purpose is to oxidize perillaldehyde to perillic acid (carboxylic acid). The reagent is a solution of chromium(V) trioxide in dilute sulfuric acid in acetone. The aldehyde is converted to the corresponding carboxylic acid via a chromate ester intermediate, with reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III). Typical conditions: add perillaldehyde dropwise to cold (0 °C) Jones reagent in acetone, stir 0 °C to rt for 30 min–1 h. Quench with isopropanol or methanol, filter off Cr(III) salts. Solvent: acetone; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution of the two primary alcohol groups of hexitol with hydrogen bromide, yielding 1,6‑dibromo‑1,6‑dideoxyhexitol and water; typically performed with excess HBr (often in aqueous or glacial form) under reflux.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 3‑hexanone to 3‑hexanol using H₂ gas and palladium on carbon; carried out under 1–5 atm H₂ in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature to moderate heat.

Swern oxidation of 2‑octanol to 2‑octanone employing dimethyl sulfoxide activated by oxalyl chloride at –78 °C, followed by addition of triethylamine; reaction usually run in dichloromethane under anhydrous conditions.

Oxidation of p‑methylphenylacetaldehyde to 2‑(4‑methylphenyl)acetic acid using potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium; heated gently, producing MnO₂ precipitate and potassium salts as by‑products.

O‑methylation (SN2) of 1‑butanol by methyl triflate; purpose is to form the methyl ether. Key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on the methyl electrophile, producing butyl methyl ether and triflic acid. Usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

[4+2] Diels‑Alder cycloaddition; dimethyl maleate acts as the electron‑poor dienophile and furan as the diene, forming the bicyclic oxabicyclo[2.2.1]hepta‑2,5‑diene di‑ester. Usually performed neat or in a non‑polar solvent (toluene, xylene) at 80–120 °C, often in a sealed tube to increase temperature. No catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds thermally and provides a stereospecific endo adduct.

Oxidation; direct combination of plutonium metal with oxygen gas to form plutonium dioxide; a straightforward oxidation used to produce the stable PuO₂ oxide for storage or fuel fabrication; proceeds readily at room temperature but faster at elevated temperature (≈200‑400 °C); no solvent or catalyst required.

Base‑mediated oxidation of 5‑methylsalicylaldehyde to 5‑methylsalicylic acid with potassium permanganate in water; the mixture is heated generating potassium hydroxide and insoluble manganese dioxide as the oxidant is reduced.

Anhydride formation from trifluoroacetyl chloride and sodium trifluoroacetate, yielding trifluoroacetic anhydride and NaCl; typically conducted in an aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to room temperature with pyridine or a similar base to scavenge HCl.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); NaOH in aqueous methanol or ethanol hydrolyzes furan‑2‑ylmethyl acetate to give sodium acetate and regenerate furan‑2‑ylmethanol; generally refluxed for 1–3 h; after reaction, acidification affords the free alcohol.

Redox oxidation of carbon monoxide by lead dioxide (Pb(IV) → Pb(II)); CO is oxidized to CO₂ and PbO₂ is reduced to PbO; typically carried out by heating a mixture of CO gas and solid PbO₂, sometimes in a tubular furnace; gas‑phase reaction, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Comproportionation (redox) of elemental mercury with mercuric iodide to afford mercurous iodide (Hg₂I₂); Hg(0) and Hg(II) combine to give Hg(I); usually performed in aqueous solution at mild temperatures; no additional reagents or catalysts required.

Nucleophilic S_N2 alkylation of sulfide ion by allyl bromide to give diallyl sulfide; potassium sulfide supplies S²⁻ which attacks the primary carbon of allyl bromide, displacing Br⁻; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO under reflux; no catalyst, potassium bromide is the by‑product.

Acid–base neutralization of sodium carbonate with tetrafluoroboric acid; carbonate is protonated, releasing CO₂ and H₂O while forming sodium tetrafluoroborate; conducted in aqueous solution, often at 0‑25 °C to control gas evolution; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

S_N2 alkylation of the thiol group of mercaptoacetic acid by 1‑bromotetradecane, producing tetradecyl thioacetic acid and HBr; typically carried out in the presence of a base (e.g., NaOH or NaH) to deprotonate the thiol, in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF, under reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition of solid silver nitrate; upon strong heating (~440 °C) AgNO₃ breaks down to metallic silver, nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen gas; performed in a dry crucible, no solvent or catalyst required.

E2 elimination (dehydrohalogenation) of 2‑bromopentane using potassium tert‑butoxide to give pent‑2‑ene; typically performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as tert‑butanol, THF or DMSO at reflux or 60‑80 °C; strong, non‑nucleophilic base abstracts a β‑hydrogen, potassium bromide precipitates.

Nitrosation of dimethylamine by pentyl nitrite forming N‑nitrosodimethylamine and n‑pentanol; a nitroso‑transfer reaction commonly carried out at 0–25 °C in a non‑protic organic solvent (e.g.,loromethane or ether) under inert atmosphere; the amine attacks the nitroso electrophile, releasing the alkyl alcohol.

Free‑radical chlorination/substitution of 1,1,2,2‑tetrachloroethane with chlorine gas to afford pentachloroethane and HCl; initiated by UV light or heat, usually in an inert carbon‑chloride solvent (CCl₄ or CHCl₃); chlorine abstracts a hydrogen atom and adds to the remaining carbon, completing the substitution.

Direct oxidation (combustion) of dysprosium metal by molecular oxygen to give dysprosium(III) oxide (Dy₂O₃); performed at high temperature (typically >800 °C) in a furnace under an oxygen atmosphere; no solvent; the metal is converted to its stable oxide with evolution of heat.

Catalytic aerobic oxidation of 2‑methyl‑3‑pentanol to 2‑methyl‑3‑pentanone using copper(II) acetate and TEMPO as the redox mediator; reactions are run under₂ (balloon or air) in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 25‑60 °C; Cu(OAc)₂ is reduced to Cu(I) acetate while TEMPO cycles between oxoammonium and nitroxyl forms, water is formed as by‑product.

Chemical reduction of 3‑nitrobenzenesulfonic acid to 3‑aminobenzenesulfonic acid using sodium dithionite in aqueous medium; typically carried out at ambient temperature, pH ~7–8, with excess water as solvent; dithionite donates electrons to convert the nitro group to an amine, generating sodium bisulfite (NaHSO₃) as the oxidized sulfur species.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of bromocyclohexane by n‑propylamine giving propylhexedrine (N‑propyl‑cyclohexylamine) and HBr; typically run in a polar aprotic solvent such as ethanol or THF under reflux, often with excess amine or a base (e.g., triethylamine) to capture the HBr; purpose is synthesis of the stimulant propylhexedrine.

Acid-catalyzed acetal hydrolysis (deprotection); water attacks the 2,2‑dimethyl‑1,3‑dioxane‑4,6‑dione breaking the acetal to release acetone and generate malonic acid; typically performed in aqueous dilute HCl or sulfuric acid at reflux; solvent is water or water/acetone mixture.

Oxidative cleavage of melatonin with sodium hypochlorite (HOCl) to produce N1‑acetyl‑N2‑formyl‑5‑methoxykynuramine (AFMK); proceeds via chlorination of the indole ring followed by hydrolytic opening of the C2‑C3 bond; carried out in aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8) at room temperature using a commercial NaOCl solution (≈5‑10 %); no additional catalyst needed; purpose is generation of the major melatonin metabolite for biochemical studies.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination); 1‑ethylcyclopentan‑1‑ol loses water to form the alkene 1‑ethylcyclopent‑1‑ene. Typical conditions use concentrated H2SO4 or p‑toluenesulfonic acid as catalyst, heating at 80–120 °C in a non‑aqueous solvent such as toluene or acetic acid. The reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate and eliminates water.

Acid‑base metathesis (double displacement) between ferrous acetate and hydrochloric acid yielding ferrous chloride and acetic acid; performed in water at ambient temperature by adding stoichiometric HCl to a solution of Fe(CH3COO)2; no catalyst required; serves to exchange the acetate counter‑ion for chloride.

Double displacement precipitation of silver acetate with thallium(I) chloride to give insoluble silver chloride and soluble thallium(I) acetate; conducted in aqueous (or water/ethanol) medium at room temperature, protected from light to avoid silver salt decomposition; precipitation of AgCl drives the equilibrium; no catalyst needed.

Halide exchange (nucleophilic substitution) of p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride with tetrabutylammonium fluoride producing p‑methylbenzenesulfonyl fluoride and tetrabutylammonium chloride; usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature the tetra‑alkylammonium salt provides fluoride and acts as a phase‑transfer agent; used to prepare sulfonyl fluorides as electrophilic coupling partners.

Diazotization of 2,6‑dimethylaniline with NaNO2/HCl followed by hydrolysis of the diazonium salt to afford 2,6‑dimethylphenol, with evolution of N₂, formation of NaCl and water; the reaction is performed by generating the diazonium chloride at 0‑5 °C in aqueous HCl, then warming the mixture (≈50 °C) to promote hydrolysis; a classic Sandmeyer‑type conversion of an aryl amine to a phenol; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of pent‑4‑en‑1‑ol to pentan‑1‑ol; reaction type: catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; key transformations: reduction of the C=C bond to a C–C single bond, preserving the primary alcohol; typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm), Pd/C (5–10 % wt) or PtO₂ as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–50 °C; reaction proceeds to completion within a few hours under stirring.

Redox displacement (single‑replacement) reaction; aluminum metal reduces Cr(III) to elemental chromium while being oxidized to Al(III), forming aluminum sulfate. Typically carried out by grinding the solid reactants together and heating strongly (300‑500 °C) in a dry, inert atmosphere; solvent, sometimes performed in a molten salt flux.

Acid‑base/anion‑exchange reaction; aqueous hydrochloric acid protonates the hexachloroplatinate anion, converting sodium hexachloroplatinate to hexachloroplatinic (platinum(IV)) acid and precipitating sodium chloride. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with excess HCl; the solution is simply mixed and stirred, no special catalyst required.

General type: double‑displacement (ion‑exchange) reaction. Purpose: to form nickel(II) cyanide, which may be isolated or used as a precursor. Key transformation: NiCl₂(aq) + 2 NaCN(aq) → Ni(CN)₂(s or aq) + 2 NaCl(aq). Typical conditions: aqueous solution, often at room temperature; the reaction is performed under controlled pH to avoid formation of HCN. No catalyst required. Common solvent: water (or dilute aqueous solution).

Methanolysis of malonic anhydride; partial esterification gives methyl malonate and malonic acid; the anhydride reacts with excess methanol, often in the presence of a catalytic amount of acid (p‑TsOH) or base (NaOMe); reflux methanol for 1–3 h; yields a mixture of the mono‑ester (methyl malonate) and the free acid.

Peracid oxidation (O‑atom transfer) of the isoflavone daidzein to the coumestrol framework, with peracetic acid providing the oxidizing equivalent and being reduced to acetic acid and water. Usually performed in a dilute aqueous‑acetone or methanol solution at 0 °C to 25 °C; reaction is quenched with aqueous base; no metal catalyst is needed.

O‑methylation using diazomethane; the phenolic hydroxyl of 17α‑ethynyl estradiol is methylated to give mestranol (the methyl ether), releasing N₂ gas. Carried out in anhydrous ether or THF, often at 0 °C to room temperature under inert gas; diazomethane is generated in situ and used in slight excess; no additional catalyst.

Reductive amination of cyclohexanone with n‑propylamine using sodium cyanoborohydride; produces the secondary amine propylhexedrine; purpose is synthesis of a stimulant amine; key transformation is formation of an imine/iminium intermediate followed by NaCNBH₃‑mediated reduction to the amine; typically carried out in methanol or ethanol at ambient temperature, mildly acidic (pH 5–6), with NaCNBH₃ as the reducing agent.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of decyl acetate (hydrochloric acid): Same ester hydrolysis mechanism as with sulfuric acid, but using aqueous HCl (approximately 1–6 M). Reaction heated to reflux; decanol and acetic acid are formed. Often carried out in a water‑organic solvent mixture (e.g., dichloromethane/water) to extract the alcohol.

Enzymatic hydrolysis (lipase‑catalyzed ester cleavage); the acetyl of ethyl 6‑acetyloxyhexanoate is hydrolyzed to the free hydroxy group, producing ethyl 6‑hydroxyhexanoate and acetic acid. Performed in an aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8) at 30‑40 °C, often in a biphasic system (water/organic solvent) with a commercial lipase preparation; no chemical catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); replaces the aryl bromine of 3‑bromo‑2‑methyl‑1H‑indole with hydrogen to afford 2‑methyl‑1H‑indole and HBr; performed under H₂ pressure (1‑5 atm) with Pd/C (or Raney Ni) in a protic solvent like ethanol at 25‑80 °C.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of phenothiazine with ethyl iodide to afford the N‑ethyl product fenethazine and hydrogen iodide; used to introduce an ethyl group onto the nitrogen of phenothiazine for pharmaceutical modification; typically performed in an aprotic polar solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or DMF) with a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to trap HI; reflux or gentle heating under inert atmosphere.

Oxidation of propanal to propionic acid with potassium permanganate; aldehyde carbonyl is oxidized to carboxylic acid, MnO4⁻ reduced to MnO2. Conducted in aqueous alkaline solution (e.g., NaOH) at 0–25 °C to reflux, followed by acid work‑up to isolate propionic acid.

Nophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on a chlorotriazine: methanol attacks the electron‑deficient 6‑chloro position of 2,4‑bis(isopropylamino)-6‑chloro‑1,3,5‑triazine, displacing chloride as hydrogen chloride and forming the corresponding methoxy derivative. Conducted in refluxing methanol, often with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl; inert atmosphere is advisable.

Halogen exchange redox reaction where fluorine gas oxidizes chloride to chlorine while being reduced to fluoride, converting thallium(III) chloride to thallium(III) fluoride; used in preparative inorganic fluorination or elemental halogen purification; performed in a dry, inert‑gas‑filled vessel at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) with careful control of F₂ flow; no solvent, solid TlCl₃ is exposed directly to gaseous F₂.

Acid‑base neutralization between acetic acid and barium oxide forming barium acetate and water; a standard method for preparing soluble barium salts; typically carried out by adding solid BaO to aqueous acetic acid with stirring and gentle heating until gas evolution ceases; dilute aqueous medium is sufficient, no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between copper(II) sulfate and sodium formate producing copper(II) formate and sodium sulfate; used to obtain copper formate, which can serve as a reducing agent or precursor to other copper complexes; performed in water with stoichiometric amounts, often at ambient temperature; copper(II) formate precipitates out and is filtered, while the sodium sulfate remains dissolved.

SN2 O‑alkylation of a carboxylate salt; methyl triflate serves as a powerful methylating agent to convert sodium benzoate into methyl benzoate. Reaction is carried out in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, typically at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere. No catalyst is required; the by‑product is sodium triflate.

Reductive amination of a ketone; 1‑phenyl‑2‑propanone condenses with dimethylamine to form an imine, which is reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to give N,N‑dimethyl‑2‑phenylpropan‑1‑amine; carried out in methanol or ethanol at ambient to reflux temperature, pH ~5‑6, NaBH₃CN as mild reducing agent.

Acid‑base neutralization of nitric acid with methylamine to give methylammonium nitrate; the reaction generates a soluble nitrate salt used in propellant and fertilizer formulations; usually conducted in an ice‑bath to control the exotherm, with aqueous methylamine added slowly to dilute HNO₃; no catalyst required, water is the reaction medium.

Nucleophilic addition of ethanol to phenyl isocyanate to afford ethyl phenylcarbamate; serves to prepare a carbamate ester; ethanol O‑H attacks the carbon of the isocyanate, forming an N‑C=O intermediate that protonates to give the ethyl phenylcarbamate; carried out at 0 °C to rt, inert gas, in solvents like dichloromethane, THF or toluene; usually no catalyst required, though a small amount of base may be used.

Type: strong hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Purpose: convert 1‑naphthylacetic acid into 1‑naphthylmethanol. Key transformation: C(=O)‑OH → CH2‑OH via delivery of two hydride ions from LiAlH4, followed by aqueous work‑up that generates aluminum hydroxide. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, addition of LiAlH4 at 0 °C then reflux; quench with water or dilute acid. No additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of a thioester; converts methyl propanethioate to propionic acid and methanethiol. Nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon cleaves the C–S bond, releasing the thiol. Typically carried out under acidic (e.g., 1 M HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH followed by acid work‑up) aqueous conditions, often in a water–THF mixture at reflux.

Hydrolysis of a trialkylborane; converts trimethylborane to boric acid and methane; key transformation: B(CH3)3 + 3 H2O → B(OH)3 + 3 CH4; typically done by adding water to a solution of BMe3 in an ether or THF solvent at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base reaction (metal sulfide + strong acid) producing a soluble metal sulfate and gaseous hydrogen sulfide; typically carried out in aqueous dilute H2SO4 at ambient to mild heating, with vigorous stirring to release H2S gas; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Type: aerobic oxidation of azylic alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Purpose: produce protocatechuic acid (3,4‑dihydroxybenzoic acid) from 3,4‑dihydroxybenzyl alcohol using molecular oxygen. Key transformation: –CH2OH → –COOH while the aromatic dihydroxy ring remains unchanged; O2 is reduced to H2O2 as a stoichiometric by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous or buffered medium at ambient temperature or mild heating, often with a metal catalyst (e.g., Cu‑TEMPO, Fe‑based) or enzyme to accelerate O2 reduction; otherwise the reaction proceeds slowly by autoxidation. No special solvent beyond water or mixed water/organic is required.

Type: catalytic hydrogenation reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Purpose: obtain cyclohexylmethanol from cyclohexanecarboxylic acid. Key transformation: –COOH → –CH2OH via addition of H2 across the C=O bond. Typical conditions: high‑pressure H2 (30–100 atm) with a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO2, in a polar protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) or sometimes in THF; temperature 50–120 °C. No additional reagents are needed.

Triphosgene cyclocarbonation (formation of cyclic carbonate); reaction of glycerol with triphosgene to give glycerol carbonate and HCl; typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at  °C to RT, with a stoichiometric base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine, 2 eq) to capture generated HCl; reaction proceeds under nitrogen, and the crude mixture is washed to remove salts and isolated by evaporation and purification.

Reaction type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: recover propionic acid and precipitate insoluble silver chloride; key transformation: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) and CH₃CH₂COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃CH₂COOH; typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at 0‑25 °C to maximize AgCl precipitation; common solvent: water.

Type: acid–base neutralization / salt formation (formation of a rare‑earth phosphate). Purpose: prepare samarium(III) phosphate from samarium(III) oxide. Key transformation Sm2O3 + 2 H3PO4 → 2 SmPO4 + 3 H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous suspension of Sm2O3 heated to reflux with excess phosphoric acid; pH adjusted to around neutral to favor precipitation of SmPO4. Common solvent is water; solid product is isolated by filtration and washing.

Type: oxidative conversion (inorganic redox) of ruthenium(III) chloride to ruthenium(IV) dioxide. Purpose: generate RuO2 while liberating chlorine gas. Key transformation: RuCl3 + H2O2 → RuO2 + Cl2 + H2O (balanced as 2 RuCl3 + 4 H2O2 → 2 RuO2 + 3 Cl2 + 4 H2O). Typical conditions: aqueous solution, added dropwise at 0–25°C to control exotherm; excess H2O2 ensures complete oxidation; reaction may be carried out under vigorous stirring. No additional catalyst is required; the medium is usually acidic to keep Ru species soluble.

Type: acid‑base proton transfer forming an ammonium chloride salt. Purpose: convert free 2‑methylpiperidine into its hydrochloride salt for isolation or further use. Key transformation: RNH + HCl → [RNH·H]Cl. Typical conditions: dissolve or suspend 2‑methylpiperidine in anhydrous ether, diethyl ether or THF, cool to 0 °C, bubble dry HCl gas or add aqueous HCl; the resulting solid precipitates and is filtered, washed with cold ether and dried. No catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization; carbonic acid is deprotonated by potassium hydroxide to give the bicarbonate salt and water; used to generate potassium bicarbonate or adjust pH; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Synthesis (combination) reaction: a redox process where elemental ytterbium is oxidized by chlorine gas to form ytterbium trichloride, an ionic halide. Typically carried out by passing dry Cl2 over heated Yb metal (300‑400 °C) in a dry, inert atmosphere; no solvent is used.

Acylation (N‑acetylation) using acetyl chloride; the amino group of DL‑Leucine attacks acetyl chloride, yielding N‑acetyl‑DL‑Leucine and HCl. Commonly carried out in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to neutralize HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

Thermal dehydrohalogenation (high‑temperature elimination) of γ‑hexachlorocyclohexane, producing 1,3,5‑trichlorobenzene and three equivalents of HCl gas. Typically performed in the gas phase at 300–400 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent required.

This is an acetal formation reaction. It protects an aldehyde group via conversion to a dimethyl acetal. Performed under acidic conditions using excess methanol, typically with a catalytic amount of sulfuric or hydrochloric acid. Commonly conducted at room temperature or with gentle heating.

Base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (saponification) of N‑(2‑hydroxy‑1‑phenylethyl)acetamide with aqueous NaOH, cleaving the acetamide to give phenylglycinol and sodium acetate. Conducted in water or water/ethanol, refluxing for 1–3 h.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification of p‑hydroxybenzoate (sodium salt) with methanol using HCl as catalyst, converting the carboxylate to methyl p‑hydroxybenzoate (methylparaben) and forming NaCl and water. Reaction carried out in methanol, reflux, with catalytic HCl (often gaseous or aqueous).

Appel‑type bromination of 1‑pentanol with carbon tetrabromide and triphenylphosphine, converting the alcohol to 1‑bromopentane, generating triphenylphosphine oxide and bromoform (CHBr₃) as side product. Conducted in CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; stoichiometric reagents.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: preparation of cadmium sulfide pigment or semiconductor material.
